Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Among the losers were several candidates Trump had personally picked, in an election he had sought to nationalise around his name.
Democrats also made substantial gains in the House, with a distinct possibility of reaching 258 members, a gain of more than 40 seats, while governorships won in traditionally Republican states, including Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada, showed that the backlash extended well beyond Washington into the Republican Party's geographical and demographic foundations.
The price of the Iran war
The national exit poll found that nine in 10 voters considered government corruption a major or crucial factor in their decision, that 63 percent regarded the decision to attack Iran as wrong, and that 87 percent worried about the price of fuel.
The same poll found that nearly three-quarters of voters said the war was a crucial or major factor in their decision, and about a third called it crucial. Nearly eight in 10 said inflation was causing their families hardship, and only 38 percent approved of Trump's performance.
Trump had promised peace, prosperity and an end to costly foreign entanglements. Americans got mounting economic pressure and Trump's war of choice
The war on Iran may not have been the sole cause of the Republican collapse, but its military, economic and political consequences contributed greatly to the backlash.
By late October, average petrol prices had reached about $4.27 a gallon, more than a third higher than when Trump returned to office less than two years earlier. Diesel had climbed even more sharply, to about $6.35. Disruptions to energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and damage to regional infrastructure were the main reasons.
Vice President JD Vance attributed the Republican defeat directly to the war. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance declared, adding that Trump himself had acknowledged its electoral consequences. Trump subsequently conceded that the conflict and higher fuel prices had damaged Republican prospects.
Vance's admission went to the heart of the contradiction between Trump's promises and his record. He had promised peace, prosperity and an end to costly foreign entanglements. Instead, Americans got mounting economic pressure and Trump's war of choice. Trump had squandered much of the political capital that enabled his return to power in 2024.
Michigan and Texas
The deeper implications of this election were clearest in Michigan. The victory of Abdul El-Sayed over Republican Mike Rogers was significant not simply because it preserved a Democratic Senate seat, but because it challenged assumptions about the viability of candidates openly critical of American support for Israel.
Sayed, a progressive Egyptian American physician and former public health official, became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. His victory followed a contentious Democratic primary in which establishment figures questioned whether his progressive positions, particularly his opposition to Israel's assault on Gaza, would sink him in a competitive state.
Michigan's electorate proved more complicated than those calculations suggested. The state contains substantial Arab and Muslim communities, particularly around Detroit, alongside organised labour, African American voters, progressive activists and other constituencies whose priorities cannot be reduced to a single issue.
In 2024, anger over the Biden administration's support for Israel's war on Gaza had opened a profound rupture between sections of these communities and the Democratic establishment, and the "Uncommitted" movement gained national prominence in Michigan.
Sayed's victory demonstrated that a broad electoral coalition can be built without abandoning criticism of Israeli policies or accommodating every demand of Aipac and the pro-Israel political machine. This does not mean that Michigan has become uniformly pro-Palestinian, or that Gaza determined every race. It means that the political boundaries surrounding the Palestinian question are shifting.
Talarico's victory in Texas, which had not elected a Democratic senator since 1988, pushed the same boundary further.
Talarico made his position on the Israel lobby and Gaza explicit: "I've never taken money from Aipac, and I'm not taking money from Aipac in this campaign. Seeing what's happening in Gaza makes me sick to my stomach as a teacher, as a Christian, as a human being."
For years, Democratic leaders operated on the assumption that unconditional support for Israel was both strategically indispensable and politically necessary. The emergence of winning candidates who openly reject Aipac's money and criticise Israel's conduct suggests that this assumption is becoming untenable.
The significance of Talarico's victory is not merely that a Democrat won in Texas. It is that a Democrat could win in Texas while openly challenging one of the most entrenched orthodoxies of American foreign policy.
The Democrats' contradiction
Sayed and Talarico will enter the Senate as critics of their own party's record on Gaza. President Joe Biden's administration armed Israel during its genocide in Gaza and defended it at the UN.
In December 2023, the administration bypassed congressional review to sell Israel tank shells and vetoed a resolution in the UN Security Council calling for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire. The Democrats' victory over Trump cannot erase that shameful record.
According to Brown University's Costs of War project, Washington provided at least $21.7bn in military assistance to Israel in the two years after 7 October 2023, under Biden and Trump.
Yet the Democratic Party is increasingly divided over the very policies its last administration pursued. This election produced at least 11 newly elected members of Congress, two senators and nine House members, who have publicly advocated for Palestinian rights, criticised Israel's conduct in Gaza or opposed aspects of American military assistance to Israel.
Some have called for ending military assistance altogether, while others demand conditions, accountability or a reassessment of the relationship.
They join established congressional critics such as Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, while figures such as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani represent a broader political challenge to Israel's defenders. Together, they expand a constituency willing to challenge longstanding assumptions about the influence of the Israel lobby and unconditional American support for Israel.
None of this means that the Democratic Party has abandoned its traditional commitments to the Zionist state. Its establishment remains closely connected to the foreign policy institutions, influential donors and strategic consensus that regard Israel as a central American ally. A Democratic congressional majority should not be confused with an antiwar majority, much less a consensus in favour of Palestinian liberation.
The election results were not simply a repudiation of Trump and his war on Iran, conducted in partnership with Israel. They were also a challenge to the Democratic establishment of Biden, Antony Blinken and Jake Sullivan, whose policies enabled and sustained Israel's assault on Gaza.
The question is whether the dissenters remain a minority or become part of a more fundamental transformation of the party. The electoral victory has created an opening, but it has not resolved the struggle over the party's direction on Palestinian self-determination and freedom from occupation.
What changes in January
When the new Congress convenes on 3 January, the balance of power in Washington will shift dramatically. For the first time in Trump's second presidency, both chambers will be controlled by the opposition, which will substantially weaken his ability to pass legislation, secure senior appointments and avoid scrutiny.
Democrats will have considerable power to obstruct, investigate and expose administration policies, but much less power to impose an alternative foreign policy
Democratic committees will acquire the power to investigate, subpoena and hold hearings on the Iran war, military spending and arms transfers, and Congress's powers over appropriations could be used to condition support for Israel.
Trump nonetheless retains constitutional authority over diplomacy and military command, and overriding his veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats do not possess.
The outgoing Republican Congress is under pressure to pass the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) and associated appropriations during the lame-duck session, while it still controls both chambers. That could fold Israel's massive military funding into broader defence and intelligence legislation.
For Israel, this period deserves particular scrutiny. The existing military relationship includes long-term assistance arrangements, weapons contracts and the War Reserve Stockpile Allies-Israel programme, whose authorisation runs to 1 January 2027. Any attempt to renew or expand these arrangements before the transition could constrain the incoming Congress's ability to exercise real leverage over dangerous Israeli policies.
Democrats will therefore have considerable power to obstruct, investigate and expose administration policies, but much less power to impose an alternative foreign policy. The immediate consequence is likely to be institutional confrontation rather than a new strategic direction.
A turning point, not a revolution
For Palestine, the election has created opportunities but offers no guarantees. A larger congressional bloc critical of Israel could increase scrutiny of arms transfers, settlement expansion and the treatment of Palestinians under an entrenched system of apartheid and military occupation.
Congressional hearings could give greater visibility to first-hand Palestinian testimony and independent investigations, and Democratic leaders could face pressure to reconsider the longstanding practice of shielding Israel from accountability.
The relationship is nonetheless deeply institutionalised. According to the Council on Foreign Relations, Israel has received more than $300bn in American assistance since its founding, adjusted for inflation, underpinned by military cooperation, intelligence arrangements, domestic political networks and decades of bipartisan commitments. These structures will not disappear because of one election.
On Iran, the implications may be more immediate. Congressional investigations into who authorised the war, what it cost and what it achieved could constrain further escalation and strengthen demands for diplomacy.
Vance's admission matters here. When a sitting vice president identifies a foreign war as the principal cause of his party's defeat, he is acknowledging that military intervention has become a serious domestic liability.
Opposition to Trump's war does not, however, imply support for a different approach to Iran: many establishment Democrats share Republican positions on Iran's regional influence and nuclear programme, even when they disagree over the use of force.
Washington's strategic relationships with regional authoritarian regimes, including Saudi Arabia, the Gulf states, Egypt and Jordan, are equally unlikely to change suddenly. The coming debate will be about the methods, costs and sustainability of American dominance in the region, not its abandonment.
The November elections have produced three developments. First, they have delivered a sweeping repudiation of Trump and weakened his ability to govern without institutional resistance. Second, they have shown that criticism of American support for Israel is no longer confined to the margins of Congress.
Third, they have exposed a visible contradiction between the Democratic establishment's record and the demands of a growing constituency seeking accountability, restraint and a different relationship with the Middle East.
Electoral change is not necessarily structural change. The system that produced bipartisan support for Israel's assault on Gaza remains largely intact, and its military institutions, lobbying networks and strategic assumptions continue to exercise enormous influence.
The question for the next two years is whether the new congressional balance will merely constrain Trump or begin to challenge the deeper foundations of American foreign policy.
The flood may have swept away Republican control of Congress. It has not yet swept away the structures that sustain America's wars or its blind support for Israel.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay starting 12-day Latin America tour
The 71-year-old pontiff is visiting three countries despite undergoing surgery to remove a tumour last month.
Pope Leo XIV has arrived in Uruguay as he begins a 12-day tour of South America, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.
The 71-year-old head of the Roman Catholic Church touched down in Montevideo on Friday after a 13-hour flight from Rome, telling reporters he feels “fairly good”.
“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place,” Leo told reporters on board the papal plane. “I had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward. And I am very happy to say praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistance, I’m here today, I think in fairly good shape.”
On his trip, the pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in one of the most intense papal foreign trips in decades.
His packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay – the region’s least Catholic and most secular country – will include a visit to a neighbourhood with heavy gang violence, a mass in Paysandu, about 375 kilometres (230 miles) from Montevideo, and another mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometres (60 miles) from the capital.
Cardinal Daniel Sturla, archbishop of Montevideo, told the AFP news agency that there was “widespread interest in the pope’s visit that goes well beyond the confines of the Catholic Church”, with tickets for masses in Paysandu and Florida quickly running out.
The regional trip is somewhat of a homecoming journey for Leo, as he will finish in Peru in three weeks, where he served for almost two decades as a missionary, forming a deep attachment to the continent.
The trip will take the pope to the former Inca capital of Cusco and the Amazon rainforest, and he will also revisit his old diocese of Chiclayo for a private visit to a chapel he helped rebuild.
Leo said on Wednesday that he was looking forward to returning to a region “so dear to me”.
The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics said he hoped the trip would “strengthen faith, renew hope, and rekindle the fire of charity” in the countries he is visiting, which face rising inequality and violence, as well as a decline in Catholic followers.
Despite undergoing an operation on October 13 to remove a cancerous tumour, doctors have given him the all-clear to travel, and the Vatican said no special medical measures were necessary beyond the standard care on papal trips.
“His stamina is fantastic. The way that he’s singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief. She noted that Leo had passed the 14-day convalescence period required by doctors after his surgery and was eager to get on the road.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: USA women throttle Switzerland 7-0 to open hockey worlds amid jersey dispute
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The United States opened their defense of the women’s ice hockey world championship with a 7-0 victory over Switzerland on Friday in Esbjerg, Denmark.
Hannah Bilka and Laila Edwards scored twice each, while Kirsten Simms, Hilary Knight and Casey O’Brien also found the net as the Americans pulled away after a competitive opening period. Caroline Harvey contributed three assists.
Bilka broke the deadlock nine minutes into the game, but Switzerland goaltender Andrea Brändli kept the favorites at bay for the remainder of the first period. The Americans took control in the second, with O’Brien doubling their lead before Edwards converted a power play just 15 seconds after a Swiss penalty.
The US outshot Switzerland 15-3 in the second period before adding four more goals in the third, including Bilka’s second and a solo effort from Simms.
Knight, the United States’ longest-tenured player making her 16th world championship appearance, scored midway through the final period to extend her tournament records to 68 goals and 121 points in 88 games. The 37-year-old is the competition’s all-time leader in both categories.
Aerin Frankel earned the shutout in goal, stopping all eight shots she faced as the Americans improved to 14-0 all-time against Switzerland, bronze medalists at February’s Olympics.
All but one member of the American roster, forward Joy Dunne, plays in the Professional Women’s Hockey League.
Canada opened their tournament by easing past Sweden 5-1 on Friday in Herning.
The youngest Canadian team since 2013, with an average age of 26, jumped to a 3-0 lead in the opening period with goals from Eldridge, Emily Clark and Rebecca Leslie.
Kendall Cooper added the fourth on a power play midway through the second period.
Hanna Thuvik pulled one back for Sweden on a power play in the final period before Eldridge completed the scoring with her second goal.
Canada goaltender Ann-Renée Desbiens stopped 13 shots in the Group B game.
In Group A, the Czech Republic rallied to beat Austria 4-1. Austria are playing in the top division for the first time. Katerina Mrazova led the Czechs with two goals and an assist.
Last year’s bronze medalists Finland faced hosts Denmark in Herning later Friday.
The US and Canada are the tournament favorites, continuing a long-standing cross-border rivalry. Canada have won 13 world titles, followed by the US with 11 across the previous 24 championships.
The Americans have won 10 of the past 14 world championships and arrived in Denmark as reigning world and Olympic champions, having claimed the 2025 title in the Czech Republic and gold at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, beating Canada in overtime in both finals.
Finland are the only other team apart from Canada and the US to reach the final, doing so in 2019.
The 11-day, 10-nation tournament in the Danish cities of Esbjerg and Herning is the first to take place in November after the IIHF moved it to begin before the PWHL season.
Rather than having the top five teams grouped together as before, the field has been split into two groups of five based on rankings, with the US leading one group and Canada the other.
The top four from each group qualify for the playoffs, with the final set for 16 November. The bottom two will play a relegation game.
Canada and the US are wearing generic jerseys without their national logos, mandated by the International Ice Hockey Federation and designed by IIHF supplier True Hockey.
Hockey Canada and USA Hockey have their own apparel and jersey contracts with Bauer and CCM, respectively.
The two federations are suing the IIHF over the dispute in a Swiss court.

New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
More than half of New Zealand’s voters cast early ballots in the tightly contested race.
Polls have opened on the final day of voting in New Zealand against a backdrop of concerns over the rising cost of living and the broader state of the economy.
Polling stations opened at 9am on Saturday (20:00 GMT Friday) and close at 7pm (06:00 GMT Saturday).
Voting already began on October 26. More than 1.6 million voters, out of nearly 3.8 million in total, had cast their ballots by the end of Thursday, according to the country’s Electoral Commission.
The country has strict laws banning any talk of politics on election day.
The 19-hour election day blackout, which ends when polling places close on Saturday evening, bars everyone, including political parties, news outlets and social media users, from commenting on likely election outcomes, campaign issues and anything else that might encourage or discourage people from voting in a particular way.
Billboards and advertising must be removed. Bumper stickers, T-shirts and even social media profile pictures are also covered by the law.
Breaches of the law can incur a fine of up to 20,000 New Zealand dollars ($11,000).
Opinion polls ahead of the tightly contested election suggest the governing centre-right National Party and the opposition centre-left Labour Party neck and neck, with neither on course to win enough seats to govern alone.
New Zealand’s Electoral Commission aims to release preliminary results from 95 percent of polling stations by the end of election night on Saturday. A final result, which will reflect ballots cast by New Zealanders abroad, is expected by November 27.
New Zealand elections
Most parties are campaigning on the economy, but their suggested solutions differ widely.
The National Party is pledging to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme.
The Labour Party is focusing on the cost of living, promising cheaper healthcare and transport.
Recent polls show no clear winner. A handful of seats either way could decide who governs.
New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional system.
Voters do not elect a leader of the country but instead select a local electorate candidate and a political party.
Electorate winners earn a seat in the typically 120-seat parliament, as do the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.

Iran's health ministry denies report on iodine distribution over US strike fears
Iran's health ministry has denied a report by The Times of London that it was distributing iodine tablets near its nuclear sites to prepare for possible US strikes.
"No Ministry of Health official has spoken to The Times, and the quote attributed to the ministry is false," Hossein Kermanpour, head of the ministry's public relations and information centre, wrote on X.
He said the health system was prepared for various scenarios and threats from "an enemy that does not even spare children". But he added that declaring a state of war was not within the ministry's authority.
He called publishing unverified reports at such a time "irresponsible".
The Times of London had cited an unnamed health ministry official who said Iran was handing out iodine tablets to communities near its nuclear facilities.
The official was quoted as saying, “Trump can no longer be trusted. He may go through with this crime," and that in every war, Iran had tried to distribute the tablets, which help protect the thyroid gland from radiation, within two to three kilometres of its nuclear sites.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: EU tells TikTok to fix ‘harmful’ For You feed, threatens fines
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
EU tells TikTok to fix ‘harmful’ For You feed, threatens fines
TikTok’s algorithm ‘leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from’, European Commission says.
The European Union has ordered TikTok to change the algorithm powering its For You feed, threatening the social media platform with large fines.
On Friday, Brussels accused TikTok of violating the EU’s Digital Services Act over the “harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect” by feeding users similar video clips based on what they’ve previously viewed or liked, even if they are “triggering”.
“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same, leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” European Commission Executive Vice President Henna Virkkunen, who oversees tech sovereignty, said in a statement.
“Today’s preliminary findings show again that TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ well-being, including those of minors.”
The algorithm, according to the EU, results in the “endless” exposure of users to “content about sadness, isolation or body image.”
The EU said that although TikTok had made some changes to mitigate the risks highlighted by the commission, the tweaks were not enough.
TikTok rejected the EU’s findings, saying they are “fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety”.
TikTok has “a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience”, a spokesperson for the tech giant said.
Brussels’ fines on the Chinese-owned platform could increase by up to 6 percent, according to regulators, unless the platform resolves the issue. The company will have a chance to respond before the commission issues its final decision.
Recent efforts in countries like France, Spain and England have focused on protecting minors on social media platforms from predatory behaviour, cyberbullying, deteriorating mental health and eating disorders. Several countries introduced social media bans for children below the age of 15.
Earlier EU findings
In February, the EU found that TikTok did not “adequately assess how these addictive features could harm the physical and mental well-being of its users, including minors and vulnerable adults”.
Whereas the EU’s February findings focused on features such as the impact of notifications, Friday’s order went after the algorithm itself, a senior EU official told the AFP news agency.
In July, the bloc accused TikTok of exposing children to risks like cyberbullying and predatory behaviour.
In the same month, Brussels ordered Meta to change Facebook’s and Instagram’s feeds in an investigation into the platforms’ violations of the bloc’s Digital Services Act.

Macklemore says US venues rejected his Free Palestine tour
American rapper Macklemore said on Friday that major US concert venues, including New York's Madison Square Garden, refused to book his Free Palestine tour that just concluded three dates in Europe.
The rapper launched the effort after he was removed as the opening act on musician Ed Sheeran's concert tour in August, because the stadium owners had objected to him saying "Free Palestine" on stage.
Since then, nine US venues declined to allow him to book available dates through the end of the year, Macklemore said on social media. The venues included Madison Square Garden and the Kia Forum in Los Angeles.
"The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues," he said in a post. "In over 20 years of touring, I've never experienced anything like this."
Macklemore played Free Palestine shows in Dublin, Paris and London to raise funds for organisations that support Palestinians. The musician said he would work with other artists and organisers to do more performances for the cause.
"We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech," he wrote. "Yet we've reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending."

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
Trump-Xi Busan deal aimed to ease tariffs and tech restrictions; progress hinges on China’s fulfillment of commitments.
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to urge Beijing to immediately implement commitments under the Busan trade agreement.
“Secretary Bessent emphasised the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments made in Busan and raised concerns about recent Chinese actions. He underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement,” the US Department of the Treasury said in a statement announcing the discussions on Friday.
The announcement refers to a trade deal negotiated between Washington and Beijing in which US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to ease tariffs and lift restrictions on tech to de-escalate tensions amid tit-for-tat tariffs imposed first by Washington and then by Beijing.
On Thursday, China said it was open to buying more US farm goods if the world’s two largest economies agreed to implement the reciprocal tariff cut.
“China has consistently been open to expanding purchases of agricultural products from the US, but only on the condition that the two sides implement their agreed ’30 billion for 30 billion’ reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement,” Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson Huang Ling said in a statement.
The move follows a September meeting between Trump and Xi, when the White House proposed $60bn in cuts, including $17bn worth of US farm goods.
In May, the White House said Beijing agreed to buy $17bn of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year’s target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made last October to buy US soya beans.
“Secretary Bessent reiterated the Trump Administration’s commitment to pursuing trade and economic policies that benefit American workers, farmers, and businesses and strengthen U.S. economic and national security,” the Treasury added.

Attacks, raids and forced demolitions mark another day of Israeli violence in West Bank
Israeli forces and settlers carried out 20 attacks on Palestinian olive pickers in six West Bank governorates on Friday, according to the Palestinian Wall and Colonization Resistance Commission.
The attacks included detentions, assaults, uprooting of trees and theft of crops, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing the commission. Farmers were also blocked from their fields.
West of Jericho, Israeli settlers entered farmland in ad-Duyuk at-Tahta with their sheep. They destroyed crops and greenhouses, resident Mustafa Fheidat told Wafa.
He estimated the damage at hundreds of thousands of shekels.
East of Ramallah, Israeli forces raided the Abu Fazaa Bedouin community for more than three hours, smashing vehicles, assaulting residents and detaining one man.
In Hebron, Israeli forces closed several Old City neighbourhoods for Jewish holidays, including the Ibrahimi Mosque, which will stay closed to Muslims until Saturday night.
Forces also detained three Palestinians, including a journalist, in Hebron and Masafer Yatta, assaulting a fourth.
Among them was Mohammad Yousef Makhmareh, a man with a disability, who was detained in Khirbet al-Markaz after soldiers tried to take his sheep. He lost a hand years ago to a landmine left by Israeli forces.
In occupied East Jerusalem, two Palestinians were forced to demolish their own homes, which housed 18 people, in Jabal al-Mukabber.
The families had paid 25,000 shekels trying to prevent the demolitions.

Chuck Schumer dismisses opposition to his leadership from progressive Democrats
US Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is facing opposition from progressives and a new group of Democratic lawmakers-elect to become Senate majority leader, in a rift that underscores the party’s divide on Israel.
Senators-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Troy Jackson of Maine, and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan all said on the campaign trail that they will oppose Schumer as Senate majority leader.
Meanwhile, progressive groups have said the Democrats’ sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday should start the process of new lawmakers leading the party.
“Voters made it very clear that they want a new generation of Democratic fighters,” Indivisible, a progressive Democratic group, said this week. “We need a Leader in the Senate who is capable of leading that fight. It’s time for Senate Democrats to choose new leadership.”
One key difference between the 75-year-old Schumer and the new cohort of Democratic lawmakers is his position on Israel. Schumer is a longtime supporter of military aid to Israel and has manoeuvred to stop bills in Congress that would condition military assistance.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
In February 2026, Schumer said that one of his most important jobs as Senate minority leader was to “fight for aid to Israel”.
“I have many jobs as leader… and one is to fight for aid to Israel, all the aid that Israel needs,” he told a group of pro-Israel Jewish leaders at the time.
“As long as I’m in the Senate, this programme will continue to grow from strength to strength, and we won’t let anyone attack it or undo it,” Schumer said, even referring to US taxpayer aid for Israel as his “baby”.
Schumer is Jewish-American and has received support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). But recent polling shows that he is out of step with the majority of Jewish voters in the US, who lean heavily Democratic.
A supermajority of Jewish Americans think Israel and Aipac’s actions are increasing antisemitism in the US, a poll commissioned by J Street and published this week found.
Still, the division on Schumer reflects a wider ideological divide within the Democratic Party. Senator-elect Sayed represents members who want to end the US’s support for Israel amid the genocide in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank. Other senators, like John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, are staunchly pro-Israel.
But Schumer is likely to return as Senate majority leader, partly because no senior Democratic senators have expressed interest in the role.
Schumer on Thursday dismissed talk of a rift within the party after a historic victory.
"The bottom line is: first... we’ve had a very, very strong finish here, and I have worked really hard to get the results we got. But second, the issue is not me,” he told MS Now. “The issue is unity, fighting together. We still have a big job to do.”

Houthis and Yemeni government blame each other for Taiz market attack that killed 30
Yemen’s Houthis and the internationally recognised government have blamed each other for a deadly attack on a market in Taiz province earlier on Friday.
The Houthis said Saudi aircraft carried out the strikes, while the government accused the group of firing a ballistic missile at the market and called the attack a “war crime”.
“Saudi enemy aircraft targeted the market in Al-Waziya city with several strikes,” Houthi health ministry spokesman Anis al-Asbahi said, according to the Houthi-run Saba news agency.
The group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the aircraft had taken off from Saudi Arabia’s Khamis Mushait base.
Meanwhile, local authorities in Taiz blamed “indiscriminate Houthi missile fire” and denied any air strikes had taken place.
The Houthi health ministry put the toll at 30 dead and eight wounded, and said rescue teams were still searching for bodies under the rubble at the market, which lies in a Houthi-held area of the province.
Government forces said on Friday that they had recaptured several areas of Taiz from the Houthis. The province lies near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key oil shipping route.

Syria sends military advisers to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks, sources say
Syria has sent a small number of military personnel to Saudi Arabia to advise and train forces as the kingdom comes under attack from Yemen’s Houthis, Reuters reported, citing two Syrian military sources and a senior US official.
The US official said Syrian advisers and training teams were travelling to Saudi Arabia to improve the combat effectiveness of Saudi and Yemeni units based there. The two Syrian military sources, who had direct knowledge of the matter, said scores of personnel had travelled to Saudi Arabia in recent weeks.
A senior Syrian diplomat told Reuters that "any suggestion of military deployments at this stage is premature" and that Syria remained focused on internal security, border protection and reconstruction.
The diplomat added that a defence cooperation agreement the two countries signed on Wednesday "specifically includes advisory support, training and exchange of expertise".
The two countries signed the agreement in Riyadh during a visit by Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for the second time in less than a month. The full terms of the deal were not made public.
Turkey, a close ally of Damascus, recently ratified a defence pact signed in Mecca in August by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani told a recent conference in Bahrain that talks were under way on Syria joining the pact.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Hamilton v Leclerc: how can Ferrari solve problem of two number one drivers?
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Giles Richards
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Going into this weekend’s São Paulo Grand Prix, all indications are that the status quo at Ferrari will no longer suffice for Lewis Hamilton if the Scuderia’s ambition to return their first drivers’ Formula One championship since 2007 is to be taken seriously.
This year’s drivers’ title is already decided with Kimi Antonelli triumphant at the last round in Mexico and Ferrari are looking towards next season where they are hopeful of genuinely being in the mix against the Italian and Mercedes.
However, after Hamilton and his teammate Charles Leclerc clashed at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, the Briton clearly believes that a title tilt in 2027 might be at risk, as the team apparently vacillate on how to manage having two No 1 drivers, both determined to be the top dog around which Ferrari should coalesce.
In Mexico, with Leclerc attempting to pass Hamilton, the move cost them both, Leclerc with a penalty and Hamilton in going wide and being passed by Max Verstappen who went on to win. The outcome denied Ferrari what would have been a likely victory and potentially a one-two. The team principal, Fred Vasseur, condemned the incident as demonstrating a lack of respect for the team and was expected to hold a crunch meeting with them both at Interlagos on Friday.
It was not the first time this season the two Ferrari drivers have been uncompromising with one another. At Zandvoort Hamilton was frustrated when, on a different tyre strategy, Leclerc did not pit when first instructed to do so by the team in order to let the British driver past. A race later at Monza, Hamilton went down the inside of Leclerc into the first chicane and was squeezed wide by his teammate into the gravel.
The notable difference after Mexico was Hamilton’s reaction. Previously he has been politic in stating they would deal with incidents behind closed doors – “offline” as he refers to it. After Mexico he publicly criticised Leclerc and before the race in Brazil was more bullish, refusing to be silenced in his criticism and making his position clear.
“Naturally it’s not so easy having someone like me come into a team because I’m very outspoken,” he said. “I push and push and push for so many changes and I’m going to be pushing for more and as long as I’m here that’s how it’s going to be. I’m here to win.”
That he is talking about it publicly indicates the seriousness of the situation. The team have no formal rules of engagement between the two and pointedly neither is considered the top driver in the way that Verstappen is at Red Bull.
Last year with the team struggling it was irrelevant. This year the problem has been brought sharply into focus. With a title at stake in the future it could be the difference between winning and losing but this is far from a straightforward situation. Hamilton came to Ferrari on the back of enjoying de facto No 1 status at Mercedes, pretty much since Nico Rosberg retired after thein 2016 season. Leclerc, who is no less competitive, has enjoyed similar pre-eminence at Ferrari, with whom he has forged a strong relationship since he joined in 2019 and was long the favoured choice as their expected next champion.
The complex demands and the fallout from letting them battle for dominance is far from new, as seen with Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost and Nigel Mansell and Nelson Piquet. Hamilton also knows about it, not least after his acrimonious fight with Rosberg in 2016. The latter was such that Mercedes, having been at pains to allow their drivers to race, had to impose rules of engagement.
Vasseur has been painstaking so far in avoiding that scenario but he was left enormously frustrated after the incident in Mexico and knows how costly it could be.
His is a very delicate balancing act however. McLaren had a similar problem with Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris in 2024 and 2025, and their efforts to allow their drivers to race without favour but also in managing them to the team’s advantage led to the adoption of their torturously complex “papaya rules”. These were satisfying to neither drivers nor fans, and did not appear particularly edifying to the team themselves. Notably however they did come out of it with the constructors’ title in 2024 and the double in 2025, a result that will not be lost on Ferrari.
It has largely not been a problem for McLaren this season, with Norris enjoying a distinct advantage over his Australian teammate, of which Hamilton and Leclerc are aware. Both are determined to make themselves the focal point of the team; both are aware how important that is if the title is at stake.
This has led to another fundamental problem for Ferrari. By not intervening in the process, they have seen the trust between the pair seemingly stretched to breaking point. Perhaps, it feels, within a whisker of becoming actively counterproductive from which a further, more damaging deterioration threatens.
As Hamilton appears to be now insisting, Ferrari must address the issue but Leclerc cannot be faulted for simply following his instincts as a competitor. Both drivers are committed to the team but both are as equally determined to win, ambitions that match those of the Scuderia, which if they are to be met they must surely now look to manage.
In first practice at Interlagos, McLaren’s Norris topped the timesheets in front of the new champion Antonelli in second, with Verstappen third and Hamilton fourth.
In the afternoon Antonelli was on top, from Norris and Verstappen with Mercedes’ George Russell in fourth. Russell is, however, set to take a five-place grid penalty on Sunday for using a new engine in Brazil. Hamilton and Leclerc were in sixth and seventh.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/right.title: Rights groups condemn Bahrain's largest mass trial of Shia clerics in history
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/right.author: Alex MacDonald
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/right.text:
Rights groups condemn Bahrain's largest mass trial of Shia clerics in history
Bahrain is set to hold the largest mass trial of Shia clerics in the country's history, with rights groups accusing the judiciary of obtaining confessions through coercion and torture.
On Sunday, a Bahraini court is set to hand down judgments to 69 defendants, among them 60 clerics, on charges of membership of a terrorist group, attempting to overthrow the "constitutional regime" and trying to promote Iran's political ideology.
According to testimony obtained by the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (Bird), the defendents were subjected to a range of abuses, including forced standing, prolonged blindfolding and handcuffing, sleep deprivation, and threats of physical and sexual violence against them and their families.
They were also threatened with revocation of their citizenship and deportation.
Sheikh Mohammed Saeed Al-Taitoon, a 62-year-old cleric, told investigators he was blindfolded and restrained for a week, and forced to stand despite severe urinary bleeding and kidney stones, while being denied necessary surgery.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Another, 57-year-old Sayed Moosa Jawad Alwedaie, told investigators he had been beaten, tortured with electricity and left naked.
Twenty rights organisations, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, called on the authorities to release those arbitrarily detained and drop charges based on peaceful religious activities, and to investigate allegations of mistreatment and torture.
Iran tensions
There has been repeated international criticism of the Bahraini authorities since their crackdown on a pro-democracy movement launched during the Arab Spring in 2011.
The Sunni monarchy that rules the kingdom has repeatedly targeted the religious leaders of the country's Shia majority, often accusing them of links to the Islamic Republic of Iran.
The US-Israel war on Iran led to the Islamic Republic launching a series of retaliatory attacks targeted US-allied states in the Gulf, including Bahrain, which has provoked a further crackdown on those with suspected links to Iran.
Sixty-nine Bahraini citizens of Iranian heritage have also had their citizenship stripped.
Tariq Al Hassan, head of Bahrain's agency responsible for internal security, told Reuters in an interview on Friday that the crackdown was aimed at confronting "an ideology that demands obedience to Iran's leadership above Bahrain's sovereign authority".
Critics, however, say the move is a further attempt to suppress dissent in the kingdom.
Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, advocacy director at Bird, described the trial as an "attack on the faith and identity of Bahrain’s Shia community" and one of the "ugliest forms of persecution" meted out by the state since 2011.
"When allegations of torture are brushed aside and defendants are denied a meaningful opportunity to challenge the evidence against them, the judiciary becomes an instrument of persecution," he said in a statement.
"This mockery of justice must end. It will leave lasting wounds and deepen divisions across the country."

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Israel closes Hebron’s Ibrahimi Mosque to Palestinians for Jewish holiday
Ibrahimi Mosque reopened exclusively for Israelis, deepening tensions over control of contested West Bank holy site.
Israeli forces have closed the Ibrahimi Mosque in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron to Palestinian worshippers as thousands of Israeli settlers converge on the site for a Jewish religious celebration.
The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Endowments said worshippers and mosque employees had been barred from entering and the call to prayer suspended.
Mosque director Moataz Abu Sneineh told Al Jazeera that Israeli authorities intended to open the mosque’s prayer halls and courtyards exclusively to Israelis.
The closure, imposed on Friday afternoon and set to last until 10pm on Saturday, coincides with an annual Jewish observance to commemorate Sarah, a wife of Prophet Abraham, who is traditionally believed to be buried at the site.
Israeli troops tightened checkpoints and restricted movement across Hebron’s Old City, where the mosque is located, preventing some residents from entering or leaving their homes.
Israeli forces told The Jerusalem Post they expected about 20,000 visitors at the site for the Jewish holiday, with hundreds of security personnel deployed.
Israel’s encroaching control
The Ibrahimi Mosque, known to Jews as the Cave of the Patriarchs, is revered by Muslims and Jews as the burial site of the Prophet Abraham and members of his family.
Under a 1997 Hebron Agreement signed between Israel and the Palestinian Authority, Israel assumed security control over the Old City, while Hebron’s Palestinian municipality holds planning and construction powers.
However, in June, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced a takeover of those powers, undermining Palestinian oversight of the holy site and raising fears that Israel was seeking to seize the site for exclusive Jewish use.
The closure comes just days after Israeli forces ended a 10-day siege of Hebron, which saw hundreds of arrests, 15 home demolitions and the displacement of more than 3,300 Palestinians.
Israeli settlers have steadily expanded their presence in Hebron’s Old City, seizing Palestinian properties and establishing new outposts under Israeli military protection.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Seth Meyers on Republicans: ‘Furiously backpedalling away from Trump’
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Late-night hosts ridiculed the many Republicans who are now trying to distance themselves from Donald Trump after the Democrats scored a midterms victory this week.
Seth Meyers
On Late Night, Seth Meyers said that Republicans were “furiously backpedalling away from Trump” after the result which has been referred to as a blue tsunami for the Democrats.
He said it’s been “a long 10 years since Trump was first elected” and in that time he has gone from “crusading outsider” to “depressed old man”.
He played footage of him miserably talking about renovations this week looking “like a substitute teacher with a hangover”.
Meyers reminded viewers that the Republicans claimed to be appealing to and working for the “forgotten working class” yet “the only workers who have actually benefited from Trump’s second terms are the ones who do rush jobs on reflecting pool renovations”.
He said that after claiming politics would be changed forever and for the better, “now they’re singing a very different tune” with many calling it the death of Maga.
One major figure now trying to backtrack is JD Vance who wrote a long post this week about how the war was the reason for the loss and that the right need to be better at analysing the mistakes that have been made.
“No one’s fucking buying it,” Meyers said in response, saying that his “whole thing is lying”.
When Trump was asked about Vance running, his low-energy response suggested that he thought no one might bother running in 2028. “What do you mean nobody is gonna run?” Meyers asked, wondering if he had gone “full nihilist”.
He joked that Trump “can’t even pretend to be upset” before moving on to the stuffy response from senior Democrats like Chuck Schumer. “You guys are killing the vibe!” he said, suggesting that they should “just let the young people talk” instead.
Jimmy Kimmel
On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host called it the “biggest midterm sweep in more than 50 years” and that Trump’s response is to rant and rave “about the least important things imaginable”.
This week saw the president complain about daylight savings time once again on social media with Kimmel joking that he is “arguing with the sun”.
He has also been going on about his 250ft $100m arch which Kimmel said drew “inspiration from his own neck vagina”.
Trump has also tried to make his iteration of the Oval Office a landmark that must remain untouched despite Kimmel saying that is resembled the “gift shop at the Liberace museum”.
He also wondered if “he’s planning to leave sooner than we think” while adding that in 2029 we will gladly “yank that crap down and throw it out”.
Kimmel also poked fun at Newsmax, which he referred to as a “cut-rate Fox with a dash of Grandpa Simpson thrown in” as hosts spiralled over the result.
“Trump made a lot of promises he couldn’t keep and they finally caught up to him,” he added.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
Susie Wiles steps down as White House chief of staff; Stephen Miller assumes the role amid post-election reshuffling.
Could Trump's veto stop the Democratic majority?
United States President Donald Trump has announced that Stephen Miller is replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
In a post on his Truth Social account on Friday, Trump said Miller would start his new job on Monday, calling him “one of my most trusted advisors”.
“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”
Wiles, the most high-profile departure yet from the White House after Republicans’ overwhelming midterm losses, said Friday would be her last day.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honour of a lifetime”, she wrote in a social media post. “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together, from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First”.
Al Jazeera learned that Wiles, who oversaw Trump’s return to the presidency in 2024, handed her resignation to Trump in the White House’s Oval Office on Thursday. A Republican Party official confirmed it was accepted by the president, who has since said he wanted to make a change.
Miller has been one of Trump’s closest confidants throughout both presidential terms, after joining the president’s first election campaign as an adviser in 2016.
Democrats are widely expected to launch investigations into Miller upon taking control of the US House of Representatives and Senate in January.
“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, the likely incoming chairman of the US House’s Oversight Committee, said in a statement to Al Jazeera. “Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts.”
He added, “Stephen Miller should lawyer up”.
Trump was widely expected to shake up his staff after the midterm drubbing, which saw Democrats net seven US Senate seats, with two states, Alaska and Mississippi, still counting their results. Democrats, as of Friday, have also won 253 seats in the 435-member US House, with 27 races still set to be counted.
Despite the vote, which was widely viewed as a referendum on Trump, Miller’s appointment largely represents a doubling down on his most controversial policies, offering a potential view of the course the president plans to chart for his final two years in office.
Miller, a domestic adviser to the president, has been the driving force behind some of the Trump administration’s most controversial policies, including its far-reaching immigration crackdown in the US.
Garcia called Miller “the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorised our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families”.
Some White House staff members immediately praised the announcement soon after it was announced.
“Stephen Miller is a Trump OG, someone who has been with the President since the very beginning”, White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on X. “There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen, and he will help the Administration deliver on monumental victories for the rest of this historic second term”.
Miller has not yet commented on the election results, but on election day, he urged Trump supporters to vote in a post on X.
“Send a message to the corrupt media, corrupt Democrats and corrupt left-wing politicians who want to steal your future and destroy the inheritance of your children,” he wrote. “Get to the polls and protect the ones you love.”

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: ‘He left the world in ruins’: the author who defied the Taliban and burning tyres to tell Alexander the Great’s epic story
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Lisa Allardice
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
He was the most powerful man in the world but he was brought down by one battle too many after a decade at the top. The story of Alexander the Great might be more than 2,000 years old, but it seems timely that a new biography of the ancient ruler won the Baillie Gifford prize for nonfiction just as President Trump took a battering in the US midterms. “This is a moment,” says its author Edmund Richardson, “where people are finding that there are limits to what unlimited wealth and power can do, and that humanity catches up with you, whether you like it or not. Alexander wants to transform the world – and he leaves it in ruins.”
Wearing a purple velvet jacket, purple scarf and matching socks, with a high forehead and corona of auburn curls, Richardson himself might have stepped out of an earlier age. It is hard to imagine anyone less like history’s favourite mob boss than this softly spoken professor of classics. We are having coffee at the offices of the PR company for the Baillie Gifford prize, the view of the City of London skyline from the floor to ceiling windows a reminder of 21st-century power and economics.
It would, we agree, have made the perfect backdrop for an interview with Patrick Radden Keefe, a previous winner of the £50,000 Baillie Gifford prize and the favourite this year for London Falling, a forensic investigation into the death of a teenager who falls from one of the city’s luxury skyscrapers. “I would never, ever have imagined this,” Richardson says, almost in a whisper. “I am fully expecting someone to tap me on the shoulder and say, ‘I’m so sorry, there’s been a terrible mistake, Mr Radden Keefe is waiting. You can take a coffee as you go.’”
Richardson’s exhilarating, exhaustively researched Alexander: God, King, Man is another triumph for the classics in a year when Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey stormed the box office (Alexander liked to sleep with a copy of Homer under his pillow, apparently). Like many, Richardson first encountered the figure in the pages of Alexander, Mary Renault’s 1969 fictional trilogy, when he was a boy. Critics have described his book as “part novel, part history”.
Richardson doesn’t just make the ruler of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon flesh and blood for a new generation. He also makes bold claims for his subject. “Alexander reshaped reality more profoundly than almost anyone else in history,” he writes. His expansionist campaigns might have been brutal, even by ancient standards, with his empire unravelling before his death, but for Richardson its true legacy is in the “ripple effects” that we still feel today. “It’s in the ways that Babylonian science turns up in Greece, that Greek art turns up on the borders of the Indus, that Egyptian scholarship finds its way into how we understand Homer. It’s in the world becoming far more connected.” He was antiquity’s answer to the internet.
“Alexander’s story is on this impossible scale,” he says. “This is someone who is capable of extraordinary violence and cruelty, extraordinary kindness and love.” Richardson describes the book as a “beautiful monster” to write. From Plutarch to Horrible Histories, there have been countless takes on Alexander’s story: the boy from the Macedon hills, who became king aged 20 in 336BC after his father was assassinated; marched his army into the heart of the Persian empire; had conquered much of the known world by the time he was 30, killing 1% of the population along the way; and who died “brokenhearted” in Babylon aged 32.
“Up until this book,” says Richardson, “my thing has always been writing stuff that no one reads about people no one has heard of. That’s my happy place!” His previous book, Alexandria: The Quest for the Lost City, was a biography of 19th-century archaeologist Charles Masson. But when his editor suggested he write about Alexander himself, he was horrified. “The idea of coming up against Alexander, and all of these thousands of versions of his story written by some of the people I admire the most in the world – absolute terror!”
Richardson, however, wanted to discover the real Alexander, before he became “great”. His search took him on his own decade-long adventure from the storage rooms of the British Museum in London to the catacombs of Egypt and the foothills of the Himalayas. Computer simulation and new discoveries gave him access to evidence and contemporary sources unavailable to earlier historians. But his travels back in time were interrupted by modern-day unrest. “There was a short encounter with a barricade of burning tyres,” he says, referring to a protest he stumbled upon in Cairo, while his visit to Afghanistan was abandoned after the Taliban ransacked his hotel.
“Terrible things tend to happen to people who take up papyrus or laptop to write the Alexander story,” he says. The first, Callisthenes, Aristotle’s great nephew, was crucified, according to some sources. “So for me, there was a sense of the story being something that consumes people. I felt my own fallibility as a writer, as a historian, vividly.” He also had to confront his own mortality.
Around three years ago, Richardson was diagnosed with cancer. He first had a melanoma as a teenager and “they’ve been back a couple of times since”. At this point, he was barely 40. “I was writing this book not knowing if I would be around when it was out in the world,” he says. He wasn’t even sure if he would finish it. His universe narrowed to the fluorescent lights and corridors of hospital. Writing became his way of travelling – “but to the world of ideas. The book, and the people I loved, reminded me that there was a version of myself that was less frightening.”
Although he was given the all clear, this time last year he was back in hospital after he collapsed, probably due to all the stress. When he came round the next day, two patients on his ward were handcuffed to police officers. “And there was me with my laptop and my hieroglyphs,” he laughs. It was a turning point, though. He had been struggling with the ending (“Obviously everyone dies and everything goes wrong”) but he returned to his “tangled” manuscript with “a feeling of trying to find a ray of hope where the light seemed to have gone out”.
Richardson, now 44, grew up in Bristol, the only child of two academics. His father, an American, is a mathematician; his mother, from northern England, is an art historian. There were “layers upon layers” of books in the house. He went to a Bristol grammar school, where he thought he might follow his father into maths, but he couldn’t resist the ancient world.
“Obsessions are my weakness,” he says. “Even when I was a kid, I would find myself getting lost in stories and falling down rabbit holes.” He made it to Cambridge to study classics, where he was taught by Mary Beard. On a postdoctoral fellowship to Princeton, he met his fiancee, “the love of my life”, the journalist and writer Yepoka Yeebo, who was studying at Columbia. They lived together in New York, before returning to London. “If there is good in what I write, it is her,” he whispers. “She makes me see the world entire, the wonder of things.”
His next subject – although his editor doesn’t know it yet – is the British Egyptologist Flinders Petrie. “I’m going back to books about people no one has ever heard of,” he says. “It’s the story of an archaeologist who, in the deserts of Egypt in 1888, thinks that he’s come up with a plan to defeat death.”
More immediately, he’s off to the BBC next, to talk more about Alexander. “It’s very strange as an academic to find people actually wanting to listen to what you say,” he jokes. “I feel so, so honoured.” Why does he think there is such interest the ancient world today? “It’s not just a story about the distant past,” he says. “We work with fragments, with ghosts, with things that have almost vanished – but that also lets us make these stories our own. There’s no such thing as the definitive book about Alexander. You know that there will be so many books after yours.”
How does he feel about his 10-year battle with Alexander ending in victory? “There have been some difficult times,” he admits. “It’s lovely to come out of that and into light.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Armed men kill at least 33 in village in Ebola-hit eastern DRC
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Armed men kill at least 33 in village in Ebola-hit eastern DRC
Locals blame ADF armed group, which pledged allegiance to ISIL in 2019, for the deadly raids on North Kivu villages.
Armed men thought to be linked to an ISIL (ISIS)-affiliated group have raided villages in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), killing dozens of people, according to authorities and civil society groups.
The attackers also set fire to a health post during their overnight assault on Cantine, about 50km west of Beni in North Kivu province, forcing patients with confirmed and suspected Ebola infections to flee.
Fighters with the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) armed group set fire to several houses and killed civilians, Beni territorial administrator Colonel Charles Omeonga told the Reuters news agency on Friday.
Justin Paluku, head of a local civil society group, also blamed the ADF for the attack.
“So far, we have counted 33 bodies and more than 50 houses set on fire, along with various other forms of material destruction,” he told the AP news agency.
Tchetche Aliamini, another local civil society leader, confirmed the death toll to Reuters and said that most of the victims suffered gunshot wounds, while others had been burned or hacked with machetes.
The violence forced many villagers to flee to other parts of the province, where the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history is raging.
Among those who fled were 180 patients from the local hospital, including suspected Ebola cases and one confirmed Ebola case, said Christian Kakule, medical director of the Kelekele Hospital Centre in Cantine.
“High-risk contacts and other individuals under monitoring have all fled,” he said. “Our concern is that when probable cases end up out in the open like this, they can become a source of transmission and trigger an outbreak of the disease.”
He said there was gunfire and homes were set ablaze as close as 50 metres from the hospital.
North Kivu currently accounts for almost half of all new infections in the DRC’s Bundibugyo outbreak and is the second most affected province after the epicentre, Ituri.
North Kivu was the epicentre of three previous Ebola outbreaks, including one in 2018-2020, which until this year was the DRC’s largest and deadliest.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has recorded more than 10,000 cases and 5,300 Ebola deaths across the DRC.
The ADF, which has roots in Uganda and pledged allegiance to ISIL in 2019, has long operated in the border region and routinely attacks civilians. In July 2025, it killed 66 people in eastern DRC in what the United Nations called a “bloodbath”.
About 100 other armed groups operate in the DRC, most prominently the Rwanda-backed M23, which has seized key cities in the east of the country while Ebola cases increase.
“This represents a major security failure,” Paluku, of the civil society group, told AP. “Given the number of loyalist and security forces deployed in this area, it is incomprehensible how the enemy managed to bypass their defences to kill civilians and inflict such significant material and human casualties.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: If Dune is this generation’s Star Wars, we are all in big trouble
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Ben Child
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
A long time ago, far far away, in a galaxy called the 1970s, kids dreamed of joining the rebellion, rescuing a princess and blowing up the Death Star. Peer into the cosmic tea leaves and it would become immediately clear that no amount of evildoing could withstand a neurotic gold butler, a dustbin with ideas above its station and a walking seven-foot tall shagpile carpet with a very low tolerance for disagreement.
It is worth remembering this when considering Florence Pugh’s recent declaration, ahead of next month’s Dune: Part Three, that Dune is her generation’s Star Wars. And then wondering how much trouble we might be in if she’s actually right. “I think they brought back movie-going. What an event the second [Dune] was,” Pugh cheerfully told the New York Times. “It was just so lovely to be a part of something that we know is our generational kind of Star Wars.”
Ponder this for a moment. George Lucas’s space opera boasted a hero who wanted to rescue his friends and free the galaxy from tyranny. Denis Villeneuve’s Dune gives us a young aristocrat who arrives in somebody else’s desert and ends up with a personal army so fanatically devoted to his greatness that his girlfriend appears to be the only person still bothering to check whether he has gone completely mad. Star Wars had a vaguely Buddhist mystical order who wanted you to trust your feelings. Dune has one that would prefer you to stop having feelings for anyone whose genetic profile hasn’t already been approved by their committee of sinister space nuns. What does it say about us if this is the defining cosmic fantasy of the modern era?
Pugh’s analogy becomes stranger the more you think about it. Lucas may have drawn heavily on Frank Herbert’s original 1965 book when he dreamed up the desert planet of Tatooine, but the two sagas offer distinctly different views of the universe. The original Star Wars trilogy asked us to believe that its central villain was ultimately worthy of redemption, despite having been a powerful cog in a regime responsible for billions of deaths. Dune, by contrast, is flowing grimly in exactly the opposite direction.
Next month’s Part Three may well be the point at which we discover that this saga’s chosen one, Timothée Chalamet’s Paul Atreides, is actually Darth Vader with better hair. However this all ends up, and cast members have been hinting that Villeneuve’s finale may not follow Herbert slavishly, it is unlikely to involve a bunch of teddy bears somehow bringing down a galaxy-spanning fascist superpower. We know from having watched the first two films that Paul has already glimpsed the horrors that could follow his rise to power. His ability to see possible futures means part three is a particularly uncomfortable prospect: a ruler who can foresee catastrophe yet may still be unable to prevent it. The boy who seemed destined to save everybody has become the man who could destroy it all.
There is one department in which Dune already has Star Wars beaten: Villeneuve’s films look absolutely astonishing. Lucas gave us twin suns, vast Imperial warships and the Death Star, but he then also gave us CGI space critters wandering across the foreground for no obvious reason, a digital Jabba you could almost see buffering and a Sarlacc pit given a face only its programmer could love. Villeneuve’s universe feels heavier, stranger and more genuinely alien: huge ships hanging over deserts, armies reduced to specks beneath impossible architecture, sandworms arriving with the rumble of ancient, inexorable doom. Even when Dune is telling us something dreadful, it looks better than almost anything else in modern blockbuster cinema.
And perhaps this is where Pugh’s comparison begins to make a bleak sort of sense. In a world where powerful men keep promising to save us from disasters they helped create, the closest thing to escapism is a dictator who can see the future he is ruining, but is unable to stop himself because the whole damn thing looks so utterly glorious in Imax.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Yaxel Lendeborg is the NBA’s most entertaining rookie – and he’s not holding back
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Owen Lewis
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
If a screen-addled pickup basketball player teleported into the body of a high-level athlete, they might resemble Yaxel Lendeborg. The most commonly cited fact about Lendeborg is that he used to spend 12 to 14 hours a day gaming, and didn’t debut on his high school basketball team until he was an upperclassman. Professional athletes often have origin stories that resemble the superhero more than the mortal, but Lendeborg really was just like us at one point. Lendeborg has also said that prior to entering the NBA, he didn’t really watch it, either. The Puerto Rican forward racked up more than enough accolades in college to qualify for the NBA, including helming Michigan to their first national championship in 37 years, but still. Any of you reading this could smoke the man who may be this season’s rookie of the year in trivia about his profession.
The 24-year-old Lendeborg is a forward on the Golden State Warriors, a team caught between the ancient, gleaming remnants of the most fearsome dynasty of the 2010s and its future. The balance didn’t work out last season, as the Warriors produced flashes of old greatness to win one play-in game before flaming out in the next. Such results are a frustrating waste of Stephen Curry’s wonderful form even at 38 years old. Lendeborg is the best hope in a while to help maximize it. But even more importantly, Lendeborg is the character of the season so far. He’s spent its first two weeks antagonizing superstars, firing off unselfconscious takes in the press and vacuuming up the spotlight from his blander peers. What a joy to bear witness to an athlete who probably didn’t even hear the words “media training” until college.
Lendeborg and the Warriors kicked off their season with a resounding loss to the Los Angeles Lakers, which quickly became the most talked-about blowout of the season so far thanks to Lendeborg making an enemy of the Lakers’ star, Luka Dončić. The two jawed at each other throughout the game, in which Dončić torched the Warriors as a whole but somewhat struggled when working one-on-one against Lendeborg. After the game, the rookie took issue with Dončić’s style of play – presumably too distracted by playing NBA 2K, he’d previously only watched Dončić via highlights and wasn’t familiar with the crafty Slovene’s foul-baiting abilities. “You get the foul call. Congratulations, bro,” Lendeborg said in a press conference. “Then you talk to me like you did something great. C’mon, dog. That shit is weak. It kind of threw me off because I have so much respect for him. Gone, man. Gone.”
Angering Dončić, an all-time great who famously levels up even further when furious, is certainly a choice. (Also, foul-baiting made Lendeborg lose all respect for him? I hope he didn’t see this effort from Duncan Robinson; it might propel Lendeborg into manslaughter.) Dončić has been on a historic offensive heater ever since, and if he maintains this temperature and wins his first MVP, he owes thanks to Lendeborg for the motivation. But the friction between the players was fascinating – a player shaking their head at Dončić like a disapproving uncle is certainly a new image – and nobody got hurt. Lendeborg later said that he took his complaints a little far. On the contrary, Yaxel: keep it up, your press conferences are now appointment viewing.
Not even a week later, Lendeborg was drawing fouls against the Nuggets like the best of them, taking 13 free throws and making 12. Just listen to him after that game, openly aspiring to new free-throw shooting heights that everybody seeks but nobody is shameless enough to admit to. I find Lendeborg challenging my staunchly held opinion that not a soul should start a new podcast until the current market desaturates.
It’s common for players like this to come out of the gates with color and gradually accept the beige, conflict-avoidant stock quotes spouted by the rest of the league. “Get this man a PR manager,” smirks the Redditor, perhaps unaware that they are advocating against their own interests. The more athletes succumb to the monochrome group of the media-trained, the more crucial dissenters become. The longtime reality show Survivor is in decline in part because modern contestants know the game too well, and thus often play the same way. Lendeborg brings to mind a similar truism about professional sports: the less a player cares about the PR contours they’re expected to follow, the better TV they make. Luckily, Lendeborg seems to understand his responsibility as an interesting athlete. “I’m not doing that, man,” Lendeborg said of media training to the San Francisco Chronicle. “I’m going to stay true to myself, and be honest. I’ve seen plenty of interviews where people are talking and it’s like, ‘Man, I don’t want to watch this,’ you know what I mean? And it’s not like I’m click-baiting or click-farming or whatever the heck people are saying.”
It’s a bonus that Lendeborg is also on an encouraging trajectory on the floor. At 6ft 10in, he provides the Warriors, who rely on exceptional shooting and quick ball movement over height, with some much-needed size. Lendeborg can do a little of everything: defend, shoot threes, pass sharply enough to keep up with Golden State’s manic style of play, drive to the basket and lay the ball in through contact.
Lendeborg rained 31 points, 12 rebounds and six assists upon the Denver Nuggets last week, the best performance of anybody in that game. He also helped hold the Nuggets’ Aaron Gordon, who often feasts against the Warriors thanks to their small lineup, to seven points. And yet, after that game, Lendeborg had the urge and lack of self-consciousness to ask a panel of former NBA greats for advice on his game during an interview. It’s no surprise that some of the feedback was for Lendeborg to keep up the “nasty” edge he’d established. Against the Los Angeles Clippers a few days later, Lendeborg piled up 37 points.
Even in plays Lendeborg isn’t a part of, you can see him twitching on the perimeter, calling for the ball and hopping in disappointment when it doesn’t arrive. (He may have gotten too excited in a rematch against the Lakers: the Warriors won, but Dončić repeatedly fried Lendeborg, who was benched and eventually fouled out.) In a win against the Miami Heat on Thursday night, Lendeborg drew a foul on Bam Adebayo and hopped up and down with his arms raised in celebration, an NBA finals-grade reaction for a routine play. He recorded a 17-8-6 stat line on the night (with three steals and a block thrown in for good measure) and it already felt quiet by his standards.
Don’t raise your expectations for the Warriors just yet – the ligaments holding them together are too frayed for that – but the team have won six games in a row. Behind Curry’s gleaming star, much of the credit has to go to Lendeborg. Warriors fans will delight in their maybe-savior, but Lendeborg’s personality has given the whole basketball fanbase reason to cheer.
