When artificial intelligence researcher Mrinank Sharma quit his job at Anthropic earlier this year, the news rippled across the internet. In his resignation letter, posted on X and viewed 15.3m times, Sharma warned of a world “in peril” from the technology he had helped build.
“It is clear to me the time has come to move on,” he wrote. His next move: a poetry degree.
In the months following Sharma’s resignation, AI industry defectors and workers outside of Silicon Valley alike have echoed his sentiments.
Bracing for disruption forecasted by the AI industry, white-collar professionals are voluntarily leaving established careers to pursue professions they feel are more secure or more aligned with their values. Workers across industries – from tech to public relations to consulting – say AI changed the substance and stability of their jobs overnight. They worry about AI jeopardizing their cognitive abilities, contributing to climate change, undermining value to customers and compromising security. Some, like Sharma, have left their fields entirely, shifting to vastly different careers.
So far, economic data shows that AI has not wreaked havoc on the workforce. It’s created about 1m US jobs, compared with 200,000 layoffs attributed to AI, according to the Economist. But as AI executives continue to warn of disruption, 71% of Americans believe the technology will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years, according to the Pew Research Center. As workers fear for the future, though, they’re making major decisions about the present.
The shift on the ground
Some white-collar workers have begun to look beyond the dreams they were sold as AI reshapes jobs.
After spending nearly a decade in public relations, 30-year-old Vanessa Hsia decided to seek a master’s degree in comparative literature.
“I felt very burnt out and concerned with the direction of the industry: chasing quantity over quality, relying on AI rather than critical thinking, prioritizing short-term wins over long-term strategy,” Hsia posted on LinkedIn. “I have no idea where this path will lead, but I’m taking my own advice: the world is on fire, might as well do what you want.”
Hsia and her former colleagues in PR feared AI would eventually replace them, she said, noting that specific tasks like pitching reporters over email were already being automated.
“I’ve been sold this dream that if I work really hard in my career, I’ll climb the ladder, that I will be respected in my field and paid a fair wage,” she said. “But then you have this technology that exacerbates the fact that, actually, no, that’s not guaranteed.”
The safe, tidy way of life defined by a bachelor’s degree, desk job and career ladder is in its death throes, accelerated by the encroaching tidal wave of AI, Hsia contends. It’s an opinion echoed by other white-collar workers.
“The career that I’ve had for 10 years is kind of fundamentally gone,” said a software engineer at a big tech company, who requested anonymity for fear of retribution. The engineer and his peers believe their roles will soon cease to exist as AI automates coding. “We all thought we would be software engineers for another decade or two,” he said, adding that he’s considering leaving the industry. “Now it’s completely changed.”
For some workers, AI has accelerated feelings of instability and purposelessness they already had in their careers. Hanna Horvath spent most of her twenties as a content marketer and editor. But earlier this year, the 29-year-old left her editing job at personal finance platform Bankrate to freelance in copy writing and social media marketing, serve as a financial planner and publish a Substack newsletter.
Even before the introduction of AI, Horvath felt like her day-to-day work had drifted away from what she was hired to do, becoming “meaningless”. And after witnessing multiple layoffs at her company, she no longer felt assured by the promised stability of a nine-to-five job.
Once her company mandated AI use, Horvath felt even worse. “AI doesn’t have to replace your job to fundamentally change your relationship to your job,” she said. “So many of us were just becoming project managers instead of actually editing content or writing content.”
On LinkedIn, Horvath wrote that though the larger conversation about AI has been about job displacement, the tech “has already changed worker psychology”, referring to people’s fears and loss of purpose. Now, with varied streams of income, Horvath said she feels more financially secure and less vulnerable to AI replacement.
Some white-collar workers are effecting complete professional 180s: from tech to law enforcement and advertising to acting.
Chris, who asked to go by a pseudonym for fear of retribution, left his software engineering job to join the police department of a major east coast city last year. AI had taken “a lot of the thinking” and fun out of coding, and he feared being displaced, he said.
“There’s no job security in corporate anymore,” said Chris, who spent more than a decade doing white-collar work. “You’re expendable, you’re an asset.”
Chris counts himself lucky to have left software engineering as his employer started to push AI on his team. Now, as a police officer, “there’s a satisfaction I never got in engineering … In a lot of ways I am happier,” he said, referring to working directly with his community.
Similarly, Kara, who asked to go by a pseudonym to speak candidly about her former career, said leaving her job as an advertising producer to focus on acting while moonlighting as a barista made her “feel spiritually lighter”.
Kara had experienced increasing burnout, much of which she attributes to being instructed to use AI despite her concerns over legality and creative use. She said her team was encouraged to use AI-enabled production tools like Runway, which generates AI videos and images, and ElevenLabs, an AI voice generator, to supplement its creative work. As the producer, she was charged with handling legal clearance at a time when AI-generated video and audio based on a human’s likeness is still a gray area.
Her employer “compelled” the team to incorporate generative AI, then “in the same conversation, warned about the legal dangers”, she said. The result was constant stress.
Kara also worries about AI generating art after training on the work of human artists. Between her creative opposition and the stress of overseeing AI’s legal use, the job “became untenable”, she said. She’s been transitioning to what she calls her “survival job” as a barista “quite happily”, she added.
Stoking job fears
For years, the architects of AI have insisted that their technology poses immense economic threats. In May 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei predicted AI would lead to the displacement of half of all entry-level white-collar jobs by the end of the decade. That carnage has yet to materialize.
This year, Amodei doubled down on his stance in an essay on his website.
“AI is increasingly matching the general cognitive profile of humans, which means it will also be good at the new jobs that would ordinarily be created in response to the old ones being automated,” reads his essay, which calls AI a “general labor substitute for humans”.
Workers’ fears likely stem from company leaders’ warnings and the layoffs they’re seeing, even though data doesn’t show AI is causing job loss, said Brendan Moore, a University of Notre Dame economics professor who’s studied worker sentiment on AI and job insecurity.
“Between the proclamations from tech CEOs saying there are going to be mass layoffs, to many large technology and telecommunications companies that are citing AI as reasons for layoffs … people are saying: ‘Oh, this is due to AI,’” Moore said, adding some companies likely would’ve downsized regardless.
Workers still drive the economy, so if large numbers of them change course, wages, prices and economic growth could be affected, Moore said. Following the “great resignation”, when workers quit en masse during the Covid-19 pandemic, wages and consumer inflation rose. If the fear of AI provokes mass resignations, similar economic disruption could materialize.
“Just the fear of job loss alone, even if mass job loss never comes, can affect the economy,” Moore said.
Though AI leaders have walked back their dire economic predictions in recent months, it may be too late to reverse negative worker sentiment, which has garnered the attention of lawmakers.
Earlier this year, the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders introduced a bill to impose a federal moratorium on the construction of new AI datacenters until safeguards were in place for workers facing job loss. AI leaders “do not want to just replace specific jobs. They want to replace workers,” he wrote in an op-ed for Fox News, calling AI a “nightmare” for the working class.
At the same time, some tech executives are calling out their industry’s failure to articulate a positive vision for the future.
“It is surprising that the discourse from many developing AI is so filled with doom,” Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta, wrote in an August essay. “I do not understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity’s relevance would rush to build that future.”
For workers, the issue is much simpler: AI is destabilizing their professional lives now – so they are taking matters into their own hands.
“Uncertainty is making people anxious,” said Horvath, the financial planner. But “you can’t have nihilism, because at the end of the day, it only hurts you”.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: How Gotham FC re-tooled for another NWSL title run – this time as favorites
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
By the time Gotham FC had won their second NWSL Championship in three seasons, Yael Averbuch West had already determined what was going to change.
Some of that is the nature of her job; the general manager of a perennial contender can’t rest on laurels. Before every postseason, Gotham finalize tough looming personnel decisions, assessing the roster and staff alike with clear eyes.
“I think psychologically, this is just really important,” Averbuch West told the Guardian. “Really, we knew what we needed to do. For us, it’s this continuous evolution of how we always look to improve. There’s nothing that’s ever safe from review.”
For all of their recent postseason success, with championships won as the lowest seed in 2023 and 2025, Gotham had never finished higher than third in any of their 17 seasons in NWSL or WPS. That trend was finally bucked in 2026, capped with last weekend’s capture of the NWSL Shield. But Averbuch West, alongside head coach Juan Carlos Amorós, wanted more consistency.
“I think it was massive, especially coming from Europe and understanding how important it is to win a league title,” Amorós told the Guardian. “Obviously, here it’s called the ‘regular season’, but it was the target that we had at the beginning of the year with the players, to show that consistency that we knew we had in the big moments. We already have the other titles, but this one feels special.”
The bar, as described by Averbuch West, is to finish each season in the top four. On paper, the 2026 squad looked more than capable of doing so. Gotham entered the year with the United States’ two top playmaking midfielders, Rose Lavelle and Jaedyn Shaw. They had vital veterans like Margaret ‘Midge’ Purce, Jaelin Howell, Tierna Davidson, and Emily Sonnett. Ann-Katrin Berger remains one of the world’s best goalkeepers, with Esther González among the game’s top strikers. They added veteran midfielder Savannah McCaskill to that mix.
They supplemented those pillars with youth – an easier ask after the NWSL did away with its college draft after the 2024 offseason. Gotham signed three top prospects with US youth international experience. One, Jordynn Dudley, was an instant smash and a contender for rookie of the year before her season-ending foot fracture in October. Another, Teagan Wy, is a projected goalkeeper of the future for the USWNT and is getting invaluable experience as Berger’s understudy. The third, Andrea Kitahata, shone bright at Stanford.
“It’s almost impossible to have the perfect amount of talent,” Averbuch West said. “You either have a little bit too much competition, or a little too little, and then if you have a couple injuries or things happen, you end up thin. I don’t even like to say ‘depth’ – we have an unbelievably talented roster, like 20-something players deep. I think that every single one of our players can start in the NWSL and be successful. We just have to pick.”
Then again, past rosters didn’t lack for talent. The trick for Amorós and his players was to play in a sustainable way; to enjoy greater control over matches. By the end of May, as the NWSL took its midseason break, Gotham led the league with a 58% average share of possession, yet was fifth in the standings, and ranked a pedestrian eighth in expected goals generated per game. Opponents were content to let them pass around in the defensive and middle thirds while concentrating their schemes on limiting service to González.
And so, the project evolved: Gotham won a global competition for Sam Kerr’s services, bringing the club’s record goalscorer back as a free agent after her time at Chelsea. How long could they keep four Best XI caliber attacking players getting their expected looks? That was a two-fronted task the club embraced.
“I’m going to try to hand [Amorós] as many problems as I can in terms of the roster we create, and the decisions he has to make [is] how it all fits together,” Averbuch West said. “But we know that these are human beings with lives and families, and things change and adapt, so I’m always expecting that.”
And change they did. Kerr’s arrival came after Lilly Reale, the 2025 NWSL rookie of the year and US Soccer’s young women’s player of the year, was traded to Boston for allocation and transfer funds. Amorós stepped away on paternity leave on 20 July. Eleven days later, Sonnett – an invaluable leader and stalwart defender – landed on the season-ending injury list after rupturing her left patellar tendon.
As if that wasn’t enough, González provided an unexpected wrinkle. The World Cup winner was a two-time Best XI honoree, as dependable a goalscorer as any, and had previously extended her contract through 2027. On 27 July, the club abruptly announced that they’d agreed to a mutual termination of her contract. Averbuch West issued a statement wishing “Esther and her family all the best as they return home to Spain.”
Less than a month later, they woke up to news that González had found her next club: not in Spain, but in Saudi Arabia. The player’s seeming about-face was difficult to understand. But if there are hard feelings today, the club’s leaders aren’t showing it.
“I think Esther is definitely one of the legends of this football club,” Amorós said. “We always say here ‘we are all humans before we are professionals’, and the situation of her life was going into a moment of change. We have to respect her and we have to appreciate the time that we spent together, thank her for everything she did for this football club, and wish her all the best. And we hope that life away from football is also going well for her.”
Why build and retain considerable squad depth if it can’t be leaned on when needed most?
“It’s not easy at all to adapt to losing a player of Esther’s level,” Averbuch West said. “I mean, arguably one of the best in her role in the world … There’s no preparation you can do to fill a void of that quality. At the same time, we can never just rely on one player to be successful in a season or the next game. We can’t rely on two or even three. We really need to have the full squad.”
Since losing González, the Bats surged to the top of the standings by early August. Goals still don’t come in the bulk that Gotham would hope, with their 39 goals being the second-lowest of any playoff qualifier.
“I think what we were able to do is keep building into those principles of controlling games,” Amorós said. “I think we were able to be more consistent on that side of the ball with the possessions. I think our defending game has been excellent, despite being very aggressive in terms of where we defend on the pitch and those principles. The more they are established, the more they become of our foundation. The evolution is definitely there, and hopefully next year is even better.”
So what would a third title in four years mean? To most, it cements Gotham’s status as a dynasty, a rare feat in a salary capped league. But that’s a question Amorós won’t even entertain for a couple more weeks. Not after the team’s previous title defense – in 2024 – fell just short in the semi-final.
“I just want to make sure that we give ourselves the best chance to get to the final,” Amorós said. “For that, we need to get to the semi-final, and to get there, we need to beat Seattle. So I think that’s the main thing. Who knows, if that happens, then I will be more than happy to answer the question of how I feel [about winning a third Championship].
“We know that when it comes to these games, it doesn’t matter if you’re number eight or you’re number one. We proved that last year.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Punk-Rock Appeal of the Women’s Pro Baseball League
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: G’Ra Asim
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The new competitive circuit captures the energy and DIY spirit of punk, while promoting a surprisingly sturdy vision of civic belonging.

Ashton Lansdell of the Los Angeles Queens celebrates after scoring against the San Francisco Firebells in game two of the Women’s Pro Baseball League Championship.

Cultic ecstasy seizes my body. I leap to my feet from a sitting position and thrust my hands skyward like someone who got the Holy Ghost in church. Like a contagion, the same behavior ripples across the aisle I’m sitting in. About a quarter of the way across the crowded baseball stadium, the vector peters out. Either the people roughly 10 rows away don’t notice our spirited efforts to sustain a wave across the entire crowd, or they just don’t feel like participating.

“Those guys suck, dude,” our wave leader groans. “They need to get with the program!”

It’s no less than the sixth time that this person has hectored our section to start an ill-fated wave. To the chagrin of the visibly exasperated spectators around him, he has not lost hope.

I’m in the stands for game three of the Women’s Professional Baseball League’s best-of-five inaugural championship series. The Los Angeles Queens are up two games to none on the San Francisco Firebelles, and another Queens win will secure the championship. The WPBL website boasts that “for the first time in 70 years, the best women baseball players in the world are competing on a professional stage.” Players hail from across the United States and 11 other countries. The league’s first-ever regular season began a few weeks earlier on August 1, 2026. Each squad in the league played all the other teams five times, for a total of 15 regular season games in a triple round-robin format. For now, there are four teams in the WPBL, two of whom have already been eliminated: the Boston Hunters and the New York Heights. All the games are played in impartial Springfield, Illinois. Watching teams named aspirationally after major markets compete in the neutral territory of flyover country feels like a provisional unity of these States, in a way it’d be hard to approximate by other means.

I’ve taken a road trip from St. Louis, Missouri, where I live, to Springfield, which I’m not sure I’ve heard of before now. Despite the city’s claim to fame as the adult home of Abraham Lincoln, it wouldn’t have surprised me to find the Klan posted up in the stadium parking lot. Along with my intrepid companions Jesse and Doc, I bought tickets online the night before the game, but pickings were slim. Three successive seats in the same row weren’t available. We bought a pair that were right next to each other and a third ticket a few rows behind those two. Our plan was to barnstorm the end of one row and dare anyone to challenge our claim. A group of white fans to our left look like they want to. They gawk over their shoulders at us like schoolyard extras in a Ruby Bridges movie. I almost hear my antebellum-era ancestors assembling into a bluesy chorus of telltale woe and foreboding.

When we pulled into Springfield half an hour ago, my eyes settled on a chain restaurant I’d never seen before.

“Taco Gringo?” I blurted. “Sounds a little too White Power for my taste. Is it really a selling point that gringos are back there making the tacos?”

“I don’t think the gringos are making the tacos,” Doc had joked. “They’re probably just cracking the whip.”

Though most of my teenage years and young adulthood took place on the East Coast, I’m a native St. Louisan. The MLB’s St. Louis Cardinals are our dominant sports franchise, so naturally my earliest baseball memories were formed at Busch Stadium. I’ve had difficulty rooting for the home team since the police killing of Ferguson teenager Mike Brown in 2014. That year, social media was awash in clips of mobs clad in Cards regalia spitting and cursing at Black Lives Matter protesters. It’s likely that there’s some overlap between the folks at the ballpark with me now and those justice-averse Cardinals fans. But here, as supporters of a new league, it feels like we have a clean slate.

Well, sort of. I can’t help but suspect that some percentage of the enthusiasm that radiates throughout Robin Roberts Stadium today is traceable to the 2023 NCAA women’s college basketball final, in which Caitlin Clark’s Iowa Hawkeyes fell to Angel Reese’s LSU Tigers. The widely watched showdown between two highly marketable and racially polarizing players sparked a surge in public interest in women’s sports. There is no competitive storyline Americans relish more than a clash between a Great White Hope and what they perceive as an uppity Black antagonist, and apparently the fervor is gender neutral. That revelation doesn’t exactly brighten the forecast for our crumbling empire, but it does boost the overall flashbulb wattage of women’s sports.

Here at game three of the WPBL’s inaugural championship series, fans carry signs with slogans like “I drove 300 miles to be a part of HERSTORY.” There is a palpable shared sense that the one thing better than being on the right side of history is cheering history on while you’re sitting by its third base line.

A strict, masc-of-center auntie in her 50s or 60s seated to my right foretells the outcome of each at-bat.

“That’s an out!” she yells sometimes, leaning back in her seat with her arms crossed as a fly ball lingers over second base.

“That’s a hit,” she claims other times, as soon as she hears the crack of the bat.

Growing up a baseball fan in the 1990s Midwest, I tracked the traditional box score stats in the paper every morning before school. Before the Moneyball movement, baseball diehards assessed player performance via straightforward statistical categories like batting average, fielding percentage, and runs batted in. These were the numbers you would see on the back of a baseball card. Starting in the early 2000s, those traditional statistics were phased out in favor of advanced analytics. Where sportscasters once narrated home runs by bellowing things like, “Busting out the whooping stick!,” they instead began to pepper the broadcast with references to math nerd esoterica like launch angle, spin rate, and exit velocity.

Look, I love Neil deGrasse Tyson. Physics has its place. But I doubt I’m speaking only for myself when I say I tune into baseball games to watch swaggering leviathans swing clubs at projectiles and hammer them to the moon. The shift in how baseball is discussed and understood is a microcosm for how the digital age has muddied the distinction between information and meaning. I appreciate that the experts can contextualize the game with such an impressive volume of information. This stern auntie’s play-by-play—which more than compensates with passion for what it lacks in data—strikes me as far more meaningful. The subtext of her commentary is that she’s been waiting for a league like this one for most of her life, and she’s not going to take one iota of action for granted.

Typically, yearning for baseball’s salad days would mark me as retrograde. In this case, I’m quite sure appreciating WPBL for its contrasts with MLB makes me a part of the vanguard. That said, I hesitate to position the WPBL as somehow morally superior to other professional sports leagues. Women’s sports are more often instrumentalized as battlegrounds in the culture wars than treated as legitimate ends in themselves. Moralizing is boring, and watching some of Earth’s most talented and tenacious people push their bodies to their limits in the name of autumnal glory is a good time. At least as much as we need an endless hermeneutics of ball, we need an erotics of ball.

Being taken out to this ballgame and taken out to the crowd also feels more poignant at a cultural moment defined by atomization. When things like, say, the venerable practice of wearing headphones when listening to media in public have fallen out of favor, any symbiosis between strangers feels like a sign of great respect in our culture. That’s what makes me realize why being absorbed into a fandom that’s both salutary and scintillating is so comforting, so familiar. The WPBL is the new punk rock.

As a millennial pushing 40, I’ve been a punk rocker much longer than I wasn’t one. I’m in two actively recording and gigging bands right now; I threw my first house show in my parents’ basement to celebrate my 15th birthday. Punk is about building the reconciled world in miniature and making its qualities infectious. Organizing a scene in your town is a small insurrectionary act—lining up a single domino that might, and sometimes does, kick-start a massive cascade.

A lot of the viral content about being an aging punk or emo kid focuses on nostalgia, as if the upshot of belonging to a forward-thinking subculture is to perseverate on the past. But the skills and instincts that we honed in VFW halls, garages, and church basements are just as easily applicable to the pursuit of gender equity in professional sports. Why settle into being a mark for the contrived cash grabs of your local Emo Nite when you could sublimate your ennui and residual angst into supporting a likeminded subculture like the WPBL instead?

Everyone who spent their teens and 20s working for street teams, orchestrating circle pits and Walls of Death, and tucking show flyers under windshield wipers can channel their punk-rock past in helping to secure the WPBL’s future. In 2018, Vice published a satirical article asking, “What Kind of Punk Dude Over 30 Are You?” The article joked that thirtysomething punks have a limited menu of acceptable hobbies and interests that they can cultivate to stave off the creep of cultural irrelevance. As I ponder the high jinks I might get up to as an over-40 punk, WPBL zealotry presents a compelling case.

Punks are better known for throwing bricks than laying them, but jury-rigging alternative structures is a big part of what we do. Whether we’re debuting a zine, a new band, or a DIY show space, we’ve always taken a distinct pride in supporting something precisely because it’s fledgling yet fertile, burgeoning and brimming with promise. The slightly grating wave whisperer here at the game reminds me of the dutiful mosh mentors I grew up with in the punk scene. They trained members of the audience to pick up anyone who fell down while slam dancing, reminded us to choose opportune and safe moments for our stage dives, and urged us to pass the hat for touring acts even when there wasn’t much money to go around. A movement isn’t only held together by the headliners—it’s also sustained by the energized, anonymous folks who dole out unsolicited marching orders, and those who roll with them even as we roll our eyes.

As the innings accumulate, I’m brought back to the beer-soaked stages and sweat-streaked floors where I cut my teeth. The early days of a punk band’s ascent are traditionally viewed as innocent, less cynical, driven by a genuine love of the game. Likewise, since legal gambling is now largely coextensive with professional sports, watching professional baseball for its own sake is a return to a simpler time. Cheering and jeering abound, but no one here is screaming about their parlay, or frantically refreshing the FanDuel app.

Much like navigating the street parking outside a makeshift venue or house show, figuring out where to leave the whip near the stadium was a riddle. My friend Jesse ended up pulling her SUV onto a muddy strip of grass next to some train tracks nearby. The demand for women’s professional baseball for the moment outpaces the real estate set aside for its patrons. We figured Springfield was still adjusting to the influx of fans from other cities, and strict parking enforcement would be unlikely. On his way to the ticket line, a man in a Chambray shirt and jeans looked back at our car and grinned impishly.

“Looks like a parking spot to me!” he declared, flashing us a thumbs-up. A nascent iteration of the American pastime foments the same constructive lawlessness as Warped Tour or the Fest.

A newfangled women’s baseball league and a punk scene both recall the architectural principle of flex space—a term that describes any versatile, adaptable, lightly zoned area in a commercial building. Some rooms or settings are designed for specific purposes. The construction of the room circumscribes how the room can be used. By contrast, flex space is meant to be pliable enough that occupants can customize it to suit the fluctuating needs and aims of their business. The punk scene and the WPBL are both flex spaces where norms can shift in real time. They’re both underground pockets that can slip the generally totalizing yoke of unfettered capitalism. In these flex spaces, the conditions of possibility are developed and implemented on the fly.

This includes a temporary suspension of the “customer is always right” ethos that otherwise guides American commerce. Jesse ventures into the bowels of the stadium to brave the concession line in the third inning. By the top of the fifth, she still hasn’t returned. I hop out of my seat and pace the stadium corridors until I find her in line, where an interminable trail of sweaty, hungry WPBL supporters are being surprisingly civil about the slow, disorganized food service. Jesse herself mentions being on the verge of becoming hangry, but exercises some commendable and not totally characteristic restraint. It’s as if the entire concession line is down for the cause. They know the WPBL is an embryonic but well-intended enterprise that calls for a level of patience and indulgence that the more established sports institutions may not require.

The phrase “social construct” penetrated the mainstream during the height of what is now derisively described as Woke 1, those pathbreaking days from early 2014 to 2021 when American culture seemed more mutable and benevolent than it has felt since. Whenever I heard gender, sexuality, or race described as social constructs, I always wondered why we couldn’t consciously build some new, more humane structures from scratch. Where was the social construct factory? Who among us might put on their hard hat and start hammering out frameworks meant to shelter rather than subjugate? In the stands at a WPBL championship game, I feel that construction effort commence.

It turns out the crowd of murmuring, staring white folks in the section next to us were actually marveling at Doc’s service animal, a preternaturally adorable toy Australian shepherd. Dogs are the ultimate social lubricant. When paired with baseball, they form a diversion powerful enough to neutralize racial reticence.

“His name is Dodger,” Doc tells a middle-aged white couple behind us. “The energy here almost reminds me of Dodger Stadium.”

“You’ve been to Dodger Stadium?” the husband breathes, as if Doc had seen the gates of Valhalla. I don’t directly observe this conversation, since I was wary that eye contact with the couple behind us would prolong the engagement. So I imagine Doc adjusting her sunglasses and tossing her fabulous Afro as she says, “Yeah, I’m originally from LA. The Dodgers are my favorite team. Where are you guys from?”

“We’ve seen Bush Stadium and Wrigley Field,” goes the husband.

It’s not quite an Obama-era beer summit, but it is a quiet coalescence of coastal elites and heartland dwellers, a glimmer of baseball’s potential to patch up tattered social fabric. The moment recalls the words of legendary folk-punk troubadour Frank Turner. Addressing the crowd at an Amityville Music Hall solo show in 2025, he explained how and why a punk performance—like a WPBL game—is always more than meets the eye.

“If we all do our parts, we will achieve two things. The first of which is, we’ll make a cool noise. And arguably, that’s what this is all about. But the other thing we’ll do is demonstrate a point which is important to me. Which is that live music, rock ’n’ roll, folk music, punk rock—whatever name you wind up calling this—is not about raised pieces of flooring and backstage passes and tour buses and egos and all that stuff. It’s about bringing people together. It’s about a room full of strangers who leave as friends, a room full of strangers who achieve something together that’s more than the sum of their parts, thereby demonstrating to themselves and to the rest of the world that we can be a community if we choose to be one.”

Doc, Jesse, and I rocked up to the ballpark expecting the Los Angeles Queens to close out the series with a 3–0 sweep. San Francisco had other plans. They overpowered the Queens from the jump, racing out to a commanding seven-to-nothing lead in the second inning and not letting up. Attendance at the decisive victory of a best-of-five series would certainly be more historic, but San Francisco’s fighting spirit won the crowd over. We all needed reminding that no deficit is too daunting if you come out swinging. A few weeks later, a sitting president will casually fantasize aloud about sacrificing two major Californian cities to the war against Iran. For now, we’re galvanized by the collective exercise of manifesting a future where the San Francisco Firebelles’ smoking baseball bats are as American as smoking gun barrels.

During a seventh-inning stretch, the wave’s most vocal advocate finally sees his wish fulfilled. The wave breaks out on the side of the stadium opposite ours. Our section exults and keeps it going when it reaches us. As fireworks shimmer across the late-summer sky, the glass ceiling feels like a piñata visibly starting to give way, sprinkling rewards that will only multiply if we all keep swinging on target. I’m filled with enough goodwill and forbearance to consider stopping at Taco Gringo on the way home.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Eyes on Iowa
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: D.D. Guttenplan
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Where with a little bit of luck—and a ton of grassroots organizing—decency has a fighting chance.

You can see it in the polls, which show Rob Sand, the Democratic state auditor running for governor, consistently ahead of Republican Zack Lahn, in a state where the outgoing incumbent, MAGA Republican Kim Reynolds, was reelected by a 19-point margin four years ago—and where Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris by over 13 points.

You can see it in Dubuque, where hundreds of protesters gathered for a No Kings rally before Trump’s visit to the state earlier this month. And in Sioux City, where 12 percent of the city’s residents are foreign-born, and in Des Moines, where thousands of demonstrators turned out at the State Capitol in the spring, and where the most recent protest, on October 17, was focused on encouraging early voting.

I first saw it for myself in late July in Guthrie Center, a town of about 1,500 people spread out along the South Raccoon River. This was the second day of RAGBRAI, the 53rd running of the Des Moines Register’s Annual Great Bicycle Ride Across Iowa. Invented by John Karras, a feature writer for the paper, and columnist Don Kaul, as a stratagem to get their employer to pay for a newsman’s holiday, the pair invited readers to join them for a weeklong bicycle jaunt across the state. Some 300 riders turned up back in 1973—of whom 114 stayed the distance.

This year there were 20,000 of us at the start in Onowa, a town that claims the widest Main Street in the country, but whose chief attraction these days is the Blackbird Bend Casino, operated by the Omaha tribe of Nebraska, and which boasts 350 electric slot machines—but no table games. After dipping our rear wheels in the waters of the Missouri River (the ceremonial start to every RAGBRAI) our route climbed over 3,500 feet, and 59.3 miles, to Harlan, where the temperature briefly hit triple digits. The road to Guthrie Center the next day brought an even greater number of hills—by the end of the day, several riders could be heard cursing whoever had assured them Iowa was flat—with the heat index reaching 110 degrees.

The Iowans on the ride were not surprised; indeed, many wore jerseys with the slogan “Iowa: Flat as a waffle.” But after pedaling under the blazing sun for hours between cornfields on one side of the road and soybeans on the other, without a stick of shade between them, it was a great relief to come into the shade and think about politics. The topic would have been on my mind anyway—I’d been given my first lessons in prairie populism by David Leshtz and Jeffrey Cox, co-editors of The Prairie Progressive, back in 2015 when the two of them were all in for Bernie Sanders. Jeff died in 2020, but Dave keeps up the fight, and it was partly his influence that made me say yes when a Vermont friend asked me if I’d ride RAGRAI with him. But I’d also brought along a native informant from Brooklyn.

I met Peter Hedges because we shared a physical therapist in Cobble Hill, and after weeks of groaning side by side every Thursday, we began to talk and discovered a shared passion for movies and left politics. Peter is a playwright and screenwriter by trade; when I asked him if he’d written anything I might have seen, he said “I wrote the screenplay for What’s Eating Gilbert Grape.” Turns out he wrote the novel, too. Peter was born and raised in West Des Moines, where he graduated from Valley High School. And that’s where the story gets interesting.

Because it turns out that Ashley Hinson, the Trump-endorsed candidate to replace retiring MAGA loyalist Joni Ernst, is also a graduate of Valley High. Back in the spring, a bipartisan group of Hinson’s former teachers joined with Valley High alumni to form Iowans for Decency, a PAC dedicated to marshaling local grassroots opposition to the Republican’s campaign—months before Josh Turek had even secured the Democratic nomination. Peter was already deeply involved, so when I asked him if he might want to come along on RAGBRAI, I didn’t have to twist his arm. “My brother rode RAGBRAI, and my cousin, and I always wanted to do it. But I never did.”

What I was thinking about in Guthrie Center—once my brain stopped boiling—and kept thinking about all the way to the finish line in Dubuque, was the way his fellow Iowans responded to Peter, who wore an “Iowans for Decency” jersey during the daytime, and a “What’s Eating Iowans?” purple T-shirt in the evening, when he’d turn up at the local high school to talk to the theater kids, or at the town library for the Iowans for Decency Listening Tour.

It wasn’t the issues that were surprising: the devastating effect of Trump’s tariffs on farm incomes, the price of gas and diesel, fear for their sons and daughters sent to fight Trump’s wars of choice, or the way, thanks to Big Ag dumping chemicals into the water table, Iowa has seen a sharp rise in cancer diagnoses (even while rates keep falling elsewhere in the country). What I kept hearing, and seeing, was some kind of limit being reached. It wasn’t exactly a prairie fire of populist enthusiasm—though Turek, who was politicized by his experience as a person with spina bifida navigating the American healthcare system, does describe himself as a “prairie populist.” (Sand, the Democratic nominee for governor, describes his politics as “radical centrist populism.”)

But then, in a state that sent Tom Harkin to the House for five terms and then to the Senate for five more terms, the Democratic Party brand is still sufficiently toxic for Sand’s yard signs to use green and orange rather than blue; I saw hundreds of them as I rode east across the state, without any idea which party the candidate was in.

So while Iowa may lack the high-stakes ideological drama of Abdul El-Sayed’s race in Michigan, or the presidential potential of Jon Ossoff’s expected triumph in Georgia, I’m going to be keeping my eyes on Iowa, where with a little bit of luck—and a ton of grassroots organizing—decency has a fighting chance.

D.D. Guttenplan is a special correspondent for The Nation and the former host of The Nation Podcast. He served as editor of the magazine from 2019 to 2025 and, prior to that, as an editor at large and London correspondent. His books include American Radical: The Life and Times of I.F. Stone, The Nation: A Biography, and The Next Republic: The Rise of a New Radical Majority.

https://www.propublica.org/article/plast.title: “Peak Greenwashing”: Two Bills in Congress Endorse Misleading Recycling Claims
https://www.propublica.org/article/plast.author: Lisa Song
https://www.propublica.org/article/plast.text:
The plastics industry spent decades convincing consumers that throwing used products stamped with the “chasing arrows” symbol into a curbside bin meant they would be recycled.
Now, amid growing awareness that many of those items never get reprocessed, the industry is championing a pair of proposals in Congress that would give misleading recycling claims the support of federal law.
On the surface, the two bipartisan House bills promise transparency for consumers by establishing national standards for recycling and recycled content labels.
But the legislation — promoted by oil, chemical and packaging companies that spend millions of dollars lobbying Congress each year — would forbid states from setting stricter requirements. That would neutralize efforts like California’s “truth in labeling” law, which bans the chasing arrow symbol on plastic products that contain toxic chemicals or that can’t realistically be recycled.
One of the measures would endorse a controversial form of “mass balance” accounting that allows companies to claim a product contains recycled content when virtually none of it came from reprocessed plastic. Two years ago, a ProPublica investigation exposed the misleading, mathematical sleight of hand used in that type of mass balance, which the Biden administration subsequently prohibited for specific products.
Both bills, which have gained momentum and could face a full House vote after the midterm elections, “are peak greenwashing,” Rachel Fullmer, a staff attorney on toxics and environmental health at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said in an email. They “champion deceptive, anti-consumer policies which would result in an increase in plastic production and plastic waste incineration, all while hiding behind the false brand of ‘recycling.’”
Experts say the best solution to the plastics crisis wreaking havoc on human health and the environment is to make and use less of the material; recycling remains a marginal solution at best.
The bills tackle a growing threat to the industry, as several states have proposed or passed laws that require manufacturers to more honestly acknowledge the challenges of recycling plastic. Those measures could force companies to spend money changing their packaging or labels.
The Consumer Brands Association, which represents the packaged goods industry including Amazon, PepsiCo and Land O’Lakes, praised the House bills.
These proposals “work in tandem to reduce consumer confusion and plastic waste while providing much-needed clarity to support new domestic innovations and investments,” the organization wrote to the leaders of the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July. They “demonstrate that consumer protection and recycling-focused efforts go hand-in-hand with promoting affordability and manufacturing investments, and we strongly encourage your support for both bills.”
The association spent $2.4 million in the first half of 2026 lobbying on these bills and other issues, according to data from OpenSecrets. In September, the two recycling bills cleared the House committee.
Five Democratic House members, including three from Texas, are among the 13 co-sponsors of the bill that endorses mass balance accounting. The other has 19 co-sponsors, including one Democrat.
A few weeks ago, Sen. John Curtis, a Utah Republican, introduced the mass balance bill in the Senate; it currently has no other co-sponsors.
Sheen of Recyclability
Consumers have long been confused by the chasing arrows symbol on many plastic containers. The label was created in 1970 to encourage paper recycling. The plastics industry began placing it on its products in the 1980s to quell public outrage over plastic pollution.
The symbol gave plastic the sheen of recyclability, even though most items cannot be reprocessed due to economic or technical barriers. The Environmental Protection Agency estimated that 8.7% of U.S. plastic waste was recycled in 2018; the rest ended up in landfills or was incinerated. In 2019, the Department of Energy estimated the national plastic recycling rate at 5%.
In recent years, the plastics industry has touted the promise of chemical recycling, a set of costly, often polluting technologies that break plastic into its molecular building blocks. Theoretically, these processes could take the most stubborn, unrecyclable plastics, like grocery store bags or string cheese wrappers, and rebuild them into new products.
That rarely happens.
Take ExxonMobil’s chemical recycling plant in Baytown, Texas. It uses oil refinery equipment to heat up the plastic and transform it into different chemical compounds.
Lee Zeldin, the EPA administrator, visited the Baytown plant last year. He later appeared in a promotional video, calling the facility a “proof of concept” for chemical recycling that could inspire “this entire country.”
But only 8% of the plastic waste processed by ExxonMobil gets transformed into new plastic, according to the California attorney general’s office, which sued the company in 2024 over “deceptively” promoting chemical recycling as an environmental solution. The other 92% mostly becomes fuel, which is burned rather than made into plastic products.
Citing internal company records, the lawsuit states that the recycled plastic is so heavily diluted with new plastic, the resulting products contain less than 0.1% recycled content.
In response, the company said in a court filing that while the state of California may not believe ExxonMobil’s recycling technologies are sufficient to solve the plastic waste crisis, “ExxonMobil did not assume liability for global pollution by innovating solutions to the problem.”
The company has marketed its chemically recycled products as containing “30% ISCC PLUS certified-circular” content, a technical term that could easily be misinterpreted as meaning 30% recycled material. That label is possible through a specific type of mass balance, which allows companies to claim credit in a new plastic product for the recycled molecules going into other things made in the chemical recycling process. Manufacturers can inflate the reported recycledness, or “circularity,” of the more lucrative products like plastic, while reducing the advertised recycled content of less valuable products.
The Recycled Materials Attribution Act, introduced by Rep. Nick Langworthy, a New York Republican, would require the Federal Trade Commission to edit the Green Guides — advertising guidelines designed to prevent greenwashing — so mass balance is recognized as “an acceptable method for substantiating recycled content claims.”
It would bypass the FTC’s own process for revising the Green Guides, which began several years ago. The agency had collected more than 1,000 public comments, including ones on whether limits should be placed on mass balance.
The bill also prevents states from adopting stricter laws on mass balance.
The Recycling Leadership Council is an industry consortium supporting Langworthy’s bill. The consortium quoted Langworthy in its February press release, touting the legislation as modernizing recycling guidelines “with a uniform national standard that protects consumers from misleading claims while giving American manufacturers the certainty they need to invest, innovate, and compete.”
In the first half of this year, the council spent $120,000 lobbying for Langworthy’s bill and related issues, including “advanced recycling” — the industry’s preferred term for chemical recycling.
“Advanced recycling technologies offer an important opportunity to keep more plastic waste out of landfills,” John Hewitt, spokesperson for the Recycling Leadership Council, said in an email.
Hewitt, who also represents the Consumer Brands Association, cited a report from a center-left think tank, which concluded that investing in chemical recycling could more than double the U.S. plastic recycling rate.
Hewitt also defended the bill’s endorsement of mass balance, which “is an established method for tracking recycled materials through complex manufacturing processes, allowing companies to incorporate more recycled content into products.”
Chemical recycling has struggled to operate at scale. If the mass balance bill passes, it could help ExxonMobil and other companies grow their business, as consumers are willing to pay a premium for sustainable products.
ExxonMobil spent more than $5 million in the first half of 2026 lobbying on the mass balance bill and many other energy or environmental issues. The company didn’t return requests for comment.
Langworthy’s campaign committee received $157,000 from the energy sector in the 2026 election cycle, including oil and gas producers and chemical companies. He did not respond to requests for comment.
Bound for a Landfill
The other bill, the Packaging and Claims Knowledge (PACK) Act, would regulate which items can be marketed as recyclable, compostable or reusable. Consumer product packaging could only be stamped with the chasing arrows recycling symbol if at least 60% of consumers have access to recycling programs that accept the product. The item must also be technically recyclable, meaning it “can be” reprocessed into a new product — but there’s no requirement to show it’s economically feasible to do so.
Recycling programs sometimes accept plastic products even when there’s no affordable way to ship them to a factory that will make them into something new; as a result, plastic that’s been collected for recycling ends up in a landfill or incinerator.
Products not meeting the 60% criteria must include qualifying language, such as “check locally” to see if it’s accepted for recycling.
The bill, introduced by Rep. Randy Weber, a Texas Republican, targets states like California that have stronger requirements for the chasing arrows symbol. A recent California law requires 60% of Californians to have access to facilities that routinely collect, sort and sell the products for reprocessing. In addition, products will be disqualified if they have inks or labels that prevent recycling, or if they contain certain levels of heavy metals and the “forever chemicals” known as PFAS, some of which are carcinogenic.
When Weber introduced the bill last December, his press release called out California’s law: “Packaging and labeling standards in the United States are increasingly influenced by state-level regulations, particularly those adopted in California.”
“The PACK Act cuts through that confusion,” he said in the press release. “It’s pro-environment, pro-business, and rooted in common sense.”
Weber did not return calls for comment. His campaign committee has received $206,000 from the energy sector and chemical companies during the 2026 election cycle.
The bill provides little detail about who will make the crucial decisions on which products qualify or what data will be used.
But at least some power will be given to unspecified “accredited third-party certification” groups, which will certify every product’s recyclability claim. These nominally independent organizations provide sustainability labels for various companies.
One example of such a group is How2Recycle, which provides recycling labels — for a fee — to companies. The labels are meant to erase consumer confusion, by instructing them to “empty and replace cap” before recycling a particular kind of bottle, for instance.
These third-party groups are supposed to be independent, but they’re easily captured by industry interests, said Kate O’Neill, an environmental science professor at the University of California-Berkeley who specializes in the politics of recycling.
How2Recycle’s parent organization, the Sustainable Packaging Coalition, has a membership dominated by retailers, brands and packaging companies. Members include Google, Chobani, 3M, Clorox and Lego. (The EPA and United States Postal Service are also members.) Several years ago, How2Recycle made the questionable claim that No. 5 plastics, used in yogurt tubs, were widely accepted for recycling.
How2Recycle and the Sustainable Packaging Coalition didn’t return requests for comment before publication.
California’s law is under a preliminary injunction due to a lawsuit from food producers and packaging companies. However, consumers can still bring private lawsuits if they suspect companies of falsely using the recycling symbol on their products, Lynn Dyer, president of the packaging trade group Ameripen, said in an email.
“AMERIPEN recognized early that differing state rules could make it harder for businesses to explain how consumers should handle packaging after use,” Dyer said. So Ameripen brought together a coalition and “helped make the case to Congress,” resulting in Weber’s bill. The group has “been engaged in discussions with congressional staff from the outset, have closely followed the bill’s development, and draw on the experience of organizations across the packaging value chain.”
In July, Ameripen urged manufacturers, retailers and brands to tell their members of Congress to back the bill. Ameripen spent $160,000 lobbying for the legislation and other environmental issues from January to June 2026.
ProPublica reached out to every co-sponsor of the House bills. Rep. Earl L. “Buddy” Carter, a Republican from Georgia who supports the PACK Act, was the only lawmaker who responded.
“American consumers deserve clear, consistent, and reliable information about the products they purchase, and our manufacturers deserve a predictable set of rules to follow,” Carter said in a statement. “The PACK Act is about establishing a uniform national standard that eliminates confusion, supports American manufacturing, and provides greater certainty for businesses and consumers alike. We can promote responsible recycling practices without forcing American businesses to navigate a patchwork of conflicting state regulations.”
The co-sponsors of the Packaging and Claims Knowledge (PACK) Act are:

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/demo.title: If Democrats Win, Thank the Left
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/demo.author: Jessica Washington, Noah Hurowitz, Akela Lacy, Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/demo.text:
Democrats are on the verge of reversing their political fortunes. The party is heading into the midterm elections Tuesday under the kind of conditions campaign consultants dream of, after two years wielding hardly more power than a strongly worded letter.
Donald Trump has spent the erratic waning years of his presidency leading his party into a political wilderness by waging a deeply unpopular war on Iran and driving the cost of living ever higher. Republicans who enjoy a governing trifecta have tried to distance themselves from the party’s decision-making and its leader, a once-animating force who has turned himself into a liability. Poll after poll says the same: Democrats are poised to take control of one or both houses of Congress — and spend the next two years thwarting Trump’s agenda.
But after a primary season dominated by an ascendant left wing and a broader rejection of centrist politics, the question isn’t just whether Democrats win on Tuesday. It’s what kind of Democratic Party emerges on Wednesday morning.
“I really like the socialism aspects,” said Gibrel Said, a supporter of Abdul El-Sayed at his closing rally in Detroit Monday night. In the marquee contest serving as a referendum on the Democratic Party’s future, the Michigan Democratic Senate nominee espouses progressive politics and has often been associated with the the left’s agenda-setting socialists, though he doesn’t identify as one. His race has been rocked by the kind of left-versus-right identity crisis that presents a perennial challenge for Democrats.
“One, Medicare for All; two, how do we fund things that help us as constituents,” Said told The Intercept, ticking off things he appreciates about the candidate. Said, who lives in the Arab enclave of Dearborn, Michigan, especially praised El-Sayed’s willingness to buck party leadership and speak out on U.S.–Israel policy. “Instead of tiptoeing around the subject, he very adamantly says, hey there’s a genocide happening here, we shouldn’t send our money.”
Cycle after cycle, in state after state, an insurgent band of Democrats critical of the political establishment’s ties to corporate interests and its unflinching commitment to Israel has had to overcome the barriers erected by its own party’s centrist leadership. Both sides present themselves as the true representatives of working people: the centrists by arguing that more transformative ideas will scare off lower-information voters, the left by saying they represent the masses.
How much of this trickles down to actual voters? On Monday, The Intercept followed canvassers and spoke to voters in Michigan, Maine, and Texas, asking about which issues had permeated and taking the temperature of voter enthusiasm. Some rolled their eyes at the spats that have dominated the headlines, dismissing the idea that eleventh-hour backstabbing would make a difference. Others regurgitated right-wing misinformation. Many complained of too many campaign mailers.
“They’re wicked mean,” said Sharon McDonnell, a supporter of Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine. Speaking to The Intercept in the town of Yarmouth, she described one mailer that included a photo of Jackson chomping a cigar and describing him as “evil.” “It’s just nasty.”
In Maine, the party’s left flank seized power in the nominating process for the Democratic Senate candidate — then fought to hang onto it after onetime rising star Graham Platner flamed out after a sexual assault allegation (which he denies). With Jackson, a former state Senate leader, Maine now offers progressives one of two opportunities to test their message at the Senate level, where a candidate has to secure appeal statewide, not just in deep-blue House districts.
The other is Michigan, where the intraparty battle is still raging. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., demolished her past attempts at fence-mending when she endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday and abandoned El-Sayed, who beat Stevens in a Michigan primary that saw $30 million in outside spending from the super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
The dustup has had Democrats biting their nails and moderate party leaders making the cable news circuit to demand party discipline — this time, to scold a centrist. The party leads in the polls for 218 of the 435 seats up for grabs in the House of Representatives, but they need to perform well in seven key states — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas, in addition to Maine and Michigan — if they want to win the Senate.
“I think she’s counterintuitively, perhaps, given people a reason to rally some more,” said Kathleen Britton, an El-Sayed supporter at the Detroit rally on Monday, of Stevens. “I really don’t think it’s gonna help Mike Rogers.”
Earlier that day, in a predominantly Black neighborhood of Detroit, a prominent Black supporter of El-Sayed preparing to knock on voters’ doors described Stevens’s endorsement as an “ego-driven statement.”
Mike Bland, the executive director of the Black Men Vote PAC, highlighted that Stevens made her public endorsement of Rogers in a Black church in Detroit. He doubted that Stevens, whose criticism of El-Sayed centers primarily on his skepticism of the U.S. relationship with the state of Israel, would be able to pull Black voters to Rogers, a conservative former House representative whose campaign has repeatedly peddled anti-Muslim tropes against El-Sayed.
“How can I say this without cursing? She used a Black church as a prop, and we have seen that time and time again,” Bland said. “Black folks aren’t stupid.”
Over the past month, El-Sayed has rallied with Barack Obama and Kamala Harris, the two most prominent Black politicians in America — and hardly radicals estranged from the establishment power center. At the same time that Stevens was making her endorsement of Rogers public, El-Sayed was attending a get-out-the-vote event at another church in Detroit. The two primary foes were supposed to appear together that day with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C.
One of the Democrats’ most coveted Senate pickups didn’t present much of an opportunity for the left in the primary, but it has still been characterized by intraparty animosity.
In Texas, where both Democratic Senate primary contenders espoused relatively moderate politics, outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, has declined to campaign with state Rep. James Talarico, though she endorsed him after he beat her in the state’s March Democratic primary.
Talarico has been performing well with Latino voters, a massive voting bloc that helped fuel his primary victory. But Crockett — who, unlike Stevens, is Black — has suggested that Talarico has not done enough to excite Black voters, a demographic she carried in the primary. On a canvassing operation targeting Black voters in the Dallas–Fort Worth area on Monday, few Black Texans who spoke to The Intercept expressed excitement for Talarico. But most had already voted for him, saying they were motivated to do their civic duty.
Black voters frequently discussed concerns over affordability, gas prices, and homelessness. Canvassers told The Intercept they had heard some of those voters express concerns over their perception of Talarico’s policies toward transgender children, at times espousing blatant misinformation, such as the idea that Talarico supported arresting parents who refused to give their children gender-affirming surgeries.
“ I don’t stand for that,” said voter Jermiah Robinson, referring to her belief that Talarico pushed “sex-change” surgery for minors. Like many voters, she cited the cost of living as her most pressing issue. Robinson said she would “want to vote for him if he stands by his words, and he’s actually like ‘Yeah, I’ll help out as far as prices and everything.’”
Talarico appears to have improved his margins with Black voters in the final stretch. According to the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas, Talarico is leading with 79 percent of the Black vote, signaling a significant increase in support from Black voters from just last month. The conventional wisdom suggests that he could barely ask for a better opponent than the scandal-plagued Republican candidate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
In 2015, Paxton was indicted on felony securities fraud charges in Texas, in a case that dragged on for roughly nine years, and ended with Paxton being required to do community service and pay restitution. And in 2023, the Texas House of Representatives voted across party lines to impeach him as attorney general for alleged corruption and retaliation against whistleblowers.
Scandal kept rocking the race for Senate in Maine, where longtime Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins faces her toughest reelection challenge yet from Jackson. Before Jackson, who lost a race this cycle for the state’s Democratic nomination for governor, there was Platner, hailed early as a working-class champion who faced a series of personal scandals in his successful primary campaign. There was the revelation of a Nazi tattoo that he claimed not to understand until last October. There were crudely worded Reddit posts and stories of cruelty from women he’d dated. One former girlfriend’s allegations of sexual assault ultimately ended his campaign — and set off a scramble to find a replacement that progressives ultimately won by elevating Jackson.
By Monday, Mainers who spoke to The Intercept appeared exhausted by the lengthy, contentious, and expensive Senate race that has dominated the state.
“There’s a lot of fatigue. People are tired of it,“ said Charlie Dingman, who chairs the state Democratic Party. “I have had some conversations at doors with people that have led me to think that the extremely negative and extremely untruthful ads may be backfiring.”
Tyler Echard, in Norway, said he’d already cast an absentee ballot for Democrats down the ticket. He was disgusted with a deluge of political mailers and eager to stop seeing them pile up on his doorstep.
“The amount of mailers we get — just mailers, not just handed at the door but in the mail — especially from the Republican side, the amount of money is probably more than I will make in my lifetime, spent in this election,” Echard said. “At some point, we gotta get legislation because money’s just gonna run everything into the ground. I ain’t got it, so I can’t influence it.”
Frustration with the status quo in Congress could spell the end for Collins’s 30-year career in the Senate. On Monday, a University of New Hampshire poll found Jackson leading Collins by 4 percentage points. And in September, Collins found herself thrust into a scandal of her own, when ProPublica revealed that the FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating an alleged pay-to-play scheme between Collins and a donor eager to secure government contracts.
The Intercept later exposed that, alongside a series of campaign donations, defense contractors cozy with Collins had received lucrative carveouts in defense spending. (Collins has denied wrongdoing in all cases.)
But the incumbent senator has faced controversy and come out victorious before. And some Mainers doubt they’ll see change either way.
“I can’t vote for either side,” said a man, who declined to share his name with The Intercept, walking down a rural road in Norway with a hunting rifle slung over his shoulder. “You can’t trust neither of them.”
Noah Hurowitz reported from Yarmouth and Norway, Maine; Akela Lacy reported from Fort Worth, Texas; Matt Sledge reported from Detroit, Michigan.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
