https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
WTA apologises to Pegula for broadcast of ‘diva’ comment about Andreeva
Pegula’s conversation with her coach on a practice court at Indian Wells was broadcast on a WTA YouTube livestream.
Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) chief Valerie Camillo apologised after a courtside microphone captured United States star Jessica Pegula making disparaging comments about rival Mirra Andreeva.
Pegula was plunged into controversy after her conversation with coach Mark Knowles on a practice court at Indian Wells in California was broadcast on a WTA YouTube livestream of the session.
In the exchange, Pegula can be heard describing 19-year-old Russian Andreeva as a “diva”.
World number four Pegula was also heard criticising Andreeva’s coach, former Wimbledon champion Conchita Martinez, for not addressing French Open champion Andreeva’s behaviour.
Speaking before Sunday’s opening matches of the WTA Finals, WTA chairperson Camillo blamed the controversy on “several breakdowns in our execution of the livestream given our own policies and procedures”.
“I want to apologise on behalf of the entire WTA for these occurrences,” Camillo said at a news conference on Friday.
“The WTA is sensitive to player privacy and has policies and procedures in place to balance players’ needs for safe spaces with opportunities to bring fans closer to the game.
“There was a lack of advanced notice and clear signage to assist players about the recording equipment operating in the area,” she added, confirming that all audio recording equipment in practice areas had since been removed.
Camillo said microphones had been installed on practice courts to pick up “ambient sound” – such as the noise of balls being struck – rather than conversations between players and coaches.
“So clearly there was a failure in our technical execution and monitoring,” Camillo said, before directly apologising to Pegula and Knowles.
“I want to specifically apologise to Jessica Pegula and Mark Knowles,” she added.
“What happened was regrettable and unacceptable. Jess is one of the WTA’s best advocates and biggest stars. She does not deserve this distraction.”
The WTA Finals begin on Sunday, with the top eight women’s singles players divided into two round-robin groups of four before advancing to the knockout rounds.

'It would facilitate Gaza genocide': Protesters storm Microsoft planned site
Several hundred activists occupied the construction site of a planned Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam on Friday, protesting the technology giant's alleged role in facilitating Israel's genocide in Gaza, as well as the environmental impact of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The demonstration, organised by climate and justice collective Geef Tegengas and environmental group Fossielvrij, halted construction work for the day in the city's Sloterdijk district.
The protesters argued that the facility could be used to support AI-powered warfare and Israel's military operations in Gaza.
"It's so many things, so many struggles that come together in this data centre," Nathan Timmer, a spokesman for Geef Tegengas, told AFP.
Timmer, 30, accused the project of helping to facilitate "AI warfare" and what he described as the "genocide" in Gaza.
Dutch news agency ANP reported that police arrested between 150 and 200 protesters, while others left voluntarily.
The protest was part of a wider two-day mobilisation across Europe called by the Stop Dirty Data Centers coalition, which is demanding a pause in the construction of new data centre facilities.
Report by AFP

https://taz.de/Wohnungslosigkeit-in-der-.title: Wohnungslosigkeit in der Hauptstadt: Wenn es dunkel und kalt wird in Berlin
https://taz.de/Wohnungslosigkeit-in-der-.author: Ali Çelikkan
https://taz.de/Wohnungslosigkeit-in-der-.text:
Wohnungslosigkeit in der Hauptstadt: Wenn es dunkel und kalt wird in Berlin
Frank-Walter Steinmeier promovierte zu Wohnungslosigkeit. Heute leben mehr als 6.000 Menschen auf Berlins Straßen. Eine Begegnung mit einem von ihnen.
D er Winter kommt bald. Zwischen den Blättern, die mit einer kaum wahrnehmbaren Traurigkeit zu Boden gefallen sind, liegen einzelne Handschuhe, die gleich beim ersten Tragen verloren gingen. Mit sinkenden Temperaturen verlassen die Berliner*innen nach und nach die Stadt.
Kolumne Keep me updated
Vor zehn Jahren, als Ali Celikkan als junger Journalist aus der Türkei gerade in Berlin angekommen war, traf er Frank-Walter Steinmeier unerwartet im Parlament. Ganz beiläufig und ohne Kontext sagte er einen einzigen Satz zu ihm: „Keep me updated.“ Seitdem ist viel passiert. Diese Kolumne ist sein lang ersehntes Update, über all jenes, das er (als Bundespräsident) sonst verpasst. Alle Texte dieser Kolumne finden Sie hier.
Manche vermieten ihre Wohnungen mit Aufschlag an Neuankömmlinge und überwintern in Mexiko. Für alle, die sich nicht längst auf Weihnachten freuen, wird nun alles schwieriger. Besonders für diejenigen, die keinen Wohnraum haben, den sie untervermieten oder selbst bewohnen können. Diejenigen, die aus den U-Bahn-Stationen vertrieben wurden, suchen Zuflucht in Kellern, Treppenhäusern oder Schrottautos.
In den vergangenen 15 Jahren ist die Zahl der Wohnungslosen in Berlin auf rund 57.000 gestiegen – mehr als die Zahl der in Kreuzberg lebenden Türk*innen. Sie schlafen in befristeten Notunterkünften. Über 6.000 leben inzwischen ganz ohne Unterkunft auf der Straße.
Herr Bundespräsident, ich habe gelesen, dass Sie Ihre Doktorarbeit zum Thema Wohnungslosigkeit in Gießen verfasst haben. Ich bin sicher, dass die Arbeit nicht plagiiert war. Und bestimmt beschäftigen Sie sich auf eine Art mit wohnungslosen Menschen. Denn sonst hätten Sie bei einer Preisverleihung in Berlin im September nicht gesagt: „Nicht über wohnungslose Menschen reden, sondern mit ihnen.“ Das sehe ich auch so.
Nach einem Unfall wurde er obdachlos
Dennoch kann ich mir nicht vorstellen, dass Sie, wenn Sie mit der U-Bahn fahren würden, nicht hastig in den nächsten Wagen flüchten würden, wenn eine wohnungslose Person einsteigt und plötzlich ein Geruch aufkommt. So machen es viele, als könnten sie darüber hinwegspringen wie über eine Pfütze. Weil das Leid zu groß ist, können wir nicht direkt hinsehen. So war es auch, als ich eines Tages auf Nikolais verrottenden Finger blickte.
Nikolai hat hellbraunes Haar, einen vollen Bart, halb geschlossene Augen und Zähne, die ihre besten Tage hinter sich haben. Jeden Tag trägt er andere bunte Kleidung. Manchmal schlägt er mit einem Stock gegen alles, was ihm in die Quere kommt. Manchmal läuft er den Jogger*innen im Görlitzer Park hinterher oder treibt Mütter mit Kinderwagen dazu, ihre Entscheidung, noch immer in Kreuzberg zu wohnen, zu bereuen. Manche Ladenbesitzer halten ihn für abhängig von Feuerzeuggas, weil er in zahlreichen Kiosken Feuerzeuge gestohlen hat. Dabei ist Nikolai cracksüchtig.
Wenn er auf Entzug ist, dauert es nicht lange: zehn Euro zusammenkratzen, zum Park bringen, einen Zug nehmen – und das zehn Minuten später von vorne. Mit schnellen, kurzen Schritten marschiert er dann die Oranienstraße entlang. Nikolai hat nicht immer so gelebt. Früher, erzählt er mir, war er alkoholabhängig. Von Estland nach Finnland, von Karlsruhe nach Berlin. Dann hatte er einen trunkenen Unfall, der seinen Körper in unbeschreibliche Schmerzen stürzte. Danach schwor er, dass er nie wieder trinken würde. Er hat sein Wort gehalten.
Nikolai sagt, er sei die Kälte aus Estland gewohnt. Doch im Winter auf der Straße zu leben, ist nicht dasselbe, wie im Sommer im Schatten eines Baumes auf der Naunynstraße einzuschlafen. Jetzt trägt er einen Schlafsack auf dem Rücken, wirkt erschöpft, seine Schritte sind schwerer geworden. Man sieht ihm an, dass es ihm nicht gut geht. Vielleicht hat er längst den Punkt überschritten, an dem er seinen Schmerz noch ausdrücken oder überhaupt wahrnehmen kann. Vielleicht hat er heute einfach keine Kraft zum Reden. Trotzdem werde ich, wie von Ihnen geraten, weiterhin mit ihm sprechen. Keep you updated.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Pineapple on pizza is an insult to our great Italian cuisine – and here’s why we secretly love it  | Luca Cesari
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Luca Cesari
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
You may have smiled at the news a few days ago: the Italian chef Davide Tamburella was sacked by a Brisbane restaurant after refusing to put pineapple on a pizza. Never mind that Queensland grows almost all of Australia’s pineapples. Tamburella would not give way to his customers or his boss, insisting that the combination was an insult to Italian culture.
Strange as it may sound, he is not the first. In 2017, Maurizio Landi, a chef from Bologna, was sacked by a bistro near Lyon after resisting pressure to cook his pasta for longer and to serve spaghetti bolognese, a dish that does not exist in his home town. For anyone who doesn’t know, Bologna is the only city in the world where ragù is eaten solely with tagliatelle, and putting it on spaghetti borders on an outrage.
Why would Italians rather lose their jobs than question their culinary certainties? The answer lies somewhere between anthropology and history. Food fashions are changing faster than ever. There are more chefs on television than grandmothers cooking at home, and Italians can sense the dangers hanging over their beloved cuisine.
It is a bit as if Renaissance paintings were crumbling before our eyes while we stand by, powerless. Yet there is one crucial difference between the Sistine Chapel and a pizza. Michelangelo’s frescoes have looked the same for half a millennium, whereas a pizza from a century ago was nothing like the one we eat today.
Some of the most glaring sins against Italian recipes are simply old ways of eating that Italians themselves no longer recognise. Overcooked pasta and pasta as a side dish are two of them. Leaf through old recipe books and you will find that pasta was eaten soft for centuries, while macaroni with cheese was served alongside meat dishes from the middle ages onwards.
But it takes far less to drive an Italian mad. One spoonful of cream in a carbonara is enough to get you thrown out of the country. A pity, then, that this too is an old habit, introduced in the 1960s by a few Roman cooks and kept up for at least 40 years, a small detail everyone seems to have forgotten.
Then there is grated cheese on pasta with fish, an outrage to many Italians, who stand ready to scientifically prove that cheese ruins the taste of fish, while forgetting such ultra-traditional pasta dishes as mussels with pecorino.
No list of extreme pairings would be complete without the cappuccino, which foreigners order at the end of a meal under the horrified gaze of the waiters. Ask for a caffè macchiato, which is a cappuccino in miniature, and nobody bats an eyelid. Not all Italians are so rigid, and even pineapple on pizza has its admirers among the great pizza makers.
A few years ago, Gino Sorbillo, one of the world’s most respected pizzaioli, opened the door to it, though only on a white pizza with no tomato, which would otherwise make it too acidic. Franco Pepe, considered by many the best pizza maker in the world, came up with the AnaNascosta (“hidden pineapple”), a cone of pizza filled with pineapple, San Daniele ham and Grana Padano fondue, making the heretical match respectable. And this summer, Berberè, a pizzeria chain with five sites in London, launched a pizza with a spiced pineapple sauce, to break with the prejudice once and for all.
Pineapple is only the latest blasphemy to land on a pizza. An article headlined “Neapolitan pizza”, in the Morning Post of 17 December 1860, reads: “There are other modes of preparing the pizza, by the substitution of freshly-caught anchovies, or slices of sausage, or mushrooms for the cream and grated cheese; but the highest authorities on these points treat with disdain all such modern innovations, and protest that a pizza compounded after that fashion has no right to the name at all.”
The toppings change, but the “authorities” will always have something to say about what can go on a pizza. It is hard to see why all the hatred should fall on pineapple, when Italian pizzerias offer frankfurters and chips, speck and mascarpone, tuna and onion, and the traditional pizza of Pesaro, in the Marche region, is a margherita with hard-boiled eggs and mayonnaise.
The truth is that we Italians don’t need pineapple pizza to eat. We need it to despise. It stands for everything we fight against to keep our traditions intact, and loathing it makes us feel like better people, on the right side of the barricade.
- Luca Cesari is a food historian and the author of The History of Pizza

https://taz.de/Todesstrafe-in-den-USA/!6.title: Todesstrafe in den USA: Kalifornien wandelt alle Todesurteile in Haftstrafen um
https://taz.de/Todesstrafe-in-den-USA/!6.text:
Todesstrafe in den USA: Kalifornien wandelt alle Todesurteile in Haftstrafen um
Der scheidende kalifornische Gouverneur Gavin Newsom macht von seinem Gnadenrecht Gebrauch. Am gleichen Tag wurden in den USA drei Todesurteile vollstreckt.
afp/ap | Der US-Bundesstaat Kalifornien wandelt insgesamt 548 Todesurteile in lebenslange Haftstrafen um. Der scheidende demokratische Gouverneur Gavin Newsom erklärte am Donnerstag, er übe damit sein verfassungsmäßiges Gnadenrecht aus. Newsom kommt damit einem Appell von Amnesty International und anderen Organisationen nach, vor Ende seiner Amtszeit Anfang Januar ein Zeichen gegen die Todesstrafe zu setzen.
Kalifornien vollstreckt die Todesstrafe bereits seit 20 Jahren nicht mehr, der Schritt gilt deshalb als symbolisch. Allerdings ist die Entscheidung Newsoms auch ein politisches Signal an Präsident Donald Trump, der ein Verfechter der Todesstrafe ist. Der 59-jährige Newsom gilt als möglicher Bewerber um die Präsidentschaftskandidatur der Demokraten im Jahr 2028.
In einem Brief „an alle Kalifornierinnen und Kalifornier“ schrieb Newsom: „Meine heutige Entscheidung erfolgt nach fast drei Jahrzehnten, in denen ich als gewählter Amtsträger offen gegen staatlich gebilligte Hinrichtungen Stellung bezogen habe.“ Er sei überzeugt, dass eine Gesellschaft ohne „staatlich sanktioniertes Töten“ stärker sei. Die betroffenen Häftlinge haben demnach keine Möglichkeit zur Berufung gegen ihre Haftstrafen.
Drei Hinrichtungen an einem Tag in den USA
Derweil sind in den USA am Donnerstag (Ortszeit) in drei Bundesstaaten insgesamt drei Menschen hingerichtet worden. Florida vollstreckte dabei zum 19. Mal in diesem Jahr ein Todesurteil. Damit erreichte der Bundesstaat erneut die Zahl des Vorjahres, als ebenfalls 19 Hinrichtungen vollstreckt worden waren. Auch in Alabama und Indiana wurden Todesurteile vollstreckt. Seit August war es damit das zweite Mal, dass in drei Bundesstaaten am selben Tag Menschen hingerichtet wurden. Dennoch bleibt dies ungewöhnlich. Zuvor hatte es einen solchen Fall zuletzt 2010 gegeben.
In Florida wurde der 64-jährige Jesse Guardado durch eine tödliche Injektion hingerichtet. Er war wegen des Mordes an einer 75-jährigen Frau im Jahr 2004 zum Tode verurteilt worden. Guardado hatte sein Opfer erstochen und anschließend Schmuck und Geld gestohlen. Vor seiner Hinrichtung entschuldigte er sich bei den Angehörigen der Frau und seiner eigenen Familie.
In Alabama wurde der 54-jährige Michael Taylor wegen eines Doppelmordes hingerichtet. Er hatte 1991 ein Ehepaar im Alter von 83 und 79 Jahren bei einem Raubüberfall mit einer Metallstange erschlagen. In Indiana wurde der 50-jährige Jeffrey Weisheit wegen des Mordes an zwei Kindern durch Brandstiftung hingerichtet. Er hatte 2010 das Haus seiner damaligen Freundin in Brand gesetzt, wobei deren Kinder ums Leben kamen.
In den USA hatte zuletzt der Fall der Todeskandidatin Christa Pike für Diskussionen um die Todesstrafe gesorgt. Die 50-Jährige hatte Ende September in Nashville im Bundesstaat Tennessee zwei Giftspritzen überlebt – als erster Häftling der jüngeren US-Geschichte. Pike war 1995 wegen Mordes an einer Klassenkameradin zum Tode verurteilt worden.
Befeuert wurde die Debatte zwischenzeitlich durch die Ankündigung von Verteidigungsminister Pete Hegseth, die Exekution des Attentäters Nidal Hasan durch ein Erschießungskommando im Dezember live zu übertragen. Nach massiver öffentlicher Empörung sagte Trump die Liveübertragung allerdings ab.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: The Good Daughter: Rose Byrne’s legal thriller is so full of calamity it borders on Mr Bean-like farce
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Stuart Heritage
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
At first glance, The Good Daughter (Thursday 12 November, 9pm, Sky Atlantic) should make you a little worried about Rose Byrne. Here is an actor not only at the top of her game, but quite frankly at the top of anybody’s. Her Apple TV show Platonic all but depends on her combination of emotional nuance and flawless slapstick to exist, and earlier this year she won a Golden Globe (and was nominated for an Oscar) for her wired, frayed lead performance in If I Had Legs I’d Kick You. In other words, Byrne should be able to make anything she wants.
So it’s bizarre that, of all things, she has chosen this. The Good Daughter is a paperback thriller show. It’s one of those slightly preposterous programmes about trauma where everyone somehow manages to look astonishingly beautiful all the time. It’s David E Kelley territory. It’s Harlan Coben territory. It’s Nicole Kidman in a silly wig territory.
Still, at least it delivers on the trauma front. Written by Karin Slaughter, adapting her own novel, it is one of the most hilariously frontloaded things I have ever seen. In the very first scene, two young girls witness their mother being shot in the face by masked intruders. In the second, we learn that this was a flashback remembered by Meghann Fahy (playing Byrne’s sister). In the third, Fahy accidentally walks in on a school shooting and ends up being beaten up by the police.
So dense with unpleasantries is the opening that you start to worry that The Good Daughter will end up being a sort of trauma-based Mr Bean where Fahy just blunders from catastrophe to catastrophe; maybe she’ll stand in a bear trap, then fall down some stairs while noticing a stain that reminds her of the time she watched her grandmother die. Unfortunately, this doesn’t quite turn out to be the case, but it isn’t far off.
However, once this early energy burns off, it does settle into a very good version of what it is. Fahy is a lawyer, whose father (Brendan Gleeson) is also a lawyer. In the wake of the school shooting they are joined by Byrne who, what are the chances, is also a lawyer. However, while Fahy and Gleeson are scrappy backwoods lawyers, Byrne is a rich and successful New York lawyer, as evidenced by the fact that she spends a lot of her time riding around in the back of expensive cars, zooming in and out of blueprints on an iPad, like someone from the future would.
What follows is a twisty, turny thriller about how the family managed to process the violent death of the matriarch, while realising that the shooting implicates much of the broader community. Of the two strands, the first is more successful. Fahy – the highlight of the second White Lotus season – holds up tremendously against Byrne, sharing a warm if occasionally fractious relationship.
The series is best when it drops the plot and offers them pure character beats, such as a scene where they both perform a madcap scrabble to shut a coffin lid. These are enough to make you hope that the pair continue to work together, maybe on something that’s a little more lively and requires them to gaze mournfully into the middle distance a little less.
Perhaps as a UK viewer I’m just spoilt. In terms of plot, there isn’t a lot separating The Good Daughter from something like Sherwood, which is hardly fair. But Sherwood was able to embellish its soapy dramatics with boiling hot political anger and moral outrage. This doesn’t have that. It’s primped, glossed and diluted to be palatable to the biggest possible audience.
And that might answer my first point. The Good Daughter isn’t a logical choice for a performer such as Byrne who finds herself in the middle of a hot streak. But if there is one thing Apple TV shows and critical indie hits aren’t particularly known for it’s a large viewership. If nothing else, something as slick as The Good Daughter has the potential to be the most-watched thing Rose Byrne has made in years. At this point in her career, who could deny her that?

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: ‘Every person has their luck’: Morocco’s beach metal detectorists
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
‘Every person has their luck’: Morocco’s beach metal detectorists
For many, the search is driven less by profit than by the thrill of an unexpected discovery.
Agadir, Morocco – Mustapha Harmouch moves slowly across the sand at Agadir’s Corniche, sweeping his metal detector in low, even arcs. He tunes out the surfers paddling beyond the shore, the children shrieking in the waves and the chatter of families, all his attention is on one sound: the beep that means the coil has passed over something buried beneath the sand.
For the 33-year-old content creator, that uncertainty is the whole appeal. The detector does not distinguish between treasure and rubbish, it gives the same signal whether the object below is a coin, a ring, a discarded piece of aluminium, or an old piece of fishing equipment.
“The excitement comes partly from not knowing what lies beneath the sand,” he told Al Jazeera English.
Harmouch bought a Tianxun TX 850 metal detector online about four years ago. What began as a hobby has since become an occasional part of the videos he posts on Stofishing, a YouTube travel and spearfishing channel with roughly 123,000 subscribers.
“It’s a nice hobby because it’s the kind of exploration where I find something and learn something new,” he said. “Each outing is a chance to encounter something I would otherwise never have known about.”
That curiosity has led him to old coins, including some associated with historical periods and places such as the Al Haouz region and Fez.
In the coastal town of Sidi Ouassay, about 65km south of Agadir, he says he found one of his rarest hauls: 14 Moroccan falus, old bronze or copper coins, in a single spot.
Some were too damaged by salt and the passage of time for their markings to be easily read, but Harmouch says the oldest dates to 1289 on the Hijri calendar.
For Harmouch, the coins’ value lies less in their price than in what they reveal about the past.
“I just collect them as a memory,” he said with a glint in his eye.
In the same area, he once found what he thought was a meteorite, only to learn it was a common, inexpensive mineral.
“Before asking, I thought I had found the best discovery,” he said, laughing at the memory.
That sense of possibility and adventure is what keeps him returning to the beaches around Agadir.
Harmouch goes detecting about four times a month, often with fellow members of the Moroccan Association for Research and Exploration Enthusiasts. He favours Taghazout and Agadir’s Corniche, where there is less rubbish for his detector to pick up.
The beaches have yielded jewellery, Moroccan coins and foreign currency, including a French 20-franc silver coin.
The possibility of finding something valuable is still part of the appeal. He once found a small gold ring in Taghazout.
“I always try to identify and return valuable lost items to their rightful owners,” Harmouch says.
Where the law draws the line
Morocco’s main legal framework for protecting historical monuments, archaeological sites, works of art and antiquities dates to Law 22-80, which regulates archaeological prospecting and the treatment of historical discoveries. The government has reiterated that unauthorised archaeological searches on land or at sea are prohibited.
Under the law, searches intended to uncover monuments or moveable objects of historic, archaeological, or anthropological importance require authorisation, while accidental discoveries are subject to reporting requirements.
If a non-archaeological activity uncovers monuments, coins, works of art, or antiquities, the discovery must be reported to authorities. The objects should not be damaged or moved, except where necessary to protect them.
Finding a modern coin lost by a holidaymaker is one thing; deliberately searching for archaeological material is another.
But on Morocco’s coastline, archaeologists say the context in which an object is found can be just as important as the object itself.
Underwater archaeologist Basma Oumaima explains why context matters: “Sometimes something as simple as a fragment of metal, a coin, or a small tool can become important because of where it was found and what was found around it”.
“That does not mean curiosity itself should be discouraged. Metal detectors themselves can actually be useful tools in archaeology when they are used as part of a proper archaeological survey, where every find is located, recorded and studied within its context”.
Harmouch says he respects the law. Members of the association carry identification, avoid private property and heritage sites and treat detecting as a hobby rather than a job. His source of income, he says, comes mainly from content creation and a fishing equipment store.
‘Every person has their luck’
For Mohamed Botaib, metal detecting has never been his main source of income. A former sports coach currently looking for work, he searches beaches, forests and mountains as a hobby.
His finds have been modest: ordinary coins, Moroccan dirhams and rings.
“Every person has their luck,” he said.
For Jalal Zegnoune, another detectorist, removing unwanted metal is one of the hobby’s practical sides. His detector has produced coins, jewellery, glasses and watches, along with less glamorous finds, including rusted sardine-can fragments, nails and lost fishing gear.
“I remove such objects from the beaches because some can be dangerous to beachgoers,” he said.
Zegnoune works full-time as a maintenance technician in Casablanca and goes metal detecting when he’s free or for limited hours in the evening.
“I also enjoy meeting other people who practise the hobby and sharing the objects they find.”
“When we look at the beach, it’s not to find treasure,” Botaib says. “It’s also our way of contributing to keeping our beaches clean. We collect pieces of metal and aluminium that we find and throw them away.”

https://taz.de/Kommunalwahlen-in-Suedafr.title: Kommunalwahlen in Südafrika: Historisches Debakel für den ANC
https://taz.de/Kommunalwahlen-in-Suedafr.author: Tintswalo Baloyi
https://taz.de/Kommunalwahlen-in-Suedafr.text:
Kommunalwahlen in Südafrika: Historisches Debakel für den ANC
Bei Südafrikas Kommunalwahlen schrumpft die einstige Befreiungsbewegung ANC auf ein Drittel der Stimmen. Sie könnte alle Großstadträume verlieren.
Noch sind Südafrikas Kommunalwahlen vom Mittwoch nicht komplett ausgezählt, aber schon jetzt sind die Ergebnisse für den im Land regierenden ANC (African National Congress) ein Desaster, und die älteste Befreiungsbewegung Afrikas fügt sich still in ihr Schicksal: Ihre mehr als drei Jahrzehnte Dominanz der Politik in Südafrika sind zu Ende.
Freitagvormittag, mit rund 73 Prozent der ausgezählten Stimmen, lag der ANC bei etwas über 31 Prozent landesweit, sein schlechtestes Ergebnis seit Südafrikas Demokratisierung und dem Ende der Apartheid 1994. Der ANC dürfte in allen acht Großstadtregionen die Macht verlieren, prognostiziert das respektierte Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR).
Die amtlichen Endergebnisse werden am Sonntag erwartet. Die Wahlbeteiligung ist gegenüber 2021 nach ersten Erkenntnissen deutlich gestiegen.
Der Absturz ist dramatisch. Bei Südafrikas ersten freien Kommunalwahlen 1995 errang der ANC über 58 Prozent, erst bei den letzten 2021 fiel der Stimmenanteil erstmals unter die 50-Prozent-Marke auf 45,5 Prozent. Jetzt sind es weniger als ein Drittel.
„Freiheit bedeutet das Recht, auseinanderzugehen“
ANC-Geschäftsführer Gwede Mantashe versuchte, einen zuversichtlichen Eindruck zu machen, als er am Freitag im Auszählungszentrum von Johannesburg vor die Presse trat. „Wir haben für Freiheit gekämpft“, sagte er. „Freiheit bedeutet das Recht, sich zusammenzuschließen und auseinanderzugehen. Das sehen wir jetzt.“
Eine Rekordzahl von Parteien sei bei diesen Wahlen angetreten, und dies habe zum Rückgang des ANC-Stimmenanteils geführt, so seine Analyse. „Es bedeutet, dass Leute sich nach Optionen umschauen. Manche tun es zu ihrem Vorteil. Sie haben sicher sogar in der Weltpolitik bemerkt, dass Dinge sich in die eine oder andere Richtung verändern. Wir sind keine Ausnahme.“
Der ANC zahlt mit seinen schlechten Ergebnissen den Preis für schlechte Regierungsführung. Landesweit nehmen in Südafrika Kriminalität, Korruption, Arbeitslosigkeit und Armut zu. Bei den Parlamentswahlen 2024 verlor der ANC erstmals die absolute Mehrheit und willigte in eine „Regierung der Nationalen Einheit“ mit bisherigen politischen Gegnern ein. Unter der Führung von Präsident Cyril Ramaphosa verstärken sich auch Flügelkämpfe innerhalb des ANC.
„Nach dem Verlust der Parlamentsmehrheit zeigt das kommunale Debakel, dass der Nimbus des ANC als historische Befreiungsbewegung nicht mehr ausreicht, damit frustrierte Wähler ihm einen Sieg bescheren“, analysiert der Kommentator Andile Majola.
Die liberal-weiß geprägte DA (Democratic Alliance), historisch der Hauptgegner des ANC und seit 2024 sein Hauptpartner in Südafrikas Regierungskoalition, verzeichnet deutliche Zugewinne. Sie ist nach aktuellem Stand von 21 auf 24 Prozent der Stimmen geklettert und wichtiger noch: In den meisten der acht Großstadtregionen kommt sie auf den ersten Platz.
„Dies ist ein guter Tag für Südafrika“, sagte DA-Chef Geordin Hill-Lewis am Freitag. „Das südafrikanische Volk hat uns die historische Chance gegeben, in vielen Städten eine Wende herbeizuführen. Wir müssen sie ergreifen.“
Erfolge verzeichnet auch die ANC-Abspaltung MK (Umkhonto weSizwe), die Südafrikas Expräsident Jacob Zuma vor den Wahlen 2024 gegründet hatte und die nun erstmals zu Kommunalwahlen antrat. Mit über 9 Prozent behält sie den dritten Platz hinter ANC und DA, den sie schon bei den Parlamentswahlen 2024 errang und dominiert Zumas Heimatprovinz KwaZulu-Natal. MK könnte dem ANC dort sogar die Großstadtregion Ethekwini (Durban) abnehmen.
„Unser Fokus ist jetzt, das Mandat des Volkes zu erfüllen und die Versprechen an die Südafrikaner zu halten“, sagte MK-Sprecher Sifiso Mahlangu.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: Do not investigate Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
Do not investigate Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office
The United States’ presidential pardon power has created a constitutional absurdity in which exposing corruption may protect those responsible.
In a functioning constitutional democracy, allegations of corporate corruption would ordinarily invite immediate investigation. Congress would demand documents, summon executives and expose wrongdoing to public scrutiny.
With Democrats having won control of both houses of Congress, the expectation will be that they exercise these oversight powers vigorously. In Donald Trump’s America, however, there is a compelling argument for doing precisely the opposite.
If the objective is criminal accountability rather than political theatre, the incoming Democratic majorities might be better advised to preserve the evidence but postpone public congressional investigations and disclosures concerning potential criminal wrongdoing by Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office in January 2029, thereby avoiding the possibility of presidential pardons that could place those responsible beyond the reach of federal criminal prosecution.
This may sound absurd, but it follows from the extraordinary breadth of the presidential pardon power. Under the US Constitution, a president may pardon individuals for federal crimes before they have been charged, investigated or convicted. What was conceived as an exceptional power of mercy can become an instrument for protecting political associates, wealthy benefactors and corporate executives from criminal accountability.
A Washington Post investigation published on October 26 reveals that powerful technology and defence companies that cultivated close relationships with Trump are increasingly anxious about the prospect of a Democratic Congress. Companies including Palantir, Anduril, OpenAI and Meta face possible congressional scrutiny over government contracts, political contributions and their relationships with the administration. Some executives are reportedly scrambling to establish relationships with Democratic politicians as the prospect of congressional investigations approaches.
The financial stakes are considerable. The Post reports that 15 companies backed by Trump’s sons received $3.2bn in federal contracts, investments and loans, most after Trump returned to the White House. Congressional Democrats have raised questions about potential conflicts of interest and whether politically connected companies received preferential treatment. These relationships provide legitimate grounds for investigating how public resources were allocated.
Ordinarily, such investigations would be welcomed as an essential exercise of congressional oversight. But consider what might happen if congressional hearings uncovered evidence of fraud, bribery or corruption. The findings could identify those responsible and establish compelling evidence of criminal misconduct. Trump could then issue sweeping pardons protecting the individuals concerned from federal prosecution. Investigators might succeed in exposing wrongdoing only to discover that their efforts had furnished the president with a list of people to protect.
Trump’s record provides ample reason to take this possibility seriously. His official clemency record includes pardons for individuals convicted of securities fraud, wire fraud and other financial offences. In March 2025, he pardoned Trevor Milton, the founder of electric-truck manufacturer Nikola, who had been convicted of defrauding investors. He also pardoned HDR Global Trading Limited, the corporate entity associated with the cryptocurrency exchange BitMEX. The crypto firm had pleaded guilty to violating the Bank Secrecy Act. Several individuals associated with the company also received pardons.
The pardon of HDR Global Trading deserves particular attention. Trump extended clemency not only to company executives but to the corporation itself, which had pleaded guilty to a federal offence. The consequences for corporate accountability in an era of enormous corporate wealth and political influence deserve far greater attention than they have received.
The Supreme Court laid the groundwork for this extraordinary authority in Ex parte Garland (1866). The Court interpreted the pardon power as extending to federal offences after their commission, regardless of whether criminal proceedings had commenced. Congress could not impose ordinary legislative restrictions on its exercise. The ruling effectively recognised the president’s authority to forgive federal crimes without waiting for the criminal justice system to establish guilt.
The implications are staggering. An executive might have committed fraud involving millions of dollars, or a government contractor might have secured contracts through bribery. If those offences fall within federal criminal jurisdiction, a sufficiently broad presidential pardon can extinguish criminal liability for the covered conduct. Presidential pardons cannot authorise future crimes, prevent state prosecutions or generally extinguish civil liability. Nor do they prevent congressional investigations. But the elimination of federal criminal punishment for past offences is consequential enough.
This is not simply a Trump problem. Joe Biden demonstrated the extraordinary reach of the same constitutional power when he issued a sweeping pardon to his son Hunter Biden in December 2024. The pardon covered federal offences committed or potentially committed over almost 11 years, extending far beyond the specific charges on which Hunter Biden had been prosecuted or convicted.
In his final hours in office, Biden went further, issuing preemptive pardons to members of his family and several public figures, including Anthony Fauci, retired General Mark Milley and individuals associated with the congressional investigation into the January 6 attack. Biden justified these measures as necessary protection against politically motivated prosecutions by the incoming Trump administration. His stated motivations differed from protecting corporate financial misconduct, and the pardons did not establish wrongdoing by their recipients. Nevertheless, his actions demonstrated how easily the power could be used to shield selected individuals from federal criminal proceedings without any independent determination that clemency was warranted.
The precedent should trouble Americans regardless of their political loyalties. Biden’s supporters may regard his actions as justified protection against threatened political retribution. Trump can invoke the same constitutional authority for entirely different purposes. The central difficulty is that the legal power does not depend upon the president’s motives being honourable, the beneficiaries being deserving or the public interest being served.
This brings us back to the peculiar dilemma facing congressional Democrats. Why assemble and publicise evidence of alleged criminal misconduct while the president retains the authority to pardon those implicated? Why identify potential defendants and present the allegations against them before the administration leaves office? Trump might issue preemptive pardons regardless. Indeed, he has already signalled his willingness to do so, declaring in a November 2 interview that he would protect Elon Musk and other allies facing Democratic investigations and grant pardons if necessary. A detailed congressional investigation could therefore provide him with a convenient inventory of possible beneficiaries.
This is not an argument for destroying evidence, suppressing whistleblowers or preventing investigations necessary to stop ongoing illegality. Records must be preserved, relevant limitation periods protected and unlawful practices halted. State authorities must remain free to exercise their independent jurisdiction. The narrower argument concerns the timing of public congressional disclosures that could frustrate eventual federal prosecutions. Even that limited postponement carries costs for transparency and democratic oversight.
The objection is obvious. Citizens are entitled to know whether public money has been misused and whether government contracts have been awarded improperly. Delaying disclosure may permit wrongdoing to continue, allow witnesses to disappear or give those implicated additional opportunities to conceal evidence. These are serious concerns that cannot simply be brushed aside. Yet the fact that withholding potentially incriminating findings must even be considered as a means of preserving criminal accountability exposes a troubling defect in the constitutional system.
The US Constitution is almost 240 years old. It requires fundamental reform in several respects, but few provisions illustrate the urgency more clearly than the presidential pardon power. The framers entrusted this authority to a single individual in the expectation that it would be exercised with wisdom and restraint. They could scarcely have anticipated an era in which vast corporate fortunes, political patronage and presidential power would become so closely intertwined.
The Constitution should be amended to establish meaningful limits on presidential clemency. Pardons involving the president’s family, personal financial interests or political associates implicated in misconduct connected to the administration should be subject to strict constitutional safeguards. Sweeping preemptive pardons covering years of unspecified criminal conduct also deserve reconsideration. An independent clemency commission, operating under constitutionally prescribed standards, could provide scrutiny of controversial pardons without eliminating the legitimate humanitarian purposes of executive mercy.
Such reforms would require constitutional amendment. The Supreme Court has interpreted the existing pardon power so expansively that ordinary legislation cannot simply curtail it. Article V makes constitutional change exceptionally difficult, but difficulty cannot justify preserving a power susceptible to serious abuse merely because it has existed for more than two centuries.
There are compelling reasons to retain presidential clemency. Criminal justice systems make mistakes, sentences can be excessive, and mercy has an important place in the justice system. But mercy must not become a privilege reserved for the politically connected, or a mechanism through which presidents protect their associates from the consequences of criminal misconduct.
For now, the perverse logic of the system suggests that those seeking meaningful federal criminal accountability might be wiser to postpone public exposure of potential offences until Trump leaves office. It is an astonishing proposition for a country that prides itself on the rule of law. A constitutional system in which exposing corruption can become the means of protecting those responsible is badly in need of repair.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

This is an entry from: Live: Qatar PM says Iran-US mediation ongoing to prevent escalation
Iran will not allow US bases in the region to be rebuilt, army spokesman says
7 November 2026 05:32 GMT
Iranian Army Spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia has said Iran's army will not allow US military bases in the region to be rebuilt.
Akraminia said more than 228 locations or facilities at US bases across the region had been severely damaged or destroyed, according to Iran’s Fars news agency, claiming no US base in the region remained capable of operational missions, forcing US forces to bring in fuel for their vessels and supplies for personnel from outside the region.
“We will never allow the enemy’s bases in the region to be rebuilt,” Akraminia said.

Britischer Schauspieler und Comedian: Russell Brand wegen Vergewaltigung schuldig gesprochen
Ein Londoner Gericht hat Brand unter anderem der Vergewaltigung schuldig gesprochen. Ihm droht nun jahrelange Haft.
Achteinhalb Stunden hat sich die Jury beraten, um zu dem Schluss zu kommen: Der Comedian und Schauspieler Russell Brand ist schuldig. Das ist deutlich weniger Zeit, als für den Prozess, der am 12. Oktober im Londoner Southwark Crown Court begann, ursprünglich veranschlagt wurde. Sechs Wochen lang sollten sich die Geschworenen für Termine bereithalten. Am Ende dauerte der Prozess nur dreieinhalb.
Sechs Frauen sagten innerhalb dieser Zeit gegen Brand aus. Vorgeworfen wurden ihm Vergewaltigung, sexualisierte Gewalt und versuchter sexueller Übergriff in insgesamt sieben Fällen während einer Zeitspanne zwischen den Jahren 1999 und 2009. In vier dieser Fälle wurde der 51-Jährige nun für schuldig befunden, darunter ein Vergewaltigungsfall und drei Fälle sexualisierter Gewalt. In zwei weiteren Fällen von Vergewaltigung und einem Fall eines versuchten sexuellen Übergriffs wurde Brand freigesprochen.
Dementsprechend „erheblich“ wird Brands Strafe ausfallen, wie der zuständige Richter diese Woche erklärte. Die Höchststrafe für Vergewaltigung ist laut englischem Recht lebenslange Haft. Üblicherweise variiert das Strafmaß aber eher zwischen 4 und 19 Jahren. Wie lange Brand ins Gefängnis muss, soll kommenden Montag bekanntgegeben werden.
Während des Prozesses berichteten die sechs Frauen, denen laut englischem Recht lebenslange Anonymität zusteht, über ihre Begegnungen mit Brand. Dabei ähnelten sich die Schilderungen: Viele Frauen nahmen Brand, der in der Zeit unter anderem als Moderator für MTV, später als Schauspieler für einige Hollywood-Produktionen arbeitete, zunächst als charmante Person kennen. In intimen Momenten habe sich sein Verhalten aber schlagartig verändert. Brand soll seine Bekanntheit ausgenutzt haben, um sich dann teils gewaltsam Zugang zu Sex mit Kolleginnen und Fans zu verschaffen. Vor Gericht bestritt Brand, der zum Prozess oft mit seiner Frau Laura Brand erschien, alle Vorwürfe.
Vor aller Augen
Vorwürfe sexueller Übergriffigkeit gegenüber Brand wurden erstmals 2023 einer breiteren Öffentlichkeit bekannt. In dem Jahr erschien ein Dokumentarfilm über Brands Umgang mit Frauen auf dem britischen Sender Channel 4. Immer wieder spielte seine Verteidigung während des Prozesses darauf an, dass die Aussagen der Klägerinnen von der Dokumentation „inspiriert“ sein könnten und stellte die Vorwürfe als Medienkampagne dar.
Nicht zufällig lautet der Untertitel der Dokumentation „In plain sight“, sprichwörtlich übersetzt: „Vor aller Augen“. Bereits früher machte Brand in zahlreichen öffentlichen Äußerungen kaum Geheimnisse aus seinem Verhalten. Sexuelle Handlungen und Andeutungen gehörten regelhaft zu seinem Repertoire als Comedian und Moderator.
2008 soll er sich vor einer Frau in einem Badezimmer entblößt haben, später machte er Witze über den Fall in seiner Radiosendung. Ein Essay in einem bekannten britischen Magazin aus dem Jahr 2013 beginnt mit den Worten: „Als ich gefragt wurde, ob ich Gastherausgeber für eine Ausgabe des New Statesman sein möchte, habe ich ja gesagt, weil es eine schöne Frau war, die mich gefragt hat.“
Weitere Ermittlungen
In späteren Videoblogs, in denen sich Brand unter anderem Verschwörungserzählungen und christlichem Spiritualismus hingab, räumte er promiskuitives und „unschönes“ Verhalten ein, beschwor aber, im Hinblick auf Frauen immer einvernehmlich und „im Rahmen des Gesetzes“ gehandelt zu haben.
Im Nachgang des Gerichtsprozesses teilte die Metropolitan Police mit, dass sie zwei weitere bereits bekannte Vergewaltigungsvorwürfe untersucht. Einer davon bezieht sich auf eine Zeit, in der Brand im Alter von 30 Jahren eine sexuelle Beziehung zu einer 16-jährigen britischen Schülerin unterhielt.
Bis zur Verkündung des Strafmaßes befindet sich Brand in Haft. Die Möglichkeit einer Freilassung auf Kaution bis dahin wurde ihm vom zuständigen Gericht untersagt.

How the Iran war helped Democrats win the midterms
Trump sought to bring Iran to its knees. Instead, Tehran brought the costs of war into American homes, fuelling the backlash against his party.
This week, Iran’s response to the US-Israeli attacks led to one of the most dramatic political turnarounds in modern American history. Trump’s failed war on its own, however, is not why the Democrats pounded the Republicans and now control the Senate and House of Representatives for the next two years. Rather, it reflected and amplified many dynamics in American society that caused discontented, angry and fearful citizens to repudiate Trump’s Republicans and support Democrats.
The US president wrongly believed that his war on Iran would pummel the country into submission and turn it into a vassal state of the US and Israel. Iran survived, attacked the US, Israel and Arab lands, and brought the painful economic costs of war into every American home. It also humiliated Washington by revealing that America’s military prowess, like Trump’s behaviour and electoral promises, is erratic at best, and ineffective at worst.
The Iran war also sparked a cascade of consequences that hurt every American and, in some areas, exposed how national values such as democracy, equality and the rule of law, along with claims of global dominance, could prove illusory. Iran’s move with the greatest impact on ordinary Americans was restricting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up the prices Americans paid for groceries, gasoline, diesel, travel, most imports and other everyday necessities. Some 90 percent of voters said the cost of living was a major or crucial factor in how they would vote.
This was compounded by the inability of the US and Israel to force Iran to surrender, even after months of brutal attacks on political leaders, infrastructure, civilian and economic sites, and military installations. Instead, Iran’s counterattacks left US bases in the Arabian Peninsula and Jordan incapacitated or evacuated, and caused huge damage to Arab energy and transport systems, disrupting global energy flows and driving up prices. The balance of the war was clear after the first few weeks: the pain the US and Israel inflicted on Iran would be matched by pain in every household in the US and other countries that assisted in the attack on Iran.
Iran simultaneously exposed critical flaws in American militarism, leaving ordinary Americans confused, frustrated and often humiliated in different ways:
a) Trump ignored Americans’ repeatedly expressed opposition to attacking Iran, along with the constitutional requirement for congressional authorisation of war. CBS exit polls confirmed that voters opposed the war for both its useless militarism and its impact on the economy. The Trump administration’s disdain for both the law and ordinary Americans’ views angered many voters who took their constitutional rights more seriously than Trump did. Many voters rejected Republicans because Trump had insincerely promised in 2024 that he would end useless foreign wars.
b) More narrowly, Trump attacked Iran without clear, consistent or credible strategic goals; his main stated reason for attacking was to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, a prospect Israeli officials repeatedly told him was imminent, even though existing US and international inspections and intelligence assessments had repeatedly found no evidence of this.
c) When it dawned on Americans that Trump went to war mainly because Israel pushed him to do so, they reacted negatively in two ways. They felt humiliated that their country’s immense military power was unable to achieve its stated goals; they also felt angry and demeaned that a small, dependent, foreign country like Israel, with its extensive and sophisticated lobbying power in the US, could initiate this calamity that hurt American households and damaged US standing and credibility abroad.
Behind the anger, vulnerability and helplessness of most Americans who voted Democratic this week were deeper grievances that predated the Iran war. These included citizens’ fury at outrageous corruption in Washington; the privileged oligarchs, political donors, bankers and corporations that saw the US as their personal profit centre more than anything else; military and high-tech sectors that were out of control and threatened innocent lives; over-aggressive anti-immigration policing; and corporate media that seemed more interested in serving all of the above, and Israel, than in conveying truth and facts to the American people.
The election brought together voters’ household economic concerns with questions of national morality and foreign policy. Equally noteworthy, the day after the vote, Vice President JD Vance wrote on social media: “The reason we lost is the war.” He identified four demands among voters who had turned away from the Republicans: “End the war”, “Focus on the cost of living and inflation”, “Put America First” and “Change our relationship to Israel”.
An unprecedented aspect of this election and Iran’s policies has been the centrality of the US-Israeli genocide in Palestine to many progressive Democrats’ campaigns and to Iran’s approach to war and peace. Vance’s explicit mention of Israel was startling enough in a political system that, for nearly a century, has largely shaped its West Asia policies according to Israeli demands. Equally striking was President Trump’s last-minute promise, on election day, to end the nearly $4bn in US military aid to Israel. It was another insincere Trump con job meant to deceive voters, because the money would not stop flowing but would simply be channelled differently. It also emphasised the huge impact that conditions in Israel-Palestine and US complicity in the genocide had on voters.

Israeli settler attacks on West Bank olive harvest hit record since 2006, UN says
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has said Israeli settlers have carried out a total of 377 attacks on olive harvest across the occupied West Bank since September, a record since 2006 when the UN began recording them.
In a statement, OCHA said that during these attacks, one Palestinian was killed by a settler, more than 200 Palestinians were injured, and over 3,850 olive trees and saplings were damaged or vandalised.
Combined with official Israeli restrictions on Palestinian access to groves, this has undermined the livelihoods of many by reducing the produce that Palestinians could collect, the statement read.
Food security partners estimate that 80,000 to 100,000 Palestinian families across the West Bank depend on the annual olive harvest for their livelihoods and income.
*Gaza: OCHA said restrictions continue to hamper aid to Gaza despite widespread humanitarian response.
Humanitarian partners warn that the entry of engine oil, spare parts, generators, heavy machinery and specialised equipment remain particularly restricted. This prevents the implementation of more sustainable shelter solutions and risks shutting down critical services if back-up generators fail, according to the statement.

https://taz.de/Nach-der-Wahl-in-Israel/!.title: Nach der Wahl in Israel: Bekommt Eisenkot das Mandat, eine Koalition zu bilden?
https://taz.de/Nach-der-Wahl-in-Israel/!.author: Tamar Ziff
https://taz.de/Nach-der-Wahl-in-Israel/!.text:
Nach der Wahl in Israel: Bekommt Eisenkot das Mandat, eine Koalition zu bilden?
Netanjahu-Gegner und Oppositionsführer Eisenkot erhält von den israelischen Parteien die meisten Empfehlungen. Was das für eine Regierungsbildung bedeutet.
Alle Parteien in Israel haben nun ihre Empfehlungen an Präsident Isaac Herzog abgegeben, wer das Mandat zur Bildung einer neuen Regierung erhalten soll. Bis Donnerstagabend hatte Oppositionsführer Gadi Eisenkot 67 Empfehlungen erhalten – von der arabischen Partei Ra’am, der Mitte-links-Partei Demokraten, den Mitte-rechts-Parteien Bejachad und Jaschar, seiner eigenen Partei. Außerdem sprach sich die arabisch-nationalistische Joint List überraschenderweise für Eisenkot aus.
Der derzeitige Premier Benjamin Netanjahu erhielt hingegen nur 46 Empfehlungen – und zwar von der ultraorthodoxen Partei Schas und den beiden am ganz rechten Rand stehenden Parteien Religiöser Zionismus und Otzma Jehudit sowie seiner eigenen Partei Likud. Die ultraorthodoxe Partei Vereinigtes Thorah-Judentum (UTJ) weigerte sich – obwohl sie Teil der scheidenden Koalition ist –, einen der beiden Kandidaten zu unterstützen.
Der Präsident erhält zwar die Empfehlungen, hat aber weitreichenden Spielraum bei der Entscheidung, wen er nun mit der Regierungsbildung beauftragt. Herzog hat nun bis zum 11. November Zeit, eine Entscheidung zu treffen. Danach hat der ausgewählte Kandidat 28 Tage Zeit, eine Regierungskoalition zu bilden, mit der Möglichkeit einer zweiwöchigen Verlängerung.
Doch bis dahin werden bereits Entscheidungen getroffen: Ganz oben auf der Agenda der derzeitigen Opposition steht die Ablösung des Knesset-Präsidenten Amir Ohana von der Likud-Partei. Der hatte jüngst erklärt, er werde einer Abstimmung über seine Ablösung bei der Knesset-Eröffnung in der kommenden Woche zustimmen, falls eine Mehrheit der Abgeordneten dies fordere. Weitere Tagesordnungspunkte sind die Aufhebung der von der Netanjahu-Regierung verabschiedeten Gesetze zur Justizreform, die Einrichtung einer staatlichen Untersuchungskommission zum 7. Oktober 2023 sowie die Verabschiedung eines Gesetzes, das für alle Bürger einen zivilen oder militärischen Dienst vorschreibt.
Weiter Stimmungsmache gegen arabische Parteien
Und Netanjahu zeigt wieder einmal, dass er noch nicht geschlagen ist: Am Mittwochabend, während Herzog sich mit der Führung kleinerer Parteien traf, veröffentlichte Netanjahu seine erste aufgezeichnete Videobotschaft seit den Wahlen. Darin warnte er davor, sich auf „islamistische Parteien zu verlassen, die die bloße Existenz eines jüdischen Staates leugnen“. Er betonte, dass er eine „breite nationale Koalition“ anführen solle, und behauptete, die Sorgen „der überwiegenden Mehrheit der israelischen Bürger würden von den Spitzenpolitikern des linken Blocks leichtfertig beiseitegeschoben“, die eine Regierung bildeten, die „sich auf Terrorismusbefürworter stütze“.
Außerdem wiederholte er die Behauptung, dass „ernsthafte Verdachtsmomente bestehen, dass ausländische Staaten mit riesigen Geldsummen in die Wahl Ergebnisse im Staat Israel eingegriffen haben“. Diese Behauptung hatte allerdings keinen Einfluss auf die erfolgte Anerkennung des Wahlergebnisses durch den Vorsitzenden der Wahlkommission, Richter Noam Sohlberg.
Der Chef des Inlandsgeheimdienstes Schin Bet, David Zini, ein von Netanjahu ernannter Beamter, hatte jüngst eine Untersuchung wegen angeblicher ausländischer Finanzierung eingeleitet – ohne irgendwelche Beweise für Fehlverhalten vorzulegen. Das Bestreben: Zweifel an den Wahlergebnissen zu säen. Zini hatte jüngst verkündet, dass gegen den arabischen Abgeordneten Ayman Odeh wegen des mutmaßlichen Empfangs von „Hunderttausenden Schekel“ von externen Parteien ermittelt werde. Er erklärte außerdem, weitere arabische Parteiführer verhören zu wollen, ohne dafür Beweise vorzulegen.
Die israelische Zeitung Ha’aretz beruft sich in einem Text auf Schin-Bet-Beamte, die der Zeitung mitgeteilt hätten, dass die Behauptungen über Einflussnahme übertrieben seien und keinen Einfluss auf das Wahlergebnis hätten. Die Polizei unter dem rechtsextremen Sicherheitsminister Itamar Ben-Gvir von der Partei Otzma Jehudit hatte am Wahltag mehrere Aktivisten der arabischen Partei Ra’am wegen des Verdachts der Bestechung und Wahlbeeinflussung verhaftet – ohne Beweise vorzulegen. Bis Mittwoch, acht Tage nach der Wahl, waren alle wieder auf freiem Fuß.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Tim Dowling: it seems the real moral of this story is that I’m easily led
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Tim Dowling
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Early on Friday morning my wife finds me sitting in bed, looking at my phone. She is dressed already, and holding keys.
“They’re blocking off the whole road,” she says.
“Really?” I say. “How come?”
“I don’t know,” she says. “But you just lie there while I find out what’s going on.”
After a few minutes, I go downstairs to peer through the curtains. My wife is talking to a man in a hi-vis vest and hard hat, who is pushing a barrier aside for her. His colleague, meanwhile, is drawing marks on the road with a paint sprayer.
An hour later, I climb the stairs to my wife’s office, with its commanding view of the street, now cordoned off with cones. A digger is parked across the road, surrounded by temporary fencing. Rain is bucketing down.
“Can I help you?” my wife says.
“I had no idea this was happening,” I say, looking out.
“There was supposed to be a letter,” she says, “but apparently nobody got one.”
The man in the hard hat walks past our gate, pursued by two other men: our nextdoor neighbour, and the guy who runs the car garage on the other side of the garden wall from my office shed. They are both clearly offering strong objections to the proceedings.
“People aren’t pleased,” I say.
The guy from the garage glances up and sees me standing at the window, looking at him. He raises his arm like he’s throwing something over his shoulder, beckoning me to come down.
On my way out the door, I grab a raincoat and hold it over my head, joining the discussion at my gate.
“Did you get a letter?” says the guy from the garage.
“No,” I say. I notice the man in the hard hat is holding what appears to be a sodden example of the letter in question.
“Can I read that?” I say. He hands it to me.
“I’ve got five cars coming today,” says the guy from the garage. “How am I gonna get them past this?”
I scan the dripping letter, which is headed Essential Sewer Repair Works. A key sentence reads: “We politely ask that you remove any vehicles you may need to use.”
“Two weeks?” I say. My neighbour shakes his head.
“What are we supposed to do?” says the guy from the garage. I feel as if I’m part of a tiny mob ganging up on an accidental representative of intransigent officialdom. It feels good.
“My car is an electric car,” I say, thinking: I really have to stop telling people that.
“Yeah?” he says.
“So I’d like to just charge it here before I move it,” I say. “Can I do that?” The man nods and extends an upward palm: your wish is my command.
Having solved my problem and absolutely nobody else’s, I return indoors, thinking: sorted.
I’m sitting in the kitchen when my wife comes back from the supermarket in the early afternoon.
“So now they’re not closing the road after all,” she says, “because I was so nice. They’re leaving one lane clear so we can all get in and out. Everyone was rude to them, but I was nice, so they’re doing it as a favour to me.”
“There’s something weird about this story,” I say.
“The road is open, I’m nice, the end,” she says.
On Sunday morning, my wife and I set off somewhere in the car, edging past the fence protecting the hole, which is already big enough to bury a bus in. The man in the hard hat is busy directing the digger, but when he sees my wife he smiles and waves. She rolls down her window.
“Are people still giving you grief?” she says.
“Oh yeah,” he says. “One lady just pulled up and swore at me.”
“She didn’t?” my wife says.
“I said, ‘Where are you going?’ and she was like, ‘I’m trying to get to church.’”
“How rude!” my wife says.
“Even your husband was joining in the other day,” he says.
“I wasn’t really rude,” I say. “I was just being mordant.”
“I’m afraid he’s easily led,” my wife says. “See you later!”
As we drive off I think: the roadworks haven’t been in place for 48 hours, and already the moral of this story has changed three times.
“See?” my wife says. “Nice.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Carlos Alcaraz saves match points to reach Paris Masters semifinals
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Carlos Alcaraz saves match points to reach Paris Masters semifinals
Seven-time Grand Slam champion Alcaraz is through to the Paris Masters semifinals for the first time in his career.
Carlos Alcaraz produced another miracle in the French capital as the seven-time Grand Slam champion fended off two match points to beat Taylor Fritz and reach the Paris Masters semifinals on Friday.
The 23-year-old fought back to win 6-7 (10/12), 7-5, 6-3 and advance to the last four of the event for the first time.
He will next take on former world number two Casper Ruud on Saturday after the Norwegian eliminated Portuguese lucky loser Nuno Borges 7-6 (7/5), 6-4.
In scenes reminiscent of his iconic French Open final comeback win over Jannik Sinner last season, when he saved three championship points, Alcaraz again wowed the crowd in Paris as he snatched another improbable victory from the jaws of defeat.
“Probably this match is going to be one of the most special matches that I ever played, and I’m going to remember this match for a long time,” Alcaraz told reporters.
Despite only playing one match en route to the quarterfinals, Alcaraz showed no signs of rust as he seized his first break opportunity in the fifth game of the opening set, whipping a forehand passing shot around the stranded Fritz.
The Spaniard’s serve then started to wobble, and Fritz pounced to break to love and level at 5-5.
In a tie-break of thrills and spills, both players had set points come and go before Alcaraz dumped a forehand wide to cede the opener to the Californian.
After recovering from 0-40 to hold early in the second set, Alcaraz pointed to his ear and held his fist aloft in a bid to get the Parisian crowd going – the first but not last callback to his five-set Roland Garros epic.
But he continued to struggle to make inroads on Fritz’s serve, and it was the American who produced the first break of the set in the seventh game.
Alcaraz staved off a match point and then secured a hold that kept his campaign alive with a sensational backhand slice from well wide of his own tramlines.
“After that game… I started to enjoy it because I just thought I pulled off great shots, great points; I started to smile; I started to bring the energy from the people to the match,” the former world number one said.
A fine passing shot saved a second match point in the next game before Alcaraz wiped out the break and then completed his Houdini act by breaking Fritz again to set up a decider.
The rampant Murcian had a chokehold on the match and went in front 3-1 in the third set when Fritz pushed a volley wide.
Alcaraz still had to save break points in a match that always threatened another twist but, as it rumbled towards a conclusion, he brought up two match points on his own serve, sealing the first with a powerful forehand that Fritz could only get a frame on.
Shelton also advances to semis
Earlier, Ben Shelton edged Tommy Paul 6-4, 4-6, 6-3 in an all-American quarterfinal.
The defeats for Paul and Fritz ended both players’ hopes of qualifying for the ATP Finals, with American Frances Tiafoe and Spanish 20-year-old Rafael Jodar now set to make their debuts at the season-ending showpiece, which will run from November 15-22 in Turin.
“Frances has had an outstanding year. One of my best friends, and to see him make Turin for the first time is amazing,” Shelton said of the 28-year-old Finals debutant.
Shelton will meet Luca Van Assche in the last four after the Frenchman ended Australian Rinky Hijikata’s fairytale run from qualifying to the last eight.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans.
But as Israel took stock of the results, there was also a sense that the elections marked a longer-term shift in US politics that will make the job of any new Israeli leader far more difficult.
The United States provides Israel with critical military and diplomatic support, so nurturing bipartisan ties was the cornerstone of foreign policy for decades. Netanyahu ripped up that commitment to throw his lot in with the Republicans in general and Trump in particular.
The opposition had always attacked his decision as ill-judged. By the end of the week, they were warning that it was positively dangerous.
“These people aren’t against Israel,” prominent opposition politician Yair Lapid said of incoming Democratic lawmakers, urging his country to rebuild bridges. “They’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.”
“The easiest thing is to scream that ‘America is lost,’ because if it’s lost, you don’t have to work. That’s just not true. Not at all.”
Lapid laid out a plan to “rebuild trust” in the US, but it perhaps did more to demonstrate the scale of the problem than reassure Israelis.
His proposal of a transatlantic charm offensive by officials of a prospective new government drew a swift and sharp rebuke from the New York congressman-elect Brad Lander.
Lander, a Democrat who is Jewish and describes himself as a liberal Zionist, was detained in the occupied West Bank last month while joining Palestinians trying to harvest olives.
“Minister Lapid: As someone who won a seat in Congress last night, and who cares about Israel: you’re not listening to what American voters – Jewish and non-Jewish – are saying,” Lander wrote in a direct response.
“We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”
In his exchange with Lapid, Lander also highlighted the arrest of journalist Abed Abu Shehada, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, as an example of how Israel violates international law. He drew a direct link with the ICE “regime of detention without charges, based on secret evidence, designed to intimidate and chill speech” that he said was rejected by US voters.
Abu Shehada was reportedly taken from his home by 15 masked security officials in a night-time raid, without an arrest warrant. Interrogators have only questioned him about a podcast interview with a public figure, lawyers acting for Abu Shehada said.
On Friday, Lander and two other incoming Jewish members of Congress, Daniel Bliss and Scott Wiener, wrote to Israel’s ambassador to the US calling for the immediate release of Abu Shehada.
“Detaining a reporter for conducting an interview — the only issue that interrogators questioned him about — is a violation of international law,” Lander said when he published the letter. “It comes at a time when senior Israeli officials are trying to delegitimize the participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s recent elections.”
Nor do Israel’s problems end with angry Democrats. The wounded Republican establishment lost no time looking a few thousand miles away to find reasons for the collapse of its voter base.
Soon after the election results came in, the vice-president, JD Vance, put “our relationship with Israel” on a short list of reasons for voter fury, and on election day Trump made a last-ditch attempt to woo voters with a pledge to cut off $4bn (£3bn) in annual military aid to Israel.
The announcement caused panic in Israel’s defence establishment. “When the commander of the Israel air force hears something like that, he might slit his wrists,” one official told Channel 12 news. “Where are we going to come up with 15 billion shekels every year, and what does that mean for Israel’s future defence budget?”
Netanyahu only responded to Trump’s electioneering on Friday with an attempt to spin the cut as a joint decision reflecting Israel’s economic strength. It demonstrated a “move from aid to partnership”, his office said in a statement.
Netanyahu has long flaunted his relationship with Trump, his fluent English and experience in the US, presenting himself as the only man with the international standing to guarantee Israel’s security in a hostile world.
After Tuesday’s US election, he looks more like an agent of its destruction to many in Israel. “One thing is clear: we are losing America,” Ben Caspit wrote in Ma’ariv, a daily newspaper.
“This isn’t a process; it isn’t happening in stages; it is happening all at once. It is an avalanche. It is a reverberating collapse of the foundation of Israel’s national defence doctrine. This isn’t a decree of fate. It is a decree of Netanyahu.”
Some advocates for change inside Israel found cause for hope in the Democrats’ victory, if Israel’s opposition can turn their mandate for change into a new government. They won 67 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but more than a quarter went to Palestinian citizens of Israel, and some of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out sitting with them.
US administrations have for too long equated support for Israel with blind support for its government, said Nadav Tamir, a former senior Israeli diplomat in the US who is now executive director of J Street Israel.
That consensus is cracking, but the majority of lawmakers from both parties still see Israel as a key US ally in the Middle East, he wrote in the Times of Israel.
External pressure from those who support its security but see current policy as self-destructive might push the country towards necessary change, including a resolution of the Israel-Palestine conflict.
“Perhaps this will be the paradox of the new [US] Congress,” he wrote. “It will be less willing to define support for Israel as automatic alignment with every policy of its government, but precisely for that reason, it may offer Israel more meaningful support in breaking out of the cycle of wars and building a future of security and prosperity.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: Governing party ahead in early results of New Zealand’s knife-edge vote
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Governing party ahead in early results of New Zealand’s knife-edge vote
Early count suggests New Zealand’s National and Labour parties are neck and neck, with neither likely to govern alone.
New Zealand’s governing centre-right National Party leads with 31.19 percent of votes, followed closely by the opposition centre-left Labour Party with 28.35 percent, according to early results.
The country’s Electoral Commission said on Saturday that the centrist Opportunity Party will meet the 5 percent threshold to enter parliament.
Polling stations opened at 9am on Saturday (20:00 GMT Friday) and closed at 7pm (06:00 GMT Saturday).
New Zealand’s Electoral Commission aims to release preliminary results from 95 percent of polling stations by the end of election night on Saturday. A final result, which will reflect ballots cast by New Zealanders abroad, is expected by November 27.
There is no time frame for when a government must be formed.
The National Party pledged to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme. The Labour Party promised cheaper healthcare and transport.
New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional system.
Voters do not elect a leader of the country, but instead select a local electorate candidate and a political party.
Electorate winners earn a seat in the typically 120-seat parliament, as do the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.
All votes are counted by hand, not by machine.
