'Crisis cannot be left unresolved': Qatar PM says mediation efforts continue
Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, has said that efforts at mediation between Iran and the United States remain active to prevent escalation, warning that the crisis "cannot be left unresolved".
During a public interview at Oxford University on Friday, Al Thani said that “for the past couple of weeks, we have worked with colleagues in the US administration who have very genuine intentions to find a way to contain the situation and de-escalate it".
He said that mediation efforts continue “to prevent the situation from spiralling out of control,” adding that “thanks also to some wise voices in Tehran, we have prevented that from getting out of control.”
The prime minister also stressed that “we will never have a perfect peace deal, but we cannot just wait for this moment of a perfect deal and avoid having a good deal”.
He said that even after the US midterm election, the "intentions are still there, the willingness to take steps toward finding a solution is still there and we are building and capitalising on this".
Al Thani said that "our engagement did not stop and will not stop", although the current pace of diplomatic exchanges may not "be as active as it was a few days ago”.
Qatar earlier dismissed reports claiming negotiations between the US and Iran have failed, warning that such claims benefit “only those seeking to prolong the war”.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Blind date: ‘I told her I don’t like the theatre. In retrospect, I can see why a playwright would be offended’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
William on Abigail
What were you hoping for?
 
To have a spark of some kind.
First impressions?
 
She looked very glamorous and suited the smart restaurant far more than I did.
What did you talk about?
 
Our love of Robert Pattinson. The play she’s working on. Shucking oysters. She asked lots of questions, so I’m worried I dominated. She did a palm reading on me too and it said I’m not a good writer.
Most awkward moment?
 
When I told her I don’t like theatre. In retrospect, I can see why a playwright and actor would be offended by that.
Good table manners?
 
I’m gonna go for “impeccable”. She was very friendly and chatty to the staff too.
Best thing about Abigail?
 
She has a lovely smile and a great sense of humour. I laughed a lot.
Would you introduce Abigail to your friends?
 
Lots of my friends are performers, so they would have loads to talk about.
Describe Abigail in three words
 
Funny, kind-hearted, genuine.
What do you think Abigail made of you?
 
I hope she thought I was kind and easy to talk to. I realised I wasn’t making much eye contact at one point, so “awkward” may be a safer bet. Funny would be a lovely addition.
Did you go on somewhere?
 
We stayed at the restaurant until closing. Then she walked me back to King’s Cross so I could catch a train back to Cambridge, which was very kind.
And … did you kiss?
 
I would never say.
If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?
 
I forgot the bathroom was a push door and thought I had locked myself in.
Marks out of 10?
 
9/10.
Would you meet again?
 
We’ve shared numbers.
Abigail on William
What were you hoping for?
 
Love, obviously.
First impressions?
 
Polite, gentle. Nervous in a sweet way. He was very concerned about being underdressed, but he looked lovely.
What did you talk about?
 
Standup comedy. Socialism. Academia. His disdain for contemporary British theatre and my adoration of it.
Most awkward moment?
 
He seemed keen to show off his American accent at a few points.
Good table manners?
 
Yes, knows his way round a wine list too!
Best thing about William?
 
He has lived a fantastically varied life of travels and extracurriculars. It’s good to meet people who have life by the horns.
Would you introduce William to your friends?
 
I’d consider it. But he said he loves lying to strangers. That gives a woman pause.
Describe William in three words
 
Charming, roguish, amiable.
What do you think William made of you?
 
I gave him a flirty palm reading and I’m worried he thinks I’ve got a hand fetish.
Did you go on somewhere?
 
I don’t kiss and tell …
And … did you kiss?
 
… see above.
If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?
 
I would have stolen his gorgeous thick-rimmed emerald green glasses.
Marks out of 10?
 
7/10.
Would you meet again?
 
I fear his love line looked a bit unsteady. But he’s got my phone number if he’d like to tempt fate.
Abigail and William ate at Kobe, London W1. Fancy a blind date? Email blind.date@theguardian.com

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: ‘Alien-cortical’ mice: Can human brain cells grow inside animals?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
‘Alien-cortical’ mice: Can human brain cells grow inside animals?
Modified mice with human brain cells ignite debates over neurohybrids and the future of cross-species medical research.
In a laboratory in California, in the United States, mice are scurrying around their cages, as mice do. But inside their brains are millions of working human neurons.
Researchers at Stanford University have implanted lab-grown human cells into mice genetically engineered to lack parts of their brains, including the cerebral cortex, the outer region that plays a major role in perception, movement, decision-making and attention.
According to a study published in Nature, these so-called “alien-cortical mice” may offer a new way to study neural circuits and brain disorders such as schizophrenia, cerebral palsy and dementia.
Putting human brain tissue inside an animal sounds like something out of Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, but how “human” are these mice, really? And what have the researchers found?
Here is what we know.
How did the experiment work?
Researchers genetically modified the mice so they were born and grew without most of the cerebral cortex and the neighbouring hippocampus, which are needed for movement, learning and memory.
When the animals were two days old, researchers injected human “organoids” into the empty spaces. Organoids are miniature masses of cells grown in a laboratory from stem cells or tumour tissue which mimic real human organs. Each was grown from healthy donors’ stem cells and holds about 100,000 human cells.
Overall, researchers removed about 14 million mouse neurons and added about 4 million human ones.
This is not the same thing as a brain transplant, and the animals are not “mice that think like humans”, the researchers emphasised.
They tried the transplants on 29 mice, and it worked on 25 of them.
What happened to the mice?
Within three months, the human tissue had grown about five times larger inside the mice’s brains, connected to their blood supply and filled more than 90 percent of the cavities.
The “alien cortex” mice walked and vocalised mostly normally, even though human tissue made up about half their brain volume.
In a maze test, mice without the implanted human tissue kept getting lost, however, while those with human cells did better, suggesting the human tissue contributed to cognition.
Unexpectedly, some of the tissue developed into von Economo neurons, which are long, rare cells normally absent in mice and almost impossible to make in a lab. They are found in highly social animals such as humans, apes, whales and elephants.
The experiment might also help explain cerebral palsy.
While human infants can suffer from oxygen deprivation as a result of more frequent complications during much longer and trickier childbirth, mice infants rarely do, which has made the condition hard to study in rodents.
When the modified mice in this case were exposed to low oxygen, they showed brain damage, an altered gait and poor limb coordination.
Why put human neurons in a mouse?
Human brain diseases are among the hardest conditions to study. The brain contains about 86 billion nerve cells linked by trillions of connections. Ethical and safety barriers, along with the brain’s high biological complexity, limit access to living human brain tissue.
Scientists have spent years growing “organoids” instead: Small clusters of human nerve cells grown in a lab. But they are not brains in a dish. They lack the connections, inputs and environment of a living brain.
Sergiu Pasca, senior author of the research paper and a professor of psychiatry and behavioural sciences at Stanford University, said this has the potential to give researchers unprecedented insight into the human brain.
“For the past two decades, there’s been a quest to try to build models of the human brain outside of the human body,” he said.
“This is not going to replace all the models we had before, but it’s going to provide us access to other aspects of human brain function that would be very difficult to study otherwise.”
What are the ethical concerns?
As research into brain organoids advances, so too do calls for clear regulations and oversight, given the sensitive ethical questions raised by these technologies.
These questions centre on the possibility that cell clusters and brains grown outside the bodies of their owners possess the capacity for sensation or consciousness, and whether this can be scientifically verified.
The researchers stopped the experiments when the human nerve cells implanted in the brains of mice were six months old, before they could form more neural connections with the animals’ brains, and before any signs of consciousness appeared.
John Evans, a sociology professor at the University of California, San Diego, who was not involved in the study, said this experiment does not in itself raise major ethical issues, but it provides evidence that other animals could be created that might raise more serious ethical concerns.
Setting clear boundaries for this research remains a challenge.
According to Evans, the problem lies in the lack of clear stopping points on the gradual path that research could take from mice to non-human primates.
Accordingly, he suggested that researchers should not go beyond rodents for the time being, in order to avoid creating neurohybrid organisms that combine human and animal characteristics and could provoke an ethical controversy.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya, Turkey
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.
Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”
“They have decided that there is no appetite for negotiation, with the US out of Paris,” said another developing country diplomat. “Countries won’t engage.”
The summit ended with a deal, although few loved it. But, as the faultlines from the Brazilian decision deepen going into this year’s summit, it is clear that the Paris agreement, and climate action around the world, has reached an impasse.
And it is not just Cop insiders who are worried. For many outside the vast white air-conditioned conference halls, the question, as this year’s summit begins, will be: what is the point?
Those same governments have pledged year after year since the Paris agreement was signed in 2015 – and entered into force a year later – to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Yet temperatures for two years have exceeded that threshold, and the UN revealed a few weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate was now for about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating.
There could be no clearer evidence that the Paris agreement, on the face of it, has failed. It is impossible not to wonder whether the Cop process itself is just not fit for purpose.
The charge sheet against Paris is long, with the central issue being the failure to achieve its goal. Beyond that immediate failure, the negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris “rulebook” under which the treaty is interpreted and put into effect.
The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein. Donald Trump’s allies – in Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and some other petrostates – frequently veto measures and obstruct progress.
It took more than 30 years of negotiation since the UN framework convention on climate change was signed in 1992 for fossil fuels even to be addressed directly. This was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away from fossil fuels” but failed to set a timeframe or any policies to back up the resolution.
The US, the world’s biggest economy and responsible for about one in every eight tonnes of carbon dioxide emitted today, has withdrawn from Paris under President Trump.
Even parts of the developed world which support the process have mostly failed to come up with convincing plans: Australia, co-host of Cop31, has set no end to fossil fuel exports; its fellow co-host Turkey plans to increase its carbon output. The UK is opening a gasfield and mulling a new oilfield, Germany has dropped its electric vehicle sales targets and scrapped a renewable heating law. Meanwhile, most rich countries are reducing their contributions to climate finance for the poor.
Most of all, the slow pace of the Paris timetable might have seemed fine in 2015, when temperatures were rising at 0.2C a decade. Today, the rate of rise is 0.4C a decade and still accelerating.
“The structures of Cops and Paris are labyrinthine, bureaucratic, and ultimately dispiriting,” said Paul Bledsoe, a former Clinton White House climate adviser, now with the American University. “It may be time to streamline them to focus more deliberately on national emissions reduction goals.”
As ordinary people watch these failures outside and inside the process, some are losing faith. The Paris agreement was a sensation, celebrated around the world. In the years since, the aura of Cop has faded, as meetings seem to disintegrate into arguments over wording and compromise.
“A lot of the commitments, the promises that were made, just turned out to be a bunch of hot air,” said Juan Carlos Monterrey, former climate envoy for Panama, now chief executive of the Vanglabs consultancy. “Under that measure, we have failed.”
Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said: “The fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast, that Earth’s resilience is showing worrying signs of decline, and that we still allow ourselves to follow a global path that will take us to a catastrophic 2.6C-3C, and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”
But, like most involved in international climate efforts, both refuse to concede that Paris is done for. “On the other hand,” said Rockström, “Paris is all we have. And we know that the global climate crisis can only, in the end, be solved if all countries in the world simultaneously move away from planet-damaging heat injection.”
Monterrey agrees. The most important fact about the Paris agreement, and the Cop process, he says, is that they exist. “Paris is our moral compass. It has told us where we should go. The speed of travel is not what it needs to be, but Paris has set the direction.”
A messy compromise
This year’s Cop is the first to have a split presidency and host. Being held in Turkey but presided over by Australia, Cop31 is a messy compromise between two countries whose other chief point of commonality is an admiration for coal.
Unexpectedly, however, the skies are a little brighter over this year’s meeting than anyone might have expected. Brazil has decisively re-elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva who has already overseen the biggest reductions in deforestation for decades.
The US midterms delivered a drubbing for the right, while in Serbia and Hungary this year democracy has won out over authoritarianism. Though the far right is still on the march across much of Europe, and autocrats still rule in most of the countries with the biggest fossil fuel industries and highest emissions, the replacement or weakening of anti-climate authoritarians by pro-climate parties is a positive sign. Globally, a large majority of people support climate action.
Action beyond the framework of Cop is marching on. After the failure of last year’s Cop30 in Brazil to provide a strong statement on phasing out fossil fuels, a group of nearly 60 countries held an alternative meeting in Colombia in April and agreed to draw up their own national roadmaps for the “transition away from fossil fuels”.
Three major countries have so far done so: France, Germany and the Netherlands. Bledsoe wants to use this model for more side agreements on the “super pollutants” such as methane, refrigerant chemicals called HFCs, ground-level ozone, nitrous oxide and black carbon, or soot.
Cutting methane by 40% could alone hold down temperatures by about 0.3C in the next decade, and deeper cuts beyond that could yield a 0.5C decrease by 2100.
“Paris was never intended to do all the hard work itself,” Bledsoe said. “We need to use the G7, the G20 and other forums too, and we need to elevate the climate to the level of national security concern, and see it as an economic threat.”
While the failures of Paris might seem obvious, its “moral compass” has also translated into greater success in the real world than many people realise.
“The solar panels on my roof and the BYD Dolphin [electric car] my neighbour drives are exhibit one and exhibit two of Paris’s success,” said Claudio Angelo, of the Observatório do Clima thinktank. “Will Paris prevent overshoot of 1.5C? No way. Will it prevent 2C of warming? Unlikely. But the transformation it has triggered can’t be exaggerated.”
Perhaps the clinching argument lies in China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and second-largest economy.
“China is taking multilateral climate efforts more seriously than many other countries, and certainly more seriously than it did a few years ago,” said Li Shuo, director of the China climate hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “The reason is simple: its economic stakes have grown enormously. If the world abandons decarbonisation, where will China sell its solar panels and electric vehicles?”
And, stung by high fossil fuel prices, many developing-country consumers are grasping clean technology without waiting for assistance. In Pakistan, plagued by blackouts and grid supply issues, rooftop solar panels have taken off, now making up about a quarter of electricity use in the country. Similarly, drivers in Vietnam are increasingly opting for cheap electric vehicles from China, which now make up more than 40% of its car sales.
Meanwhile, the conference hosts themselves, from unpromising beginnings, have brought forward one of the biggest new ideas in the last decade for putting the world on track to lower emissions – changing fuel sources for cars and heating to electricity. The electricity should be from clean sources where possible – but its efficiency means that even if the energy source is fossil-based, it still uses less power.
Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University, estimates that the superior efficiency of electricity over fossil fuels will mean that the world’s total final energy use can be halved by switching to electric for everything – meaning we need to generate a lot less, too.
If countries can agree a target at Cop31 of deriving 35% of final energy use from electricity by 2035, up from 23% today, that would be a major boost to decarbonisation efforts. Adair Turner, former chair of the UK’s climate change committee and now co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission thinktank, said: “Electrification is the single most important thing you have to do [to reach net zero emissions].”
Cops provide a place where countries can come together to share experiences, to seek advice, to find support and fellowship. “That’s very valuable,” said Ilana Seid, ambassador of Palau and chair of the Pacific Small Island Developing States. And in a world in which the bulk of current and future emissions, and fossil fuel production, comes from non-democracies or authoritarian states, Cops also provides one of the few forums where they can be held to account.
That “societal pressure” is crucial, said Seid. “We small islands and vulnerable nations are on the frontline. For us, this is existential. We are all very committed to Paris.”
After all, despite all the doubts, the power of a decision at Cop should not be underestimated. While “coalitions of the willing” are a “good thing” according to Nick Stern, the economist, the universality of the Paris agreement and Cops give them a unique authority.
Sue Biniaz, a former US climate negotiator, said: “Any time you have a consensus decision, it sends a signal to investors, to people who finance things, and to countries. I think that’s true these days with the geopolitics of the world – if something can be agreed by the whole world, it’s impactful.”
Cop31 may bring progress on electrification, on climate finance and on the transition that countries, rich and poor, need to make to a low-carbon world. But we already know that whatever the summit produces, it will not be enough.
However flawed yet substantive they are, Cops last only a fortnight, while efforts to tackle the climate crisis will require such wholesale transformation of our economies and societies that they should top governments’ agendas all year.
“Imagine you have lost your loved one without having their bodies to bring back home. Lost livelihood where you spent your whole life to accumulate those assets. We faced a horrific situation,” said Sujeeta Mathema, executive director of ActionAid Nepal, who was quickly on the scene to help people after the catastrophic glacier collapse there.
“It feels like living with grief, fear and uncertainty about the future. The devastation is not just physical; it is deeply emotional and psychological.”
People are traumatised, she says, and deeply feel the injustice of how the climate crisis is created by the rich while hurting the most vulnerable. But Cop can still be a place of hope, Mathema adds.
“Cop is an important space for us to raise our voice, clearly putting our agenda. Cop can help prevent such disasters if the commitments come off paper and are put into action.”

Trump says US knocked out Iranian 'little bit of anti-aircraft device'
US President Donald Trump says Washington had made considerable progress in its dealings with Iran, while acknowledging that US forces had carried out limited strikes against targets on the country.
"I don't want to talk about it. We do minor strikes. But they knocked out... and they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device. And we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five," Trump told reporters when asked about reports of strikes near Iran's Qeshm Island.
Speaking to reporters after arriving aboard Air Force One at Donald J. Trump International Airport, Trump said the United States was taking out more Iranian oil than before the conflict.
"We've made a lot of progress with Iran, we're taking out more oil now than we were before the war. It's not a war," he said.
"You know, in Russia-Ukraine, they lose 25,000 people a month. We haven't lost anybody in seven months, so I don't think that's a war. Total control. But we're dealing with the Iranians, we'll see how that all works out."
Report by Reuters

https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.title: ‘My biggest fear was being shot down’: how an injured Ukrainian soldier was evacuated by drone
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.author: Luke Harding in Lviv
https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.text:
Artem Lytvyn was crossing a field when the bang happened. Up ahead was a tree line. Not far beyond that the Russian border. The 25-year-old Ukrainian soldier had spent five days trekking to a dangerous forward position in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. Along the way he and six comrades dodged drones, and killed two Russians in a foxhole.
A few hundred metres short of his destination, he trod on a mine. “I didn’t hear anything. It was a magnet type. My rifle set it off,” Lytvyn said. He applied two tourniquets to his shattered right leg and pulled off his combat boot. Fellow soldiers dragged him and another wounded platoon member, Siava, into bushes. The same blast ripped off Siava’s leg. He died two days later.
Evacuating casualties from the frontline of Russia’s war in Ukraine is notoriously difficult. In the five years since Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, it has become a heavily surveilled and ever-widening “kill zone” where constant drone attacks mean even armoured vehicles can no longer be used. Soldiers are often forced to spend months in dugouts without rotation.
Members of Lytvyn’s brigade, the 129th, tried to evacuate him. They dispatched a remote-controlled land robot used to deliver supplies and transport casualties but it and three further robots got stuck. The terrain was unfavourable: rivers, muddy fields, a forest of oaks and aspens. A 10-person stretcher party set off but after five days it had covered just 6.8 miles (11km) – half the distance to where Lytvyn lay.
“I felt really bad. I couldn’t eat or sleep. I slept one night in eight days,” he said “The guys dropped pain killers, cigarettes and food – porridge and stewed meat – by drone.” With no prospect of rescue he requested a crutch, determined to hobble out. But when he tried to stand up he immediately fell over.
Soon after this hopeless moment, Lytvyn’s radio crackled into life. “They told me they were sending a huge bird,” he said. The “bird” was a gigantic drone capable of carrying a 150kg (330lb) payload. Manufactured by the Ukrainian company SkyFall, the unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) came with a coffin-like capsule suspended beneath six powerful black rotor blades.
A rescue using this kind of purpose-built evacuation vehicle had not been tried before. One of the pilots involved on the unmanned mission, Andrii, described it as complex and risky. The StarGate drone they would use was big and conspicuous – a tempting target for Russia’s elite Rubicon drone force, which could either bring it down using smaller UAVs, or simply jam it so it tumbled to the ground.
Andrii said he and his colleagues from the 475th Separate Assault regiment (also known as Code 9.2) plotted the route for a week. “I didn’t sleep because I was thinking about this situation. I just napped on the couch for 15 minutes,” he said. The drone was fitted with a navigation module using AI so it could continue to fly on a mapped route even if its GPS system was scrambled – at least in theory.
Eight days after his foot was blown off, at 3am on 21 October, Lytvyn heard a faint noise in the inky distance. The whirring grew louder and soon the drone landed next to him. The next few minutes would determine whether he survived or perished. A remarkable video filmed by the drone’s onboard camera shows Lytvyn crawling out of his hiding place, pushing himself forward using his hands and left leg.
“I climbed into the capsule. I lit a cigarette, closed the hatch. That was it – I looked out at the horizon and took off. I left my radio and my assault rifle behind,” he said. “At that moment I felt happy and excited.” The drone flew low over a night-time landscape. “I wasn’t worried about technical failure. My biggest fear was being shot down.”
Andrii followed its progress nervously from a remote location. “Our hands were sweaty and shaky. It was completely silent in the room. Everybody was anxious,” he said. His unit had dispatched other drones to escort Lytvyn on the 18-mile journey. They included heavy duty Vampire drones, which bombarded known Russian positions. The idea was to create a diversion. It worked.
Twenty minutes later the StarGate drone landed in a clearing. A voice cried out: “Are you friendly?”. Lytvyn shouted back: “Friendly”. In the control room there was relief and applause. “I’ve never done anything scarier and more important in my life,” Andrii said.
Ukrainian soldiers materialised out of the gloom and carried Lytvyn into a small cellar. They cut off his uniform and doused his leg with hydrogen peroxide to kill the maggots – a frequent problem with untreated battlefield wounds. The soldier had previously cut away parts of his foot with a knife. The treatment did not work. “The maggots were still there. There were loads of them,” Lytvyn said.
A few hours later, around lunchtime, an armoured Humvee rolled up and took him to an ambulance, which drove him to an operating theatre in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s under-fire second city. There, surgeons gave Lytvyn a blood transfusion and amputated his right leg at the knee.
He was transferred to a military hospital in the western city of Lviv, where he is now recuperating on a ward with four other soldiers who have lost limbs.
“What happened to me is a miracle. I rose into the heavens,” Lytvyn said, adding: “Travelling by StarGate is better than by land robot. A ground robot moves slowly and throws you around as if you are in a washing machine. If you are hurt, it can be painful.”
Lytvyn’s girlfriend, Alyona, and his younger brother, Nikita, perched on the end of the bed. They only learned that Lytvyn was seriously wounded after his extraordinary escape. From time to time they brought him cups of tea and cake. The soldier added: “The ride was cool. I’d love to fly again. Not in a situation like that, of course, but I’d just like to have a go. We need to develop this system further.”
Last month, another wounded soldier, 49-year-old Kostiantyn Vlasenko, became the first to be airlifted by drone from the frontline after 491 days at his position. It was a different drone to the StarGate one and Vlasenko dangled from a harness on his nine-mile journey. A third soldier, 54-year-old Andriy “Donbas”, was last week rescued by drone.
Europe’s biggest war since 1945 has in the last years evolved into an all-out drone battle, characterised by competition and rapid technical innovation. SkyFall is just one of many Ukrainian defence industrial startups. The company also manufactures heavy bombers, mid-range strike drones and a high-speed interceptor that can ram the Russian jet-powered UAVs terrorising Kyiv and other cities.
By the end of the year it plans to produce 1,000 StarGate drones a month. “I believe that thanks to them dozens of lives will be saved. Maybe hundreds,” Andrii said.
The extreme efforts made by Ukrainian regiments to rescue wounded combatants contrast with the attitudes shown by Russian commanders who order soldiers into “meat assaults” with little chance of survival. According to Kyiv, 54,400 Russian soldiers were killed or injured in October – the highest figure since the war began.
Lytvyn’s plans for the future are uncertain. Home is Dnipropetrovsk oblast in south-eastern Ukraine. “I need to recover first,” he said, adding that he wants to spend time with his seven-year-old daughter, Mia.
But he said he had no regrets about going on a risky mission to the edge of Ukrainian-held territory – from where he very nearly did not return. “This is our country, our territory. We are defending it.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Khawaja claims entire Australia team knew about 2018 ball-tampering scandal
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Khawaja claims entire Australia team knew about 2018 ball-tampering scandal
The ‘Sandpapergate’ scandal saw Australia scuffing the ball with sandpaper in the March 2018 test in Cape Town.
Former opener Usman Khawaja claimed on Saturday that the entire Australian team knew about the 2018 “Sandpapergate” scandal in Cape Town and said they also employed the tactic during the previous Test at Port Elizabeth.
Captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were sent home in disgrace and found by a Cricket Australia investigation to be the only three players with prior knowledge of the ball-tampering plot.
Smith was banned for a year and sacked as skipper, Warner was suspended for 12 months and stripped of all leadership roles, while Bancroft was slapped with a nine-month ban. Head coach Darren Lehmann was cleared of direct involvement but resigned soon after the series.
But Khawaja, who retired this year after 88 Tests, told The Sydney Morning Herald everyone had prior knowledge.
“It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” he said ahead of the release of his autobiography next week, where a chapter is dedicated to the issue.
Bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly in 2021 that they knew about it.
Khawaja said he spoke in the dressing room after the Cape Town Test, urging the team to take collective responsibility, rather than scapegoating Warner, Smith and Bancroft.
“In an ideal world, I don’t want to do this,” Khawaja said.
“I don’t want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.
“Maybe I thought Davey [Warner] would have exposed it, or someone else would have talked about it more. I just didn’t think it was going to come down to this.”
In the book, according to the newspaper, Khawaja recounts that discussions about ways to rough up the ball were also held in the dressing room during the second Test at Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha.
It culminated in the discovery that sandpaper was effective, and at this point Smith allegedly walked away, saying he did not want to know about it.
Bancroft then allegedly volunteered to use sandpaper in South Africa’s first innings in Gqeberha, where the ball swung significantly.
Cricket Australia said in a statement it was “comfortable” with the findings of its original investigation, but remained open to new evidence.
“There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month’s series in South Africa,” it said.
“During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.
“All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: President Herzog faces key choice as Israel struggles to form government
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
President Herzog faces key choice as Israel struggles to form government
Palestinian-led parties have backed Eisenkot in a bid to oust Netanyahu, but the prime minister could stay on if no government is formed.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog must decide who gets the first attempt at forming a government, after an inconclusive election left both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, short of a parliamentary majority.
Herzog has said he will task a candidate with forming a government on Sunday. Eisenkot has received the endorsement of a majority of lawmakers – but only thanks to parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record 19 seats in October’s election, but whom Eisenkot has ruled out bringing into government.
Here is what we know:
Who is Herzog likely to ask to form a government?
During consultations between party heads and Herzog, which ended on Thursday, 67 out of 120 Knesset members endorsed Eisenkot, while only 46 endorsed Netanyahu.
Netanyahu’s endorsements fell seven short of his bloc’s 53 seats after United Torah Judaism, one of his longtime allies, withheld endorsements over his coalition’s failure to exempt ultra-Orthodox Israelis from military service.
Herzog has not publicly committed to either side, saying that while the numbers may look clear, “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” made it hard to tell who could build a coalition.
Prior to the October 27 elections, reports emerged that the president wanted to push for a national unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s rival parties to avoid another election.
How difficult will it be to form a government?
No bloc has secured the 61 seats needed to form a majority government. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious alliance has 53, four Jewish-led parties backing Eisenkot hold 48, and the Arab-led parties hold 19.
Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.
United Torah Judaism has signalled that its support was available for the right price, but Shas endorsed Netanyahu on Wednesday.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, would need to lure an opposition party to his side. A unity government with the two men rotating as prime minister – and excluding Arab-led parties from government – is another option, but many Netanyahu rivals have ruled out serving under him.
Will Arab-led parties be part of the next government?
So far, it seems unlikely that they will.
The Arab-led parties are the Joint List, an alliance of three parties, and the United Arab List (Ra’am). They hold 11 and eight seats, respectively.
Ra’am says it is willing to join an Eisenkot-led government, while the Joint List has ruled out joining but offered to help put him in office from the outside.
Both endorsed Eisenkot during consultations with President Herzog, but he has refused to bring either into government unless they meet certain conditions, including recognising Hamas as a “terrorist organisation”.
Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas, whose party joined an anti-Netanyahu coalition in 2021 and became the first party representing Palestinians to enter government in Israel, has expressed support for disarming Hamas, but declined to label it as a “terror” group.
However, Israeli law allows Eisenkot to become prime minister with fewer than 61 seats if his proposed government wins a parliamentary confidence vote – which the two could help him secure.
Eisenkot could form a minority government in the meantime and later secure a majority by luring the two ultra-Orthodox parties by making concessions on the conscription issue.
In positions that many observers see as highlighting the second-class nature of Palestinian citizens in Israel, some of Eisenkot’s allies have opposed any reliance on Palestinian lawmakers, while Netanyahu’s Likud has threatened that cooperating with the Arab-led parties would be “dangerous to Israel”.
Senior Joint List member Ahmad Tibi told The Associated Press that rejecting a partnership would prove Israel is “an ethnocracy, not an absolute democracy for all citizens”.
What do Palestinian-led parties want from the next government?
First, an end to Netanyahu’s rule.
The Joint List said its unanimous backing for Eisenkot answered a “public demand” to stop Netanyahu and his government returning to power.
By widening Eisenkot’s lead, it said, it hoped to narrow the path to a unity government that keeps Netanyahu in office. Its support, it added, did not mean dropping its reservations about an opposition that had not shown readiness to confront Netanyahu’s approach or incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel.
In return for outside support, Arab-led parties are seeking guarantees for Palestinian citizens, including an end to house demolitions and incitement, action against crime, and a political horizon for Palestinians.
Tibi told The AP he had no illusions that this would end Israel’s wars or bring a Palestinian state, but said a “repair government” would improve Palestinian citizens’ lives, including, potentially, by tackling violent crime in their communities.
Ra’am leader Abbas has also said ending the government of Netanyahu, and far-right figures such as Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, is a priority.
What happens if no government can be formed?
The nominee chosen by Herzog will have 28 days to form a coalition, extendable by 14 more. If they fail, another nominee will be chosen and granted 28 days.
If the second nominee fails, a parliament majority can back a third candidate, and be granted a final 14 days.
If once again no government is formed, the Knesset will be dissolved and an entirely new election called within 90 days. This would mean Netanyahu staying on as caretaker prime minister.
Nehru Jamhour, an analyst of Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera that this drawn-out impasse was the likeliest outcome, and Netanyahu’s preferred one. He said that Netanyahu was hoping that a repeat election could weaken his rivals and depress turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Deputadas negras de esquerda recebem ameaças de morte com conteúdo neonazista
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
As deputadas estaduais Dani Monteiro e Renata Souza, do Psol do Rio de Janeiro, pediram que a Polícia Federal apure as ameaças de morte que ambas receberam em e-mails com conteúdos neonazistas enviados na madrugada de quarta-feira (4) a seus endereços eletrônicos funcionais.
Além delas, as ameaças também são direcionadas às deputadas estaduais Dani Balbi (PCdoB), também do Rio de Janeiro; Ediane Maria, Paula da Bancada Feminista e ao Movimento Pretas, todas do Psol de São Paulo.
Os e-mails trazem ameaças de morte contra as parlamentares, de estupro contra crianças trans e afirmam que os autores são parte de uma célula neonazista e integralista atuante no Brasil.
“Infelizmente, não é a primeira vez que sou alvo de ameaças, mas é a primeira vez que sofro um ataque explicitamente supremacista. Assim como Renata, sou uma mulher preta e favelada, eleita para o meu terceiro mandato. O racismo e o fascismo não vão nos silenciar. Exigimos investigação célere e responsabilização. Seguiremos enfrentando essas forças na defesa dos direitos e da democracia”, afirmou a deputada Dani Monteiro.
As parlamentares enviaram ofícios à Coordenadoria Institucional de Segurança da Assembleia Legislativa do Rio de Janeiro (Alerj) e à Presidência da Casa, solicitando a preservação do e-mail original, dos registros de recebimento e dos metadados que podem ajudar a identificar sua origem.
Também solicitaram providências à Coordenação de Repressão a Crimes Cibernéticos e de Ódio da Polícia Federal e pediram uma reunião com a participação de todas as parlamentares atingidas. O material será encaminhado formalmente à PF assim que os arquivos originais e os registros técnicos estiverem disponíveis.
“A violência política de gênero e raça precisa ser combatida de maneira efetiva. Essas ameaças atentam contra a democracia, uma vez que tentam nos violentar diante da nossa atuação parlamentar. As ameaças que atentam contra a minha vida são encaminhadas diretamente à Polícia Federal. E eu não vou recuar um milímetro diante da defesa do povo”, declara a deputada Renata Souza.
Crimes diversos
Na terça-feira (3), a Polícia Federal (PF) deflagrou uma operação para apurar crimes de ameaça, injúria racial, racismo e violência política contra a deputada federal Talíria Petrone (Pol-RJ) e seus familiares por meio da internet.
“A investigação teve início em agosto de 2026, após o envio de mensagens eletrônicas contendo ameaças de morte e ataques de cunho racista e misógino direcionados à parlamentar e à sua família, além da divulgação não autorizada de dados pessoais da vítima”, informou a PF.
Durante a operação, foi cumprido um mandado de busca e apreensão no município de Teresópolis, no Rio de Janeiro, expedido pela Justiça Eleitoral do Distrito Federal. Além disso, a PF identificou um suspeito de autoria das mensagens.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: Russia launches missile attack on Kyiv, injuring residents
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Russia launches missile attack on Kyiv, injuring residents
Missile attacks damage a residential building and injure civilians after Zelenskyy warns of potential for new strikes.
Russian forces have launched a missile attack on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor said, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned in his nightly video address that Russia was preparing new attacks on energy targets, bridges and other infrastructure.
Debris from Saturday’s attack damaged a residential building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
“Explosions in the Kyiv suburbs. The enemy is hitting infrastructure with ballistic missiles,” Klitschko wrote on Telegram.
Klitschko said debris had struck a five-storey apartment building in a western district of the capital. The facade of another residential building was also damaged.
The city’s military administration said on Telegram that two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was damaged.
Officials continued to warn residents of the potential for more strikes hours after the attack.
The attacks come as Zelenskyy said his government is seeking specific guarantees from Western allies on how post-war security support would function. He made comments in an interview aired late on Thursday, following two days of discussions among allies in Brussels.
The talks in Brussels discussed post-war reconstruction, funding for next year and security guarantees backed by the Ukrainian government’s Western allies.
The meetings brought together officials from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and the European Union, along with representatives from the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock, Ukrainian lead negotiator Rustem Umerov wrote in an online post.
US-led talks
The attacks occurred three days before US-led Ukrainian-Russian talks were to open in Abu Dhabi seeking a resolution to the war that has gone on for more than four years. The last such talks took place in February.
On Thursday, US President Donald Trump said a deal between Russia and Ukraine may be imminent, following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, at the White House.
Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.
The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came on the same day as First Lady Melania Trump hosted a diplomatic gathering with Russian and Ukrainian representatives to mark and build on a localised truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October.
The truce expired last Sunday, a day before a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhia region.
The death toll from the attack has risen to 50, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said on Friday, making it one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: MST realiza final da maior Copa Camponesa do Brasil neste sábado (7), em Caucaia
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Aline Oliveira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A grande final da 4ª edição da Copa e Feira Estadual da Reforma Agrária acontece neste sábado, 07 de novembro, a partir das 14 horas, no Estádio Municipal Raimundo de Oliveira, em Caucaia (CE). Conhecida como a maior Copa Camponesa do Brasil, a competição chega à sua decisão depois de cinco meses de jogos.
As atividades começam com música ao vivo, com Vanessa a Cantora, seguida de um ato solene e de uma partida entre MST e Amigos/as. Na sequência, acontecem as finais das competições masculina e feminina. O encerramento será com a entrega da premiação às equipes campeãs e vice-campeãs.
Na competição masculina, Croatá Jandaíra, do Assentamento Croatá, em Russas, enfrenta o Clube Esportivo Massapê, do Assentamento Massapê, em Mombaça. Na competição feminina, a decisão será entre Mulungu, do Assentamento Mulungu, em Tururu, e Meninas do 25, do Assentamento 25 de Maio, em Madalena.
A Copa
Nesta edição, a Copa reuniu 150 equipes e mais de 3 mil atletas nas categorias masculina e feminina, vindos de assentamentos e acampamentos da Reforma Agrária espalhados por 36 municípios de todas as regiões do Ceará.
Os jogos foram disputados em fases. A competição começou na etapa municipal, passou pela regional e seguiu pelas quartas de final e semifinais. Agora, as duas melhores equipes de cada categoria disputam o título.
Joel Gomes, coordenador geral da 4ª Copa e Feira Estadual da Reforma Agrária, destaca que a Copa e Feira estadual das áreas de Reforma Agrária do Ceará é uma ação de grande significado, considerando que é construída a partir de concepções de esporte e lazer, de perspectiva crítica, formativa e integradora a outras dimensões como a agroecologia e o enfrentamento às violências.
“Com palavras de ordem estampadas nas camisas, chama a atenção dos territórios para o compromisso com outras relações entre as pessoas e com a terra. Outro aspecto importante é a reafirmação do esporte como direito humano, com importante potencial de mobilização e participação dos sujeitos, homens e mulheres, em sua execução”, informa Gomes.
O evento é realizado pelo Governo do Estado do Ceará, por meio da Secretaria do Esporte (Sesporte). A execução é da Associação de Cooperação Agrícola do Estado do Ceará (ACACE), com apoio do Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST).
