GOAL! Leeds United 1-0 Tottenham (Okafor 79)
Premier League: It’s been in the post and Noah Okafor delivers for Leeds United, less than two minutes after being introduced from the bench. Harry Wilson, who came on at the same time as him, provided the assist. The goal survives a VAR check for handball in the build-up.
Championship: Stoke have turned things around at Fratton Park, where Ben Wilmot has scored their second to put them 2-1 up against Portsmouth. At Ashton Gate, Norwich now lead Bristol City 5-0 courtesy of a Mathias Kvistgaarden spot-kick.
Premier League: It’s still scoreless between Leeds United and Tottenham at Elland Road, where Spurs are second best and Antonin Kinsky has just pulled off an excellent save to deny Leeds midfielder Sean Longstaff. There are 13 minutes of normal time remaining and Scott Murray has the latest …
An email: “As a USA born Stoke supporter who came into the whole thing in 2008 during the elder Delap era, it does the soul good to see fellow countryman Jack McGlynn come over from MLS and bang them in,” writes Joshua Reynolds.
Championship: Free-scoring Norwich are piling the pain on Bristol City, with Jovon Makama getting in on the goalscoring action to make it 4-0 to the visitors at Ashton Gate. It’s the 22-year-old’s second goal in as many games and his side’s 11th in a week, following last Saturday’s 3-2 win over Watford and Tuesday’s 4-0 victory at Derby County.
Everton 3-1 Coventry City
Premier League: Thierno Barry scored twice as Everton made the most of some benevolent officiating to come from behind, beat Coventry City and go fifth in the table. Andy Hunter reports from Hill Dickinson Stadium.
FA Cup first round
In yesterday’s Football Daily email, John Brewin previewed his pick of the weekend’s first round games featuring the return of his beloved Macc, a 40-year-old cult hero lining up for the lowest ranked team in the competition and the club that purports to be the oldest in London. Read on …
For the FA Cup, the early rounds are the juice. The first round proper to be played out over the long weekend is looking, well, proper. And on Saturday at 3pm GMT, a proper time, 31 ties will kick off. No VAR, either. At the stage when the bottom two Football League divisions join the competition, focus remains on those non-league clubs fighting for the honour of the pyramid …
Mansfield v Macclesfield 
  
In January, Macclesfield achieved the greatest shock in the competition’s history, knocking out the holders, Crystal Palace, in the third round. John Rooney’s National League North team head through the Pennines to face soundalikes Mansfield. Those from Macclesfield often find themselves having to correct others on coming from the Cheshire town rather than the one in Nottinghamshire. Macclesfield are such a modern club these days they have a sporting director in Keith Curle, a former Stags manager. Curle and current Mansfield boss Nigel Clough were England teammates at Euro 92, of which the less said the better.
Bradford City v Marine
  
Merseyside’s most authentic, proper football club? Neither Everton nor Liverpool can compete with Crosby’s Marine. When modern football gets too much, the temptation to savour a pie and pint at Rossett Park, the club of Roly Howard, legendary manager for 33 years, becomes strong. On Saturday, Marine travel to Bradford City, on something of a slide since Graham Alexander de-camped to manage Preston.
Burton v AFC Rushden & Diamonds
  
Fans at Burton’s Pirelli Stadium will see Billy Sharp’s comeback at 76. One of the Football League’s very top marksmen, the Championship’s all-time scorer on 130 recently retired but has returned with AFC Rushden & Diamonds, the phoenix club of a former temporary employer for whom he scored his first goal when loaned there in 2005, before they were liquidated six years later. A striker who defines the term “well-travelled” – including a spell at LA Galaxy – blink and you will miss Sharp, as the prodigal return is for one game only, in search of his 300th career goal. He departed Doncaster on the tantalising total of 299.
Plymouth Argyle v Alvechurch 
  
Alvechurch, representing a Worcestershire village, was previously most famous for giving the world Alan “Smudger” Smith (incidentally another member of that Euro 92 squad). The less said about his substitution for old pal Gary Lineker against Sweden the better. Smith’s alma mater, in the Southern League, travel to Plymouth Argyle, led by Tom Cleverley, the former brand turned aspirant tracksuit manager. Two seasons ago the Pilgrims’ progress down to League One was offset by beating eventual Premier League champions Liverpool in the third round. Should that fall flat, the city gets another helping on Monday night when Parkway take on Berkhamsted, the commuter town’s community club.
Cray Wanderers v Stockport County
 
Representing the Isthmian League are Cray Wanderers, who claim to be London’s oldest football club, whose origins are traced to 1860, older perhaps than even Notts County. Playing in Chislehurst, best known for its caves, “The Wands” take on high-flying League One Stockport County, led by The Wire’s Jimmy McNulty.
Peterborough v Reading
  
All that and a Savage family reunion as the Posh, managed by Robbie, host son Charlie’s team, the Royals. The Cup properly runneth over.

Championship: Harry Darling has doubled Norwich City’s lead at Bristol City, making it 2-0 for the Canaries v the Robins in the Battle of the Songbirds.

Beyond the top flight, there’s plenty of Championship action to keep us entertained, while there are no fewer than 33 FA Cup first round matches slated for today. 89 min: Wilson steps across Tonali, who swings an arm to bring him down and picks up a booking.
88 min: Meanwhile, Leeds are doing a marvellous job of containing Spurs, who are trying to respond, but can’t get anywhere near their opponents’ box. Leeds’ xG is now exactly 2 to Tottenham’s 0.28.
87 min: No, is the answer to that. Not a single one.
86 min: TNT are interviewing Nmecha as the game goes on, a box popping up and invading the action. Did any football fan ask for this sort of thing?
84 min: Kudus makes way for the 18-year-old Williams-Barnett. When the game restarts, Calvert-Lewin once again tears clear down the right, but doesn’t back himself to shoot, turning around instead and laying off to Okafor. The move breaks down. That’s a couple of big chances butchered by Calvert-Lewin today.
82 min: Spurs haven’t won any of their last 49 matches in which they’ve gone behind. No wonder Roberto De Zerbi looks thoroughly miserable. That goal was no more than Leeds deserved; they’ve been by far the better team in this second half.
80 min: VAR has a look at a possible handball by Wilson, but there was no touch with his arm. The goal stands!
GOAL! Leeds United 1-0 Tottenham Hotspur (Okafor 79)
Bard throws in from the left. Wilson swivels just inside the box, chesting down and teeing up Okafor, who takes a touch infield before lashing a shot across Kinsky and into the bottom left! Lovely move, and what a substitution!
77 min: Kinsky annoys Longstaff again by pawing his corner clear. Then Leeds make a double change, sending on Wilson and Okafor for Tanaka and Nmecha.
76 min: … but Spurs don’t clear their lines particularly well, and Tanaka strides down the left to win another Leeds corner. Longstaff, who must be wondering how he didn’t score, to take.
75 min: Bogle advances down the right and crosses low for Longstaff, who turns and launches a rising shot goalwards from 12 yards. It’s a superb effort, and heading in, but met by the fingertips of Kinsky. What a save! The ball clears the bar, and nothing comes of the corner.
73 min: Kulusevski and Bentancur combine down the right, but at such slow speed that Leeds close down all avenues to their box. Spurs have not created very much this afternoon.
71 min: From the set piece, Bogle shoots. The ball hits Bentancur. Leeds claim a penalty, but that’s hit Bentancur on the chest. No sir!
70 min: Bard loops down the middle. Nmecha tries to loop over Kinsky, who tips onto the bar. But he was offside. Then Calvert-Lewin fails to hit the target. But Kinsky takes his sweet time over the restart, so the referee awards a corner to Leeds!
68 min: Spurs play some possession stuff. They don’t really go anywhere for a while, but suddenly spring into action, Gallagher bringing the ball down on the edge of the Leeds D before pearling a low drive inches wide of the bottom left. Not entirely sure Trafford was getting to that. Spurs fans thought that was in, so are jeered for their cheer not long after.
66 min: … so Spurs make a triple change, replacing the ineffective Marmoush and Fernandes, plus Porro, who is on one-and-a-half yellows, with Kulusevski, Bentancur and Gallagher. Gray will take over from Porro at right-back.
64 min: Leeds have had seven attempts on goal during this second half. Spurs are yet to generate a single one.
63 min: Calvert-Lewin, Bard and Longstaff combine well down the left. The ball’s rolled infield for Ampadu, who shoots from 25 yards. The ball takes a huge deflection to the left, and had it stayed on target, it was a goal, because Kinsky had committed to diving the other way. But it squeaks out for a corner, which Kinsky claims. Leeds are getting closer and closer.
62 min: Van de Ven again over-eggs his dribble out from the back. This time he loses the ball, allowing Nmecha to enter the box from the left and aim a curler towards the top right. It’s not a good effort, and easily blocked.
61 min: Leeds are romping ahead in the xG stakes. It’s 1.11 to 0.22.
60 min: Porro clips Bard, who was advancing down the left, from behind. It should be a yellow. It’s not, though, presumably because it would have been a second yellow for Porro, and you know how referees process that sort of situation. Porro is now in the last-chance saloon. Meanwhile nothing comes of the resulting free kick.
58 min: The pace doesn’t drop, but passes are no longer sticking. All a bit messy for now.
56 min: Van de Ven over-elaborates when dribbling out from the back, and is nearly stripped by Longstaff. Had the Leeds man completed the challenge, he was through on goal. Van de Ven breathes out.
55 min: Tonali, dropping deep, tries to release Kudus down the right but has to settle for a corner. Kudus ambles across to take it. He exchanges passes with Solanke, then Robertson finally crosses long. Leeds deal with it. A bit of a waste.
53 min: Calvert-Lewin romps into space down the inside-right channel, chasing a fine Longstaff pass. He should shoot upon reaching the area, but lays off to Tanaka instead, who leans back and skies over the bar. Huge chance spurned.
52 min: Porro slides in, over the ball, and catches Nmecha on the shin. It’s a yellow. It should be a yellow. But Bogle’s far worse action in the first half should have been that at the very least. Roberto De Zerbi highlights this inherent contradiction, and is also booked for his trouble. Consistency? Good luck in your search for that.
50 min: Bogle crosses from the right. Calvert-Lewin prepares to sidefoot home from six yards, only for Van de Ven to nip in ahead of him, and slice the ball over his own bar and wide left. Then from the corner, hit long by Longstaff, Calvert-Lewin heads goalwards. Solanke blocks on his own line, then Elvedi heads wide left from close range. It should be 1-0.
48 min: Ampadu throws long from the right. Van de Ven clears. Leeds have had no joy with their long-throw weapon so far.
46 min: Bard’s very first act is to whip in a glorious low cross from his position on the left. Calvert-Lewin is on his heels and can’t connect. That was begging to be rammed home.
Leeds get the second half started. They’ve replaced Gudmundsson with Bard.
Half-time postbag. “Both feet are off the ground. That’s Bogle’s entire weight on Tel’s Achilles. That can lead to a serious injury. Bizarre decision” – Martin Perring
“Why do red cards exist if not precisely to protect players?” – John from Norway
“The most insane thing about VAR, and there are so many insane things about it, is that we have to watch replays of a player OBVIOUSLY doing a red-card challenge one thousand times in slow-motion, and it ends with not even a yellow. The chicken-shit nature of it all, the incompetence, all elevated because of technology. I hate it so, so much” – Øivind Idsø
“There’s overthinking it, as you say, but this is like they’ve been given a task to find a reason for not giving that as a red, rocking and rolling desperately, frame-by-frame. The explanation they release for not giving a red should be a corker. Meanwhile, whatever happened to ‘clear and obvious’? VAR is almost single-handedly turning me into a grumpy old man. I’ll be off out now to shout at some pigeons” – Rob Knap
“I’ve supported VAR from the start. It was always going to have teething issues as it was implemented, and it was never going to 100% eliminate mistakes. Subjectivity is still a thing. But, my word, they don’t half make it hard to defend at times. It should be established now, a mature technology with most of the errors ironed out. If anything, though, It’s getting worse. I’m not in the ‘Bin it’ camp yet, but I’m a lot closer than I was at the start of the season” – Matt Dony
“Committees are an extremely useful method for decision making, especially when people have time to deliberate. But perhaps football refereeing isn’t suited to committees” – Kári Tulinius
“That would have been a red card at Elland Road in the 70s” – Gary Naylor
HALF TIME: Leeds United 0-0 Tottenham Hotspur
Leeds should have had a penalty; they should also have had a man sent off. The players walk down the tunnel. The referee was planning to drive away in his car, but the doors and square wheels have fallen off and there’s all smoke coming out of the radiator.
45 min +5: Ampadu throws long from the left. Van Hecke powers a header miles clear. Ampadu has another go. Van Hecke batters clear again. The xG does not change.
45 min +4: The xG, for what that’s worth, is 0.19 to 0.22. Meanwhile Roberto De Zerbi continues to give the fourth official the what-for. His post-match interview could make for good entertainment.
45 min +2: Fernandes slices a low drive miles off target. After nearly boiling over, this half is now fizzling out, which is probably for the best all round.
45 min: There will be six minutes of additional first-half time, most of which a result of the on-field referee and VAR spending ages failing to make a decision.
44 min: Kudus fizzes a tempting low cross through the Leeds six-yard box from the right. What a ball. But neither Gray nor Solanke respond. Any touch and it was the opening goal.
43 min: Tel limps off. A heavy trudge, he’s in some difficulty. He’s replaced by Solanke.
42 min: Marmoush clips Muharemovic from behind. That should be a booking as well, but the referee has lost control of this with his unwillingness to make any sort of decision whatsoever. Meanwhile Tel goes down, he looks really unhappy.
40 min: Tel is getting dog’s abuse now. He’s also moving very gingerly, having recently had someone stand on his ankle.
39 min: Roberto De Zerbi isn’t happy about that. You can’t blame him. Meanwhile the game restarts, with Bogle, who shouldn’t be on the pitch, crossing for Nmencha, who plants a header straight at Kinsky. Had that gone in, there would have been some wild scenes all right.
38 min: No red card, no serious foul play. That is preposterous enough in itself; that there’s not even a yellow is beyond a joke. The on-field referee should have seen that, at the very least.
37 min: VAR is flapping taking a long time over this. You can overthink these things, you know.
36 min: It’s a really poor challenge, studs landing on Tel’s achilles, the Spurs player’s leg bending. It should be a red card.
35 min: VAR is in fact checking for a red card. The on-field referee, it should be noted, has completely abdicated responsibility.
34 min: Bogle leaves one on Tel, who was in the process of spinning him. It’s a really poor challenge, studs on ankle. A red card wouldn’t be out of the question here; there’s not even a yellow shown.
33 min: A long pass down the left confuses Elvedi into conceding a corner with a misjudged backwards header. One corner leads to another, then Marmoush heads harmlessly wide. To be fair, Trafford has had next to nothing to do as well, if you ignore a couple of long-range shots scuffed straight at him.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.author: Christian Lelek
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.text:
- Berlin
- Berlin
Stillstand am Fließband
Noch keine Lösung im Tarifkonflikt der Metall- und Elektroindustrie. In Berlin und Brandenburg ist die IG Metall offen für phasenweisen Lohnverzicht.
Es scheinen vor allem die Arbeitgeber zu sein, die in den Angriffsmodus geschaltet haben. »Die IG Metall schürt bei ihren Leuten Erwartungen von einem anderen Stern«, schäumte Henning Brandes, Verhandlungsführer des Verbands der Metall- und Elektroindustrie in Berlin und Brandenburg (VME). Und weiter: »Mit Plakaten und Trillerpfeifen wird es nicht gelingen, die Probleme unserer Branche aus der Welt zu schaffen. Das gelingt nur am Verhandlungstisch.«
An diesem waren zuvor am Freitag die Verhandlungen zwischen dem VME und der IG Metall ergebnislos zu Ende gegangen. Die ganze Woche über hatte die IG Metall zahlreiche Betriebe bestreikt, auch noch am Freitag. Bis zur Wochenmitte zählte die Gewerkschaft 7000 Mitglieder, die ihre Arbeit mindestens zeitweise niedergelegt hatten.
Die Arbeitgeber verbreiteten ihrerseits düstere Zukunftsperspektiven. Den Abbau von branchenweit 300.000 Jobs stellte Gesamtmetall für die kommenden zwei bis drei Jahre in Aussicht und damit mit 3,4 Millionen Beschäftigten den niedrigsten Stand in dieser Branche seit der Wiedervereinigung. Seit 2019 seien bereits 350.000 Arbeitsplätze abgebaut worden. Wie zur Bestätigung hatte nur einen Tag vorher der Autozulieferer Schaeffler den Abbau von Arbeitsplätzen hauptsächlich in Deutschland verkündet. Der Standort in Berlin, wo unter anderem Elektromotoren und Antriebstechnologien entwickelt werden, soll komplett schließen. Dadurch fallen 259 Stellen weg.
Die Arbeitgeber führen ihre Zurückhaltung in der laufenden Tarifrunde auf die fortwährende Krise zurück: fehlende Aufträge, steigende Kosten und immer schärfere Konkurrenz aus dem Ausland. »Die extrem schwierige Lage bei dem Großteil unserer Betriebe verbietet es, Arbeit noch weiter zu verteuern«, sagte VME-Verhandlungsführer Brandes. »Die Strukturprobleme lassen sich nicht wegstreiken.«
Die IG Metall hält das bisherige Vorgehen der Arbeitgeber für das falsche Krisenmanagement. »Verzicht ist keine Zukunftsstrategie und sichert keinen Arbeitsplatz und keinen Standort. Das geht nur mit Investitionen und Innovationen in die Werke bei uns in der Region«, sagte Jan Otto, Leiter des Bezirks Berlin-Brandenburg-Sachsen.
Nichtsdestotrotz legte die IG Metall am Freitag ein Konzept vor, mit dem »Investitionen in Zukunftsprodukte mit verbindlichen Zusagen für Standorte, Arbeitsplätze und Ausbildung verbunden werden«. Eine Tarifforderung der IG Metall ist die Absicherung von Standorten und Arbeitsplätzen. Das nun vorgelegte Konzept soll als Tarifvertrag für klar begrenzte Fälle vereinbart werden. Wie ein Sprecher auf Nachfrage von »nd« mitteilte, müssten Details hierzu noch ausverhandelt werden. Aus Sicht der IG Metall könne das aber auch den phasenweisen Verzicht auf Teile des Lohns bedeuten.
Während die IG Metall am einen Ende auf schwache Unternehmen Rücksicht nehmen will, fordert sie von profitablen Unternehmen für ihre Mitglieder eine Gewinnbeteiligung. Das Bild der Arbeitgeber von einer »Krise überall« entspreche nicht der Realität, sagte der IG Metall-Sprecher weiter.
Die Gewerkschaft verweist auch mit Blick auf ihre Lohnforderungen auf sich bessernde Konjunkturprognosen. Das bisherige Angebot der Arbeitgeber, die Gehälter erst im Juli 2028 um 1,3 Prozent anzuheben, bezeichnete Bezirksleiter Otto als ein »freches Minus-Angebot«, das hinter die allgemeinen Preissteigerungen zurückfalle. Die IG Metall war mit einer Forderung von fünf Prozent mehr Gehalt bei einer Vertragslaufzeit von zwölf Monaten in die Tarifrunde gegangen.
Die Arbeitgeber bezeichneten ihren Vorschlag als ein Zeichen des Entgegenkommens. Sie wiesen darauf hin, dass es erst im April dieses Jahres 3,1 Prozent mehr Geld für die 96.000 Beschäftigten in Berlin und Brandenburg gegeben habe.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

Le sénateur PCF des Bouches-du-Rhône Jeremy Bacchi demande l’amnistie pour les « lycéens victimes de sanctions administratives » dans le cadre du mouvement social en cours. Il a écrit au ministre de l’Éducation nationale. « Dans plusieurs établissements, des directions ont prononcé ou s’apprêtent à prononcer des sanctions administratives impliquant l’inscription d’avertissements dans les dossiers scolaires à l’encontre de jeunes ayant participé à des actions de mobilisation ou s’étant trouvés à l’extérieur des grilles de l’établissement malgré des interdictions préfectorales ou de direction », dénonce Jeremy Bacchi dans sa missive à Edouard Geffray.
« Qualifier d’absences injustifiées des actes d’engagements de la jeunesse et les assortir d’un avertissement porté au dossier scolaire constitue une réponse d’une extrême gravité », critique le dirigeant communiste, qui s’inquiète de sanctions « notifiées de manière immédiate » sans « instruction » qui permette « de faire valoir le principe du contradictoire ». Aussi demande-t-il de garantir le respect des procédures.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: Why are oil traders refusing to buy Russian diesel after Trump-Putin deal?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Why are oil traders refusing to buy Russian diesel after Trump-Putin deal?
Zero Russian diesel has reached the US under the deal as buyers fear legal action, with Congress’s ban on Russian energy imports still in place.
At least three tankers carrying Russian diesel to the United States have changed course, casting doubt over US President Donald Trump’s October deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin.
Nearly a month after Trump agreed to let Russia release diesel stocks to the US and global markets, despite existing sanctions, zero diesel has reached the US, where prices have nearly doubled since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Russia has sent out a total of four tankers loaded with diesel since the deal was agreed.
Here’s what we know.
What’s happened to tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US?
The Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leone-flagged Leruo left the Baltic port of Primorsk last month, with the US East Coast as their declared destination.
As of Thursday, however, one was heading towards Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to marine analytics firm Kpler and the vessel-tracking site MarineTraffic.
A third tanker, still in the North Atlantic, has changed its destination from New York to “for orders”, leaving its unloading point open.
The Financial Times also reported that Beast, a sanctioned Seychelles-owned tanker that was loaded at the Russian port of Primorsk in late October, has set sail towards the US and is currently signalling “Atlantic”.
What did Trump and Putin agree?
A deal big on numbers, but scant on details.
Trump first announced the agreement following a call with Putin on October 9. He said Russia would make more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel available immediately to US and global markets.
Long-range product tankers, which carry diesel supplies, can carry up to about 100,000 tonnes of diesel at a time.
Another 500,000 tonnes would follow in November, then 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
The agreement Trump brokered with Putin allows Russian diesel to be sold, delivered, unloaded and imported until April 7. It came after Trump blamed Ukraine for causing diesel shortages by targeting Russian energy facilities amid the Russia-Ukraine war.
It also reversed years of US policy after Washington banned imports of Russian energy following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the US Department of the Treasury has since issued a temporary sanctions exemption, much to the ire of a cross-party group of lawmakers in the US Congress who passed a new sanctions package in the name of the late, pro-Ukraine Senator Lindsey Graham in September.
In a statement to the AP news agency, the Treasury said the exemption was “in compliance with all applicable laws”.
Russia announced its first shipment of diesel during a visit to St Petersburg in October by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.
Yet much about the deal remains unclear.
Neither the White House nor the Kremlin has said whether the agreement was put in writing, and neither has revealed the price to be paid for the diesel, the payment terms or which companies are involved.
How much Russian diesel is now waiting to be sold?
It’s not clear exactly, but it’s less than was promised.
The volumes involved have not been made public, but analysts say the first shipment is unlikely to deliver meaningful relief to US consumers.
US retail diesel prices topped $6 a gallon ($1.59 per litre) in September – nearly twice their pre-war levels – and have remained elevated.
“The reported shipment is equivalent to roughly two hours of US distillate consumption,” Aarathi Krishnan, CEO of Raksha Intelligence, told Al Jazeera, referring to the first tanker to be dispatched by Russia.
“Even if it arrives as planned, it will make very little difference to national supply,” he said.
Why don’t traders want to buy Russian diesel?
Because of the legal risk.
Despite the US Treasury temporarily authorising Russian diesel sales that would normally fall under sanctions, Congress’s ban on Russian energy imports remains in place, leaving a high level of uncertainty for traders.
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill wrote to port and terminal operators in her state on Monday, telling them to turn away ships carrying the fuel.
She warned that “any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.”
Sherrill argued the Trump administration had no authority to override the ban.
Lawmakers have also warned banks, port authorities and fuel distributors that handling the imports could expose them to civil or criminal liability, as well as future congressional investigations.
The Trump administration claims the exemption is lawful, and no court has ruled on the dispute.
“It’s clear there’s hesitancy here in bringing these barrels onshore just because of the implications of doing so,” Matt Smith, an analyst at Kpler, told AP.
Where will the diesel go now?
Probably not to the US, experts say.
The first two diverted tankers are heading towards Brazil and the Mediterranean, according to Kpler data, and the third tanker could follow.
“Because of regulatory [and] sanctions concerns, we may not see this cargo discharge on the US Atlantic coast,” Smith told AP.
Moscow, however, insists the deal is on track.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said “all the diesel will find its buyers.”
Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, went further, writing on X that the reports were “fake” and “tankers destined for the US continue on course.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: Qeshm island and Hormuz hit, as mediators try to prevent US-Iran escalation
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Qeshm island and Hormuz hit, as mediators try to prevent US-Iran escalation
US strikes have continued on Iran after more ships in the Strait of Hormuz were attacked.
Tehran, Iran – The United States has bombed Iran after vessels were targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, as mediators continue to try to prevent large-scale fighting between the two countries.
Two projectiles hit Iran’s Qeshm on Friday night, the latest in a series of air strikes on the southern island over recent weeks targeting Iranian air defences and launchers. President Donald Trump called them “minor strikes”, amid increasing concerns of a potential escalation in the war between the countries.
Iran’s army said in the early hours of Saturday that it destroyed a US-made MQ-9 drone using an unnamed new system. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) separately claimed on Friday that its air defences intercepted an MQ-1, reportedly the 16th aircraft of this model to be destroyed since the start of the war.
At least 11 ships were attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the week ending on November 6, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which said three of them sank. The Western military intelligence agency has recorded 88 projectile strikes since hostilities resumed in early July, although it has cautioned that most attacks are going unreported.
UKMTO’s weekly report also identified 170 outbound and 155 inbound transits in the Strait of Hormuz, approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels. Most of the vessels that travel with their transponders switched on are using the Iranian route to the north. But many ships are still attempting the southern route near Oman with their tracking systems offline to shuttle oil out of the waterway.
Iranian armed forces also claim that, in addition to being hit with missiles and drones, tankers and commercial vessels using “unauthorised” routes also run the risk of being hit by naval mines.
The Iranian military’s naval force said on Saturday that a tanker with its transponder turned off caught fire in the eastern area of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine. Washington says the mines have been cleared.
No range limit on missiles
For years, the IRGC maintained that it was limiting the range of its ballistic missiles to about 2,000 kilometres (1,240 miles) to reassure European countries that they would not be targeted.
But with Trump threatening to resume extensive air strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure, commanders say nothing is off limits now.
“This limitation has been lifted for us,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told reporters during an event on Saturday, in reference to missile range constraints.
His comments came after Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered an unrestrained military response to any future threats from Israel and the US. Iran’s aerospace division of the IRGC has prepared “surprising defence achievements” that will be deployed in action if another wave of major attacks starts, he added.
“The operational unveiling of these [advanced] achievements in case of new conflict will not only frustrate and fascinate enemies, but will further solidify Iran’s military authority on the global stage, make the resistance front happy, and fully neutralise aggressors’ calculations,” Mohebbi said.
The spokesman said the IRGC plans to unveil another underground “missile city” soon, and will deploy some combat systems to public spaces so the people can personally inspect them.
Mohebbi added that if the Islamic republic decides to alter its nuclear doctrine and build a bomb, the necessary preparations will be made.
On state television’s war-focused Be Vaght-e Iran (At Iran’s Time) programme over the weekend, presenters and analysts said Iranian armed forces had their fingers on the trigger and were especially eyeing any movement from Israel.
“Our military information about the strategic chokepoints of Israel is complete. If our water, electricity and natural gas is cut off, they will also be plunged into darkness and lack of water,” one analyst said. “This is not a bluff, but a serious warning.”
‘Pendulum swing between war and talks’
Over recent weeks, diplomatic efforts by mediators to avoid attacks that could damage the entire region have picked up, although with limited gains.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that he held talks with 12 foreign ministers over the past 48 hours, including top diplomats from Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
He said he explained the “fundamental positions” of Tehran, including the seven demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and stressed the need to form “regional security arrangements without the interference of superregional powers”.
Security chief Mohsen Rezaei reportedly emphasised the same conditions to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a visit to Moscow on Thursday, which was also aimed at delivering a message from Khamenei.
Developments between Iran and the US resemble a “constant pendulum swing between war and negotiations” that is increasingly leaning towards conflict, according to political analyst Mostafa Najafi, who is said to be close to Iran’s security chief.
“What is clear for now is that the movement of this pendulum will continue; a conflict whose ending is much more complicated and time-consuming than imagined,” he wrote on X. The historic defeat for Trump and the Republicans in US midterm elections this week may further complicate the picture, he added.
Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said three factors increase the risk of war in the short term after the elections, unless negotiations lead to a breakthrough.
The political cost of high fuel prices, brought about largely due to the war on Iran, has already been paid, he said, and there won’t be another point on the political calendar soon for Trump to worry about this issue.
“On the one hand, the pressure to get a deal will dissipate,” he told Al Jazeera.
Pressure from pro-war hawks will also escalate significantly because they will be constrained in their efforts to step up the conflict after the Democrats take control of Congress in early January. The appointment of far-right, pro-Israel hawk Stephen Miller as chief of staff also hints that Trump might not be ready to wind down the war.
“Finally, there is a new psychological element to Trump’s mindset following this humiliation: Trump’s desire for vengeance. There has been a vindictive element to his calculations in the past weeks because of his anger over how Iran – in Trump’s mind – has ruined his presidency,” Parsi said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Dozens killed as humanitarian crisis mounts in Yemen: What next for war?
Government forces reclaim key territories in Taiz and Lahij but face setbacks under Houthi resistance in certain areas.
Dozens were killed in Yemen on Friday when a missile struck a market in Taiz governorate, with each side of Yemen’s brutal war blaming the other for the attack.
It has been a month since Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched its “Dawn of Yemen” offensive on the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel group after it took swaths of territory along the country’s Red Sea coast.
As the fighting continues, the humanitarian crisis is only intensifying, with hundreds of thousands displaced so far.
Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council has said the government will continue with its “irreversible” drive to dismantle Houthi military capacity and restore sovereignty, meaning the war may get worse before there is any resolution, observers say.
Here’s what we know.
What is Operation Dawn of Yemen?
The operation was launched by the head of the Presidential Leadership Council of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Rashad al-Alimi, on October 5.
Its aim is to recapture areas under Houthi control and liberate the capital city of Sanaa, which has been under the rebels’ control since September 2014.
The operation has relied on air support from the Saudi-led coalition, as well as ground operations carried out by government military coalitions and units to weaken the Houthis’ military capabilities.
In the Red Sea corridor, breaking the Houthis’ maritime chokehold and securing the Bab al-Mandeb strait has been an essential goal after the group captured the strategic port city of Mocha (Mokha) in September.
How much territory have the government forces taken back?
After launching the operation, the government said its forces recaptured positions around Dhubab and Bab al-Mandeb the same day, though the extent of their gains could not be confirmed.
It also said they captured mountain positions in Haifan, western Taiz and around al-Waziiya.
By October 13, fighting spread to Marib, where the government forces claimed gains around the Maas camp and north of Harib.
It did, however, lose territory in Taiz governorate, which led to a Houthi siege that continues to suffocate the city as it reaches its first month.
On Friday, the government forces said they had recaptured many areas in the governorate, including al-Nidani village, Shaab al-Sarari, large parts of the Sanamat area and the Ribat al-Qarn area in Dhi al-Barh in Taiz governorate.
Government troops and coalition fighters also secured the Tavat Wathib and Habil al-Saram hills along the Al-Aqroud front.
They announced the execution of 1,211 operations against Houthi positions on the different battlefronts, as they confirmed control over new positions on the Tur al-Bahah front in the Lahij governorate.
However, government forces are far from being able to take back Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, Thomas Bonnie James, an assistant professor in politics and international relations at Aberdeen University in the United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.
“[Defeat] won’t happen if it means taking back Sanaa and ending Houthi rule. Not any time soon,” he said. “The government’s forces look big on paper, but they are spread across too many fronts and use old equipment.
“Sanaa is surrounded by mountains, which makes it easy to defend. A much stronger Saudi-Emirati coalition tried from 2015 and never came close,” he explained.
What else has the government achieved since the operation began?
James told Al Jazeera that Dawn of Yemen’s aim is to apply pressure to, rather than achieve the total defeat of, the Houthis.
“Dawn of Yemen is better understood as a way to apply pressure than as a bid for total victory,” he said. “The aim is to make the war more costly for the Houthis and to give Saudi Arabia a stronger position before any peace deal.
“What happens in the next three months matters more than the slogans.”
The Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council announced on Thursday that the armed forces have carried out 40,761 military operations since the beginning of Dawn of Yemen.
The council also said the attacks resulted in the “neutralisation” of about 20,000 Houthi leaders and elements, and more than 5,000 vehicles.
Previous announcements from the military command said they conducted 17,000 targeting operations during their first weeks and daily figures ranging between 951 and 1,272 operations throughout the month.
Last month, the Yemeni government also said its forces were able to kill or wound 1,540 Houthis in 24 hours.
Last week, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.
The Houthis did say that the total number of attacks the group has been subjected to since the beginning of the escalation reached 3,930 raids and missiles up until early November.
Al Jazeera has not been able to verify these figures.
How are the Houthis striking back?
The Houthis, who are also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have caused hundreds of casualties since the beginning of the escalation.
Yemen’s government forces have blamed the Houthis for an attack on the al-Hadara market on Friday in the Taiz governorate that killed and injured dozens, mostly civilians.
Government military spokesperson, Colonel Majed al-Nazili, said the “terrorist” Houthis hit the market with ballistic missiles, calling it a war crime.
The Iran-backed Houthis rejected the accusation and said Saudi Arabia, which backs the Yemeni government, was responsible for the attack.
After taking the capital and state institutions in 2014, the Houthis have had access to a large number of weapons that once belonged to the Yemeni military.
Analysts say with the external support from Iran and their reliance on international black markets, the Houthis’ military capabilities continued to advance.
Their increasingly long-range missile strikes have allowed them to reach many areas across Saudi Arabia and even Israel in June.
One of the Houthis’ latest deadly attacks killed at least 70 government security recruits in Shabwah.
How is this affecting people in Yemen?
As the government and the Houthis continue fighting, the humanitarian situation in Yemen is heading towards catastrophe.
More than 323,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the escalation began in August, with Taiz governorate taking in most of them, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported on Friday.
More than two in five of the internally displaced in Yemen are in Taiz, where the Houthi blockade continues to encircle the city, cutting off supplies to about 800,000 people.
The UN Human Rights Office has reported 281 civilian casualties since August, with 69 people killed and 212 injured. Children make up more than one-third of casualties.
In Taiz, Salah Ahmed Ghaleb al-Majidi, acting director of the governorate’s Siege Affairs Department, described the situation to Al Jazeera as “catastrophic”.
Essentials, including medical supplies, food, fuel and water, are unable to reach the governorate due to the Houthi blockade.
An Al Jazeera report found that the remaining diesel stocks in the city have dwindled and have less than 48 hours left to run.
Hospitals are warning that once they run out of fuel, departments and medical centres will have to shut down, including emergency services.
Taiz’s deputy governor for health affairs, Ilan Abdul Haw, told Al Jazeera that about 40 percent of hospitals have closed, while those still open are operating at 50 percent capacity due to the lack of fuel.
What next for this war?
James told Al Jazeera that as the winter approaches in Yemen, and the siege on Taiz tightens, conditions will only worsen for Yemenis caught in the conflict.
“The biggest worry is the people of Taiz. More than 800,000 of them have been cut off from aid since the Houthis surrounded the city in early October,” he said. “Winter is coming, aid money is short, and the city is under siege. That is what more fighting will mean for ordinary Yemenis.”
The war has also spread beyond Yemen, as the Houthis continue strikes on Saudi airports and oil sites.
“The Houthis are firing at Saudi almost every day. Saudi Arabia is now openly bombing inside Yemen again for the first time since 2022,” James said. “Both sides are hitting where it hurts most, and that is how wars get bigger”.
Other fighting in the region could also pull Yemen into a wider war, and vice versa, as the US-Israel war on Iran remains in a deadlock, James told Al Jazeera.
“Yemen is now tied to the wider conflict with Iran. If the US strikes Iran again, Iran will want to use the Houthis to put more pressure on Saudi Arabia,” he said.

Nepal’s fight to rebuild after flood disaster
101 East reveals Nepal’s efforts to save lives and rebuild communities after a devastating natural disaster.
On the morning of August 26, 2026, a devastating flash flood of rock and ice thundered from a high Himalayan mountain through Nepal’s valleys, sweeping away homes, villages and bridges.
At least 1,400 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing.
It was the latest in a series of natural disasters that have battered Nepal in recent years as climate change accelerates.
This programme follows the rescuers risking their lives to search for the missing and those providing aid and refuge for traumatised children and families.
101 East reveals Nepal’s efforts to save lives and rebuild communities after a deadly natural disaster.

https://www.theguardian.com/membership/2.title: ‘Some photos imprint upon us’: How our Saturday magazine puts together special issues about world-changing photographs
https://www.theguardian.com/membership/2.author: Gautam Malkani
https://www.theguardian.com/membership/2.text:
Can photographs still exert power in an age when millions of pictures are taken and shared every minute, and when a viewer’s first response is to question whether an image is even real?
Every few months, a team of editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine puts together a special photography package in print and digital formats. It features photographs that don’t just stop the scroll, they have also prompted the rewriting of history books. They are the kind of images that have changed the world in some way or radically shifted people’s perceptions.
Each issue has a particular theme. Earlier this month, the magazine featured photographs that have changed how we view masculinity – from a 1950 portrait of Marlon Brando in a white T-shirt to a paparazzi shot of David Beckham in a sarong and a bare-chested Vladimir Putin on horseback. Previous issues have focused on photographs that have reshaped sport, forced people to confront the reality of the climate crisis and upended the world of fashion.
Beyond the impact each image had back when it first came out, they still feel powerful and affecting today – reminding us how great photography can command a kind of reverence and stillness in the viewer. “Working on these issues, you realise that there’s something about the power of the images that’s elemental,” says Rebecca Liu, a commissioning editor on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine. “Some photos imprint upon us before we even can think about them. They just immediately hit our bloodstream.”
The first special issue featured protest images that have prompted social or political change. It was initially conceived as a one-off feature in 2022 amid protests in the US that year against the overturning of Roe v Wade and demonstrations against police brutality. But the feature resonated so strongly with readers that it spawned an occasional series.
That regularity means the process of putting the issues together is now fine-tuned, though not without its own drama and headaches. “Sometimes on the day of going to print we’re waiting on two or three final things to be confirmed,” says Rebecca. “It’s a massive act of organisation and coordination and a real collective effort with a lot of moving parts.”
Selecting which pictures to include involves tapping the collective minds of picture editors and journalists on the magazine and across the Guardian. Different colleagues will have different criteria. How to weigh up a photograph’s social or political impact against its technical importance to the medium? Should it be an image that, in itself, has changed the world or a photograph of a world-shifting moment?
“Everyone working on the magazine has a different take on it,” says Louis Siroy, the magazine’s deputy picture editor. “Some editors will ask how a particular photograph shaped society; what does it mean? Whereas I might be asking what are the important photographs or photographers that fit into that theme or category.”
For example, the first special issue about protest photography didn’t just include the famous image of a protestor standing in front of a tank in Tiananmen Square, it also included a less famous but equally powerful photograph of a boy sitting on the shoulders of relatives above the sea of soldiers’ helmets. Taken by the photographer Dario Mitidieri, the image was suggested by Louis. “That to me is a great photograph, and I was trying to bring something that wasn’t necessarily the image people are familiar with,” he says. “Hopefully these selections inspire people to value and appreciate the breadth and power of great photographs.”
By drawing on colleagues’ different perspectives and experience, each special issue sheds unique light on its theme. “So while the selection can’t possibly be comprehensive and definitive, it’s still authoritative,” says Rebecca.
Other images included in the initial protest photography issue include the famous picture of US athletes John Carlos and Tommie Smith raising their fists in a black power salute during a medal ceremony at the 1968 Olympics. There are also several photographs of protesters facing off against riot police or soldiers, including a powerful image of a young girl in Santiago, Chile, during a 2016 demonstration marking the anniversary of the country’s 1973 military coup.
One of the most time-consuming challenges involves obtaining the rights to publish the images. “Some of the greatest challenges involve finding the right copyright holder for some lesser-known photographs,” says Caroline Hunter, the magazine’s picture editor.
Even well-known photographs can present hurdles. “Sometimes you have to get permission from the subject of the photo as well as from the photographer, particularly when it comes to photos of celebrities or fashion,” explains Louis. “It can get really hard to track down the person you need. For instance, the masculinity special featured a famous second world war photo of a US aeroplane gunner that was taken by the photographer Horace Bristol, who is now deceased. It took some time to contact the photographer’s son Henri in California and explain the context in which we wanted to use the photo. And even when dealing with well-known photographers, it still involves negotiating the rights for editorial use rather than commercial use.”
Another challenge that can arise is the quality of the photographs. “We have to ensure the image is large enough or good enough quality to reproduce, especially for very old images that previously existed only as prints,” says Caroline. “Works by famous and art photographers often have specific rules around usage, so it’s important to ensure that we keep within their guidelines. We had a really good response from photographers after our recent photo special marking America at 250. I think this was because there were so many great, iconic images from seminal photographers.”
The team also has to decide the best layout for the print and digital editions – which images to give prominence to, how they might best fit together, and the range of black-and-white and colour images. Maggie Murphy, the magazine’s art director, experiments with different layouts, sometimes on a screen, sometimes with printouts strewn across the desks.
As well as the images, a huge amount of work goes into the words. Each special issue includes a short guest-written essay, and each photograph has an extended caption about that particular picture’s significance or backstory.
The journalists who are commissioned to write these captions undertake extensive research. For example, the masculinity issue includes a famous 1970 advertisement depicting a pregnant man, for which the journalist tracked down the original campaign’s photographer, who is now 98. “I encourage original interviews and research wherever possible,” says Rebecca. “We want the words to illuminate something about the picture and for people to learn things. That’s not something you necessarily have to do for a 150-word caption, but we want to do it because the editorial component is so important to us at the Guardian.”
Researching the captions also reveals something about the nature of photography. “It really shows the importance of not just taking an image at face value,” says Rebecca. “I’m always surprised by what you discover when you look into things. You might find a complicated backstory behind the person who is photographed – perhaps their ambivalence about being pictured, for instance.”
The same applies to the thought that goes into the introductory essays. The novelist Anne Enright wrote perceptively about how women are captured on camera, for better or for worse, in her introduction to an issue that featured photographs that have changed the way society sees women. “As you look at a Kardashian selfie, consider how many rules had to be broken to get her to this moment of self-commodification,” writes Enright.
The masculinity issue contains an accompanying essay by the poet and novelist Luke Kennard, who reflects on how the images seem to capture extremes of masculinity, with little in between: “To judge from our media, one would think we were either waifs or muscle-men… Even the bang average is barely represented.”
Rebecca noticed that gap in representation back when the team was initially selecting which photographs to include in the issue. “I remember thinking, where are the other male bodies? It was difficult to find any – at least with the quality and artistry that we look for in these stories. You’d Google the words ‘dad bod’ and you’d just get screenshots of Seth Rogen and grainy paparazzi shots of celebrities on the beach.”
The team is very mindful of the power of images to subtly reinforce or subvert people’s preconceptions. “Working on these issues makes us reflect on how much we subconsciously absorb images,” says Rebecca. “And how they feed into our imaginations.”

An annual report published by the Themed Entertainment Association (TEA)—a nonprofit trade association that represents creators, developers, designers, and producers in the visitor attractions and immersive experiences industry in forty countries—has found that institutions cross China ranked as the world’s most-visited museums in 2025.
According to Ocula, TEA recorded 161.4 million visits across its global top twenty museums in 2025, an increase of 5.4 percent from the same institutions in 2024. Chinese museums held twelve of the top twenty spots. Beijing’s Palace Museum was the most popular, with nineteen million visits—an increase of 11.8 percent from the previous year.
TEA also found that Gen-Z accounted for more than half of museum visits across China, attributed to an increased focus on technology in these museums, including immersive and AI-focused exhibitions.
By contrast, visitor numbers for Washington, D.C.’s federal museums declined steeply following the US government shutdown, which lasted forty-three days. Visits to the National Gallery of Art, for instance, fell to 2.8 million in 2025, a decrease of 28.9 percent. Similarly, attendance at the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of Natural History and National Museum of American History declined by 15.4 percent and 14.3 percent, respectively.
Unlike federally funded institutions, privately funded ones saw increases in attendance, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Art Institute of Chicago, the latter of which had an increase of 13.3 percent. The only American museum to break into the top twenty was the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, whose visitor numbers increased by 4.5 percent to 5.98 million.
Outside of China, the most visited institution was the Musée d’Louvre in Paris. As the fourth most-attended museum globally, it attracted 9.05 million visitors in 2025. Also of note is the National Museum of Korea, which saw its year-on-year visitorship increase 68.3 percent, the top 20’s biggest percentage increase.

https://taz.de/Berichte-CDU-will-Ilse-Ai.title: Nachfolge von Frank-Walter Steinmeier: CDU will laut Medien Ilse Aigner als Bundespräsidentin
https://taz.de/Berichte-CDU-will-Ilse-Ai.text:
Nachfolge von Frank-Walter Steinmeier: CDU will laut Medien Ilse Aigner als Bundespräsidentin
Nach der CSU legt sich offenbar auch die Schwesterpartei CDU fest: Die bayerische Landtagspräsidentin soll Deutschlands erstes weibliches Staatsoberhaupt werden.
afp/dpa/kna/rtr | Die CDU will Medienberichten zufolge die CSU-Politikerin Ilse Aigner für das Amt des Bundespräsidenten nominieren. Dies berichteten „Bild“, „Spiegel“ und „Süddeutsche Zeitung“ am Freitag übereinstimmend. Die Deutsche Presse-Agentur erfuhr es aus mehreren hochrangigen Quellen der Union.
Die 61-Jährige wäre die erste Frau an der Staatsspitze der Bundesrepublik. Aigner ist derzeit Präsidentin des bayerischen Landtags. Im Kabinett von Kanzlerin Angela Merkel war sie einst Bundeslandwirtschaftsministerin. Das neue deutsche Staatsoberhaupt und Nachfolger von Frank-Walter Steinmeier (SPD) wird von der Bundesversammlung am 30. Januar kommenden Jahres gewählt. Aigner hat bereits aus den Reihen von SPD und Grünen Zustimmung erfahren, womit ihre Wahl im Januar als gesichert gelten dürfte.
Offiziell soll sie eigentlich erst am Montag verkündet werden. Die derzeitige bayerische Landtagspräsidentin würde damit Deutschlands erstes weibliches Staatsoberhaupt – nach zwölf Männern. Und das erste mit CSU-Parteibuch. Der Niederbayer Roman Herzog war bei der CDU.
Eine weitere doppelte Premiere wäre mit ihrer Person verbunden: Aigner hat nicht studiert – und sie ist ledig. Was bedeutet, sie müsste Bundespräsidentin und First Lady in einem sein.
Hohe Zustimmungswerte auch bei SPD und Grünen
Wegen hoher parteiübergreifender Zustimmungswerte dürfte ihr eine satte Mehrheit in der Bundesversammlung am 30. Januar sicher sein. Zuletzt sprachen sich auch führende Sozialdemokraten und Grünen-Politiker für die Oberbayerin aus. Eine Gegenkandidatur mit Siegchancen erscheint unter diesen Umständen ausgeschlossen.
Lange ließ sich Aigner nicht entlocken, ob sie überhaupt Ambitionen auf Schloss Bellevue hat. Das war offenbar ein kluger Schachzug. Nicht nur, weil sie sich nicht so ohne weiteres des Rückhalts in ihrer eigenen Partei vollständig sicher sein konnte. Sondern auch, weil zu forsches Auftreten aufseiten der CSU regelmäßig Abwehrreflexe bei der größeren Schwesterpartei auslöst.
„Schicksalsgemeinschaft“ mit Söder
Mit CSU-Chef und Ministerpräsident Markus Söder verbindet sie eine „Schicksalsgemeinschaft“, hat Aigner einmal gesagt. Beide zogen 1994 in den Landtag ein, waren Kollegen im Landesvorstand der Jungen Union und im Kabinett von Horst Seehofer. Den Wettstreit um Seehofers Nachfolge 2018 verlor sie gegen den fränkischen Rivalen.
Seinen Traum vom Kanzleramt müsste Söder wohl endgültig begraben, sollte seine 61-jährige Parteifreundin nach Berlin wechseln. Andererseits hätte er eine potenzielle Konkurrentin für den Regierungssessel in München vom Hof. Dieser Aspekt ist nicht zu unterschätzen, denn der Amtsinhaber ist in seiner Partei keineswegs so mehr so unangefochten wie früher.
An seiner Unterstützung für eine Bundespräsidentin Aigner hatte Söder seit einem halben Jahr keinen Zweifel mehr gelassen. „Wenn sie möchte, hat sie meine volle Sympathie und Unterstützung“, sagte er im April in einem Interview. Im Sommer legte er nach, Ende Oktober nutzte er den CSU-Parteitag für eine regelrechte Werbeoffensive.
Ein vielsagender Versprecher
„Die Entscheidung wird woanders gefällt, aber ich würde mir es von Herzen gönnen, wenn Ilse Aigner nächster Bundespräsident würde. Das wäre eine tolle Sache“, sagte Söder wörtlich. „Mir?“ Nur ein Versprecher?
Wer aber ist die groß gewachsene, dunkelhaarige, kinderlose Katholikin? Aigner stammt aus Feldkirchen-Westerham. Das liegt auf halber Strecke zwischen München und Rosenheim. Nach der Mittleren Reife 1981 ließ sie sich zur Radio- und Fernsehtechnikerin ausbilden. Später bildete sie sich zur Systemelektrikerin für Hubschrauber weiter.
An der Berufsschule war sie unter 100 Männern die einzige Frau. Eine gute Vorschule für das, was sie später in der Politik erwartete. Schon mit 27 wollte Aigner Bürgermeisterin ihrer Heimatgemeinde werden. Männerseilschaften bremsten sie bei der Nominierung aus. Nach einer kurzen Zeit im Landtag sprang Aigner für einen ausgefallenen CSU-Direktkandidaten bei der Bundestagswahl 1998 ein. Und gewann auf Anhieb das Mandat.
„Bin Single, aber nicht einsam“
Seehofers Angebot, im Kabinett von Angela Merkel 2008 Agrarministerin zu werden, kam für sie überraschend. Sie sagte erst zu, nachdem sie sich mit ihren Schwestern bei einer Bergtour beraten hatte. Im Podcast „Grant & Gloria“ gab sie Mitte Oktober einen seltenen Einblick in ihr Privatleben: „Ich gehe als Single durchs Leben.“ Das bedeute aber nicht, dass sie einsam sei. „Ich lebe in einem großen Familienverbund, in einem sogenannten Dreigenerationenhaus, wo immer irgendwas los ist.“ Mehrfach habe sie versucht eine Partnerschaft einzugehen, „mit mehr oder weniger Erfolg“.
Die Politikerin hat schwere Krankheiten durchgemacht. Im Jugendalter wurde ihr ein Tumor im Rücken diagnostiziert. Durch eine Operation entging sie einer drohenden Querschnittslähmung. Als Bundeslandwirtschaftsministerin überwand sie Schilddrüsenkrebs mit einer Strahlentherapie.
Technikerin der Macht
Als bayerische Parlamentspräsidentin hat sich Aigner weit über die CSU hinaus Respekt verschafft. Schon bei ihrer ersten Wahl erzielte sie mit 198 von 205 Stimmen eine überwältigende Mehrheit. Als ausgleichend und nahbar gilt die Technikerin der Macht.
Nicht nur in ihren öffentlichen Reden hat Aigner ihr Profil als Verteidigerin der Demokratie und als Brückenbauerin geschärft. Auf Krawall gebürsteten AfD-Abgeordneten zeigte sie im Landtag mehrfach die Grenzen auf. Den Laden zusammenzuhalten, diese Fähigkeit wäre im höchsten Staatsamt in Berlin noch einmal stärker gefragt.

BSW in Aufruhr: Nahostkrieg unter Friedensfreunden
Das sächsische BSW entsendet den prominenten Israel-Unterstützer Constantin Schreiber in die Bundesversammlung. Die Antizionisten in der Partei sind auf den Bäumen.
Der stellvertretende Bundesvorsitzende des BSW ist empört. Er distanziere sich „ausdrücklich und entschieden“ von den sächsischen Parteikolleg:innen, teilte Michael Lüders am Donnerstag mit. Das Vorgehen des BSW im Dresdener Landtag sei „falsch“ und „politisch in keiner Weise“ nachvollziehbar. Die Aufregung ist groß. Nicht nur bei Lüders. Auch das JSW, das Jugendbündnis der Wagenknecht-Partei, echauffiert sich: „Ohne uns. Sachsens Jugend bleibt antizionistisch.“
Der „antizionistische“ Furor gilt dem früheren „Tagesschau“-Sprecher Constantin Schreiber. Der dezidierte Unterstützer Israels ist am Donnerstag zum offiziellen Vertreter des sächsischen BSW in der Bundesversammlung bestimmt worden, die Ende Januar eine neue Bundespräsidentin wählen wird. „Antizionistischen“ Kreisen gilt Schreiber wahlweise als „Genozidleugner“, „Israel-Propagandist“ oder „Islamhasser“.
Der sächsische BSW-Fraktionschef Ronny Kupke kann die Aufregung nicht verstehen. „Constantin Schreiber ist ein etablierter Journalist, Nahost-Korrespondent, ehemaliger Tagesschausprecher und kritischer Beobachter gesellschaftlicher Entwicklungen, auch über deutsche Grenzen hinaus“, sagt Kupke zur taz. Die Differenzen von Schreibers „transatlantischen und proisraelischen Positionen“ zu denen der Wagenknecht-Partei seien offensichtlich: „Und natürlich macht sich das BSW diese nicht zu eigen.“
So wie das BSW in Sachsen aber die Brandmauer ablehne, so habe die Partei „kein Problem damit, mit Menschen in Kontakt zu kommen, deren Ansichten wir nur bedingt teilen“, sagt Kupke. Das gelte auch für die Nominierung von Wahlleuten für die Bundesversammlung: „Was also spricht nun dagegen, jemanden zu entsenden, der anderer Meinung ist?“
BSW-General Ruhnert überrascht
Ursprünglich wollte das BSW Sachsen gar nicht Constantin Schreiber, sondern den Generalsekretär der Bundespartei, Oliver Ruhnert, ins Wahlrennen schicken. Der Journalist, der zuletzt als „Global Reporter“ für den Axel-Springer-Verlag tätig war, kam nur deshalb zum Zug, weil Ruhnert nach eigenen Angaben Ende Januar aus terminlichen Gründen verhindert ist.
Die Begeisterung des BSW-Generals über seinen Ersatz-Wahlmann hält sich dabei schwer in Grenzen. „Ich war auch überrascht und teile Schreibers Aussagen zu Nahost nicht“, sagt Ruhnert zur taz. „Meinungspluralität tut unserer Partei gut. Aber ich hätte mir eine andere Entscheidung gewünscht. Vor allem aber hätte ich mir gewünscht, dass man diese Personalie zunächst intern bespricht.“ Die Aufregung könne er daher nachvollziehen.
Gleichwohl gebe es jetzt auch keinen Grund, die Personalie der sächsischen Kolleg:innen „zum großen Politikum“ zu machen. Es handele sich schließlich „nur“ um die Vertretung in der Bundesversammlung und nicht um ein Amt im BSW oder im Landtag, so Ruhnert weiter.
Auch Ronny Kupke vom sächsischen BSW-Landesverband versucht, den Ball flach zu halten. Der Fraktionschef im Landtag sagt: „Unser Anspruch war dabei nicht, eine geopolitische Debatte vom Zaun zu brechen, sondern eine Persönlichkeit des öffentlichen Lebens zu entsenden, die glaubhaft vermittelt, dass sie das Weiter-so der Altparteien nicht mitträgt.“ Eben einer wie Constantin Schreiber.
Schreiber kündigt Erklärung an
Der Bundesversammlung gehören alle 630 Bundestagsabgeordneten an, dazu nochmal ebenso viele von den Landesparlamenten bestimmte Wahlleute. Diese müssen nicht zwangsläufig Abgeordnete sein.
Constantin Schreiber wird dann auch nur einer unter etlichen Nicht-Politiker:innen sein, die am 30. Januar eine neue Bundespräsidentin wählen. So wollen die Grünen im niedersächsischen Landtag unter anderem die Klimaaktivistin Luisa Neubauer nominieren, während ihre Parteikolleg:innen in Baden-Württemberg etwa auf Hartmut Engler setzen, den Sänger der zumindest musikalisch schwierigen Schlagerband „Pur“.
Sachsen entsendet insgesamt 33 Wahlleute, 3 davon das sächsische BSW, einer davon ist Constantin Schreiber. Auch diese Relation müsse man sich mal vor Augen führen, sagt Ronny Krupke. „Daraus nun ein fundamentales Problem zu konstruieren, erscheint gewagt.“ Schreiber selbst äußerte sich bislang nicht öffentlich zu der Nominierung. Für Freitagabend kündigte er eine Erklärung an.

https://taz.de/Greenpeace-warnt-fuer-Deu.title: Greenpeace warnt vor Rechenzentren: Mega-Datenfabriken verursachen Mega-Wasserstress
https://taz.de/Greenpeace-warnt-fuer-Deu.author: Kai Schöneberg
https://taz.de/Greenpeace-warnt-fuer-Deu.text:
Greenpeace warnt vor Rechenzentren: Mega-Datenfabriken verursachen Mega-Wasserstress
Einige geplante Rechenzentren in Deutschland könnten so viel Wasser wie eine Kleinstadt verbrauchen, warnt Greenpeace. Das gefährde die Versorgung.
Große Rechenzentren können in trockenen Regionen Deutschlands zu Wasserstress führen. Laut einer Kurzstudie des Öko-Instituts im Auftrag der Umweltorganisation Greenpeace verbrauchten die hiesigen Serverfarmen im Jahr 2025 rund 13 Milliarden Liter Wasser zur Kühlung. Bis 2030 könnte dieser Bedarf durch neue Mega-Datenfabriken auf bis zu 27 Milliarden Liter pro Jahr anwachsen – was dem Trinkwasserverbrauch einer Großstadt mit rund 580.000 Einwohnern entspricht, etwa so viel wie Essen.
„Das kann lokal durchaus desaströse Effekte haben“, sagt Greenpeace-Expertin Linda Klapdor der taz. Bereits im vergangenen, besonders heißen und trockenen Sommer habe es in einigen Kommunen Beschränkungen der Wassernutzung und historische Tiefstände in Flüssen und Seen gegeben. Greenpeace fordert von der Bundesregierung verpflichtende Wassergutachten vor Genehmigungen, ein Verbot wasserintensiver Anlagen in Trockengebieten und konsequente Sanktionen bei Verstößen gegen behördliche Meldepflichten.
Die Bundesregierung plant bis 2030 eine Verdoppelung der Rechenzentrums-Kapazitäten in Deutschland. Während bisherige Anlagen meist weniger als 5 Megawatt Anschlussleistung haben, entstehen nun Anlagen mit über 1 Gigawatt, mehr als 200-mal so viel. In Deutschland sind aktuell knapp 30 Riesenprojekte mit mehr als 100 Megawatt Serverleistung in Planung.
Die Studie modelliert deren jährlichen Wasserbedarf auf jeweils bis zu 930 Millionen Liter pro Jahr, etwa den Trinkwasserverbrauch einer Kleinstadt mit 20.000 Menschen. In bereits trockenen Regionen könnten die neuen Datenfabriken „akuten Grundwasserstress, Verteilungskonflikte mit steigenden Belastungen für die Menschen in den betroffenen Gemeinden und Schäden am lokalen Ökosystem verursachen“, heißt es in der Studie. Problematisch sei zudem der hohe Strombedarf.
Digitalwirtschaft hält Wasserverbrauch für „sehr gering“
Diese Berechnungen stehen im Kontrast zur Darstellung der Digitalwirtschaft. Der Branchenverband Bitkom hatte den Wasserbedarf von 65 Prozent der deutschen Rechenzentren jüngst als „sehr gering“ eingestuft. Fast zwei Drittel der hiesigen Anlagen verbrauchten maximal 0,1 Liter Wasser pro Kilowattstunde IT-Stromverbrauch, heißt es in einer in dieser Woche erschienenen Bitkom-Untersuchung.
Das Öko-Institut kommt nach der Bereinigung von zum Teil unvollständigen Datensätzen aus dem behördlichen Rechenzentrumsregister hingegen auf einen gewichteten Mittelwert von 0,67 Liter Wasser pro Kilowattstunde IT-Stromverbrauch. Bereits der aktuelle Jahresverbrauch deutscher Rechenzentren von 13 Milliarden Litern entspreche dem Wasserinhalt des Berliner Wannsees.
„Das Problem ist die fehlende Transparenz der Betreiber“, erklärt Klapdor die unterschiedliche Darstellung. Weniger als die Hälfte der rund 1.200 meldepflichtigen Rechenzentrumsbetreiber in Deutschland hätten überhaupt Daten an die Behörden geliefert, nur 139 Meldungen seien für die Studie verwertbar gewesen. Auch laut Bitkom erklären sich die unterschiedlichen Werte „möglicherweise durch die unterschiedlichen Berechnungsansätze und die zugrunde liegende Datenbasis“, heißt es in einer Stellungnahme für die taz.
Zudem widerspricht Greenpeace einem zentralen Argument der Betreiber, wonach niedriger Stromverbrauch technisch zwangsläufig durch einen höheren Wassereinsatz erkauft werden müsse. In der Praxis lasse sich kein statistischer Zusammenhang zwischen Strom- und Wassereffizienz nachweisen. Eine hohe Energieeffizienz könne komplett ohne Wasserkühlung realisiert werden. Eine moderne Trocken- oder Kompressionskühlung könne den Wasserverbrauch der Serverfarmen sogar vollständig auf null senken.
Börsen brechen nach Ankündigung von Bernie Sanders ein
Während es in Deutschland erst wenige Proteste gegen neue Datenzentren gibt, waren sie in den USA eines der wichtigen Themen im Wahlkampf zu den Midterms. Laut einer am Mittwoch veröffentlichten Umfrage von Nachrichtenagenturen waren für 56 Prozent der Wähler*innen die Themen Datenzentren und künstliche Intelligenz ein entscheidender Faktor für ihr Votum. Viele demokratische Kandidaten warben damit, den Bau von Rechenzentren stärker zu regulieren. In drei der Bundesstaaten, die die Demokraten den Republikanern bei den Senatswahlen abgenommen haben, gibt es besonders viele geplante Datenzentren: Texas, Ohio, Iowa.
In den USA sind sie nicht nur wegen ihres hohen Energie- und Flächenverbrauchs umstritten, sondern auch wegen der Luftverschmutzung. Aus Mangel an Netzkapazitäten bauten die Betreiber vielfach Gaskraftwerke zur Stromversorgung in die Nähe.
Das hat auch einen negativen Klimaeffekt. Nach einer Untersuchung der Umweltorganisation Sierra Club verursacht die Energieerzeugung für die derzeit in den USA bis 2030 geplanten Datenzentren 618 Millionen Tonnen CO2. Zum Vergleich: Deutschland verursachte im vergangenen Jahr 649 Millionen Tonnen. Vielerorts scheiterten US-Rechenzentrumsprojekte an örtlichen Protesten der Bevölkerung, allein 45 waren es im zweiten Quartal 2026.
Unter anderem die Forderung des demokratischen Senators Bernie Sanders nach einem US-weiten Moratorium für den Bau von Rechenzentren sorgte am Donnerstag und Freitag für Unruhe an den Börsen weltweit. Vielerorts brachen Aktien rund um die Chipbranche ein, die als Profiteure des KI-Hypes gelten.
Das war auch in Deutschland zu spüren. Der deutsche Leitindex DAX sackte am Freitag um 2,3 Prozent auf 25.706 Punkte ab. In Japan brach der Nikkei-Index in der Spitze um 7 Prozent ein, in den USA war der Index der Technologiebörse Nasdaq am Donnerstag um 5,5 Prozent abgestürzt. „Die Angst vor einer rigorosen KI-Regulierung nach dem Erdrutschsieg der US-Demokraten löste an der Wall Street und in Asien regelrechte Panik aus“, sagte ein Analyst zur Nachrichtenagentur Reuters. Bereits im Vorfeld der Wahlen hätten KI-Aktien an Anziehungskraft verloren.
