https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Katherine Hearst
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Rains flood Gaza displacement camps as Israeli authorities block entry of shelter materials into territory
Thousands of tents sheltering displaced Palestinians have been flooded by heavy rains overnight, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation.
Scarce aid entering the territory has left tens of thousands of Palestinians in the war-torn enclave exposed to the elements for a fourth winter in a row- with no fuel and nothing but makeshift tents and shelters for protection.
Red Cross spokesperon Amani Al Naouq told Al Jazeera that she has seen footage of “entire families, entire camps” inundated with water and scrambling to drain their tents and protect their belongings and lives.
In October, Director General for the International Organization for Migration Amy Pope warned that nearly all of Gaza's population require shelter assistance, with the combined supply pipeline of humanitarian shelter partners covering barely 17 per cent of identified winter needs.
"Families who have already endured repeated displacement and devastating loss must be able to face the winter in safety and dignity," Pope said. "Shelter materials must enter quickly, predictably and at the scale required."
Israel has continued to tightly restrict the entry of aid into the territory, with shelter items- including tent poles, construction materials and mobile homes- almost completely barred as the Israeli authorities consider them "dual use" items.
IOM said that around 8,600 IOM emergency shelter kits are waiting outside Gaza, but continue to be turned away from crossing points by the Israeli authorities.
This has forced humanitarian workers to repurpose salvaged materials to construct makeshift shelters, as storms turbochared by the strengthening El Niño phenomenon batter the territory.
“The solutions are known, the supplies are ready and humanitarian teams are prepared to deliver,” Pope said. “Immediate and sustained humanitarian access is essential to protect lives, strengthen damaged shelters, and help families move beyond temporary solutions. All parties must facilitate principled humanitarian action and support a response equal to the severity of the crisis.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Buildings damaged in Israeli bombings risk collapse as rain inundates Gaza
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Buildings damaged in Israeli bombings risk collapse as rain inundates Gaza
Floods have swept through Gaza after heavy rain, endangering families and putting war-damaged buildings at risk.
Gaza City – Rana Adnan Hmeida, 29, stands at the entrance to her tent in al-Mina camp in northern Gaza, holding her two-month-old daughter as she tries to keep her warm after rainwater has flooded their shelter overnight. The family’s bedding, blankets and clothes are all soaked, with her children exposed to the cold and wind of Gaza’s latest storm.
Hmeida, her husband and children have been awake since midnight as heavy rain and strong winds swept through the camp. Water seeped into the tent and drenched their belongings. With all their clothes wet, Hmeida had to ask neighbours to help dry their clothes.
“Since midnight, we have been sitting awake. Water came into our tent, and the bedding, blankets and everything else got soaked. In the morning, I found my son and little daughter shivering. My two-month-old baby was freezing,” Hmeida told Al Jazeera.
“What am I supposed to do? Hold my children or try to stop the water? I was trying to keep them warm while carrying my little girl, but the water kept coming in. The wind was so strong that we felt the tent was about to be ripped out of the ground.”
Her husband, Sameh Hmeida, 30, said the family’s tent is particularly exposed due to its close proximity to the sea. It has no tarpaulins or insulating materials that might have helped in the storm.
Heavy rain has flooded camps and cities across Gaza over the past days, where many Palestinians are spending the fourth winter outside their homes since Israel began its genocidal war on the enclave in October 2023.
Water levels have risen by 30 to 40cm (12 to 16in) at several camps in Gaza due to Saturday’s rain, with Gaza’s civil defence agency receiving hundreds of calls.
Rainwater has flooded many tents in al-Mina camp, where about 1,700 Palestinian families live, turning the ground into pools of muddy water.
Raed Abu Amsha, 40, said his tent collapsed on top of his family during the storm. The clothes and blankets of all nine children in his care, four of them from his late brother, were soaked.
“I am responsible for orphans as well as my own children, and I cannot provide for their needs. This storm lasted only two hours, and look what it did to us. We need tents, tarpaulins and anything that can protect our children. How long are we going to keep living like this?” he said.
In Nuseirat, a decades-old camp in central Gaza with permanent structures, rainfall also threatens families living in buildings damaged by Israeli bombardments.
Nasser al-Hajj, 54, lives in a tower block that was hit in an Israeli strike in September 2025. Debris from upper floors fell onto his home, leaving a large hole in the ceiling where water now enters every time it rains.
Although the ceiling has been reinforced with support beams, an engineer has warned al-Hajj that the apartment is dangerous, with the risk of further rubble falling from the building if more bad weather hits Gaza.
During the latest storm, al-Hajj took his children to a neighbour’s home and waited for the debris to stop falling from the roof. Two of his children, who have autism, sleep in the tower block’s guard room, away from the damaged area.
“I am forced to live somewhere that could collapse over our heads at any moment. But where am I supposed to go? Rent is expensive, and a tent is not safe either,” he told Al Jazeera. “I know how dangerous this place is, but I have no other option,” he added.
According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.
About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.
The Gaza Municipality is also struggling to respond to the storms. About 15 kilometres of rainwater drainage lines and 212 kilometres of sewage networks have been damaged. Eight pumping stations and three main stormwater collection basins are out of service.
The remaining system can handle no more than 20 percent of rainwater under the best of circumstances, according to municipality spokesperson Hosni Muhanna.
“[We] continue to clean drainage systems in preparation for the rainy season,” Muhanna said.
The municipality has deployed workers to clean drains and manholes, remove rubbish and clear water channels, repair damaged sections of drainage lines and operate water pumps.
But Muhanna warns that these efforts cannot restore the network’s capacity amid shortages of fuel, equipment and spare parts.
More than 2,000 buildings in Gaza City alone are at risk of collapse, he said, and the volume of rubble in Gaza City has exceeded 25 million tonnes.
Emergency committees in displacement camps are also struggling with shortages of shelter supplies. Adli Awad, an official with the emergency committee in Nuseirat refugee camp, said his team is trying to distribute tents and tarpaulins, particularly to families affected by the rain. But the number of people in need far exceeds available stocks.
“We are trying to provide as many tents and tarpaulins as possible. We are also helping families dig channels to divert rainwater away from tents and reduce flooding,” Awad said.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with election ‘too close to call’
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Eva Corlett in Auckland
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.
On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.
But with some seats won by very slim margins, and special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November.
Special votes include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate. In 2023, 600,000 such votes were made, 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them.
With nearly 100% of the regular votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just three seats behind.
Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could begin.
National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote.
Labour, led by Chris Hipkins, secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party, Opportunity, the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government.
Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”.
“As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final count land in its favour.
The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helped propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time.
Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need the party to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, its predicted role could come to fruition.
Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the other minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from larger parties.
The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”.
“It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.”
In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote.
However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.
National won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an extra five seats to make up the balance.
That will be good news for its path to power, but comes with some significant trade-offs for the party. Four of its most senior ministers, including Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Bishop and Gerry Brownlee, will not return to parliament because they did not win a seat, or the party didn’t win enough votes to bring in list-only MPs.
On the other side of the house, Te Pāti Māori picked up five overhang seats.
With all the extra seats, there could be 130 in the next parliament – a record under MMP – which means 65 seats are needed to form a coalition.
The country faces a two-week wait until special votes are announced, followed by the possibility of weeks of negotiations. Luxon said caretaker government conventions would apply in the meantime.
“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well-established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

Yemeni government forces have claimed three air attacks on Houthi positions in the al-Misrakh district of the Taiz governorate.
The city of Taiz- which is government-held- has been subject to an ongoing Houthi siege. The blockade has triggered a spiralling humanitarian crisis in the city, as road closures bar vital supplies, including fuel, from entering.
Laurent Bukera, the United Nations Humanitarian Coordinator for Yemen warned that the city's health system is "close to collapse", while the UN World Food Programme (WFP) said that the conflict has blocked lifesaving assistance from reaching 800,000 people, including 600,000 who depend on aid in the city.
Meanwhile, Houthi media reports that at least 15 people have been killed, mostly women and children, in a series of Saudi strikes in the al-Shariyah area of Yemen’s Bani Hashish district. According to the reports, some 30 others have been wounded.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Luke Harding in Kyiv
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said.
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts, Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that the American military carried out a new round of "minor strikes" on Iran's Qeshm Island, which he claimed "knocked out" Iranian air defence systems.
Iranian state media reported that two blasts were heard in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which lies in the Strait of Hormuz, the contested waterway which has been disrupted since the US launched its assault on Iran in February.
The Iranian army said in comments carried by state broadcaster IRIB that their air defences downed a US drone over the island.
But Trump told reporters shortly after that the attacks "knocked out" the air defence systems "in about 15 minutes, maybe five".
Responding to reports of the explosions, US Central Command (Centcom) said that the situation is "relatively calm".

In a post on X late on Friday, it said that the US is “offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.
This comes after the US military reported that it had conducted what it described as "defensive strikes" on Monday.
The latest round of strikes is the first since Trump's Republican Party suffered a crushing defeat in the US midterm elections- a loss which was fuelled in part by Trump's war on Iran and subsequent rocketing of energy prices.
Since then, Trump's messaging has been erratic- oscillating between threats to "destroy" Iran and claims that the war is close to being concluded.
Also on Friday, Trump repeatedly claimed to reporters that talks with Iran are ongoing.
“We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal,” the US president said.
“We’ve made a lot of progress with Iran,” he added.
Meanwhile, Qatar's foreign ministry has rejected "false claims" that negotiations have stalled.
“Promoting such false claims serves only those seeking to prolong the war and destabilise the region,” Majad al-Ansari, spokesperson for the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a post on X.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Pro-Russian hackers leak Italian foreign minister’s data on dark web
The prime minister blames pro-Russian hackers for the leak, as her top diplomat says the cyberthreat was ongoing.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has said his personal data had been disseminated on the dark web, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blaming pro-Russian hackers for the leak.
Tajani announced in a social media post on Saturday that “for days now, cybercriminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation”.
The threats against Tajani, who is also vice prime minister of Italy, come amid a spate of hoax bomb threats across Europe that have forced flight diversions, security alerts at broadcasters, and attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems.
“They are also targeting my family; they are willing to pay for more details about me and my loved ones,” Tajani added in his X post. “My response is very simple: I will not be intimidated in any way.”
‘Matter of grave concern’
Meloni expressed solidarity with Tajani “following the revelations about the activities of pro-Russian hackers, and the publication on the dark web of personal data”.
She called attempts to sell confidential information about government officials “a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination”.
Tajani added in his statement that Italy’s “position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted: defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation’s democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities”.
He also suggested that the cyberthreats may also be a reaction to the Italian government’s efforts to strengthen the Foreign Ministry’s digital defences.
Tajani did not specify what kind of information had been shared, but suggested that the cyberthreat was ongoing.
He added that the ministry was taking the threats seriously and was coordinating its response with allied countries.

Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: La Liga – predictions, team news, lineups
Barcelona and Atletico clash on Sunday in a blockbuster encounter which could upend the La Liga title race this season.
Who: Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona
What: La Liga, match day 12
Where: Riyadh Air Metropolitano, Madrid, Spain
When: Sunday, November 8, at 9pm (20:00 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 17:00 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream
A top-of-the-table clash headlines Sunday’s La Liga action, with Barcelona looking to retain their top spot before the international break as they face challengers Atletico Madrid.
With only two points separating the teams, the blockbuster clash could well be the turning point in the 2026-27 title race should Atletico upset Barcelona.
Diego Simeone’s side have been in terrific form all season and take on Barcelona, bolstered by a seven-game winning streak in the Spanish top flight.
Atletico’s striker Julian Alvarez struggled to find his feet early in the campaign, with a dramatic transfer saga involving Barcelona adding to the uncertainty. But the Argentinian has since rediscovered his form, scoring in each of his last two league outings.
If Atletico have been impressive, Barcelona have been irresistible.
Hansi Flick’s team have netted an incredible 46 goals in just 11 league games; the only team to score more in their first 11 matches of a campaign were Athletic Club in 1930-31 (49).
Raphinha and Lamine Yamal have been the architects of Barca’s lethal attack, with the Brazilian winger leading the goal-scoring charts this season with 15 league goals in 10 games. He is just the second player to reach this tally within 10 games at the start of a campaign after Real Madrid icon Cristiano Ronaldo, who did so in 2014-15 (18 goals in 10 matches).
Ahead of Atletico vs Barcelona, here’s everything to know:
How have Atletico played this season?
Atletico are second in the La Liga standings, with 28 points from 11 games. They have won nine matches, lost once and drawn as many.
How have Barcelona played this season?
Barcelona lead the La Liga points table with 30 points from 11 games. They have won 10 games and lost only once, suffering a 2-1 Clasico defeat to bitter rivals Real Madrid last month.
Raphinha thriving where Barca envisaged Atletico’s Alvarez
Raphinha is back to his devastating best as Barcelona’s centre-forward, suggesting the Catalan giants have little reason to regret missing out on Atletico’s Alvarez this summer.
The Argentina international tried to force his way out of Atletico to join Spanish champions Barca, whose attempts to engineer a deal angered the Rojiblancos. Barcelona were fined about 600 euros ($675) for their approach for striker Alvarez by the Spanish football federation in October.
Alvarez stayed and later apologised to Atletico fans to try and rebuild bridges, while Barcelona moved on fast, with winger Raphinha developing into an unstoppable force in a previously unfamiliar number nine role.
Raphinha’s form has made the chances of Barca returning for Alvarez next summer remote, and, after penning a new contract until 2030 on Thursday, he will look to underline that against Atletico.
With the Brazilian firing on all cylinders, Flick’s side won 11 games straight across all competitions at the start of the season.
Currently, he has 19 goals in 13 games across all competitions, including a brace each in the last two games.
After joining Barcelona from Leeds United in 2022, the winger grew frustrated under coach Xavi Hernandez, who did not seem to trust him completely.
However, Flick’s arrival and his high-pressing game suited Raphinha to the ground, and the winger has gone from strength to strength, becoming one of the team’s most influential players and one of the captains.
What happened the last time Atletico played Barcelona?
The last time the teams met was in a 2025-26 Champions League knockout game on April 14.
Although Barcelona defeated Atletico 2-1 in Madrid that day, Atletico edged their Catalan opponents 3-2 on aggregate and reached the semifinals.
Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: Predictions
Opta’s supercomputer gives Barcelona a 49.3 percent chance of winning, while Atletico’s probability of a win stands at 27.5 percent. There is a 23.3 percent chance of a draw.
Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: Head-to-head
Atletico have won two of their last five games against Barcelona in all competitions (L3), all of which have taken place in 2026.
The teams faced off twice in the Copa del Rey semifinals in March, with Atleti grabbing a solid first-leg 4-0 win at home before holding on for a 4-3 aggregate triumph, while they also won 2-0 at Camp Nou in the Champions League quarterfinals in April, going through 3-2 on aggregate on that occasion.
In La Liga, though, Barcelona have won in each of their last four trips to the Metropolitano. They are bidding to become just the third team in La Liga history to clinch five straight away wins over Atletico, after Athletic Club in 1955 and Real Madrid in 2013 (both runs of six).
Form guide
(Last five games in all competitions; latest match first)
Atletico: L-W-W-D-W
Barcelona: W-W-L-L-W
Team news
Atletico Madrid
Cristian Romero is out with a muscle injury.
Predicted starting XI:
Jan Oblak; Marcos Llorente, Marc Pubill, David Hancko, Alejandro Grimaldo; Giuliano Simeone, Obed Vargas, Morten Hjulmand, Alex Baena; Kang-in Lee, Julian Alvarez
Barcelona
Barcelona midfielder Rodri has been ruled out of Sunday’s clash because of a hamstring injury. He was substituted at half-time of Barcelona’s 3-0 Champions League win over Aston Villa on Tuesday.
Spanish media have reported Rodri could miss up to a month.
Jules Kounde (sprained ankle), Xavi Espart (ankle), Dani Olmo (thigh) and Roony Bardghji (knee) are also sidelined with injuries.

Joan Garcia; Brian Farinas, Pau Cubarsi, Frenkie de Jong, Joao Cancelo; Gavi, Pedri; Lamine Yamal, Fermin Lopez, Karim Adeyemi; Raphinha

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New ‘high safety’ chemicals in plastic food packaging linked to lower birth weight, study finds
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Exposure to a new generation of allegedly “safe” plasticizers is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications, which could cause serious health problems later in life, a new peer-reviewed study found.
As the health risks in exposure to common phthalate plasticizers became clear over the last few decades, industry began switching to a new type of chemical, called Dinch, that it claimed was a “high safety”, nontoxic alternative. It is widely used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union, and is found in children’s toys, medical devices, some textiles, flooring and other consumer goods.
But it may not be as safe as industry has claimed, the New York University Langone Health analysis of federal US health data suggests. There is a dearth of research into Dinch health risks, though what exists points toward the chemicals being hormone disruptors that can impact kids’ development.
The new paper is the first to link Dinch to lower birth weights and birth lengths. Fetal growth problems can raise the risk for heart disease, learning difficulties, obesity and other issues that can echo into adolescence and adulthood, the authors wrote.
“Chemicals should be properly tested for their safety before they become a widespread exposure for unwitting people in the general public,” said Leonardo Trasande, a lead author on the NYU paper.
The chemical is formally named 1,2-cyclohexane dicarboxylic acid diisononyl ester. It is used to make plastic more flexible and durable, and is found in common kitchen products such as cling film and plastic wine corks.
Researchers looked at data for over 6,600 pregnancies collected as part of the National Institutes of Health Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (Echo) Program. Up to 70% of women showed Dinch in their urine, and higher levels increased the risk of the child being classified as “small for gestational age”, or below the 10th percentile for babies born at the same stage of pregnancy.
Each tenfold increase in Dinch exposure resulted in a 27-gram reduction in newborn birth weight. An average newborn weighs about 3,400 grams (about 7.5lbs). Hispanic mothers or those with lower education levels were more likely to have children affected by Dinch, the study found.
Previous research on animals and human cells has found that Dinch by-products can interfere with the hormones in a pregnant woman that guide fetal development, and may trigger inflammation that affects how nutrients and oxygen reach the baby, NYU’s authors wrote.
The paper appears to expose yet another classic example of industry replacing one dangerous chemical with a compound that has similar health effects. This resets the regulatory and research process, even though the new chemical is very similar in structure or has the same health risks.
After the US and EU regulators began taking action in the aughts over toxic phthalates such as DEHP, industry began increasing the use of Dinch. German chemical giant BASF is among Dinch’s major producers and overall global production volume jumped from 25,000 tons in 2002 to 400,000 tons in 2024.
This process is called “regrettable substitution”, and is common. For example, many chemical companies and goods producers replaced the most dangerous Pfas “forever chemicals”, such as Pfoa, with GenX compounds. But after years of research, the latter have been found to be more toxic.
Researchers with the Switzerland-based Food Packaging Forum said they are concerned about Dinch and the lack of health information around it. But there is evidence that it migrates from food packaging into food, and levels in the EU population have been increasing across recent decades. The Food Packaging Forum is currently conducting health research on DINCH.
The NYU findings “raise pretty serious concerns about regrettable substitution”, Trasande said.
“These results underscore the need for stronger oversight of chemicals used in food packaging and other household products by requiring they be tested before they are introduced to the market, instead of after they are connected to health concerns,” Trasande said, noting that the plastics treaty under negotiation at the United Nations is an opportunity to establish better policies.
Women can protect themselves and their children by buying plastic-free products as much as possible, including clothing and toys. Look for food at the grocery store that comes in glass packaging, and use glass or wood storage and utensils in the kitchen.

I see a little silhouetto of a man. Scaramouche, Scaramouche, will you do the Fandango? Thunderbolt and lightning, very, very frightening.
Now I know how the over-by-over team feel when it rains.
Bernd Mayländer back on track in the safety car. But “it’s grim out there” says Croft. “It’s murky, it’s miserable.”
David Croft and Martin Brundle increasingly sceptical that we will actually get qualifying today. Apparently a rule change for this season means that if qualifying cannot take place in time for the race, then it would start in championship order.
Oops. Lightning.
“I think it’s fantastic to have so young champion … I knew Kimi from five, six years old.” He raves over the champion’s win from 19th at Monza.
Drivers stepping out of their cars. Craig Slater now with Emerson Fittipaldi, the earliest F1 champion I can remember watching drive. He was once the youngest champion.
Sisyphus’s team of marshals sweeping water off the track.
“We just see lots of standing water,” comes over the radio.
Ted Kravitz fears that the next band of rain is in. Things are getting worse, not better.
The safety car is going round, and it doesn’t look clever.
Brundle wondering how it will go if sunset approaches. We have a couple of hours to go but a crash might make life difficult. In 2024, qualifying had to be moved to the Sunday morning.
Ger Nugent asks: “How does that work, 3 drivers at the back of the grid – a coin toss?” Based on what has happened previously, in effect it is a mini-qualifying battle between them. Whoever does worst will be at the back, etc.
Rain is continuing. Bernie Collins trying to regain her status as the oracle, predicting it will get heavier soon too. We could be here a while.
Here’s Felipe Massa. After what happened to him at Interlagos in 2008, it’s a surprise he can raise a smile. Of course the battle over that season’s championship goes on; not because of Hamilton’s last-gasp recovery but the Crashgate events in Singapore.

The medical car is going round. Ted Kravitz explains that it has a higher clearance than the safety car, so can go round more easily.
Brundle explains the difficulty of driving on a resurfaced track, where new asphalt will ooze resin. The traditional wet line at Interlagos may not work, Croft says.
Should be about 10 more minutes of rain – but David Croft gets a storm warning on his phone. When the weather does stop, the medical car will assess conditions.
The drivers that went out are trying to get dry. Ollie Bearman noted for reversing in the pit lane …
Neither Hamilton nor Verstappen went out in the rain. Smart thinking, or not that bothered because of the penalties?
To be clear, here are the grid penalties as far as I know:
George Russell 5 places

They ran for 2min 23sec before it had to be called off. My faith in Bernie Collins is shattered, she was saying some time during Q2.
And it’s a red flag.
Cars crawling round. Antonelli says he is already aquaplaning.
Cars pulling out of the queue to change their boots.
Looks like everyone will have to go round on intermediates and change to wets, notably Mercedes.
The rain is here!
It sounds as if the rain will come sooner than previously expected. Most of the cars ready to go, as the start of Q1 could be the best time for running.
David Croft talks about the weather, which should be interesting tomorrow too.
Portentous musical countdown time.
Ted Kravitz talking through the pole chances of Antonelli, Russell and Norris in the upgraded McLaren.
Verstappen is going to be at the back of the grid too! Have had technical problems and somehow I missed that. Apologies.
Bernie Collins says Q3 is going to be “very, very interesting” given the incoming rain.
Isack Hadjar has been talking to Naomi Schiff about his love for Ayrton Senna, at the scene of one of the Brazilian great’s most famous wins, the 1991 Brazilian GP, stuck in sixth gear.
In other news, the São Paulo Grand Prix is here to stay, come rain or shine. A five-year extension has been agreed, guaranteeing a race there till 2035. Who can forget the 2007 and 2008 finales, with the title wins for Kimi Räikkönen and Hamilton? The latter had a remarkable late rain intervention that so nearly cost the Briton the first of his seven titles before the weather deteriorated in his favour.
Kravitz adds that Hamilton will take part in qualifying, despite being relegated to the back of the grid. Last week’s winner topped the times in FP3:
 Red Bull’s Max Verstappen set the fastest time in final practice on Saturday for Formula One’s São Paulo Grand Prix, finishing ahead of Kimi Antonelli. The four-times champion clocked 1min 11.622sec, 0.025 faster than the 20-year-old Mercedes driver who had topped the second practice at Interlagos circuit on Friday.
Verstappen is set to start Sunday’s race from the back of the grid after collecting a penalty for an engine change, while Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc also face grid drops for taking new internal combustion engines.
McLaren’s Lando Norris, fastest in FP1, was third quickest on Saturday, 0.131 off the pace, with Mercedes’ George Russell fourth. Russell will take a five-place grid penalty, also for an engine change.
…
Brazilian Rafael Camara, making his season debut after replacing Esteban Ocon at Haas, finished the session 15th, ahead of his teammate Oliver Bearman. Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto, the other local driver, was 10th fastest. Reuters
Ted Kravitz standing in a wet pit lane, and more rain is expected to midway through qualifying.
How has free practice gone generally? Well, Antonelli was not resting on his laurels on Friday:
 Kimi Antonelli set the pace in second practice for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Friday after McLaren’s Lando Norris was fastest in the opening session at Interlagos.
The Mercedes driver Antonelli topped the timesheets with a lap of 1min 10.763 seconds under dry but humid conditions, with Norris second, 0.253 slower, and Red Bull’s four-times world champion Max Verstappen third, 0.259 off the pace.
“There’s a bit of work to do, but overall feeling good and excited for tomorrow. I think we have a good chance,” the Italian said, referring to Saturday’s qualifying.
George Russell was fourth fastest for Mercedes despite a looming five-place grid penalty for taking a fresh engine, ahead of McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, while Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc were sixth and seventh.
The 20-year-old Antonelli, who secured the world title with third place in Mexico last weekend, had ended the first session second fastest behind Norris after returning to action for the first time since clinching the championship.
“FP1 was a little bit of a surprise, a pleasant surprise,” said Norris. “FP2, I think we seemed to struggle a little bit more compared to the Mercedes, just two tenths off on every lap, basically. But relative to some of the others, I think we seem pretty good.” Reuters
Half an hour to go to qualifying, and it has not been a good day for Lewis Hamilton, who will start at the back of the grid tomorrow.
Today, in third practice, he had smoke coming out of his car. Hamilton and Charles Leclerc had already replaced their engines, leading to 10-place grid penalties, but as Reuters reported: “The 41-year-old Briton reported ‘strange’ engine vibrations and smoke in the cockpit over the radio before stopping.”
Ferrari then said: “Following today’s FP3 session, the power unit fitted to car #44 was removed for further checks. After completing our analysis, we have decided to replace the entire power unit. Lewis will take part in qualifying but will have to start tomorrow’s race from the back of the grid.”
Giles Richards, meanwhile, has been looking at how Ferrari will try to cope with having two wannabe championship contenders.
Preamble
Andrea Kimi Antonelli, F1 world champion at just 20 – has this special AKA done too much too young? You have to hope there is plenty more to come from the Italian, but if he needed a reminder of how much talent is around him on the grid he had only to look at the other men on the podium in Mexico City last weekend: the race winner, Max Verstappen, and the runner-up, Lewis Hamilton, have 11 world championships between them.
While Mercedes have won a majority of the races – Antonelli (nine) and George Russell (three) have stood on the top step 12 times out of 19 – Verstappen has won three of the past four races for Red Bull. McLaren have two victories from Lando Norris, the deposed world champion. And Ferrari have … one. More of that later.
Even as Antonelli got over the line in Mexico City, his Mercedes was one of four different marques in the top five places. What remains of 2026 can offer pointers for 2027, for teams and drivers.
So there are plenty of reasons to join me from 5.30pm GMT for the buildup to qualifying for what is now called the São Paulo Grand Prix. In the meantime, here’s Giles Richards look back at how Antonelli made history

https://www.middleeasteye.net/discover/c.title: Covering Palestine: Historic news clippings reveal US media complicity in Israel's crimes

Covering Palestine: Historic news clippings reveal US media complicity in Israel's crimes
For years, mainstream media has been criticised for its failure to report accurately on Israel’s genocide in Gaza, allowing Israel to commit crimes with impunity.
In July the UN special rapporteur for the Palestinian territories, Fransesca Albanese, released a report about the media complicity in genocide.
Her report details how the systematic targeting of Palestinian journalists, Israeli media’s incitement, and the legitimisation from international coverage have facilitated genocide and obstructed accountability.
Outlets relied heavily on Israeli sources, using the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 to justify Israel’s subsequent onslaught and present the conflict as though it began exclusively with the attack.
It was frustration with this narrative that prompted Maria Robles, an independent researcher and artist, to begin research into archival American newspaper stories.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
She wanted to “share the reality” of what was happening in Palestine through “public history and public memory - not based on opinion, but aggregating existing materials, existing research, existing journalism and making it as accessible as possible to the public”.
Over three years, Robles collated more than 3,000 clippings from almost 700 papers dating from 1724 to 2023, using online archives and physical records, and in doing so, establishing Covering Palestine.
Robles had previously worked on a research campaign to raise awareness about the history of slavery in New York using publicly available archive material.
“Covering Palestine similarly is about education or access to it, being a tool. So is data,” she told Middle East Eye. “I think both of them move us toward liberation, one step at a time.”
The website allows users to filter material by year, newspaper and subject, tracing patterns, names and key events.
She hopes the archive will help the public understand Palestine’s history prior to 2023 and allow researchers and organisations to “look and understand, criticise and question how the information was shared, and talked about and reported on”.
From 'colonisation' to 'settlement'
“The media bias has always been there,” Robles explained, but the language used has changed with the times: for example, it was striking that Israel was discussed explicitly as a colonial project when the term was less of a dirty word.
“Plan of colonising Palestine with Jews,” one New York Times headline announced on 6 January 1902.
“Jews set up six colonies,” another said on 24 May 1939.
In 1926, the Buffalo Jewish Review reported that “Jewish Colonisation will Extend Beyond Palestine Frontier”.
Covering Palestine traces how the word “colonisation” became controversial and was replaced with “settlement”; a shift beginning in the 1920s, with the term having mostly disappeared by 1948.
Today, critics accuse papers such as the New York Times (NYT) of routinely whitewashing Israeli imperialism, comparing headlines describing Israel’s illegal occupation of southern Lebanon as “cementing its foothold” or “plans to control” with much less euphemistic ones about the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
In an NYT opinion piece, columnist Bret Stephens dismissed the description of Israel as a settler-colonial state as “invidious, hypocritical and historically illiterate” and called Zionism “the oldest continuous anticolonial movement in history”, contradicting how the paper he wrote in once presented it.
The passive voice
A 2024 study from The Intercept found a clear pro-Israel bias in mainstream media coverage, particularly the NYT, with outlets consistently applying a double standard when using emotive words such as “massacre” and “slaughter” to describe civilian deaths.
During the first 100 days of the conflict following 7 October, the NYT used the word “massacre” 124 times to describe violence against Israelis and never against Palestinians; during the first year, CNN used it 225 times for Israelis and 16 times for Palestinians - despite a far higher Palestinian death toll.
Palestinian deaths, meanwhile, are frequently reported on using the passive voice: a headline from the Washington Post read “Israel’s war in Gaza claims thousands of young lives”. Another stated “more than 1,000 people have been killed in Gaza during ceasefire, Palestinian authorities say”.
This pattern is not new.
On 29 October 1956, Israeli border police shot dead 48 unarmed Palestinian civilians, including 23 children, in Kafr Qasim, who were returning home from their fields for violating a curfew imposed by the Israeli army on the town earlier that day that they had not been informed of.
Covering Palestine’s archive revealed all too familiar patterns of passive and euphemistic language
The story was suppressed by Israeli military censorship for 44 days.
Nothing on Kafr Qasim appears in the archive until 12 December 1956, the day David Ben-Gurion, the prime minister, broke his own ban and told the Knesset.
Of the papers in the archive that carried the disclosure, not one put “massacre” in a headline, and it was not until 13 October 1958, after a military court had convicted eight border police, that the word appeared in a headline to describe the event.
When reports eventually emerged, Covering Palestine’s archive revealed all too familiar patterns of passive and euphemistic language.
“Israel Discloses Killing of Arabs In Curfew Tift” was how Oregon’s News Review reported on the incident on 12 December 1956.
Meanwhile, the New York Newsday labelled it “Bare Slaying by Error of 48 Israeli Arabs”: indicating the event was accidental before any investigation had been opened.
One New York Times headline said “48 Arabs Killed; Israel Penitent”.
Alongside a scan of the clipping, Robles transcribed the headline, adding citations for researchers and linking to further context.
She noted the NYT headline was the only one that led with the death toll, but used the passive “killed”, without naming the perpetrator, before turning to “the condition of Israel’s conscience”.
Censorship
In April 2024, a leaked NYT memo instructed journalists to avoid terms including “genocide”, “ethnic cleansing” and “occupied territory” in their reporting on the conflict.
Robles noted that historical reports were often explicit about Israeli censorship: a 1980 NYT article declared “Israeli Censorship Strikes a Discordant, Insistent Note”, beginning “this dispatch has been subjected to Israeli censorship”.
By contrast, she said, “now…the reporting has to rationalise, maybe not successfully…why they are reporting it the way they are”, repeating Israeli talking points without acknowledging them, such as “Israel’s right to defend itself” or claims Hamas uses civilians as “human shields”.
The censorship of the Palestinian press was also reported on by the New York Times, detailing how “Israel Tightens Control Over Arab Newspapers” when Israeli authorities intercepted trucks and confiscated papers being transported for distribution in the West Bank in 1982.
Today, Palestinians document the genocide committed against them directly through social media, reaching international audiences without their language being filtered through American media or Israeli censorship.
However, Israel’s systematic targeting of Palestinian journalists has made Gaza the deadliest place to be a journalist.
The early reports of Palestinian newspapers being shut down are reflected in Israel’s attacks on journalists today, Robles explained, “not allowing [Palestinians] the opportunity to do their own reporting or speak about what is happening”.
Israel frequently labels Palestinian journalists “terrorists” to justify these attacks - lies that their western colleagues uncritically echo without adequate scrutiny.
Dehumanisation
Similarly, strikes on Gaza are often reported as “targeting Hamas”, regardless of civilian casualties, while death tolls are attributed to Gaza’s “Hamas-run health ministry”, casting doubt on their reliability.
Yet long before Hamas existed, American papers used dehumanising language to rationalise Israel’s atrocities, diminishing their readers’ empathy for Palestinian victims.
In July 1972, Palestinian novelist Ghassan Kanafani was killed alongside his teenage niece by a bomb planted in his car in Beirut.
Reporting on his death, US news outlets presented him as an “Arab Militant leader”, “Revolutionary”, or “Palestinian Guerrilla”, with only one headline in 11 calling him an artist, according to Robles.
A central motivation behind Covering Palestine was to humanise Palestinians by documenting their experiences across generations, including rare occasions when they were named or their lives and culture covered without the association with death and suffering.
“That humanising of people…reminding [the public] that these are really people that these experiences are really happening to” is important to counteract the dehumanisation they face, Robles said.
She also wanted to challenge Zionist myths that Palestine was a “land without people” or not a real country.
The historical record reveals a people and community that existed for many years prior to Israel’s establishment: one clipping from 1891 described “the Fellaheen [peasants] of Palestine” as “an ancient and historic people”; similarly in 1910 they were referred to as “the aboriginal inhabitants of the Holy Land”.
As genocide seeks to eradicate a people and their past, Robles wants to use Covering Palestine to preserve and expose the history of a place whose story began long before 7 October.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Amy Winehouse inspired me to quit a soul-crushing job
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Emily Phillips
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
At 6am on a bleak October morning in 2006, I was driving down the North Circular in London to a job I hated. I usually kept the radio low, a background murmur to keep me focused on the road. But that morning I turned up the volume allowing the buoyant bassline from Amy Winehouse’s Rehab to reverberate through my Ford Ka. As Amy’s rich voice conveyed the depths of her despair, I stared blearily at the empty road ahead and wondered how I’d taken such a wrong turn.
It was a disorienting time for me. Two years out of uni, I’d accepted a job in the back end of London’s Docklands area, in a freezing cold, windowless office, staring at four giant screens to check whether any of the world’s stock exchanges had technical faults. My shift pattern meant I would wake at 5am, then endure a male colleague relentlessly monitoring me – the way I had to monitor those blinking screens. From two desks behind, he would send me Myspace messages with inappropriate observations about how tight my outfits looked.
But it was better money than my previous job, an admin role that had been sold to me as a graduate media position. And perhaps it would look good on my CV if I just surrendered to the grownup notion of a sensible job in finance. (Who did I think I was, expecting to be paid to pursue my passion as a writer anyway?) Maybe one day I’d be able to clear some of my debt and move out of my parents’ house. But I hadn’t seen my friends, who were partying every night in east London, for more than six months. In my bleakest moments, I’d will a minor car accident on my drive in, in the hope I wouldn’t make it to my desk. The moment in Rehab when a man tells Amy he thinks she’s depressed had never felt so close to home.
The weekend after I first heard the song, Amy’s album Back to Black was released, and I rushed to HMV to buy the album on CD. Delving into her storytelling, I was astonished at her unflinching brilliance, but I should have known. Amy and I grew up on parallel tracks. As a teenager, she’d play pool with my brother at our local pub in Whetstone, north London. We were both suburban girls who wanted something different, and found it in little retro dresses, tattooed men and raucous nights in Camden. I may not have been suffering a searing breakup, as she was when she wrote Back to Black, but I was lonely and despondent.
Amy’s visceral take on life, told through frank lyrics, arresting melodies and powerful vocals, shook me out of my stupor. If she could wade through all of this pain, all of this addiction, then I could surely stop writing myself off and get back out there.
So I signed myself up to night school to study journalism, letting the money from a bad job pay for what I hoped would be a better future in magazines. I rang my friends and told them how low and cut off I had been feeling, and they gathered me up and placed me right back in the mix for those nights in Camden that fuelled me on. And I finally worked up the courage to tell my manager, a woman, about the office creep. It warned him off and, while it was many years before #MeToo would roll around, he thankfully didn’t so much as look my way again.
Before long I was still doing the 6am drives to Docklands, but when I finished there I’d drive straight on to night shifts at newspapers, where I’d write headlines and upload copy on to websites as the printing press whirred in the building’s underbelly. I began to feel a burning in me again to do something I loved, and a new confidence that I might actually have a chance. Eventually, I was able to drop out of my dead-end role and get paid for doing the job of my dreams.
Nearly 20 years into my journalism career, I’ve written a book about how Amy and so many other immense female singer-songwriters have pulled us through our most heartbreaking moments. It’s a testament to women’s ability to restore each other in tough times. Love might be a losing game but, against the odds, loving myself was something I needed to bet on.
I Hate You So Much Right Now by Emily Phillips is published by Blink (£16.99).

Iran’s IRGC says building underground sites for weapons production, storage
IRGC says underground military complexes allow missile production to continue even under heavy bombardment.
Iran is building underground military complexes able to sustain weapons production and storage even under heavy bombardment, according to the country’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi made a series of announcements on Saturday about the military’s capabilities during a news conference in Tehran, Iranian media reported.
Among the achievements listed were an “underground missile city” set to be unveiled, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported.
Mohebbi said the IRGC had rapidly transferred its missile and drone production lines from the surface to underground facilities. This allows Iran to continue producing missiles while its adversaries assumed its stockpiles were dwindling, he explained.
The spokesperson also outlined advances in stealth technology. He maintained that such improvements had allowed Iran’s missiles and drones to pierce air defence systems and accurately strike targets during previous rounds of fighting with the United States and Israel.
“Today, every weapon used by the IRGC Aerospace Force is manufactured using homegrown knowledge and expertise. Moreover, our products are not even derived from reverse-engineering captured enemy war material,” Iran’s IRNA news agency quoted Mohebbi as saying.
A recent report by US newspaper, The Wall Street Journal, shows that Iran caused billions of dollars in damage to US bases throughout the Middle East during previous rounds of fighting.
Meanwhile, a separate report by the Reuters news agency found that Iran had successfully targeted Gulf infrastructure on at least 135 occasions during the same period, causing billions of dollars in damage and lost revenues.
Mohebbi also warned on Saturday that restrictions on the range of Iranian missiles had been lifted. The warning follows a statement from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who said that there would be “no geographical limits” to Iran’s response if it were attacked again by the US and Israel.
The US-Israeli war on Iran was launched on February 28, prompting Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz and triggering a global energy crisis. Mediation efforts have stepped up recently, as regional countries hope to bring the war to an end.
On Friday, President Donald Trump said the US military launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, while also claiming Washington had made “a lot of progress” in talks with Iran.
Tehran has repeatedly warned that it will target Gulf energy infrastructure if the fighting resumes. Such attacks would likely push energy prices even higher.
Meanwhile, Washington has also imposed additional sanctions on Iran as it seeks to force Tehran to concede to its demands. The restrictions have further strained the country’s economy, forcing Iran to adopt new trade routes.
On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced it was establishing a new task force that will support ongoing US efforts to prevent Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.
The US has also imposed a naval blockade on Iran to prevent it from exporting oil.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Pedro Volpe had just woken up last Tuesday when he saw a message from a friend asking whether his bank account was down, too.
It was a day after payday, and Volpe, 50, a writer and lawyer, opened his banking app and panicked: he could not even see his balance.
Volpe was among nearly 3 million Paraguayans, about 60% of the country’s adult population, whose accounts had been frozen overnight. All were customers of Ueno Bank, a digital lender that aggressively expanded across the South American country in recent years, and which, on Monday night, the central bank ordered into resolution over insolvency.
Ueno is at the centre of a political and economic crisis that has brought Paraguay’s banking system to the brink of collapse. On Friday, it led to the impeachment and house arrest of the rightwing president, Santiago Peña.
Peña had resigned the day before in a vain attempt to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents – who, under the constitution, become senators for life. Lawmakers stripped him of the seat anyway, meaning Peña will face criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.
In just a few days, he went from being a market favourite among Latin American presidents and one of Donald Trump’s key allies in the region to facing fierce mass protests, being voted out and placed under house arrest.
The now former president is the subject of an investigation by the public prosecutor’s office over alleged favouritism towards Ueno, which, in just a few years since Peña took office in 2023, went from an obscure digital lender to the bank of choice for most Paraguayans.
“It was very easy to use and to open an account,” said Volpe, recalling that everything could be done quickly on a mobile phone. The bank also offered far more generous investment returns than its competitors did.
“Now I’m having to work miracles to pay my bills,” added Volpe. “A lot of people can’t even afford basic everyday things like food; luckily, I still had some money saved elsewhere, but that has only got me this far. I don’t know what I’ll do next week.”
Ueno was so popular – sponsoring the national football team, the league and the country’s biggest football clubs – and served such a large share of the population that businesses have already reported an overall fall in sales of up to 80% this week. Media outlets belonging to the same financial group as the bank had their operations suspended, including radio stations and the century-old newspaper La Tribuna.
The impact on ordinary Paraguayans was perhaps even wider reaching. The media freeze saw 300 workers having their salaries suspended, initially for 90 days. About 32,000 pensioners whose public pension funds had been invested in the bank were left without payments.
“A lot of people are also not working because they can’t get paid or make payments,” said the historian and political analyst Fabián Chamorro. “Meanwhile, the protests were growing every day, and Peña’s impeachment was the way congress found to prevent a popular explosion.”
A former finance minister and ex-employee of the central bank and the International Monetary Fund, Peña was elected by promising to restore a “great Paraguay” and attract foreign investment.
Soon after taking office at age 44 as the youngest president in Paraguay’s democratic history, he appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, who had until then been Ueno’s CEO, to lead the central bank. Less than three months later, Spalding authorised Ueno, then a finance company, to become a digital bank.
Peña himself had about $1m in shares he bought in 2019 in a company that would become Ueno Holding in 2022, the parent company of the conglomerate that controlled Ueno Bank. Even after becoming president, he only disposed of the shares in April 2025. He said he had bought them purely as an “investor”.
“During Peña’s administration, Ueno began receiving various benefits, and the government relaxed the rules to allow public funds to be invested in the bank,” said Chamorro. An estimated $800m to $860m in state and pension funds were invested in Ueno.
A series of internal central bank reports pointing to irregularities – including loans to companies within the same group – were revealed by local media in recent months, but Peña dismissed them as a “false media campaign” against his government.
With the bank having less than half the solvency required to meet its obligations, the central bank ordered it into resolution only after mounting pressure from other banks and opposition lawmakers.
Spalding resigned and, like Peña, was ordered arrested on Friday night. During the week, police had already arrested eight senior executives and directors of Ueno and its controlling group on suspicion of concealing the bank’s deteriorating financial position for months.
The public prosecutor’s office is investigating Peña on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling. He denies all the allegations, and his lawyers said there is no evidence he directed the allocation of pension funds to the bank.
Meanwhile, most affected people still have no access to their own money.
A guarantee fund covers deposits of up to $38,000, which would apply to more than 90% of individual account holders. On Friday, the central bank began making payments to customers with up to $1,565, no outstanding debts and an existing account at another institution.
Paola Benítez, a 25-year-old chef from the capital, Asunción, met all three requirements, but by late Friday afternoon had not yet recovered the money she had been saving for her wedding.
“This has made me a bit anxious, a bit desperate too, because honestly, who am I supposed to go to and ask about this? It’s very strange, very confusing, very sad,” she said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: At least six people killed in shooting in Poland’s Krakow
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
At least six people killed in shooting in Poland’s Krakow
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk says police are investigating after ‘tragic shooting’ in second-largest city.
At least six people have been killed and 15 others wounded in a shooting in the centre of Krakow in southern Poland.
Police said that a man drove onto the city’s Main Market Square at about 3pm (14:00 GMT) on Saturday and “began firing at random people from his car”.
Four women and two men were killed in the shooting, authorities said.
The gunman, who acted alone, was shot by officers and detained, police said. He has since been transported to hospital to receive treatment for his injuries. The Interior Ministry confirmed that the suspect is a Polish citizen.
Police officers were also among the wounded.
“According to information from police officers, the man was wearing military-style attire,” a police spokesman told reporters.
“During the arrest, officers used their weapons, but the man returned fire; as a result, two police officers are among the injured,” he added.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said that one of the officers is in a critical condition.
In a post on X, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk praised the “heroic” police response to the “tragic shooting”.
“I am being kept informed by the Minister of the Interior about the situation in Krakow,” he wrote, adding that “the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack”.
President Karol Nawrocki said his thoughts were with the victims, those affected, and their families.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said on social media that he was “receiving dozens of messages from foreign ministers from all over the world offering their condolences”.
Tom Rose, the US ambassador to Poland, called the incident a “horrific mass shooting … a savage and murderous attack that’s shattered the peace of Poland”.
“America stands with Poland at this dark hour,” as Poland stands with the citizens of Krakow, he said on X.
Located about 250km (155 miles) south of the capital, Warsaw, Krakow is the second-largest city in Poland and a popular tourist destination, attracting about 15 million visitors each year.
Deadly shootings are extremely rare in Poland, a European Union and NATO member with 38 million people. But the country was on high alert following a series of stabbings in October, which Tusk denounced as a “cult of violence”.
The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas said on X on Saturday that “Poland does not stand alone”.
“The tragic loss of life in the shooting in Krakow is a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland,” Kallas said. “My thoughts are with the victims and their families and the first responders.”
Poland, a staunch ally of Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, has repeatedly warned of Russian sabotage and hybrid warfare on Polish soil, accusations rejected by Moscow.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy offered condolences, condemning what he called “a shocking crime”.
“Ukraine stands in solidarity with Poland and the Polish people. People have the right to safety,” he said on social media.

The Lions by the River Tigris: Restoring Mosul’s artefacts
When the ancient Iraqi city of Mosul is devastated after liberation from ISIL, three men strive to revive its beauty.
In the heart of war-ravaged Mosul, two carved lions stand as a fragile link to the city’s shattered past. Bashar, a fisherman, lost his once-grand family home during the battle to liberate the city from ISIL (ISIS) nearly 10 years ago. All that remains is a marble gate crowned with lions, which he fiercely guards.
Fakhri, a devoted collector determined to save Mosul’s heritage, becomes obsessed with acquiring the lions gate for his unofficial museum. His friend Fadil, a musician once silenced under ISIL, challenges him to see the human cost behind every artefact. As Mosul rebuilds, a quiet cultural revival reflects the resilience of a city with 8,000 years of history.
The Lions by the River Tigris is a documentary film by Zaradasht Ahmed.
