Iraq’s FM says external parties using Iraqi soil to attack neighbours
Iraqi foreign minister warns of potential regional war, says Baghdad seeking to resolve disagreements with Saudi Arabia.
Iraq has evidence that external parties have been using its territory to launch attacks on neighbouring countries, its foreign minister told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview on Saturday.
Baghdad is investigating attacks launched from Iraqi territory against Gulf states and is seeking to resolve disagreements with Saudi Arabia through dialogue, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said.
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran-aligned groups operating in Iraq of attacking its oil infrastructure. In September, Baghdad confirmed that drone attacks on the kingdom’s East-West pipeline originated from Iraqi territory.
Hussein told Al Jazeera that Baghdad was negotiating with Iran-aligned armed factions to bring their weapons under state control and the process must be pursued through dialogue rather than force.
He also said Iraq was in contact with Tehran regarding the issue of weapons held by Iraqi factions.
Iraq’s government had initially established a deadline for armed factions to bring their weapons under state control by September 30, when the US-led international coalition to combat ISIL (ISIS) was set to end their mandate and leave the country.
However, it pushed back the deadline to June 2027 after encountering resistance to the policy, despite long-standing pressure from the US to fulfil its disarmament pledge.
On Iraq’s balancing act between Tehran and Washington, Hussein confirmed that the US had formally requested the closure of all but two border crossings with Iran.
He added that while Iraq welcomed friendship and an alliance with Tehran, it rejected interference in its internal affairs.
The foreign minister also said that Iraq had lost about $60bn from the suspension of oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, but that shipments have resumed after understandings were reached with Washington and Tehran.
On the issue of combatting ISIL after the coalition pullout, Hussein said that Iraq, Syria, Jordan and Turkiye have formed a committee to fight the group’s presence in Syria.
For Al Jazeera’s full interview with the Iraqi FM, tune in at 21:00 Doha time (18:00 GMT) on Sunday.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: TikTok accused of helping to promote sex industry to girls
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Amelia Gentleman
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
TikTok is helping to promote and normalise the sex industry, allowing “sexfluencers” to post videos aimed at marketing pornographic content they have uploaded elsewhere on sites such as OnlyFans, a report indicates.
After studying non-explicit content posted on TikTok over the course of a year by some of OnlyFans’ most popular young female performers, researchers said the women buried coded references to pornography in “girly lifestyle content” that showed them shopping, playing with their pets, baking or offering skincare advice.
While mentioning OnlyFans or directly linking to OnlyFans from TikTok accounts is prohibited, euphemisms, emojis and crude gestures are used to indicate that performers’ adult content is available for sale on other platforms. TikTok prohibits sexual solicitation, including invitations to share explicit images, but the platform distributes so-called safe-for-work material produced by popular OnlyFans performers.
The report analyses how hints about adult content are hidden in widely shared TikToks that show OnlyFans stars filming their hair and makeup routine for “get ready with me” posts – known by the acronym GRWM. Performers may use the word “corn” instead of the word “porn”, or add the corn emoji next to a star emoji, to avoid the content being blocked.
The “TikTok to OnlyFans pipeline” study was conducted by researchers from the campaigning organisations Cease (Centre to End All Sexual Exploitation) in the UK and Collective Shout in Australia. Researchers spent months scrolling through posts from a number of key “sexfluencers” and then following recommendations offered up by TikTok’s algorithm.
In viral posts, OnlyFans performers told their followers on TikTok about the money they had earned from selling sexual content. “One of the most pervasive messages across these posts is that selling sexual services on OnlyFans gives you a fabulous life – a life filled with freedom, fun, friendship and lots of money,” the report states.
Many posts promoted this message with images of cash, big houses, private jets and expensive cars, beneath headlines such as “how it feels knowing I own all of this at 23 thanks to 250,000 men”.
In some posts, OnlyFans was presented as the answer to poverty and unemployment by performers who described rag-to-riches stories. Opening an OnlyFans account was marketed as a solution, “rescuing women and girls from bleak, underprivileged lives, gifting them with the nice, luxury items that they – and their struggling families – have always deserved”, the report says.
OnlyFans’ own data indicates that its top 5,000 creators have made more than $1m each on the site since the platform launched in 2016. But the average earnings of the site’s 5 million registered performers are estimated to be about $1,000 a year, the report states.
Melinda Tankard Reist, of Collective Shout, condemned TikTok as “an industrial-scale digital pimp funnelling girls into the sex industry”. She said: “It is our view that young women and girls deserve to be protected from a predatory industry grooming them to be producers of explicit content.”
Tankard Reist said the research was commissioned in response to an awareness that OnlyFans stars such as Sophie Rain and Ari Kytsya had a huge following on TikTok among teenage girls, and concern that they were using the site to promote benefits of creating pornography.
Rain became famous with content filmed in the “Bop House”, a luxury pornography production house in Miami, which is home to a rotating group of women who sell sexual content on OnlyFans. Auditions to join the Bop House are shared on TikTok and would-be recruits respond by posting sexually suggestive dances tagging Bop House recruitment.
OnlyFans performers rely on building up their followers on TikTok and other social media platforms, so they have become adept at finding ways to make subtle nods to the presence of explicit content that is for sale elsewhere. The report focuses on the ties between TikTok and OnlyFans because TikTok has such a high proportion of young users and because it is where the careers of many on OnlyFans start out.
Many OnlyFans stars do brand promotion alongside their lifestyle content on TikTok, advertising household items such as pet food, burgers and pineapple juice, as well as sex toys and condoms. The global cosmetics brand L’Oréal last year appointed Kytsya – who refers to herself as a “mattress actress” – as a brand ambassador for Urban Decay, a makeup brand popular with teenagers and sold globally. In these advertisements, viewed millions of times on TikTok, she calls for makeup that performs well on mattresses.
The report’s authors have called for an extension of the ban that exists in many countries on showing explicitly pornographic content to under-18s so that it also includes posts that promote or are related to the sex industry.
A TikTok spokesperson said: “TikTok strictly prohibits the sharing or showing of sexual content and we use advanced technologies to enforce our community guidelines. In addition, our systems are designed to prevent age-inappropriate content from reaching teens.”
An OnlyFans spokesperson said: “OnlyFans is a platform for people aged 18 and over and we have strict onboarding processes to prevent minors accessing the platform.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Wladymir Ungaretti: um flaneur radical contra a invisibilidade da vida
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Alexandre Haubrich
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Talvez seja um pouco injusto começar esse texto pela minha narrativa pessoal, já que essa experiência, definitivamente, não foi individual. Mas o professor Ungaretti, o jornalista Wladymir Ungaretti, que faleceu nesta sexta-feira, 6 de novembro, foi quem, na minha formação, me permitiu enxergar o jornalismo com toda a sua potência. Pode parecer paradoxal, mas a verdade é que essa delimitação de “isso é bom jornalismo, isso é só ‘showrnalismo’ e ‘perfumaria’” é, em realidade, não limitadora, mas libertadora.
Ungaretti ensinou, a mim e a centenas de jornalistas (alguns aprenderam melhor, outros pior), a infinitude das possibilidades de liberdade e como a busca pelo conhecimento pode nos empurrar nesse caminho, no qual subversão, radicalidade e liberdade são formas diferentes de dizer e viver a mesma coisa.
Eu entrei na faculdade de jornalismo porque gostava de escrever e porque via no jornalismo uma chance de ajudar a mudar o mundo. Mas tinha 17 anos e essa ideia ainda era bastante abstrata e errática. Naquele momento, o Ungaretti já dava aulas na Faculdade de Biblioteconomia e Comunicação (Fabico) há uns 15 anos, e, entre outras coisas, tocava com os alunos duas revistas, a 3×4 e a Sextante. Conheci ele a partir do convite de uma colega para me juntar a um pequeno grupo e produzir uma edição especial da 3×4, por fora da grade curricular regular, com o tema “Indígenas”. Foi no trabalho de construção dessa revista que tive meus primeiros contatos com o Ungaretti e com o jornalismo.
Este texto vai ficar longo para os tempos de hoje, talvez ninguém ou quase ninguém chegue ao final agora, mas o próprio Ungaretti ensinou que fazemos textos e fotos não só para agora, mas, principalmente, para registrar a história, para dar ao futuro elementos para olhar para o que é hoje o presente. Ele queria que suas fotos e textos fossem utilizados daqui a muitos anos para que as pessoas do futuro olhassem para o mundo de hoje e integrassem essa perspectiva ao olhar retrospectivo: o Ungaretti queria atrapalhar os planos de quem gosta de contar a História apenas sob o olhar dos vencedores, dos de cima, e por isso registrava, em texto ou imagem, tudo o que era marginal e que, no futuro, talvez ficasse invisível.
Ele “flanava” pelas ruas, por livros, por reportagens, por imagens. Esse flanar fazia com que suas referências se misturassem e complementassem, complexificando seu olhar sobre o mundo. O melhor é que ele absorvia tudo e devolvia para o mundo em seus próprios textos, fotos, aulas e conversas. Tudo para combater a invisibilidade, para lançar luz sobre o que o poder e a loucura do sistema querem apagar.
As conversas com o Ungaretti sobre as pautas para a revista 3×4 iam muito além das pautas que iríamos apurar e dos textos que iríamos escrever. A preocupação dele não era com detalhes técnicos, distanciamento do olhar, construção do “lide”, etc., mas com os problemas de fundo: como aprender a ouvir os entrevistados para além do que diziam, como entender aquelas histórias em sua profundidade histórica, cultural e humana, como ir à raiz das histórias, como produzir material jornalístico que, no dia seguinte, não servisse apenas para embalar peixe.
A produção dessa revista foi meu primeiro trabalho jornalístico e, da visão que construí naquele momento sobre o jornalismo, não me desviei mais. Na verdade, em alguns momentos a expandi, em outros a encolhi, puxei para um lado, puxei para o outro, mas sempre a partir daquela base. Tudo o que fiz depois como jornalista se relaciona com a forma como minha visão foi moldada a partir do Ungaretti.
Não é uma experiência individual
Falo da minha própria formação, mas sei que não é uma experiência individual: Ungaretti deu aula na Fabico por 25 anos e, de uma forma ou de outra, centenas de jornalistas foram impactados por sua forma única de estar em sala de aula e, mais do que isso, nos corredores da faculdade e nas ruas da cidade. Porque suas aulas não respeitavam paredes.
Para cada encontro em sala de aula, ele chegava carregado de jornais, revistas e livros, que espalhava pela mesa, grudava no quadro-negro ou dispunha pelo chão. Ele gostava de dizer que não se via como professor, mas como jornalista. Mesmo assim, chegava sempre bem cedo, muito antes do horário das aulas, para terminar de preparar o que iria falar, para reler textos que considerava fundamentais e para se concentrar para a atividade febril de ensinar que desempenharia pelas horas seguintes.
As aulas traziam tantas referências, conexões e inspirações que, em diversos momentos, se tornavam caóticas. O Ungaretti parecia eletrificado, sacudindo à nossa frente reportagens de jornais, puxando de um canto da mesa um livro que aprofundava o tema de certa reportagem, catando no chão um outro que complementaria a discussão por outro ângulo. E assim iam os encadeamentos, sem parar nem quando chegava o final da aula formal, porque aí estava sempre disponível para seguir a conversa — primeiro nos corredores da Fabico, depois tomando um café ou, mais tarde, uma cerveja.
Antes de entrar na Fabico, nos anos 1990, o Ungaretti trabalhou como jornalista em diversos veículos. Ele falava muito de seus tempos da Rádio Continental. Também falava muito de sua participação na luta contra a ditadura, como jornalista e como militante — não que essas atividades fossem excludentes, pelo contrário.
Ungaretti fez da sua vida, em todos os espaços, uma bandeira da liberdade e da radicalidade. Não se atinha a convenções, a limites ou a aparentes contradições. Aceitava suas próprias contradições e as exercia com gosto. Era uma pessoa extremamente fraternal, preocupada em ajudar e ensinar, mas nem sempre era fácil de lidar, porque não recuava, porque não aceitava menos do que tudo. Ele foi uma pessoa complexa também porque refletia a complexidade do mundo que, como poucos, foi capaz de enxergar. Não gostava das amarras e formalismos acadêmicos, mas era feliz em sala de aula, orientando pesquisas e aprendendo junto com os alunos. Não gostava da institucionalidade, nem de corporativismo, mas se manteve por décadas filiado ao Sindicato dos Jornalistas. Era um anarquista convicto, mas nunca deixou de defender os governos de Lula e Dilma, mantendo sempre um aguçadíssimo espírito crítico.
A radicalidade e a profundidade de cada fala do Ungaretti dialogavam com a prática que exercia em todas as suas atividades. Ele queria aguçar o próprio olhar e o dos outros, fazer ver o que era escondido, fazer gritar o que era calado. Como professor, como jornalista e como fotógrafo — e fotojornalista —, ele queria iluminar o que era marginal, fossem recortes das cidades, fossem pessoas invisibilizadas, esquecidas, rejeitadas. O olhar cuidadoso e fraterno sobre o que para a maioria é objeto de repulsa e de negação. As texturas e formas que ele buscava como imagem em suas fotos também estavam ali como conceito, como discurso e como bandeira.
O Ungaretti foi um revolucionário, um marginal, um subversivo, uma bandeira da liberdade e do jornalismo comprometido com as lutas sociais. Não gostava de dizer que era professor, sempre ressaltava que era JORNALISTA. Mas a verdade é que, com suas falas e com sua prática, ensinou dezenas ou centenas de alunos a serem melhores jornalistas e melhores cidadãos, mais críticos, indignados e capazes de olhar para as coisas além da superfície.
Uma máxima que ele gostava de repetir trata dos trotskistas: que têm uma função fundamental de puxar os governos para a esquerda, mesmo que não ganhem. O próprio Ungaretti também teve, de alguma forma, essa função: mesmo que nem todos consigam ser livres como ele, as suas ideias, palavras e ações nos oferecem uma possibilidade constante de entender que nada é natural, que tudo pode ser transformado. A liberdade como objetivo e exercício, a radicalidade como caminho, a subversão como urgência. Ele viveu tudo isso intensamente e, assim, se manteve jovem, por se manter curioso, interessado e em movimento. E, agora, se mantém vivo.
Um olhar para além do tempo presente
Os livros que recomendou aos seus alunos foram a base da formação de muitos. Incontáveis vezes chegou em sala de aula, ou em um café, ou em um bar, brilhando inteiro pela descoberta ou redescoberta de algum autor que ajudava a explicar o mundo sob um olhar inesperado. Ele puxava da essência de escritores, historiadores, artistas e fotógrafos o que poderia ser incorporado às suas próprias reflexões e vivências e assim o fazia: produzia imagens pensando em Flusser e Robert Capa, olhava para a História a partir de Hobsbawm, flanava pela cidade de mãos dadas com João do Rio. E reunia tudo isso em suas derivas, fotografando com estética artística e olhar jornalístico pedaços da realidade que ajudavam a contar histórias muito maiores do que o tempo presente.
Muitas dessas fotos ilustraram contracapas do Jornalismo B, jornal que editei por vários anos e que sempre contou com as colaborações e o estímulo do Ungaretti. Ele foi um estimulador da mídia alternativa, isso também é bom lembrar. Desde a revista O Dilúvio, outro marco do jornalismo alternativo em Porto Alegre, até seu próprio blog, o Ponto de Vista, nascido na primeira onda de blogs políticos e jornalísticos, passando também por seus perfis nas redes sociais, onde nunca deixou de publicar fotografias e pequenas reflexões.
Ele gostava de lembrar a análise do Hobsbawm de que o século XX só terminaria quando Fidel Castro morresse. Essa análise faz a realidade do mundo passar por cima do que é convencionado, se impor como a realidade que de fato é, feita de movimento. No nosso pedaço de mundo, o jornalismo do século XX também teve uma Era encerrada com a morte do Ungaretti.
É bastante clichê, mas a certeza mais clara neste momento é que o Ungaretti segue vivo pelas suas ideias e pela sua capacidade de transmiti-las. A missão a que se propôs, de transformar radicalmente o mundo, foi, dentro das possibilidades que tinha, plenamente cumprida, porque transformou muita gente, porque muitos jornalistas formados a partir da influência dele não esquecem, ou ao menos de vez em quando se lembram, que JORNALISMO É SUBVERSÃO.
*Alexandre Haubrich é jornalista ungarettiano, doutor em Comunicação pela UFRGS, diretor do SindjoRS
*Este é um artigo de opinião e não necessariamente representa a linha editorial do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Democrats finally decided to take rural America seriously – and won big | Anthony Flaccavento and Erica Etelson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Anthony Flaccavento and Erica Etelson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Long before Jamie Ager entered politics, he was making a name for himself in a very different place: the meat counter of a grocery store in Boone, North Carolina.
It was the early 2000s, and Ager owned and operated Hickory Nut Gap, a regenerative farm near Asheville. Over the next 20 years, he helped build a regional food system that delivered healthier food to thousands of people, improved land stewardship and made farming a bit more profitable.
We’ve long believed that American politics would be a whole lot better if people like him – working folks who care for the land and their communities so well – were representing us.
And now he is. On Tuesday night, Ager won the House race for North Carolina’s 11th congressional district, resoundingly flipping a Republican seat that Donald Trump won handily in 2024.
He wasn’t alone. Democrats tore into Republicans’ rural vote margins, wiping out almost half of Trump’s colossal 40-point advantage in 2024. Of the 21 most rural-populated states that held elections for US Senate, Democrats won in 10 of them, including states like Kansas, Mississippi and Iowa, all long surrendered to the Republican juggernaut.
Rural voters still favor Republicans – but by a whole lot less. They swung 15 points toward Democratic US Senate candidates, compared to their 2024 presidential vote choice. (Nationwide, Republican turnout was down, so we don’t yet know what percentage of the swing was toward Democrats versus the couch).
Non-college voters swung hard as well. For the first time since 2012, a majority (51%) of non-college voters voted for a Democrat for the US House of Representatives, a stunning 17-point improvement over 2024.
The campaign platforms of winning (or leading) candidates in red and purple states demonstrate a clear pattern: concrete economic issues of working and rural people were central.
In Kansas, Adam Hamilton’s “prairie populism” railed against the crushing costs of farming inputs, something Iowa’s Josh Turek also stressed. In Mississippi, Scott Colom emphasized the loss of labor and delivery departments in rural communities. Texas’s Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico both spoke out for rural schools against defunding and voucher programs. Keisha Lance Bottoms spoke openly about the rural-urban divide and her own roots in the Georgia countryside.
In South Carolina, Annie Andrews focused on kitchen table economics, rural healthcare and farmland preservation. And Sam Forstag, the first Democrat Montana has sent to the US House since 1994, emphasized the protection of public lands that Montanans rely on for recreation and sustenance.
All nine of the Senate candidates who flipped (or are projected to flip) their seats focused unrelentingly on easing voters’ pocketbook pain, reining in corruption, putting the brakes on AI datacenters, and supporting workers, farmers, veterans and small businesses. With the exception of Troy Jackson and Andrews, you’d be hard pressed to find more than a glancing mention of a single culture war issue on any campaign website.
The same goes for the five Democrats who flipped governorships. Hinojosa, Texas’s governor-elect, told the New York Times: “I have no interest in fighting culture wars. There is just one fight [against tech giants], and we are so caught up fighting each other … over the ways we disagree about social issues … I’m not going to perpetuate that any more.”
That stance earned her an eight-point Democratic shift in Texas’s 17 rural counties.
It’s taken Democrats several painful cycles to learn the benefits of sitting down at the kitchen table and staying there, a strategy that will serve them well for the foreseeable future.
Having learned the hard way that ignoring rural and factory town voters is the road to ruin, House and Senate candidates flocked to small towns. Abdul El-Sayed showed up at barns, union halls and fairgrounds in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. Colom visited almost every county in Mississippi, held 60 townhalls and even showed up at a small town Maga rally to talk to Trump supporters.
Rob Sand undertook a 100-stop tour across Iowa, including all of its rural counties. Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton met with local agricultural extension districts to advocate for rural broadband and 4-H. Jake Johnson, who flipped Minnesota’s first congressional district, had teams of volunteers fan out across the district for one-on-one conversations with voters, contributing to a six-point swing in their rural county.
For the first time ever, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee fielded a rural engagement program that included local organizing in rural districts, mobilizing volunteers and assisting with ad buys and mailers. Grassroots organizations, like Every State Blue, Dirt Road Organizing and many others fought for every vote, mobilizing the base while also reaching out to swing voters and disaffected Trump supporters.
The combined effect of all of these rural outreach efforts was gamechanging: When Democrats play ball in rural areas, they can win or, at least, begin to make significant inroads in those districts.
Democrats won big on Tuesday, most noticeably in rural regions and red states. The actions they take next will determine whether this is a short-lived repudiation of Trump or the start of a movement that finally, truly takes on elite power in service of working people everywhere.
As Corbin Trent, a media strategist and former communications director for congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, put it, the Democrats “have been given the keys by the American people. It’s time to drive the car to a better place.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/netan.title: Leak reportedly exposed Netanyahu and Mossad chief's plan to attack Iran before Israeli election
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/netan.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/netan.text:
Leak reportedly exposed Netanyahu and Mossad chief's plan to attack Iran before Israeli election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Mossad chief Roman Gofman sought to carry out an operation against Iran on the eve of Israel's 27 October election, but the plan was thwarted after Washington was inadvertently alerted, Israeli media have reported.
A report by Channel 12 said the proposed operation was opposed by senior officials in Israel's security establishment, who feared it could trigger a major escalation with Iran and lead to the postponement of the vote.
It said preparations nevertheless continued until an Israeli security operative mistakenly alerted the United States, prompting Washington to move quickly to stop the plan.
Netanyahu's office denied the account, saying: “The prime minister himself clarified in real time that an attack before the Israeli elections was not on the agenda.”
The report adds to allegations of tensions between Netanyahu and senior military officials over proposed action against Iran in the days before the election.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
On 25 October, two days before Israelis went to the polls, Channel 12 reported an “unprecedented confrontation” between Netanyahu and Israeli military chief of staff Eyal Zamir over a military action that defence officials feared could provoke a confrontation with Iran.
The network said Zamir had resisted carrying out the action and sought further deliberations, as well as signed documentation from Netanyahu confirming its legal authorisation.
A military source quoted by Channel 12 said: “This relates to an action that could lead to a flare-up with Iran, at a sensitive and dramatic moment, creating this [potential] miscalculation.”
The report also cited unnamed sources who said military leaders were concerned that the political leadership was seeking to “utilize the Iranian issue for political benefit”.
On 26 October, a day before the election, Channels 12 and 13 reported that Zamir was the only senior Israeli security chief to oppose military action sought by Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz, amid concerns that it could trigger an escalation with Iran and disrupt the vote.
The New York Times also reported that Netanyahu had “sought for weeks to orchestrate a new airstrike on Iran” but was blocked by Zamir.
It said the military chief had become concerned that Netanyahu was pushing for a separate operation short of an overt strike, which Zamir believed could provoke an Iranian response.
Former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak, a critic of Netanyahu, said in an interview with Channel 12 on Thursday that the prime minister had planned to carry out “a provocation” involving Iran “via the Mossad, behind the back of the IDF chief of staff”.
Threat of renewed strikes
The reports of the alleged operation come amid diplomatic efforts to end the war between the United States and Iran, with Qatar mediating between the two sides as Washington weighs its next steps.
On 1 November, Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu had urged US President Donald Trump to resume the war against Iran immediately after the 3 November US midterm elections.
The report, citing Israeli and American sources familiar with a phone call between the leaders, said Trump wanted to give negotiations with Tehran more time.
Netanyahu reportedly feared that a diplomatic agreement could lead to a significant easing of pressure on Iran, while Trump wanted Israel to avoid disrupting the negotiations.
Qatar's mediation efforts have continued since the US midterm elections.
Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani said on Saturday that Washington remained willing to reach an agreement with Tehran and that significant progress had been made.
“We cannot wait to reach a perfect agreement; we hope to reach a good agreement,” he said, according to Reuters.
Trump said on Friday that the United States was talking to Iran, while insisting that Washington had the upper hand in the conflict.
“We've beaten Iran. We are doing very well with Iran. We're talking to Iran. We haven't lost a soldier in six or seven months,” he told reporters outside the White House.
He also repeated his claim that “Israel and, in fact, the entire Middle East, WOULD NOT EXIST TODAY if I did not stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon”.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.title: Doping | Die Wada im Zahlenrausch der Ermittlungen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.author: Tom Mustroph
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120372.text:
- Sport
- Doping
Die Wada im Zahlenrausch der Ermittlungen
26.000 Dopingkunden, 90 illegale Labore, 100 Tonnen Substanzen – die Weltantidopingagentur feiert die Erfolge ihres Investigativnetzwerks.
Zum zehnjährigen Bestehen ihres internationalen Investigativprogramms gab die Weltantidopingagentur Wada am Mittwoch durchaus beeindruckende Zahlen heraus. Das Programm mit dem komplizierten Namen Global Anti-Doping Intelligence and Investigations Network, kurz GAIIN, hat in den vergangenen Jahren 260 Polizeiermittlungen eingeleitet, in deren Folge 90 illegale Labore geschlossen und 100 Tonnen leistungssteigernde Substanzen beschlagnahmt wurden. Außerdem seien Namenslisten mit etwa 26.000 Dopingkunden sichergestellt worden, erzählte Chefermittler Günter Younger in einem Videocall.
Was bislang allerdings fehlt, sind die prominenten Sportler und Betreuer unter den Kunden. Da werde man noch ein, zwei Jahre warten müssen, vertröstete der frühere LKA-Ermittler aus Bayern auf Nachfrage von »nd«. »Wir haben die Namen von den internationalen Strafverfolgungsbehörden. Wir helfen ihnen dabei, sie zu identifizieren. Einige Festnahmen gab es bereits. Es ist aber auch herausfordernd, aus den Listen die richtigen Personen herauszufiltern«, erklärte Younger.
Eine Pille hier, eine Spritze da
Diese Diskrepanz ist ärgerlich. Sie unterstreicht einmal mehr das klassische Dilemma des Antidopinggeschäfts. Doping selbst ist eine ziemlich schnelle Sache. Eine Pille hier genommen, eine Spritze dort gesetzt. Die Jagd auf jene, die diese Substanzen zu sich nehmen und sich über Siege, Medaillen und Sponsorenverträge freuen können, ist hingegen eine sehr mühsame Angelegenheit.
Bestes Beispiel ist die Tatsache, dass das Internationale Olympische Komitee (IOC) Anfang dieser Woche neue Olympiaurkunden für einige Athletinnen der Spiele 2022 und 2024 zustellte. Die Koreanerin Yelim Kim etwa durfte sich über die Urkunde für Platz acht in der Eiskunstlaufkonkurrenz in Peking 2022 freuen. Grund dafür war, dass das IOC erst jetzt die Ehrentafel in dieser Disziplin aufgrund des Dopingfalls der russischen Sportlerin Kamila Valieva änderte. Diese war damals Vierte geworden, wurde aber 2024 rückwirkend gesperrt. Alle ab Platz fünf rückten nun vor. Und weil es Urkunden nur bis Platz acht gab, bekam Kim als ursprünglich Neunte nun erst ihr Dokument.
Auch beim Marathonlauf der Frauen von Paris 2024 gab es neue Urkunden, weil nun die zunächst auf Rang sieben platzierte und später des Dopings überführte rumänisch-kenianische Athletin Delvine Relin Meringor aus den Listen gestrichen wurde. Der ganz frische EPO-Dopingfall der Olympiasiegerin von 2021, Peres Jepchirchir, hatte auf die Pariser Urkundenvergabe dagegen keinen Einfluss. Die Kenianerin wurde in Paris nur 14., ihr positiver Dopingtest erfolgte auch erst in diesem Jahr.
Erfolgsquote unter einem Prozent
Der Frust darüber, dass vergleichsweise wenig Athletinnen und Athleten durch Dopingtests auffliegen, war auch Motiv für die Einrichtung der internationalen Ermittlungsabteilung der Wada. Die Erfolgsquote bei Tests liegt seit Jahren unter einem Prozent. Younger ist allerdings überzeugt, dass die tatsächliche Doperquote weit höher liegt. Deshalb begann er vor zehn Jahren, die Abteilung aufzubauen. »Anfangs waren wir zwei Mitarbeiter, jetzt sind wir 15«, blickte er zurück. Aufgeteilt sind sie in das Ermittlerteam und eine zweite Abteilung, die sich ausschließlich mit den Kronzeugen und Hinweisgebern beschäftigt.
Mehrere hundert Whistleblower dürften es inzwischen sein. Younger zeigte sich stolz darüber, dass keiner dieser Namen bisher bekannt wurde, dass ihre Identität also geschützt blieb. Um das zu garantieren, trennte er auch beide Abteilungen. »Die Ermittler kennen nicht die Namen der Whistleblower, bekommen aber die Informationen und Sachverhalte übermittelt«, betonte er.
Im Windschatten der Strafverfolger
Für das eindrucksvolle Ergebnis von 260 Ermittlungen und 90 geschlossenen illegalen Laboren war aber ein zweiter Schritt verantwortlich: Die Überzeugung von Strafverfolgern weltweit, dass es sich lohne, auch in Sachen Doping zu ermitteln. Younger machte dafür vor allem die Tatsache verantwortlich, dass die organisierte Kriminalität (OK) wegen des vergleichsweise geringeren Verfolgungsdrucks den Handel mit Doping-Präparaten in ihr gewöhnlich auf Drogen- und Waffenschmuggel ausgerichtetes Portfolio aufnehme. Das mache Doping-Ermittlungen auch für OK-Spezialisten interessant. Und in deren Windschatten kann die Wada wiederum Netzwerke aufdecken.
Workshops mit Strafverfolgern in mittlerweile 99 Ländern führten zu der Vielzahl von oft länderübergreifenden Ermittlungen. Bestes Beispiel ist die in diesem Jahr erfolgte Schließung einer Fabrik für pharmazeutische Rohmaterialien in China, die auch auf Hinweisen europäischer Ermittler über Vertriebsstrukturen beruhte.
Richtig rund wären die Erfolge aber erst, wenn auch jene Spitzensportler und Betreuer aufgespürt würden, die sich vermutlich noch im Dschungel der sichergestellten Tarnnamen und Kundenlisten verbergen. Es wird Zeit, dass das passiert – auch damit nicht erst Jahre vergehen müssen, bis Olympiaurkunden an die Sportlerinnen und Sportler verteilt werden können, die sie wirklich verdienen.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/we-do.title: ‘We do not want to die from the cold’: Gaza families struggle as rain floods shelters
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/we-do.author: Ahmed Dremly
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/we-do.text:
‘We do not want to die from the cold’: Gaza families struggle as rain floods shelters
Mansour al-Sakni, 33, watched helplessly as rainwater flooded the makeshift shelter on the roof of a building in Gaza City's al-Tuffah neighbourhood, where he lives with his wife and four children.
The family had replaced their old tarpaulins with new ones just two weeks ago. Sakni had sold two water barrels so they could buy new sheets to keep them dry and sheltered.
But when the first winter storm swept across the Gaza Strip, the canopy offered little protection.
“We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water. The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too,” Sakni told Middle East Eye.
“We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room.”

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Sakni lives in a 30 square metre room with tarpaulin walls which have been damaged by the weather.
“I sold the two water barrels to buy new tarpaulins to protect my family from the rain and wind, but it was no use. Last night we were again flooded by the rain,” he said.
Before the war, Sakni earned a living selling newspapers. Now, he has no steady income and the family relies fully on food given out by the community kitchen, known locally as a takiya.
His 10-year-old daughter Jana suffers from bad eyesight. She requires glasses, but Sakni can’t afford to buy any.
A friend gave him 200 shekels to buy a pair, he said, but he used the money to purchase wood to reinforce the shelter instead.  
“We are poor people in Gaza. We want to live. We do not want to die from the bombing or the cold. Enough. Have mercy on us.” 
Sakni said he was wounded by shrapnel in 2024 while standing in a queue outside a bakery on al-Nasr Street. The fragment struck his back, he said, and the injury causes him severe pain in cold weather.
Heavy rainfall flooded thousands of tents across Gaza on Saturday, leaving displaced families exposed to cold, rising water and the risk of further damage to already weakened buildings.
Gaza's Civil Defence agency said it had received about 1,500 distress calls in 10 hours after the rain began early on Saturday.
At some shelters, water rose by 30 to 40 centimetres, Al Jazeera reported.
Civil Defence spokesperson Mahmoud Basal said: “What we feared has actually happened. A few shelter centres were completely flooded, and everyone inside them has now been forced out into the unknown.”
‘The rain came inside’
For Nasmeh al-Khatib, 26, the storm brought back the fear of losing her home and the uncertainty that has defined life since her husband was killed during the family's displacement in Gaza City in 2024.
Khatib lives with her two-year-old daughter, Alina, in her family's home in Mashrou Amer in northern Gaza. Five families are sheltering in the partially destroyed building.
The house was struck in October 2025, days before the ceasefire, she said. It once had four floors, but three were destroyed. The families now live on the ground floor, which she fears may also be unsafe.
“We have covered the house with tarpaulins, but every time it rains, we are flooded,” Khatib told Middle East Eye.
She said heavy rain and strong winds battered the building overnight, bringing down the sheets used to cover openings and allowing water to enter. Thunder also frightened the children, who woke believing the sounds were from bombs.
“My two-year-old daughter cried throughout the night. She asks me, ‘Mum, why is the rain inside the house and not outside? I don't like the rain'," Khatib said.
The family has solar panels, but the electricity repeatedly cut out and returned during the night. She said parts of the walls and floor began giving electric shocks, while lights and phone chargers stopped working.
“We do not know what to do. All our belongings are wet. Since morning, we have been trying to seal the holes in the walls and tie the tarpaulins in any way we can,” she said.
“We know that everything we are doing is in vain and that when it rains again, we will be flooded once more. We need a solution to this suffering.”
Winter crisis
The storm has exposed the vulnerability of hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians living in tents, makeshift shelters and buildings damaged during Israel's ongoing genocidal war on Gaza.
Gaza's emergency committee said more than one million displaced people face winter-related risks and that the territory needs about 200,000 tents, as well as heating supplies, Al Jazeera reported.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha), in a report published on 5 November, said people in Gaza still needed approximately 121,000 tents and 561,000 tarpaulins as of 1 November.
It said available stocks included about 2,800 tents and 76,000 tarpaulins, while no emergency shelter kits were available.
Ocha said the entry of timber needed for shelter kits continued to be rejected by Israeli authorities.
It also warned that restrictions on supplies, delays in approvals and funding shortages could mean some materials would not arrive until the second half of the winter.
The Norwegian Refugee Council said on 5 October that Israeli restrictions on the entry of shelter materials and funding shortfalls were likely to leave 1.65 million people facing a fourth winter in worn-out tents and war-damaged buildings.
Aid organisations have also warned that many displacement sites are at risk of flooding.
Ocha said in an October report that an estimated 950,000 people were living at displacement sites facing medium to high flood risks, including more than 400,000 at high risk.
The latest storm also damaged buildings already weakened by bombardment.
Gaza's Civil Defence said residents were evacuated from a partially collapsed building in Nuseirat, while two people were injured when a wall collapsed in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Civil Defence officials have said their ability to respond is limited by shortages of equipment and supplies.
Raed al-Dahshan, director of Civil Defence in Gaza governorate, told Al Jazeera that the agency did not have “a single tarpaulin or a single tent” to distribute to families affected by the flooding.
For families such as Sakni's and Khatib's, the problem is not simply the arrival of winter rain, but the absence of a safe place to shelter from it.
“I am tired of this life,” Sakni said. “We want the world to find a solution for us."

IRGC spokesman announces lifting of restrictions on Iranian missiles
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards has said that it has lifted restrictions on the range of Iran's missiles.
IRGC spokesman, Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi reportedly made the comments at a press conference on Saturday, in response to question regarding the country's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei's warning to the US against further attacks on the country.
Khamenei had previously said during a meeting with senior military commanders, that any renewed US or Israeli attck would be met with "with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response".

“Our duty is to show our capabilities on the battlefield,” he added.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Guatemalan lawmaker and three police officers killed in armed attack
It happened in a region of the country known to have drug trafficking activity.
A Guatemalan lawmaker and three police officers have been killed in an armed attack, according to the country’s authorities.
The attack on Friday targeted Congressman Julio Portillo, who was in the town of Rio Hondo, in the eastern Zacapa department, which is known for drug trafficking activity.
Portillo was initially taken to a hospital with serious injuries. His death was later confirmed by the National Unity of Hope party, or UNE, to which he belonged.
“President Luis Contreras, members of the Board of Directors and lawmakers mourn the tragic passing of Congressman Julio Cesar Portillo Paz, representative of the Zacapa district,” Guatemala’s Congress posted late Friday on X.
President Bernardo Arevalo said the three National Civil Police officers killed in the attack had died in the line of duty and instructed security forces to cooperate with prosecutors investigating the killings.
Authorities have not disclosed a motive for the attack or identified who was responsible.
The Lorenzana family cartel, which has links to Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel, controls the drug trade in Zacapa.
Portillo won his seat in 2023 for the opposition party Cabal, but has since switched to the National Unity of Hope party led by former First Lady Sandra Torres.
She is expected to run for president in Guatemala’s elections next year.
The killings come about three weeks after former anticorruption prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa was shot dead in Guatemala City, a case that heightened concerns about organised crime’s influence and the possible return of politically motivated assassinations.
Authorities have not established a connection between the two attacks.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Black voter turnout surges in US south despite Republican redistricting drive: ‘They could not stop the momentum’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adria R Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Black voter turnout surged across US southern states where Republicans were accused of redrawing electoral maps to “diminish Black political power” in the wake of a seismic supreme court ruling.
Democrats flipped or held seats in Alabama, Texas and Florida with the support of this voting bloc, building on a decades-long, dedicated movement to protect and build Black political power in the region.
The redistricting drive “blew up” in Republican lawmakers’ faces, said Ashley K Shelton, CEO and president of Power Coalition for Equality and Justice in Louisiana. “There’s nowhere to go but up from there,” she said. “We still have to fight to protect representation. We have to continue to fight for that representation.
“Let’s be clear: voters overcame unbelievable voter suppression across this country, and in particular in the south, to make sure that they were able to cast their vote in their voice.”
It comes after the supreme court effectively gutted a major section of the Voting Rights Act (VRA) in April with the Louisiana v Callais decision, rendering ineffective the last remaining powerful provision of the 1965 civil rights law that prevents racial discrimination in voting.
Even before Callais, Republican lawmakers in Texas, following directives from Trump, had redrawn maps in an attempt to consolidate their party’s political power. With the supreme court decision, multiple southern states – Alabama, Tennessee and Louisiana – did the same, redrawing majority Black districts.
Voters and voting rights groups across the south were incensed – both by the supreme court decision and by the actions of Republican lawmakers, leading to protests across the region, including All Roads Lead to the South in Alabama, which drew thousands of people from across the country.
But Tuesday’s midterm elections provide the first opportunity to see the impact of redistricting efforts on voters.
“There is a direct correlation between the Callais decision, the behavior of these state assemblies, and Black voters turning out during the primary, and then the results that we saw on Tuesday,” said Ashley England-Albright, co-founder and legal director of Black Voters Matter (BVM).
In 2024, Black voters in Alabama celebrated when Shomari Figures, who is Black, was elected as the first congressman in the state’s then-newly drawn, majority-Black second congressional district.
The district – which includes most of the state capital of Montgomery – “for years didn’t have the representation that they needed to push certain things, like more for the schools, better housing, things like that”, Jamey Thompson, who was elected to a local school board that year, said at the time.
But, after Callais, Alabama swiftly reinstated an old map that reverted Figures’s district to one that a court previously found diminished the influence of Black voters in the state’s Black belt.
Still, facing a tougher election contest after his district was redrawn to be more favorable to Republicans, Figures – a Democrat – won by nearly eight points on Tuesday.
Majority-Black counties in Alabama, like elsewhere in the south, had distinctively high turnout this election: voter turnout increased on average by 65% across the state, from 28% in 2022 to 44% in 2026, according to data reviewed by the Guardian.
Black-majority turnout in Figures’s district increased by 81%. The three counties with the highest voter turnouts in the district were Black-majority.
“So much of what this administration has done has been to roll back the protections that give us access to the ballot, while simultaneously flooding us with propaganda that tells us that it doesn’t matter,” said Nadine Smith, president and CEO of Color of Change, which worked to mobilize voters across the south before the election. “What you saw was Black voters showing up in the face of an administration that has spent two years attacking our rights, weakening voter protections and redrawing maps specifically to diminish Black political power.
“Even in early voting, we were seeing a surge. We organized anyway, and we voted anyway. Even in places where they, not all, but many of the places where they redrew maps, they could not stop the momentum.”
A study from July that analyzed voter turnout in the south during the primaries indicated that Callais, even then, was spurring increased participation from Black voters.
Alabama’s Greene county surpassed 50% turnout in the primary election, while Bullock, Lowndes, Macon and Montgomery counties – all of which are in Alabama’s second congressional district – also experienced significant turnout. Bullock county, which is more than 70% Black, had the third-largest turnout in the state.
In Louisiana, which triggered the Callais decision, Black voters made up 35.7% of the primary electorate during the primaries, despite making up only 32.1% of the population.
Louisiana maintained increased Black voter turnout through to this week’s midterms, when more Black voters cast early ballots than in any other midterm or gubernatorial election in the past decade.
“The turnout and the exit polling that we’re hearing from partners and the boots on the ground that we had was that folks were not going to allow the court decision to undermine the power and the authority that they had with their votes,” said Sarah Whittington, advocacy director of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Louisiana.
Organizers in the south have been working for decades to mobilize voters. The fall of the VRA reminded them of how hard previous generations had fought to secure it.
Five months prior to the VRA being signed, about 600 people who marched in support of voting rights on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Alabama were brutally attacked by law enforcement officers, who confronted them with teargas, billy clubs and other weapons.
“Bloody Sunday”, as the march is remembered due to the viciousness of the attacks, was a turning point in the civil rights movement. That was one of the fights that voting rights advocates uplifted frequently to remind voters of what is at stake.
“This is the lesson of the south,” said Smith, of Color of Change. “There’s power in community, in connecting with each other. We saw HBCU students marching to the polls. We saw so much of that sense of: ‘I vote not simply about the candidates in front of me. I vote as an expression of my love for my community, for my people, for my family. I’ll do everything in my power, and my power is considerable to make the path more humane.’”

https://taz.de/Deutsch-polnische-Beziehu.author: Gabriele Lesser
https://taz.de/Deutsch-polnische-Beziehu.text:
Deutsch-polnische Beziehungen: Hass auf Bundewehrsoldaten ohne Ende
Die deutsche Botschaft dementiert Falschmeldungen in Videos. Der Nato-Verbündete Polens habe mit der Krise um das Verfassungsgericht nichts zu tun.
„Zamach, Zamach!“ – „Staatsstreich“ skandieren polnische Rechtsradikale nun schon eine Woche lang vor dem Verfassungsgericht in Warschau. Polens Internet ist voll von dramatischen Videos mit angeblichen Staatsfeinden und Volksverrätern.
Seit kurzem rasen in vielen Social-Media-Kanälen rechter Politiker bedrohlich wirkende Bundeswehrlaster über Polens Autobahnen Richtung Warschau. Bundeswehrsoldaten in grüner Tarnkleidung werden vor dem polnischen Parlament „erwischt“ und zu harten Klängen der Gruppe „Rammstein“ in Szene gesetzt. Unter dem Video steht in fetten Buchstaben und auf Englisch: „Brüssel sendet deutsche Truppen nach Polen“, so als sei der „Staatsstreich gegen Polen“ ein Werk der bei den Rechten verhassten Mitte-links-Regierung von Donald Tusk, der Europäischen Union und der Deutschen.
Die antideutschen Hassvideos nahmen in den vergangenen Tagen dermaßen zu, dass sich die Deutsche Botschaft in Warschau gezwungen sah, zu reagieren. Etwas umständlich heißt es da: „Aktuell lädt die Deutsche Botschaft zu Feierlichkeiten anlässlich des 71. Gründungstages der Bundeswehr ein, an deren Rande eine Ausstellung zum 70-jährigen Jubiläum der Luftwaffe gezeigt wird, und der an allen deutschen Auslandsvertretungen begangen wird.“ Am Ende der länglichen Pressemitteilung heißt es auf X: „Jegliche Desinformation, die eine Involvierung Deutschlands in innenpolitische Angelegenheiten Polens suggeriert, oder eine Instrumentalisierung zwischen Verbündeten unterstellt, wird strikt zurückgewiesen.“
Das Problem: Das Dementi der Botschaft haben gerade mal 20.000 X-User angeklickt. Die Hassvideos hingegen werden von Millionen Polinnen und Polen gesehen und für bare Münze genommen. Auch der rechtsnationale Präsident Karol Nawrocki wiederholt gerne, dass die Gefahr für Polen nicht so sehr vom Osten, sondern vom Westen ausgehe und Polens Gesellschaft bereit sei, die Westgrenze Polens zu verteidigen.
Uraltbilder von Putin und Tusk
Politiker der rechtsnationalen Partei Recht und Gerechtigkeit (PiS), die von 2015 bis 2023 in Polen regierte, lassen keine Gelegenheit aus, den liberalkonservativen Premier Donald Tusk als deutschen Agenten zu brandmarken. Aber PiS-Politiker zeigen auch gerne Uralt-Bilder von Russlands Präsidenten Wladimir Putin und Donald Tusk auf der Mole von Sopot, und dann wieder Bilder von Tusk in einer angeblichen SS- oder Wehrmachtsuniform.
PiS-Partei-Chef Jarosław Kaczyński behauptet seit Jahren, dass die Deutschen alles täten, um Polen „unter ihren Stiefel“ zu bekommen und Brüssel und Berlin gemeinsam versuchten, Polen seine staatliche Unabhängigkeit zu nehmen. Vor Jahren forderte Kaczyński lautstark angeblich nie erhaltene Reparationen von Deutschland ein, was zu seinem Sieg bei den Parlamentswahlen beitrug.
Dabei hat Polen nicht nur die höchsten Reparationen nach der Sowjetunion erhalten, sondern auch – nach Israel – die höchsten finanziellen Hilfen für NS-Opfer. Doch das eine war direkt nach dem Zweiten Weltkrieg und das andere nach der politischen Wende in Polen 1989 und der Wiedervereinigung Deutschlands 1990. Da erinnert sich heute kaum noch jemand daran.
Vorwürfe an die Adresse Brüssels
In den rechten Hassvideos wird den Internet-Usern die immer gleiche Botschaft eingebläut: Die Mitte-links-Regierung unter Premier Donald Tusk, der Nachbar Deutschland und die EU seien Feinde. Die Tusk-Koalition, die mit Deutschland und der EU kollaboriere, müsse weg, die politische Bedeutung Berlins in der Welt moralisch untergraben und die Rolle der EU auf die des Geldgebers reduziert werden.
Kaczyński forderte unlängst, mit den polnischen EU-Austrittsverhandlungen zu beginnen, da Brüssel sich zu oft in die Souveränität Polens einmische. In einem der Soldaten-Hassvideos des rechten Parlamentariers Konrad Berkowicz hört sich das dann so an: „Demokratie à la Europäische Union, die deutsche Armee in Polen. Ursula von der Leyen schickt die deutsche Armee nach Polen. Donald Tusk gibt seine Zustimmung. Die Medien schweigen. Das muss die Welt sehen.“
Der PiS-Politiker Dariusz Matecki schreibt auf X: „Die deutschen Soldaten erklären, sie seien auf dem Weg zu einer Ausstellung in der deutschen Botschaft“. Dann stellt er die typische und schon Tausendfach wiederholte PiS-Wahlkampffrage: „Wann zahlt Berlin endlich die Polen zustehenden Reparationen für die unermesslichen Schäden des Zweiten Weltkriegs?“
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. https://taz.de/Flavio-Bolsonaro-in-New-Y.title: Flávio Bolsonaro in „New York Times“: „Wie ich dorthin gelangt bin, nehme ich mit ins Grab“
https://taz.de/Flavio-Bolsonaro-in-New-Y.author: Christine Wollowski
https://taz.de/Flavio-Bolsonaro-in-New-Y.text:
Flávio Bolsonaro in „New York Times“: „Wie ich dorthin gelangt bin, nehme ich mit ins Grab“
Nach seiner Flucht in die USA zweifelt der brasilianische Wahlverlierer erneut das Wahlergebnis an. Die Brasilianer haben nur Spott für ihn übrig.
Nachdem er sich durch pathetische Nachrichten auf X lächerlich gemacht hatte, in denen er sich als den „wahren gewählten Präsidenten“ bezeichnete, war es ein paar Tage stiller um den Wahlverlierer Brasiliens geworden. In den sozialen Medien kursierten weiterhin Spottvideos. Mit Bezug auf den Linksrutsch bei den Midterm-Wahlen in den USA hieß es: „Flávio hat es nicht gereicht, in Brasilien zu verlieren, er musste auch noch Trump beim Verlieren helfen.“
Am Mittwoch hat der Senator der New York Times ein ausführliches Interview gegeben, bei dem er sich wie schon zuvor als Opfer darstellt, aber auch heldenhaft gibt. Die Flucht habe er allein ohne jegliche Hilfe von anderen Personen oder Regierungen organisiert, behauptet der 45-Jährige im Widerspruch zur Angabe US-amerikanischer Behörden, die bestätigt hatten, an der Flucht beteiligt gewesen zu sein.
Frei heraus gab Bolsonaro junior zu, er habe gewusst, dass er im Gefängnis landen würde, falls er in Brasilien bliebe. Vorwürfe gegen ihn lauten unter anderem: Geldwäsche, Korruption und illegaler Geldtransfer ins Ausland. Sobald der Senator im Januar seine Immunität verliert, weil sein Mandat endet, kann er deswegen zur Rechenschaft gezogen werden.
Humanitäres Visum für maximal ein Jahr
Zur Flucht habe er sich spontan nach einem Besuch bei seinem Vater Jair entschlossen, der zurzeit seine 27-jährige Haftstrafe wegen eines Putschversuchs im Hausarrest absitzt. Offenbar wollte er nicht wie der Papa enden. Einzelheiten zur abenteuerlichen Reise in die USA nannte er keine, die werde er „mit ins Grab nehmen“.
Der Wahlverlierer und seine Familie dürfen mit ihrem humanitären Visum maximal ein Jahr in den USA bleiben. Durch den Wahlsieg der Demokraten wird eine eventuelle Auslieferung bei einer Verurteilung wahrscheinlicher.
Zweifel am Wahlergebnis in Brasilien
Gegenüber der New York Times zweifelte der Sprössling des Putschisten Jair erneut das Wahlergebnis an, bei dem Präsident Luiz da Silva mit 4,4 Millionen Stimmen Vorsprung im Amt bestätigt wurde. Dieser Vorsprung sei „mathematisch unmöglich“, behauptete Flávio, weil er doch im ersten Wahlgang noch vorn gelegen hatte. Donald Trump, dem die Flucht des Brasilianers politisch geschadet hatte, distanziert sich: Er habe nicht vor, Flávio zu treffen, sagte der US-Präsident.
Flávio Bolsonaro betonte, er werde aus dem Ausland durch seine Verbündeten seine Agenda vorantreiben, etwa die Herabsetzung der Strafmündigkeit und die Begnadigung seines Vaters Jair Bolsonaro. Im Falle von Neuwahlen werde er selbstverständlich kandidieren. Bei X ist ihm auch dafür wieder Spott sicher: „Entweder hat ihn der Reporter reingelegt oder er hat auf Englisch nichts davon verstanden, worum es in dem Interview geht, in dem sie ihn fertig gemacht haben“, vermutete ein Brasilianer dort.

Spiel „Trading Card Shop Simulator“: Deo für die Nerds
Im „Trading Card Shop Simulator“ verkauft man Sammelkarten. Bis man den Fehler macht und selbst zur Ware greift – beziehungsweise zum Hausverbot.
Als Jugendlicher ging ich nie ohne Feinwaage aus dem Haus. Weed interessierte mich nicht, ich wollte Pokémonkarten.
Die gibt’s für ein paar Euro zufällig abgemischt in kleinen Packungen, sogenannten Booster-Packs. Damit meine Freunde und ich unser Taschengeld nicht für wertlose Karten verprassten, sollte die Waage helfen: Booster-Packs, die eine seltene holografische Karte enthalten, waren angeblich um ein paar Milligramm schwerer.
Und ja, wir zogen daraufhin sogar ein paar seltene Karten, erhielten in den Läden dann aber Hausverbot. Im „Trading Card Shop Simulator“ („TCSS“) drehe ich nun den Spieß um.
„Trading Card Shop Simulator“
„Trading Card Shop Simulator“, PC, Playstation, Xbox und Switch
In dem Spiel befülle ich ein Geschäft mit geschmacklosen Tischen, Stühlen und Vitrinen, Regale preisen die heiße Ware: Booster-Packs. Die sind im Spiel aus lizenzrechtlichen Gründen mit fiktiven Monstern bedruckt. Das macht aber nichts, weil Fans bereits Programme entwickelt haben, mit denen ich sie in Pokémonkarten umwandle.
Der Schweißgeruch der Nerds
Ich locke die männliche Kundschaft mit Sonderangeboten in meinen Shop und verkaufe ihnen dann überteuerte Karten. Deodorants vertreiben den Schweißgeruch der Nerds, die ich nun am Haken habe.
Leider verstieß ich gegen die wichtigste Dealer-Regel und vergriff mich an meiner eigenen Ware. Eigentlich sollte ich die Booster-Packs verkaufen, um die Geschäfte zu finanzieren. Stattdessen öffnete ich alle Päckchen und verkaufte Seltenes an andere Sammler.
Das lohnt sich auch in echt, der feuerspeiende Drache Glurak etwa ist auf Ebay mehr als 138.000 Euro wert. Der „TCSS“ ist toll, weil er diesen Moment des Päckchenöffnens zelebriert, meinen Sammeltrieb befriedigt und ich viel Geld spare. Ich frage mich, ob es bald auch eine Feinwaage im Spiel gibt. Damit mir niemand meine seltenen Karten wegnimmt, klingt Hausverbot nach einer sehr guten Idee.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.title: The end of Maga as we know it
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.author: David Smith in Round Rock, Texas
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text:
Walking by a tattoo studio and medical spa on the pretty main street of Round Rock, in Texas Hill Country, Tarik Bakir recalled voting for Barack Obama in 2008 and Donald Trump in 2024. But when it came to the 2026 midterm elections, he was firmly back in the Democrats’ column.
“I’m not happy with the Iran war,” said Bakir, 41, a financial adviser who served with the US military in Afghanistan. “The economy’s OK, but not great. This election was a rebuttal to Trump. This time people said they didn’t like him, or his policies.”
Once a reliably Republican suburb north of Austin, Round Rock is the birthplace of James Talarico, whose victory this week in a US Senate election – Democrats’ first in Texas since 1988, the year before Talarico was born – symbolised a nationwide “blue-nami” that swept away Trump’s Maga (Make America Great Again) coalition.
It was the most sweeping midterm repudiation of a sitting president since the Watergate election of 1974. Unlike typical midterms, where losses are concentrated in swing districts or isolated suburban pockets, the 2026 midterms saw the Republican floor drop out across deep-red strongholds, suburban corridors and rural heartlands alike.
Democrats stormed once impregnable fortresses such as Kansas and South Carolina, taking control of both chambers of Congress and redrawing the political map. In Texas, for decades a bedrock of conservatism, the senator Ted Cruz is now the last statewide Republican still standing.
For Trump, it was a scathing rebuke after a madcap campaign that left some wondering: if the president had deliberately tried to sabotage his own party’s chances, what, precisely, would he have done any differently?
The president heaped praise on Ohio senator Jon Husted’s “ass” but, in the words of Cruz, his party got an “ass-kicking”. Florida governor Ron DeSantis called it “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country”.
Patrick Gaspard, a former official in Barack Obama’s White House, said: “Anyone who says that they were not surprised is lying. This busted all of the models across all demographics and geography. You would think that 2024 was the last century, not just two years ago.”
Why did Maga fall apart so fast, and in such colossal fashion? The short answer is that costs, corruption and conflict with Iran left Trump supporters feeling betrayed.
Frank Luntz, a veteran pollster and strategist, hosted a focus group on the eve of the election with people who voted for Trump in 2024, but would be voting for Democrats in 2026.
Affordability issues were “hurting Trump voters more than others because they are more likely to be paycheck-to-paycheck voters”, said Luntz. “They are more likely to have no money at the end of the week, and very little money at the end of the month, and so they were susceptible to food and fuel prices more than the average voter.”
“They were promised in 2024 that prices would come down, and we wouldn’t have forever wars, that we would drain the swamp,” Luntz added. “They looked in 2026 and they felt not nearly enough had been accomplished on this and so they wanted to punish Republicans. This is not about rewarding Democrats. This was about holding Republicans accountable for these voters believing what they were promised.”
‘His fingerprints are all around’
Instead of focusing on the economic pressures hurting many of his own supporters, like farmers struggling to pay for diesel and fertiliser, Trump diverted his public commentary towards vanity projects, legal grievances and high-profile spats.
“He lost the plot,” according to Luntz. “He was talking about topics that they didn’t fully understand and didn’t care about. He wasn’t talking about the things that mattered most to them and in the end they took it out on the Republican party.”
Gaspard, a distinguished senior fellow at the Center for American Progress thinktank in Washington, agrees that the Maga coalition fractured because Trump violated every pledge made to working-class voters – from sweeping tariffs on foreign goods and an unpopular military conflict in Iran to cryptocurrency self-enrichment schemes and federal immigration overreach that terrorised local communities.
The result has broken the psychological chokehold Trump exerted over his party, Gaspard believes. “We’re seeing it already. When your approval hits the low 30s, politicians think about survival,” he said. “What happened creates a permission structure finally for Republicans to develop a spine to move away from him on their political choices, their policy choices and how they navigate their cultural choices as well.”
He added: “Donald Trump can’t act as if he wasn’t present at the scene of the crime. He personally picked the candidates in Texas and South Carolina. His fingerprints are all around it, and he can’t proclaim his innocence.”
Republicans lost most of Trump’s gains with Latino voters in 2024, according to an Associated Press voter poll, while only about one in 10 Black men voted Republican in their local House race, down from roughly one in four who backed Trump in 2024. Voters under 30, who had been roughly evenly divided between Trump and Kamala Harris two years ago, backed Democratic House candidates by about seven-to-three this time.
Gaspard noted that the collapse extended to Trump’s prized demographic strongholds: “When you end up in an election where the Republican party ended up splitting men 50/50 with Democrats, that is a death knell for the manosphere, the bro platforms that they saw as their firewalls.”
Some observers were quick to pronounce the death of Maga and the end of the Trump era. But the past decade of US politics has been characterised by whiplash elections with both parties lurching between triumph and disaster. Trump was written off after his defeat in 2020 only to bounce back four years later. He still has more than 800 days left in office.
Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster, said: “Is this the end of Maga? No. As long as Donald Trump is in the White House, it’s still a danger. But it’s been badly wounded and, like a cornered ferret, it can still be quite dangerous. But this is a collapse of generational significance across the map and it has to deliver a massive shock to a Republican party that has been enthralled to Donald Trump for 10 years.”
Sykes, author of How the Right Lost Its Mind, added: “It takes a massive defeat like this for a political party to come to its senses. That’s what history tells us. It’s not because of op-ed pieces or commentators, or critical podcasts. It’s losing on this kind of epic level.”
The populist right may have lost some recent battles in Brazil, Serbia and Hungary, where close Maga ally Viktor Orbán was defeated, but it has hardly lost the war. From Argentina to India, its leaders remain in power, while in France, Germany and Britain its movements are challenging the established political order.
‘Like a cornered ferret’
Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, cautioned against assuming that the midterms marked the permanent demise of populist conservatism, comparing its persistence to illiberal movements in Europe.
He said: “I would hesitate to say that it’s the end of Maga, any more than the defeat of Viktor Orbán means the permanent defeat of illiberal democracy, any more than Donald Tusk’s comeback in Poland means that the forces arrayed against him have gone away.
“Maga has deep social roots in the American population. It expresses something that’s real and isn’t going away. But the question is whether it will be as dominant as it has been for more than a decade inside the Republican party in the United States and around the world. I think the answer to that question is no.”
Galston does believe that the midterms have created a vacuum within the Republican party and an opening for a reform candidate to challenge the Maga orthodoxy before 2028.
“These questions are never settled in the abstract,” he continued. “They’re settled when someone steps forward and says: ‘I stand for something different,’ and then convinces enough people that that is the right thing to stand for. That’s the way Donald Trump took the party away from the Reaganites.
“I don’t think we’re going back to the status quo ante, but is somebody going to stand up with a coherent counter-agenda? I don’t know who that would be but there’s a market opportunity.”
Trump responded to his humiliation at the ballot box like a man in denial. The following morning, he retreated to his safe space, the construction site of a new White House ballroom, and concentrated on signing a structural beam rather than addressing the electoral defeat. “Trump is still your president,” read an official White House social media post superimposed over an image of the 80-year-old, glowering into the camera.
But the race to succeed him has been blown wide open by the Republican debacle. Newt Gingrich, a former speaker of the House, wrote on social media: “The scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open.”
The biggest loser was the vice-president, JD Vance, who responded by posting an essay-length message on X, publicly identifying Trump’s deeply unpopular war in Iran as the catalyst for the defeat. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in what many saw as a calculated move to align himself with rightwing podcasters – and to put daylight between himself and his boss.
Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, said: “It’s going to be very challenging for JD Vance, because he’s hitched his wagon to Donald Trump so closely as his vice-president. But he’s going to try: he’s a professional political chameleon. I don’t think he has the chops to do it. He’s not very good at this.”
Other Republican contenders for 2028 could include DeSantis; Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Nikki Haley, the former US ambassador to the United Nations; Utah governor Spencer Cox; and former Virginia governor Glenn Youngkin. Winning the nomination may depend on harnessing Maga populism while also presenting a new vision.
“Trump is a toxic brand, underwater with every demographic, including his own base,” added Setmayer. “It’s fair to say it’s the end of Maga as we know it under Donald Trump. Be prepared for it to morph into something else with the same basic foundation.”
For Democrats, the challenge meanwhile will be to turn an anti-Trump coalition into a positive political programme. The midterms highlighted a new wave of young, dynamic leaders including Talarico in Texas, Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, a progressive and the first Muslim elected to the Senate. His victory could encourage the representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to throw her hat into the ring in 2028.
‘Our economy’s hurting’
Galston believes that the sweeping wins across deep-red states have effectively rendered traditional debates over candidate “electability” obsolete in the upcoming Democratic primary contest.
“There was something for everyone,” he said. “The arguments over electability have been mooted because it turns out that different kinds of Democrats can win in different kinds of places. That’s good news because, rather than shadow-boxing about electability, Democrats can actually have the discussion that they need substantively.”
They will be aware that Trump has an unearthly survival instinct. He has weathered controversies, impeachments, assassination attempts, criminal charges and electoral defeats and is not yet halfway through his second term. But this week’s national reckoning suggests that, after pulling off a comeback for the ages in 2024, he has squandered his last shreds of political capital.
Back in Round Rock in Texas, the epicentre of this week’s electoral tremors, there was little sympathy for the president.
On Main Street, Billy Joe Wilson, 47, who was wearing a long beard, tattooed arms and a bright yellow T-shirt, said: “The guy’s given us six years now of who he is and we keep believing him, and yet everything he says is going the opposite way: gas is up, diesel is up, cost of goods is up. Our economy’s hurting.”
Wilson, who runs bars and restaurants in the area, added: “Texas was a big supporter of the Republican party and Trump. But my generation got tired of realising that we’re getting screwed in the deal. We want to make sure that our kids or grandkids are set up to be successful, not living under a rule where the rich eat the poor.”

https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/jeremy-bacch.title: Jeremy Bacchi demande la levée des sanctions administratives contre les lycéens mobilisés
https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/jeremy-bacch.text:
Le sénateur PCF des Bouches-du-Rhône Jeremy Bacchi demande l’amnistie pour les « lycéens victimes de sanctions administratives » dans le cadre du mouvement social en cours. Il a écrit au ministre de l’Éducation nationale. « Dans plusieurs établissements, des directions ont prononcé ou s’apprêtent à prononcer des sanctions administratives impliquant l’inscription d’avertissements dans les dossiers scolaires à l’encontre de jeunes ayant participé à des actions de mobilisation ou s’étant trouvés à l’extérieur des grilles de l’établissement malgré des interdictions préfectorales ou de direction », dénonce Jeremy Bacchi dans sa missive à Edouard Geffray.
« Qualifier d’absences injustifiées des actes d’engagements de la jeunesse et les assortir d’un avertissement porté au dossier scolaire constitue une réponse d’une extrême gravité », critique le dirigeant communiste, qui s’inquiète de sanctions « notifiées de manière immédiate » sans « instruction » qui permette « de faire valoir le principe du contradictoire ». Aussi demande-t-il de garantir le respect des procédures.
