https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.title: Thunderstruck: what does the future hold for lightning?
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.author: James Bradley
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.text:
In a rock shelter in Kakadu national park in the north of Australia is an image of a being the Bininj people call Namarrkon. His flesh bleached away to reveal the bones beneath, he wears stone axes on his head, elbows and knees, and wields a great band of lightning that runs from his ankles up, over his head.
Namarrkon’s journey from the Arafura Sea to the Arnhem Land escarpment helped shape the landscape, according to the dreamtime stories of the Bininj. And in the great storms that arc and rumble across the landscape during the buildup and the wet season, it is Namarrkon who splits the clouds with his stone axes to create the thunder and lightning and release the life-giving rain.
Around the world there are an average of 60 lightning flashes a second, some extending more than 800km. Each flash can release up to seven gigajoules of energy, the equivalent of 1.67 tonnes of TNT, fleetingly heating the air around it to about 30,000C, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. This constant discharge of energy plays a vital role in regulating Earth’s electrical field and the ionosphere. It helps drive the nitrogen cycle by cracking open nitrogen molecules in the atmosphere and making them available to plants, aiding in the production of ozone, and helping break down greenhouse gases such as methane. And it underpins the cycles of fire that shape the ecologies of forests, savannahs and grasslands across the planet. Lightning, as the story of Namarrkon captures, is an integral part of life on our planet.
Yet as the planet heats up, not just lightning’s role in these systems but lightning itself may be changing. And the consequences of this could be severe. In July more than 48,000 lightning strikes ignited massive wildfires in Canada and the north-west United States, destroying homes and casting a pall of smoke over cities across North America. During last summer’s British heatwave, nearly 30,000 lightning strikes hit south-east England in a single day.
Already, globally around a quarter of a million people are struck by lightning every year, resulting in about 24,000 deaths. In Australia alone lightning kills five to 10 people a year and injures about 100.
Invisible fluids and cosmic rays
The awesome power of lightning is written deep into human cultures around the world. Frequently it expresses a kind of duality, conjuring beauty as well as terror: from the earliest-known poet, the priestess Enheduanna, describing her goddess as having a “glance like striking lightning” to gods whose domain includes both storms and agriculture in ancient Mesopotamian, Maya and Aztec cultures.
Often those who wield the lightning are protectors of humankind: in the Rig-Veda of ancient India, Indra slays the evil serpent Vritra with a thunderbolt and releases the rains and the rivers, while the Norse thunder god Thor was a guardian of humans. And many Native American cultures across the Pacific north-west, Great Lakes and Great Plains incorporate a powerful being known as the Thunderbird, who safeguards humankind.
Although writers and philosophers have sought a physical explanation for lightning for more than 2,000 years, it was not until the 18th century that the American polymath Benjamin Franklin proved the connection between the discharge of static electricity and lightning. Franklin theorised electricity was an invisible fluid that could be passed from object to object or held in substances such as water vapour.
Scientists no longer speak of invisible fluids. Instead, lightning is understood to be created when warm, moisture-laden air rises into the cold upper reaches of storm clouds. As the temperature falls, the water vapour condenses and forms tiny ice crystals. These collide with particles of soft ice called graupel, passing electrons from the ice crystals to the graupel. Now positively charged, the smaller, lighter ice crystals begin to rise into the upper reaches of the cloud, while the heavier, negatively charged graupel sink. As they move away from each other the resulting electrical field grows more intense, until finally the difference between the two neutralises in a sudden discharge of energy. It’s this discharge we see as lightning.
However, the question of precisely what triggers the discharge is still not yet fully understood. This is partly because the electrical fields generated by this process are only about a tenth as strong as they need to be to generate a spark. Recent research suggests it is cosmic rays that provide the spark, although other studies point to the runaway buildup of “streamers” of ionised air.
More than 80% of these discharges take place over land, and although the distribution of lightning changes with the seasons, it is concentrated in central Africa, parts of South America and the Himalayas. The most lightning-prone place in the world is in Venezuela, in an area known as Catatumbo, or “House of the Thunder” in the language of the Bari people, where warm, water-laden air blowing in over Lake Maracaibo collides with the high ridges of the Andes and can generate thunderstorms on 140 to 160 nights a year. By contrast lightning is extremely rare in polar regions.
But while the bulk of lightning occurs over land, particularly storm-prone areas of the ocean can achieve far higher densities of flashes: in one 1998 storm in the Indian Ocean lightning flashed eight times a second, so often that to the human eye it would seem the sky was permanently illuminated. And, in a testament to the power of human activity to shape the weather, storms over the ocean are also enhanced over shipping lanes. Aerosol particles emitted in the exhaust of ships appear to be changing the process of cloud formation.
Lightning without storms
As the climate crisis heats the atmosphere it seems reasonable to assume that thunderstorm activity will increase. A warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour and the additional heat provides more energy to drive deep convection within thunderclouds. Yet the reality is more complicated than this suggests.
A recent review of lightning studies now under peer review finds that projections ranged from an 11% decrease to a 44% increase in lightning per degree of global warming, with a mean increase across all projections of 7.5% per degree. Despite considerable uncertainty about how tropical regions will be affected, it also finds broad agreement lightning will increase in high latitudes.
Andrew Dowdy is associate professor in climate science in the School of Geography, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at the University of Melbourne, and one of Australia’s leading experts on lightning. He says that while “it’s clear that in a warmer world, some of the conditions that are conducive to thunderstorms and lightning can be enhanced”, there are still “large uncertainties” when it comes to understanding how lightning will be affected by climate change.
Some of these uncertainties relate to the difficulty of modelling the fine-scale processes that cause lightning, others to the relative paucity of high-quality, long-term data relating to lightning; until the launch of satellites capable of measuring lightning from space in the 1990s it was necessary to rely on ground-based observations and regional radar. Nonetheless, by combining records relating to cyclones and fronts with thunderstorm data, Dowdy and his colleagues have been able to track the frequency of such events as far back as 1979. This has revealed an increase in such events along the eastern coasts of continents alongside a poleward shift in cyclone activity in the southern hemisphere.
Separate research by Dowdy has found that while thunderstorm activity has increased in eastern and south-easternAustralia, other areas, especially in the tropical north, have experienced a decline.
But lightning can strike without a storm.
Just last week, a report released by the Emergency Leaders for Climate Change in Australia warned that the number of fires started by dry lightning – lightning that strikes the ground without accompanying rain – was increasing. The advocacy group noted that forests in Australia’s south-east recorded 50% more dry lightning strikes in 2000–2016 than in the previous two decades, helping create a “step change in fire conditions”.
“Lightning is the natural ignition source of fires,” says Dowdy, who also notes that “lightning fires tend to burn larger areas on average compared to fires that are ignited by humans. And that’s because lightning can occur in remote places that are hard for response crews to get to, but they can also occur in large clusters.”
The connection between any increase in dry lightning and fire is not straightforward, however. In Tasmania the number of fires sparked by dry lightning events has increased significantly since the 1990s. The fires that devastated Tasmania’s remote north-west in 2025 were sparked by a massive lightning storm that saw more than 1,200 lightning strikes reach the ground in less than 24 hours. Yet while it was lightning that started the fires, the landscape was already primed to burn by a combination of unusually dry conditions, strong winds and high temperatures, a convergence of factors that is rapidly intensifying as the planet heats up.
“It’s clear that in a warmer world you get more dangerous conditions for fire weather in many places,” Dowdy says.
Similar mechanisms are at work elsewhere in the world, perhaps most visibly in the United States, where dry lightning is combining with increasingly dangerous fire conditions to create megablazes such as the August Complex blaze, which burned more than 4,000 square kilometres in northern California in 2020.
Lightning in the fire cloud
More intense fires are driving an increase in another form of lightning, however.
When fires grow ferocious enough they can begin to create their own weather, as the heat and moisture they release can combine into giant thunderheads known as pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb). Turbocharged by the intense heat of the fires, these terrifying formations reach far higher than ordinary storm clouds, often boiling up into the stratosphere, creating a massive vortex which sucks the moisture released by the fire up into the upper reaches of the atmosphere at speeds that can exceed 200 km/h. There, in the swirling darkness of these monstrous structures, this moisture freezes, collides and creates lightning.
Until recently, pyroCb storms were relatively unusual, but in the past decade they have become increasingly frequent, not just in Australia but in the United States, Canada and Russia, and most recently Europe, where one was reported during the fires that devastated France in July and August of this year.
Jason Evans is a professor at the Climate Change Research Centre at the University of New South Wales. He says there has been a “massive increase” in the number of pyroCB events in Australia. In the black summer fires of 2019-2020, he notes, there were almost as many recorded as in the 40 years prior combined.
PyroCb are not just a symptom of our planet’s increasingly deranged fire cycle, they also create feedback loops, spreading and intensifying the fire, as lightning strikes and embers borne by the strong winds they generate start new fires. This process can extend across very wide areas: during Australia’s black Saturday fires in 2009 pyrogenic lightning from a 15-kilometre high pyroCb ignited new fires 100 kms ahead of the fire front.
Evans says that once a pyroCb “kicks off”, it’s “not containable. We can’t control it really at all. All we can do is get out of the way. They’re even too dangerous for the firefighting aircraft to try and get close enough to get their water on to.”
The spectacle of pyroCbs is just one more example of the way human activity is transforming the planet. Whereas we once were at the mercy of the lightning, now we are helping create it. What this will mean for us and our world remains unclear. For as the stories of the Bininj and others remind us, lightning has always embodied an uneasy duality. Simultaneously beautiful and terrible, feared as well as exalted, it can be both life giver and destroyer.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: They have gone 10 weeks without answers. Will these families ever know what happened to loved ones missing after Nepal’s floods?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Cait Kelly
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Every day, Nikhila Agastya answers more questions from her two children: has she heard anything about their father? Is he with anyone? Is it snowing in Kathmandu? Is he cold, and does he have warm clothing? Will he come home? The answer is: probably not.
“They know that [their] father is missing,” Nikhila says. “And they are still looking for him. They always wait; every day they wait for him. They won’t give up, they think he will come home.”
Her husband, Gopi Agastya, had travelled from Sydney to Nepal to go on a pilgrimage with the Isha Foundation when a flood hit on 26 August. He did not return home.
It has been 10 weeks since the catastrophic floods wiped away whole villages, reaching settlements as high as 82 metres above the river level.
The number of dead has risen to 1,459. Another 5,285 people are unaccounted for. More than 700 of them are foreigners – including 34 Australians – with families who have had no answers for 10 long weeks.
Nikhila last spoke to her husband the morning of the floods, before he entered the immigration centre at the border with Tibet. Gopi was excited about coming home – he missed their two girls, aged 13 and 7, and wanted to eat a home-cooked meal with them. The two parents planned to take the children on a cruise when he returned.
The days that followed are now a blur to Nikhila. She travelled to India to be with family, while a friend whose husband was also missing went to Nepal and filtered any small pieces of information back: the border was still inaccessible; the Isha Foundation was trying to get in; families were putting up posters of loved ones on hospital walls in a desperate hope they would be found.
Nikhila sent images to Australia’s department of foreign affairs – of the shoes he would be wearing, his jacket, beanie, sun goggles – anything that could help identify him.
“He’s a very lovable person. Everyone likes him. He had good friends. I recently spoke to a friend of his, and he said Gopi is not just his name; Gopi is a brand.”
He was also the sole breadwinner of the family. The pair married 15 years ago and moved to Australia: he worked in IT for a major supermarket chain and she focused on their children. But Nikhila is now looking for work, with a government parenting payment nowhere near what Gopi was earning.
Amid these pressures, she can’t help but hope Gopi might come home.
No answers
Every morning for the last 10 weeks, Linda Govender has sent a WhatsApp message to her daughter. And every day, she receives no reply.
Her daughter, Terricia, was in an immigration centre when the floods hit. Now her mother is running a global campaign on behalf of the families of missing foreigners.
“The uncertainty is unbearable,” Govender says from South Africa. “You wake up every morning hoping for news, checking your phone, reading messages and wondering whether today will finally be the day somebody has an answer.”
Govender travelled to the flood zone in the days after, hiring a helicopter with other families to search by air. She returned home to Isipingo Beach, south of Durban, with no answers.
Realising many others were in the same situation, she then set up Global Voices for the Missing – an online community where families can share information and advocate. She says they want Nepal’s government to keep searching to find the whereabouts of the deceased and to maintain regular communication with affected families.
“We understand that difficult decisions have to be made following a natural disaster,” she says. “But families deserve to know that every reasonable avenue has been explored.
“For the families, the disaster does not end. We are still waking up every morning wondering where our loved ones are. We are still waiting for information.”
Soon after the floods, the government of Nepal sought to help speed up that information and set up DNA testing that could match families with the remains of their loved ones.
More than 2,000 people have given their DNA. At the start of October, only 112 bodies were transferred back to families. The process is slow and the backlog is large.
Governments around the world have also been working with their Nepali and Tibetan counterparts to begin the official process of issuing death certificates.
‘We keep continuing’
In the days after the floods, families from around the world rushed to Kathmandu. They hired 4WDs to take them as far as they could into the flood zones, they spoke to embassy officials and politicians, they visited the hospitals, sticking images of their loved ones up on the walls.
Last month, Nepal officially ended the search-and-rescue operation, moving into the “search-and-rehabilitation phase”, according to Phanindra Paudel, the chief of the National Emergency Operation Centre.
Authorities would no longer actively search for bodies but would recover any remains, property or other valuables found during the rehabilitation process, he said.
For hundreds of families around the world, waiting for any news, it was a blow.
Those who took it upon themselves to search for loved ones have not found it easy. Nepal’s government is still trying to clear debris to get up to the border with China, with many roads still closed. Nepal has said rebuilding will cost close to US$4.78bn (A$6.93bn) and has called for greater support for that mammoth undertaking, which will take years.
Thousands were displaced – now living in centres, tents, monasteries, or with extended family. They do not know when they will be able to return home.
Sagar Pandey is the chief executive of the Himalayan Glacier Company. His company had 47 people – including 15 Australians – in tour groups in Nepal’s north when the floods hit. His brother was guiding one of them.
“It was scary, it was bad,” Pandey says. “But now, people are trying to overcome; people are trying to continue their lives in a new way.
“It’s been really hard; they can’t forget, but also people don’t have a choice.”
Nepal has been reeling from the floods, which hit during one of the country’s peak tourist times. Adding to the impact is the fact that overseas visitors are no longer coming. Last year, the country welcomed more than 1.1 million visitors, contributing about 6.7% to the gross domestic product (GDP): now, the number has dropped off. Pandey has lost almost 80% of his usual bookings for this time of year.
“We have the missing guides’ children we have to support, to pay for the future for their schools. So we keep continuing.”
Anita Cook is among that small group of visitors returning to Nepal. She owns iNeeta cafe, a world away from the Himalayas, and one of the few shops in the small Australian town of Moyhu, Victoria. She has been to Nepal twice, and is now taking her two boys to hike the Annapurna circuit.
“Once you’ve been there, it just really leaves a really strong impact on you,” she says. “The way these people live, they’ve got nothing, but they’re the happiest people on the earth and they would do anything, anything to help you.”
Her cafe is full of plants she is selling to raise funds, while the local pub is contributing $1 for every parma sold. She is taking $12,000 the small community has raised and putting it straight into the hands of the guides she knows well – they’ve lost families, are connected to the community and she trusts they can give the money to the right people. But she says the best thing she can do is get on a plane and trek.
“[When it happened] I would have jumped on a plane and went straight away. But we are going now, because trekking in the mountains is the bread and butter of all these people.”
‘I just hope’
For people who went missing at the border, the process has been harder – determining which country they were in when the flood hit has been difficult.
The family of Renee Spry, a woman from the Sunshine Coast, have been waiting while this process happens along with the 49 other families from her group.
“There was some confusion about where they were lost,” Renee’s sister Jacinta says.
“But at the end of it, Nepal agreed that they were on the Nepalese side, and they would be the ones who would be trying to issue death certificates.”
A fortnight after the flood, Renee’s husband and two daughters travelled to Nepal. They could not get to the border area, but provided DNA samples, put pictures of her up and visited the temples she had gone to before her pilgrimage. They raised the money to travel through GoFundMe and donated $10,000 to the Emergency Action Alliance.
“They were prepared they might go there and not really get any answers,” she says. “I still think it was a therapeutic thing that they did it.”
Jacinta says “it is a funny kind of grief”: to lose someone and have no answers, no physical representation that they are gone. “The uncertainty has probably been the hardest bit,” she says. “Feeling just a bit hopeless about it, feeling removed and a long way away.”
The family want people to keep paying attention to Nepal – on the redevelopment and also the increasing disasters the climate crisis is causing in the small country.
“If you were talking to Renee, she would say there are all these people still trying to live there,” Spry says. “In this ongoing danger, in this evolving climate catastrophe.
“She would be worried about them. She would be like, ‘what’s everyone doing about this?’”
For many families, like Nikhila’s, the lack of information has not extinguished their hope that, one day, their loved ones will be found.
“I always feel like that,” she says. “I just hope, still, something, he might be there, somewhere. I just hope.”

https://taz.de/Staats--und-Finanzkrise-i.title: Staats- und Finanzkrise in Paraguay: Haftbefehl gegen abgesetzten Präsidenten
https://taz.de/Staats--und-Finanzkrise-i.text:
Staats- und Finanzkrise in Paraguay: Haftbefehl gegen abgesetzten Präsidenten
Paraguays Parlament entmachtet Santiago Peña. Wenig später wird gegen ihn Haftbefehl erlassen. Was ist los in dem lateinamerikanischen Land?
dpa | Die turbulente Finanz- und Staatskrise im südamerikanischen Paraguay hat sich weiter zugespitzt. Das Parlament tauschte am Abend den Staatspräsidenten des Landes aus. Der Senat votierte einstimmig für die Amtsenthebung des bisherigen Staatschefs Santiago Peña, nachdem die Abgeordnetenkammer zuvor dasselbe getan hatte, wie im paraguayischen Fernsehen zu sehen war. Wenig später erließ die Generalstaatsanwaltschaft Haftbefehl gegen Peña. Ihm wird eine Verwicklung in den derzeitigen Bankenskandal vorgeworfen.
Neuer Staatschef ist der bisherige Vizepräsident Pedro Alliana, der kurz nach Peñas Absetzung im Kongress im Amt vereidigt wurde. Er lenkt zunächst bis August 2028 die Geschicke Paraguays, das derzeit durch eine Finanz- und Staatskrise erschüttert wird.
Nahezu gleichzeitig mit der Vereidigung Allianas leitete die Justiz Schritte gegen Peña ein. Gemäß der Anordnung der Staatsanwaltschaft muss dieser unter Hausarrest bleiben, bis er der Fachabteilung für Wirtschaftskriminalität und Korruptionsbekämpfung vorgeführt wird. Das soll laut lokalen Medien am Samstag passieren.
Das Online-Portal „abc“ übertrug Aufnahmen, die Einsatzkräfte der Polizei vor dem Haus Peñas zeigen. Ein Haftbefehl wurde auch gegen Zentralbankchef Carlos Carvallo erlassen.
Amtsenthebung statt Rücktritt
Die Senatoren waren sich während der Sitzung zur Amtsenthebung einig, dass Peña sich der Pflichtverletzung im Amt schuldig gemacht habe. Dieser war selbst nicht zur Anhörung im Senat erschienen und ließ sich durch seine Anwälte vertreten.
Zuvor hatte er vergeblich um einen Aufschub des Termins um 72 Stunden gebeten. Peñas Anwälte argumentierten, das Amtsenthebungsverfahren laufe ins Leere, da Peña zuvor seinen Rücktritt erklärt hatte.
Peña hatte so versucht, dem Amtsenthebungsverfahren zuvorzukommen. Senat und Abgeordnetenkammer nahmen sein Gesuch aber nicht an. Wäre der Kongress Peñas Ansinnen gefolgt, wäre er als ehemaliger Präsident Senator auf Lebenszeit geworden – was parlamentarische Immunität bedeutet hätte.
Bankenkrise stürzt Land in Krise
Paraguay wird in diesen Tagen von einer Finanzkrise mit politischen Folgen erschüttert. Millionen Menschen fürchten um ihre Ersparnisse, seit die im Mittelpunkt eines Skandals stehende Ueno Bank faktisch insolvent ist. Die Zentralbank leitete ein Abwicklungsverfahren gegen das Geldinstitut ein, nachdem dessen Eigenkapitalquote unter die Hälfte des vorgeschriebenen Mindestwertes gefallen war. In der Folge konnten Kunden zeitweise nicht mehr auf ihre Konten zugreifen. Die Digitalbank war in den vergangenen Jahren zu einer der größten Banken Paraguays gewachsen.
Peña unterhielt bis März 2025 Geschäftsbeziehungen zur „Grupo Vázquez“, zu der die Ueno Bank gehörte. Der Politiker hatte Vorwürfe möglicher Interessenkonflikte stets zurückgewiesen. Die Generalstaatsanwaltschaft leitete am Donnerstag nun mehrere Ermittlungen gegen Peña ein. Dabei geht es um die Aufsicht über die Bank, deren Abwicklung und die Bereitstellung öffentlicher Mittel für das Geldinstitut.
Die Staatsanwaltschaft bestätigte Festnahmen von Führungskräften der Bank. Zentralbankchef Carlos Carvallo musste seinen Posten räumen, nachdem ihm wegen seiner früheren Tätigkeit bei der Ueno Bank ebenfalls ein Interessenkonflikt vorgeworfen worden war.
Ihre Rücktritte erklärten auch Innenminister Enrique Riera, Kabinettschef Javier Giménez und Roberto Moreno, der Rechtsberater des Präsidentenamtes.
Der 52-jährige Alliana gilt als wirtschaftsliberal und konservativ. Der Kaufmann gehört wie Peña der traditionellen Colorado-Partei an, die das Land über Jahrzehnte führte.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Paraguay’s ousted president charged over banking scandal
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Paraguay’s ousted president charged over banking scandal
Santiago Pena was impeached over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which left millions unable to access their accounts.
Paraguay’s former President Santiago Pena has been charged after spending the morning at the attorney general’s office in Asunción for questioning, a day after being impeached over his alleged involvement in a banking scandal that has left nearly half the country unable to access their savings.
The former president, who was placed under house arrest on Friday, was charged over the scandal. The Reuters news agnecy reported that Pena was charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain.
The scandal centres on Pena’s ties to Ueno, a digital bank that grew rapidly during his presidency, partly through an injection of more than $800m in public funds, and attracted millions of customers.
The bank’s collapse has prompted days of protests across Paraguay, with thousands taking to the streets demanding access to their savings. Some demonstrations have turned violent, with protesters clashing with police.
Pena, who held a stake in Ueno’s parent company until March 2025, has denied wrongdoing, arguing that the bank’s problems were a regulatory matter.
What is Pena accused of?
Among the allegations against Pena are that he used his political influence to direct hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while shielding the bank from regulatory scrutiny as concerns grew over its risky lending practices.
They point to his appointment of Carlos Carvallo, a former executive at the company that later became Ueno, as head of Paraguay’s central bank in 2023. On Saturday, Carvallo was charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain.
Pena is further accused of allowing Paraguay’s state pension fund to deposit $355m at Ueno, above legal limits.
Pena had offered his resignation on Thursday, but lawmakers rejected it and pressed ahead with impeachment proceedings to prevent him from having the political immunity he would have gained had he stepped down.
An arrest order was issued shortly after he was removed from office.
On Saturday, after announcing the charges, prosecutors are also seeking pretrial detention for both Pena and Carvallo.
Bank collapse sparks political crisis
The scandal erupted after regulators took control of Ueno on Tuesday over concerns about its solvency, leaving nearly three million people unable to access their savings or use their bank cards.
Paraguay’s central bank said Saturday that 1.2 million customers had already received partial or full reimbursement of their insured deposits.
But that has done little to quell public anger, with many still waiting for their money back. Some protesters have also expressed frustration over Pena’s replacement, Pedro Alliana, who belongs to the same conservative Colorado Party and is himself under investigation in connection with the bank’s collapse.
Alliana, who was sworn in as president on Friday, has pledged to help those affected.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: Pope Leo hold first mass in Uruguay, urges crowd to be ‘bridge builders’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Pope Leo hold first mass in Uruguay, urges crowd to be ‘bridge builders’
Vatican says some 40,000 people gathered to listen to the head of the Roman Catholic Church in western city of Paysandu.
Pope Leo XIV has addressed tens of thousands of people who gathered for his first mass in western Uruguay as he continues his 12-day tour of Latin America.
The head of the Roman Catholic Church urged the crowd at Paris London Park in Paysandu on Saturday to be “bridge builders” and “share the joy” of their faith.
More than 30,000 people – many from Uruguay but also from neighbouring Argentina and Brazil – had registered in advance to attend the service, about 375km (230 miles) from the capital, Montevideo. The Vatican said another 10,000 had shown up beyond that, despite the morning rain and blustery, grey skies.
It was the first mass of Leo’s three-nation South American tour – which also includes Argentina and Peru – which had been in doubt after the 71-year-old American pope underwent lung cancer surgery last month.
The pontiff appeared to be in good health on Saturday. While flying from Rome to Montevideo, Leo told reporters his speedy recovery was due to “trusting God, good doctors, good surgeons, and overall, I think a healthy lifestyle”.
His visit to Latin America comes as the region contends with sharp political divisions, with several right-wing leaders coming to power since United States President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January last year. Bucking the trend, left-wing Brazilian President Lula da Silva was re-elected for a fourth term in office last month.
In Paysandu, Leo urged the crowd to “forward the mission of evangelisation with enthusiasm” and to be a “fraternal community that comes together and shares life, projects, dreams and hopes”.
During Saturday’s address, he also paid homage to the region’s beloved mate tea, which is regularly shared among groups who drink from the same straw in a symbolic show of community.
It “teaches us to share and be together”, the pontiff said.
Approximately 60,000 people are expected to gather for a night-time prayer vigil led by the pope in Montevideo later on Saturday.
Leo’s visit to Uruguay is the first to the country by a pope in nearly four decades.
He will head to Argentina on Sunday before finishing his tour in Peru.
During his trip to Argentina, the pope will address President Javier Milei, a strong proponent of free markets and a close ally of US President Donald Trump.

Palestinian Minister of Health warns of outbreak of disease in storm-battered Gaza
Palestinian Health Minister Majed Abu Ramadan has warned of the risk of the outbreak of disease in Gaza as tens of thousands of displaced people have faced flooding while sheltering in makeshift tents.
Israeli restrictions have meant scarce aid- and in particular, shelter materials- is entering the strip, leaving almost all of Gaza's population exposed to the elements and health risks amid rapidly deteriorating sanitation conditions.
Abu Ramdan emphasised that the razing of infrastructure by Israel as part of its onslaught on Gaza has amplified the health risks. Overcrowded displacement camps and the cold and damp conditions inside damaged tents could expose children, infants and elderly people to an elevated risk of respiratory infections.
Meanwhile, lack of clean water, busted sewage systems, and mounting waste pose the risk of water and food contamination, as well as the spread of rodents and insects.
Abu Ramadan also emphasised that widespread malnutrition, particularly among children and pregnant women, means their bodies will be less able to fight off infections.
"What is happening in Gaza is not a passing winter crisis, but an escalating threat to public health and people's lives that requires immediate international action commensurate with the scale of the catastrophe," Abu Ramadan said.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: The best plastic-free ice cube trays in the US won’t crack, stink or taste like a freezer
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Marian Bull
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
For those of us without a luxury refrigerator, an ice cube tray can be a tether to sanity. On hot summer days, it refreshes. At 6pm, it turns booze into a cocktail. In the morning, it can be an essential ingredient in the smoothie you drink while rushing to work.
Most classic ice cube trays, however, are made from hard plastic. If you’re like me, you grew up with them: stacking trays, that, if they were fancy, came with covers. So if you’re trying to cut plastic out of your kitchen and home, as so many people are, an upgrade is probably in order.
In the nearly 10 years that I have spent in my current apartment, with my current (imperfect) freezer, I have cycled through a few different options, from silicone and back to plastic. For years, I had a set of silicone ice cube trays, without a cover. These have the benefit of being plastic-free, looking sleek (with various color options), and releasing the ice easily: you never have to crack them on the counter, but instead pop the cubes like one of those fidget toys kids go wild for these days. Plus, if you’re into making cocktails for yourself or friends, they often come in big square options that look sexy in a rocks glass.
A few years in, though, I encountered an issue: my ice began to taste off, like an old freezer: like long-forgotten plastic, stubborn nubs of fat, abandoned recipes – a completely nontoxic but haunting stain. After some internet sleuthing, I learned that silicone absorbs smells over time. You can bake off some of these smells in a 200F (93C) oven for about an hour. (The downside of this is that your kitchen will, briefly, also smell like an old freezer.) This works, but I will probably never regularly bake my ice cube trays.
This year, I was determined to find new options. I was curious about the charmingly old-school stainless steel ice cube trays I had been seeing around, plus I wondered if finding a silicone ice cube tray with a lid might help with the whole smell situation. I set my sights exclusively on platinum-cured silicone, which is durable, odorless and doesn’t leach out potentially toxic siloxanes. This significantly narrowed down our options, especially as I refused to settle for a silicone tray with a plastic lid. I believe I have found some of the best plastic-free options out there for cocktail enthusiasts and hydration enthusiasts alike.
Why you should trust me
I’ve been writing about home cooking for nearly 15 years, and am always thinking of ways to circumvent the small issues that plague regular cooks every day. I also tend to use my ice cube trays every day, mostly for my morning smoothies. And I have been known to stir up a few Saturday evening negronis, chilled with a fat ice cube.
How I tested all these trays
There are only so many stress tests to put an ice cube tray through. I focused on all the subtle details of the basic ice-making process, mostly surrounding filling and release. I was particularly interested in testing out some of the newer stainless steel models. Some have a classic crank lever (which operate along a dramatically wide range of success), and some have a more traditional ice cube tray shape: rectangular cavities set into a rectangular tray, or miniature spheres shaped by two identical trays. The problem with these latter options was that they were nearly impossible to get out of their trays without a bit of melting. While I’m all for friction-maxxing, this was untenable for me. A good tray’s baseline is how easy it is to remove cubes. Shape and size also matter – I loved a silicone tray that had bigger cubes, but I found the ice unwieldy for my morning smoothies. Ultimately, the best ice cube tray should produce cubes suitable for a variety of icy needs.
I’ll be donating the ice cube trays I tested to St Mary’s Clothing Drive, a wonderful charity near my apartment in Brooklyn.
At a glance: the best ice cube trays in 2026
- Best all around ice cube tray:
    
Just Smart Kitchenware’s No-Spill Small Ice Cube Tray
- Best tray for cocktail enthusiasts:
    
Viski Ice Cube Tray
- Best tray for tiny (or crowded) freezers:
    
Firgi Silicone Ice Cube Freezer Tray
- Best stainless steel ice cube tray:
    
Ecozoi Large Cubes with Easy Release
Best all around ice cube tray:
This tray from the Australian kitchenware company Just Smart Kitchenware comes in a set of two, with a lid that easily lifts off, thanks to a corner tab.
Why we love it: This pair of happy green trays is the Goldilocks option of everything I tested. The cubes produced were mid-sized: not tiny, not huge; small enough for smoothies and big enough to plink a few into a glass for a cocktail. The lid attaches and detaches by “snapping” on to the outside of the tray, so you never have to worry about fitting a frozen bit of silicone into a groove. And since this is a pair of trays with sturdy lids, you can stack them easily right after filling.
The LFGB-certified silicone means that it’s rated even higher than the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) food-grade standard, and you can easily pop it in the dishwasher if you want. (While I don’t have a dishwasher, I’ve read on various forums that using scented dishwasher liquid can impart smells into silicone.)
It’s a shame that … Even high-rated silicone can still absorb smells. (For advice on how to deal with this, head to the FAQs below.)
Best tray for cocktail enthusiasts:
Viski Ice Cube Tray
Why we love it: Viski’s silicone tray comes with a lid and the cubes pop out super easily, thanks to the large cavities. The resultant ice is a little too large for, say, a smoothie or a narrow water glass. But they’re perfect for a spirit-forward drink, like a Manhattan or a negroni, or what I like to call “booze in a cup” (any liquor of your choosing, on the rocks). Viski also makes a handful of other cocktail-focused ice cube molds, so you can tailor the shape to your preferred at-home drink– from long, rectangular highball ice cubes to a more dramatic mountain mold. Their cube molds all have lids, which allow for easy stacking and keep an errant fleck of food from attaching itself to your precious cocktail ice.
It’s a shame that … The large ice cubes aren’t suitable for my morning smoothie.
after newsletter promotion
Best tray for tiny (or crowded) freezers:
Firgi 12-Cavity Silicone Ice Cube Freezer Tray
Why we love it: My freezer can get pretty packed – with CSA meat, random containers of homemade stock, bags of seafood and occasionally unlabeled bags of scraps. This slim, narrow ice cube tray is a great option because of its size: narrow enough to wedge itself in between a pint of ice-cream and a whole chicken. The silicone here sort of snaps into itself, with a double airtight lid. I liked how sturdy this seal felt, but it did require about one or two extra seconds of thought from my brain to make sure that everything was sealed correctly.
It’s a shame that ... I bought the single pack instead of the double, which would have solved the issue of occasionally not having enough ice cubes.
Best stainless steel ice cube tray:
Ecozoi Large Cubes with Easy Release
Why we love it: The great thing about stainless steel ice cube trays is that they don’t absorb smell the way that silicone does. The bad thing is that most of them don’t work.
Many of the “easy release” trays that I tested made it impossible to do so – the cubes were really more of an ice block that I banged endlessly on my counter in an effort to separate them. These trays come in two pieces: a tray and a lever mechanism that fits inside it, shaping the cubes. When your ice is frozen, you pull the lever, which is supposed to individuate the cubes by shifting the pressure among the “walls” separating them. The cheaper options offered on Amazon did not work at all. Even the more expensive Ecozoi easy release model in the traditional long shape was finicky: if I filled it up all the way, I didn’t find that the lever was strong enough to break up the ice. Luckily, the large square cube model I tested worked like a 1950s charm. The release works easily, and I actually liked that the resulting cubes were a little irregular.
It’s a shame that … Since this is metal, grabbing it from the freezer occasionally felt like sticking my tongue to a snowy telephone pole.
The Filter also tested these ice cube trays
- Myyaowl Six-Cube Easy Release Tray
- Vortihive Stainless Steel Ice Cube Tray
- Captain Cranberry Metal Stainless Steel Ice Cube Tray
- Ecozoi Small Round Ice Cube Trays
- Ecozoi Stainless Steel Ice Cube Trays
- Ecozoi Ice Maker Tray with Easy Release Handle
What you need to know about ice cube trays
Are silicone ice cube trays safe?
Silicone ice cube trays are generally nontoxic and safe to use, especially when they’re labeled “food-grade”. The best, or safest, are made from platinum-cured silicone, which is safe at the widest range of temperatures and ensures that potentially toxic siloxanes don’t leach out.
What is the difference between food-grade silicone and platinum-cured silicone?
Most silicone is cured with peroxide, while platinum silicone is cured with, well, platinum. This is the highest-grade silicone currently on the market, and is the safest for those concerned about leaching toxins. So if you’re worried about anything contaminating your ice cubes, platinum-cured silicone is a safer bet than food-grade silicone.
How long do ice cube trays take to freeze?
This will depend on your freezer, but they usually take about three to four hours; larger cubes tend to take longer, between four and six hours.
If my silicone does take on a smell, how do I get it out?
There are a few strategies for getting smells out of silicone. The simplest is to soak your tray in a 1:1 solution of water and vinegar for a few hours. Or you can try washing and drying your tray, then baking it in a 250 oven for 30-60 minutes. You can also rub the silicone with a 1:1 paste of baking soda and water, and let it sit overnight.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/us.title: US midterms: Not even Trump's Israel aid stunt could rescue the Republicans
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/us.author: Mohamad Elmasry
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/us.text:
US midterms: Not even Trump's Israel aid stunt could rescue the Republicans
There is nothing particularly unusual about an election stunt. Politicians routinely perform them. Rarely, though, is a stunt as obvious as the one US President Donald Trump pulled on 3 November, Election Day, when he announced that America would, at year's end, stop providing $4bn in annual military aid to Israel.
Trump had clearly read the room, and the polls.
For all his public disdain for polls he claims are "fake" or "rigged", the president understands their political significance.
Polling data suggests that American voters are increasingly uncomfortable contributing their tax dollars to Israel's military, particularly as costs rise in the US and Americans struggle to afford basic necessities.
An August Marquette Law School poll, for example, found that 52 percent of American adults believe Washington provides Israel with too much military aid. Only 16 percent said it provides too little. Even among Republicans under 30, 54 percent said Washington gives Israel too much.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Appearing on Fox & Friends that morning, Trump asked why Republicans should "suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed", a reference to Abdul El-Sayed, who hours later would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Funding for Israel, Trump said, had become "a bad talking point" for Republicans.
The admission was remarkable, and it demonstrated, perhaps more clearly than anything else, the extent to which a mainstay of American foreign policy has turned into an electoral liability.
Trump's funding cut declaration should be seen for what it was: a desperate, last-ditch attempt to rescue the sinking Republican midterm ship, a political life jacket thrown to Republican candidates running for governorships, the Senate and the House of Representatives.
It did not work. The election results look less like a blue wave than a blue tsunami. Democrats gained control of both chambers of Congress, flipping at least seven Republican-held Senate seats and winning important governorships, including in Texas, where a Democrat will govern for the first time in more than three decades.
Why the stunt failed
Why did Trump's bold attempt to save the midterms for Republicans fail so miserably? There are at least two reasons.
First, the midterms were not simply a referendum on Israel. An announcement about aid to Israel, even a significant one, was never going to erase broader American concerns about the economy, the war on Iran, the state of democracy, immigration policy, racism and other issues, some of which overlap.
Second, and perhaps more importantly, many Americans likely recognised that Trump's announcement was nothing more than a stunt.
Almost as soon as Trump made his declaration, scholars, journalists, activists, and political commentators expressed doubts about various aspects of the supposed aid cut.
Academic Marc Owen Jones said only "gullible" people would believe Trump's announcement.
The annual aid package represents only a relatively small part of Washington's overall military support for Israel
The journalist Glenn Greenwald noted that the US provides Israel with significantly more than $4bn in annual military aid. The commentator Ana Kasparian suggested that a new provision in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is moving Israel's military into more of a direct partnership with the US military.
These cautions are important. America's $4bn annual military aid package to Israel only scratches the surface of overall US military support for the country.
Brown University's Costs of War project estimated that Washington provided $21.7bn in military aid to Israel in the two years following 7 October 2023, while spending up to a further $12bn on military operations in the wider Middle East. In other words, the annual aid package represents only a relatively small part of Washington's overall military support for Israel.
The package is also not Trump's alone to cancel. The $3.8bn a year Israel currently receives is set by a 10-year, $38bn memorandum of understanding signed under Barack Obama in 2016 and running to 2028, and it is Congress, not the president, that appropriates it each year.
Beyond annual aid
Kasparian's point about the NDAA is worth pausing over. The version of the 2027 NDAA passed by the House in July includes a provision, Section 219, that establishes a "United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative".
The provision would deepen cooperation between the American and Israeli military establishments, including joint training exercises and information sharing on jointly developed technologies. Republican Congressman Thomas Massie warned on the eve of the vote that the House was about "to merge our military technology and supply chains with Israel's".
The legislation does not formally merge the American and Israeli armed forces. More formal, more intense cooperation in these sensitive areas nonetheless represents a move towards greater interdependence. For Israel, the much smaller nation, such interdependence would be invaluable. A letter from 56 civil rights and advocacy groups, including Amnesty International, has described the provision as "exceptionally dangerous".
Set against that support, cooperation and integration, the $4bn in annual military aid looks modest.
It is noteworthy, too, that Trump said he had made the decision to cut annual military aid to Israel in concert with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In an October interview, days before an election in which he lost his governing majority, Netanyahu indicated that US financial support would slow.
"If you think we're going to continue receiving ... tens of billions of dollars in American aid ... it won't happen, because America has changed," he said.
Israel's defence ministry announced in June that formal talks had begun on replacing the memorandum with a "completely reciprocal partnership" built on joint research, development and co-production.
Section 219, then, raises an important question: could the Trump-Netanyahu agreement involve replacing direct annual military assistance with deeper defence cooperation? After all, greater integration of American and Israeli defence would be more consequential than $4bn.
Importantly, this would also be a way of maintaining US support for Israel amid declining support from American liberals and, increasingly, among American conservatives.
An unravelling consensus
That declining support is becoming more difficult to ignore. For decades, unconditional support for Israel was a given in American politics, the one issue on which Democrats and Republicans reliably agreed. The Washington consensus about Israel is unravelling.
A February Gallup poll found that more Americans now sympathise with Palestinians than Israelis. The poll showed that among young Americans, the gap in Palestinian-Israeli support is substantial: about half sympathise more with Palestinians and a quarter with Israelis. On 15 July, 103 House Democrats joined Massie in voting to block $3.3bn in military aid to Israel.
There is evidence that the growing discontent extends beyond American liberals. Prominent conservatives, including Tucker Carlson, Marjorie Taylor Greene, Candace Owens, Matt Walsh and a host of others, have become vocal critics of both Israel and America's support for it.
Even Vice President JD Vance has grown increasingly critical of Israel. In recent months, he has made several provocative statements about Israel and the US-Israel relationship.
In June, he lambasted Israel, warning that the country had almost no friends left in the world. Vance then said in September that US foreign policy should not be "subservient to the state of Israel".
On 4 November, the morning after the vote, Vance posted a lengthy midterm commentary on X, outlining what he considers the four primary reasons why Republicans lost.
Citing polling data, Vance said that Americans who had abandoned the Republicans identified four changes that could bring them back: ending the war on Iran, controlling inflation, putting America first and changing "our relationship to Israel". "The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
Vance's admission is a bombshell. Only hours after a major electoral defeat, the sitting Republican vice president admitted that America's "relationship to Israel" had become a political liability.
In Israel, too, one journalist commented that his country had "suffered a very serious blow" in the midterms because Israel "was on the ballot".
A growing body of polling data, the public positions of influential American conservatives and Vance's own criticisms of Israel suggest that a true reckoning for the American-Israeli relationship is coming soon. Trump's election day stunt may have been an acknowledgement that the reckoning has already started.
