https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.title: Gotta buy ’em all: how Pokémon card collecting became race against scalpers
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.author: Zoe Wood
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/n.text:
The runaway demand for Pokemon cards is because they are being hyped “like crypto”, according to one young fan who had spent the night queueing outside a London store to make sure he did not miss out on the latest card release.
Before its 10am opening on Friday, the line outside the pop culture store Forbidden Planet in central London snaked past five others and, despite its strict sales policy, was probably “50/50” fans and resellers, said Kai, who had been there since 3am.
The 25-year-old has loved Pokémon since he was a child but the immense rise in reselling and scalping in recent years means fans like him are being priced out. “The cards used to be cheap but they have ballooned in price,” he says.
Kai blames the fact that “people in the crypto space have got into Pokémon” for fuelling the now rabid interest in buying cards for profit, and even gambling, with fans targeted by livestreams to bid on cards.
The signs on the door of Forbidden Planet spell out the rules. Like other stores, it limits high-demand products – in this case the £49.99 Delta Reign “elite trainer” box – to one a customer. (The set will be selling with big markups on eBay by the end of the day.)
It also has what it calls a “supplier-requested unsealing policy”. This approach deters some resellers because an opened product cannot be sold on as brand new.
“It’s calmer here,” said Kai of the queue of more than 120 people. “The people and workers are nice here.”
Like others in the queue he has (Pokémon) war stories of fights and overwhelmed security staff.
The clamour for cards has the most determined buyers zooming from store to store by e-bike. Others reportedly get around purchase limits by changing clothes or paying cash for other people’s hauls.
The traders were identifiable by their multiple shopping bags, said Kai, who added that “as a collector there is no reason to have that many”.
Some stores, such as Argos, only sell the trading cards online. On Amazon, high-demand lines are sold by an “invite-only” process designed to combat scalper bots.
With tattoos of his favourite Pokémon, Gengar and Dragonite ,on his leg and arm, Anthony, 26, started collecting when he was five. He secured the third queue spot after coming straight from his waiting shift at 1am.
He admits to doing “everything” – buying, selling and exchanging cards – and using the sale proceeds to subsidise his collection.
Like Luke, second in the queue, and Hiep, who secured first place at 11pm, he wanted to buy the expensive elite trainer sets. Luke, 30, said nostalgia around Pokémon’s 30th anniversary this year was the “straw that broke me”.
He had a binder with placeholders for missing cards. It was an “expensive” hobby with scalpers being the reason “people like us turn up so early”.
Frustrated parents are increasingly found lurking in Reddit threads and Facebook groups looking for advice on how to buy cards for their children.
Even though Pokémon produces about 10bn cards a year, Calvin Innes, a fandom and pop culture strategist, said the demand had “outrun the machines, so everything else – bots, scalpers, queues etc – sits on the fact that there is a hard supply limit”.
“It’s not impossible for kids to get cards but the buying experience has gotten really ugly,” said Innes, author of Fandom Power: Marketing in the Age of Nerd Culture. “As a father of three kids who are all into Pokémon, it sucks.”
While elite trainer and booster box sets, plus Pokémon Center exclusives, were the hardest products to get, Innes said single packs and blisters were more accessible, although smaller high street retailers sold out quickly.
He also advised parents to buy singles from a UK card shop, singles marketplace, such as Cardmarket, or top-rated sellers on eBay UK.
Another option for parents was to go to a prerelease or league event at a game shop. Innes said they typically cost £25-£30 and the child usually got guaranteed cards, and the opportunity to play the game.
Daniel Garnett, who owns the Hull Pops Gaming Centre in Hessle, East Yorkshire, runs a free kids club and said he tries to keep product back for regular players. “We teach kids all about the Pokémon game, about the cards and how to play. We also have a qualified Pokémon judge that helps out.
“Sadly, however, about a month ago, we had lots of parents bring their kids in purely to buy product, and had no intention of playing or staying for the session.”

https://taz.de/Serpil-Midyatli-ueber-Ung.title: Serpil Midyatli über Ungleichbehandlung: „Frauen werden wundgeschossen“
https://taz.de/Serpil-Midyatli-ueber-Ung.author: Esther Geißlinger
https://taz.de/Serpil-Midyatli-ueber-Ung.text:
Serpil Midyatli über Ungleichbehandlung: „Frauen werden wundgeschossen“
Schleswig-Holsteins SPD-Fraktionschefin Serpil Midyatli findet, dass Frauen und Männer in der Politik mit zweierlei Maß gemessen werden. Immer noch.
taz: Frau Midyatli, die Berliner Linke Elif Eralp spricht von Angst um ihre Familie, und die Öffentlichkeit zweifelt an ihrer Regierungsfähigkeit – wäre die Reaktion bei einem männlichen Politiker ebenso gewesen?
Serpil Midyatli: Ich habe den Eindruck, dass Frauen und Männer mit zweierlei Maß gemessen werden. Wenn eine Frau sagt, sie habe Angst, dann gilt sie als zu emotional, dabei sollen Politiker:innen doch nahbar und emotional sein. Was denn nun? Ohne zu sehr auf den konkreten Fall einzugehen, finde ich Sorgen um Familie und Kinder verständlich. Ich weiß nicht, ob es bei einem Mann auch so thematisiert worden wäre. Aber bei der Eignung für ein Regierungsamt müssen für Frauen und Männer dieselben Maßstäbe gelten.
taz: Sie haben den Eindruck, dass zurzeit im öffentlichen und politischen Raum die Männer wieder nach vorn stürmen und die Frauen zurückdrängen. Woran machen Sie das fest?
Midyatli: Ich sehe wieder häufiger Podien, auf denen nur Männer sitzen, ohne dass sich jemand daran stört. Auch die Sprache und die Themen verändern sich. Ja, wir haben in Folge des russischen Angriffs auf die Ukraine eine neue Bedrohungslage, aber warum sprechen dann jetzt vorrangig Männer über technische Fragen? Sicherheit hat etwas damit zu tun, wie resilient die Gesellschaft ist, und dazu braucht es alle Gruppen. Mich ärgert auch, wie gerade die CDU und der Kanzler über Frauen sprechen – sie sollten mehr Vollzeit arbeiten, einen stärkeren Beitrag leisten. Das klingt, als würden wir bisher alle in der Hängematte liegen. Wenn die Teilzeitquoten hoch sind, wie auch in Schleswig-Holstein, hat das Gründe, etwa fehlende Betreuungsplätze oder die Struktur des Arbeitsmarkts. Aber anstatt diese Probleme anzugehen, wird erwartet, dass wir die strukturellen Benachteiligungen individuell lösen.
geboren 1975 in Kiel. Mit 19 Jahren übernahm sie die Leitung eines Restaurants ihrer Familie und betrieb später mit ihrem Mann, mit dem sie zwei Kinder hat, einen Kultur- und Veranstaltungsservice. Seit 2000 ist sie SPD-Mitglied und wurde nach mehreren kommunalpolitischen Stationen 2009 in den schleswig-holsteinischen Landtag gewählt. 2019 übernahm sie den Landesvorsitz, den sie 2026 an Ulf Kämpfer abgab. Sie ist Fraktionsvorsitzende der SPD im Landtag.
taz: Der Landtag in Schleswig-Holstein hat eine Frauenquote von knapp 44 Prozent, so viele wie nie. Im Bundestag sind es weniger als ein Drittel, vor allem wegen der stark männerlastigen Fraktionen der AfD und der CDU/CSU. Ist damit das Ergebnis in Kiel eine Ausnahme, fürchten Sie einen Rückschlag in der kommenden Wahlperiode?
Midyatli: Ich würde mir sehr wünschen, dass der nächste Landtag auf 50 zu 50 kommt. Was einfacher geht, wenn die AfD nicht einzieht. Frauen machen nicht automatisch eine bessere Politik, aber sie bringen andere Themen und Sichtweisen ein.
taz: Sie wünschen sich eine Bundespräsidentin?
Midyatli: Es ist ein starkes Zeichen, dass wir das höchste Amt des Staates mit einer Präsidentin besetzen wollen. Das Hin und Her bei CDU und CSU war peinlich. Es gibt viele starke und kompetente Frauen, der Kanzler hätte früher eine Entscheidung treffen sollen, um eine Hängepartie zu verhindern. Mich freut, dass sich viele Stimmen für Ilse Aigner stark gemacht haben.
taz: So viel Rückhalt hat Bärbel Bas offenbar nicht gespürt, sie ist auch wegen Angriffen auf ihre Person zurückgetreten. Wie haben Sie das Ausscheiden Ihrer Parteifreundin erlebt?
Midyatli: Ich fürchte, man muss generell sagen: Frauen werden wundgeschossen. Trotz des Schicksalsschlages, der Bärbel Bas getroffen hat, ging die Kritik weiter. Immer noch oder wieder werden Frauen eher Kompetenzen abgesprochen. Und wenn es keine Argumente gibt, geht es ums Aussehen oder um puren Hass. Das finde ich krass, ich dachte, dass wir weiter sind.
taz: In Schleswig-Holstein will die Grüne Aminata Touré Ministerpräsidentin werden – auch wenn Sie natürlich Ihrer Partei den Sieg wünschen, ist Schleswig-Holstein nach Heide Simonis wieder reif für eine Landesmutter?
Midyatli: Am Ende kommt es darauf an, welche Politik für die Frauen gemacht wird. Unser SPD-Spitzenkandidat Ulf Kämpfer setzt sich sehr stark für Gleichstellung und Familien ein. Von Frau Touré höre ich viele Pläne, aber sie ist bereits Sozialministerin und hätte schon in dieser Legislaturperiode mehr auf den Weg bringen müssen.
taz: Sie selbst haben als Parteichefin in Schleswig-Holstein vor fünf Jahren Thomas Losse-Müller zum Spitzenkandidaten gemacht. Jetzt tritt die Landes-SPD wieder mit einem Mann an. Also stimmt der alte Satz, dass Frauen selbst schuld sind, weil sie nicht nach vorn drängen?
Midyatli: Man muss Entscheidungen dann treffen, wenn sie anstehen. Damals habe ich es so entscheiden, weil es inhaltliche Gründe gab. Diesmal habe ich mich beworben, aber die SPD-Mitglieder haben sich in der Urwahl mit klarem Votum für Ulf Kämpfer entschieden. Ich bin fein damit. Ich bereue weder die eine noch die andere Entscheidung.
taz: Wie merken Sie selbst als Frau mit türkischen Wurzeln den Druck?
Midyatli: Ich weiß, dass ich mich doppelt beweisen muss. Aber ich finde es weit schlimmer, was in der Kommunalpolitik passiert. Das Netz setzt keine Schranken, und wenn es Anfeindungen gibt, werden gerade Kommunalpolitiker:innen leiser. Wir brauchen stärkere Regeln, um die Plattformen zu kontrollieren, und wir brauchen die Sensibilisierung dafür, dass man im Netz nicht alles sagen darf.
taz: Was sollte sich noch ändern, was wünschen Sie sich?
Midyatli: Wenn wir mehr Frauen in höchsten Ämtern haben wollen, braucht es Allianzen. Männer schaffen den Aufstieg auch nicht allein, und solche Netzwerke müssen wir Frauen auch bilden. Wenn einer Frau die Kompetenz pauschal abgesprochen wird, dürfen wir das nicht dulden.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: ‘They’re just live experiments’: the dark and deadly world of looksmaxxing
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
If you’ve heard the term looksmaxxing – the manospheric pursuit of male aesthetic beauty via steroids, peptides, cosmetic surgery and total commitment – you probably know the name Clavicular. With more than 2 million followers and a cluster of mainstream media profiles, the 20-year-old streamer born Braden Peters has become the chiseled face of a once fringe movement to achieve algorithmically defined good looks by any means necessary, from daily methamphetamines to breaking your jaw with a hammer. Clavicular has courted attention for a nihilistic worldview expressed in blunt, idiosyncratic argot: “hardmaxxing”, “bone smashing”, anything to increase your “SMV” (sexual market value).
Baffling, horrifying or grimly compelling, depending on your view, Clavicular would be a fascinating documentary subject. Indeed, news of a possible Clavicular documentary has percolated all year, after the influencer filed a cease and desist letter against Disney/Hulu for allegedly filming him backstage at a New York fashion show in February. (It’s far from his most serious legal matter this year – last month, he pleaded guilty to charges that he raped a 17-year-old girl at his family’s Massachusetts home in May 2025.) But the docuseries in question, Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death, was never actually about Clavicular, who appears only in publicly available snippets. It instead trains its focus upstream of the bone-smashing, on the infamous influencer’s influences: the so-called “biohacking” scene that inspired the youths’ fixation on extreme body modification. And in particular, supplement guru Dr Tony Huge and his acolytes, in the aftermath of the suspicious death of his close associate, the “penis enlargement” expert known as “Leo Longevity”.
“This was a very fringe movement when we began this documentary,” said Stacey Lee, the director of the three-part series. But its influence seemed to expand as rapidly as the subjects’ roided muscles once filming commenced in 2024. “Clavicular grew up on Leo Longevity,” Lee said. “These kids are growing up on that. They are feeding on these projections of masculinity, and we are watching it in real time. What Tony was putting online 10 years ago is being recreated in shorter, faster, far more extreme forms.”
To be clear, the man born Anthony Hughes never advocated for moderation. A former bankruptcy attorney turned bodybuilder with muscles that appear perpetually at risk of bursting through his skin, Tony initially made his “biohacking” name for trying, on camera, the “fat-burning” “supplement” DNP that could, in even mildly excess doses, melt internal organs. A prolific user of steroids and experimenter with substances from the dubious to illicit, Hughes projected brawny confidence at a time when, as he puts it in the first episode, “Society doesn’t have a place for masculine men any more.” (Get Huge is, among other things, a very difficult watch for those with an aversion to “manosphere” bluster, or needles, which jab with stunning frequency.)
To his 250,000 online followers, Hughes hammered the mantra: “a day natty [natural] is a day wasted”. To not be biohacking was to be “beta and controllable”, missing the opportunity to be bigger and better. “They’re just live experiments,” said Lee of the mindset. “Every day is another science experiment to see what I can do with my body in order to augment it.” Ubiquitous daily injections in the face, neck, arm, rear is “the world. To them, it’s like drinking water.” To skirt US regulatory scrutiny – and, as later episodes explore, civil lawsuits and criminal investigations – Hughes relocated to Pattaya, Thailand, in 2017, where he gathered a clique of “passport bros” for content and a self-proclaimed “harem” of paid women. (“A man should only have as many girlfriends as he can leg press,” he says while holding up a pyramid of Thai women.)
Lee, a mother of a nine-year-old son concerned by the far-rightward lurch of male influencers, caught up with Hughes there in 2024, “and immediately it was just doors wide open”, she recalled. “Tony’s whole philosophy is radical transparency – ‘come on in, nothing to hide here’.” The camera crew trailed Tony and two close associates, Elon Muscular and Connor Murphy, as they gym, roid, rip through Pattaya’s sex-work scene and, above all, film. But it was transparency in name only. “We realized quickly that these guys are performers,” Lee said. “They create characters for the internet. And the character for the internet projects radical transparency. What does the human, when the internet is turned off, what are they like?” For young men, “these guys are projecting this blueprint for how to live their lives. We wanted to puncture that and get beneath it.”
Part of that was simply asking questions about what happened to Leo, born Laith Abdullah Algaz, who was found dead in the house he shared with Hughes in January 2023; authorities ruled the cause as blunt force trauma, source unknown. A self-proclaimed penis enlargement expert who fled to Thailand after his estranged wife filed a restraining order, Leo quickly developed an intense bromance with Hughes. (As Elon recalls: “They were more than friends. There was fire between them.”) But the relationship was souring by the end – and Leo, as Lee uncovered, was not the first Tony Huge “ride or die” to actually die. As Get Huge gets deeper, Lee learns that four other close Hughes associates have either died or disappeared under questionable circumstances since 2018, ranging from overdoses to house fire to hanging. And the camera pans out to the making of the documentary itself, as Hughes, Elon Muscular and Murphy, each surely surpassing the daily injectables limit – Murphy claims to be taking anywhere from a dozen to 100 “compounds” per day – snipe at each other and scrap for narrative control.
Lee declined to offer a theory on what happened to Leo or the other men in Hughes’s orbit. “It was more important for us that the theories become a conduit to expose the different systems of this masculine philosophy,” she said. “When people die, I think most people would just be like, ‘Hold up, let’s pump the brakes.’ But that doesn’t happen because they’re part of a community, there is a sense of belonging and they’re almost reinforced in this mindset of like, ‘Oops, we got the experiment wrong, let’s not do that next time.’
“It is really disconcerting when these really complex emotional problems that everyone faces are simplified down to like, get a bigger jaw. Fix your brow line. And make your penis bigger.”
Get Huge certainly contains many disconcerting observations, from the ridiculous (Elon Muscular’s attempt to brand Hughes “the Hugh Hefner of biohacking”) to the sinister (Hughes requesting his “girlfriends” always be naked or wearing “sexy clothes” in his bedroom). But it is a surprisingly empathetic look at an emotionally stunted scene. At one point, Lee point-blank tells Elon that he is enough. “Someone should tell me how I’m supposed to be enough,” he responds.
“I don’t think anyone sets out to do extreme dangerous, violent things,” Lee said of her approach. “I think this really begins in a very human place that we can all relate to, which is how do we become the best version of ourselves. But in this looksmaxxing, biohacking, bodybuilding world where there’s this notion of perfection – and I think we can relate to this as women, too – when those goalposts keep shifting, it’s very hard to know when enough is enough.”
It may never be; in July of this year, two months after filming wrapped, Murphy drowned in the lake behind his house at the age of 32. Eyewitness and police accounts suggest he was experiencing a psychotic break; he had recently documented his attempts to inject himself with pure gold. His death was an emotional blow to Lee and her crew. “Just tragic,” she said. “We were completely floored. We were really upset.” Murphy had, she said, “seemingly become more unstable”, over 18 months of filming. “And I said to Tony and Elon and the friends around, like, ‘Are you guys worried about Connor?’ And this is the hard thing with someone like Connor – he’s like, ‘I’m just performing. This is an act.’ We were trying to penetrate that. Like, what is a performance? What is real?”
“We were definitely witnessing and trying to document what we were experiencing in real time,” she added. “But I think what was the more surprising thing was how everybody else didn’t have any concerns.” The series, she hopes, will present “a more complicated, multidimensional person behind this online performance”.
Get Huge offers few answers, either to the question of what happened to Leo Longevity and Connor Murphy, or how to get someone out of nihilistic spiral in an interminably aesthetics obsessed world. “Where the solutions lie in all of this is what we’re consuming online – looking for more authentic, real role models for young men to look up to,” Lee said. Short of that, Get Huge proposes two supplements in short supply: compassion and skepticism. “We weren’t coming in here pointing a finger,” said Lee. “We want audiences to have these conversations. We want audiences to think, decipher, discern what is real and what is not.”
- Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death is available on Hulu in the US on 10 November and Disney+ elsewhere

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: Narrative threads: How to write a Booker-shortlisted novel, by Marlon James, Douglas Stuart, Elizabeth Strout and more
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
Douglas Stuart 
  
John of John
Who knows where a novel really comes from? I spend years gathering loose threads and then, when I feel like the cloth will hold, I start to weave them into a narrative. I suppose I began internalising John of John back in 1994, the year I went to college and chose to become a weaver myself.
But it was in 2019, in the anxious period waiting for Shuggie Bain to be published, that I really found the thread for John of John. I decided I would go to the Western Isles. It was a place I had been longing to see all my life and I had a vague idea that I might set a novel there about an adult son who has been called home to a crofting community to care for his difficult father. I reasoned that even if a novel didn’t emerge from the trip, at least I would have seen more of my own country.
I was drawn to the Western Isles for many reasons. I was keen to see the Harris tweed weavers, but I’d also just finished writing Young Mungo, a novel about sectarian violence where young Glaswegians seemed intent on destroying beauty, and so without being able to articulate it, I had set out seeking a spirit of gentleness, to write about creativity within working-class lives – about beauty, and colour, and nature, and music.
People have a romantic notion of the islands – and perhaps I had a little too. Although they are stunning, they are very real, very practical places, where it can be difficult to earn a living and raise a family, where managing your relationship within a community is of the utmost importance.
I started in Vatersay and, after slowly travelling up the archipelago, I finally arrived on the Isle of Harris. It was there, in the home of a local woman, that I saw what my third novel might become.
We were sitting at her kitchen table, talking about her involvement in the local church. I mentioned that I’d been struck by the number of spinsters and bachelors I’d met on my trip. It seemed unusual given that crofts seemed to benefit from larger families. When I asked her why she thought some folk had never married, she replied that they had probably just “missed their moment”. I agreed that it must be tricky to find love in a settlement with so few people, and then I ventured that it would be harder still if some of these older people had been gay. The woman looked at me with such cool horror that I realised, in that moment, that the novel was going to be less about a son returning home, and more about the father he had left behind; a weaver who was tied to the land, a man who had never been able to find love, or any sense of himself, in the only place where he belonged.
Elizabeth Strout 
   
The Things We Never Say
A woman works in the drugstore in the town in which I live in Maine, and one day almost two years ago, she whispered to me – no one else was in the store – “I just want it over!” She cupped both hands on the sides of her mouth and said: “The election.” I told her I felt the same. She said, looking around nervously: “I never, ever say anything about it to anyone, but I just want it over.” I told her I knew what she meant, and off I went. I have no idea who she voted for, but her pain was palpable. As was mine.
The Things We Never Say is a tribute to people such as her, people who are distressed about the way things are, and have been for a few years, in our country, the United States of America. We live it, breathe it, it is everywhere among us, and while people will talk to like-minded people (sometimes) there is much that people will not say to each other about our current situation.
Not only was this true as I was writing the book, it is even more true now; the book shows the decline of our democracy. And through it all we continue living our daily lives. We go to work, we shop for groceries, we take walks with friends and laugh, we go to our quilting clubs, and all around us terrible things are happening, and most of us are not talking about it.
I have spoken publicly about my inspiration for Artie Dam, the protagonist, how I found an old photo in an obituary and saw a splendid ordinary face … This is all true, and it gave me the visuals I needed for him, but the book itself came forth because of what is happening in our country. I made Artie a high school history teacher because he would have had – perhaps – a deeper understanding of what was going to happen, and in fact, has happened.
I interwove his personal story – because we all have a personal story as we move through our time in history – and I wanted his inner life to somehow reflect what was happening in his outer life. Artie’s time in history has caught up with him, and this is his story. It is our story.
Marlon James 
  
The Disappearers
There is a blind man in Mallorca who could tell this story better than I could. What he might not have in art he has in truth, and he could tell you about his life before he went blind, his hopes when he still lived in Jamaica, the night that took his vision, the mob that nearly took his life, and the last thing he saw: the man who took his eyes out. All alleged of course. The blind man was gay – is gay – and the last thing he saw was what Jamaican men do to gay people. But until three years ago I thought this man the stuff of urban legend, a story that shook my young gay self down to the bone and sent me hurling into the closet with the door slammed shut.
The thing is I knew it happened. The rumour was that on a night in the early 90s, a mob descended on a group of gay men in Kingston, gathered at either a support group or a branch of Jamaica Aids support, and beat them within an inch of their lives. That among the mob was law enforcement, men in business and a very famous musician. All alleged, of course. There has never been a written record of it, no police report, no news article, no lead in the nightly news, and so I was convinced it happened.
Rumours are ephemeral, which is why in Jamaica they are almost always true. We know that you pay a price for standing on fact. Espousing a truth means making yourself a target. Speaking truth to power in the end attracts power to stop it. Because it is the kind of news that fades, the kind of news that is untraceable, the rumour speaker knows that he has the safety of knowing that his truth will never come back to expose or convict him. So, he speaks it freely. They killed a gay man. One of the mob was Jamaica’s biggest reggae singer. The gay men were getting safe sex advice. The gay men might have been having sex. The men were all black. The men were a mix of black and white. The men all had Aids. All alleged of course.
I tend to make novels out of stories that haunt me. The stories that haunt the most sometimes tell me the least, leaving me with gaps and leaps, and holes that stop the tale from adding up. This is where I feel most useful as a novelist; as something between a historian and a journalist, making real the lives of imagined people. Or filling in the other dimensions of a one-dimensional event. Or, most importantly, conjuring what might have been the consequences of a singular, sometimes forgotten action. It might not be exactly as the blind man in Mallorca would tell it, or it might be totally different. But a story can be real if not factually true, and sometimes that is truer than reality itself.
Rebecca Perry 
  
May We Feed the King
Poetry had left me and I missed writing. Bolstered by publishing a short work of creative nonfiction about my childhood as a competitive trampolinist, I started working on two separate short stories, testing if fiction was something I could do.
One story was about a young attendant to a dying king, and another about a lonely woman using replica food in her home to create scenes and their resident spirits, with the ultimate goal of cohabiting with them. At a point it became clear to me that she was working her way towards the young attendant, and that I was writing one book and not two separate stories at all.
A year or so before that I said to two of my friends, while visiting the Royal Magdalene Almshouses in Glastonbury and feeling transported by one of the dressed bedrooms, that I was interested in writing about staging and replica.
Thirty years before that I squeezed a plastic grape in a sofa showroom.
I had no idea what would happen in the book when I started writing it, or how it would end. Iris Murdoch once said, “One should sit quietly and let the thing invent itself”, and I took that as a mantra, letting the book emerge. It turns out that can be quite messy, and it took a while to find its final form. Initially the chapters were alternately contemporary and historical. At one point I cut and rewrote half of it. Some decisions, like the short chapters, were instinctive. Others were the work of much stylistic experimentation. All the usual messy business (I assume, having only done it once) of writing a novel.
On that journey, what surprised me most was that the wider world fed more into the writing of the medieval part of the book than it did the present-day sections. I was already thinking about power and empire, but writing at the height of the genocide in Gaza and watching in horror the results of unchallenged, untethered absolute power, certainly shaped the writing of the king and many of the characters around him. Before this, I assumed that novels exist in a state of purity in the mind, untouched by current events. I’m sure that’s sometimes true, but in my case the contemporary and medieval worlds had to be in conversation.
Luke Kennard 
  
Black Bag
It was March 2021, and I had chronic neck and back pain from spending eight hours a day teaching on Zoom during the lockdowns. I was also temporarily head of my department (which anyone in academia will know to be a completely thankless and enervating role). I had given myself a night off to work on some poems because I go absolutely spare when I’m not writing. It was about 10pm, I probably had a glass of wine next to me, and I was looking for interesting phrases in social psychology articles. I had 12 tabs open, when I found, in a footnote, a brief precis of the black bag experiment (University of Oregon, 1967). It struck me as beautiful and ridiculous. I wasn’t really interested in the findings of the experiment, which focused more on others’ gradually more affectionate reactions to black bag over time. What obsessed me was the experience of portraying black bag: what kind of actor would leap at the chance to do it? The fact that it was a pretty neat symbol of the status of the artist in the 21st century … The fact that I wasn’t averse to the idea of doing it myself because, ugh, just being a person at all is so wearying.
It was a really lucky and completely arbitrary find and I felt utterly rejuvenated by it as a concept. I like writing that has some kind of constraint (like Georges Perec’s novel A Void, composed without a single letter “e”), a rule that starts to generate the work; that becomes its own inspiration. But this was a constraint for a character within the book, and that struck me as even better. Within minutes of reading about it I felt like I was black bag, my constant inner monologue turned into even more of a bathysphere than usual.
I immediately abandoned the poem I was working on and started writing a first-person scene where an out-of-work actor talks to a psychology lecturer about the role of black bag. It was pretty much all I wrote from that point on. I wrote BLACK BAG on the front of a notebook and vowed to do as little research as possible.
M John Harrison  
   
The End of Everything 
I always start writing from an interest in form, rather than from ideas for characters or scenes or stories. They come later. As soon as I find the form, I look for its weak points so I can break it. The two forms that interested me when I began to think about The End of Everything were the UK novel of catastrophe after the second world war, expressed best in John Wyndham’s The Day of the Triffids and its outbreak of ambulatory carnivorous vegetables; and the novel of the alien invasion of Earth epitomised by HG Wells’s classic The War of the Worlds.
In both, the disaster is bounded, understandable and, most importantly, solved. This is not necessarily true of disasters in the real world; they’re constant, unmanageable, entangled with one another and with global politics; and wherever possible they go unacknowledged by people whose comforts are not immediately threatened. The classic disaster stories burst in on a fictional population, rag it about, and then, having taught the reader a lesson, recede. They encourage us to feel good by presenting unpredictable upheaval followed briskly by the defeat of the threat and a return to some form of the author’s preferred cultural ground state.
I wanted this book to offer a different shape: a catastrophe the nature of which is impossible to parse, and which continues unabated for the foreseeable future. In short, actual change. Nested inside the novel are various parodies, pastiches and political metaphors; a certain amount of grotesque humour. The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It’s a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend. It’s an alien invasion narrative in which the aliens arrive not as Wells’s invaders from Mars but as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast. Their motives are so unhuman that we aren’t sure even they know how – or why – they came.
As a favour – and with a whispered You’re welcome! Enjoy! – I’ve passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien. I hope, though, that the issues are transparent: the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet, and which consciously confounds the ability to make a factual statement about anything; humanity’s inexplicable attempt to break down and abandon the environment it can’t live without; the loss of any sense that we actually know how to manage the world except via a Netflix empowerment fantasy.
In an early film of The Day of the Triffids, the triffids are defeated by spraying salt water on them; in the novel itself, the hero and his dependents ignore the issue of giant carnivorous plants and retreat to the Isle of Wight, where they return to the ground state by starting an allotment. We don’t have those options.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Infantino caught in the web as tide turns against Trump in midterms and leaves Fifa exposed | Barney Ronay
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Barney Ronay
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Oh baby, clamp me in your repulsive mouthparts. Sink your unusually large and venomous fangs into my abdomen. And yes, we are doing this in the White House cabinet rooms, out there in plain sight of the watching world, just a gleaming golden ball between us. But it’s fine. Probably. Now take a sip of those sweet, sweet tiny male arachnoid entrails.
An exciting new study was published over the summer into the habits of the Australian redback spider. The research made headlines for its focus on reproductive behaviour, specifically the male’s urgent and very willing engagement in what is known as sexual cannibalism, AKA copulatory suicide.
Scientists observing these tiny arachnoids discovered that during the act of lovemaking with the larger, more decorative female, the male will perform a spectacular sexual death-somersault, flipping himself upside down, presenting his underbelly to the female’s fangs, and urging her to literally consume his intestines mid-coitus as an energy snack and self-dooming sweetener. You’ve already ripped my heart out, babe. Now take my guts as well.
This doesn’t paint a very flattering picture of the male redback’s sense of himself, his ability to recognise boundaries in a relationship. Overall, the picture is of a craven, fawning, hairless entity, entirely in thrall to its power-master. Yes, it might make sense for a while to place your prospects in the hands of a glassy-eyed red-tinged predator at the heart of a toxic web of power. But it can land you in a spot of bother down the line.
In unrelated news, there was a sense this week that Gianni Infantino’s entanglements with Donald Trump may have now moved one step closer to scrutiny, sunlight, consequences, perhaps even some kind of decisive intestinal devouring. The sight of Infantino cavorting for the US president was one of the more grotesque sport-adjacent spectacles of recent times. What kind of relationship was this?
How will history remember that display of power-fluffing, the supposedly apolitical Fifa president sat nodding gravely at the walnut-veneered table as the latest immigration policy is trailed, beaming along as some random crypto-waffle is chucked into the mix, and becoming through this an ever more contorted figure, as though essence of human mendacity has been condensed, reconstituted into a fine paste, pumped into a serge blue suit and taught to walk around saying the phrase: “My magic ball unites the golden peace world.”
At the time it felt as though this was some kind of warning siren, a real-time satire on the idea of unaccountable executive power. Is this just allowed now, confirmation in human form that acting as though you exist outside the rules is halfway to actually being there?
Well, maybe not. As of Wednesday there is for the first time a sense of something potentially self-dooming about that public two-hander. Perhaps this is the best way to picture those interactions now, Infantino backflipped in supplication, thighs clamped around the presidential shoulders, presenting his tenderest parts to those razor-sharp mandibles. Feast on my entrails. Consume my borrowed sporting soul. Empower me. Or don’t. Whatever. We’ll talk later.
Trump may be heading into a diminished final two years in office. But Trump Exposed Reactor Core Syndrome is still very much in play, a principle that states, yes, he will give you heat, light and a deathly glow. But he will also melt your face in the process. And maybe this process is now finally coming for the world’s second-most-provocative elected president.
The headline Fifa news this week was the council member Kozo Tashima’s announcement that he will stand as a candidate in March’s leadership vote. There is, at the very least, someone else to vote for now. In the wider world, but potentially more significant to the Infantino regime, the US midterm elections brought a Democratic landslide in the Senate and the House of Representatives.
Football is, as ever, just a tiny notch on the to-do list. To date those results are simply a rejection of something, the chance to luxuriate in the defenestrating of some of those High Trump oddities, the senator who believes a cabal of Sikhs is trying to steal the moon, the House representative on record as saying all Eritreans are genetically derived from yoghurt, the one-term governor who looks as if he bites the heads off sparrows and wears a suit made entirely from recycled human fingernails.
What comes next is not clear. But there is talk of cleaning house. Internal judicial matters are now firmly in the hands of Trump’s opponents. Some Democrats have warned of the need to “lawyer up”, have spoken about correcting the most excessive acts of opportunism over the past two years.
Even as Infantino is out there bartering for his future, bothered at mosquito-level by a cloud of revelations – the use of Fifa resources to electioneer, talk of having his maid’s visa raised at government level – the one thing that may actually get close to him is force majeure.
At which point enter the tantalising figure of Jamie Raskin, representative for Maryland’s 8th district, and widely tipped to become the new chair of the House judiciary committee. Raskin is a hawk on what he describes as “the corruption” of aspects of the Trump regime. And these include Fifa.
Raskin’s letter to Infantino dated 26 July bears re-reading. First he brings up the wire fraud and money laundering case against Full Play Group that was part of the 2015 indictments against the Blatter regime and that was dropped by the Trump administration because it was “not a priority”.
He refers to “Fifa’s brazen campaign to curry favour with Donald Trump since his re-election”, the “hilariously fake ‘Fifa Peace Prize’”, the leasing of office space in Trump Tower at an economically irrational rate, describing this and other elements as a “strategy of outright bribery”.
Examples of price gouging and “fraudulent sales tactics” are mentioned as a lever for a potentially fascinating disclosure of Fifa communications with the Trump organisation, and the promise of a full congressional investigation.
This was sabre-rattling at the time. It isn’t any more. The letter was also sent before the Joshua Kushner-linked scheme to sell off part of the World Cup to private equity, described by Raskin as a “smash-and-grab scam of colossal proportions”. “Now we see where all the bribes, kickbacks and sweetheart deals have been leading,” he told the Guardian. Are you excited yet? Does this sound like possible fangs of doom stuff?
This is the same Democrat who could now have the authority to compel testimony and documents from Fifa, JP Morgan – the bank involved in the sell-off process – and entities associated with the Kushner family. The Trump White House has in the past dismissed such allegations as politically motivated. Fifa has kept its head down. Well, good luck with that now.
Who knows? Even the noise, the heat and the potential ripples may be enough for some of those being asked to vote in Rabat next year. Infantino’s self-promotion as a one-man global brand, the royal court persona, the selfie with Pelé’s coffin, the micromanaging of the vote for Saudi 2034. All this creates its own internal tensions.
There would of course be satisfaction at witnessing a redback-style ending. Even if, as ever, the worst part is the feeling of sadness, of chances missed, the thought of what could have been done with all this power in larger, less grasping, less mandible-like hands.
The wheels of justice can be disappointingly clogged and reluctant to grind. But this feels motivated and public enough to carry some energy. There is at least a ball rolling now. Plus the central irony, that Infantino made himself a player here, dared the world to watch, and willingly hurled himself into that cannibalistic embrace.

US military says it disabled cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman
A US military aircraft fired on and disabled a commercial vessel that tried to break the US naval blockade of Iran on Saturday, US Central Command (Centcom) said.
The St Kitts and Nevis-flagged cargo ship had visited an Iranian port and was trying to leave regional waters when a US plane fired precision munitions at its stern, after US forces ordered the crew to clear the targeted areas of the vessel, Centcom said.
The US military also said on Saturday it was launching a task force to crack down on Iran’s movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material across its land borders and through the Caspian Sea, expanding on its months-long naval blockade.
Centcom estimated that the blockade had prevented Iran from exporting more than $25bn worth of crude oil.

Iran's army says forces 'stronger' than at start of war, Hormuz to stay closed
Iran's armed forces are "on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war" with the United States, an army spokesman said on Saturday.
"They now possess greater motivation, commitment and self-confidence," Mohammad Akraminia told the official IRNA news agency, adding that the Strait of Hormuz would stay closed until Washington met Tehran's demands.
"Under the order of the Supreme Leader, the response of the armed forces will be immediate, effective and without geographical limitations," he said.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told the Fars news agency that "the increase in the range of Iran's missiles continues steadily".
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Instagram that he had held calls with counterparts from 12 countries over the past 48 hours, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkey, Egypt, Iraq and Pakistan.
He said he had stressed "the legitimate right of our country to defend its sovereignty and national security" and called for "regional security arrangements without the interference of superregional powers".
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani on Friday to discuss efforts to end the war.
On Friday, the US military offered a $20m reward "and possible relocation" for information on Iran's nuclear programme.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: NWSL playoffs: Cooper’s extra-time penalty sends Kansas City through as Utah stun San Diego
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Michelle Cooper converted an extra-time penalty to give the Kansas City Current a 1-0 victory over Angel City on Sunday in the quarter-finals of the National Women’s Soccer League playoffs.
The fourth-seeded Current will face the winner of Sunday’s quarter-final between top-seeded Gotham FC and No 8 Seattle Reign FC in next weekend’s semi-finals.
Kansas City, the only NWSL team to finish the regular season unbeaten at home, extended that run into the postseason.
Angel City goalkeeper Angelina Anderson made five saves in regulation. Four minutes into extra time, Kansas City defender Izzy Rodriguez sent in a corner kick. Before the ball went over the crossbar, Current defender Kayla Sharples went to ground near the goal line after contact with Anderson and midfielder Ary Borges. Kansas City were awarded a penalty, which Cooper converted.
The teams combined for 25 fouls in a physical encounter. Fifth-seeded Angel City collected three yellow cards in regulation, the first in the 13th minute when Sveindís Jónsdóttir slid into Gabrielle Robinson from behind as the Kansas City defender shielded the ball near her end line.
Borges was booked in the 58th minute after catching Vanessa DiBernardo with her cleat as they challenged for a ball in the air. In second-half stoppage time, Maiara Niehues clipped Cooper’s heel and knocked off her cleat. Kansas City’s only yellow card went to Temwa Chawinga in the 114th minute.
San Diego Wave 0-1 Utah Royals
The seventh-seeded Utah Royals earned their first playoff victory with a 1-0 upset of the second-seeded San Diego Wave in Friday night’s NWSL quarter-final.
Cloé Lacasse delivered a pinpoint low cross to Kiana Palacios, who took a touch before firing home the game’s only goal in the 30th minute. It marked the first time Utah had led San Diego in any competition this season.
Royals goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn made four saves to record her sixth clean sheet of the season.
“Unbelievable, it’s just everything you could hope for,” McGlynn said. “I’m like in shock, no words can describe this feeling.”
The Royals snapped a four-match winless streak and will travel to face either the third-seeded Washington Spirit or sixth-seeded Portland Thorns in the semi-finals. Washington host Portland in Sunday’s remaining quarter-final.
Both teams were missing key players. San Diego midfielder Kimmi Ascanio was unavailable with a thigh injury, while Utah midfielder Mina Tanaka, initially listed as questionable with a hamstring injury, was ruled out.
The Wave were held scoreless despite dominating possession (62% to 38%), shots (16-8) and shots on target (5-2).
San Diego entered the match on a seven-match unbeaten run but have now lost four consecutive playoff matches.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: Richard Lloyd, founding member and guitarist of punk band Television, dies aged 75
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
Richard Lloyd, known for his sophisticated musical style as a founding member and guitarist for the influential punk band Television, has died at the age of 75.
His family confirmed that Lloyd died Saturday morning at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. “His loving wife Sheila and his dog Willie Mays were with him at the end,” his family said in a statement to Rolling Stone.
According to his family, Lloyd’s death was caused by cholangiocarcinoma, a form of bile duct cancer that he was diagnosed with in March 2026.
A crowdfunding campaign had revealed that Lloyd had developed tumors in his liver and, crucially, there was one that could not be surgically removed.
Television, which formed in 1973, played a significant role in the emerging punk rock movement that grew up around CBGB, the legendary former music venue on the Bowery in New York City. The group was among the earliest punk acts to perform at the downtown venue, which had previously focused mainly on country and bluegrass music.
During a 2007 interview, Lloyd reflected on his role in shaping the club’s history, declaring: “CBGB’s is the most famous rock ‘n’ roll club to have ever existed and I fucking created it! I was the invisible force behind it.”
Television recorded just two studio albums during its peak in the late 1970s. The band’s first album, released in 1977, was Marquee Moon, which has since earned widespread recognition as a landmark recording. Rolling Stone ranked it No 107 on its 2023 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. The record is still considered one of the most influential guitar-driven albums in rock history.
In a 2005 review, the Guardian described his performance, writing that “Lloyd’s guitar was the louder in a lopsided sound mix, so it was impossible to overlook the amount of ground he was covering. Crisp, crunchy chords, dextrous fills and torrential Van Halen-style solos tumbled from his fingers.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: FAA announces first US digital air traffic control towers in Florida and Alaska
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US are officially operational, bringing new technology first to smaller airports in Florida and Alaska as the Trump administration presses ahead with updating the country’s ageing aviation infrastructure.
The systems are now online at the Bartow executive airport (KBOW) in Florida and the Kenai municipal airport (PAEN) in Alaska, with five additional regional airports slated to receive the technology next.
The digital towers use advanced camera systems and digital displays to give air traffic controllers a continuous, 360-degree view of airport operations, including runways, taxiways and surrounding airspace, according to the agency.
The FAA maintains that the technology is not intended to replace human controllers. Instead, the systems are designed to provide greater visibility and additional information to help controllers perform their existing duties.
“Our air traffic controllers continue to do the critical job of keeping aircraft safely separated, and we’re giving them better technology to do that,” said the FAA’s administrator, Bryan Bedford, in a statement.
“Digital towers provide controllers with greater visibility of airport activity and more information to make critical decisions,” he added.
Bedford is scheduled to appear before the House transportation and infrastructure committee next week, where he will face questions about the progress and challenges surrounding the administration’s ongoing $12.5bn modernization initiative.
The effort aims to replace decades-old equipment still used throughout the aviation system, including copper telecommunications lines, floppy disks and paper strips used to track aircraft.
Congress approved $12.5bn over five years in June 2025 to support air traffic control reforms, but the Trump administration is seeking another $30bn from the legislative branch to fund additional improvements.
Concerns about the types of technology being implemented within air traffic control have been gaining traction alongside the increasing unease about artificial intelligence as a whole. In September, the FAA rolled out a new AI software tool called the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (Smart).
Trump has been heavily criticized for his response to a national shortage of air traffic controllers following last year’s government shutdown.
Staffing levels in control towers and many related aspects of US air traffic safety systems have been under especially close scrutiny since a midair collision between a passenger jet and a military helicopter on the outskirts of Washington DC in 2025 that killed 67 people. It was the deadliest crash in the US for more than 20 years and the authorities later deemed it “100% preventable”.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.title: Israel's president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to try to form new government
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.text:
Israel's president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to try to form new government
Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Saturday chose opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a new government, Israeli media reported, after an inconclusive election left neither he nor Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with a clear path to power.
Eisenkot, a former military chief, is due to formally receive the mandate on Sunday evening.
He will then have 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension.
Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc won 53 seats in the 27 October election, short of the 61 needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, though it remains the largest grouping in parliament.
The opposition alliance led by Eisenkot won 48, while Arab-led parties secured a record 19 seats between them, giving them a potentially decisive role in coalition talks.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Both Arab-led parties backed Eisenkot during consultations with Herzog this week.
Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, endorsed him with its eight lawmakers on Wednesday, followed by the Joint List on Thursday.
That brought Eisenkot’s total to 67 lawmakers, against 46 for Netanyahu.
United Torah Judaism, which had backed Netanyahu after the previous five elections, declined to recommend him this time, though it did not back Eisenkot either.
The Joint List said its unanimous decision reflected public demand to stop Netanyahu and his government from returning to power, and was aimed at widening Eisenkot’s lead to improve the chances of replacing the incumbent government.
After the consultations, Herzog said on Thursday it would be logical to give the mandate to Eisenkot.
Netanyahu turns on Arab-led parties
Eisenkot’s bloc has so far refused to formally ally with the Arab-led parties, even though they could hand it a majority.
But the opposition has opened the door to a once unlikely partnership with ultra-Orthodox parties, which could give Eisenkot enough seats for a coalition that might also include Ra’am, a Palestinian-led party, with outside support from the Joint List.
In a pre-recorded speech on Saturday, Netanyahu said that a government relying on Islamists would destroy Israel from within, comparing it to what he said was happening in Europe.
He has also gone on the offensive against Arab-led parties, accusing them of receiving foreign funding ahead of the election, in which Palestinian citizens of Israel turned out in record numbers.
He renewed his call for a national unity government of Zionist parties, an idea Herzog has previously signalled he wants to explore.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party responded by urging Likud and its allies to cut ties with what it called extremists and join a unity government under him.
On Friday, Eisenkot called for an emergency government and did not rule out a minority government.
He said he would move quickly to build a coalition around the four Jewish opposition parties of the Change bloc: Yashar, Naftali Bennett’s Together, Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu and Yair Golan’s Democrats.
Any party that accepts his conditions could join, either at the start or later, he added.
Eisenkot has repeatedly rejected the idea of a Palestinian state alongside Israel.
While serving as army chief between 2015 and 2019, he publicly advocated closer ties with Saudi Arabia, saying the two countries should work together to counter Iran’s influence in the region.
He also said Israel would be willing to share intelligence with Riyadh to confront Tehran.

Iraq has evidence outside parties use its territory to attack neighbours: Foreign minister
Iraq has evidence that external parties have been using its territory to attack neighbouring countries, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in an interview with Al Jazeera on Saturday.
Hussein said Baghdad was investigating attacks launched from Iraqi soil against Gulf states and wanted to resolve its differences with Saudi Arabia "through frank dialogue".
Riyadh has accused Iran-aligned groups in Iraq of targeting its oil infrastructure. In September, Baghdad confirmed that the drones that struck the kingdom’s East-West pipeline had been launched from Iraqi territory.
Last month, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi assured Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that Iraq would not be used as a launchpad for attacks on the kingdom.
During the interview, Hussein said Baghdad was negotiating with Iran-aligned factions to bring their weapons under state control, a process he said must rely on dialogue, not force.
He added that Iraq had told Tehran it welcomed friendship and an alliance but rejected interference in its internal affairs.
Iraq lost about $60bn while oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz were suspended following the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, Hussein said.

Trump orders DOJ to investigate Democrats for ‘threatening’ people
Trump lashed out at them on Truth Social and called the Democratic lawmakers “extortionists”.
United States President Donald Trump has ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to look into Democrats for “threatening a lot of people” with impeachment and other forms of punishment, following their midterm election victory.
In a Truth Social post on Saturday, Trump said what Democrats had done amounted to a “criminal act”, without providing evidence.
The post comes days after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress from Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers and newly elected candidates have said they would pursue probes into the Trump family’s financial dealings, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), as well as investigations into Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Attorney General Todd Blanche.
“The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people,” Trump wrote, adding that some of his cabinet have been threatened with impeachment. “This is extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable for this.”
Trump also said, without evidence, that some Democrats were threatening his donors, whom he called “some of the most respected people anywhere in the World”. He said Democrats were targeting them for their political views, specifically calling out Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin. He gave no evidence of her threatening people over their views.
When Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will be able to conduct a range of investigations, in which they can order access to documents, summon Trump officials to testify, and hold hearings.
Democratic Representative Robert Garcia of California, who is likely to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee, which serves as the investigative committee in the House and has broad jurisdiction and power, posted “LAWYER UP” on social media after it was clear Democrats would take the House.
During his second term, Trump has called for investigations into his political enemies, including the former director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), James Comey, and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.title: How did AIPAC-backed candidates fare in the US midterm elections?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
How did AIPAC-backed candidates fare in the US midterm elections?
Many candidates the pro-Israel group backed still won, but most of the money it spent went to candidates who lost.
Nearly a year before he stunned many by winning a seat in the United States Senate from Texas, James Talarico drew attention for his vehement rejection of campaign funding from the country’s largest pro-Israel lobbying group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
“I’ve never taken money from AIPAC, and I’m not taking money from AIPAC in this campaign,” Talarico said in a clip for a podcast that later went viral. “Seeing what’s happening in Gaza makes me sick to my stomach as a teacher, as a Christian, as a human being.”
On November 3, Talarico won by more than 12 percentage points. Pro-Israel groups allied with AIPAC gave modest support – about $6,000 – to Talarico’s opponent, Ken Paxton, but Talarico’s willingness to be so open about his disdain for AIPAC is still a notable part of a shift in US politics.
In races across the country, AIPAC and political spending groups linked to it poured tens of millions of dollars into backing one candidate or another. While the group did back many winning candidates, nearly two-thirds of the total money it spent this election cycle went to those who ended up losing.
Even among Republicans, candidates are thinking twice about taking funds from the group, said Rina Shah, a geopolitical adviser and strategist and a former senior GOP congressional aide.
“A few years ago, taking AIPAC support was a no-brainer for most GOP candidates,” she told Al Jazeera. “Now, with a younger, more America First wing asking hard questions about foreign entanglements, and Gaza weighing on voters across the spectrum, it’s become a real topic, not a niche one.”
More opaque spending
How AIPAC spends money has become more opaque. In October, for instance, the group said it would stop endorsing candidates and making direct contributions to them after this election cycle. Much of its spending already runs through affiliated political action committees, such as its super PAC, the United Democracy Project (UDP), making donations harder to track.
AIPAC has funded hundreds of candidates in the midterm elections, in both primaries and the general election on November 3, according to Track AIPAC, an organisation that records the group’s funding of US politicians. The organisation tabulates spending by UDP as well as nearly 50 other PACs tied to the pro-Israel lobbying group.
On November 4, the day after the Democratic Party roundly defeated Republicans and won control of both the House and Senate, AIPAC said it had already counted some 234 candidates it backed, from both parties, as having won their contests.
Candidates won, but most money went to waste
In terms of the number of winning candidates, the group still has a strong record. Pro-Israel groups like AIPAC and UDP backed candidates in at least 32 of 35 Senate races this election, according to Track AIPAC. In 26 of those races, the groups spent more than $100,000 on a candidate, and 21 of those candidates won their races on November 3.
“AIPAC members are determined to expand their political activism in the cycles ahead,” the group said in a post on X that specifically pointed to support for the two most powerful Democrats in Congress – Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries – who have also continued to call for maintaining strong US ties with Israel.
But nearly two-thirds of the total money pro-Israel groups spent in the midterm elections went to candidates who lost, according to a tally by the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. Around $55m of the $84m that AIPAC, UDP and linked groups spent in the election cycle went to candidates who did not win, according to the findings.
“We have entered a new era,” said Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute, a foreign policy think tank that advocates for less US foreign involvement. “It is not just that AIPAC is spending millions of dollars and losing. You also have a new reality now in which candidates find AIPAC’s donations toxic and are rejecting it.”
The most notable race in which an AIPAC-backed candidate lost was for a Senate seat in Michigan, where the group and affiliated PACs spent some $30m on Representative Haley Stevens, a Democrat who unsuccessfully sought the party’s nomination for the contest. According to the New York Times, AIPAC then poured an additional $9m into backing Republican Mike Rogers, who lost on November 3 to Abdul El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel who has called for the US to stop giving financial support to the country.
“Thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice,” El-Sayed said in his victory speech on election night, addressing the pro-Israel lobbying group.
In Maine, AIPAC-linked groups gave more than $4.8m in support of Senator Susan Collins’s re-election campaign. Collins lost to Democrat Troy Jackson, who flipped a seat long held by Republicans.
In California, Melissa Hernandez received more than $6m in backing from UDP and other pro-Israel groups this year, as she sought to defeat Aisha Wahab, a left-leaning Afghan American who has frequently been critical of Israel, in a contest for a seat in the House. Wahab won that race.
Backing candidates who won again in Democratic strongholds
But in other races, the pro-Israel groups have successfully backed candidates, especially in primary races in recent years, ensuring that the Democratic Party ends up nominating candidates who are not too far to the left and not overly critical of Israel.
In Missouri, AIPAC-related groups provided more than about $3m in funding to support Representative Wesley Bell. Bell, a Democrat running in a traditional stronghold for the party, won a seat in the House on November 3 with more than 81 percent of the vote. Most of that money was spent in primaries, where AIPAC financially backed Bell’s campaign against former Representative Cori Bush, who was one of the first lawmakers in Congress to call Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide and who had lost to Bell in a primary in 2024. Previously, AIPAC-related groups funneled $8m into beating Bush that year. Jeffries supported Bell in this year’s primary rematch.
In another Democratic win in a party stronghold, George Latimer was re-elected to the House to represent a New York district just north of New York City. AIPAC spent some $14m defeating his opponent in 2024, when he ousted left-wing Israel critic Jamaal Bowman.
UDP also spent more than $4m in 2024 on another primary, this time helping Democrat Sarah Elfreth beat out more left-leaning candidates to win the party’s nomination. Elfreth again won in the heavily Democratic district on November 3.
Not the only lobbying group on Israel in town
AIPAC is no longer the only lobbying group on Israel, though.
J Street, a Jewish American group that describes itself as pro-Israel and pro-peace, said on November 4 that it had backed more than 200 candidates with more than $13m in funding, in a campaign aimed especially at candidates backed by AIPAC.
It has especially sought to back Democratic candidates who offer a more moderate view on Israel, even as some party leaders have claimed that being more overtly critical of Israel would alienate Jewish voters. But a poll commissioned by J Street found that 72 percent of American Jewish voters still backed the party in the midterm elections.
“In an election with so much at stake for American democracy, we are proud to have supported a record number of candidates who share our commitment to Israel’s future, democracy and a peaceful resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” J Street President Jeremy Ben-Ami said in a statement.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Malaysian king warns against defying house arrest order for ex-PM Najib
Attorney general postponed Najib Razak’s transfer from jail after court cleared him for house arrest on Friday.
Malaysia’s king has warned that any attempt to challenge his order granting jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak house arrest could amount to defying his decree, a day after authorities delayed Najib’s transfer.
The 73-year-old Najib was jailed for his role in one of the largest-ever global plunders of a sovereign wealth fund, the now-defunct 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
But King Sultan Ibrahim granted him a conditional pardon in September, allowing him to serve out the rest of his sentence at home provided he paid a $12m fine.
On Friday, the country’s attorney general blocked the former prime minister’s transfer to house arrest after the fine was paid, saying his office needed more clarification on the pardon.
The king said on Saturday there was nothing to clarify, calling the pardon “clear, evident and without any ambiguity”.
“There should be no confusion in interpretation,” King Ibrahim said in a statement, adding it was not tied to any other cases against the former leader.
“Given that all conditions in the conditional pardon order have been fulfilled, any argument questioning the order leads towards denying the order of His Majesty the King.”
Najib’s lawyers thanked the monarch on Saturday, saying there was “no basis” for authorities to keep Najib in prison “a moment longer”.
“They must transfer him immediately to his residence at Jalan Langgak Duta to serve his house arrest, as His Majesty has ordered,” lawyer Farhan Shafee said in a statement.
The Attorney General’s Office issued its own statement shortly afterwards, denying it was challenging the king’s authority while giving no indication if it intended to immediately release Najib.
“This step is not aimed at delaying or denying the implementation of the Conditional Pardon Order, but to avoid any conflict in the implementation of the orders in force and to ensure no sentence is implemented unlawfully,” it said.
Hours later, the prime minister’s office said the attorney general was seeking an audience with the king to “seek pardon” and express an intent to comply, while insisting that legal questions remained that only a court could decide.
The house arrest order applies only to Najib’s first conviction.
He faces an additional 15 years in prison after being found guilty last year in another 1MDB-linked case, with the sentence set to begin after his stint in house arrest ends. Najib is appealing the verdict.
The king, a position held in rotation by Malaysia’s nine regional sultans, plays a largely ceremonial role but has the authority to grant pardons under discretionary powers granted by Malaysia’s constitution.
Malaysians hold the monarch and the country’s other sultans in deep respect. Negative remarks about the royalty can be prosecuted under the colonial-era Sedition Act.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7.text:
Yemeni gov’t forces report advances as Houthis say deadly strikes hit Sanaa
Civilians bear the brunt of fighting as 27 people reported killed in strikes on a village in Sanaa province.
Yemeni government forces say they have repelled Houthi assaults in Marib, as the armed group said strikes on a village in Sanaa province had killed at least 27 people.
In a statement on Saturday, government forces said troops backed by warplanes and drones had fought for hours to halt Houthi advances in Marib province, destroying fortifications and combat equipment.
It said troops were also pushing into Houthi-held areas of al-Jawf province, where fighting entered a third consecutive day as part of the “Dawn of Yemen” operation launched more than a month ago by the internationally recognised government, to take control of territory from Houthi fighters.
In a separate statement, government forces spokesman, Colonel Majed al-Nazili, said the army had carried out 875 attacks on Houthi positions on Saturday, “neutralising” about 130 Houthi commanders and fighters and destroying or disabling 50 vehicles and missile launchers.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.
‘Two narratives’
Also on Saturday, a series of strikes killed at least 27 people and wounded about 30 others in Sanaa province, the Houthi-run Saba news agency reported.
Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Sanaa-based Ministry of Health, said the attacks struck al-Shariya village, north of the capital. He said most of the casualties were women and children.
The Iran-backed Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – blamed the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government forces for the attack. The President of the armed group’s Supreme Political Council, Field Marshal Mahdi al-Mashat, vowed to “avenge” the attack.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have not commented on the reported strikes.
The incident comes a day after the Houthis and Yemen’s government traded blame over a separate attack that killed civilians at a market in Taiz.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the Houthis put the civilian death toll from the past two days at 55, blaming Saudi air strikes, while Yemeni government officials have held the Houthis responsible for most of the casualties.
“Two narratives are blaming each other and pointing the finger at each other, while this is taking a toll on civilian casualties,” Mawry said.
As fighting continues in Yemen, the Houthis separately claimed to have launched six attacks on Saudi targets using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones, but did not say when the attacks were carried out.
The group said it had targeted King Khalid international airport and oil facilities in Riyadh, an oil site in Khurais, an oil pumping station in Dawadmi, a National Guard camp in Najran and what it described as Saudi troop gatherings in Yemen’s al-Jawf and Marib provinces.
Colonel Turki al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-backed coalition supporting Yemen’s government forces, said early on Saturday that they had shot down a Houthi ballistic missile over the Riyadh region.
