https://gothamist.com/news/strand-bookst.title: Strand Bookstore admits it took a pandemic loan despite being ineligible
https://gothamist.com/news/strand-bookst.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/news/strand-bookst.text:
Strand Bookstore in Union Square acknowledged it accepted a pandemic-era Paycheck Protection Program loan for which it was not eligible, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia announced on Tuesday. The office stated that the bookstore would pay nearly $1.5 million to account for the error.
The Strand is owned by Nancy Bass Wyden, who is married to Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden. The U.S. Attorney’s Office said The Strand was ineligible when it applied in February 2021 for a loan of more than $930,000, as federal law prohibited businesses controlled by a member of Congress or their spouse from receiving the second round of PPP funding.
“The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief,” U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a statement. “No one gets a pass when it comes to defrauding the American taxpayer.”
A spokesperson for The Strand described the application as an honest mistake, saying that neither the bookstore’s accountant nor the bank handling the loan were aware of the law barring a congressman’s spouse from receiving a PPP loan. The funds were returned as soon as The Strand became aware of the issue, according to the spokesperson.
The store has not responded to an inquiry to clarify whether it paid the original $932,350 loan amount or the new, higher sum announced by the U.S. Attorney's Office.
Ron Wyden, a Democrat, has been outspoken in his criticism of President Donald Trump, who appointed Pirro to her position in May 2025.
The Strand, which is known for the “18 miles of books” housed in its flagship store, has been open about its financial struggles in the past. In March 2021, responding to worker complaints of mismanaged funds, a Strand spokesperson told New York magazine that limited sales and a PPP loan were the only things keeping staff members paid in a period of struggle.
In December 2024, the Strand’s 110 unionized employees went on strike amid tense contract negotiations to demand they make more than New York City’s minimum wage of $16 an hour. Both parties reached a tentative agreement to raise the base pay rate by 50 cents an hour and grant employees a raise of $1.50 an hour in their fourth year working at the store.
Nancy Bass Wyden's grandfather, Ben Bass, founded the bookstore at its original Greenwich Village location in 1927. It moved 30 years later to its current location on East 12th Street and Broadway.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/hungary-ussr.title: The 1956 Hungarian Uprising Was a Working-Class Revolt
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/hungary-ussr.author: Adam Fabry, Anita Zsurzsán
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/hungary-ussr.text:
The 1956 Hungarian Uprising Was a Working-Class Revolt
Seventy years ago today, Soviet forces crushed the Hungarian uprising that had electrified Eastern Europe. Latter-day conservative narratives distort the true history of the 1956 revolution and the crucial role of workers’ councils in driving it forward.
On October 23, 1956, tens of thousands of Hungarians took to the streets of Budapest. What began as a demonstration led largely by students rapidly became a popular uprising against the country’s Stalinist government.
Within days, the authority of the Hungarian Communist Party had crumbled, Soviet troops had been forced to withdraw, and workers across the country were establishing their own councils to organize production and exercise political power.
The Soviet leadership called it a “counterrevolution,” while Western governments celebrated it as a “revolt against communism.” Both interpretations obscured something fundamental: the Hungarian Revolution was driven by workers and ordinary people who wanted to free themselves from a system that claimed to represent their interests.
The uprising was ultimately crushed by Soviet military intervention on November 4. Thousands were killed; hundreds were executed in the repression that followed; and some two hundred thousand Hungarians fled the country. Yet the revolution remains one of the twentieth century’s most important challenges to authoritarian rule in the name of socialism.
For the international Left, its significance is difficult to overstate. As the Hungarian Marxist philosopher G. M. Tamás observed, Eastern Europe was precisely where socialism had supposedly been put into practice. What, then, were we to make of workers rising en masse against a self-proclaimed socialist government?
The answer begins with the contradictions of the Hungarian state itself — and with the people who dared to challenge it.
The Crisis of Stalinist Hungary
By the mid-1950s, Hungary was a country of roughly ten million people still recovering from the devastation of World War II. Following the defeat of Nazi Germany, it had been incorporated into the Soviet sphere of influence. Its economy was reorganized around state ownership, central planning, and rapid industrialization, while political power was concentrated in the hands of a Communist Party modeled on the ruling party in Joseph Stalin’s Soviet Union.
Under the leadership of Mátyás Rákosi, the party pursued an especially brutal version of this model. Heavy industry received priority over consumer goods, agriculture was subjected to forced collectivization, and living standards were sacrificed to ambitious production targets. The secret police, known as the State Protection Authority (ÁVH), became the instrument of a pervasive system of surveillance, intimidation, and repression.
The government justified these policies on the grounds that they were necessary for building socialism. But workers had little control over their workplaces, peasants faced coercive agricultural policies, and ordinary citizens had virtually no say in political decisions. Although the state owned the factories, that did not mean power was in the hands of the people who worked in those factories.
From a critical political-economic perspective, this exposed a deeper contradiction. The state mobilized society for rapid industrial accumulation while subordinating workers to the demands of production. The bureaucracy determined what was produced, how resources were allocated, and how much people were expected to sacrifice. The facade was socialist, but the relationship between rulers and ruled remained profoundly authoritarian.
The New Course
The unexpected death of Stalin in 1953 opened a small space for change. Under pressure from Moscow, Rákosi was replaced as prime minister by Imre Nagy, a reform-minded Communist who recognized that the existing economic model was unsustainable. The new government introduced economic and political reforms, known as the “New Course,” which promised to reduce the emphasis on heavy industry, improve living standards, expand consumer production, and ease political repression.
The reforms generated widespread hopes. Forced labor camps were closed, restrictions on private enterprise were relaxed, and peasants received greater freedom to cultivate their land. But the success of the reform program was far from guaranteed. Rákosi retained control of the party apparatus, and powerful Stalinist factions opposed Nagy’s attempts to change course. In 1955, with Soviet support, Nagy’s opponents accused him of “right-wing deviation” and had him removed from office.
His dismissal signaled that the state would not tolerate even limited reform when it threatened the authority of the party bureaucracy. The following year, Nikita Khrushchev’s denunciation of Stalin’s crimes at the Soviet Communist Party’s Twentieth Congress further undermined the regime’s legitimacy. If Moscow now acknowledged the terror and injustice of Stalin’s rule, what did that mean for the Hungarian leaders who had faithfully reproduced his methods?
Students, intellectuals, writers, and increasingly workers began demanding answers. By October 1956, Hungary was like a tinderbox waiting to explode.
A Revolution Takes Shape
The immediate spark came on October 23. Students gathered in Budapest to demand political reform, the return of Imre Nagy to government, the withdrawal of Soviet troops, and greater national independence. Their demands also encompassed changes to workplace conditions, including opposition to the unpopular piece-rate system that tied workers’ wages to production quotas.
The demonstration grew dramatically as people joined the march through the capital. By evening, a vast crowd had assembled outside parliament. Elsewhere, demonstrators pulled down a monumental statue of Stalin, an unmistakable declaration that the old order had lost its authority.
The turning point came when demonstrators gathered outside the Hungarian Radio headquarters, hoping to broadcast their demands. ÁVH security forces opened fire, killing and wounding people. The violent response by the government transformed a mass demonstration into an armed uprising. Weapons were seized, police vehicles were set ablaze, and insurgents began confronting the state’s armed forces.
The following day, Soviet troops entered Budapest, but their intervention failed to restore order. Some Hungarian soldiers refused to fight the insurgents; others defected or handed over weapons. Nagy returned to the premiership as the authorities struggled to regain control.
What had begun as a protest against political repression was becoming something much more radical. The uprising spread beyond the capital to industrial towns, provincial centers, and rural communities. Factories stopped working, local revolutionary committees appeared, and workers began organizing independently of the party and the state.
Workers’ Councils
This is where the conventional Cold War story becomes inadequate. The revolution cannot be understood simply as a national revolt against Soviet occupation, nor as an uprising orchestrated by anti-communist politicians. Its most consequential development was the emergence of independent working-class organization.
Across Hungary, workers established revolutionary councils, elected by their colleagues and answerable to them. These bodies coordinated strikes, organized supplies, represented workers in negotiations, and increasingly asserted authority over factories and local institutions. They were not merely trade unions demanding higher wages. In many cases, they challenged the state’s right to govern workplaces and society without popular consent.
Historical estimates suggest that more than two thousand workers’ councils were established during the revolution, involving more than 28,000 members. Their demands varied, but recurring themes included the withdrawal of Soviet troops, political freedoms, the release of prisoners, and genuine worker participation in economic decision-making.
For a brief moment, the factory floor became a site of political power. Workers who had supposedly constituted the ruling class discovered that they could organize production and articulate political demands without the supervision of party officials.
The revolution was not ideologically uniform. It brought together students, industrial workers, peasants, intellectuals, reform Communists, and supporters of different political traditions. Nor did all its participants share the same vision of Hungary’s future. But the workers’ councils gave the uprising a distinctive social character that neither the Soviet leadership nor its Western adversaries could comfortably accommodate.
Beyond Budapest
The working-class dimension of the revolution was particularly evident in Budapest’s industrial districts and in provincial manufacturing centers. Workers in Csepel, Újpest, and Kőbánya joined the resistance, while industrial towns such as Miskolc, Ózd, and Dunapentele (which had been renamed Sztálinváros under the Stalinist regime) became important sites of revolutionary activity.
These developments matter because the revolution is often remembered primarily through images of street fighting in Budapest. Yet the uprising spread through the networks of industrial production, workplaces, and communities that underpinned the Hungarian economy.
In Dunapentele, workers insisted that their town was socialist precisely because its inhabitants were workers and power belonged in their hands. They declared their intention to defend it against both fascist excesses and Soviet troops. Their statement captured the central contradiction of 1956: they were not necessarily rejecting the ideal of socialism but rejecting a political order that invoked socialism to justify its own domination.
Peter Fryer was a correspondent for the Daily Worker, the official newspaper of the Communist Party of Great Britain. He witnessed the uprising and described the devastation inflicted on Budapest by Soviet forces. Working-class districts suffered particularly heavily. Fryer’s reports challenged the official Communist account of a fascist conspiracy and helped expose the reality of the intervention to readers abroad.
Workers’ participation was not limited to the construction of councils or the organization of strikes. They also formed a substantial part of the armed resistance. Fighting was particularly intense in industrial neighborhoods, where insurgents used their knowledge of local streets and buildings to resist a much-better-equipped military force.
Young workers were especially prominent. Many had grown up under the Communist regime, experienced its workplace discipline and political restrictions, and reached adulthood with little memory of the prewar order. The motivation behind their revolt cannot be reduced to nostalgia for the old Hungary. They were challenging the society in which they had actually lived.
The distinction is crucial. The revolution did contain nationalist and anti-communist currents, and some participants sought a restoration of political arrangements from before the war. But these currents do not explain the independent organization of workers across the country, nor do they justify the Soviet claim that military intervention was necessary to defeat a fascist counterrevolution. The revolution’s social diversity should not obscure its central achievement: ordinary people began to exercise political power for themselves.
The Soviet Counterattack
By late October, the uprising had forced the government into a series of concessions. Nagy announced a coalition government and, under mounting pressure, moved toward political pluralism. On October 28, the government declared a ceasefire and acknowledged the revolutionary movement. The prospect of Soviet withdrawal appeared increasingly real.
But the Soviet leadership faced a dilemma. Allowing Hungary to break decisively from Moscow’s control risked destabilizing the entire Soviet bloc. The danger was not merely that another government might leave the Warsaw Pact. It was that a successful revolution organized from below might inspire workers elsewhere to challenge their own rulers.
The crisis also unfolded against a wider international backdrop. Western powers were unwilling to risk a direct military confrontation with the Soviet Union, while the Suez crisis was exposing the limits of Western claims to defend freedom and national sovereignty. Hungary’s fate would ultimately be decided by the balance of power between states, not by the rhetoric of either superpower.
On November 1, Nagy announced Hungary’s withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact and appealed for international recognition of the country’s neutrality. Meanwhile, Moscow had already begun preparing a second military intervention. In the early hours of November 4, Soviet forces launched Operation Whirlwind, attacking Budapest and other centers of resistance.
This time the assault was overwhelming. Some 58,000 Soviet troops advanced against a revolution that lacked the military resources to withstand a prolonged offensive. Hungarian army units were rapidly disarmed or neutralized, while workers and insurgents continued fighting in several areas.
Nagy broadcasted a desperate appeal for help announcing that Soviet forces had attacked the capital and were attempting to overthrow the government. He subsequently sought refuge in the Yugoslav embassy, but was later arrested. In 1958, following a secret trial, he was executed alongside other leaders of the revolution, including Pál Maléter.
By November 11, the main centers of armed resistance had been crushed. More than 2,500 people had died during the revolution. The workers’ councils, however, did not immediately disappear. Their continued existence forced the new authorities to confront a problem that military victory alone could not resolve: how to govern a population that had demonstrated such open hostility to the regime.
Defeat and the Consolidation of Kádár’s Rule
While Soviet tanks were reentering Hungary, a new Soviet-friendly government, led by János Kádár, was formed. However, the new government initially faced widespread opposition. Factories remained closed, transport services were disrupted, and workers organized strikes against the Soviet intervention. The Central Workers’ Council of Greater Budapest, established in November, became a focal point for efforts to coordinate resistance and negotiate with the authorities.
The government responded with a mixture of concessions and repression. Kádár’s representatives negotiated with workers’ leaders, seeking to persuade them to resume production. But when negotiations failed to break the resistance, the authorities turned decisively toward coercion.
On December 9, the headquarters of the Central Workers’ Council was raided and prominent activists were arrested. Martial law was imposed, strikes were criminalized, and imprisonment and execution became instruments of political control. By early 1957, organized resistance was increasingly difficult to sustain. Many young workers fled Hungary, while those who remained faced the prospect of prison, dismissal, or forced submission.
The repression was followed by a longer process of political consolidation. Kádár rebuilt the Communist Party (now renamed the Hungarian Socialist Workers’ Party, MSZMP) and sought to win the acquiescence of a population exhausted by conflict.
Over time, his government developed a more pragmatic approach to economic management and everyday life. Compared with the brutalities of the Rákosi period, Kádár’s Hungary eventually became associated with relative material security and a degree of private autonomy.
But these accommodations rested on the defeat of independent political organization. Workers could enjoy certain improvements in living standards, provided they did not seek to reclaim the political power they had briefly exercised in 1956.
The revolution therefore left a complicated legacy. Its defeat did not mean that Hungarian society returned unchanged to the prerevolutionary order. The authorities had learned that permanent mobilization, relentless austerity, and indiscriminate terror could undermine the stability they sought to secure. The memory of 1956 placed limits on the state’s room for maneuver, even as it tried to erase the revolution’s independent working-class character.
The Legacy of 1956 Today
The struggle over the meaning of 1956 did not end with the defeat of the revolution. In contemporary Hungary, its memory remains contested. Following the democratic transition in 1989–90, political commemorations have often emphasized themes of national independence and resistance to Soviet domination that primarily resonate with the emphasis of right-wing political parties on national sovereignty.
Under Viktor Orbán’s sixteen-year rule, the state invested heavily in creating an institutionally revisionist memory culture in Hungary, presenting the revolution as a reactionary struggle for “national sovereignty.” However, this picture is utterly detached from the reality of what was happening on the ground in 1956. While reactionary forces sought to co-opt the revolutionary movement at the time, as often happens in mass politics, the struggle did not lose its principled socialist character.
The interpretation that stresses the issue of national sovereignty obscures the revolution’s equally important challenge to domestic authoritarianism and the power of political elites. The workers’ councils should remind us that we cannot separate opposition to foreign domination from the question of who exercises power within society. The revolution was not simply a nation asserting its independence; it was also a population challenging a ruling class that claimed to represent it.
The lesson extends well beyond Hungary. At a time when authoritarian movements are gaining ground across Europe and elsewhere, 1956 challenges the assumption that political alternatives must be confined to a choice between authoritarian state control and the existing capitalist order. It also offers a warning to the Left: governments cannot claim to represent working people while denying them the freedom to organize independently, challenge political authority, and determine the conditions under which they live and work.
The legacy of 1956 is therefore neither simply nationalist nor merely anti-communist. It is a reminder that emancipation cannot be imposed from above, whether in the name of socialism, national security, or economic progress.
The Hungarian workers who challenged their rulers demonstrated that democracy means more than choosing between competing elites. It also means the collective capacity of ordinary people to shape their own lives. This crucial class aspect is often excluded from today’s discourse: many commentators attempt to draw parallels with the war in Ukraine, which often reduces this pivotal socialist revolution to merely a struggle for national sovereignty.
What 1956 Means for the Left
The Hungarian Revolution was neither a vindication of liberal capitalism nor the reactionary conspiracy portrayed by Soviet propaganda. It was a heterogeneous popular uprising whose most radical expression lay in the independent organization of workers.
That distinction remains politically important. If socialism means only state ownership, central planning, and rule by a party claiming exclusive authority to represent the working class, then the Hungarian workers’ revolt poses an uncomfortable question: What happens when the people supposedly represented by the state rise up against it?
We cannot find the answer by dismissing the revolution as an aberration or by ignoring the political diversity of its participants. It requires taking seriously the experience of workers who challenged bureaucratic control, organized their workplaces, and demanded the right to determine their own future.
The councils did not offer a complete blueprint for a socialist society. They operated under extraordinary circumstances, and their political projects were neither uniform nor free of contradictions. But they demonstrated that opposition to Stalinism could emerge from a desire for greater democracy and collective control, rather than simply a wish to restore capitalism.
For the Left, the lesson is not that the revolution should be claimed uncritically by any particular tradition. It is that socialism cannot be reduced to the power of the state, and workers cannot be treated as passive beneficiaries of policies devised in their name. Emancipation requires their active participation in shaping economic and political life.
In 1956, Hungarian workers confronted a regime that claimed to have abolished exploitation while denying them meaningful control over their labor and society. Their defeat exposed the violence required to preserve that contradiction. It also revealed the possibility of another kind of politics — one rooted in collective self-organization, political freedom, and the struggle against domination.
The Soviet tanks crushed the revolution. They could not entirely extinguish its challenge to the meaning of socialism. For anyone on the Left still committed to a society governed democratically by those who create its wealth, that challenge remains unfinished.

https://gothamist.com/news/incumbents-bo.title: Incumbents booted from Jersey City school board after years of dysfunction
https://gothamist.com/news/incumbents-bo.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/incumbents-bo.text:
A quartet of political outsiders swept Jersey City’s school board election on Tuesday, taking a majority of seats governing a school district with a roughly $1 billion budget and 26,000 students.
This year’s election brings the biggest swing in power on the school board in more than a decade with the powerful Jersey City Education Association teachers union losing control of the board after years of dysfunction.
For Stronger Schools, a slate of outspoken parents who have been critical of the current board and district leadership, won the three full-term seats and the single one-year-term seat that were on this year’s ballot. They had the backing of multiple progressive city leaders as well as a groundswell of parents.
Jessica Taube, Danielle Walker and Chloe Williams won the full-term seats, according to unofficial results. Gina Verdibello, who has previously served on the board, won the one-year term.
The four candidates held commanding leads with about 94% of voting districts reporting. Taube, Walker and Williams each had at least 10,000 votes more than their competitors. Verdibello secured more than half of the votes for the one-year-term.
For Stronger Schools ousted three incumbent board members — Dejon Morris, Alpa Patel and George Blount — who were running along with Vanessa Rodriguez on the Education Matters slate.
Critics and opponents blamed incumbents, especially Morris, for hostile board meetings, tensions between the board and parents, and a ballooning tax burden on residents. This year the board approved a $1.1 billion budget that included a roughly 14% tax hike, and extended Superintendent Norma Fernandez’s contract, which made her the highest paid superintendent in the state.
“People wanted change,” Taube said Wedensday. “We were the slate for change, and we're going to bring change.”
There are two current board members — Tia Rezebala and Lorenzo Richardson — who ran under the For Stronger Schools banner in recent elections. When this year’s winners are seated in January, the faction will hold six of the school board’s nine seats.
The winners said their first focus after being sworn-in will be the district’s budget.
“Figuring it out and digging into it, see what works, what didn't work,” Verdibello said.
Ron Greco, the Jersey City Education Association president, said Morris’ actions in particular made it clear that change was needed on the board, citing the arrest of a parent at a school board meeting earlier this year as an example. Morris was listed as the complainant on police reports. The charges against the parent were later dropped. Morris has previously defended his approach to running meetings, saying he balanced the public's right to speak with keeping order.
The union had backed Leadership That Listens, made up of Videsh Bahadur, Fernando Garcia, Julietta Vogt and Zebedayo Masongo. Vogt was an aide to County Executive Craig Guy, but the Hudson County Democratic Party — which got hammered in last year's municipal election — didn't officially endorse a slate.
The last time there was a this big of a shift on the school board was in the early 2010s, when a faction backed by then-Mayor Steve Fulop took control of the district and was frequently at odds with the teacher’s union.
Greco said he doesn’t expect a repeat of that dynamic. He said he’s optimistic that the union and the new For Stronger Schools majority will be constructive partners.
“I wish our people won, but I'm not sad. I'm not dejected walking around,” Greco said. “I think that they're going to work well because they have a vested interest in the school system.”
Taube and Verdibello said they plan to sit down with the union as they prepare to take office.
“ We've kept a very positive relationship with union leadership,” Taube said.
Mayor James Solomon, who did not publicly endorse any slate but did say he wanted the incumbents voted out, congratulated the For Stronger Schools candidates on their win.
“Jersey City families want change in our public schools — responsible spending and academic excellence,” Solomon said in a statement. “As a public school parent — those are my priorities too.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/democratic-p.title: We Need a Socialist Congressional Caucus
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/democratic-p.author: Nick French
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/democratic-p.text:
We Need a Socialist Congressional Caucus
Though still a small minority, socialists will soon have more members in Congress than they ever have before. A socialist caucus can help them build their power.
With last night’s election results, it’s official: after new members are sworn in this coming January, socialists will hold more seats in Congress than they ever have in US history.
Six freshmen congress members backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) — Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Chris Rabb of Philadelphia, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, and Angela Gonzales-Torres of Los Angeles — are joining fellow DSA members Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib in the House of Representatives. Counting also Sen. Bernie Sanders, long a self-described democratic socialist though not officially affiliated with DSA, the United States will have nine socialist members of Congress.
The new socialist legislators, all of whom ran on the Democratic Party ballot line, can be expected (like Tlaib, AOC, and Sanders) to caucus with the Democrats. Despite achieving a meaningful beachhead in the legislature and being joined by left-populist allies like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Maine’s Troy Jackson, socialists will still be a tiny minority within the Democratic caucus.
The growing left wing will have to figure out how to coordinate effectively with each other while operating within the “big tent” of the larger congressional party. That party is full of members committed to pro-corporate and militarist agendas, and avowed anti-socialists Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer are likely to be its leaders. The socialist legislators, on the other hand, have their own policy priorities and were elected in large part because of their criticisms of the party establishment: for failing to address the cost-of-living crisis, for backing Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and for mounting an ineffective opposition to Donald Trump’s attacks on workers and civil rights.
To navigate the terrain of Congress effectively, including the inevitable conflicts with corporate-friendly Democrats and party leaders, socialists need their own congressional caucus.
The Need for a Socialist Caucus
Members of Congress on both sides of the aisle have long recognized the utility of cooperating with ideologically like-minded legislators in smaller caucuses within the larger legislative parties. The Democrats’ three main ideological caucuses are the Blue Dogs, representing the right wing of the party; the New Democrat Coalition (NDC), representing a basically socially liberal but economically moderate faction; and the Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC), representing the party’s left-leaning members.
These caucuses are venues for legislators to formulate ideas and coordinate strategy. They can serve to advance particular priorities that don’t have the support of the broader party, or at least not yet. They also signal members’ broad alignment with distinct ideological currents within the broad Democratic tent.
Sanders, Tlaib, and AOC are already members of the CPC, and Sanders himself helped found the caucus (along with late DSA member Ron Dellums and others) in 1991. So it may seem like the new socialist electeds are better off simply joining the CPC and attempting to advance their priorities that way.
Yet that caucus long ago ceased to be an ideologically cohesive organization, let alone one that can be expected to fight for socialist legislative goals.
As Jacobin contributor Neal Meyer has written, many CPC members have refused to back left-wing priorities like Medicare for All or reducing our country’s obscene military budget. And today, many CPC members are also members of the centrist, pro-business NDC. In fact, the incumbents ousted by DSA challengers this cycle — Adriano Espaillat, Diana DeGette, Shri Thanedar, and Jimmy Gomez — were members of the CPC.
What a Caucus Can Achieve
So there’s a real role to be played by a new caucus that can cohere left-wing elected officials and continue efforts to build a socialist pole within the Democratic Party, expanding on the work that politicians like Sanders, AOC, and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani have done already.
In the short term, a socialist caucus may be able to make strategic interventions to advance its policy aims (and block bad policy). Here they might learn a thing or two from the House Freedom Caucus (HFC), the hard-right GOP caucus founded in 2015 that was instrumental in ousting House Speaker Kevin McCarthy and replacing him with Mike Johnson.
The Freedom Caucus has often played “legislative hardball” against its own party to try to push policy further right. Looking at the HFC experience, scholar of the GOP Paul Heideman writes, “The conditions in which socialist legislative hardball is most likely to be successful are those in which the Democratic Party has a majority in Congress and an opposite-party president.”
That is the situation in which socialists will soon find themselves. In similar circumstances, the HFC was able to “use its size and discipline to compel the House leadership to enter into fights with the administration that it otherwise would have avoided” and “succeeded in winning more power for itself in the form of committee appointments and so on.” The very large congressional majority that Democrats just won, however, means that socialists will not be able to constitute a winning vote margin, which puts limits on their leverage.
Heideman has also observed that the hardball strategy has often been counterproductive. Sometimes, when Freedom Caucus members refused to vote for legislation because it was insufficiently right-wing, Republican leadership was forced to seek Democratic votes to pass the legislation instead. As a result, the legislation ended up more liberal than it would have been otherwise. The HFC has in recent years seen its numbers and influence dwindle.
The HFC experience reveals the limits of the power of a small minority of legislators. Especially if and when socialist lawmakers find themselves working under a Democratic president, they will need to be creative and strategic about how they approach fights with their own party.
The efforts of the Squad — the informal grouping of young legislators including AOC, Tlaib, and others who are generally regarded as the leftmost members of the House — under the Biden administration are also instructive. In 2021, the Democrats were attempting to pass both a major infrastructure spending bill, which had broad congressional support, and Build Back Better (BBB), an expansive social welfare bill that was opposed by centrist Democratic senators Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin. The CPC, including the Squad, argued that Democratic leadership should hold a vote on the two bills together, to use the infrastructure bill as leverage to convince the centrists to vote for BBB.
Ultimately, party leaders decided to split the votes — holding a vote on the infrastructure bill first, then BBB — and convinced most of the CPC, but not the Squad, to go along. The result was predictable: the infrastructure law passed, and BBB did not. Only the socialists and a few progressive allies held the line until the end, insisting correctly that splitting up the votes would likely doom the welfare bill.
That’s exactly the kind of principled tactical intervention a socialist caucus can help make.
Of course, in many cases, as with the Squad’s stand for BBB, the socialist minority will lose out to moderates, especially because they can’t rely even on the support of most of the CPC. But as socialists continue to grow their numbers in Congress, they will have more weight to throw around.
In any case, the congressional left can’t avoid conflicts with the rest of the Democratic Party, as evidenced by party moderates’ continued denunciations of socialism and the concerted efforts of groups like the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and Third Way to discredit DSA and take down left-wing Democratic candidates.
Building a Socialist Pole
That fact points to one of the longer-term reasons socialists would do well to form a caucus. Given the ideological divisions among the Democrats and the unavoidable fights to come with politicians to their right, socialist legislators need their own congressional organization, one that can articulate and keep its members cohered around a distinctive political vision.
Even when the socialist left can’t prevail in intraparty conflicts, being able to communicate what socialists stand for to the broader public is indispensable. A caucus will allow the Left to point to the legislators who have a demonstrated commitment to their priorities, making the case for electing more socialists and building up the broader institutional forces that can support them, like the labor movement and DSA. It will allow the socialist left to distinguish itself from the unreliable “progressives” of the CPC and other caucuses, helping it to consolidate support among the electorate.
The value of a caucus will be all the greater if, as seems likely, socialists keep winning elections, and the conflict heightens. Over the last decade, the socialist left has hotly debated how to relate to the Democratic Party: whether to try to win control of it, or form a third party immediately, or tactically exploit the Democratic ballot line with the eventual goal of forming a party of our own. For now, it seems undeniable that, in most places, running on the Democratic line is the surest way to build up our forces in Congress as well as state and local offices.
Yet it is clear that many in the party see socialists as an existential threat, and that in the long run this house divided against itself will not stand. There will be a struggle between those who are fighting for greater redistribution of wealth and the democratization of political and economic power, on the one hand, and those who bitterly oppose that on the other. That struggle might result in the triumph of one group or the other, staying within the confines of the Democratic Party or producing a splintering into two or more parties. Whatever happens, socialists in Congress can only benefit from starting to organize themselves for that battle now.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-tru.title: In the Midterms, America Rebuked Trump’s Authoritarianism
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-tru.author: Ben Burgis
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-tru.text:
In the Midterms, America Rebuked Trump’s Authoritarianism
The reaction of the bulk of the American people to the cruelty and authoritarianism they’ve seen in the last two years has been abject disgust. They voted like it in the midterms.
Perhaps a more competent would-be despot than Donald Trump could have pulled it off. He could have consolidated his power gradually, choosing his battles against immigrants and the Left and imagined foreign adversaries wisely and making sure he didn’t alienate his existing base of support by keeping his finger on the pulse of American sentiment and staying in tune with the struggles of average people, like the high cost of living and the exhaustion with illegal foreign wars. We’ll never know.
The reaction of the bulk of the American people to the cruelty and authoritarianism they’ve seen in the last two years has been abject disgust. And they have reacted positively to the pro-worker rhetoric of Bernie Sanders and the rising Left he has inspired. Candidate after candidate seemed to have finally gotten the memo to steer clear of culture war and rhetorically emphasize affordability. What it all added up to was a “blue wave” so powerful that Republicans lost in states like Texas and South Carolina and Kansas.
For those who despaired at the electorate’s handing the presidency to Trump for a second time in 2024, last night was deeply heartening: the American people decisively rejected what Trump has to offer them.
First Time Farce, Second Time Tragedy
Donald Trump’s first turn at the presidency was more bark than bite. He did a tremendous amount of harm, but mostly the kind of harm that a hypothetical President John McCain or President Mitt Romney would have perpetrated: he lowered taxes for rich people, slashed benefits for poor people, undermined health and safety regulations, and busted unions. There were moments where he went beyond this consensus GOP agenda, usually in the direction of performative cruelty toward immigrants, but he tended to back down in the face of judicial pushback or public outrage. Often he and the constantly rotating cast of second-rate con men he surrounded himself with seemed unsure how to wield the levers of power.
There were portents of what an unleashed form of Trumpist authoritarianism might look like, particularly in his desperate attempts to overturn the results of the 2020 election. Ultimately, though, this too was a flop, and a reasonable argument could be made that Trump had simply tried to do a coarser, more “populist” version of what smarter Republicans had successfully pulled off when George W. Bush stole the 2000 election from Al Gore.
The second round of Trumpism has been so much worse. Reversing Karl Marx’s formula about what happens when history repeats itself, it has been “first time farce, second time tragedy.” Trump returned to power surrounded by true believers dedicated to carrying out the president’s will, and the result has been a sustained two-year assault on liberal democracy.
On his first day in office, Trump signed an executive order attempting to overturn the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of birthright citizenship. He bullied universities across the country into harsher crackdowns on students who protested the genocide in Gaza. He had legal permanent residents arrested and tried to have them deported for attending protests or writing op-eds. He had migrants, some of whom had entered legally and broken no laws, imprisoned in a Salvadoran gulag because of guesswork about what their tattoos might mean. And he sent thousands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents to occupy the city of Minneapolis as a swaggering show of force to intimidate his political opposition. When those agents murdered American citizens Alex Pretti and Renée Good, in broad daylight and on camera, the administration smeared the victims as “domestic terrorists” while their bodies were still warm.
Socialists, Liberal Democracy, and “Resistance Liberalism”
One important thing that “resistance liberal” types got right during and after the first Trump administration was that the president’s ambitions were more rabidly authoritarian than presidents of either party in America’s recent past. Part of what left-wing and socialist critics of “resistance liberalism” got right is that Trumpism was a natural outgrowth of that recent past, and attempts to “just get back to normal” in coalition with Never Trump Republicans very badly misread the moment.
Those of us who want to fight for a better, more materially egalitarian, and more authentically democratic society understand perfectly well that liberal democracy is an indispensable starting point from which we can wage that fight. It’s what gives us the room to agitate, organize, and maneuver. So democratic socialists have stood consistently against Trumpism, as we have against previous forms of authoritarianism. Even in the early months of the administration, when many establishment Democrats didn’t seem to know what had hit them, Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were crisscrossing the country building anti-Trump enthusiasm with their Fighting Oligarchy tour, which married a defense of democracy against authoritarianism with a critique of economic inequality.
This time around, many grassroots Democrats were ready to listen to that message. Enough were willing to support out-and-out socialists that a Democratic Socialists of America member is now the (wildly popular) mayor of the most important city in the capitalist world. And last night’s blue tidal wave more than doubled the number of socialists in Congress. Some degree of “Berniecrat”-style messaging crept into the rhetoric of Democratic candidates across the country. And Democrats in hotly contested states like Maine and Michigan openly championed substantive social democratic policies like Medicare for All.
All of this represents a belated recognition that Trumpism wasn’t just a random eruption of bigotry from some toxic depth of our collective national psyche. It was a demagogic response to the material realities of a profoundly unequal and increasingly precarious society. And it’s best fought by uniting a defense of liberal democracy with a pro-worker economic message.
Of course, campaign rhetoric and governance are two very different things, and the country is far from out of the woods. A profoundly dangerous authoritarian is still president — and will be for the next two years. And establishment Democrats are adept at finding creative new ways to turn even the most inspiring victories into fresh defeats.
For now, though, the fact remains that the American people just handed MAGA a historically massive rebuke. That’s well worth celebrating.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-soc.title: In Last Night’s Midterms, the Left Proved It Can Win
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-soc.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-soc.text:
In Last Night’s Midterms, the Left Proved It Can Win
Democratic voters have long sided with socialists on policy but feared they were a liability in elections. Last night’s results finally proved that wrong.
The Left has been so conditioned in the Trump era to look aghast and horrified at election results that it is still hard to fully believe the outcome today. Yet the historic events of last night really did happen: Donald Trump and Republicans suffered a historic rebuke from voters, handing Democrats wins up and down the ballot all across the country, flipping both chambers of Congress in their favor, and handing them the largest congressional majorities they’ve had since Barack Obama’s election.
In many ways, the result is simple. Across poll after poll leading into the election and exit poll after exit poll leading out of it, the message from voters was the same: they think the economy sucks, they think prices are too high, and they’re angry at Trump and blame him squarely for this entire situation. To send this message, voters turned out in droves to hand power to a Democratic Party that these same polls show they have very little love for, sometimes viewing the Dems even more dimly than they do Trump.
Democrats were expected to take the House. They were not expected to win a majority of more than 250 seats in it, as current estimates have them winning. Nor were they expected to win a Senate majority, let alone a Senate majority of at least fifty-four seats. And they were not expected to flip deep red seats across the country, to sweep Republicans from control of Texas at nearly every level of power, and to win a majority of the country’s governorships, achieving wins and trifectas in states they’ve been practically locked out of for sometimes decades. Obama referred to his 2010 midterms rout as a “shellacking.” Last night was an annihilation.
This is not just good news for Democrats. For the Left, which operates within these Democratic majorities at both the state and federal levels, the results present a historic opportunity to turn its political priorities from words into tangible reality across the country, further building the power it has patiently and, for a long time, quietly been constructing from the ground up these past ten years.
That includes at the federal level. Even though Trump has two more years in the White House, and Democrats are threatening to zealously turn their powers of oversight on the vast record of abuse and criminality he’s racked up during that time, there is some, extremely slim reason to believe something could actually get done.
Trump phoned Politico last night to make clear he was open to working with the Democrats and didn’t “want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything.” The last time Trump was in the White House with a Democratic Congress, the pandemic, the United States saw the largest expansion of the welfare state in decades. Trump’s ideological malleability and the fact that he is currently looking at a legacy as a historic failure presents at least the possibility of an opening for something better to happen.
It’s an opening the Left will be able to take advantage of, too. The Left will enter this new Congress with far more formidable numbers than it’s had in decades: at least seven members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), creating the historic opportunity to for the first time form a distinct socialist caucus in Congress and a Squad-like progressive “Bloc” that could have as many as twenty members.
The massive Democratic House majority means “the Bloc” will not have the expected leverage of being able to block House Democratic leader’s Hakeem Jeffries’s bid for Speaker, or to hold up legislation Freedom Caucus–style. But it will have influence. Much of the generous pandemic policies of 2020, including both Trump and, later, Joe Biden’s stimulus checks, originated with the public demands of socialist and progressive members of Congress that later found their way into legislation on the back of their clear public need and popularity.
This time, the Left will be making these arguments in a world in which socialists have already transformed the way even centrist Democrats talk about politics. The party’s years-long obsession with “norms” and rescuing democracy having largely faded into the background in favor of the affordability-focused and anti-billionaire rhetoric popularized by, respectively, New York’s socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and the socialist duo of Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour.
Just as importantly, it’s a world in which the Left, thanks to a spate of major wins last night, has thoroughly discredited the arguments used to marginalize and dismiss its basic case.
Earthquake in Michigan
No left-wing victory last night was bigger than Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan Senate win over Republican Mike Rogers by a whopping 7 points. It was the exact, hefty margin El-Sayed himself had promised he would win by back in May and defied the incessant predictions that he would end up badly underperforming.
There was arguably no more important race this year than for the purple state’s Senate seat: for the Left, which sought to prove progressives could run and win outside of blue strongholds; for corporate Democrats, a segment of whom feared losing the ability to fearmonger about supposedly risky left-wing candidates; for the pro-Israel lobby, which feared that the success of a stridently pro-Palestinian message would obliterate its claim that blind fealty to Israel was “good politics”; for Trump and the MAGA movement, whose loss of the key state could be a harbinger of even worse political defeat to come.
El-Sayed’s win has confirmed all of these. It represents not just a failure for MAGA, in the form of now two-time loser and career-long warmonger Mike Rogers. It’s an absolute disaster for the pro-Israel lobby and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) in particular, which blew tens of millions of dollars over the course of both the primary and general to defeat El-Sayed and tried every trick in the book to defame and make voters, particularly Jewish ones, fear him.
Instead, both exit polls and voting data indicates El-Sayed comfortably won Jewish voters despite this ugly, Islamophobic campaign against him. He outperformed Kamala Harris in the heavily Jewish Oakland County, the home base of his Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, who humiliated herself trying to kneecap him in the final days of the race.
Catastrophically for the pro-Israel lobby, he did all this while maintaining an unabashed opposition to further US aid to Israel, proving unambiguously that left-wing criticisms of Israeli policy are not only broadly shared by voters in battleground states, but that they are shared by Jewish voters, too.
That he managed this is especially impressive given that, unlike his Democratic colleague running for governor, El-Sayed had to overcome not only an avalanche of big money spending but also members of his own party working around the clock to sabotage him, from Stevens’s last-minute endorsement of Rogers to Rep. Hillary Scholten’s support for a write-in campaign against the Democratic nominee in the final days.
Democratic defectors to the GOP had a variety of motives, but at least some of them made publicly clear they hoped El-Sayed’s defeat would nip the growing Democratic opposition to US aid to Israel in the bud — something they were willing to elect a candidate who included actual antisemites in his campaign to do, as well as to empower an administration that makes common cause with literal neo-Nazis and white supremacists. Instead, they lost and disgraced themselves for nothing.
El-Sayed also did it on a progressive platform of Medicare for All and taxing the rich, two ideas that, when Bernie Sanders first popularized them in 2016, the public was told were too controversial with swing voters and risky to run on. A decade later, these ideas have such widely understood, popular support that Republicans didn’t even bother attacking them. Instead, they put all their eggs in the race-baiting basket, making El-Sayed’s Arab ethnicity and Muslim faith the overwhelming focus of their attacks in what turned out to be one of the most shockingly racist election campaigns this century — and another disgraceful failure.
Wins and Losses
El-Sayed’s win wasn’t the only bright spot for the Left last night. There was also Troy Jackson’s win in Maine, who succeeded where four others had failed in unseating the seemingly untouchable thirty-year Republican incumbent Susan Collins from her Senate seat. Though Jackson, an eighteen-year state legislator and former state senate president and Democratic leader, was far from your typical image of a left insurgent, he quickly consolidated socialist and progressive backing after former nominee Graham Platner’s personal scandals pushed him out of the race.
Though not a socialist, Jackson’s genuine working-class background — as a fifth-generation logger who entered politics to win collective bargaining rights for his fellow woodworkers — and robust progressive record made him closer to the kind of candidates the Left hopes to see in power. In the end, Jackson was able to secure victory by neutralizing Collins’s ability to run up big scores in otherwise blue-voting areas.
The other major progressive win was by James Talarico, who became the first Democrat to win a Texas seat in thirty-eight years, part of a historic blue sweep across Texas that saw Democrats end nearly three decades of GOP rule of the state. Talarico is not a socialist, despite old comments criticizing capitalism that briefly became a campaign issue, and like El-Sayed, he took pains to insist that he was a capitalist. Even so, he was backed by groups like More Perfect Union and the Progressive Change Campaign Committee and drew support from prominent socialists like Hasan Piker, who has said that the Left was “the force that backed him early on” and “allowed him to win.”
Maybe more important, Talarico ran on a class-based message decrying “billionaire mega-donors” — one of whom, Elon Musk, lit at least $47 million on fire trying and failing to beat him — and insisting that the fundamental political divide in the United States was “top versus bottom,” a more progressive message than many Democrats ran on even in solid blue states. So his emphatic 12 point victory over the scandal-plagued Ken Paxton is a victory for the kind of populist message the Left has long advocated, even as Talarico did things like refusing to back Medicare for All and declining to campaign with Bernie Sanders when he visited the state.
Speaking of Sanders, as of the time of writing, seventeen of the twenty-one candidates endorsed by the socialist senator have won their races, while only two have lost, and two are in races that are still to be called. Sanders’s endorsements were less straightforwardly left-wing than those of organizations like DSA or Justice Democrats. They included candidates like El-Sayed and Jackson, but they also included more establishment candidates like Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, who beat corporate-friendly rivals in their primaries. They ran the gamut from DSA candidates like New York’s Claire Valdez and Colorado’s Melat Kiros to candidates like Rebecca Cooke, the less progressive candidate in her primary but someone who flipped a Trump-voting, rural Wisconsin district that for decades was represented by a Democrat.
They also included William Lawrence, the Sunrise Movement cofounder who has flipped a swing district in the swing state of Michigan despite having one of the more left-wing résumés of any Democratic candidate — something that, like El-Sayed, we were told would make him a guaranteed loser. The fact that Lawrence left DSA mid-campaign and had to distance himself from old tweets that included calls to nationalize the fossil fuel industry should not take away from the magnitude of his win. On the back of a progressive populist campaign that pushed a data center moratorium and Medicare for All, Lawrence won a purple district that used to belong to the Democrats’ patron saint of centrism, former CIA analyst Elissa Slotkin.
Even some of the defeats were surprisingly good for the Left. In ruby-red Florida — where Republicans outnumber Democrats by 1.5 million and a Democrat hasn’t won statewide office since 2012 — DSA member Angie Nixon lost by less than 3 points, little different from the 2 point losing margin of the ex-Republican candidate who Democrats ran for governor. The state’s last three Democratic losing margins for Senate are 13, 16, 0.2, and 8 points. And that’s after being outspent nearly four-to-one and getting no help whatsoever from the national Democratic Party, which should be kicking itself for missing the opportunity to win another gettable Senate seat.
That a DSA member would even be competitive in Florida — the heartland of right-wing Cuban extremism and the home of both Marco Rubio and now two Bolsonaro sons — would have sounded laughable five years ago, or even five months ago. That Nixon could do this well with this little help will, together with El-Sayed’s win, make it that much harder to argue that the socialist label is an inherent electoral liability.
It should spark some soul-searching among the Democratic establishment and its decision to preemptively write off the race as a foregone loss. But it will no doubt also spark debate within the socialist movement, too, given Nixon’s result was built partly on distancing herself from alienating positions like defunding the police and abolishing prisons. Her strong showing, along with the success of other left-wing candidates who similarly moderated or eschewed contemporary left orthodoxy on some issues, points to the benefits of DSA candidates having the flexibility to tailor campaigns to local electorates.
The Left also suffered a defeat of sorts in Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn fell short at a second tilt at a Senate seat in a state where a Democrat hasn’t won statewide election for twenty years. Osborn, a union leader who led a successful 2021 strike against Kellogg’s over planned benefit cuts, was something of a proof of concept for the Left: that, as per research from the Center for Working-Class Politics, the way to win in such states is to run genuine working-class candidates with populist platforms outside of the Democratic Party brand.
To some extent, both of Osborn’s campaigns proved this true. The last four Democratic losing margins in Nebraska Senate races were 41 points, 19 points, 24 points, and 16 points; by contrast, Osborn has fallen short by roughly the same, single-digit margin of 7 points both runs. Clearly, if pro-working-class candidates are going to flip a deep red state like Nebraska, Osborn’s campaign is a model for how to do it.
But a losing margin is still a loss. Despite combining left-populist policies like “right to repair” with centrist messaging on issues like immigration — Osborn famously ran ads declaring he backed Trump’s border wall — the former union leader was unable to shake attacks that he was a secret Democrat. A particularly damaging set of “scandals” had Osborn on tape bashing the border wall and other Trump policies and using insulting language about his voters. On top of an avalanche of outside spending aimed against him, it proved too much to overcome.
These are on top of a few other stinging defeats for the Left, including Justice Democrats–backed Justin Pearson’s razor-thin loss in Tennessee’s Ninth District, who looked like he might be able to overcome a Republican gerrymander thanks to a surge in black voter turnout.
Socialists may instead be heartened by the victory of Scott Houldieson over a Trump-endorsed candidate in the Republican-held Indiana First Senate District. Houldieson, a union autoworker who cofounded and led the reform effort within the United Auto Workers that resulted in Shawn Fain’s leadership of the union, easily flipped the seat with a 14 point victory on the back of an affordability-focused campaign. Though not DSA-backed or a statewide race, it is to some extent a vindication of the kind of approach the Left believed would see success in Nebraska.
The Local Game Continues
Meanwhile, as usual, socialists and progressives continued their steady accrual of elected office at the state and local levels.
As of the time of writing, DSA has notched 130 wins in everything from state legislatures and city councils, to mayor’s offices and ballot measures, with forty-two losses and fifty-eight races still to be decided. While Angie Nixon fell short of her Senate bid, environmentalist Ashley Herrmann became only the second socialist to win elected office in Florida and the first to be elected to its state legislature in more than a century, flipping a swing district that the Republican incumbent had won with 58 percent of the vote two years earlier. Other notable socialist wins included Robert LeVertis Bell’s election to the Kentucky state house and Mathewos Samson’s election to the Georgia General Assembly, which, together with Gabriel Sanchez’s reelection, makes him one of two socialists in the state legislature.
Particularly notable are several mayoral races that were foregone conclusions after the primaries. Janeese Lewis George is now officially Washington, DC’s first socialist mayor, having won on the back of an affordable housing plan that combines “abundance”-style reforms with expanding rent stabilization. In Providence, Rhode Island, socialist David Morales has similarly cruised to an expected win and, together with a socialist-led city council, will now work to pass a robust rent control measure in the housing-crisis-stricken city — a measure the incumbent mayor he successfully primaried had vetoed.
More complicated is the Los Angeles mayor’s race, where socialist City Councilor Nithya Raman is currently on track to unseat Karen Bass as Los Angeles mayor. Raman’s candidacy was the subject of some controversy, after she was endorsed by the local DSA chapter despite not fully embracing the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement against Israel and not being questioned about it, leading the DSA’s National Political Committee to nearly strip her of the endorsement, an effort that failed by one vote. If Raman does win, she’ll be the first candidate to unseat an incumbent LA mayor in twenty-one years.
This is on top of a host of progressive ballot measures pushed through by majorities of voters countrywide: the defeat of an abortion ban ballot measure in Missouri, a successful ban on dark money in elections in Montana, and divestment from Israel in Providence, to name a few. Maybe most notably, ballot measures restricting the construction of data centers have so far won overwhelmingly around the country, thirty-eight to one, with eight still to be counted — a clear public vindication of a position championed and popularized by the broad Left.
What’s Smart Is What’s Right
For the past decade, socialists and progressives have often had good election nights even when the Democratic Party has suffered, and they have had bad nights while Democrats rejoiced. Last night may be the first one where both the Left and the centrist party establishment have seen historic wins in tandem.
Over the past two years, the Left showed it was the force most willing to fight against Trump’s right-wing assault and to come up with an effective argument — affordability and fighting oligarchy — to do it. Last night finally proved left policies and rhetoric are not the electoral liability Democratic voters have been told for decades it is.
For decades, Democratic voters have had to make the agonizing decision every election to choose between their heads and their hearts. The Left may have just freed them of it.

Ansage der Berliner Linkspartei: Mit Emde soll Ende sein
Die Linkspartei in Berlin beschließt, die umstrittene Abgeordnete Emde zum Verzicht ihres Mandats aufzufordern. Zusätzlich droht ihr der Fraktionsausschluss.
High Noon war es nicht, als die beiden Landesvorsitzenden der Berliner Linkspartei den Beschluss bekannt gaben, aber die Verkündung kam noch rechtzeitig für die „Tagesschau“ zur Prime Time. „Wir vertrauen ihr nicht mehr“, erklärten Kerstin Wolter und Maximilian Schirmer am Freitagabend nach einer Sitzung des Landesvorstands der Hauptstadt-Linken.
Die, der die Spitze der Landespartei nicht mehr vertraut, ist die umstrittene Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde. Mehrfach hatte sie das Existenzrecht Israels geleugnet, hat sich mit Ibrahim Ibrahim fotografieren lassen, einem Sympathisanten des Hamas-Terrors. Emde soll, das hat der Vorstand nun beschlossen, ihr Mandat als Abgeordnete der Linksfraktion im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus abgeben.
„Sie hat sich wiederholt und bewusst über unsere gemeinsamen Beschlüsse hinweggesetzt“, sagten Wolter und Schirmer am Freitag zur Begründung. Ein Mandat sei keine Ich-AG. „Mandate werden kollektiv errungen: durch die Arbeit und die Stimmen von Kandidierenden, Mitgliedern und der gesamten Partei. Daraus erwächst Verantwortung für das eigene Handeln.“ Am Ende stand die unmissverständliche Ansage der beiden Landeschefs: „Es reicht, genug ist genug.“
Der Druck auf die Linkspartei, endlich das Ende vom Emde einzuleiten, war in den vergangenen Tagen noch einmal größer geworden. In der taz hatte die Linken-Bundestagsabgeordnete Katalin Gennburg bereits am Mittwoch Emde zum Rücktritt aufgefordert. „Für mich ist ein Punkt erreicht, an dem ich denke, jetzt reicht’s“, hatte Gennburg gesagt.
Emde, die in Neukölln ein Direktmandat geholt hatte, hatte zuvor nicht nur ihre Aussage wiederholt, Staaten hätten kein Existenzrecht. Während des Parteitags am vergangenen Samstag, auf dem die Linke beschloss, Koalitionsverhandlungen mit Grünen und SPD aufzunehmen, hatte sie vor dem Tagungsort auch gegen die eigene Partei demonstriert. „Gewählt für Palästina. Verraten für den Senat“, lautete das Motto der Kritiker eines rot-grün-roten Bündnisses aus den Reihen von palästinasolidarischen Gruppen.
Eine kleine Tür bleibt offen
Zuletzt hatte sich auch noch Parteiikone Gregor Gysi zu Wort gemeldet. „Ich hoffe, dass wir sie ausschließen“, hatte Gysi im Podcast von Paul Ronzheimer gesagt. Emdes Äußerungen nannte er „antisemitisch und vor allen Dingen indiskutabel für meine Partei“.
Ob Vanessa Emde ihr Mandat tatsächlich zurückgibt, ist offen. Tut sie es nicht, könnte sie aus der Linken-Fraktion im Abgeordnetenhaus ausgeschlossen werden. Diese tagt am Dienstag. Sollte der Fraktionsvorstand beantragen, Emde aus der 44-köpfigen Fraktion rauszuwerfen, könnte am Dienstag darauf darüber abgestimmt werden. Nötig für einen Ausschluss ist eine Zweidrittelmehrheit.
Dass diese zusammenkommt, gilt inzwischen als immer wahrscheinlicher. Wie aus Kreisen der Fraktion zu hören ist, hätten einige der Abgeordneten, die neu in der Fraktion sind, sich zunächst ein eigenes Bild machen wollen. Emdes Auftritte, nicht zuletzt ihr Auftritt während des Parteitags, hätten aber viele Abgeordnete davon überzeugt, dass es keine Vertrauensgrundlage für eine Zusammenarbeit mehr gebe.
Mit der Aufforderung, ihr Mandat niederzulegen, und einem möglichen Antrag auf Ausschluss aus der Fraktion kommt die Linke auch einer Forderung der Berliner SPD entgegen. Deren Fraktions- und Landeschef Steffen Krach hatte erklärt, dass es mit Vanessa Emde als Teil der Linksfraktion kein Linksbündnis geben werde.
Allerdings haben die beiden Linken-Vorsitzenden Emde noch eine kleine Tür offengelassen. „Vanessa Emde hat eine Woche Zeit, zu uns zurückzukehren“, fügten Wolter und Schirmer hinzu. „Dazu soll sie ihren Instagram-Beitrag löschen, sich für ihren Auftritt am Rande des Parteitags entschuldigen und eine konstruktive Zusammenarbeit auf Grundlage unserer Beschlüsse zusagen.“
Ob Emde durch die Tür geht? Unwahrscheinlich.

https://taz.de/Union-will-Aigner-als-Bun.text:
Union will Aigner als Bundespräsidentin : Es ist keine Schwäche, sich hinter eine starke Frau zu stellen
Ilse Aigner soll Bundespräsidentin werden. Das verdankt sie nicht Friedrich Merz, der erneut nicht wie ein Antreiber, sondern ein Getriebener wirkte.
E s scheint festzustehen, Ilse Aigner soll Bundespräsidentin werden. Auch die CDU stellt sich nach übereinstimmenden Medienberichten hinter sie. Die offizielle Bestätigung steht noch aus, aber zuletzt lief alles auf die bayerische Landtagspräsidentin zu. Es gab in den vergangenen Tagen kaum noch eine Politikerin in Union und SPD, die sie nicht für eine „hervorragende“ Kandidatin hielten, auch die Grünen funkten Zustimmung.
Alle warten nur noch darauf, was Friedrich Merz sagt. Der Kanzler und CDU-Vorsitzende will sich nach bisheriger Planung am Montag äußern, nach einer Sitzung des Präsidiums. Die CDU-Führungsebene, darunter auch zwei Frauen, deren Namen ebenfalls im Laufe der Debatte als mögliche Kandidatinnen aufploppten, trifft sich bereits am Sonntagabend zum Abendessen. Der Austausch darüber, wen die CDU, die formal das Vorschlagsrecht hat, als Nachfolgerin von Frank-Walter Steinmeier aufstellt, dürfte kurz werden.
Interessanter ist die Erörterung, warum Merz auch dieser Findungsprozess mal wieder komplett entglitten ist und er sich von Markus Söder so vorführen ließ. Der CSU-Chef hatte Aigner bereits im April zum ersten Mal vorgeschlagen. Der Kanzler hielt sich lange bedeckt, legte sich zuletzt lediglich darauf fest, dass eine Frau Bundespräsidentin werden soll. Wieso nutzte Merz nicht den CSU-Parteitag Ende Oktober, um das Thema abzuräumen? Stattdessen hieß es kurz zuvor, die CDU werde einen eigenen Vorschlag machen und vor zwei Wochen streute sein Umfeld noch den Namen der hessischen Fraktionsvorsitzenden Ines Claus. Ein Testballon oder eine Trotzreaktion?
Jedenfalls keine konsistente Strategie. Der CDU-Vorsitzende hat erneut keine glückliche Figur gemacht und dokumentiert, dass Personalplanung nicht sein Ding ist. Er, der sich selbst gern als Antreiber sieht, wirkte wie ein Getriebener. Aber egal, am Ende ist es kein Zeichen von Schwäche, sich hinter eine starke Frau zu stellen.

https://taz.de/Bundespraesidentschafts-K.title: Bundespräsidentschafts-Kandidatin Aigner: Die Bundespräsidentin als Demokratiewächterin
https://taz.de/Bundespraesidentschafts-K.author: Christian Rath
https://taz.de/Bundespraesidentschafts-K.text:
Bundespräsidentschafts-Kandidatin Aigner: Die Bundespräsidentin als Demokratiewächterin
Die Bundespräsident:in sollte eine Jurist:in sein, raunte es in der CDU, was sich gegen Ilse Aigner richtete. Doch sie soll es nun offenbar werden.
In unsicheren Zeiten mit zerbrechlichen Koalitionen und einer immer stärker werdenden AfD sollte die/der Bundespräsident:in ein/e Jurist:in sein. Dieses Argument war seit dem Sommer regelmäßig zu hören. Das Argument kam nicht aus dünkelhaften Juristenkreisen, sondern vor allem aus der CDU und zielte recht offensichtlich darauf ab, die CSU-Kandidatin Ilse Aigner als Bundespräsidentin zu verhindern.
Ilse Aigner hat im elterlichen Betrieb eine Ausbildung zur Radio- und Fernsehtechnikerin absolviert. Später machte sie eine Fortbildung zur staatlich geprüften Elektrotechnikerin. Juristin ist sie eindeutig nicht.
Dabei wurde der Wunsch nach einer/m Jurist:in an der Staatsspitze nicht offensiv gegen Aigner vorgebracht. Vielmehr wurden eigene Kandidat:innen damit beworben, dass sie Jurist:innen seien, etwa Hessens Ministerpräsident Boris Rhein, die CDU-Fraktionsvorsitzende im hessischen Landtag Ines Claus und Ex-Verfassungsrichter Udo Di Fabio.
Bei bisherigen Bundespräsidenten hat die Frage nach der Ausbildung keine große Rolle gespielt. Von den bisherigen 12 Amtsinhabern waren nur 6 Juristen: Gustav Heinemann, Karl Carstens, Richard von Weizsäcker, Roman Herzog, Christian Wulff und Frank-Walter Steinmeier. Roman Herzog war vor Amtsübernahme sogar Präsident des Bundesverfassungsgerichts.
Aber immerhin sechs Bundespräsidenten waren keine Juristen: Theodor Heuss (Ökonom und Journalist), Heinrich Lübke (Vermessungsingenieur, Bauernfunktionär und Agrarminister) Walter Scheel (Bankkaufmann und Außenminister), Johannes Rau (Buchhändler, Journalist und Ministerpräsident), Horst Köhler (Ökonom und IWF-Direktor), Joachim Gauck (Pfarrer und Leiter der Stasiakten-Behörde).
Nun wird also voraussichtlich Ilse Aigner nominiert und Ende Januar zur Bundespräsidentin gewählt. Sie muss dann auch in staatspolitischen Krisen Entscheidungen von hoher Tragweite treffen. Dabei hilft ihr im Bundespräsidialamt ein Referat von vier Jurist:innen, das seit 2025 von Claudia Spoerhase geleitet wird. Zuvor war Spoerhase im Bundespräsidialamt sieben Jahre lang für die Vergabe von Orden zuständig.
Zudem kann sich die Bundespräsidentin jederzeit externen juristischen Sachverstand organisieren. So ist es nicht unüblich, dass das Bundespräsidialamt renommierte Rechtsprofessor:innen um Rat fragt und diesen auch stets erhält. Allerdings lebt die Rechtswissenschaft von Diskussionen und es gibt meist viele sich widersprechende Meinungen. Schon die Auswahl der juristischen Berater:innen kann vorentscheidend sein. Letztlich muss die Bundespräsidentin allein entscheiden, welcher Rechtsauffassung sie folgt.
In drei Konstellationen könnte die Bundespräsidentin mit heiklen verfassungsrechtlichen Fragen konfrontiert werden.
Prüfung von Gesetzen
So wird jedes Bundesgesetz im Bundespräsidialamt auf seine Verfassungsmäßigkeit geprüft, bevor die/der Bundespräsident:in unterschreibt und das Gesetz anschließend im Bundesgesetzblatt veröffentlicht wird. Wenn die/der Bundespräsident:in nicht unterschreibt, kommt das Gesetz nicht zustande. Üblicherweise scheitern Gesetze nur bei „schweren und offensichtlichen“ verfassungsrechtlichen Mängeln am Bundespräsidialamt. Bisher gab es acht entsprechende Fälle, zum Beispiel weil eine erforderliche Zustimmung des Bundesrats fehlte.
Während es bislang oft um eher technische Fragen ging, könnten künftig vermehrt der Schutz von Grundrechten und die Sicherung der Demokratie in den Vordergrund rücken, insbesondere falls die AfD an der nächsten Bundesregierung beteiligt ist und versucht einen autoritären Umbau des Staates voranzutreiben. Denkbar ist aber auch, dass die etablierten Parteien versuchen, die AfD mit verfassungswidrigen Gesetzen zu benachteiligen und von der Macht fernzuhalten.
Die Nicht-Unterzeichnung eines Gesetzes ist der schnellste Weg, ein beschlossenes Gesetz zu verhindern. Die/der Bundespräsident:in kann aber in weniger eindeutigen Fällen auch unterzeichnen und dabei ihre verfassungsrechtlichen Zweifel öffentlich machen. Sicher wird dann bald das Bundesverfassungsgericht mittels Verfassungsbeschwerde oder abstrakter Normenkontrolle eingeschaltet und kann das Gesetz prüfen.
Ernennung von Regierungsmitgliedern
Die/der Bundespräsident:in schlägt dem Bundestag vor, wer Bundeskanzler:in werden soll. Das ist in der Regel die Person, die es geschafft hat, eine Koalition zu schmieden, die sie im Bundestag dann wählen will. Die/der Bundespräsident:in kann sich aber weigern, eine Person vorzuschlagen, die verfassungsfeindliche Ziele verfolgt. Sollte sich eine AfD-geführte Koalition etwa auf Björn Höcke als Kanzler einigen, könnte die Bundespräsidentin die Kanzlerwahl verhindern.
Die/der Bundespräsident:in ernennt zudem auf Vorschlag der Bundeskanzlerin bzw. des Bundeskanzlers die Minister:innen. Auch hier könnte sich die Bundespräsidentin bei verfassungsfeindlichen Politiker:innen weigern. Bloße Zweifel an der Kompetenz genügen nicht.
Entsprechende Fälle hat es bisher noch nicht gegeben. Das Vetorecht gegen Verfassungsfeinde in der Regierung steht auch nicht ausdrücklich im Grundgesetz. Sollte sich die Bundespräsidentin auf ein solches Vetorecht berufen, dürfte dies zu Verfahren beim Bundesverfassungsgericht führen.
Entscheidung über Neuwahlen
Wenn die/der Bundeskanzler:in eine Vertrauensabstimmung verliert, kann sie/er der Bundespräsident:in vorschlagen, den Bundestag aufzulösen. Die/der Bundespräsident:in kann hier frei entscheiden, ob Neuwahlen ermöglicht werden oder die Bundesregierung zur Weiterarbeit als Minderheitsregierung verpflichtet.
Die Beispiele zeigen, dass die Bundespräsidentin in unruhigen Zeiten eine enorme Verantwortung als Demokratiewächterin haben kann. Verfassungsrechtliche Kenntnisse wären dabei sicher hilfreich. Diese sollte eine Berufspolitikerin wie Ilse Aigner aber auch ohne Jurastudium haben. Wichtiger als bloße Kenntnisse ist ohnehin verfassungspolitische Klugheit und Standfestigkeit. Autorität wird eine Bundespräsidentin in diesen Zeiten aber nur gewinnen können, wenn sie deutlich macht, dass es ihr um Grundrechte und Demokratie geht und nicht um den Machterhalt der etablierten Parteien.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
