Is unconditional support for Israel becoming a liability for Republicans?
JD Vance’s response to the midterm defeat suggests a once-untouchable Republican consensus may be starting to crack.
The sweeping Republican defeat in the November 3 midterm elections may have opened a debate that, until recently, would have been almost unthinkable within the party: whether the United States should fundamentally reconsider its relationship with Israel.
For decades, unwavering support for Israel was a defining feature of Republican identity, sustained by evangelical Christians, the conservative foreign policy establishment, influential lobbying organisations, and a deeply entrenched congressional consensus. Now, following the electorate’s repudiation of Donald Trump and his administration, that consensus is showing unmistakable signs of strain.
The clearest indication came from Vice President JD Vance, who acknowledged in an unusually candid post-election assessment that dissatisfaction with America’s relationship with Israel was among the reasons Republican voters abandoned their party. Identifying four concerns driving former Trump supporters towards Democrats, Vance cited the Iran war, the cost of living and inflation, the principle of putting America first, and, significantly, changing the American relationship with Israel.
His admission was remarkable not simply because of what he said, but because of who said it. As the administration’s second-highest official and a potential Republican presidential contender in 2028, Vance effectively acknowledged that unconditional support for the Israeli government is no longer politically cost-free, even within the Republican coalition.
More importantly, he brought into the open a question Republican politicians have traditionally been reluctant to entertain: whether America’s commitment to Israel continues to serve America’s own interests.
Does this represent a genuine reassessment, however, or merely an attempt to explain an electoral disaster and reposition the party for 2028?
There are compelling reasons to believe that something more consequential is under way. The Republican alliance with Israel has rested on several overlapping foundations: evangelical Christian support, strategic and intelligence cooperation, military interests, and conservative political organisations that have made backing Israel an almost unquestionable test of political loyalty.
But those foundations are increasingly being challenged by a younger generation of conservatives, particularly within the emerging America First movement, who question why American resources and military commitments should be directed towards foreign conflicts while economic pressures mount at home.
Their scepticism does not necessarily reflect sympathy for Palestinians or opposition to Israel’s existence. Rather, it challenges the assumption that American and Israeli interests are automatically identical. Increasingly, these voters want to know why Washington should continue providing extensive military assistance, diplomatic protection, and political support regardless of the policies pursued by the Israeli government.
The wars in Gaza and Iran have brought that question into sharper focus. Israel’s devastating military campaign in Gaza, the resulting humanitarian catastrophe, and Washington’s continued military and diplomatic backing have imposed mounting moral, diplomatic, and strategic costs on the United States. The subsequent confrontation with Iran further exposed the dangers of allowing Israeli security priorities and regional calculations to influence American decisions about war and peace.
Vance’s intervention, therefore, did not emerge from a political vacuum. It reflects tensions that have been developing within the Republican electorate for years. Earlier polling had already identified declining enthusiasm for Israel among younger Republicans, even as traditional constituencies remained considerably more supportive. The Chicago Council’s 2026 survey also found declining Republican favourability towards Israel compared with 2022, although Republicans continued to favour maintaining or increasing military assistance. The picture is consequently not of a party abandoning Israel, but of one increasingly divided over the terms and consequences of the relationship.
That division could become central to the Republican Party’s struggle over its post-Trump future. By identifying dissatisfaction with Israel policy as a factor in the electoral losses, Vance has effectively legitimised a debate that conservative politicians have long avoided. He has also signalled that the issue could become an important point of differentiation among potential presidential contenders preparing for 2028.
For Trump, the contradiction is particularly damaging. He built his political movement around putting America first and ending costly foreign entanglements, yet his presidency has become closely associated with extraordinary support for Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, including military cooperation, diplomatic backing, and confrontation with regional adversaries.
The Iran war has made that contradiction harder to defend. Voters who supported Trump expecting him to prioritise domestic concerns may reasonably question why the United States became entangled in another Middle Eastern conflict, particularly when the consequences include economic uncertainty, higher energy costs, and resources diverted from domestic priorities.
While Trump has acknowledged that the Iran conflict contributed to Republican losses, he has continued defending the decision to launch it. Vance, meanwhile, has been more explicit in recognising the political price of the administration’s foreign policy choices. That difference could become an important fault line within the Republican leadership.
Yet recognising the political costs of the relationship is not the same as changing it. The institutional forces sustaining the US-Israel alliance remain formidable. Congressional Republicans have traditionally supported substantial military assistance, while evangelical organisations, influential donors, lobbying networks, and defence sector interests continue to exercise considerable influence. Beyond domestic politics, the relationship encompasses intelligence sharing, military technology, regional security arrangements, and decades of diplomatic commitments.
Consequently, even an administration persuaded that unconditional support carries electoral risks could find it difficult to translate that recognition into meaningful policy. Changing the rhetoric is considerably easier than changing military appropriations, arms transfers, diplomatic positions, and the strategic architecture underpinning the alliance.
Nevertheless, the midterm results have altered Washington’s political calculations. With Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress, continued military assistance and diplomatic protection will face greater scrutiny. Republicans contemplating their political future must also consider whether defending every decision of the Israeli government remains electorally advantageous, particularly among younger voters and independents whose support increasingly determines national outcomes.
The real test, therefore, will not be what Republican politicians say in the aftermath of their defeat, but what they are prepared to do. Will they support conditions on military assistance? Reconsider automatic diplomatic protection when Israeli policies violate international law? Challenge settlement expansion and annexationist ambitions? And will they recognise that a sustainable regional settlement must address Palestinian freedom, security, and political rights rather than treating them as secondary considerations?
These are the questions that distinguish a genuine reassessment from electoral opportunism.
For Palestinians, the stakes are considerable. A meaningful Republican shift could create political space for greater accountability, a less permissive American approach to Israeli military operations, and renewed pressure for a political settlement grounded in Palestinian rights. But expectations should remain measured. A change in Republican rhetoric does not necessarily translate into a change in America’s strategic priorities, much less an immediate departure from decades of established policy.
Ultimately, the significance of the midterm defeat may lie less in an immediate transformation of American policy than in the erosion of an assumption that has governed Washington for generations: that support for Israel is politically untouchable. The Republican Party now faces a choice: ignore the warning or recognise that its political future may depend, in part, on responding to it.
The alliance is not about to disappear. But the political immunity that has long shielded it from serious scrutiny may finally be eroding. Whether that erosion produces a substantive change in American policy towards Israel remains the defining question of the post-election period.

https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.title: Walking with spirits in Cambodia’s sacred forests
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.author: Jonnie Bayfield
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.text:
I’m two hours downriver from the Chi Phat community ecotourism camp, in the Koh Kong region of Cambodia, when my phone signal fizzles out completely. It’s dawn and we’re chugging through the snaking Preak Piphot River towards the starting point of a 9-mile (15km) overnight trek into the country’s sacred, spirit-filled Cardamom mountain range. The region, a six-hour bus ride west of the capital Phnom Penh, recently made global news for being home to a raft of new species of fauna and a sanctuary for rare and endangered wildlife.
As well as its plant and protection initiatives, it is also known for its storied history, from ancient burial grounds to the last stronghold of Pol Pot’s fleeing Khmer Rouge fighters into the late 1980s. If trees could talk … Well, many believe these ones can.
Unlike the western way of managing belief – sealed in gated graveyards or glimpsed on infrequent Sundays – Khmer spirituality (as with the national, Buddhist faith) is as integral to daily Cambodian life as the ticking-over tuk-tuk or the churn of the streetside sugarcane crusher.
 
The Cardamoms has long been a land I have tried to reach. I’m here for a few days, hoping to feel the spiritual power of such a sacred place, as well as check out its diverse yet elusive wildlife, from forest elephants to wild dogs (or dholes).
Luckily, I won’t be entering the jungle alone – Chea Singhtararith, or Rith, is my tourist board chaperone, alongside a team of guides from the Chi Phat ecotourism community – including a forest cook, known simply as Mr Crab. Oh, and we’ll be joined by a host of omnipotent spirits …
In Cambodian animism, neak ta are powerful, just spirits who protect and watch over the country’s boundless, ever-threatened natural wonders: from the mighty Tonlé Sap River, one of the few in the world that reverses its flow twice yearly but is threatened by increasing pollution, to its dense, diverse, frequently devastated forests.
The Cardamom range is one of the largest unfragmented rainforest corridors in mainland south-east Asia. It has a double line of defence: armed government rangers who enforce national park law on the ground, and deep-seated animist traditions that keep vast areas of the forest untouchable, and thus a haven for wildlife.
As we float down the river, a young guide called Daro points to a small shrine balanced on a seemingly levitating stone. “Lok Ta Esey Tmar Andet [the Hermitage of the Floating Stone] protects this river.”
And what a river it is – flanked by dense, green jungle, all fortified by twisted fists of mangrove, with the fresh, young roots rising up from the riverbed sharp as spears. This spot is considered so sacred that many local people believe it to be the home of one of Cambodia’s most notorious mythic visions – the White Crocodile, a portent of death or inescapable fate.
It’s everyday crocodiles I’m more concerned about, along with venomous snakes and my own, personal nemesis: dengue fever-harbouring mosquitoes. I’ll take all the spirits’ help I can get.
In recent years, rural communities like Chi Phat have been forced, by economic and environmental pressures, to re-evaluate their dialogue with nature. Founded in 2007 by the Wildlife Alliance, the Chi Phat ecotourism community offers a range of extremely well-priced excursions, tours and activities across the area, including treks into the Cardamoms, with overnight stops at their deep-jungle base camp.
However, it’s local people like 60-year-old Mr Crab (arguably the finest forest cook in the Cardamoms) who best symbolise what the initiative set out to achieve: prior to his life in the community’s ecotourism project, he was a truck driver for the loggers, ferrying out the very trees he now works to protect. Many others in the Chi Phat community come from a similar background: loggers, poachers, hunters – all of whom have gone from exploiting their surroundings to promoting and protecting them.
On our approach to base camp, which sits by the river Stung Preat, we silence the engines and decamp into narrow row boats so as not to disturb the delicate ecosystem. This is birdland now, and the unfolding mass of jungle hisses, pops and creaks. Occasionally, a kingfisher darts in our periphery, as bright butterflies (such as the Indo-Chinese chocolate albatross) flutter through hard heat, crossing still water, disturbed only by the odd gang of scrapping monkeys waiting at every turn.
It’s 8am when we ditch the row boats and begin the steady walk into the tree line, about 2½ miles in the direction of a small river where we will take lunch. The humidity is intense. Within minutes, it feels as though all the fluid has left my body – wicked away by hiking clothes.
“Watch out,” Rith says, as we dodge curling roots and clamber over collapsed trunks. “We don’t say bad or negative things in the forest. Nor do we take anything. And when we need to pee, we ask the gods first. The smaller trees have smaller spirits – so pick one of them to pee on!”
It’s not simple superstition either – the jungle and the Cardamoms teem with wildlife best left in myth. One such beast we meet, a golden-backed spider (the giant golden orb weaver), is roughly the size of an adult hand and spins vast webs that, once hit by light, shimmer an iridescent gold.
Similarly, when we stumble across a crop of rare, yellow cap mushrooms they are so “magic kingdom” in appearance, I assume they will either kill us or transfigure us. Instead, Mr Crab bags them up for dinner, claiming them as a gift from the forest spirits.
Luckily, the spirits shine on us, with the mirage-like appearance of a fast-running stream. The heat is now so oppressive that I strip down and dive in.
Mr Crab and Daro (who gave up a lucrative life as a graphic designer in the city to live alongside nature again) spark up a fire. A welcome round of Khmer tea is brewed and half a chicken fried up for lunch, accompanied by a pan of steaming rice. It’s the start of the wet season, and when it rains it pours. Bruised clouds have gathered, and so we hit the trail again, hoping to reach our camp for the night, 2 miles away, before dark.
It’s some time later, as a Kurtz-like delirium is about to set in, that a small campsite appears amid the dense vegetation: a clearing with several hand-built covered sleeping platforms, Mr Crab’s outdoor kitchen and a small bathing pool fed by a trickling waterfall.
Night draws in, and with it the cyclic choral purr of cicadas, that, much like the forest spirits perhaps, are never seen yet all around. Dinner is served by torchlight, hung from the roof by a krama (the symbolic, all-purpose Khmer scarf). The remaining half a chicken is roasted on an open fire alongside those yellow cap mushrooms fried up with fresh garlic, all washed down with sips of “Khmer whisky” – fruit-flavoured rice wine that could strip paint.
That night, I’m lulled to sleep by a colossal downpour that hammers at the tin roof over our heads. Come morning, we head off on the final leg of the Cardamom trek, winding back into the heart of the Chi Phat community. Paths widen and the jungle begins to open up. But it’s not this that marks our return from the wilderness – it’s the cicada-like ping of all our phones coming back online.
Almost as soon as the trees open up entirely, the rain comes down, and we make it back to Chi Phat drenched and blistered. Miraculously, my flesh has survived the two-day mosquito buffet utterly unbitten. Maybe there is something to all this spirit worship after all.
The trip was facilitated by the Cambodia Tourist Board and the Chi Phat community, which offers a range of tours, excursions and activities. A five-day package, including treks, guides, food and accommodation, costs about $350pp

https://taz.de/Aigners-Nominierung/!6228.title: Aigners Nominierung: Die Frau der Stunde
https://taz.de/Aigners-Nominierung/!6228.author: Dominik Baur
https://taz.de/Aigners-Nominierung/!6228.text:
Aigners Nominierung : Die Frau der Stunde
Ilse Aigner als Bundespräsidentin – das ist eine gute Wahl. Doch wie sie es wurde, das wollen wir mal schnell wieder vergessen.
I lse Aigner wird Bundespräsidentin, und das ist gut so. Nicht weil sie nett ist, nicht weil sie mit den Leuten kann, nicht weil sie politisch erfahren ist, nicht weil sie einen klaren Wertekompass hat und auch nicht, weil sie der Rechtsextremen im bayerischen Landtag immer wieder gezeigt hat, wo der Hammer hängt. Sicher, all das sind gute, nein, sehr gute Voraussetzungen für Aigners neuen Job.
Was aber am allermeisten für Aigner spricht und ihre Nominierung letztlich unausweichlich gemacht hat, ist die breite Basis, die sie trägt. Sie ist eben nicht die Kandidatin der CSU, hinter ihr stehen große Teile der SPD, der Grünen und – wie sich zuletzt gezeigt hat – eben auch der CDU. Natürlich hätte man noch wochenlang abwägen können, welche andere mögliche Kandidatin welche Eignung mitbringt, allzu durchsichtige Argumente durchdiskutieren können, ob eine Bundespräsidentin Jura studiert haben sollte und, und, und …
Und keine Frage: Es gibt mit Sicherheit andere Frauen – vielleicht sogar Männer –, die dem Amt gewachsen wären. Aigner muss nicht die beste aller möglichen Kandidatinnen sein. Doch sie ist die Frau, auf die sich derzeit eine starke demokratische Mehrheit in Deutschland verständigen kann. Nicht im Sinne des kleinsten gemeinsamen Nenners, sondern aus Überzeugung, bisweilen sogar Begeisterung. Und das ist genau das, worauf es jetzt ankommt, wenn das künftige Staatsoberhaupt eine Rolle bei der Überwindung der Gräben unserer Gesellschaft spielen soll.
Die Frau der Stunde
Kurzum: Ilse Aigner ist die Frau der Stunde. Dass sie es wurde, hat freilich auch mit einer befremdlichen Dynamik zu tun, an deren Entstehen Friedrich Merz einen gehörigen Anteil hatte. Die „Würde des Amtes“ ist ein überstrapazierter Begriff und sollte nicht zu hoch gehängt werden. Doch dass die Kandidatinnensuche zuletzt aus dem Ruder gelaufen und zu einem wenig angemessenen Schauspiel verkommen ist, lässt sich kaum leugnen.
Der CDU-Chef hätte sich entweder rechtzeitig und aktiv in die Kandidatinnensuche einbringen, eventuell eine ähnlich starke Kandidatin in Stellung bringen müssen oder eben dem wilden Durcheinandergeplärre vor allem seiner eigenen Leute ein frühzeitiges Ende setzen, indem er sich selbst hinter Aigner gestellt hätte. Damit hätte er sogar seinem Rivalen Markus Söder eins auswischen können.
Hat er nicht. Sondern es leider vermasselt – und sein Ansehen damit weiter ramponiert. Man muss kein Freund des Kanzlers sein, um die Gefahr zu erkennen, die von dieser andauernden Selbstdemontage ausgeht. Am Ende jedenfalls werden es nicht die demokratischen Parteien sein, die von ihr profitieren.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: There is reason to hope that the Democrats might deliver this time
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
There is reason to hope that the Democrats might deliver this time
With a decisive rejection of Trumpism, US voters have given Democrats one more chance — they better not blow it.
In the days since the midterm elections in the United States, many commentators have argued that the “blue tsunami” signalled a popular rejection of US President Donald Trump, but not a new love for Democrats. They are right to warn that if the Democratic Party fails to deliver, it will likely face the same kind of anti-incumbent anger in the next election cycle.
I have personally spilled loads of ink arguing that the Democratic old guard’s embrace of neoliberalism is a huge part of what created the crisis conditions that enabled Trump’s rise to power in the first place, and has severely hampered their ability to stop him over the past decade.
But this election cycle was different in remarkable ways. To put it in plain terms, the Democrats started “sucking less” — not all of them, but a lot of them. And this recent demonstration of “sucking less” is what is presently providing me with at least an ounce of hope that the party might actually manage not to blow this historic opportunity.
How did the Democrats “suck less”? First off, there was a proliferation of progressive economic populist candidates who explicitly took on powerful corporations and positioned themselves clearly as fighters for working-class people. The economic populist insurgency within the Democratic Party gained significant ground in this cycle.
Some might wonder, what took so long? For one, it’s easy to forget that the electoral insurgency within the GOP had an eight-year head start on the insurgency within the Democratic Party — and that head start has been enormously consequential.
In the wake of the 2008 financial meltdown, it was, ironically, conservative anti-establishment energy that first captured populist momentum through the Tea Party. With the help of organisations such as FreedomWorks, that energy was quickly channelled into Republican Party primary contests. By 2014, Tea Party activists had unseated GOP House Speaker Eric Cantor and set the stage for Trump.
Nearly three years after the Tea Party kicked off, Occupy Wall Street was the left’s opening salvo in the populist era. By framing a popular class conflict (the 99% vs the 1%) and naming popular villains (Wall Street and big banks), Occupy dramatically changed the national “common sense” about the evils of runaway inequality.
But the grassroots movement was allergic to the electoral realm. Senator Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential run brought Occupy’s core message onto electoral terrain, but it wasn’t until the 2018 midterms — with the election of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC) and “the Squad” — that the left’s capacity for electoral insurgency caught up with where the right already was in 2009.
Since then, independent progressive organisations such as Justice Democrats, the Working Families Party, Democratic Socialists of America, the Sunrise Movement, and countless local and statewide organisations (for example, PA Stands Up and PA United in my home state of Pennsylvania) have been developing their capacity for recruiting and supporting working-class champions to run for office.
This has been a profound development. Over the course of a decade now, in fits and starts, this groundswell of independent grassroots organising has broken the Democratic Party establishment’s virtual monopoly on candidate recruitment. The 2026 midterms demonstrated a significant increase in capacity to run working-class champions for Congress.
And without diminishing the importance of this long-term organisational investment, it is clear that 2026 also saw an organic proliferation of candidates who ran as champions of the working class. This organic proliferation didn’t happen by chance: It was the result of a profound shift in common-sense notions of what constitutes a winning message.
Over the past decade, a growing chorus of voices in Congress and on the campaign trail has taken up the message Bernie originally popularised, arguing for the same reforms and overhauls, from passing Medicare for All and making housing and childcare affordable, to reining in artificial intelligence (AI) and taxing the rich.
But it took a confluence of events to finally start to break into the mainstream of the Democratic Party in the 2026 cycle.
One key event, unfortunately, was Trump winning a second term. An important casualty of Trump’s second victory was the median Democratic voter’s faith in party leadership. The arc of results and consequences from 2016 to 2024 suddenly cleared the fog, exposing a damning narrative about the party leadership’s negligent qualifications when it came to winning elections.
All that stuff they told us about Bernie being “too far left”, all their wisdom about “electability” was nonsense. The acceleration of the party’s already severe bleed of working-class voters in 2024 and its alarming spread to Black and Latino voters exposed the utter bankruptcy of Democratic leader Chuck Schumer’s lauded affluent suburban swing voter strategy.
The next key event was more uplifting, thankfully. In 2025, in a moment when progressive hopes were at their lowest ebb, suddenly Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani showed up out of nowhere with one of the most captivating and inspiring mayoral campaigns in US history, winning the Democratic nomination for mayor of New York City, and then the election.
Mamdani’s incredible message discipline centred around one word: affordability. With a discredited party leadership, mostly missing in action, Mamdani effectively filled a leadership and vision vacuum. Meanwhile, Bernie and AOC were crisscrossing the country, filling stadiums and energising the base with their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour.
On the eve of the 2026 midterm season, economic populism had become the only thing on offer, the only thing that seemed to credibly have a chance. Suddenly, a whole lot of Democratic candidates and officeholders were talking about affordability and the working class.
One of the few things party leadership did right in 2026 was not derailing this growing populist message and momentum. So while Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries remain unpopular, a movement among the rank-and-file and a new crop of economic populist candidates managed to land a coherent and compelling narrative.
An orthodox Marxist might argue that the explanation for the Democratic Party’s failure over the past decade to connect to working-class voters is straightforward: It doesn’t want to bite the hand that feeds it, in other words, billionaires and powerful corporations that provide millions in campaign contributions.
While big money undoubtedly provides significant incentives, I take a perspective more like sociologist Max Weber’s, where the political class has an important degree of “relative autonomy”. Most political operatives genuinely want to win elections, but their ideas about how to do so are constrained and distorted by the elite cultural milieu in which they are embedded.
It’s taken a full 10 years since Trump’s first victory for economic populism to finally break into the elite bubble of the liberal consultant class, or at least to bypass it and finally approach a critical mass of candidates and officeholders in the Democratic Party who grasp how the world has changed, what hardship and precarity most Americans are experiencing, and how to win working-class voters back.
In his 2016 run for president, Bernie was not “ahead of his time”. He was reading the times perfectly. What he was ahead of was an out-of-touch Democratic Party establishment, whose misreading of the times enabled a dangerous authoritarian pseudo-populist to ascend to power and set America’s downward spiralling course for a decade now.
Tuesday’s historic “blue tsunami” was not only the result of Trump’s failures. The 2026 midterm election cycle also saw the start of the remaking of the Democratic Party to be a party that — as Bernie steadfastly exhorts us — fights for the working class.
Yes, sure, Bernie probably would have won the general election back in 2016 and 2020. But more to the point today: Bernie is winning. That is to say, by finally moving towards an economic populist agenda and a commitment to America’s working class, the Democratic Party might just be starting to find its popular voice.
Tuesday’s results do not mean US voters have sworn loyalty to the Democratic Party. But they have given it another chance. A chance to deliver and improve people’s lives. It would be wise and electorally prudent to deliver… bigly.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Should we move back closer to family before our daughter starts school? | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Annalisa Barbieri
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
My husband and I are in a dilemma about where to live. We are in our early 30s and have an 18-month-old daughter. We are from the East Midlands but moved to the north-west three years ago to buy our first house. Our parents are in the East Midlands, as well as a few friends. My brother, who I am close to, also plans to move back from London in the next few years.
We moved to have a change, and for my husband to have some distance from our parents. He is not that close to his; I am close to my mum, but find the relationship challenging because she can behave erratically. My husband has put in quite a lot of effort to form connections in our new home city, but none seem to have stuck. I get some community from my colleagues and have tried to connect with other mums, but I sometimes long for the deep-rooted ties that come from longer term friends and family.
The choice is between moving back to be closer to parents and some friends, and for geographical familiarity, or staying in the north-west in the hope community will grow as our daughter grows up. At the moment, visits from our parents can feel intense due to them staying over. Moving back might improve relations with them through more regular informal contact, such as popping in or doing an activity together.
We would like to make the decision before our daughter starts school, and would love your advice.
My first thought is that you haven’t been in the north-west for long and could be on the verge of everything clicking into place.
I went to psychotherapist Katherine Walker, who said: “Your daughter starts school in a couple of years. This is often the time when deeper roots start to form and stand the test of time.” She also pointed out that “moving away has simply given you the opportunity to develop new bonds. It doesn’t mean the ones you already had will decline.”
She used the analogy of a relationship garden – there are tall, well-established trees that survive by themselves (family) v flowers (friends) that bring daily joy but need daily watering. “I would encourage you,” said Walker, “to focus on planting new flowers to enjoy over the coming years, and enjoy the trees you already have.”
Moving back will have costs – and not just fiscal ones. We wondered what you thought would change. Could you try to imagine what it would be like – not just your fantasy idea of it, but the reality, with all the issues that made you leave?
Walker also wanted you to think “about the decision in terms of broader opportunity, rather than what seems to be mainly about returning to deeper, older relationships. These are, of course, important, but just one factor in determining where you live. Where is better for career opportunities, schools, local amenities, ways to socialise, etc?”
The thing about moving to a place because of other people is that they may then move, or you may fall out with them, or something else may change. And your brother – another reason for moving back – may not move at all. You and your husband seem to be creating your own story. Give it a bit longer. Imagine moving back and everything being the same as when you left, and how frustrating that would feel.
As the daughter of immigrants, I understand that longing for deeper rooted connections, but the friends you make – people you have chosen – fill the gaps family can often leave.
You may find these podcasts I did on Belonging and Should We Move helpful.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Drone attack on Colombian army base kills three soldiers and wounds 16
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Drone attack on Colombian army base kills three soldiers and wounds 16
Colombian President de la Espriella says those behind the attack in Santa Rosa del Sur will have ‘nowhere to hide’.
A drone attack on a military base in northern Colombia has killed three soldiers and wounded at least 16, the country’s armed forces said.
The Colombian military said in a statement on Saturday that the attack hit a base in Santa Rosa del Sur, a small town in the foothills of the San Lucas mountain range. Authorities have not said who carried out the strike, the latest in a series of attacks on security forces as violence rises across rural parts of the country.
The area is rich in gold mines and has long been disputed by rebel armed groups including the Gulf Clan, the National Liberation Army (ELN) and smaller groups led by former members of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).
Footage shared on social media showed clouds of smoke rising from the base after three explosions, and soldiers taking cover in shelters made of sandbags.
“Those who were behind this attack… will have nowhere to hide,” President Abelardo de la Espriella wrote on X. “Every attack against our soldiers strengthens our resolve to defend Colombia.”
Rising violence
Violence has intensified in several rural areas since de la Espriella, a conservative, took office in August.
The president cancelled peace talks with rebel groups and has taken a confrontational approach, including more air strikes, deploying more troops in some cities and creating joint task forces to defend strategic assets such as a pipeline that runs from the Caribbean coast to central Colombia.
De la Espriella’s government argues that armed groups used ceasefires granted by the previous government to consolidate their grip on rural areas, where they tax local businesses and profit from the drug trade.
Some groups have responded by stepping up attacks on the country’s armed forces.
Last week, a military base in Tolima province was targeted with missiles made from gas canisters. The attack killed four civilians, including a two-month-old baby.
Police in the border city of Cucuta have been attacked several times with remotely activated bombs.
State forces and illegal armed groups carried out 34 attacks with bombs or explosives in Colombia in the four weeks to October 16, a 9 percent increase on last year’s four-week average, according to ACLED, a group that monitors armed conflicts.
A 2016 peace deal with FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters, but smaller groups have since fought over the rebels’ former territory.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.title: Earthquake hits central Japan, injuring more than 20 people
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
Earthquake hits central Japan, injuring more than 20 people
The magnitude 5.7 quake hit Shizuoka prefecture, and authorities warn of possible strong aftershocks in coming days.
More than 20 people have been injured after a strong earthquake shook central Japan, shattering store windows and sending people fleeing buildings, according to local media and authorities.
The magnitude 5.7 quake struck at 1:04am local time on Sunday (16:00 GMT Saturday) at a depth of about 40km (25 miles) in western Shizuoka Prefecture, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.
More than 20 people were injured in the Aichi and Shizuoka prefectures, the Kyodo news agency cited authorities as saying.
A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara, and the prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, and Gifu.
No tsunami warning was issued, Kyodo reported.
The quake was not felt in Tokyo, which is far from the epicentre.
Japanese television showed shattered shop windows and shards of glass scattered across streets. A bookstore was left with mounds of books that had fallen from the shelves.
Some of the injured had fallen on the stairs as they tried to flee, the Associated Press news agency reported.
Aftershock warnings
The meteorological agency warned people to be ready for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially the next two to three days.
“Please be on the lookout for mudslides, falling rocks and the possible effects from rainfall,” agency official Ayataka Ebita told reporters.
He said no apparent change had been detected so far in the Nankai Trough, an underwater ocean trench where two major tectonic plates meet under parts of Japan, where scientists say a megaquake could occur.
Some local train services were suspended, while the Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in affected areas as a precautionary measure.
Trains on the Tokaido Shinkansen line, which connects Tokyo and Osaka, were delayed between Shizuoka and Gifu-Hashima stations after safety checks, rail operator JR Central said.

Trump asks UFC chief Dana White to be White House press secretary
Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO says he will meet with the US president on Monday to discuss the offer.
Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) chief executive Dana White has said he will meet with Donald Trump after the US president offered him the job of White House press secretary.
Speaking at a new conference after a boxing event in London on Saturday, White said he would meet with Trump at the White House on Monday to discuss the president’s offer.
“Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other,” Trump wrote on Truth Social earlier on Saturday. “Dana, please take the job!”
Trump also requested that White “bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country”.
Trump listed and posted pictures of six current and former UFC title holders to join White: Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov from Russia’s Dagestan region; Americans Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier and “Kayla Harris”, likely a reference to Kayla Harrison; and Amanda Nunes, a Brazilian who became a US citizen last year.
“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left,” Trump wrote.
The White House press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia’s tenure ended last month after just five days.
Zacharia succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down from the role at the end of August.
White and Trump first worked together in the early 2000s, but they grew closer since the UFC chief publicly backed Trump’s presidential campaign in 2016.
In recent years, Trump has attended several UFC events, and in June, the White House hosted a night of UFC fights as part of celebrations marking the 250th anniversary of US independence.
The White House press office already has a former UFC spokesperson among its ranks: Director of Communications Steven Cheung, who worked for White’s organisation from 2013 to 2016.
Cheung shared the president’s message on X and said, “Hell yeah! Do it, @DanaWhite! It’ll just be like old times!”

https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.title: Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.text:
For people in the Russian industrial city of Samara on the banks of the Volga, the first they knew of the Ukrainian attack were detonations that sent a column of smoke into the air.
If the Kremlin was vague about the target, video footage on social media soon made it clear what had been hit in the early hours of 15 August: the Progress Rocket and Space Centre, manufacturer of Russia’s Soyuz-2 rockets.
Two Flamingo missiles had slammed into a pair of buildings, including a facility known as 106A, a “clean room” where motherboards for the Soyuz launch systems were assembled.
In the midst of other Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries and industry, the Samara attack stood out, providing evidence of a spreading war, the geographical impact of which – already felt across Europe via hybrid attacks, and assaults on civilian shipping in the Black Sea – has crept into the domain of space.
In a conflict that is redefining warfare through the heavy use of drones and battlefield sensors, access to space and the satellites that power those systems – as well as the ability to disrupt enemy operations there – has become ever more critical.
The attack on Samara was a case in point, hitting the rockets that deliver Russia’s new Rassvet satellite system, which is being rapidly deployed as a replacement for Elon Musk’s Starlink, from which Russia was shut out earlier this year.
In addition, Ukraine has attacked other sites belonging to Roscosmos this year, including Korolyov, a large complex north of Moscow, and a Ukrainian-built radio telescope captured by Russia in Crimea.
Russia’s attempts to rapidly deploy its Rassvet network are not the only challenge from space that Ukraine faces. Moscow has also used Oreshnik ballistic missiles on at least three occasions – a system that launches into near space, then deploys multiple independently targetable warheads initially designed for nuclear weapons.
All of this has prompted Kyiv to intensify efforts to diversify its own access to space-based systems away from the US and Starlink, which was controversially choked in recent weeks, and to develop new space countermeasures against threats such as the Oreshnik.
Ukraine has conducted at least three tests of near-space interceptions as it has sought to launch its own sovereign satellites, joining a rapidly expanding number of countries working towards a foothold in space.
That became a reality last month when Ukraine and Denmark’s GomSpace announced they had successfully launched the Obria Nano, the first test satellite for a future independent Ukrainian communications network, reportedly envisaging about 245 satellites.
‘Everyone wants their own version of Starlink’
The increasing incursion of the Ukraine conflict into space, say experts, is only the latest evidence of the rapid militarisation of a domain the treaties for which remain ill defined, outdated and difficult to enforce.
In September the US air force secretary, Troy Meink, admitted for the first time that Washington had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons” amid reports that Russia had regularly flown its satellites close to US and other countries’ assets in space.
As if to underline that point, a few weeks later a Russian satellite, Kosmos 2612, was observed aggressively manoeuvring towards a commercial radar satellite operated by the Finnish group Iceye that provides three-dimensional terrain imaging to the Ukrainian military, in what experts described as an act of deliberate harassment.
“[Space warfare] has been talked about as the future,” says Dr Elena Grossfeld, an expert on space and security at the Swedish Defence University. “But we’re already in that future.”
For Russia, Grossfeld argues, space has become essential to military success, with Moscow treating offensive operations there as a precursor to broader conflict in a new reality where war is inseparable from satellite-based intelligence and targeting.
“This started before the war in Ukraine,” Grossfield said. “The US Space Force [then second in command, Gen David Thompson] said in 2021 that the US was seeing daily attacks [by Russia and China] on US satellites.
“They are not necessarily kinetic [attacks], but now with the war and with everyone’s dependency on space for intelligence and communications, it has become front and centre.”
While Grossfield said Russia’s intention in the recent “bullying” of the Iceye satellite was not clear, one possibility was to force it to use fuel to change course and in doing so shorten its lifespan.
That is not the only tactic that has been seen. Russia has also used signal jamming, laser-dazzling of satellites, and placed “inspector” spy satellites near foreign space assets.
Complicating what is happening in space, experts say, is that treaties on governance in space, and deployment of weapons, have in recent years been overtaken.
Victoria Samson, the head of the space security and stability programme at the Secure World Foundation, which advocates for space safety and sustainability, noted a rapid increase in the number of countries operating in space, in tandem with the expansion of commercial activities by companies such as Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin.
But while many countries have opted to use SpaceX for its satellite launches, Musk’s recent actions towards Ukraine, cutting Starlink data speeds, have forced a rapid rethink of whether to rely on unreliable and sometimes ideologically led commercial ventures.
“The big shift in the past decade,” said Samson, “has been towards commercial space operations and that has been an issue in the current conflict [in Ukraine].”
Like Grossfeld, Samson sees frictions in space becoming more overt. “It’s all part of strategic competition,” she said, describing the recent Russian satellite-bullying incident. She added that with more escalation, there had been “more openness on the US side to talk about what they are doing [in relation to weapons in space] while Russia and China are working on a lot of the same stuff.
“Then there is the issue of space being used in an active military conflict. We have already seen Russia jamming GPS, which has resulted in aviation being disrupted over the Baltics. But it has been particularly visible in the issue of Starlink and in pauses by the US to sharing satellite intelligence with Ukraine [that warns] of incoming ballistic missiles.”
If there has been a consequence of Musk’s and the Trump administration’s unreliability, Samson believes, it has been to push countries to seek alternatives. “Like the Russians with [the] Rassvet network, everyone now wants their own versions of Starlink, including the Europeans.”
For Ukraine, said Fedir Venislavskyi, the head of the state security subcommittee of its parliamentary defence committee, that meant a “sovereign” Ukrainian presence in space, now achieved via the Obria Nano satellite.
“Since the war the space domain has been crucial for Ukrainian forces and that has been underlined by recent events – whether at the instigation of the US government or from SpaceX – where we saw communications drop and jeopardise our military’s command-and-control systems.
“Now we need to raise it to another level, not least because the enemy is already threatening Ukrainian territory from international space via Oreshnik missiles. It’s essential we’re not shortsighted about this risk.”
With Russian launch sites now beyond the range of Ukraine’s longest-range missiles, Ukraine has instead conducted three tests on exo-atmospheric kill systems to intercept launches in near space, including launches of weapons piggybacked on very high-flying aircraft.
“It is a priority,” said Venislavskyi. “We’ve already demonstrated launches of exo-atmospheric systems and we are working to see if we can get that in production.” However, he admitted, given the huge demands of the war, funding would be a significant issue.
In the meantime, the new race for space continues.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/8.text:
US launches task force to disrupt Iran’s land-based supply routes
The operation is to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport weapons and other materials, US Central Command says.
The United States military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) has announced a plan to block Iran’s land-based supply routes, expanding its months-long naval blockade of Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz.
CENTCOM, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced on Saturday that it had established a new task force “to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials”.
Task Force Iron Gate will reinforce “the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea”, CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.
Based in Tampa, Florida, the task force will coordinate with other US government agencies “on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea”, CENTCOM said.
Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defence secretary for the Middle East, told Al Jazeera the task force’s role will be to find out where “weapons systems are coming in, how they could potentially be cut off”, and how “Iran is transporting its energy”.
He added that if US President Donald Trump orders an escalation to the war, it will likely be attacks on this “series of targets”.
“Unlike Operation Epic Fury, which primarily focuses on military targets, I think these targets will be focused on economic and infrastructure targets, as part of this comprehensive plan to cut the regime off from its ability to fight and ability to fund itself,” Mulroy told Al Jazeera.
CENTCOM separately said on Saturday that it had disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman as part of its blockade of Iranian ports.
A US “military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, disabling the ship after CENTCOM forces directed the crew to abandon targeted spaces”, it said in a statement.
“Enforcement actions since July have resulted in U.S. forces redirecting 147 commercial vessels that complied”, and disabling “five merchant ships that refused to comply”, it added.
Explosions reported
On Saturday, Iran’s official news agency IRNA reported the sound of two explosions on Qeshm Island, located in the Strait of Hormuz.
IRNA also reported the sound of “several explosions” in the cities of Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas.
Trump confirmed new strikes on Qeshm Island a day earlier, but downplayed them as “minor”. He added that Tehran still wants a deal as Qatari-mediated talks continue.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy reported that two oil tankers struck mines near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday.
Iranian state television, citing the navy, said the tankers had passed through an “unsafe” part of the strait with their navigation systems off. They “suffered severe damage and stopped after hitting sea mines”.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Did the Bay Area just save its transit system from the brink of certain death?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Isabeau Doucet in San Francisco
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Voters in the San Francisco Bay Area overwhelmingly approved two transit measures this week that advocates hope will save the region’s financially distressed public transit agencies from a potential death spiral that could have had massive repercussions for the area’s residents and its economy.
The Regional Transit Measure (RTM), a 0.5% sales tax across four Bay Area counties and a 1% sales tax in San Francisco, will generate approximately $1bn annually to fund the region’s four largest transit operators. It received a strong 62.2% support across all five counties that voted on the measure, winning with a landslide of 78.6% in San Francisco.
In San Francisco, 73.6% of voters also approved a parcel tax to fund Muni, the first publicly owned and operated transit agency in a major US city.
Had the measures not passed, Bay Area Rapid Transit (Bart) would be forced to close as many as 15 stations as soon as early next year, dramatically reducing frequency of service and increasing the cost of rides and parking. Caltrain, a commuter rail that connects San Francisco with the South Bay region, would have closed 10 stations and ended weekend service. And Muni, the city of San Francisco’s main transit system, would have been forced to reduce a third of its service, eliminate 20 bus lines and suspend its iconic streetcars and cable cars. All agencies would have had to end evening services.
Less frequent service and fewer stations would have meant less fare revenue, fewer commuters and a downward cascade of financial austerity, creating a transit doom spiral that would have left Bay Area residents without reliable, affordable ways to get around the sprawling metropolis. The potential impacts were enormous in a region formed around a large body of water, where the freeways and bridges are notoriously jammed with traffic.
A recent report authored by Laura Tolkoff, transportation policy director for the San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association, estimated traffic delays on the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge, which sees roughly 3.5m crossings a month, and other chokepoints around the region would have more than doubled during peak hours.
Bay Area transit agencies were left uniquely exposed to the low ridership during the pandemic given their dependence on fares for operating revenue and the region’s nation-leading shift to remote and hybrid work. As pandemic relief funds were set to expire and the fiscal cliff came into view, transit advocates shifted gears into action.
In 2023, Connect Bay Area organizer Lian Chang got involved with the fight to save public transit when she made coffins and replicas of local trains and buses out of cardboard for a mock funeral procession in front of city hall. Those cardboard replicas have done considerable mileage since, some needing new paint jobs as they circulated from press conferences to campaign events and rallies, Chang said.
She had no experience campaigning then, but has since helped rally volunteers in painting many banker boxes into buses and trains to carry the signatures that got the measures on the ballot, adding a playful and visually striking element to the campaign.
The biggest challenge, Chang found, was finding ways to get transit riders to self-identify and organize themselves into a constituency. To create a sense of pride among transit riders, who tend to be immigrants, children, seniors and lower-income people, she worked with local designers to make buttons to hand out on specific bus lines slated for cuts. This also helped recruit more volunteer signature-gatherers.
In the end, thousands of volunteers collected 77,000 of the 305,000 signatures that qualified the measure for the ballot, which, according to the Connect Bay Area campaign, is the highest number in recent memory. “We don’t know of any larger signature-gathering mobilization in the Bay Area,” said Chang.
The measures could still face legal challenges from anti-tax groups, as past transit initatives have faced, tying up the funds in escrow accounts for years.
“The Public Transit Revenue Measure District is prepared to vigorously defend the will of the voters and the validity of the measure,” said Rebecca Long of the Metropolitan Transportation Commission, the agency in charge of administering the RTM funds.
Jeff Cretan, spokesperson for Connect Bay Area, the coalition that backed the two initiatives, wants to keep the momentum high so voters aren’t facing another transit catastrophe when the measures expire in about 15 years.
“This is an opportunity for us to go to the state and say, we need to change how we do this, not just here, but in other parts of the state,” said Cretan.
Compared with other world-class regions in the United States and beyond, California has historically underinvested in the public transit of its urban centers, despite priding itself on robust climate policies.
A 2022 report from the California Air Resources Board said for the state to meet its own climate goals, existing public transit networks would need to double their capacity and service frequency by 2030. Bart, AC Transit, Caltrain and Muni make up 30% of the state’s transit ridership. Yet, only 5% of Bart’s operating revenue comes from the state.
Tuesday’s election also brought a wave of new leadership to the state. Transit advocates already see an ally in state senator Scott Wiener, who co-authored the transit measures and won his bid to succeed Nancy Pelosi in Congress.
But they are also hopeful governor-elect Xavier Becerra will prioritize public transit after seeing strong support from Bay Area voters, despite not making it a central issue of his gubernatorial campaign. (Becerra’s campaign did not return the Guardian’s request for comment.)
“I hope that Governor Becerra and elected representatives take note of the messages voters just sent: transit is not controversial – it’s essential and it’s incredibly popular,” said Tolkoff.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Hilal Saki
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Paraguay's pro-Israel former president taken into custody over banking crisis
Paraguayan prosecutors charged pro-Israel ex-president Santiago Pena and took him into custody Saturday over a banking crisis that saw millions cut off from their money and sparked major protests.
Pena, Paraguay's youngest-ever president, was removed from office by the Senate on Friday, just three days after the collapse of a leading bank with which he had business links.
An indictment against Pena states that "between 2023 and 2026, UENO BANK S.A. allegedly received deposits and loans from public and pension entities" and that it "was also allegedly granting loans to companies linked to the bank's economic group in an irregular manner."
The 47-year-old economist owned shares in Ueno Holding, the controlling company of the bank, until he sold them last year.
Pena maintained close relations with Israel, and in 2024, reopened his country’s embassy in the occupied Jerusalem, making it the sixth country at the time to make the move.
Pena's removal is a further blow for US President Donald Trump's network of allies in South America.
Trump's favourite for Brazilian president, Flavio Bolsonaro, was defeated by left-wing incumbent Lula Inacio Lula da Silva last month.
Report by AFP

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Bad blood? Knicks defend Taylor Swift after players accuse her of being ‘fake fan’
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Taylor Swift’s love story with the New York Knicks caught an unexpected stray after two players from last season’s NBA champions accused the singer of being a fair-weather fan.
The Knicks released a statement on Friday defending Swift after Tyler Kolek and Miles McBride questioned whether the pop superstar was a genuine supporter of the team.
The reserve guards were asked during an NBA 2K livestream on Thursday to name the least authentic celebrity fan they had seen courtside at an NBA game.
“At the Knicks games, I would say it’s very performative because like they just want to be seen at the game,” Kolek said. “They’re not necessarily fans. Probably Taylor Swift.”
McBride agreed with the assessment, while Kolek acknowledged that his comments could provoke a backlash from Swift’s supporters.
“I’m going to get some hate from the Swifties,” Kolek said. “I guess she’s got a lot going on, so she can’t come all the time, but ... it’s a little performative.”
McBride identified actor Ben Stiller and comedian Tracy Morgan as more committed Knicks supporters, describing both as “solid” fans.
The Knicks found themselves in the delicate position of defending one of their most famous fans against their own players, moving quickly on Friday to head off any bad blood with Swift.
“Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization,” a team spokesperson said.
Swift, 36, has attended several high-profile Knicks games, including Game 4 of this year’s NBA finals, when she sat courtside alongside actor Mariska Hargitay and musicians Alana and Este Haim. Wearing a royal blue “Stevie Knicks” T-shirt with orange lettering that quickly went viral and inspired a wave of copycat merchandise, she watched OG Anunoby score a last-second tip-in to secure a famous New York victory.
She also attended Game 3 of the Eastern Conference finals in Cleveland with her husband, Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce, a longtime Cleveland sports fan.
Swift knows Madison Square Garden all too well, having first performed there as a 13-year-old in 2003 during a Knicks half-time talent contest. She and Kelce married at the arena in July.
Kolek and McBride are both eligible for contract extensions, although the Knicks said in October they were not holding extension talks with players. The team hold a $2.5m option on Kolek for the 2026-27 season.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: ‘We’re still cool’: Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd confirm split and reject WNBA draft speculation
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd have confirmed they ended their romantic relationship more than a year ago, with the Dallas Wings star backcourt tandem rejecting suggestions that their relationship influenced the team’s decision to select Fudd with the No 1 pick in this year’s WNBA draft.
The former University of Connecticut teammates announced their breakup on Friday’s episode of Fudd’s podcast, and asked fans to stop sending hostile messages to them and their families.
“Before we continue with anything else, Paige and I have something that we want to share with everyone,” Fudd said. “We are no longer together. I don’t know how else to say that.”
Bueckers confirmed the split, saying the two had been separated for more than a year, well before Fudd joined her in Dallas in April.
“We were not together before she got drafted,” Bueckers said. “So all of those narratives can go to bed. She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She’s an amazing human, amazing basketball player. And we’re still friends. We’re still cool.”
Fudd’s selection in April had prompted considerable attention to her relationship with Bueckers, who was herself the first overall pick by Dallas in 2025. The pair became the first college teammates to go No 1 in consecutive WNBA drafts since fellow UConn standouts Tina Charles and Maya Moore in 2010 and 2011.
Fudd, an Associated Press All-American and one of the country’s top outside shooters, helped UConn win the national championship in 2025 before being selected first overall in a draft without a clear consensus top prospect. She quickly made her mark in Dallas, hitting six three-pointers against the New York Liberty in May to break the franchise’s rookie single-game record previously held by Bueckers.
The attention surrounding Fudd’s arrival in Dallas reflected a broader trend in the WNBA, where players’ romantic relationships have become subjects of intense social media speculation, at times overshadowing their accomplishments on the court.
At the Wings’ media day in April, Bueckers addressed questions about their relationship and denied having any influence over Dallas’s draft decision.
“Quite frankly, I believe me and Azzi’s personal relationship is nobody’s business but our own, and what we choose to share is completely up to us,” she said.
“Azzi Fudd was a No 1 draft pick because she earned it, and it had nothing to do with me and everything to do with who she is as a human being, who she is a basketball player, her resilience, her strength and her career-best year at UConn,” Bueckers added. “She should be celebrated as such.”
The pair first met at a USA Basketball camp in 2017 and played together for four seasons at UConn, helping the Huskies end their nine-year NCAA title drought in 2025. Their relationship became public in July of that year, when Bueckers referred to Fudd as her girlfriend during an interview with the TikTok show WAG Talk.
On Friday, Bueckers said the speculation surrounding their relationship had led to negative messages directed at both players and people close to them.
“We’ve seen a lot of negativity. We’ve seen a lot of hate,” she said. “We’ve had stuff sent to us. We’ve had stuff sent to our family, our friends.”
“I hate that we have to address this, but just to control the narrative, there’s been some crazy things said about us,” she added. “Sometimes in life, there’s just seasons. And sometimes in life, two people are just at different points of their life.”
Bueckers said their separation had not affected their ability to play together, noting that they had already spent an entire season as teammates after breaking up.
“We’re the utmost professional,” she said. “We care about basketball and we’re still friends.”
Dallas finished the regular season with a franchise-record 27 wins, a 17-game improvement from the previous year, and reached the playoffs for the first time since 2023. They gave the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries a first-round scare, pushing the series to a deciding third game.
Bueckers earned her second consecutive All-Star selection, while Fudd averaged 13.1 points in 30 games as a rookie and shot 39.7% from three-point range. Fudd’s season ended prematurely because of a right knee injury that required surgery.
Bueckers said the two would continue to support each other as friends and teammates.
“We still support each other. We are still going to be great friends. We are going to be great teammates. We are going to be professionals,” she said. “At the end of the day, we still care about each other and want the best for each other.”

https://gothamist.com/news/man-accused-o.title: Man accused of pushing ex-girlfriend and baby from Bronx balcony pleads not guilty
https://gothamist.com/news/man-accused-o.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/man-accused-o.text:
Domestic violence survivors and advocates wearing purple filled a row of seats in a Bronx courtroom Wednesday for the arraignment of a man accused of pushing his ex-girlfriend and their 8-month-old daughter off a 15th-floor apartment, killing the woman.
Police found Nathaly Ramirez, 23, and her baby on the ground outside their Olinville Avenue apartment on Oct. 6, according to the Bronx district attorney’s office. Ramirez died from her injuries. The baby suffered critical injuries and is still in the hospital.
Angel Carrasco, 31, pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to second-degree murder, first-degree attempted murder and other charges. When he entered his plea, several women wearing purple socks, purple sweatshirts and T-shirts that said “Stop Domestic Violence” and “Domestic Violence Survivor” in purple lettering murmured and sighed. Purple is associated with domestic violence awareness.
Prosecutors did not share additional details in court about what may have prompted the pushing. In a statement, District Attorney Darcel Clark said the shoving had “outraged the city.”
“His callous disregard for life has left a young mother dead and his own daughter forever altered because of his heinous actions,” she said. “He now faces justice for the heartbreaking loss of Nathaly Ramirez.”
Several of Ramirez’s loved ones sat quietly in the back of the courtroom and did not speak with reporters after the arraignment. Carrasco’s defense attorney, Nathan Karnovsky with Bronx Defenders, also declined to comment outside the courtroom.
Carrasco is not expected back in court until mid-February. Justice Alvin Yearwood told members of the public in the courtroom that it would take time for the case to wind its way through the system, in order to protect Carrasco’s constitutional rights.
“I ask you to be patient and to understand that we’re working on this,” he said.
Carrasco made his first court appearance virtually from a hospital bed in a psychiatric ward. In court on Wednesday, his attorneys did not request additional psychiatric testing.

https://gothamist.com/news/rain-in-nyc-a.title: Rain in NYC and NJ will end weeks-long stretch of beautiful weather
https://gothamist.com/news/rain-in-nyc-a.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/rain-in-nyc-a.text:
It’s about to rain on New York City’s good weather parade.
Nearly three weeks of beautiful, clear-skied, mild weather days are coming to an end as a weather system moving through the area Thursday and Friday will bring cloudy skies and rainfall, according to the National Weather Service.
Local weather account New York Metro Weather, gives a daily weather vibes rating on X from 0 to 10. The account's been doling out 8s, 9,s and 10s from Oct. 19 through Nov. 3, with Wednesday receiving a 7 — an indication of the vibe shift to come.
John Homenuk, who runs the account, said that’s due to a persistent high pressure system that’s hung out over the area which no storm has yet been able to push away.
“When you have a stretch like this, it really is enjoyable,” he said. “It's not just one or two days and you have to kinda force yourself outside to go do something, you know? You have some options and the forecast is good for a while. So it's really nice, and you get to spend quite a bit of time outside. ”
Conditions are expected to stay dry through Wednesday with temperatures approaching 70 degrees in some parts of the city, but the National Weather Service predicts cloudy skies by the evening. A low pressure weather system approaching the area will likely bring showers in the first half of Thursday, which will be mostly cloudy with a high near 74, according to the National Weather Service.
Homenuk said he doesn’t expect “anything crazy” but the system will bring more humidity to the area and slightly cooler temperatures this weekend.
Things get a little more bleak Friday, with showers and possible thunderstorms after 1 p.m., and a high near 70 degrees, according to the NWS. The total rainfall will likely be under half an inch, which helps the area get closer to normal for the season after getting just half the normal amount of rain for October, NWS meteorologist John Murray said.
“ It could potentially be some heavy rain at times, it is possible Friday and into Friday night,” he said. “Could have some minor flooding here and there especially in your poor drainage, low-lying areas.”
But nothing lasts forever, even cold November rain. Conditions will be drier through Saturday and Sunday, though the chances of rain won’t be completely gone, and temperatures will remain unseasonably warm throughout the weekend, Murray said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Pessoas negras representam quase 85% dos atendidos em audiências de custódia no DF
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Ana Gonçalves
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Pessoas negras representam 84,78% das pessoas entrevistadas pela Defensoria Pública do Distrito Federal (DPDF) nas audiências de custódia realizadas no primeiro semestre de 2026. O levantamento também aponta um perfil marcado pela baixa escolaridade, pela informalidade no trabalho e pela vulnerabilidade econômica. Para o coordenador do Núcleo de Assistência Jurídica das Audiências de Custódia e da Tutela Coletiva dos Presos Provisórios (NAJCust), defensor público Alexandre Fernandes Silva, os números evidenciam a seletividade racial e social do sistema de Justiça criminal.
“A realidade do Distrito Federal comprova empiricamente o que os estudos apontam. Mais de 80% das pessoas que passam por audiência de custódia no DF são pretas ou pardas. Isso revela que o Distrito Federal é uma base empírica dessa seletividade racial tão característica do nosso sistema de Justiça”, afirma.
O 5º Relatório das Audiências de Custódia reúne informações de 2.365 entrevistas prévias realizadas com pessoas presas em flagrante e apresentadas à Justiça entre janeiro e junho de 2026. Segundo a Defensoria, o núcleo atua na defesa de aproximadamente 60% a 70% das pessoas presas em flagrante no Distrito Federal.
O levantamento foi produzido a partir de uma pesquisa por amostragem com pessoas atendidas pela Defensoria. Portanto, os dados não representam a totalidade das prisões realizadas no DF, mas permitem observar características sociais de uma parcela expressiva da população que chega às audiências de custódia.
Baixa escolaridade e trabalho informal marcam perfil
Além da desigualdade racial, o relatório aponta dificuldades de acesso à educação e ao mercado formal de trabalho. Quase metade das pessoas entrevistadas (48,84%) não concluiu o ensino fundamental. Outros 20,68% não terminaram o ensino médio.
Na situação ocupacional, o levantamento indica que a maior parte das pessoas não tinha carteira assinada. O gráfico do relatório aponta 87,26% nessa condição. A renda também revela vulnerabilidade: a faixa mais frequente, correspondente a 28,29% dos entrevistados, era de R$ 1.500 a R$ 2 mil.
Para Alexandre Fernandes Silva, esses indicadores ajudam a compreender como a atuação do sistema de segurança pública alcança de maneira desigual diferentes grupos sociais. Segundo o defensor, o policiamento ostensivo concentra sua atuação em ocorrências nas ruas, onde pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade ficam mais expostas à abordagem e à prisão em flagrante.
O coordenador chama atenção para o contraste com crimes que exigem investigações mais complexas. Na avaliação dele, a concentração de prisões em flagrante por ocorrências de rua não significa que os crimes cometidos por pessoas de maior renda estejam ausentes do sistema penal. A diferença está também na forma como essas ocorrências são identificadas e investigadas.
“Esse policiamento, por outro lado, acaba ocultando, com uma taxa de prisão alta, os crimes que têm maior complexidade, que demandam mais investigação e que, não raras vezes, são cometidos por pessoas com uma renda muito maior”, afirma.
Para o defensor, as audiências de custódia não oferecem, portanto, um retrato de todas as formas de criminalidade, mas de uma parcela dos casos alcançados pela atuação policial e encaminhados à Justiça. Essa distinção é importante para compreender por que pessoas negras e de baixa renda aparecem de forma tão expressiva no levantamento.
Crimes patrimoniais e tráfico concentram imputações
Entre as imputações registradas nas entrevistas, os crimes contra o patrimônio sem violência aparecem em primeiro lugar, com 39,47%. Em seguida está o tráfico de drogas, que corresponde a 28,10% dos registros. Os crimes contra o patrimônio com violência representam outros 11,51%.
Os percentuais se referem às acusações atribuídas às pessoas no momento da prisão e não significam condenações. O perfil também deve ser compreendido dentro do recorte das pessoas apresentadas às audiências de custódia, etapa que recebe casos de prisão em flagrante e de cumprimento de mandados de prisão.
Ceilândia aparece como a região administrativa com maior participação nos registros, com 13,78%, seguida pelo Plano Piloto, com 8,50%, e Taguatinga, com 8,03%. Os números indicam a distribuição das ocorrências registradas no levantamento, não taxas de criminalidade proporcionais à população de cada região.
Defensoria registra relatos de violência policial
Outro dado que chama a atenção no relatório é o de que 13,53% das pessoas entrevistadas relataram ter sofrido violência policial. Para Alexandre, embora o percentual possa parecer pequeno à primeira vista, ele representa uma dimensão relevante do problema.
“Uma a cada dez pessoas sofreu violência policial alegadamente na audiência de custódia”, afirma o defensor.
A audiência de custódia é uma etapa em que a pessoa presa é apresentada a uma autoridade judicial, que deve avaliar a legalidade da prisão, a necessidade de manutenção da custódia e possíveis ocorrências de violência ou maus-tratos durante a abordagem.
Quando há relatos de abuso, a Defensoria encaminha as informações aos órgãos responsáveis pelo controle da atividade policial. A depender da corporação envolvida, os casos podem ser enviados às respectivas corregedorias e ao Ministério Público, responsável pelo controle externo da atividade policial.
Ao avaliar o conjunto dos dados, o coordenador afirma que a seletividade é uma característica central do sistema de Justiça criminal. Para ele, o perfil racial e econômico das pessoas que chegam às audiências de custódia demonstra como a estrutura penal atinge de maneira mais intensa grupos que já enfrentam desigualdades sociais.
“A realidade do Distrito Federal exemplifica essa seletividade, que acaba perpetuando as hierarquias e as desigualdades existentes no país em geral e no Distrito Federal em específico”, conclui.
