https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.title: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.author: Ryan Devereaux
https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.text:
Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors.
“People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said.
Fifteen days later, her fears were realized.
ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors.
The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said.
The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted.
“The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.”
Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites.
“Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.”
Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing.
In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.”
The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio, that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental.)
Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.”
Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary.
“When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.”
U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.”
James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field.
While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.
Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.”
“Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30 calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the remains.”
In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall construction in the borderlands.
Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS has invoked its powers 66 times, with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two administrations.
When DHS uses this authority, it typically waives dozens of laws at a time. That was the case in 2019 when the department set its sights on Organ Pipe. A waiver issued by then-acting Secretary Kevin K. McAleenan set aside more than 40 of the nation’s most stringent environmental and cultural resource protection laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act and others. Also on that list was the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, the landmark 1990 law that acknowledged the nation’s long history of desecrating Native American burials and required that ancestral remains and cultural objects be returned to tribes.
In an internal 2019 report obtained by The Washington Post, park service officials identified nearly two dozen archaeological sites in Organ Pipe as at risk of damage or total destruction by government contractors.
Of particular significance is a desert oasis known as Quitobaquito Springs. Less than 200 feet from the international border, the springs provide one of the only reliable sources of groundwater and shade for miles around, and they were a longtime gathering place, grazing site and home for O’odham families.
“Archaeological evidence of human presence at Quitobaquito extends back thousands of years, at least to Archaic times,” the survey found, adding that the springs represent the “only known Hia C-ed O’odham village site in the United States.”
A park service report in 2024 noted that a cemetery at Quitobaquito holds the remains of at least two families, including Eiler’s, and 34 graves. Throughout the region, remains of 5,500 ancestors that were displaced have been made available for return to the Tohono O’odham Nation, according to ProPublica’s NAGPRA database.
“This sort of incident has happened numerous times across our homeland, and it’s always alarming to hear about a case from an O’odham point of view,” said David Martínez, a professor of American Indian and transborder studies at the University of Arizona and a member of the Hia-Ced O’odham and Akimel O’odham tribes, as well as the Gila River Indian Community.
“Those remains shouldn’t have been disturbed in the first place,” he said. “While there are protocols existing today to properly care for these remains, ultimately, whatever either the government or the corporate world is pursuing to build, we know that at some juncture that construction will continue, and it always leaves us feeling, I think, a little hollow.”
Today, Quitobaquito lies in the shadow of the border wall erected during Trump’s first term. Its construction required detonating explosives in the national monument, blasting apart an area called Monument Hill and outraging tribal leaders. According to Eiler, the remains recovered in September were not found at the springs, though government work crews are working in close proximity to the site.
This year, DHS hired Sundt Construction, an Arizona-based company, to build a second wall in the monument. The $443 million contract was finalized in May. (Sundt directed questions concerning the discovery of human remains on its job site to CBP.)
According to CBP, the 2019 waiver for Organ Pipe is still in effect, years after completion of the project that prompted it. A second waiver, exempting DHS from many of the same laws and applying to the national monument as well as a wildlife refuge to the west, was issued by Homeland Security’s then-Secretary Kristi Noem last year.
“Unfortunately, there is no end date to the effectiveness of the waivers,” said Dinah Bear, a Tucson-based lawyer who served for 25 years as a senior attorney in the White House’s Council on Environmental Quality under both Democratic and Republican administrations. What’s more, she added, “there’s nothing in the statutory language that ties the waivers to a particular project.”
The Department of Homeland Security’s waiver powers have been central to a high-profile legal fight over the department’s efforts to build a border wall through Big Bend National Park in West Texas, with a federal judge overseeing the case recently ordering a temporary halt to the project.
Borderlands advocates in Arizona are hoping for similar interventions. In Congress, Grijalva is preparing legislation to void existing waivers that have allowed DHS to disregard laws designed to protect tribal sovereignty, sacred sites and environmentally sensitive lands.
In the meantime, construction on the border continues. For Eiler, it’s not just the destruction in Organ Pipe that’s troubling. She sees the disturbance of tribal graves resulting from wall construction as reflective of a wider pattern of destruction across the border.
“It’s sad because it’s not only happening down there,” she said. “It’s happening all over the United States, and nobody’s saying much about it.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/ameri.title: After ProPublica Investigation, House Democrats Demand Answers on U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
https://www.propublica.org/article/ameri.author: Nicole Foy
https://www.propublica.org/article/ameri.text:
What Happened: Citing ProPublica’s recent investigation, House Democrats are again asking the Trump administration to explain why hundreds of U.S. citizens have been held by immigration agents and how the government verifies citizenship during immigration operations.
In an October letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, California Rep. Lou Correa and 39 other legislators demanded the administration share the number of citizens that immigration agents have detained and how the government is tracking such encounters. They also asked for more information about how agents are trained to verify citizenship and legal status.
Why It Matters: ProPublica counted more than 500 Americans detained by immigration agents — almost certainly an undercount since the government is not transparently tracking the cases.
Experts told us the cases collectively show federal agents running roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens. We found more than 100 Americans who were questioned about their citizenship, 63 Americans detained while recording, 36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family and roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children.
What They Said: “We remain concerned that the Department’s actions are violating American citizens’ constitutional rights to due process, equal protection, and freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, and request transparency regarding the Department’s actions,” the representatives wrote in their letter to DHS.
DHS has long insisted it is not arresting U.S. citizens, and it defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.”
“These members of Congress have shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who’ve broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than they ever have for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray, and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America,” a spokesperson wrote to ProPublica.
Background: Democrats have been pushing the second Trump administration for more details about how immigration agents are interacting with U.S. citizens since early 2025. Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens in response to our earlier reporting that found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents.
Last month, Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, a New Mexico Democrat, introduced a bill, Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act, that would make it easier for citizens to sue immigration agents for wrongful arrests.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Peggy Flanagan Makes Her Closing Argument Against Trump’s “Cruelty and Chaos” in the Minnesota Senate Race
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Joan Walsh
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Peggy Flanagan Makes Her Closing Argument Against Trump’s “Cruelty and Chaos” in the Minnesota Senate Race
Flanagan opponent Michele Tafoya’s extreme and erratic stands on Operation Metro Surge may well cost her the Senate seat.
Minnesota GOP Senate candidate Michele Tafoya has had nearly a year to take a solid stand on Donald Trump’s “Operation Metro Surge,” which sent ICE and other federal agents into her state to seize immigrants, snatch children from parents, and murder two Minneapolis citizens, poet and mother Renée Good and nurse Alex Pretti. The former NFL sideline reporter has failed to do so, and now it’s Minnesota’s turn to weigh in on Tafoya. Her extreme and erratic stands on Metro Surge may well cost her the Senate race, against consistent surge critic Democratic Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan.
Just to recap: As the siege began in December, Tafoya defended it on her podcast. “Look, Immigration and Customs Enforcement is a law enforcement group and they are trying to enforce the law and they’re trying to do it in cities that have major issues. They’ve determined that Minneapolis is one such city.” In her campaign rollout video, she included glowing footage of ICE operations. Maybe most outrageously, she blamed Good for her own murder.
Related Article
“I’m sure you guys are seeing on the Internet this car that was driving right toward an agent,” she said the day Good died, on The Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show. “You can’t run people over with a car. The car is a deadly weapon.” When multiple forensic examinations showed decisively that Good was driving her car away from Customs and Border Patrol agent Jonathan Ross, Tafoya shifted blame to Minnesota Democrats she claimed were leading people like Good, and later Pretti, to interfere with Metro Surge.
“They have created an environment where people think, ‘Oh my gosh, I have to go resist,’” she told The Will Cain Show. “‘I can’t just peacefully protest. I’ve gotta put my body, my car… This is what I have to do in order to stop this.’”
Pretti’s gruesome killing—video captured ICE agents shooting him multiple times in the back, while he knelt on a Nicollet Avenue sidewalk subdued by other agents—turned public opinion sharply against Metro Surge. So Tafoya calibrated, a little, applauding the departure of Department of Homeland Security director Kristi Noem and praising Trump for putting “border czar” Tom Homan in charge in February. But she quickly returned to blaming Minnesota Democrats, and protesters she repeatedly called “violent,” for the clashes in the streets of Minneapolis. And in her October debate with Flanagan, Tafoya bizarrely blamed Minnesota protesters, and Flanagan herself, for worsening Operation Metro Surge.
“This was not about peaceful protesting. This was about violence and criminal conduct. And she should know because she has participated in illegal protests in the past as well,” Tafoya said. Flanagan countered by noting that Tafoya accused Good of causing her own death, and Tafoya replied, “That is a hideous statement.” The debate moderator didn’t follow up.
I began putting together this brief recap of Tafoya’s many defenses of Operation Metro Surge when I saw multiple reports that, at least 10 days before the election, Minneapolis’s early vote totals had already reached 101 percent of its early vote in the 2024 presidential election. The New York Times noted that the city was “the heart of Operation Metro Surge.” That seemed like bad news for Tafoya. A few days later a Times/Siena College poll showed Flanagan up 54–40 percent over her GOP challenger.
I caught up with Flanagan, while she was on a last-weekend bus tour of her state, to discuss the role she thought Operation Metro Surge was playing in her contest with Tafoya.
The early voting numbers, she told me, “are incredibly encouraging and hopeful. But what I also know is that it matches the energy that we are feeling on the ground. People are fired up to vote. I think this is the biggest opportunity that people who’ve been impacted by Donald Trump and Operation Metro Surge have, to push back on this administration, and to send folks to Washington, DC, to be a check on the cruelty and chaos that we have experienced firsthand.”
Flanagan went on: “I think this has really been the arc of this campaign, right? From Operation Metro Surge, and how people showed up to march, and to feed their neighbors, and to drive kids home from school who weren’t even their kids. Then going to precinct caucuses, to becoming delegates to the state convention, to a 20-point win in the primary.” Flanagan beat Democratic rival Angie Craig, who has since endorsed her, by that much in August.
“And now headed into the general election, where Donald Trump has endorsed my opponent multiple times in the last couple of weeks.”
I asked Flanagan how she’d chart Tafoya’s evolution on Operation Metro Surge. “There’s no evolution,” she said flatly. “The thing you can count on her to do is be two-faced. She has said that ICE should be called ‘NICE.’ She said that ICE treated children really, really well, in response to 5-year-old Liam Conejo Ramos’s being detained.
“I just think that every time she opens her mouth to express outrage about this,” Flanagan continues, “she tells on herself, that she does not know the people of Minnesota, and frankly, they do not know her. What I witnessed in Operation Metro Surge: literally packing bags [of groceries] to feed my neighbors. It was marching in negative 30-below, bundled up with 50,000 people. It was simply telling the truth about what it is that we have experienced. For me, it was Christmas Eve, at Mass.” Flanagan attends the multiracial, bilingual, activist Catholic Church of the Ascension in northern Minneapolis, whose Latino members were hard hit by Metro Surge. ”And there were maybe 40 people, when usually that night you can’t even get a seat, because people were so afraid.” She sounds increasingly fed up with Tafoya. “Give me a break, lady. You have no idea what you’re talking about.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But Flanagan insists that her base of support goes well beyond Minnesotans outraged by Operation Metro Surge. She had just finished an energetic tour of Indian Country, including her own home base of White Earth, where she’s an enrolled member of the Ojibwe tribe (her Irish Catholic mother signed her up, even though she’d separated from Flanagan’s father, the late Ojibwe leader Marvin Manypenny). She ticked off the issues she says are propelling her campaign.
“We’ve done 340 events in 125 communities, and every single place I go, people talk about affordability, specifically around healthcare. This is the thing. that I hear about in every community, urban, rural, suburban. And I did not start off in this campaign supporting Medicare for All, but having these conversations with Minnesotans I was like, oh, this is what we have to fight for, and this is what we’ve got to do.” As we hang up, I ask Flanagan about Tafoya’s calling the NYT-Siena poll that showed her 14 points behind “an outlier.” She laughs.
“Listen, I’ve always run for office like I’m 10 points behind. I’m not taking anything for granted. We are gonna run it through the tape.” Her staff signals to both of us that it’s time to get back on the bus and continue her final-weekend travels, and we say goodbye.

https://www.propublica.org/article/five-.title: “Chaos” in the Air: Five Ways Voting Could Be Disrupted on Election Day
https://www.propublica.org/article/five-.author: Jen Fifield, Peter Elkind
https://www.propublica.org/article/five-.text:
As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.
Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.
The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.
The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.
Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.
“The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”
“Paper Trail” Podcast
Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “Paper Trail.”
In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”
The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”
Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.
Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.
Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:
1. Will There Be Federal Interference?
An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.
Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.
He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.
“Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said.
It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.
Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.
“We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”
A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”
It’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”
2. What Effect Will Noncitizen Voter Challenges Have?
The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.
Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.
On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”
This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.
In a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some said on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.
Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”
A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation plan” that would interfere with legal voting.
Last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”
In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”
Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She said the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”
Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”
Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.
A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.
“A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” said David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.
3. Will There Be Problems at the Polls?
States often change laws and rules related to voting.
Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.
A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.
Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.
Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two issues involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.
Every election features some issues with voting equipment.
So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.
ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.
4. How Secure Will the Election Be?
Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.
Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.”
In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.
Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.
Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.
“States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he said.
5. Where Will Postelection Challenges Come From?
Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.
Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.
Trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The New York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.
Nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.
“This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the Washington attorney general.
In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which said the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.)
Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.
Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.
“I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown said.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Donald Trump Has Lost It
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Chris Lehmann
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Donald Trump Has Lost It
At one of his final midterm rallies, the president showed just what a spent political force he has become—and what little grip on reality he still has.
Dubuque, Iowa—“It’s pure fricking genius.”
Donald Trump was, of course, describing himself—or rather his rhetorical stump style, which had been trained on the crowd of MAGA faithful assembled here at Dubuque’s Five Flags Center for more than an hour. He’d been complaining about how his wife, Melania, wants him to be less demonstrative at the rally podium—less dancing, no more impersonations of female weightlifters getting bested by transgender competitors. The first lady, Trump protested, wants him to be “more presidential,” which prompted him to do an impersonation of a typical campaign stiff: “Ladies and gentlemen of Iowa, it is a great honor to be with you this evening.” (The impression came across a good deal like House Speaker Mike Johnson, who did a cameo turn at the podium during Trump’s performance.)
Trump then gleefully went through a series of weird angular gesticulations to simulate his slantwise narrative style—the string of non sequitur grievances and resentful old-rich-guy refrains that he dubbed “the weave” during the 2024 campaign. But that descriptor has graduated, midway through his second term, into the work of a maestro.
This was one of the last Trump rallies in the 2026 midterm cycle—which is to say, one of the last Trump rallies we will ever need to care about, given that the president is hurtling toward lame-duck status. The president’s stylings on the stump had revolutionized American politics a decade ago. Now, like a good Midwest county fair touring band, Trump had revived many of his oldest MAGA hits. He laid into the “sick people” on the press risers at the back of the room, insisting that “they are the biggest threat to our country.” He railed against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, dubbing him a “jihadist” and “Communist” and proudly explaining why he’s repeatedly given his first name as “Mohammed.” (It’s something he does for “certain reasons,” he said, in a strained effort to make gutter bigotry sound somehow cagey, before gleefully announcing that he does it “because I’m the president.”) He lobbed kindred racist attacks against Minnesota Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar, whom his Justice Department has targeted with a bogus authoritarian raid and investigation, as well as Somali immigrants; like any washed-up anti-woke comic, he said, “I hope I don’t say anything too controversial” to set up his pet anti-Somali refrain: “We don’t want them here.” There were also extended riffs, even now, about Joe Biden’s cognitive failings, the de rigueur reminder that Trump has “aced” three cognitive exams himself, and some talk about Kamala Harris’s woeful turn as overseer of immigration policy at the White House—all key issues for him and essentially nobody else.
It was hard to see how any of this translates into fricking genius, though. I was in the upper levels of the stadium, and several of my seatmates were straining to make out just what Trump was talking about—especially when he went into digressive genius mode, dilating on optimal flagpole design and golf masters as models for political achievement (yes, really).
Last week, the GOP briefly canceled the rally in favor of a virtual gathering, which would ostensibly be a bigger draw (an objective that makes zero sense for an event meant to generate excitement and boost turnout for state and local politicians). Then the party reversed course, perhaps understanding how weak the move would make Trump look. Five Flags is a small facility—it boasts ads in the corridors for a February performance of a Pink Floyd Tribute band, “Think Floyd”—and it was reasonably full, despite the event’s bait-and-switch scheduling..
Trump came on stage 90 minutes late—long after all the GOP candidates in this suddenly purplish battleground state had delivered their own versions of the stiff-politician election-eve pitches. During the protracted stretch of dead air, the crowd began to get restive and bored; the playlist of classic rock standards began repeating, and at one point, people began swaying their phones in flashlight mode in time to Sinead O’Connor’s “Nothing Compares 2 U”—a singularly odd spectacle after the state’s gubernatorial GOP nominee, Zach Lahn, inveighed against the depraved and murderous character of liberal culture warfare; this was, after all, a performer best known for tearing a photo of the pope in half on live television. There was a palpable mood of the agitprop starting to lose interest in itself.
A very different brand of Kulturkampf was announced, in any event, ahead of Trump’s appearance. There was a video of white-jumpsuit Vegas-era Elvis—a performer the crowd had already heard at least a half-dozen times over on the soundtrack—delivering a demented medley of “Dixie” and “The Battle Hymn of the Republic.” Near the end of the mashup, the camera lingered uncomfortably on a Black flautist in the Elvis ensemble delivering the closing strains of “Dixie.” A nearby diehard MAGA supporter must have noted my goggle-eyed expression and volunteered, “That was really weird.”
Not as weird as the next video entry: the 2024 rally chestnut called “God Made Trump,” delivered as a riff on radio Paul Harvey’s address “God Made a Farmer,” but shot through with the militant messianic imagery of the New Apostolic Reformation. The video starts with an AI-manipulated version of Harvey’s voice announcing “On June 14, 1946, God looked down on his planned paradise and said, ‘I need a caretaker,’” and goes rapidly downhill from there, depicting Trump as an axe-wielding mortal foe of wolves, vipers, the deep state, and the fake news.
It all made for an abrupt shift of tone from the autopilot classic rock playlist, but it didn’t really come anywhere near a closing campaign argument. Iowa is facing many pressing economic and political challenges—from the soaring price of diesel and fertilizer in the wake of Trump’s war in Iran to overlapping crises in cancer and water quality to the declining standing of the state’s formerly distinguished public education system. Senate GOP nominee Ashley Hinson has belatedly positioned herself as an opponent of the Iran War, after voting in favor of it seven times in the House, in order to stay competitive with her upstart Democratic rival, state Representative Josh Turek. Lahn has broken ranks with deregulatory Republican orthodoxy to demand investigations into the cancer and water crises.
Trump, not surprisingly, didn’t mention any of these problems, or GOP proposals to address them; his prescription for electoral victory in Iowa appeared to be Worship me harder. So he stayed firmly and gleefully within his comfort zone of deriding Democrats as “lunatics” hell-bent on spreading communism and forcing sex changes on the children of unwitting God-fearing parents. He made desultory promises that gas prices would come down shortly after the midterms—presumably by resuming the same large-scale attacks on Iran that have already caused those prices to skyrocket while completely failing to defeat the Islamic Republic. He reprised his bribery pledge of $5,000 to every voter who will preserve and expand the GOP majorities in Congress. But he relied mostly on more video footage to drive home the theme of the GOP 2026 campaign: “craziness versus common sense.” One scattershot set of supercuts sought to dramatize the socialist orthodoxy and transgender fetishes of the Democrats, while another highlighted the alleged open-border excesses of the Biden White House, and dwelled on lurid details of murders and sexual attacks from undocumented immigrants. By the time the second video kicked in, people in my section and many on the main floor began to leave. They’d seen this show before—and besides, they could watch Fox News in the comfort of their home, without having to see Elvis hymn the Confederacy or Donald Trump cosplay as Jesus.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Haley Stevens’s Betrayal Is a Fiasco for the Democratic Establishment
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Haley Stevens’s Betrayal Is a Fiasco for the Democratic Establishment
Centrist, pro-Israel Democrats helped Stevens undermine Abdul El-Sayed for months. Now they are reaping the consequences.
Michigan Representative Haley Stevens likes to tell the world what she’s dreaming about. Sometimes, she even overshares a little bit, as in her notorious December 2023 statement that “Israel comes to me in my dreams.”
On Saturday, Stevens dipped into her well of nocturnal visions in a bid to calm the waters she’d started churning up over her clear antipathy toward Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Michigan Senate nominee who defeated Stevens in a bitter primary in August. Responding to concerns that she might break with her party and endorse El-Sayed’s Republican rival, Mike Rogers, Stevens reportedly texted a Michigan Democrat, “I am voting straight Dem!!!! I had a dream last night we won. And I believe he will win! P.S. it was a happy dream.” She reportedly said much the same thing to multiple friends and congressional colleagues up until early Sunday morning—until, without warning, she appeared with Rogers at a Detroit church and announced that she was endorsing him.
The drama of Stevens’s life over the last few weeks has been a battle between these competing dreams. Her pro-Israel politics were in tension with her partisan identity after she lost the primary in August to El-Sayed, who is strongly critical of Israel. AIPAC spent more than $30 million supporting Stevens. After her loss, AIPAC and allied groups such as the United Democracy Project have continued to pour tens of millions of dollars into the effort to defeat El-Sayed, although the full spending on the race hasn’t yet been tabulated. Stevens, meanwhile, kept insisting that her dream of a Democratic Senate outweighed her dreams of Israel, even as she demanded that El-Sayed denounce anti-Israel ads he had nothing to do with. (El-Sayed complied.)
Now we know which dream ultimately won out. When Stevens made her announcement, one of the people in the background was Abigail Ronson, described by Drop Site News as not only a Rogers spokesperson but also “a registered foreign agent for the state of Israel.” Not surprisingly, AIPAC repeatedly posted celebratory retweets of Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers.
Stevens has a personal connection to Zionism as well. Her fiancé, Jason Turkish, is strongly pro-Israel and a megadonor to both political parties. He has donated more than $24,000 to the campaign of Maine Republican Susan Collins. Last week, Turkish announced that he is voting for Rogers. (A friend of Stevens told The Washington Post on Sunday that Turkish had been “really working her over” to endorse Rogers, including by saying that she was betraying Jewish voters by backing El-Sayed.)
In declaring her own support for Rogers, Stevens claimed, “Who we are as Michiganders is not hate, and it is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.” This claim is absurd, since El-Sayed has not been running a hateful campaign, while Rogers and other Republicans have targeted the Democrats with vile Islamophobia. In fact, after welcoming the support of Stevens, Rogers referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist.”
The journalist Ray Wert, who is married to Mallory McMorrow, who was also bested by El-Sayed in Michigan’s Democratic senatorial primary, offered some insights into Stevens in a long post on X.com that emphasized her personal flakiness and speculated on the role her fiancé might have played in the decision. According to Wert:
I’ve known Haley Stevens for a long time. Until now, she has always had staff to protect her, prop her up, and keep her safe from her own irrational behavior. What we’re seeing now? This is just raw, unfiltered Haley. 
The Haley who flip-flops and goes from thought to thought without rhyme or reason. The Haley that calls you at 3 AM to yell at you, and then calls you back at 5 AM oblivious to the fact that she even spoke with you at 3 AM. The Haley who bends to the last and loudest voice that tells her something. 
More often than not that last voice is now her fiancé. And…that appears to potentially be a really troubling relationship.
This account of Stevens’s personal instability is plausible enough, and other emerging accounts reinforce this narrative. So too will the train wreck of an interview that Stevens gave to CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Sunday night, in which she appeared erratic in the extreme and failed to give any coherent reason for her last-minute endorsement of Rogers.
But Stevens’s personality is only part of the story. Donald Trump is also weird, but his weirdness is amplified and given direction by his ideology as well as pressure from those around him.
In Stevens’s case, hardline pro-Israel ideology is key to understanding her decision. Danielle O’Byrne, a political strategist who has worked for Stevens as well as Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, wrote bluntly about the ideological dimensions of Stevens’s actions:
In 2022, I worked for Haley Stevens’ campaign. Over my time working there I quickly learned that she was bought and sold by AIPAC. A Democrat from the middle of America, obsessed with foreign interests and willing to sell herself and us out for it. We won that race by 20 points. With over $10 million in outside spending by AIPAC to oust another Jewish Democratic member, @andylevin, all because he wasn’t kowtowing to them.
It’s precisely because Stevens was a fierce pro-Israel warrior that she had the support of the Democratic Party establishment. In the primaries, she was the preferred candidate of Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader. After she lost the primary, Stevens started making comments that were clearly designed to sabotage El-Sayed. But this didn’t put her beyond the pale, since other party leaders such as former House speaker Nancy Pelosi and Neera Tanden (head of the Center for American Progress) were saying much the same thing.
In retrospect, centrist Democrats such as Pelosi and Tanden were playing a dangerous game. They were clearly intent on reducing El-Sayed’s margin without fatally wounding his campaign. The goal was to make sure that even if El-Sayed won, they could argue that he underperformed because his version of progressive politics—particularly when it came to Israel—was too extreme, thus making it easier to ideologically discipline him in office.
Stevens was playing the same game, but on Sunday, she went too far by actually endorsing Rogers. This robbed establishment Democrats of their plausible deniability in hamstringing the El-Sayed campaign.
Popular

Stevens also made herself toxic among Democrats. She still has a few defenders, such as Todd Richman, head of Democratic Majority for Israel. But her longtime chief of staff Justin German has quit and says many of his colleagues are also resigning. Party leaders—notably Schumer, Pelosi, and Tanden—who previously supported Stevens are now decrying what Schumer described as a “despicable betrayal.”
But the lamentations of these powerful centrist Democrats ring hollow. They sound like Dr. Frankenstein wringing his hands over the havoc wreaked by the monster he created. The monster, of course, deserves punishment—and there is already a move to expel Stevens from the Democratic Party’s congressional caucus—but so do the doctors.
The best-case scenario for the Democrats might be that they win a large enough supermajority that they can afford to expel a few wreckers within the party, not just Stevens but also Senator John Fetterman.
But Stevens is merely a symptom of a deeper problem. Even as voters are becoming more wary of the US alliance with Israel, Democratic Party elites are top-heavy with figures closely aligned to the pro-Israel lobby. Any reckoning with the Stevens fiasco has to also include radically weakening this lobby.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Ilhan Omar: “Trump Has an Unhealthy and Creepy Obsession With Me”
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
In the predawn hours of October 12, Department of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents raided the home of US Representative Ilhan Omar, DFL-Minnesota. The raid was reportedly part of a criminal fraud investigation that was focused on decades-old immigration and citizenship paperwork that was filed by Omar’s father when she was a child. Omar, an outspoken progressive, is a refugee from Somalia who came to the United States at age 12. She has been the target of attacks by Trump, his Republican allies, and right-wing media for the better part of a decade. She denied any wrongdoing and decried the raid as “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
That sentiment was echoed by former president Barack Obama, along with many other prominent Democrats and defenders of civil liberties. For his part, Trump claimed he had nothing to do with the raid. Yet, on the same day that it occurred, the president ripped into Omar as “totally crooked personally” and “a terrible person.” He also endorsed Minnesota Republican US Senate nominee Michele Tafoya, who is mounting a high-stakes challenge to DFL candidate Peggy Flanagan in Tuesday’s midterm election. With Republican prospects fading in Senate battleground states such as North Carolina and Georgia, Tafoya’s bid was on Trump’s radar to such an extent that, just hours after the raid on Omar’s home, he was telling Minnesotans, “You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who’s a very respected person.”
The Nation recently asked Omar to discuss the raid and the politics surrounding it. Here’s what she had to say.
—John Nichols
John Nichols:  There was an immediate show of support from your constituents after the raid. You can’t be too worried about your own reelection prospects. But do you think that the president and his allies are trying to stir up anti-immigrant and anti-Somali sentiment in the broader context of the midterms?
Ilhan Omar: Absolutely. This is political, and it’s a deliberate attempt to distract the American people from the failures of this administration. Republicans don’t want to talk about the soaring cost of living, the Epstein files, the war in Iran, Trump’s shady diesel deal with Russia, or a healthcare system that is spiraling out of control. So instead, Trump sends DHS to raid my home. This is what authoritarianism looks like: weaponizing the federal government against anyone he sees as an opponent, scapegoating immigrant communities, and using racism and fear to divide us. He is reaching for the same tired playbook because he knows his party is in trouble. Trump thinks he can turn our neighbors against one another to win an election. I believe the American people are better than that.
JN: Why do you think the president and so many Republicans are obsessed with you?
IO: Trump has an unhealthy and creepy obsession with me. I represent everything Trump and today’s Republican Party seem to despise. I’m a woman, an immigrant, a refugee, a Muslim woman who wears a hijab, and someone who refuses to be intimidated into silence. I know who I am and why I do this work.
The Republican Party has chosen to serve billionaires and powerful corporations over working people. They know that our vision of healthcare for everyone, an economy that works for working families, and a country where everyone can live with dignity is popular with the American people. So they resort to racism, Islamophobia, conspiracy theories, and lies. They want to make me the story because they don’t want to answer for their own failures. But I will not let their hatred define me, and I will not let it distract me from the people I came to Congress to serve.
JN: Many Minnesotans have complained about being targeted by the administration—with last winter’s Operation Metro Surge, and with all the focus on you. Why do you think this is happening?
IO: Trump has said that this is political retribution. I believe Minnesota is a target because we represent everything his politics of division cannot understand. We are a community that chooses solidarity over fear and care over cruelty. We welcome immigrants and refugees. We don’t just welcome them into our neighborhoods—we send them to Congress. When our neighbors are threatened, we show up, even in below-zero temperatures. We deliver meals, give children rides to school, check on one another, and organize mutual aid. We understand that when one family is hurting, our whole community has a responsibility to help. I have seen that love firsthand in the outpouring of support from my constituents. In moments when this administration tries to make people feel afraid and alone, Minnesotans have reminded me what this country can be at its best. Their courage and compassion mean more to me than I can put into words.
That is what Trump cannot stand. He wants us to believe that our differences make us weaker, that some people belong here more than others, and that fear is the only way to lead. Minnesota proves otherwise. Our strength comes from looking out for one another, recognizing our shared humanity, and refusing to abandon our neighbors. The antidote to authoritarianism is community. It is love. It is solidarity. It is the belief that every person deserves dignity and that none of us are free until all of us are free. Those are Minnesota’s values. Those are American values. And no raid, no threat, and no amount of hatred will take them away from us.
JN: You have often spoken about your patriotism and your pride at being an American. How does the raid—and the president’s very personal attacks on you—make you feel about your country and the people who are currently leading it? Do you think Trump is out of touch with American values and ideals?
IO: Trump’s behavior echoes some of the darkest chapters in our nation’s history. But I believe deeply in the promise of this country because generations of Americans have fought, sacrificed, and organized to make it a more just and equal place. That’s why I ran for office.
My family and I have endured death threats, relentless harassment, and years of personal attacks from this president. It has been painful, but it has never shaken my love for this country or my belief in its people. Trump may be out of touch with our values, but I know the best of America is found in people who stand up for one another, refuse to give up, and keep fighting for a country that lives up to its promise. I will never stop fighting for an America where everyone can see a doctor, afford a safe home, and put food on the table.
JN: What can Congress do to hold Trump and DHS to account?
Popular

IO: Congress has a constitutional duty to stand up to this abuse of power. We must defend our rights under the Speech and Debate Clause [outlined in Article I, Section 6, Clause 1 of the United States Constitution] and make clear that no president gets to use the power of the executive branch to intimidate or target members of Congress for political reasons.
This is bigger than party. It is about defending our democracy and protecting the independence of Congress. When we allow one branch of government to intimidate another, we weaken the very foundations of our republic.
[House Speaker] Mike Johnson has failed to meet this moment. But I promise you this—when Democrats retake the majority in November, we will stand up, hold this administration accountable, and defend the institution and the constitutional rights that every member of Congress is sworn to uphold.
JN: President Obama offered a powerful statement in your defense. It is notable that he was also a target of Trump’s conspiracy theories and a questioning of his citizenship. Were you struck by that?
IO: President Obama knows the world of right-wing conspiracies better than anyone. In many ways, the conspiracy world I find myself in was created around him. That is why he can so clearly see the purpose and contradictions of the lies being told about me. He knows that no amount of evidence or facts will ever be enough for these trolls, because they are not after the truth. The conspiracy itself is what drives them. It meant so much to me to know that President Obama sees this for what it is and was willing to speak out.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Russia’s security service detains teen over alleged terror plot targeting Moscow museum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sophia Kishkovsky
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Russia’s FSB security service has detained a teenager on charges of threatening Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum and Nature Reserve via TikTok after an unusual warning from US officials of a “credible threat of a mass casualty event” on 31 October. The alert was posted on the website of the US embassy in Moscow and social media. Der Spiegel reported that German citizens in Russia had received a similar warning.
On 1 November, the FSB distributed a video, published on sites such as Tass, the official state news agency, showing an unidentified young man being detained, footage of a knife, camouflage and neo-Nazi content on his phone, and his confession to posting “propaganda of Nazism” on his TikTok page. Russia’s National Antiterrorism Committee posted the same footage to its YouTube channel.
The US issued a similar alert several days before an attack that killed at least 149 people in March 2024 during a concert at Crocus City Hall in Moscow. Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack; before it occurred, Russian President Vladimir Putin denounced the warnings as “outright blackmail”.
In a change reflecting US President Donald Trump’s cooperation with Russia, the FSB in a statement on 1 November, posted on the agency’s website, credited “US law enforcement agencies” for warning of an impending attack at Tsaritsyno: “We are grateful to the American side for the information provided.”
The FSB statement added that “in the interest of public safety, planned cultural events at the museum-reserve have been cancelled, and security measures in the surrounding area have been stepped up”. The museum is typically closed on Mondays, while the surrounding park, known for its rolling hills, fountains and wooded paths, is open daily. Russian media reported that the park reopened on Sunday.
The FSB’s statement claims the detained minor had posted images on TikTok “showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, cap, eyewear and headset—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon” as well as “photographs taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve, accompanied by the caption: ‘I found a place’”.
The complex, which was originally intended as a summer residence for Catherine the Great in the 18th century, is consistently ranked as one of Moscow’s most visited tourist sites. Tsaritsyno’s website states that over 7 million people visit the museum and park in southern Moscow annually. The Grand Palace, its centrepiece, is known for its neo-Gothic design by the architect Matvey Kazakov, which remained unfinished after Catherine’s death. Many other buildings on the grounds were designed by Kazakov’s teacher, Vasily Bazhenov, Catherine’s court architect, who was initially commissioned to design the palace before falling out with the Empress.
Some preservationists denounced the glitzy completion of the palace, inaugurated in 2007 with Putin present. It was carried out under Moscow’s mayor at the time, Yury Luzhkov, who was known for monumental construction projects. Although some attempts have been made to show contemporary art at Tsaritsyno, its exhibitions are primarily focused on the tsars and historic Russian folk crafts.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The False Promise of Bob Woodward
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Richard Kreitner
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The False Promise of Bob Woodward
He’s always been known as an intrepid journalist. But critics in The Nation, throughout decades, identified ways he held important stories for his own gain.
The False Promise of Bob Woodward
He’s always been known as an intrepid journalist. But critics in “The Nation,” throughout decades, identified ways he held important stories for his own gain.
“Sometimes people have a vision of themselves that just doesn’t fit with reality,” Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward writes in his new memoir, Secret. For example, he does not feel the public’s understanding of him as “‘all business’ and cold” is quite right. But the problem is deeper than that. Woodward has always presented himself as a fearless and committed truth-teller, intent on getting to “the center of what was really going on.” Repeatedly, however, Woodward’s books, purporting to bring readers into the inner operations of the US government, have obscured more than they revealed.
Decades of reviews in The Nation of Woodward’s books show the consistent flaws and oversights that have marked the journalist’s work, not least a habitual reliance on the tropes and trivialities of inside-the-Beltway access-mongering. Jefferson Morley spotted the tendency early, reviewing Woodward’s 1987 book, Veil: The Secret Wars of the C.I.A., 1980-1987, which largely focused on Reagan’s CIA director, William Casey. “Woodward has not so much misreported his story as misinterpreted it,” Morley argued. Training his attention on minute “power struggles” between top officials, Woodward “tends to neglect the more fundamental and important news,” such as the Agency’s support for the contras in Nicaragua, which became international news while Woodward was reporting his book. Instead of telling readers about what the US government was actually up to—including the crimes that high officials were committing—the journalist focused on petty personal squabbles: “Because there was not much dispute among Woodward’s high-level sources about routine C.I.A. support for contra operations, he had no controversy to report on. No high-level controversy, no story.”
The excerpt of Woodward’s new memoir that recently ran in The New Yorker purports to recount a time when he courageously chose to publish the unvarnished truth about infighting within the George H.W. Bush administration, at the cost of losing a close friend who had been his source for the story. But Morley’s review highlights a consistent thread throughout Woodward’s career: His closeness to sources has often won out over a commitment to printing the truth. “Woodward probably has more access to top government officials than any other Washington reporter,” Morley noted. “But access always—always—has a price. Veil confirms that the more access a reporter has, the higher price he or she pays.” Indeed, Woodward himself acknowledged that he did not have the time to pursue the contras story because he was busy talking to Casey for the project that turned into Veil.
Reviewers have often pointed to the glaring lack of background information in Woodward’s supposedly immersive political narratives. Assessing 1991’s The Commanders, framed as an unparalleled glimpse into the (first) Bush administration’s deliberations on the eve of the (first) invasion of Iraq, Jon Wiener observed that “the book’s fatal flaw is that it contains virtually nothing about the political context in which Bush made up his mind in favor of war”— for instance, that his decision to invade was motivated by a sluggish economy and slumping poll numbers ahead of an important midterm election.
But Wiener identified an even worse problem with Woodward’s book, one that would keep cropping up throughout the journalist’s career: his tendency to keep a lid on important stories until the moment was right for him. In the run-up to the first Gulf War, it would have been useful for the public to know that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff was opposed to an invasion. Wiener asked, “What did Woodward know and when did he know it?… Why did that information become Woodward’s private property, which Simon and Schuster would sell to us months later for $24.95? The information Woodward possessed would have been a powerful weapon for the antiwar movement…. Woodward has privatized the news.”
As the Reagan era segued seamlessly into the reign of Clinton, Nation critics objected more strenuously to Woodward’s customary tricks and tics. Reviewing The Agenda, in 1994—a “work of intensive stenography,” about the early years of the Clinton administration—Christopher Hitchens wrote, “The portentous vacancy of neoliberal argot has met its chronicler in one who takes it seriously.”
Woodward’s next book was The Choice, a nearly 500-age tome about the 1996 election, which happened to be published months before that election. Republican challenger Bob Dole “cooperated readily” with the author, as Lynn Phillips wrote in her Nation review, while neither President Clinton nor first lady Hillary Clinton agreed to do so, an imbalance that Woodward never quite managed to rectify, as Phillips wrote: “And when a reporter gets so close to his candidates that he speaks from inside their mouths (Bob Dole, c’est moi!), his reportorial glasses fog up.”
Woodward’s glasses were especially foggy in the early years of this century. His 2003 book Bush at War, about the months after the September 11 attacks, was appraised in The Nation by Washington editor David Corn: “Woodward stuck with what has become in recent years his standard MO: Approach each power player and say, ‘All the other power players are telling me their side of the story, so you should do so as well.’ Woodward then weaves the various self-serving versions—supplied, of course, on background—into a quasi-official chronicle, with little overt sourcing.” While his Watergate investigations “excavated a story the big shots didn’t want public,” Woodward’s later work related only “what the powerful do want known.”
And so on, through the Obama, Trump, and Biden years, and into our own abysmal present. Most recently, in 2025, Matthew Duss, executive vice president at the Center for International Policy, assessed Woodward’s book, War, about the Biden administration’s handling of conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine. As Duss wrote, “Woodward consistently fails to interrogate any of what he is told, choosing instead to simply record and relay it and allow his readers to assemble the picture as they wish, as if the real journalistic feat was just getting the decision-makers and insiders to talk to him in the first place.”
Despite the self-serving accounts in his memoir, Woodward remains, as he has long been, a conduit for largely meaningless internecine battles among elites, a glorified stenographer haplessly doing the bidding of the powerful even while he presents himself as a heroic crusader for the vitality of the Fourth Estate. It’s a vision of himself that doesn’t fit with reality, even if Woodward’s first-draft accounts of history have done all too much to shape it.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Objects reinstalled at Museo Nacional de Colombia following removal by right-wing government
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Mercedes Ezquiaga
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Bogotá’s Museo Nacional de Colombia has reinstalled the 63 objects previously taken down from its permanent galleries over claims of “political indoctrination”. The move followed a court order that reversed the national government's removal of the items on 15 October.
On the evening of 28 October, César Enrique Osorio Ortiz—a judge at Bogotá’s 24th Family Court—ordered Colombia’s cultural ministry and the museum to return the works to their original locations within 48 hours. The ministry complied with the order on Friday (30 October).
The decision came in response to a constitutional-rights case filed by cultural groups and political opponents who had accused the government of the country's far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella of censorship. The judge also ordered both institutions not to remove works based on their content or the views they express.
Among the removed pieces were a pride flag belonging to the activist Elizabeth Castillo, a pen made from a bullet that was used to sign the 2016 peace agreement between the state and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and a poster for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.
The removals came amid calls by De la Espriella for a “cultural war” and a “direct blow to ‘wokeism’ and the ideologisation of culture”, an offensive that affected the country’s main museum.
The government’s decision sparked a series of protests during which hundreds of people gathered outside the museum, as well as a joint statement by six museums expressing “deep concern” and calling for the protection of their professional autonomy. The signatories included the Modern art museums of Bogotá, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Medellín and Tolima, as well as the Museo Rayo.
Marielsa Castro Vizcarra, the chief curator of the Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (which signed the joint statement), tells The Art Newspaper that the cultural sector responded quickly, from street protests to the statement and the involvement of the International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art. Castro described the incident as “a precedent we need to take into account” and “an authoritarian way of spreading fear”.
According to the judge's ruling, the artefacts had been removed “without a documented curatorial justification” in a decision that “disregarded the constitutional protection of cultural expressions”. The court did not rule out future changes to the exhibitions, provided they are properly justified and not based on the authorities’ objections to the works’ content.
“No government owns our history!” wrote Gabriel Becerra, a left-wing lawmaker behind the constitutional-rights case, in a post on X welcoming the court’s decision.
