https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/main.title: Polls Close in Maine as Democrats Make Final Push to Oust Sen. Susan Collins
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/main.author: Noah Hurowitz, Austin Campbell
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/main.text:
The toughest reelection campaign of Republican Sen. Susan Collins’s career is over, as Mainers await results of whether their longtime senator effectively portrayed herself as an independent force in Washington or was weighed down by the baggage of a Republican Party entering the midterms at a severe disadvantage.
Polls closed at 8 p.m. ET Tuesday night in a race that could see the 30-year incumbent lose her powerful Senate post to challenger Troy Jackson, a progressive who was virtually unknown on the national stage until his rushed elevation just over three months ago as the Democratic replacement candidate.
Tuesday night’s election results could change the control of the Senate chamber, with Maine as one of the seven critical states likely to determine whether Democrats can overcome the Republican majority in D.C.
But Maine voters may have to wait far later to learn who won. The state’s ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates by preference rather than being forced to select just one candidate, could delay results significantly.
“I think it’s possible results will take us past midnight,” Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows told reporters in Lewiston on Tuesday.
Bellows said municipalities have two business days to submit their results to the state, although election officials have requested that towns share their vote counts Tuesday night.
Collins, who has represented the state since 1997, campaigned on her record of securing federal investments for state infrastructure, such as rural hospitals, and prided herself as being a moderate Republican who breaks ranks with President Donald Trump.
However, an analysis by Congressional Quarterly Roll Call found that her votes aligned with Trump 90 percent of the time in both the president’s first and second terms.
Still, Collins’s split support among some Democratic voters was evident Tuesday in Lewiston, where several residents told The Intercept they were supporting the Republican senator despite filling their ballots out to Democrats otherwise.
“I am Susan Collins all the way,” said Anne Marie Hastings, a voter who also expressed strong support for Matt Dunlap, a progressive running against former Republican Gov. Paul LePage in a closely watched race in the state’s 2nd Congressional District.
“I’m a registered Democrat, but when it comes to things like this, I go with what I feel is right, not the party that they belong to,” Hastings said.
Another Lewiston voter, Ouellette Bertram, said he voted blue across the board, with the exception of “the Republican lady,” who he said he just plain likes.
“She’s been doing a good job, I think,” Bertram said.
Other Maine residents didn’t share the sentiment toward the Republican incumbent and the Republican Party’s decadelong legacy within the state.
One all-Democrat voter was Bryan Golay, who said he wished the Democratic Party would move to the left but voted against what he described as the GOP’s “enshittification” of America, much of which, he said, has come during Collins’s time in Washington.
“If you can’t get shit done in 30 years, why are we gonna give you another term?” Golay said.
Mags Krantz, a master’s student of social work who works with children with disabilities, said she voted for all Democrats, including Dunlap and Jackson, citing GOP-backed cuts to social services.
“They just cut funding for my job, and for my career,” Krantz told The Intercept outside a polling site in Lewiston on Tuesday. “I really voted for my future, but I also voted for every vulnerable child that I work with every single day that really wishes adults would vote for them over money.”
Speaking to a crowd of supporters on the eve of the election, Jackson toasted the grassroots organizing that has powered his rapidly assembled campaign into the most serious challenge yet to Collins’s hold on her seat.
“This government is fundamentally broken, and it only works for the wealthiest people in this country — that’s what we’re up against right now,” Jackson said. “They are going to outspend the hell out of us. There’s no doubt about it. But they don’t have people like you in rooms like this across this state and across the country.”
Jackson, who spent nearly 20 years in the state legislature, ran on a platform focusing on lowering costs for working-class families, expanding healthcare access, and combating the influence of wealthy donors and corporate PACs in Washington. He entered the race somewhat hastily in late July, after former Democratic nominee Graham Platner withdrew from the Senate race following a rape allegation, which Platner denied.
Maine is one of the two critical swing states determining control of the Senate to use ranked-choice voting. The other is Alaska, where the last polls won’t close until 1 a.m. ET on Wednesday.
The Collins–Jackson race has been one of the top targets for national attention this cycle — most of it on purpose. In October, The Intercept reported that Defending Main Street, a Republican-aligned super PAC associated with Collins spent between $20,000 and $25,000 attacking Jackson on topics such as cost-of-living and taxes. The ads mistakenly were targeted to audiences in Portland, Oregon, rather than the intended Portland, Maine.
This is a developing story that will be updated. Noah Hurowitz reported from Lewiston and Portland, Maine.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://citylimits.org/nine-homeless-new.title: Nine Homeless New Yorkers, Who Died Unclaimed in Last Winter’s Storms, Laid to Rest in Manhattan
https://citylimits.org/nine-homeless-new.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/nine-homeless-new.text:
Share This Article
The remains of the nine unhoused people, who died of hypothermia on the city’s streets, were initially slated for mass graves on Hart Island—until a group of fellow New Yorkers stepped in.
Last winter, a brutal stretch of cold weather and lingering snowstorms killed at least 18 people in New York City, including several who were homeless and on the street at the time of their deaths.
Months later, nine of those unhoused New Yorkers’ remains had yet to be claimed by friends or family, despite what one advocate described as “diligent searches” on the part of the medical examiner’s office to locate next of kin. Their bodies were headed for Hart Island, the city’s desolate potter’s field off the shore of City Island in the Bronx, which for more than a century has served as the final resting place for those without someone to plan or pay for their burial.
Instead, after several fellow New Yorkers stepped in, the nine late residents were honored with a funeral mass Monday night at Saint Thomas Church Fifth Avenue, where their ashes—contained in square golden urns, their names inscribed on the front—were interred in the cathedral’s columbarium.
“We believe that those who have been homeless deserve dignity in death, even if they did not receive it in their lives,” Charles King, CEO of the homeless services nonprofit Housing Works, said during the service, where the robed church choir sang “Amazing Grace” and other hymns set to booming organ music.
“We want our fellow New Yorkers to appreciate the cost of our collective decision to throw away human lives, as evidenced by our lack of meaningful shelter and care for the least among us,” King said.
Few details are known about the nine people laid to rest, organizers said. All of them died from hypothermia, found in different parts of the freezing city—one in the doorway of a building in the East Village, another along the Van Wyck Expressway in Queens—between November 2025 and February 2026. They ranged in age from 38 to 74, and came from South Carolina, Puerto Rico, Russia, and India; two were born in the city.
Their names were James Paul Smith, Manjeet Singh, Harold Hemphill, Tomeka Ryeshera Gibson, Jorge Elias Rivera Torres, Jeffrey Costa, Edward “Eduardo” Adames, Jose M. “Joseph” Pena, and Igor Zapevalov.
“We know little of these nine neighbors, but we do know this: they are beloved,” Rev. Mark Schultz of Saint Thomas Church said during the service.
The ceremony and interment were arranged by Community Burial Project, a new initiative founded by artist Rhonda Roland Shearer to provide memorials for New Yorkers experiencing street homelessness at the time of their deaths.
Shearer, who spent the months after 9/11 distributing supplies to first responders at Ground Zero, said she was struck by the ceremonial process for handling recovered remains there, which she described as “dignified and very emotionally present.”
She’d previously partnered with Housing Works to raise memorial funds for unhoused New Yorkers who died during the COVID-19 pandemic. She was distressed, she said, at the prospect of those killed during last winter’s deadly cold being sent to Hart Island, where the dead are buried in mass graves.
“No one’s allowed to be there to pray,” she said of burials on the island, which for years were largely inaccessible to the public.
Shearer reached out to Housing Works, which connected with the city’s Human Resources Administration and Medical Examiner’s Office to make arrangements for any victims of the cold snap who went unclaimed. A local funeral home provided the funeral services and urns, and Saint Thomas’ offered the columbarium space. Additional expenses were covered by a donation from the author Amy Tan and her husband, Shearer said.
“The ability of community to just come together on this is the big message here,” she said. Going forward, the Community Burial Project will make similar arrangements for other street homeless New Yorkers at risk of being “forgotten,” she added.
“These nine, I believe, are not only being treated with dignity and getting the respect that all humans deserve, but I think they’re going to serve, in this case, the larger effort…to continue this,” Shearer said. “That will also add another layer of what meaning was conveyed by their lives.”
King, of Housing Works, said he and the organization have pushed for years for the city to cease its use of Hart Island for burials, and to come up with a “dignified way to deal with people who don’t have anyone to claim their remains.”
“They bury people in pine boxes, often five deep in these big anonymous holes,” he said.
The public memorial service, he explained, was also a way to “to make the public aware of the homeless people we walk around all the time,” and the need to treat them with respect, both during life and after it.
He called for the city to invest in more drop-in centers to offer “humane and comfortable spaces” for unhoused people, with fewer restrictions and better conditions than the often crowded—and sometimes dangerous—city shelters that street homeless New Yorkers are reluctant to enter.
“The truth of the matter is, we tend to look at homeless people in a very one-dimensional way, forgetting that they have their own hopes, their own dreams, their own aspirations,” King said.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/mich.title: Michigan Senate Race Closes as a Referendum on Israel Policy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/mich.author: Matt Sledge, Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/mich.text:
For the left, it’s been the marquee race of the midterm cycle. Either a Republican former U.S. representative known for pushing domestic spying powers or an outspoken progressive who forced a reckoning over U.S.–Israel policy among Democrats will emerge from Election Day as the next senator from Michigan.
Abdul El-Sayed would be the first Muslim U.S. senator if elected Tuesday night, capping off a race that’s been viewed as a referendum on swing-state appeal for the Democratic Party’s left flank. If he defeats Mike Rogers, a loyal Trump ally whose campaign often peddled Islamophobic tropes against the Democratic nominee, the results will all but certainly embolden progressives ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
If El-Sayed loses, it will likely trigger a centrist backlash — and cost the Democrats a critical Senate seat as the party fights to take back the upper chamber.
Polls across Michigan closed by 9 p.m. ET on Tuesday, with anxious voters across the state awaiting the returns.
In the heavily Arab and Muslim city of Dearborn, voters across party lines said they were outraged at the Islamophobic attacks ads targeting El-Sayed that became a staple of airwaves and social media feeds in the campaign’s final days.
“I am a Muslim. And I’ve seen a lot of ads, and it’s disgusting, because we are good people,” said Gus Tarraf, a Republican running for a state House seat. “I love this country.”
Although Donald Trump carried many precincts in Dearborn two years ago due to voter frustration over the Biden administration’s support of Israel, Tarraf said his community is turning on the Republican Party this year.
“Not a lot of Arab Americans are happy with the Trump administration,” he said. “So it doesn’t matter if they know you, as soon as they know you are on the Republican ticket.”
El-Sayed’s willingness to criticize U.S. policy on Israel animated soap-opera-level drama in the final days of the race, when his former primary opponent, centrist Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, announced she would switch her endorsement to support Rogers.
After demanding an apology from El-Sayed for an outside PAC’s ad, Stevens said on social media that she came to the decision after feeling “shut out” by El-Sayed’s campaign, adding that she’s heard from “Black voters, Jewish voters, and others about how deeply these messages hurt.” Rogers, she said, gave her “the hope that he can serve in the tradition of John McCain: a senator willing to put country before party and stand up to his own side when conscience requires it.”
Stevens’s late-breaking endorsement of Rogers drew a mix of eye-rolls and outrage from voters at three precincts in Detroit and Dearborn. None of the voters interviewed by The Intercept said it had swayed them to vote for Rogers.
“People have already early voted. People have already absentee voted,” said Noora Iskander. “I don’t think many people change their minds. So I think it’s just hypocritical.”
Stevens’s decision to make the endorsement while inside a Black church in Detroit may also have generated backlash from the Black voters that Rogers was hoping to win over, according to some who spoke to The Intercept. One said the church community has been buzzing — and not positively — about the weekend’s events.
“Unfortunately, she went to a Black church to use it as a backdrop,” said Dearborn voter Dorothea Sharon. “It really was a slap in the face for the Black community that that happened.”
While El-Sayed has had to face intense scrutiny over accusations of conflating opposition to U.S. aid to Israel with antisemitism, little accounting has been made of the blatant Islamophobia and xenophobia from the Rogers campaign, the Republican Party, and Trump. But in Dearborn, the rhetoric had clearly hurt several voters who spoke to The Intercept.
The father of state Senate candidate Abbas Alawieh, a Democrat who played a prominent role in the 2024 Uncommitted movement, grew visibly upset when asked about the ads targeting Muslims.
“These are weak people who don’t have anything to do — they don’t have any programs for our economy, for our health, for our future,” Zouheir Alawieh said. “That’s why they are attacking us as Muslims and as human beings. It’s never been like this. This is a shame. America is a place where the Black with the white with the yellow, the Muslim with the Christian with the Jews, can live freely. Don’t try to tear up our society.”
Outside Dearborn, El-Sayed has tried to defuse the anti-Muslim smears against him by joking that he is only in favor of “shawarma law.” However, the Islamophobic attacks convinced at least one voter to cast her ballot for Rogers.
“I don’t want to live under Sharia law,” said Joann, a law firm employee who declined to give her last name after she voted in Detroit.
The fear of Islamic rule was the main issue for Joann, she said, although she also worried about El-Sayed’s campaign pledge of Medicare for All.
“I’ve worked my whole life, put all my stuff into the Medicare, but then I’ve got to let other people get it for free? It doesn’t seem fair to me when I’ve worked my whole life for it, and we’re not even sure that it’s going to be there when we really get ready to retire,” she said.
Yet it was that very messaging from El-Sayed’s campaign that excited many other residents in Michigan. Many voters who spoke to The Intercept said they were more focused on pocketbook issues.
“It’s the gas prices, the food. I mean, money is running out your pocket so fast,” Leigh James said after voting at Tabernacle Missionary Baptist Church in Detroit.
James said she had walked to the polling place to avoid using gas. “I’m trying to save,” she said. “So thank God I live in the neighborhood.”
Other voters said they were inspired by El-Sayed’s personality, with one woman describing him as a “fighter.”
Noora Iskander, who voted for El-Sayed in Dearborn, said she approved of his stance in favor of Medicare for All, his affordability platform, and his solidarity with Palestine.
“I think he’s going to make a lot of change. He’s going to scare a lot of people — which I believe is a good thing, because you can’t really change for the better if you don’t scare a few people,” she said.
This is a developing story. Matt Sledge reported from Dearborn and Detroit, Michigan.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: In uneasy times, Bangladesh launches its first art fair
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Rebecca Anne Proctor
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Bangladeshi capital of Dhaka is set to stage its first commercial art fair this month, which aims to transform the city’s private art sector and encourage a new generation of Bangladeshi collectors.
Art Dhaka, staged under the tagline “Art for All”, will take place at Aloki, a popular multidisciplinary cultural hub and former garment factory.
Though Dhaka is increasingly recognised on the global stage for its non-commercial exhibitions, the city has a limited number of traditional commercial art spaces, with only a few private galleries.
The fair’s founding members—Durjoy Rahman, Nahar Khan, Aumia Khundkar and Fahd Sattar—are addressing the city’s lack of commercial infrastructure by staging a curated fair of emerging and established Bangladeshi artists. Those whose work will feature in the first edition include Dhali Al Mamoon, Mojahid Musa, Najmun Nahar Keya, Bishwajit Goswami, Ayesha Sultana and Dinar Sultana Putul.
The new fair is being curated by Najmun Nahar Keya and fellow Dhaka-based artist and curator Zihan Khan, both of whom have guest curated Dhaka’s international festival for photography, Chobi Mela. The fair will feature gallery presentations, public programming and dedicated spaces for emerging artists.
“This is not like Frieze or Art Basel—it is with the ambiance of an art biennial,” says Rahman, a collector and the founder of the Durjoy Bangladesh Foundation (DBF). “We wanted to stage an event to showcase the art, culture and architecture in Bangladesh through a platform which caters to a wider ecosystem, with a commercial aspect.”
Bangladesh, emphasises Rahman, is a country of around 178 million people, making it the eighth most populous nation in the world, and one in which art has long played a key role. “Culture and art have always been important to everyday life,” Rahman says. “Craft is a part of everyone’s household. We grew up going to cultural events. But over the years, because of industrial development, art became a subject for just a few. Art Dhaka attempts to fill this gap.”
Only a handful of galleries
“We don’t have a strong gallery system,” Rahman says. Besides his own foundation, Dhaka is home to a handful of other private foundations, including the Bengal Foundation, Brihatta Art Foundation, Cosmos Foundation and the Samdani Art Foundation. The latter was founded in 2012 and has organised the Dhaka Art Summit (DAS) since 2012, arguably the most influential event in attracting international attention to Dhaka’s art scene.
The handful of commercial art galleries include Drik, internationally known for championing photography and multimedia storytelling; Galleri Kaya and Gallery Chitrak, showing Modern masters and contemporary Bangladeshi painters; and Abinta Gallery of Fine Arts, a non-profit cultural centre that opened in 2012 and shows established and emerging Bangladeshi artists.
“In a city with 36.6 million people, how do we stage something that will lure even 2% of the population when we have such few art spaces?” asks Rahman. “We want to balance the display of both Modern and contemporary art and encourage new and younger Bangladeshi collectors to invest in art.”
“For the first edition, I think we want to establish the fact that we have local patronage. We do have the calibre of artists and we have the organisational ability within ourselves and our curators to put on this show,” says Fahd Sattar, the founder of Aloki.
“We need to have cultural infrastructure between South Asian countries,” he adds, emphasising how future editions of the fair will incorporate the wider region. “This year we are focusing on Bangladeshi artists and the diaspora. Next edition, we could also venture out of Aloki to other areas of the city, and may open to international galleries and artists.”
While there is much hope the new hybrid-format fair will provide a needed boost for Dhaka’s art scene, it is taking place as the country continues to navigate a challenging socioeconomic and political landscape.
Following a historic general election on 12 February—which marked the first contested presidential election since October 1991 and resulted in a landslide victory for Tarique Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)—the nation is still finding its footing. The last few years in Bangladesh have been characterised by intense political turbulence and economic strain, particularly during the challenging democratic transition under an interim government following the ousting of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in 2024. Against this backdrop, Bangladesh’s art scene is undergoing a profound post-uprising transformation. Following the fall of Hasina’s government, the creative community has experienced a surge in politically engaged expression, alongside institutional restructuring and the formation of new international partnerships.
Globally, the Bangladesh art scene garnered much international interest due to the DAS, a biennial event staged by Bangladeshi collectors and patrons Nadia and Rajeeb Samdani. But the country’s challenging political landscape has created difficulties in staging the summit, with the last edition taking place in 2023.
“We have never censored any artist; you can’t censor artists,” says Rajeeb Samdani, emphasising that DAS cannot be staged in Bangladesh’s current political climate.
Most recently, transgender and feminist human rights activist Ho Chi Minh Islam was dropped as a speaker from the fifth Bay of Bengal Conversation in Dhaka, scheduled to take place on 5 October, following an intense online backlash. The event is an international forum on geopolitics, technology and governance, organised by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS).
A return for the summit
Rajeeb Samdani, who praises the inaugural Art Dhaka for the wealth of opportunities to be had for the Bangladeshi art scene, says he and Nadia hope to return to Bangladesh with the DAS in the next few years, once the challenging political landscape dissipates.
“It’s great an art fair is taking place in Dhaka as I think it is important for the city’s art ecosystem and the wider development of the art scene,” he says.
In the meantime, the Samdanis have been busy maintaining their programming abroad. This includes a multi-year partnership with the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, which includes a solo exhibition of Soma Surovi Jannat and the appointment of Munem Wasif as the inaugural visiting artist at the UK museum.
On 27 November the Kunsthalle Basel will present works by eight shortlisted finalists for the Samdani Art Award from Bangladesh alongside 16 artists from the wider Basel region in the exhibition Far Reach (until 2 January 2027).
The Samdanis’ much anticipated permanent space, Srihatta Samdani Art Center and Sculpture Park in Sylhet, will include permanent galleries and residency facilities. “We haven’t announced it publicly yet, but we started operations at the beginning of this year,” says Rajeeb.
During a period of uncertainty in Bangladesh, Samdani is hopeful. “It’s wonderful everyone is coming together during this period of transition,” he said, “We are looking forward to doing the summit sometime soon.”
• Art Dhaka, Aloki, Dhaka, 6-10 November

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.title: Democrats, Don’t Mess This Up
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.author: Natasha Lennard
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.text:
For two years, Donald Trump’s Republican Party has worked to push the United States further and further into a state of fascist rule. Trump’s regime has turned the federal government against ideological enemies, enriched and entrenched the power of billionaire allies, and done its utmost to decimate any checks and balances on the actions of the despotic leader and his loyalists.
It is, then, an extraordinary and overdue moment of relief to see the processes of democracy — however flawed in our barely representational system — offer the opportunity to take an off-ramp away from technocapital-backed fascism. Across the nation, Democrats secured historic victories. Even in Republican strongholds including Texas, Georgia, and South Carolina, voters delivered a rebuke to Trump’s GOP.
Democrats in Congress now have a mandate to do two things: Stop Trump, and improve the welfare of the U.S. working class. This should be understood as no less than a moral imperative to act immediately to curb the regime’s fascism in every possible way.
Americans are above all furious at the dire economic conditions in which they’re expected to struggle. The midterm results reflect a limit of Trumpian false consciousness: People know when they are poor, and they can see when billionaires, federal armed forces, genocidal governments, and presidential family members are profiting.
Despite their newfound congressional majority, Democrats now face an uphill battle to deliver legislation that will improve people’s material conditions. But that is not an excuse for inaction, mealy-mouthed gestures, or nods to bipartisanship. Democrats must push legislation that Republicans cannot stop, as well as legislation that Trump is all but sure to veto.
For one, Democrats must immediately roll back cuts to programs like Medicaid and supplemental nutritional programs. They must go further, too, and deliver on campaign promises for robust healthcare provisions, welfare spending, and restrictions on the ruinous depredations of Big Tech.
Trump bypassed Congress to prosecute his illegal war of choice on Iran, which has cost over $47 billion to date. But Congress has the power to curb military spending. Democrats must pass further resolutions to end the war, and they must pull the plug on military budget, directing funds instead to healthcare, housing, and investments in green infrastructure, to name a few urgent priorities. Though a flailing Trump finally announced that he would end military aid to Israel on Monday, it is Democrats who must pass further legislation to end all U.S. complicity in Israel’s apartheid regime and genocide.
Democrats must also propose laws to defund and abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement. This is no outlandish proposal; the impunity-drenched militia was only founded in 2003, and it is only by virtue of Congress that it now receives more funding than any other federal law enforcement agency. It is in Congress’s power to dismantle the agency and pass legislation to nullify the $170 billion-plus allocated to the border regime in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill.
Democrats should do whatever possible to roll back and end political prosecutions and the Trump administration’s brazen efforts to criminalize dissent.
The Democratic program must, in short, reject the austerity logics that have dominated the party for four decades. As sociologist Melinda Cooper has pointed out, and Trump’s Republicans have again and again proven, such austerity is not even austere: Pro-austerity governments since the Nixon administration in the 1970s have overseen lavish public spending in the shape of tax cuts and subsidies for holders of financial wealth (which does not trickle down), as well as funding for policing, border enforcement, prisons, and war machines. These are choices, and Democrats have been given a mandate to make choices that instead benefit — to revive a classic — the many, not the few.
Democrats such as Rep. Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., have stressed that their focus will be on the “affordability agenda” on which the party has run. This must include taking swift action to investigate and impeach the president and the worst offenders in his Cabinet, including Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In no way does insisting on accountability for Trump and his acolytes’ lawlessness distract from an economic focus. No affordability agenda can be achieved with an authoritarian executive in place. Challenging Trump’s despotism and self-dealing with every possible tool goes hand in hand with legislating to deliver on so-called kitchen-table issues.
Will Democrats in Congress, many of whom continue to reject the progressive and left-wing energies that have helped drive this blue wave, succeed in this anti-fascist political and economic agenda? No doubt, they will be thwarted at every turn by a desperate and dangerous executive and an embattled Republican minority. That is no reason to compromise, and constant pressure must be kept on Democrats who pretend otherwise. As the votes tonight make clear, in their millions, Americans know who to blame.

https://apache.be/2026/11/04/welke-impac.title: Welke impact heeft de Democratische overwinning bij de Amerikaanse midterms?
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/welke-impac.author: Redactie Apache
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/welke-impac.text:
De Democraten hebben overtuigend de midtermverkiezingen gewonnen. Hoe is hen dat gelukt? De verkiezingsuitslag laat zich niet zomaar in één conclusie vatten. In de aanloop naar de verkiezingen verschenen tal van analyses, die elk een ander licht werpen op de politieke verschuivingen. Om het overzicht te bewaren, selecteerde de redactie een aantal leestips die helpen de uitslag en zijn mogelijke gevolgen beter te begrijpen.
Amerikaanse media en opiniemakers klinken alvast eensluidend: de overwinning van de Democraten bij de midterms is zonder meer historisch te noemen. Ze overstijgt de voorspellingen die afgelopen weken werden gedaan. De Democratische partij behaalt zowel in de Kamer als de Senaat een meerderheid en kan zo de komende jaren extra druk leggen op het beleid van de Amerikaanse president Donald Trump.
Het valt op dat de Democraten de meerderheid konden halen in staten die traditioneel sterk naar de Republikeinse kant leunen. Voor het eerst sinds 1988 wint een Democratische kandidaat zo de senatorszetel in Texas. 
En ook de arts Abdul El-Sayed heeft geschiedenis geschreven door de veelbesproken verkiezingsstrijd in Michigan te winnen. Hij versloeg de Republikein Mike Rogers en werd daarmee de eerste moslimsenator in het land, ondanks de islamofobe campagne die tegen hem werd gevoerd.
Slecht nieuws voor Trump
Onder Donald Trump is de Amerikaanse strijd tegen corruptie zowel binnen als buiten de landsgrenzen drastisch ingeperkt. Door anticorruptiewetten af te zwakken, toezichthouders te ontslaan en internationale initiatieven af te bouwen, neemt het risico op fraude, machtsmisbruik en illegale geldstromen toe. Nu ze gewonnen hebben, krijgen de Democraten een ruim arsenaal aan middelen in handen om anticorruptie weer op de agenda te zetten, schrijft OCCRP. Toch is er een lange weg te gaan vooraleer ook zij het vertrouwen van de bevolking kunnen herwinnen.
Met de controle van zowel de Senaat als het Congres, kunnen de Democraten stokken voor de wielen steken van Trumps beleid. Het Witte Huis beschikt echter over veel middelen om zich te verweren, schrijft The insider. De machtsstrijd tussen de twee belangrijkste takken van de overheid dreigt vooral vast te lopen bij de derde macht: de rechterlijke macht. Historisch gezien lagen de kaarten daar vaker in het voordeel van het Witte Huis.
Impact op Oekraïne
The Kyiv Independent stelt de vraag hoe het Oekraïnebeleid van Trump zou kunnen veranderen, wanneer de Democraten het Huis en de Senaat veroveren. Buitenlandse zaken blijven een bevoegdheid van de president die zelfs de door de Democraten gecontroleerde kamers niet zomaar kunnen beïnvloeden. De belangrijkste verandering zou zijn dat pro-Oekraïense Republikeinen nu sneller zouden aansluiten bij bipartizane initiatieven
Ondertussen volgde ook Rusland met argusogen de verkiezingen. Hoewel analisten voorspellen dat een Democratische overwinning niet noodzakelijk Trumps buitenlandbeleid erg kan beïnvloeden, valt het Steve Rosenberg, Moskoucorrespondent bij de BBC, op dat Russische media benadrukken dat dat wel het geval zal zijn. Een manier om de schuld alvast niet in de schoenen van preisdent Poetin schuiven?
De gevolgen voor Europa
Welke gevolgen hebben deze uitslagen voor Europa en de Europese Unie? The Conversation wijst op twee belangrijke domeinen: veiligheid en handel. Europa ondervindt de economische gevolgen van de Amerikaanse oorlog in Iran, maar heeft slechts beperkte invloed op Amerikaanse beslissingen. Een Democratisch Congres zou het toezicht op militaire operaties kunnen verscherpen en kunnen beperken door via wetgevende initaiteven en begrotingsmaatregelen.
Wat met de techbro’s?
De Democraten zouden in het geval van een overwinning beter in staat moeten zijn om big tech in te tomen, schrijft The Guardian. De afkeer bij grote delen van de Amerikaanse bevolking tegen AI en de komst van datacenters speelde een belangrijke rol bij enkele lokale verkiezingsstrijden. De grote techbedrijven gooiden alle middelen in de strijd: hun financiële bijdrage aan verkiezingscampagnes was nog nooit zo groot.
De sponsorcampagne van de bigtechbedrijven lijkt alvast niet al te best uit te pakken. Volgens Tech Influence Watch ging de meerderheid van de financiële steun van de techbro’s naar kandidaten die vannacht verloren.
De Democratische golf van dinsdag zou kunnen leiden tot beperkingen voor datacenters en hogere belastingen voor bedrijven en topverdieners, en dat is al meteen voelbaar op de beurs, schrijft NBC News. De aandelenfutures – termijncontracten om aandelen aan te kopen - daalden dinsdagavond na de overtuigende overwinning van de Democraten. De omvang van de “blauwe golf” verrast beleggers, en dan vooral zij die in AI-bedrijven belegden.
Verzet tegen ICE
Opvallend veel latino kiezers brachten tijdens deze midterms hun stem uit en dat zou weleens aan het gewelddadige optreden van ICE hebben kunnen liggen, schrijft WIRED. Keert het migratiebeleid van Trump zich als een boomerang tegen hem?
It’s the economy, stupid
Nu de Democraten de verkiezingen wonnen, zullen ze worden opgezadeld met de economische problemen die op til zijn de komende jaren, schrijft Semafor. De overwinning kan dus ook slecht uitpakken: elk vastgelopen wetsvoorstel, elke shutdown en elk matig rapport over werkgelegenheid zou kunnen worden toegeschreven aan degenen die de wetgevende macht in handen hebben – de Democraten.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Women behind the lens: ‘I learned early what I was meant to become: a wife, a cook, a keeper of the home’
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Remofiloe Nomandla Mayisela
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
MilkMaid is part of my photographic series Lipservice, which stars Mrs Martha May, a contemporary makoti (a colloquial South African term for a wife). Mrs May is always dolled up, poised, ready to serve. Here she stands before a wall of long-life milk, face painted in the patches of a dairy cow, a crate balanced on her head. Rubber gloves, a frilled apron over shweshwe (coloured fabric). Milkmaid and milk, server and served, in one body.
The idea grows from the old line: the way to a man’s heart is through his stomach. In Lipservice the kitchen is a stage with food the script women are handed. Milk felt like the most intimate ingredient, the first thing a woman gives and the easiest to package and sell back. The carton reads like a job description: long life, full cream, UHT process. Made to last on a shelf. Stacked in repetition, the cartons speak to how women are consumed: branded, endlessly replaceable.
I was raised in a strong matriarchal household. I learned early what a woman is meant to become: a wife, a cook, a keeper of the home. My work began there, with coming of age and the quiet curriculum of the perfect woman. Who wrote it?
Mrs May is less an alter ego than an extension of that role I was raised to rehearse, played out loud.
I direct, style and do my own makeup, gather the props, set the self-timer and step into frame. Kitsch and pop colour keep it playful, so humour invites people close before they notice what they are looking at. The pinks are sweet. The idea underneath is not.
The term Makoti is popularly traced to the Afrikaans maak ons tee – “make us tea” – naming the wife as the one who serves.
Self-portraiture is how I tell this story honestly. The work speaks to many women, but I can only testify from my own body. It is auto-ethnography in a costume. She watches you watch her, and the gaze turns back to ask who the performance is really for.
Lipservice was the entry point. My practice is an ongoing investigation into the performance of womanhood, and the makoti is the role on a pedestal, held up as the ultimate goal, or so they say. That inquiry continues through my current research and a new body of work, Aftertaste.
MilkMaid laughs, but it also asks you to taste what you are being served. A bite of truth.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Vienna Recession? Four galleries in Austrian capital shut shop amid a tougher market
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Melanie Gerlis
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Vienna’s contemporary art scene seems to be collapsing. Three of its galleries—Layr, Exile and Zeller van Almsick—are either closing or “evolving”, all citing the unsustainability of running increasingly costly businesses in an unpredictable market. Meanwhile Eva Presenhuber, who opened a space in Vienna in 2022, has confirmed she is also leaving the Austrian capital amid a downturn in sales.
Those that have confirmed they are closing for good—Exile after 18 years and Zeller van Almsick after nearly ten—are clear-eyed. “There is no point in sugarcoating the fact that the past two years have been financially extremely challenging,” says Magdalena Zeller, a co-founder of Zeller van Almsick. For Christian Siekmeier, the founder of Exile, “there are simply no new collectors emerging”.
Emanuel Layr, who is closing his corner-hugging Layr gallery in favour of a more nomadic, project-based business (including a smaller, by-appointment space in Vienna), says: “The gallery model as we know it is increasingly reaching its limits.” The relentless commitments, to art fairs and the customary six-weekly exhibition, are not paying off. “It’s harder to sell some things, costs are getting higher, then there’s a big art fair coming and taking another €100,000,” he says. “I had to be more realistic, and think, ‘How much profit do I get? How much does the artist get?’.”
Yet Layr and his Viennese counterparts identify a groundswell of enthusiasm from younger generations. September’s new Astoria Artshow, an event held in Europe’s oldest garage (founded in 1918), was a hit, and notably from a young crowd. Its cash tills might not have been ringing, but galleries paid only €500 to participate so had much less to lose. The gallery-led gathering, which returns as a “fair” next year, seemed a breath of fresh air in the slot of previous events, such as Viennacontemporary, which is not showing any sign of returning.
A unique month-long festival
Long-time collectors were also fans of Astoria Artshow. “This will be the future,” says Eva Frey, who with her husband Manfred has been buying contemporary art for more than 30 years, and who sits on the board of Mumok, another bright spot in Vienna’s cultural offerings. Frey points out that the gallery closures will come after the city’s unique, month-long Curated By festival, supported by the city and state and which has been a boon to the contemporary art scene since it launched in 2009.
Frey says that the issue for Vienna’s cutting-edge galleries is that collectors of her vintage (which she defines as “over 70”) are not enough to keep business going. The problem, she says, is not so much the youngest generations, but that “there are fewer people between 45 and 55, who are established in a profession, and who used to be the main collectors in the market”. Layr finds too that “for middle-income professionals, there is less money around, so they are more careful”.
The middle-income strains seem a microcosm of what is happening in the wider art market
Many of the issues might be Vienna-related. It’s a small market and Zeller identifies “a significant gap between the cultural importance of the city and the depth of its local collector base”. But the middle-income strains seem a microcosm of what is happening in the wider art market, namely plenty of enthusiasm from the younger generations and a relative handful of older buyers keeping the top end just about managing. This requires a holding pattern of flexibility, at best, from the galleries who stick it out. For those that do, and can, hope rests on the juniors, but we just might have to wait a while to know if they can fill the gaps.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/vill.title: In California’s Central Valley, ICE Might Swing a Red District Blue
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/vill.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/vill.text:
In California’s Central Valley, some surprising voters are lining up behind a progressive upstart: A law enforcement officer who calls for the abolition of ICE. A millennial who once voted for a Republican congressman.
They found themselves among supporters of Randy Villegas, a Democrat poised to oust longtime incumbent Republican Rep. David Valadao in a district dominated for decades by conservatives in California’s Central Valley.
With Democratic victories across the nation, California’s 22nd Congressional District is the kind of historically red stronghold where progressive policies may find new purchase.
Villegas’s path to the general election mirrors that of other progressive candidates charting a new identity within the party. Running on policies such as Medicare for All, addressing affordability, rejecting corporate donations, and halting the flow of weapons to Israel, the 31-year-old defeated a moderate Democratic state assembly member backed by the party’s establishment in the June primary.
Villegas’s opposition to ICE in a district that is 70 percent Latino or Hispanic marked the sharpest point of contrast with Valadao, who defended the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant campaign and famously uttered “It is what it is” on the debate stage last month when pressed on the issue. Valadao claimed “a lot” of the individuals captured by ICE in the Central Valley in recent weeks have criminal records, despite research showing the majority of those detained by ICE lack criminal convictions.
It was Valadao’s stance on immigration that most animated Central Valley voters who spoke with The Intercept.
“I’ve never seen him stand up to something I feel is egregious,” said Raul Castro, 53, a Fresno County probation officer who is upset with Valadao’s lack of willingness to oppose Trump on the ICE raids surging through the area in recent weeks. “I just don’t respect people like that.”
While standing on the front porch of his house in a middle-class suburb in northwest Fresno, Castro lamented ICE’s targeting of immigrants based on their appearance, language, or jobs. He spoke out against immigration agents pulling people from the street and into labyrinthine detention centers where civil rights advocates have reported a lack of access to basic necessities such as clean water and adequate healthcare. Though Castro once supported ICE, when asked whether he would support abolishing the agency altogether, he said yes.
“If you asked me that same question, ‘Hey would you abolish ICE?’ I’d say, ‘No, ‘cause they’re doing things to make sure our country is safe. I want to live in a safe Fresno, safe county, safe city,’” Castro told The Intercept. “But now, wait a minute, maybe that’s not what I thought it was going to be.”
Villegas told The Intercept he wasn’t surprised to hear he had won the support of an anti-ICE law enforcement officer.
“I don’t find it surprising because I think ICE has made it much more difficult for local law enforcement to carry out their jobs and their work — and everybody is seeing the indiscriminate profiling going on,” Villegas said at a Fresno park rally to support last-minute canvassing efforts.
Villegas himself does not support abolishing ICE but instead has called for wide-ranging reforms of the agency. The policy position makes Villegas somewhat an anomaly among his progressive peers, who are riding a wave of leftist energy into Congress, some of whom include “Abolish ICE” among their campaign platforms.
While holding key endorsements from high-profile democratic socialists Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Villegas has also rejected the socialist label, preferring “populist,” despite attempts by the Republican national party to weaponize the term against him. Unlike many of his fellow progressives, Villegas is also one of the few who is running in a historically red district. And he’s confident voters are not caught up in the ideological nuances and hopes to instead cut through them.
“People are fed up with an agency who is unaccountable, people are fed up with a member of Congress who is unaccountable, who doesn’t even have public town halls,” Villegas said. “We deserve better than that in the Central Valley, and I think that’s why our messaging is resonating across the political spectrum.”
Such reach across the political spectrum is also evidenced in voters like Aram Easter, 33, who was born and raised in Fresno. He doesn’t vote in every election, but cast a ballot for Valadao a decade ago when his district previously covered Fresno, largely because he bought the vision of someone with local Central Valley roots (Valadao was born and raised in the nearby Hanford). He also agrees with some aspects of Trump’s agenda, such as building the border wall. But he drew the line on immigration enforcement.
“You got people tearing people’s families apart,” Easter said. “My family immigrated here — I have Black and Mexican family — I’m not with them overly-aggressively doing it.”
Since early October, ICE raids have become more prevalent in the region, with more than 200 people detained by authorities throughout the surge, according to the local newsroom Fresnoland. Similar upticks in ICE have taken place recently throughout the state, including Los Angeles and San Diego. Voter rights organizations in the Central Valley have taken notice and are viewing the raids as an effort by the Trump administration to suppress the vote, especially in a key race in the 22nd District.
“This timing of the uptick in ICE is not a coincidence,” said Marisa Moraza, political director at PowerCA Action, which is doing independent expenditure work to support Villegas’s campaign. “It’s not a coincidence that this started at the beginning of October when voters received their ballots in the mail.”
The raids have also suppressed get-out-the-vote efforts, Moraza said. Last month, the group had to pause in-person canvassing operations for several days amid the surge in ICE activity, electing to instead do phone banking.
The ICE activity is also keeping would-be voters from dropping off their ballots, as recent arrests of U.S. citizens struck fear among voters, said Cirilo Ordaz, a canvasser with PowerCA supporting Villegas.
“With going out to vote, I think a lot of them haven’t done it yet because of that fear,” said Ordaz, who was one of dozens of Villegas supporters who fanned out across the region on the Monday before Election Day to urge residents to vote.
Sylvia Ramirez, another Fresno native canvassing with PowerCA said she’s noticed far fewer people outside in recent weeks, including a lack of crowds at the popular annual event Big Fresno Fair. For voters, she and her group offer to drop off people’s ballots for them if the fear is keeping them inside.
“Offering the services of dropping off a ballot for somebody really helps out with the fear that people have of leaving their houses,” she said, adding that she has told her family to stay at home as much as possible in recent days to avoid interactions with ICE.
The Central Valley, known for its significant agriculture production, has been the seat of high-profile Republican lawmakers, such as former Rep. Devin Nunes and former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy.
But after a Democrat-led redistricting in the state last year in response to Texas’s partisan redistricting effort, the district now includes the northwest sections of Fresno, a city with more Democrats.
Early voting across the state has outpaced recent midterm elections, according to a recent survey. It’s unclear how much of that is anti-Trump animus or having a candidate voters are excited to support.
Castro, the probation officer, was among those who voted early. In recent weeks, he said he noticed residents looking at him with concern while on the job in uniform, showing up at areas where ICE had previously conducted raids. It’s a fear he acutely understood. As a child, he lived in labor camps with his mother and father, who were both undocumented immigrants working in Fresno as farm laborers. He recalled similar indiscriminate sweeps by Border Patrol in the 1970s.
“When I was small, back then it was Border Patrol, and they used to show up in a van,” Castro recalled. “All the agents used to get out and run after these guys. And they used to round them up and take them out,” he said.
Seeing video and hearing of recent ICE raids targeting farmworkers in the area conjured such painful memories.
“I never thought I’d see that again,” he said.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://apache.be/2026/11/04/vlaamse-ado.title: Vlaamse adoptiedienst verzon fabel van Nepalese tapijtkinderen
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/vlaamse-ado.author: Hari Prasad Sacré
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/vlaamse-ado.text:
De Vlaamse adoptiedienst Interadoptie haalde kinderen uit Nepal om hen zogezegd te redden van kinderarbeid in de tapijtfabrieken. Maar hun broers en zussen bleven in Nepal, en geen van hen werd ooit een tapijtkind. Documenten tonen dat de dienst bewust kinderen met familie koos, en dat toezichthouder Kind en Gezin daarvan op de hoogte was.
Interadoptie bracht in de jaren 90 zeven kinderen uit Nepal naar Vlaanderen, officieel om hen te behoeden voor kinderarbeid in de tapijtfabrieken. Ik ben een van hen en ik ken het verhaal van vijf anderen. Elk van ons had nog familie, waaronder minstens één ouder en broers en zussen. Bovendien bevat mijn eigen dossier onjuiste en vervalste informatie en heeft mijn eerste moeder nooit toestemming gegeven voor adoptie.
Via het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie kreeg ik inzage in mijn adoptiedossier en in de briefwisseling tussen Interadoptie, Kind en Gezin en de bemiddelaar S.S. in Nepal, tussen 1992 en 2000. Die documenten tonen hoe de fabel van de tapijtkinderen de wanpraktijken verhulde.
“Rijp voor kinderhandel”
Dat er in Nepal risico’s waren, wist de adoptiedienst al vroeg. In een verslag aan Kind en Gezin uit 1994 schrijft Interadoptie: “Dit land is duidelijk ‘rijp’ voor kinderhandel en private adoptie.”
Elk van de kinderen die Interadoptie naar Vlaanderen bracht had nog familie, waaronder minstens één ouder en broers en zussen
De dienst stelt daarom voor om de Belgische ambassade en Bal Mandir, het staatsweeshuis in de hoofdstad Kathmandu, te verwittigen dat adopties niet privaat mogen gebeuren. Zo wil men irreguliere adopties buiten de erkende diensten om tegenhouden. Maar de waakzaamheid richt zich enkel naar buiten. Het eigen kanaal blijft buiten schot.
Want in hetzelfde verslag staat ook dit:
“Onze gevolmachtigde ter plaatse […] overweegt nu en dan een adoptie van een half-weeskind of achtergelaten kind in een hospitaal. De wachtlijsten met Bal Mandir schieten niet op en hun briefwisseling spreekt enkel concreet over donaties voor hun tehuizen.”
Lees die zinnen samen en de redenering wordt zichtbaar. De officiële weg naar wezen zat vast, en andere organisaties boden hogere donaties. Dus zocht de dienst een andere weg. Via de contactpersoon die Bal Mandir voor Interadoptie had aangeduid, mevrouw S.S., kwamen kinderen buiten het weeshuis in beeld. In de zes adopties die ik ken, ging het altijd om half-wezen. Deze kinderen hebben nog een levende ouder, broers, zussen en grootouders.
De fabel van de tapijtkinderen
Hoe verantwoordde de dienst haar keuzes? Een inspectieverslag van 1994 rapporteert de motivatie van de dienst als volgt:
“In Nepal wordt de adoptiedienst echter geconfronteerd met het feit dat de kinderen in de weeshuizen dikwijls een beter leven hebben dan de kinderen die bij hun ouders verblijven. […] ‘Tapijtkinderen’ worden al vanaf 6 jaar tewerkgesteld in tapijtfabrieken […]. Om die reden en in het belang van het kind opteert de adoptiedienst ervoor om geen kinderen uit weeshuizen te adopteren maar wel kinderen die het risico lopen om in zo'n tapijtfabriek te worden tewerkgesteld.”
Kinderarbeid in de Nepalese tapijtindustrie was in de jaren 90 echt. Het kreeg internationaal ook veel aandacht. Dat maakt de fabel zo overtuigend. Een goede fabel heeft altijd een kern van waarheid. Maar de adoptiedienst gebruikte het beeld van de tapijtkinderen en kinderarbeid om kinderen los te wrikken van functionerende families met een slinkse retoriek.
De adoptiedienst gebruikte het beeld van de tapijtindustrie om kinderen los te wrikken van functionerende families met een slinkse retoriek
Nepalese gezinnen worden in dat beeld neergezet als een risico-omgeving. Kinderen in een weeshuis zouden het beter hebben dan kinderen die opgroeien bij hun ouders. De adoptiedienst slaagt er zo in om de logica dat een kind bij zijn familie hoort volledig om te draaien. Het Nepalese gezin wordt verdacht gemaakt en opgevoerd als een omgeving waaruit het kind gered moet worden.
Daarnaast verschuift de focus van weeskinderen naar risicokinderen met familie. De dienst kiest uitdrukkelijk niet voor kinderen uit weeshuizen. Wie bewust geen wezen adopteert, adopteert intentioneel kinderen die nog familie hebben. Zo komen kwetsbare gezinnen die door een moeilijke periode gaan plots in het vizier van transnationale adoptie.
Tot slot sluit het gezegde ‘in het belang van het kind’ elk kritisch gesprek uit. Wie dat argument inroept, maakt tegenspraak moeilijk. Wie kan er tegen zijn dat een kind niet in een fabriek moet gaan werken?
Broers en zussen nooit actief in de tapijtindustrie
Wij, Nepalees geadopteerden, kennen elkaar. Van zes van ons ken ik het verhaal en de families. Telkens gaat het om kinderen die werden weggehaald uit families waar ze nog ouders, grootouders, broers en zussen hadden. Die broers en zussen bleven in Nepal. Geen van hen kwam ooit in een tapijtfabriek terecht. Het risico waarvan wij gered moesten worden, was nooit een reëel gevaar in hun leven.
Het risico waarvan de geadopteerden gered moesten worden, was nooit een reëel gevaar in het leven van hun broers en zussen
Dat de redenering rond de tapijtkinderen niet klopte, zag Interadoptie trouwens zelf in. In een brief aan mijn adoptieouders uit 1994 schrijft de dienst: “Men kan zich wel afvragen wat er met de andere kinderen gebeurt.”
Daarmee erkent de dienst het gat in het eigen verhaal. Als één kind gered moest worden van de tapijtfabriek, gold dat risico evengoed voor zijn broers en zussen. Toch bleven zij in hetzelfde gezin, met dezelfde ouders en dezelfde armoede. Dat Interadoptie hen liet waar ze waren, toont dat de adopties nooit een antwoord waren op het risico van kinderarbeid.
De geadopteerde bleef achter met de vraag waarom net hij of zij weg moest, terwijl de broers en zussen bij hun ouders konden opgroeien. Op die vraag heeft het reddersverhaal geen antwoord.
Internationale basisregel niet gerespecteerd
Dat het ook anders kon, blijkt uit een verslag van een vergadering met de vicevoorzitter van Bal Mandir in oktober 1996. Bal Mandir adopteerde lange tijd enkel wezen. “Sinds kort komen ook verlaten kinderen in aanmerking, maar enkel als ze niet door familieleden kunnen opgevangen worden.”
De vicevoorzitter van Bal Mandir noemde de private adopties via ngo’s “handel”, winstbejag zonder projecthulp of nazorg
Het officiële Nepalese kanaal zocht dus eerst naar familie. Bal Mandir paste daarmee toe wat internationaal als basisregel geldt. Een kind komt namelijk pas in aanmerking voor adoptie in het buitenland als zorg in de eigen familie of gemeenschap onmogelijk is. De Speciale VN-rapporteur voor de verkoop van kinderen rekent in een rapport uit 2016 het negeren van dat principe tot de praktijken die van een adoptie een verkoop van kinderen maken.
De bemiddelaar van Interadoptie, mevrouw S.S., koos telkens voor kinderen die nog familie hadden. In hetzelfde gesprek noemt de vicevoorzitter van Bal Mandir de private adopties via ngo’s “handel”, namelijk winstbejag zonder projecthulp of nazorg. Ook Interadoptie volgde die private weg bij zeker zes van de zeven dossiers. Dat die weg niet zonder risico was, wist de dienst zelf. In het verslag van de vergadering schrijft Interadoptie dat adoptiegezinnen bij private adopties “voor moeilijkheden kunnen komen te staan” bij het Nepalese ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken, “zoals bij onze twee laatste dossiers”.
Nazorg als ‘controle’
Ook na de adoptie bleef het reddingsverhaal de keuzes van de dienst bepalen. Een inspectieverslag van Kind en Gezin uit 1993 beschrijft hoe Interadoptie omging met nazorg:
“Nepal vraagt nazorgrapporten tot het kind 18 jaar is. Er worden hiervoor geen huisbezoeken gebracht. Inspectie deelde mee dat dit geen nazorg is […]. De adoptiedienst stelde dat als er problemen zijn bij de adoptiegezinnen zij dit wel verneemt, van de groepsverantwoordelijken […]. Bovendien is er ook een financieel probleem. Wie zal deze huisbezoeken betalen? En zullen adoptanten dit als een controle beschouwen.”
Het comfort van de adoptieouders woog zwaarder dan de noden van het kind
Nepal vroeg opvolging tot het kind volwassen was. Interadoptie zag geen nood aan huisbezoeken. Problemen zou de dienst wel horen via de groepsverantwoordelijken, adoptieouders die per land activiteiten organiseerden. Daarnaast speelden de kosten en de vrees dat adoptanten bezoeken als controle zouden ervaren. Het comfort van de adoptieouders woog zo zwaarder dan de noden van het kind. De dienst beloofde nadien de nazorg beter uit te bouwen, maar de huisbezoeken zijn er nooit gekomen.
De nood aan nazorg was er wel degelijk. Deze kinderen waren weggehaald bij familie die bleef bestaan en moesten met dat verlies leren leven. Het reddingsverhaal liet daar geen ruimte voor. Wie als gered wordt voorgesteld, krijgt immers weinig ruimte om verlies te verwerken.
Wat deed de toezichthouder?
Kind en Gezin wist van bij het begin van de risico’s in Nepal. Volgens een inspectieverslag uit 1993 begon de samenwerking met Nepal “op vraag van kandidaat-adoptanten […], die absoluut een Nepalees kindje wilden adopteren”. Toen dat koppel na zes maanden nog geen toewijzing had, wilde het toch vertrekken. “De verantwoordelijke van de adoptiedienst kon hen niet tegenhouden.”
Niet de nood van een kind in Nepal, maar de wens van Vlaamse adoptanten zette de samenwerking met Nepal in gang
Het is een schoolvoorbeeld van wat het Vlaamse expertenpanel rond transnationale adoptie in 2021 vaststelde, namelijk dat het systeem vraaggestuurd was. Niet de nood van een kind in Nepal, maar de wens van Vlaamse adoptanten zette de samenwerking met Nepal in gang.
De toezichthouder ontving ook het verslag waarin Interadoptie Nepal “rijp” noemde voor kinderhandel. De eigen inspectie noteerde dat de dienst in dat land bewust geen wezen adopteerde, maar kinderen met familie. Waarom greep de toezichthouder niet in?
Na zeven adopties stopte Interadoptie de samenwerking met Nepal. Uit de documenten blijkt niet waarom. Wel valt op dat de stopzetting kwam kort nadat de private route problemen opleverde in twee dossiers bij de Nepalese overheid.
Hari Prasad Sacré dankt de binnenlands geadopteerden die gestreden hebben voor het inzagerecht. “Zonder hun moedige strijd had ik deze analyse niet kunnen schrijven. Daarnaast dank ik de medewerkers van het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie. Ik ervaarde een grote bereidheid en zorgvuldigheid om de documenten te verzamelen en ter beschikking te stellen.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/jame.title: Even Anti-Trans Panic Couldn’t Save Republicans in Deep-Red Texas
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/jame.author: Akela Lacy, Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/jame.text:
On an election night handing Republicans a beating in critical House and Senate races across the country, the GOP fell short even in once deep-red Texas after a campaign run on a go-to outrage tactic: fearmongering over the rights of transgender people.
Democrats escaped the political wilderness in the Longhorn State on Tuesday night, when Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton — despite the far-right attorney general’s relentless attacks on the trans community and his party’s claims that Democrats would enforce so-called “transgenderism” as a kind of ideology.
The massive upset was paired with a victory for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, who beat Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott shortly after the Senate race was called for Talarico.
In Dallas, Paxton voter Rachel Fuller told The Intercept she was alarmed by what she believed was Talarico’s support for “far-fetched” ideas, like “giving children the right to decide — and making parents, calling them abusive for not letting them have transgender changes.”
Her comments suggested some of the $78 million Republicans spent on anti-trans attack advertisements in Texas were working. But they weren’t enough to help Republicans hold onto power in Texas, which hasn’t had a Democratic senator since the 1990s.
The ads made up almost half of all ad spending in support of Paxton, according to an analysis from Puck using data from AdImpact.
By and large, the ads spread blatant misinformation about Talarico’s record.
One infamous $29 million ad created by Texas PAC, a political action committee primarily funded by billionaire Elon Musk, claimed that Talarico supported jailing parents who did not support gender-affirming surgeries for minors. “Every mom in Texas should be worried about James Talarico putting parents in jail if they do not support surgically transitioning their children,” a woman in the ad warned ominously.
That attack, which according to Puck received 1.9 billion views as of October, does seem to have caught the attention of Texans — even with voters who ultimately supported Talarico.
Julius Ishola, a canvasser for Black TOP, an operation under Texas Organizing Project that targets Black voters, told The Intercept he had frequently heard Black voters raise concerns that Talarico intended to jail parents.
“I’ve been getting a lot of bad feedback regarding James Talarico,” Ishola told The Intercept, saying many voters cited concerns of “gender sex change and possibly prosecuting parents who go against that … and allowing transgenders into female restrooms.”
As a state legislator, Talarico fought bans on transgender athletes’ participation in youth sports, and famously said that God is “nonbinary,” earning him ridicule from Republicans, who nicknamed the Senate candidate “Talafreako.” In the face of those attacks this cycle, Talarico appeared to backtrack on the issue, telling Fox News in September that he supported bans on transgender children’s participation in sports if it risks “safety or fairness” — without clarifying what that meant.
His wavering does not seem to have reached many voters.
“I voted Republican all the way. And that’s my fear of Talarico going in,” said Carol Billings, a voter who cast her ballot for Paxton at the Living Waters Church in Dallas County. Like Fuller, she cited her perception of the Democratic nominee’s trans policies as a major source for concern.
Still, many voters in Black districts, which were vital to Talarico’s victory, barely mentioned Talarico.
“At the end of the day,” said Dallas Jones, a Houston-based Democratic political strategist whose firm focuses on African American voter engagement and backed Talarico, “the results show that people care more about their everyday lives than they do about trans Americans who just want to get by.”
Some voters told The Intercept they were far more concerned with issues of affordability. “ I just hope we can get these gas prices down,” said Darryl Moore, a Fort Worth voter.
This is a developing story and will be updated. Akela Lacy reported from Dallas, Texas.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
