https://www.propublica.org/article/lake-.title: Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back.
https://www.propublica.org/article/lake-.author: Jonathan Mingle, John Dillon
https://www.propublica.org/article/lake-.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Falling Behind: After a decade and nearly a billion dollars, the EPA says Vermont is “not on track” to meet its phosphorus reduction goals.
- Some Parts Getting Worse: Seven of Lake Champlain’s 15 sampling stations have exceeded the EPA’s annual phosphorus limits every year since 2015.
- Policies Pushed Back: Vermont has delayed tightening farm regulations, requiring property owners to control stormwater and fixing a system in which two agencies oversee farm pollution.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
On the last day of August, Jeff van den Noort spotted thick swirls of neon green film coating the water just steps from his home in Vermont. He waded in up to his ankles and dipped a jar to get a sample of the scum.
It wasn’t the first time he’d seen the slime. Since his parents bought the house on an island in Lake Champlain in 1966, van den Noort has spent part of nearly every summer in this quiet spot. Back then, the lake was clear.
But he began to witness the water’s deterioration as he grew older, especially after he moved into the home full time in 2010 to care for his ailing mother. That day in late August was the worst he’d seen all summer.
Later that week, van den Noort grabbed a bucket, a few Mason jars and a smartphone and got into his rusty Saab. He drove past the boat launches, frozen-in-time general stores and windswept pastures of the lake’s islands in northern Vermont and stopped at four other spots along the shore. Each time, he collected some murky water, gauged how thick the muck was, took a few photos and jotted down the weather conditions. He then uploaded his report to an online database.
Van den Noort was one part of a large volunteer effort to monitor a problem that has plagued Lake Champlain, which supplies drinking water to about 200,000 people. In recent decades, blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria, often called blue-green algae, have killed pets, forced beaches to close and hurt business and property values along the shores of this iconic Vermont feature.
“I just don’t feel like enough is being done,” van den Noort said. “And I think the state needs to take this seriously.”
Just over a decade ago, state leaders seemed to be doing just that. In 2015, then-Gov. Peter Shumlin stood a few feet from Lake Champlain by the Burlington waterfront and signed Vermont’s Clean Water Act. It promised to tighten limits on pollution and provide funding to clean up the state’s waterways.
The move was a response to ratcheting pressure from environmentalists and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA had been telling Vermont officials for years that they needed to take much stronger action. In 2016, the agency finalized tougher cleanup targets that the state must meet by 2036.
But after 10 years and nearly a billion dollars spent on water quality projects and programs, Vermont’s cleanup effort is faltering. In a little-noticed letter to the head of Vermont’s Department of Environmental Conservation last year, the EPA’s regional administrator warned that the state was “not on track” to meet its cleanup goal and would need to more than double its annual pace.
Halfway through the two-decade timetable, Vermont has achieved only 35% of the goal, according to the state’s most recent estimates. And the steps that Vermont has taken to get there, such as upgrading sewage treatment plants, represent “low-hanging fruit,” Eric Perkins, a former EPA official involved in setting the target, wrote in an email in response to questions from Seven Days and ProPublica.
The culprit behind these blooms is phosphorus, an element that is an essential building block of life, present in all organic matter. But too much of it has been pouring into the lake from farm fields saturated with fertilizer and manure, dirty stormwater, and raw sewage from treatment plants overwhelmed by heavy rains. That has tipped the lake’s ecosystem out of balance, spurring the growth of microorganisms that turn shallow bays and shorelines into no-go zones.
Ingesting cyanobacteria-laden water can cause vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and liver damage, while skin contact can lead to rashes. Researchers have also detected possible links between chronic exposure to cyanobacteria and heightened risk of Parkinson’s disease and ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. The algae blooms can also deprive fish and other aquatic life of oxygen.
While some areas of Lake Champlain have seen incremental improvements in phosphorus concentrations and cyanobacteria blooms, other parts of the lake are getting worse. Seven of the lake’s 15 sampling stations have exceeded the EPA’s annual phosphorus limits every year since 2015, a Seven Days and ProPublica analysis of lake monitoring data through 2025 shows. Four stations recorded higher average phosphorus levels over the past decade than in the decade before, including in the southern part of the lake and its northeast arm.
In September, the Department of Environmental Conservation reported to the EPA that in two northeastern sections of the lake most chronically plagued by phosphorus runoff, the state is not nearly on track to meet its targets. The department specifically acknowledged that it was not making enough progress in addressing stormwater runoff and that reductions in farm pollution in the Missisquoi River watershed have slowed since 2023.
Vermont shares the 120-mile-long lake with New York and Quebec, but it’s the source of about two-thirds of the phosphorus that flows into the water body. Agriculture is the largest polluting sector, while stormwater runoff from development, like urban parking lots and rural roads, contributes the highest amount of phosphorus per acre.
State agencies have repeatedly delayed taking more difficult and politically fraught action to crack down on pollution from farms, businesses and housing developments. Policies around them have encountered resistance from the dairy industry, property owners and lawmakers sympathetic to their interests.
The challenges in cleaning up Lake Champlain raise a salient question: If a small, conservation-minded state like Vermont can’t tackle this problem, what does that mean for other areas of the United States grappling with algae blooms in the Great Lakes, the Chesapeake Bay and the Gulf of Mexico?
State officials counsel patience as they remind Vermonters it will take more time to solve the problem.
“We are moving apace with the commitments we’ve made, in terms of the projects, but it isn’t manifesting itself nearly as quickly in the lake monitoring data,” said Julie Moore, Agency of Natural Resources secretary. “This is a complex ecosystem, and we need to come at this work with a whole lot of humility.”
Leaders of the Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets said it will take time for investments, such as programs to reduce soil erosion and help farmers upgrade their manure storage equipment, to pay off.
“The first five years, we were really developing an enormous amount of programs,” said Laura DiPietro, the agency’s water quality program director, but implementing them “doesn’t happen overnight.” She said she expects to see greater phosphorus reductions resulting from them in the coming decade.
But for van den Noort, the blooms are increasingly hard to ignore.
“The worst days ever are really, really bad,” he said. “Just as far as you can see, the whole bay is green.”
Pushing the Limits
Unlike chemicals and heavy metals, which can be removed from lakes and rivers with dredging, phosphorus isn’t technically or economically feasible to extract.
So environmental regulators focus instead on limiting the amount of phosphorus that flows into the water each day. It’s like putting the lake on a diet. The EPA sets what’s known as the total maximum daily load, a target based on the agency’s determination of how much phosphorus the lake can absorb and remain healthy. To meet that goal, the state must cut pollution from agriculture, stormwater drains, roads, forests and wastewater treatment plants.
The EPA had set previous targets for Lake Champlain in 2002, but, concerned that Vermont wasn’t taking strong enough measures, the agency set tougher ones in 2016. For the first few years after those targets were updated, Perkins, who was then the EPA’s Vermont water quality coordinator, felt that the state was generally on the right track.
During his tenure, state agencies and lawmakers set up the Clean Water Fund to finance water quality projects and dedicated tax revenue streams to support it. They put in place stronger rules for fertilizer use and manure storage on farms. They created permit programs to limit stormwater runoff from roads and municipalities. That progress was reflected in a 2020 report card the EPA issued, acknowledging that Vermont had checked off all the milestones up to that point.
“Overall, I was very impressed with the level of commitment demonstrated by the state,” Perkins wrote to Seven Days and ProPublica.
By the time Perkins retired in 2021, he and colleagues at the EPA had become concerned about signs of lagging commitment by Vermont’s agencies to water quality enforcement on farms.
One clear opportunity to speed up phosphorus reductions, according to Perkins, is to ensure farms comply with required agricultural practices and avoid spreading manure before anticipated rainstorms, which has caused “major phosphorus runoff events.”
If the state and farm operators were to make that a priority, “it could likely make a big difference,” Perkins wrote. And the state could encourage that practice by overhauling its permitting system to tighten water quality requirements and enforcement for farms that keep animals confined in barns for long periods of time. Those farms are called concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs. In recent years, many small family dairies in Vermont have closed or consolidated into larger operations that would be considered CAFOs under federal law.
Yet Vermont has delayed action on an EPA directive to strengthen its approach to regulating CAFOs. Just across the lake, New York has used such permits for decades to ensure better environmental practices on larger farms. In Vermont, a recent state task force report recommended working to develop this program for another five years.
A second, related reform the EPA has recommended is to change who leads regulation of those farms.
Vermont has two different agencies that oversee farm pollution. The Agency of Agriculture regulates how farms handle waste on site, while the Agency of Natural Resources is responsible if runoff from that waste leaves the farm. This split responsibility has caused oversight problems, including lapses in following up on reported water quality violations with inspections and enforcement actions. Environmental advocates have long maintained that the agriculture agency has a conflict because it also has a mandate to promote the state’s farm sector.
This arrangement frustrates farmers, too. In a letter to Gov. Phil Scott earlier this year, owners of one Vermont dairy farm wrote that “the lack of alignment and clear communication between these agencies” places farmers in an uncertain position. “Many in the farming community feel caught in the middle of interagency disagreements, unsure which standards will ultimately govern their operations or how enforcement will proceed,” they wrote.
In interviews, officials at the two agencies acknowledged those communication problems but said that they have taken steps to improve how they share information on potential violations and coordinate more closely on inspections.
In 2024, the EPA ordered Vermont to consolidate the regulation of agricultural pollution under the Agency of Natural Resources, Vermont’s main environmental agency, which the EPA says has sole authority to administer federal Clean Water Act rules.
In a letter that year to Moore, the agency’s secretary, EPA Region 1 administrator David Cash noted that the EPA had monitored the situation in Vermont for well over a decade. “And despite having had ample time and opportunity to cure longstanding program deficiencies,” he wrote, “ANR has failed to do so.” Cash noted that the state has failed to give ANR “sufficient resources or operational authority” to regulate runoff from farms.
Hovering over this back-and-forth is the threat that the federal government could take over enforcement of water pollution rules from Vermont.
Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms.
Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to investigate the cleanup of Lake Champlain. Have you been affected by this issue? We’d like to hear from you.
Following the letter to Moore, the divisions between the two agencies were on display as they discussed their regulatory approach in internal emails obtained under Vermont’s Public Records Act by Seven Days and ProPublica. In a 2025 email, Agency of Natural Resources general counsel Catherine Gjessing reminded her counterpart at the agriculture agency and legislative counsel staff that “there are a significant number of farms that are in fact discharging without a permit” in violation of the federal Clean Water Act. She added that the two agencies had been working under this split responsibility arrangement, with the agriculture agency taking the lead, “for decades now and we are still not in compliance.”
In an interview, the agriculture agency’s general counsel, Steve Collier, said there was never “a Wild West situation where farms were not being regulated” and that his agency’s rules protected the environment. “Whether or not the Clean Water Act was being administered exactly as it should be is a different issue,” he said.
Outside of agriculture, Vermont has yet to fully implement a third EPA demand as well as the directives of its own Clean Water Act. That 2015 law mandated the Department of Environmental Conservation to require properties with 3 or more acres of paved surface, such as parking lots, to install systems to slow and capture stormwater runoff.
Five years later, when the department still hadn’t finalized this “3-acre rule” permit system, the EPA warned Vermont that it would have to give the state “a failing grade” if it didn’t do so by Sept. 4, 2020. Vermont met the EPA’s deadline but in 2025 passed a law pushing the date for getting permits to 2028 for properties in the Champlain basin.
And those property owners don’t need to make the stormwater upgrades until 2033.
Treading Water
For a quarter century, Steve Cushing has been advocating to clean up St. Albans Bay in the northeast part of Lake Champlain near the epicenter of Vermont’s dairy industry. Throughout that time, he listened as federal and state environmental officials came through town and pledged to act. “Expect a lot of progress 10 years from now in many segments of the lake,” one EPA official told him and his neighbors in 2015.
A decade later, this summer’s cyanobacteria blooms in the shallow bay were some of the worst he’s seen in several years, he said. Since June, the public beach in the St. Albans Bay Park has mostly been closed to swimming.
“Overall, you can’t really see a big improvement in water quality in the bay,” Cushing said.
Public data supports that notion. Every three years the federally funded Lake Champlain Basin Program, which coordinates research and grantmaking across the lake’s watershed, issues a report summarizing its water quality monitoring.
Its most recent edition, from 2024, revealed “deteriorating” trends in the northeast arm of the lake for both phosphorus and cyanobacteria and no progress in Missisquoi Bay, a shallow stretch spanning the U.S.-Canada border that frequently suffers intense blooms.
That’s troubling, scientists and advocates say, because the failure to address new pollution is exacerbated by both historical pollution and the effects of climate change.
What scientists call “legacy phosphorus” has accumulated in soils and lake sediments after many decades of fertilizer use, manure spreading, deforestation and unregulated septic and wastewater systems.
“We are working on a system that’s been impacted by human activities for the past 150-plus years,” said Matthew Vaughan, the chief scientist of the basin program.
Climate change poses another headwind for the lake cleanup. Since 2003, cyanobacteria blooms have appeared earlier in the spring and later in the fall as temperatures rise, and even at lower phosphorus levels. The drought that hit Vermont in 2025 led to a spike in blooms, thanks to the combination of heat and low water levels. Meanwhile, downpours are turning Vermont’s streams and rivers into fire hoses of phosphorus-laden sediment: In just one week in July 2023, record-shattering floods pumped six months worth of phosphorus into the lake.
“All of this just makes it more urgent to do our part to address these water quality challenges,” Vaughan said.
Some state officials and researchers contend that phosphorus deposited in the lake bed and soil decades ago might play as significant a role in fueling algae blooms as today’s runoff.
But while legacy phosphorus remains a challenge, “I think it’d be wrong to just rely on that as the excuse,” said Eric Smeltzer, who worked for the Department of Environmental Conservation for 35 years, including as the state limnologist who monitors the health of Vermont’s lakes and ponds.
“The most important technical question about the Lake Champlain phosphorus cleanup is: Are these practices working? And if not, why not?” Smeltzer said. “How can it be done better? I think you can’t just explain it away based on time lags and legacy phosphorus forever.”
In reviewing the state’s data recently, one detail in particular jumped out to him, he said. Wastewater treatment still garners an outsize share of Vermont’s clean water spending, even though it has been clear for years that it’s not a major contributor of phosphorus, while agriculture and stormwater are.
Cushing traces the algae blooms back to the dairy farms that dominate the watershed and to regulators’ failure to “put any teeth behind” restrictions on manure spreading and other water quality rules.
Cushing, a former dairy farmer, has pushed for policy changes as a volunteer with the St. Albans Area Watershed Association and has led an effort to mechanically remove vegetation that contributes to the phosphorus problem in his overburdened bay.
At 78, he is now searching for someone to take over the weed removal effort. “I’m getting a little burned out,” he admitted.
Seven miles to the west, on the island of North Hero, van den Noort questioned this summer whether all the data he gathers is making any difference.
“If we really wanted to solve the problem, I think we’d have to make some tough choices,” he said. “I don’t think anybody wants to do that. It’s a head-in-the-sand thing.”
Every week, van den Noort drives up the western edge of Isle La Motte on his monitoring circuit, looking out over a stretch of water that is supposed to be one of the cleanest parts of Lake Champlain. On the worst days, a pea green broth of blooms stubbornly hugs its entire shoreline.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Scenes From a Democratic Earthquake In Iowa
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Chris Lehmann
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Scenes From a Democratic Earthquake in Iowa
The state was a MAGA citadel. Not anymore.
Des Moines, Iowa—“All along I’ve said Iowa was the center of the political universe,” Josh Turek, the Hawkeye State’s newly elected Democratic senator, told a giddy election-night crowd on Tuesday. “And man, did we prove that tonight.”
Some hyperbolic Hawkeye pride was more than a little pardonable on a night when the so-called “blue tsunami” swept Democrats into power across the country. But Turek was not wrong to highlight what was happening in Iowa. This is a state that Donald Trump carried by 13 points just two years ago, and that, thanks to a GOP-dominated statehouse and legislature, had earned the moniker “Florida of the North” for its firmly DeSantis-like lurch into a regressive, deregulatory, and woke-baiting governing agenda. It was supposed to be a firewall in the Republican Party’s doomed fight to hold on to its Senate majority. Millions in super PAC donations and vicious attack ads had flooded the state. And Turek still won.
Not only that: Rob Sand, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, captured the statehouse for the party for the first time since 2010, and Democrats also took three of the state’s four congressional seats. All those winning candidates were women—another historic breakthrough in an evening full of them.
At the same time, Iowa’s repudiation of the MAGA disease in American politics was very, well, Iowan—which is to say, humble, neighborly, and civically optimistic. I grew up in eastern Iowa, and when I moved to the West Coast, I soon learned that greeting passersby on the street was regarded not as welcoming but creepy. The obsessive punctuality and the usage of honorifics that had been drilled into me as a kid likewise were regarded as quaint throwback rituals—virtual stage directions in a community-theater production of Our Town.
But Turek, like most Iowans, is still very much at home in these traditions. Even after the bruising campaign he waged against GOP Representative Ashley Hinson, he stressed that “I have deep respect for anyone who steps up to run.” (Some Iowans in the crowd were admittedly less generous, greeting the mention of Hinson’s name with a smattering of boos.) In his speech—delivered at the ur-Iowan venue of the state historical society—Turek addressed the state in the familiar second person, as in “Now, Iowa, let us be the city on the hill—the Iowa we grew up in that was the envy of the nation…. Iowa, this is where our comeback begins.”
At the same time, Turek also channeled the capital-P Populist tradition that has decisively shaped the state’s politics over the past century. Near the end of his speech, he called former US senator Tom Harkin to the podium, telling the crowd how Harkin had “changed my life” by working to secure passage of the Americans with Disabilities Act (Turek is wheelchair-bound, having contracted spina bifida in the womb after his father was exposed to Agent Orange in the Vietnam War). Harkin also embodied the crusade to secure fair and equal representation to working-class Americans, Turek explained—a cause that now served as “the North Star” of his own politics.
In this register, the patina of Iowa niceness became something more righteous and confrontational. Turek toned down his congenital niceness when he addressed the parlous state of our politics; in lieu of the amorphous indictments of “a broken system” that many lawmakers favor, he denounced a moneyed oligarchy—not exactly the sort of bipartisan overture he was chided on social media for earlier in the day when he said he’d cast his ballot in some local races for GOP candidates. One of his biggest applause lines was “Tonight, Iowa, we outvoted the billionaires,” and he made the same point in a much more personal idiom later, saying, “In Iowa, Elon Musk does not decide elections.” And he vowed to “end the corruption we’re seeing on both sides of the aisle,” adding, “I am going to DC to overturn Citizens United.”
If Turek is a prairie populist in the Harkin vein, the state’s governor-elect Rob Sand, who celebrated at the same Des Moines gathering, is something closer to Jimmy Stewart’s title character in Mr. Smith Goes to Washington. Sand is the incumbent state auditor and has relied on a long roster of endorsements from Republicans and independents in a campaign that he described as dedicated to “the straight and narrow path of public service, not politics.” When Iowans send their children off to school, he announced, “We don’t tell them to be red or to be blue. We tell them to be good, to be kind, to tell the truth.” Sand’s campaign distilled that sentiment into another typically Iowan slogan: “Not redder and bluer, but better and truer.” Midway through his speech, he paused to revive the civic ritual that he made the signature moment in his town halls across the state, leading the crowd in “America the Beautiful.”
But Sand also went on to explain that this is more than simple goo-goo sentiment. As a matter of basic political math in a state where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats by 180,000, “the smallest party has to appeal to reasonably minded people in the other party.” And in governing a state with GOP majorities in both houses of the legislature, Sand has little choice but to seek some workable common ground with a MAGA-fied GOP.
Speaking of the loyal opposition, Sand said, “I hope you will kindly tell me why you didn’t vote for me—and since I’ll be here for a while, you’ll get to know me better, and maybe change your mind next time.” It’s a pragmatic, improbably wholesome start at charting a path out of the MAGA darkness that’s engulfed the state, but it’s again not without precedent. Throughout much of the 20th century, Iowa had some of the most liberal and most conservative members of the Senate—Harkin and the state’s now super-senior nonagenarian Senator Chuck Grassley, John Culver and Roger Jepsen, Harold Hughes and Jack Miller. This, too, was a legacy of Populism, which in its Upper Midwest iteration found later expression in left-wing movements like North Dakota’s Nonpartisan League and Minnesota’s Farmer-Labor Party. Tuesday’s results supplied a strong confirmation of the argument that the best rejoinder to the phony mogul populism of the Trump era is actual economic populism; it could be that Iowa’s incorrigibly neighborly contribution to that project is to make civic populism a going concern once again. Who’s up for a chorus of America the Beautiful?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Deathbed portrait of Vanessa Bell by Duncan Grant discovered
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Maev Kennedy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A poignant portrait of the artist Vanessa Bell, made within days of her death in 1961 by her sometime lover and lifelong friend Duncan Grant, has been rediscovered among family papers and donated to the famous home of the Bloomsbury Group, Charleston farmhouse in East Sussex.
The drawing in soft pencil and biro, from an angle suggesting Grant was sitting by her bedside, was rediscovered among family papers during research for a forthcoming exhibition of the work of both artists at Tate Britain. It may have been made just after Bell’s death, though she could just be resting peacefully with eyes closed.
Although Grant has dated the drawing “Friday April 14”, Bell actually died at the farmhouse on a week prior. In a statement from Charleston, now a museum and archive, Darren Clarke, head of collections and research, says that in later years, Grant and his friends went through masses of the work in his studio identifying and labelling pictures, so the date may have been added in error years later.
“What seems very likely here is that Duncan knew this drawing had been made around Vanessa’s death and later added a date from memory. He got remarkably close, but apparently not quite close enough. Everything about the drawing itself – its viewpoint, its intimacy and its extraordinary economy – suggests someone sitting quietly beside Vanessa’s bed and drawing the face he had known for half a century.”
The friendship and artistic partnership of Grant and Bell was one of the happiest and longest lasting of the tangled affairs of the group. Although Grant was gay and a former lover of Bell’s brother Adrian, they were lovers for a time and in 1918 had a child, Angelica—who went on to marry David Garnett, another of Grant’s lovers. Grant and Bell lived and worked at the 17th-century farmhouse for decades, covering many of the interiors with striking painted decoration. He outlived her by 17 years, and in 1978 was buried beside her in the churchyard of St Peter’s in Firle, near their home.
Grant was long regarded as the most talented artist of the group, and the first major solo exhibition of Bell’s work came only in 2017 at the Dulwich Picture Gallery. At that time most of her paintings in the Tate collection were languishing in storage, but her reputation has been growing steadily in recent years. The Tate is making amends with a major exhibition of work by both artists, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury (12 November 2026 - 11 April 2027) at Tate Britain.
Although Charleston is the largest lender to the Tate exhibition, including the entire contents of Grant’s studio, the drawing will only be included in the exhibition catalogue. It will go on public display for the first time at Charleston in May 2027, when the studio reopens after major conservation work.
The drawing has been donated to Charleston as part of the 50 for 50 campaign which aims to bring 50 major works by the group back to the farmhouse in time for 2030, the 50th anniversary of the founding of the Charleston Trust, which runs and maintains the museum.
Nathaniel Hepburn, the director and CEO of Charleston, says in a statement on the discovery: “I found this drawing deeply moving when I first saw it. We know Duncan’s drawings of Vanessa so intimately, made over the course of their long friendship, that the discovery of a previously unknown work is remarkable in itself. But there is something incredibly poignant about imagining Duncan sitting beside Vanessa, drawing her after her death.“

https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/l.title: Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms.
https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/l.author: shoshana.gordon@propublica.org, John Dillon
https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/l.text:
Despite being an iconic part of Vermont’s landscape and a large source of the state’s drinking water, Lake Champlain has been polluted for decades. Phosphorus runoff from farm fields, rural roads, parking lots, stormwater drains and wastewater treatment plants flows into the lake, fueling algae blooms that frequently choke its bays and shorelines.
Vermont is halfway through a 20-year effort to clean up the lake. In 2016, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency established new, stricter requirements for reducing phosphorus runoff that the state must meet by 2036. But more than a decade in, after spending nearly a billion dollars, the state is lagging behind. Water quality has not improved dramatically, and in some parts of the lake, it is getting worse. This past summer algae blooms shut down swimming at public beaches in St. Albans Bay in the northeast part of the lake.
Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to understand the reasons behind this lack of progress. We want to know how pollution in the lake is affecting Vermont’s economy and the lifestyles and livelihoods of Vermonters and visitors alike. We’re also interested in learning more about how persistently poor water quality in Lake Champlain affects Vermonters’ health, well-being and finances.
Do you live, play or depend on Lake Champlain? We want to hear from you. Your perspective will help us understand how longstanding pollution affects a wide range of issues, from drinking water quality to tax revenue from tourism around the lake.
We’re gathering these stories for our reporting, which can take several weeks or months. We may not be able to follow up with everyone, but we will read everything you submit and it will help guide our project.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Jon Ossoff Showed Democrats How to Channel Voters’ Anger About Corruption and Corporations
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Joan Walsh
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Jon Ossoff Showed Democrats How to Channel Voters’ Anger About Corruption and Corporations
The Georgia senator was considered the most vulnerable incument this cycle. He cruised to a commanding victory, with lots of lessons for 2028.
Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff came into his reelection contest judged the most vulnerable incumbent in the Senate, the only Democratic senator running in a state Trump won two years ago. On election night, Ossoff was the first Senate candidate called a winner. At 7:18 pm—yes, just 18 minutes after the polls closed—the respected Decision Desk declared him the victor over Republican Representative Mike Collins, 59–41 percent. What happened?
Shortly before the midterm vote, we saw polls showing that 90 percent of voters considered political corruption their top issue, while just behind were voters who said it was the cost of living. That explains Ossoff’s win. Throughout the campaign, he led the way in showing Democrats how to link the grifting of Donald Trump, as well as the white supremacy and self-dealing of his Trump-loving opponent Representative Mike Collins, to Georgia voters’ own struggles.
The link wasn’t necessarily obvious at first, but once Ossoff did it, I was surprised no one else figured it out.
Related Article
I have been covering Ossoff since his unsuccessful but close congressional race, and his victorious 2020 Senate race. I’m on the record as an admirer. But in the last year, I’d become a big Instagram fan—his staff clips the greatest hits of his campaign talks. But it was more powerful seeing him in person in Savannah, watching him twin the two devastating effects of the Trump era, elite corruption and middle-class immiseration, and put it to voters in a way that they got it.
“I don’t know if you saw the mess in Washington last week. The president was so humiliated in [the Strait of] Hormuz, he threw his toys out the stroller,” Ossoff told the Savannah crowd. “That’s after he gave some felon donor a no-bid contract for the Reflecting Pool, and it filled up with algae.”
But then he hit Trump’s domestic agenda. “He promised to bring down prices on day one,” Ossoff said. “Y’all know what today is? Today is day 524, and groceries, rent, and healthcare are at their all-time highs in American history. Donald Trump and his puppet Mike Collins—they doubled health-insurance premiums for more than a million Georgians and threw 300,000 Georgians off their insurance altogether. I heard from a woman with cancer who waits tables for a living and said she was going to lose her health coverage in the middle of chemotherapy. And they did this to pay for a tax cut that went overwhelmingly to the rich and to corporate America. Did you know that, Savannah?” Savannah knew, indeed.
Ossoff went on: “While hundreds of thousands of Georgians lose their healthcare, Mike Collins builds Trump a ballroom. They worked harder burying the Epstein files than they ever worked to lower your grocery bill. And while you pay more for everything, the Trumps are raking in billions. from all over the world. Illegal tariffs, failed war, healthcare cuts, and unmatched corruption.”
But I found myself most drawn in by the most everyday stories Ossoff tells: how most of us, even those who aren’t in crisis, feel the walls of corporate power closing in. “The corporate disrespect is suffocating,” he told the Savannah crowd. “Instead of reading to your child, that precious spare hour after work is spent on the phone, fighting your bank, or the cable company, or the insurer that’s denied your claim and dared you to fight back while you’re sick. A toddler’s ambulance is followed by a $3,000 bill. Hedge funds buy up houses till there are none left to afford, then rip off the renters. We were promised a political system that delivers for the public, but instead, it delivers for the donors.”
Maybe not surprisingly, Ossoff returned to those themes in his victory speech Tuesday night, with new polish and conviction. “While the wealthy and well-lobbied feast on inside information and official favors, America’s forgotten families are treated to systemic corporate disrespect and official indifference, working harder and harder while the treadmill just gets faster and steeper and the bills get higher and higher,” he told the Atlanta crowd.
“Instead of reading your daughter her favorite book, that precious spare hour after work, you’re on the phone begging the insurance company to cover the medicine that prevents her seizures. You report the black mold to your landlord, who doesn’t fix the leak, and the ambulance for your toddler’s asthma attack is followed by a $3,000 bill.” The senator just a year ago judged the most vulnerable found new power in channeling the growing vulnerability of American voters.
Ossoff told me back in June, as he tells everyone, that he will not run for president in 2028. I chose to believe him, since he is a 39-year-old senator running for his second term, with two small daughters and a wife with a medical practice. I still believe he has plenty of time and plenty of crossroads ahead. But he ran such a flawless campaign, he’s going to face this question incessantly.
For now, I’m going to leave him with his own summary of what his victory, and the stunning wins by Democrats from the Senate to the House to state legislatures, have to say about the country’s political health. “In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption, and incompetence of the failed lame-duck president, Donald J. Trump.” Indeed. Ossoff’s overwhelming victory Tuesday night makes him a major player in deciding what comes next, whether he decides to run or not.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: November Book Bag: from a book about broken art to a collection of Zanele Muholi’s LGBTQ+ portraits
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture, C. D. Dickerson III and Andrew Sears, Chicago University Press, 240pp, £40 (hb)
The Power of the Fragment in Sculpture explores the enduring fascination with fractured statues, focusing on the “power dynamics of iconoclastic dismantling and defacement, and how various cultures treat broken statues”, says a publisher’s statement. Highlights include Michelangelo’s terracotta Model of a Nude Woman (around 1533), which new research suggests may have been intentionally created incomplete. The publication accompanies a wide-ranging and eclectic exhibition spanning more than 4,500 years of global history, which opened in September at the Palazzo Strozzi in Florence before it travels to the National Gallery of Art in Washington DC next year.
Felix Gonzalez-Torres, Nancy Spector, Phaidon, 352pp, £39.95 (hb)
This newly revised and expanded edition assesses the relevance today of the influential conceptual artist Felix Gonzalez-Torres who died from an Aids-related illness in 1996. “Almost two decades after its original publication, the monograph accompanying Gonzalez-Torres’s 1995 retrospective at the Guggenheim Museum is still the canonical text on the artist,” says a publisher’s statement. Gonzalez-Torres is known especially for his famous sweet installations, which are usually mounted in piles in the corner of rooms. “The candy pieces, like all his works, encourage a wealth of meanings, and can be everything from stridently political to gently lyrical,” writes the critic and host of The Art Newspaper’s podcast, Ben Luke.
The Voice of the Artist(s): another vocabulary, Gabriela Galcerán (editor), Sternberg Press, 360pp, £23.50 (pb)
This publication grew out of a video project devised by the cultural producer Gabriela Galcerán in which 26 artists chose a word, one for each letter of the alphabet, and responded to it in their own way. The five thematic chapters, including “Power + Politics” and “Agency + Language”, subsequently draw connections between their ideas. Contributors include Lynn Hershman Leeson, Lawrence Abu Hamdan and Gary Hill. “They all made me flinch, each for a different reason. I love the wide range of tones and registers that make up this choral effort. Some are intimate, some political, some humorous or oblique,” says Galcerán in a statement.
Faces and Phases, Zanele Muholi, Renée Mussai (editor), Mack, 464pp, £65 (hb)
For more than 20 years, the South African artist and activist Zanele Muholi has been documenting Black lesbian and bisexual women, along with queer, trans, non-binary, and gender fluid people for the project Faces and Phases. This new volume of the work, released to mark the project’s 20th anniversary, has been updated to include new sitters in locations such as São Paulo, Salvador, London, Porto and Los Angeles. “These striking photographs are often accompanied by participants’ testimonies, sharing their personal stories, feelings, and lived experiences,” says a publisher’s statement. Muholi was born in Durban in 1972 at the height of apartheid in South Africa. In the early 2000s, the photographer began to raise awareness of the hypocrisies and hate crimes that remain prevalent against the LGBTQ+ community within the country.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/ice-.title: ICE Was Secretly Ordered to Stop All Immigration Raids on Election Day
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/ice-.author: Karl Loftus
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/ice-.text:
Orders for what one official called a “national no enforcement day” began circulating on Monday inside U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement.
Handed down through ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division through internal group chats and verbal commands, the directive called for a halt to all immigration enforcement operations on Election Day, according to ICE officials across the country who spoke to The Intercept.
“We were told all operations are canceled for Election Day,” said one ICE immigration official, who operates in the south and requested anonymity to protect their livelihood. “Word of mouth from our first-line supervisors, no official email notice.”
According to multiple ICE officials who spoke to The Intercept, the orders were handed down quietly to avoid media attention.
“Yesterday was the least amount of activity observed from ICE ERO throughout the entire year so far,” said Sherman Austin, the creator of StopICE.net, a crowdsourced platform tracking reported ICE activity across the United States. “You can kind of tell like from the morning. Usually, ICE gets started really early, and there’s a huge spike in activity between 5 a.m. and 10 a.m. That spike wasn’t there on Election Day.”
Another ICE official, who works in the Great Lakes region, confirmed the orders ahead of Election Day, referring to it as “National No Enforcement Day.”
“We were told to do ‘admin’ shit,” the official said. They said that ICE deportation officers who regularly do street-level operations were diverted to administrative office work: “I’ll be drinking coffee at the office for the first time in a year.”
In total, ICE officials working in four areas of responsibility — ICE’s jurisdictional regions — coving parts of the northeastern, midwestern, northern, and south-central U.S. regions told The Intercept that they had received orders to stand down on Election Day.
“Something Unusual Was Going On”
StopICE, the tracking website, which has roughly half a million subscribers, did record some ICE activity on Election Day, according to Austin, although most of the reports stemmed from sightings unrelated to any immigration enforcement activities.
“There were a few reports that came in about ICE being at usual spots like the jails,” Austin said, “or seen driving in certain areas in in the city, but it wasn’t the same type of activity that’s usually seen on the site. It was pretty clear that something unusual was going on.”
AntiFreeze, another crowdsourced ICE-tracking platform that allows users to report and receive real-time alerts about ICE raids, also saw abnormally low levels of ICE activity on November 3, according to Josh, the creator and developer behind the site, who requested to keep his last name anonymous.
“On Election Day, our network only logged about 56 reported ICE sightings nationwide, which is one of the quietest Tuesdays we’ve ever seen,” Josh said. “We did get about three sightings that did report ICE activity near polling stations, but most of the reports were observations of vehicles associated with ICE. We barely got any reports about actual ICE arrests yesterday.”
Local activists also observed a low level of ICE activity on the street level.
“There was no evidence of street abductions,” said an activist working with the rapid-response network in Minnesota’s Twin Cities.
“ICE, in some capacity, was still out and about, but we did not see any reports of off-the-street detainments by ICE or attempts at detainments,” said the activist, who said they got word of ICE arrests at jails, but not targeted operations among the general public. “There were a lot of folks, probably more than usual, observing, and so I think we can be pretty confident that this wasn’t due to lack of observation.”
Leo Martinez, who volunteers with VC Defensa in Southern California, told The Intercept that no one in his rapid-response group reported any sightings of ICE activity on Tuesday.
It is still unclear exactly where the orders to halt immigration enforcement operations on Election Day originated from, although some ICE officials believe the orders stemmed from ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations leadership — and not directly from the White House.
“Nobody from the SDDO level” — a reference to Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer, part of ICE’s upper management — “expected it to happen until the very last moment,” said another ICE official familiar with the matter. “But I think some of us caught on that senior leadership was making this call with fears of us being at the polls.”
The official said, “It’s crazy that The White House didn’t catch on.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Hong Kong artists create a poetic moment in Venice
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
For Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice, the Hong Kong-born artists Kingsley Ng and Angel Hui are training visitors’ attention on the quiet moments and subtle details connecting both cities. The exhibition, marking the 25th anniversary of Hong Kong’s first participation in the Venice Biennale, is curated by the Hong Kong Museum of Art (HKMoA) and continues until 22 November. It is housed in a historic Venetian residential building in the floating city’s Campo della Tana neighbourhood, a setting that underlines the meditative, lived-in quality to the works.
“What we hope visitors take away from the exhibition is a moment of reflection,” says Dr Maria Mok, the director of the HKMoA. “Through Kingsley and Angel’s attention to everyday details, we hope visitors feel invited to slow down and become more attentive to their surroundings, even within the hustle and intensity of urban life.”
One of Kingsley Ng’s installations, for instance, Laundry Nocturne (2026), consists of a projection and soundscape that evoke the play of light across laundry hung between buildings. It was inspired by the artist’s experience visiting Venice, where billowing laundry on clotheslines is still common, though for Ng it also evoked memories of Hong Kong.
“The laundry becomes a point of entry into a wider soundscape of nighttime labour: recordings from a wastewater treatment plant, a newspaper-printing facility and a postal sorting centre evoke the work that continues while much of the city sleeps,” Ng says. “These modest, often overlooked processes that keep a city alive do not only connect Venice and Hong Kong. They are like a low hum in almost every city, to be picked up by an ear that doesn’t only listen to loud grandeur.”
For her installations, Angel Hui shines a spotlight on humble features of Hong Kong’s everyday life, including goldfish in plastic bags and a neighbour’s ornate but faded window frame. In her magical rendering, glowing plastic bags embroidered with goldfish motifs are suspended overhead, while a handwrought iron window made by Hui and traditional metalsmiths rotates slowly in the gallery.
“In Hong Kong, a goldfish bag is an everyday object; in Venice, it seemed almost precious—delicate and exposed,” Hui says. “The experience reminded me that a work does not need to be grand to hold meaning. Sometimes, its poetry lies in inviting us to look more attentively, and to meet the familiar with tenderness.”
Both artists, through their site-specific installations, encourage visitors to mark a pause while heightening their attention to details of light, sound, colour and texture. This invitation to contemplation is echoed in the exhibition’s title, Fermata, which is a type of musical symbol instructing a performer to hold a note or a pause for an extra moment, and the term for the places where Venetian vaporettos stop to let off and pick up passengers. For Hui, this title and its dual meanings resonate across the exhibition’s disparate locales.
“The difference in pace is pronounced: Hong Kong often presses forward, while Venice seems to make room for pause,” she says. “This is why Fermata—a moment of stopping, of stillness—felt so resonant. In both cities, the ordinary endures, and in that endurance, everyday objects acquire a quiet radiance.”
The exhibition’s title and installations also complement the theme of this year’s Venice Biennale, In Minor Keys, set by the late curator Koyo Kouoh.
“I come to see the works as experiences to return to and live alongside,” Ng says. “For me, that is one meaning of In Minor Keys: making time for the ordinary and immediate—the air, light and weather around us—and becoming more attentive to our presence within them.”
The artists’ ability to turn familiar objects and moments into tableaux where time pauses and senses are heightened is key to the exhibition’s power. It allows their installations to resonate across localities, from the Venetian Lagoon to Hong Kong’s cityscape.
“The artworks merge into the Venetian neighbourhood, from laundry hanging across nearby alleys and above our courtyard exhibition space to the view of the neighbourhood outside Kingsley’s Laundry Nocturne gallery, to wrought-iron windows that echo Angel’s work,” Dr Mok says. “All these details are blurring the boundary between the exhibition and its surroundings. They also show how small moments of daily life can quietly synchronise across different cities and audiences.”
- Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice, Campo della Tana, Castello 2126, 30122, Venice, until 22 November 2026

https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-man-wak.title: Bronx man wakes up to a $39K nightmare after online meetup at hotel, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-man-wak.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-man-wak.text:
A man who used a social media app to meet someone at a Bronx hotel told police he believed he was drugged and was robbed of nearly $40,000 in cash, along with his car and cellphone.
The NYPD is asking for the public’s help identifying a person shown in surveillance images wearing a hot pink dress, with tattoos on their chest and silver earrings.
The incident took place on Aug. 24 at the Tremont Hotel in the Bronx.
The 31-year-old man met the person there around 10 p.m. that Monday, police said, after previous meetups. At some point during the encounter, he fell asleep and two other men entered the room, according to police.
When he woke up, his car, cellphone, about $39,507 in cash and other belongings were missing, according to police. The two men were later identified, but the person in the pink dress fled on foot, police said.
The man's car was later recovered, police said.
Emergency medical workers took the man to St. Barnabas Hospital, where he was listed in stable condition, according to police. The man told investigators he believed he had been drugged, police officials said Wednesday.

https://citylimits.org/keeping-taino-cul.title: Keeping Taíno Culture Alive: Bronx Exhibit Celebrates the Legacy of Bobby González
https://citylimits.org/keeping-taino-cul.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/keeping-taino-cul.text:
Share This Article
A new exhibit at the Museum of Bronx History explores the life of the Puerto Rican poet, storyteller and educator who dedicated nearly four decades to preserving Indigenous culture and challenging stereotypes about the South Bronx.
For Bobby González, preserving Indigenous history began close to home: inside his family’s bodega in the South Bronx.
Growing up near the Melrose Houses, González encountered people from different Indigenous backgrounds who visited the neighborhood store owned by his parents. Those conversations helped shape his understanding of his own Taíno heritage and inspired a lifelong commitment to educating others about Indigenous history.
Now, three years after his death, his work is being remembered through a new exhibition at the Museum of Bronx History.
“From the South Bronx Reservation: Bobby González, Taíno Indian,” which opened Oct. 8 and runs through March 2027, explores the life of the Puerto Rican poet, storyteller and educator who dedicated nearly four decades to preserving Indigenous culture and challenging stereotypes about the South Bronx.
Born in 1951, González grew up in a Puerto Rican family whose parents migrated to New York after World War II. His father worked as a short order cook before opening a bodega in the 1970s, where González and his brothers helped run the family business.
According to Stephen Payne, director of the Bronx County Historical Society, the bodega played an important role in shaping González’s identity.
Visitors included people with Cherokee, Quechua, Lenape and other Indigenous backgrounds. Their conversations encouraged González to learn more about Indigenous communities across the Americas and explore his own ancestry.
That experience later influenced the phrase “South Bronx Reservation,” which González used to describe the neighborhood’s Indigenous presence.
Payne explained that the phrase also reflected similarities between the South Bronx and some Native American reservations, including struggles with pollution and limited resources.
For González, the neighborhood was more than a place where he grew up. It became the foundation of his writing, poetry and cultural activism.
His widow, Maria Aponte González, remembered him as someone who remained deeply connected to his community.
“He was a very gentle spirit,” she said. “Never yelled, never raised his voice.”
She described her late husband as approachable, calm and someone to whom community members frequently turned for advice.
González co-founded the cultural organization Taíno del Norte, organized the annual Bronx Native American Festival and wrote several books, including “The Last Puerto Rican Indian.” He also traveled across the country, speaking at schools, colleges and museums about Indigenous history.
Some of González’s belongings, via the Bronx History Museum.
His mission was to challenge the belief that Taíno people—a native group that originally inhabited the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico—had disappeared centuries ago.
“We are Taíno, we are still here,” Payne said, recalling a phrase used by the organization González helped establish.
Payne explained that the exhibition highlights how Indigenous identity continues to shape Puerto Rican communities, particularly in the Bronx, where González became an important figure in the Taíno cultural revival movement.
The exhibition also arrives at a time when the Bronx is experiencing demographic changes. Payne said rising living costs have contributed to Puerto Rican residents leaving the borough or city, making it increasingly important for community members to share their stories now.
“It’s very important to preserve that part of the history while there still are people in the community who can speak to it,” he said.
The exhibition brings together personal belongings, writings and other materials preserved by González throughout his lifetime.
Aponte González, who co-curated the exhibition alongside documentary filmmaker Edwin Pagán, selected the objects from their home.
“Everything that you’re going to see in the exhibit is Bobby’s work,” she said.
Rather than focusing on how others described her husband, she wanted visitors to experience his legacy through the materials he created himself.
Among his contributions were poetry workshops, including a spoken word series that helped emerging poets develop their voices. He also used puppetry and storytelling to introduce children to Indigenous history and cultural traditions.
Aponte González launched the Bobby González Legacy Project in 2024, following conversations she had with her husband about preserving his work before he became seriously ill.
She described the exhibition as a project that took two years to develop, with support from Pagán and the Bronx County Historical Society.
For Payne, the exhibition also reflects a larger challenge facing historical institutions: preserving the experiences of working class communities whose personal records and belongings are often lost because of housing instability or limited financial resources.
He explained that families who have experienced eviction or frequent moves may no longer have access to photographs, documents and other materials that help tell their histories. In those cases, institutions often rely on oral histories and archival research to recover stories that might otherwise disappear.
González’s collection offered a different opportunity because he had preserved much of his own work, which his widow has made available through the Legacy Project.
Beyond celebrating his accomplishments, both Aponte González and Payne hope the exhibition encourages younger generations to learn about their cultural backgrounds.
“Young people need to make space in their heads. And be open to learn things,” Aponte González said.
For Payne, the larger message is that Indigenous history should not be understood only as something belonging to the distant past.
He hopes visitors recognize that Native American communities continue to preserve, reclaim and develop their cultural traditions today.
Through González’s writing, storytelling and activism, the exhibition offers visitors an opportunity to explore that living history through the experiences of a man who dedicated his life to sharing it.
The exhibition is on display at the Museum of Bronx History, located at 3266 Bainbridge Ave. in the Bronx, through March 2027.
