https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/m.text:
Illegal e-motos are common on city streets. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Dozens of businesses were hit with more than 130 violations for selling illegal e-bikes and scooters in a two-month enforcement blitz to protect consumers against fire-prone and overpowered micromobility devices.
Inspectors for the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection visited 229 retail shops across the five boroughs between Aug. 1 and Sept. 20 and found 136 individual violations that resulted in more than 75 summonses, each carrying a $1,000 fine. Three stores were shuttered.
“New Yorkers deserve to feel safe knowing that the devices they see in their communities meet the City’s safety requirements,” said DCWP Commissioner Sam Levine, whose agency ensures that stores sell only UL-certified e-bikes and batteries, display e-bike fire safety materials in their storefronts, and don’t sell illegal e-motos and scooters that have too much power and speed capability. “Our citywide sweep sends a clear message that businesses cannot put New Yorkers at risk just to make a profit.”
In addition to the three closures, Levine’s agency worked with another five shops to bring them into compliance with the law, the agency said. Stores remain closed until all outstanding fines are paid to DCWP, the department said.
Since e-bikes and scooters started growing in popularity during the pandemic there has been misplaced ire from politicians. Confusion over which devices are legal on city streets and bike lanes led to a fervent backlash to all electric bikes.
E-scooters are illegal in New York City if they exceed 20 miles per hour or weigh more than 100 pounds. E-bikes are legal if their motors don’t exceed 750 watts and their top speed is 25 mph.
The law defines a “motorized scooter” as a two-wheeled powered device that can’t be registered with the Department of Motor Vehicles, like, say a legal moped, and also doesn’t fit the city’s street-legal definitions of an e-bike or stand-up scooter. DCWP can give summonses to businesses selling these out-of-class devices, known as e-motos.
These devices, which far exceed the city’s limits for power and speed, are often sold online and in stores as legal devices.
But the tides are shifting. Two high–profile deaths involving New Yorkers riding non-street-legal e-motos and scooters sparked long-overdue action from city and state politicians.
In August, the city Law Department sent cease-and-desist letters to 42 online retailers selling the so-called e-motos, which are illegal to ride on city streets and bike lanes.
The cease-and-desists brought large retailers like Amazon, Temu, and Walmart into compliance. Such companies now block orders by geography so consumers can’t ship these devices to their New York City homes. But many small direct to consumer brands are still shipping flagrantly illegal e-motos and scooters and marketing them for city use. Aniioki, a brand that Streetsblog sees out on the streets daily, sells bikes online that can hit over 50 miles per hour.
DCWP said it also issued more than 85 cease-and-desist orders and 41 summonses to online sellers for battery safety violations.
And in July, Attorney General Letitia James issued a consumer alert to warn perspective buyers of the shady market. So far her office has received three relevant complaints.
State lawmakers are also pushing legislation to officially bar the sale of e-motos online and in stores, closing a loophole that has allowed retailers to sell devices that are illegal to ride on roadways but are legal to own for private use.
State Sen. Kristen Gonzalez (D-Long Island City) introduced the bill to establish a clear definition for these overpowered vehicles, and explicitly prohibit companies from not only selling them, but from falsely advertising them as legal, a common practice that results in unsuspecting consumers purchasing devices they can’t legally use.
The driver, Timothy McVey, 41, of Staten Island, turned himself in at the 62nd Precinct station house and was booked for failure to yield and failure to exercise due care

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.author: The Intercept Briefing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.text:
The size of the Democrats’ victory Tuesday night shattered records and even the most optimistic expectations, handing the party a governing mandate with a clear demand for change.
But what do voters want that change to look like? This week on The Intercept Briefing, politics reporter Jessica Washington and managing editor Maia Hibbett break down Tuesday night’s election and hear from voters in Maine, Michigan, and Texas about what drove them to the polls in the midterms that saw a so-called “blue tsunami.”
“The rich get richer, the poor get poorer,” said one voter in Maine. In Michigan, a voter told The Intercept that politics “feels like a game that the rich play sometimes.” A Texas voter expressed anger that President Donald Trump was “spending taxpayer money to renovate the White House and turn it into this gold sanctuary.”
Frustration with wealth inequality and money in politics came up again and again in The Intercept’s conversations with voters. So did a desire for more social welfare spending, Medicare for All, freedom for Palestinians — and responses to transphobic and Islamophobic fearmongering on the campaign trail.
“When Democrats win so far across the board, you can make an argument that any faction of the Democratic Party has the mandate,” said Hibbett, “because Democrats of all stripes won Tuesday night.”
In any case, the results indicated a clear disapproval of the way the Trump administration is governing and the use of fearmongering as a tactic of distraction.
“One lesson maybe for Democrats is there’s no point in attempting to placate people when it comes to bigotry,” said Washington. “The thing that’ll motivate voters is if you can convince them that you’re going to make their lives better, not if you can convince them that you’re playing the middle on an issue of civil rights.”
For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.

They only needed 218 for a majority, so obviously that is more, and they’re expected to pick up some more seats as some more races get called. Now, things seemed fine for a second. Haley Stevens had all of these Democratic surrogates going on air saying that she promised to support him. It was produced by this outside group Rebellion PAC, which is the group headed by Cenk Uygur, who some listeners might know from The Young Turks. He is also famously Hasan Piker’s uncle.

It really seemed strange. So we sent Matt Sledge out in Michigan to ask some voters what they thought of it, and if they thought that this was a politically savvy move that would have any resonance. And here’s what they said.

Mega-donors overwhelmingly gave to Republican candidates, including Elon Musk, who spent nearly $450 million, with large sums of that directed at boosting Ken Paxton in Texas, who, by the way, lost to James Talarico. Now, for context, the next highest donors under Musk are a Republican couple [Richard and
Elizabeth Uihlein] who spent $150 million, mostly in Wisconsin and Illinois. 
Jesse Craft: We all see where money is coming from. It’s coming from very, very wealthy billionaires. I don’t think we should be able to buy elections.
Tea Edwards: Politics, it just feels like a game that the rich play sometimes. Kind of feels hopeless when you’re just looking at all of these people and corporations giving money to each other.
MH: You hate to see Elon Musk throw away almost half a billion dollars. It only leaves him so many billions to go.
JW: Heartbreaking.
MH: But, I mean, in Texas, as you mentioned, that money really did not pan out. It didn’t seem to sway voters. It seemed like if anything from the voters who talked to our reporters in Texas, in Michigan, and in Maine, which we’ll get to later, people were really mad about outside election spending and don’t like the idea that billionaires or corporations can buy their elections.
And in Texas, a lot of that money went to propping up this anti-trans panic campaign that Paxton was running. But all that money was not enough to save Paxton from James Talarico. Paxton was a pretty bad candidate: He was mired in too many scandals to keep track of, including a 2015 grand jury indictment on felony securities fraud charges.
In 2020, eight of his top deputies reported to the FBI that he was potentially abusing his office to do favors for a donor and friend. And just earlier this year, he offered a plea deal in a child sex abuse case that seemed to anger Texans and voters.
Remember, this is the era of the Epstein files and people being very concerned about child sex abuse. It did not seem like the wisest calculation for Paxton to offer this while running for Senate.
JW: As it turns out, there is not enough money in the world to buy Ken Paxton out of being Ken Paxton and voters recognizing that. But Republicans tried this cycle to spend big on transphobia and to blanket the airwaves with these anti-trans advertisements.
Elon Musk’s Texas PAC spent $78 million on anti-transgender ads in Texas, which actually accounted for nearly half of all ad spending in support of Paxton. Republicans’ big play in Texas was transphobia — and that play failed.
While clearly it didn’t sway the election, some of those messages did appear to trickle down to voters. Our colleague, Akela Lacy, talked to voters in Dallas and the surrounding areas, and she did come across some voters who said they wanted to support Talarico or even some voters who did support Talarico but were concerned about his stance on trans rights, an issue that Republicans really fearmongered on this cycle yet again after doing it in 2024.
Akela Lacy: When you said you saw some stuff about James Talarico that made you unsure about voting for him, can you say more about that? What did you see, and what’s your impression of him?
Jermiah Robinson: I think I seen something about the LGBTQ+ community? I mean, I don’t really care about it, but I don’t know. People were saying a lot of bad stuff. I think they said something about him —
Canvasser: Encouraging sex change.
Jermiah Robinson: Yeah, on the children. I don’t really stand for that.
Maia Hibbett: The watchdog group Media Matters also put together a montage that showed just how much Republicans really leaned into this transphobic rhetoric.
Danielle Buck: He wants to trans our kids. He believes that there are six genders.
Andrew Kolvet: They wanna indoctrinate your kids. They wanna trans your kids.
Adam Sosnick: They’re gonna trans your kids. They’re gonna Talarico your kids.
Donald Trump Jr.: Trans kids back in school, trans agendas back in school, in your classrooms, with your children.
JW: Clearly, some of that rhetoric did trickle down to voters based on Akela’s conversations, and some people even believed the misinformation being spread in those ads.
But fearmongering was just clearly not persuasive enough to distract people from their lived reality, and that lived reality is that gas prices are up, rent is unaffordable, and grocery prices are up.
I think one lesson maybe for Democrats is, there’s no point in attempting to placate people when it comes to bigotry. The right can and will distort your messages, and so you can stand in your values or not, but the thing that’ll motivate voters is if you can convince them that you’re going to make their lives better, not if you can convince them that you’re playing the middle on an issue of civil rights.
MH: We saw a parallel to this in some ways in Michigan as well, where a lot of the Republican argument was based on this perception of Islamophobia and fearmongering. Ultimately, that was not enough to elevate Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed. In Texas, there’s also, of course, the strong anti-immigrant sentiment that Republicans frequently run on, and I think the statewide results showed us that that narrative really fell apart this cycle.
JW: To your point, clearly, attacks on trans people, attacks on immigrants didn’t work in Texas. Democrats had an amazing night. Gina Hinojosa toppled three-term incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott. The state has not had a Democratic governor since 1990.
MH: And speaking of toppling long-term incumbents that have been hard to get out of office, our colleague Noah Hurowitz was in Maine, where Troy Jackson defeated Susan Collins last night after many Democratic attempts to get her out of office.
This issue of disillusionment with money and politics came up quite a bit when he was talking to Maine voters.
Sharon McDonnell: It’s immoral. It is immoral to have people worried about their fuel and have that much money coming into this. It’s just wrong.
Tyler Echard: The amount they spent on just mailers, not handed at the door but in the mail, is especially, it seems, on the Republican side of things, has been absolutely insane. The amount of money is more than I will probably make in my lifetime, spent in this election.
Charlie Dingman: It’s been extraordinary in Maine, the amount of spending in this race, particularly in the Senate race. I think there’s a lot of fatigue. I think people are tired of it. I have had some conversations with voters at the doors that lead me to think that the extremely negative and extremely untruthful ads may be backfiring.
JW: It seems like those ads backfired. The last voice you heard was Charlie Dingman, Maine Democratic Party chair.
Collins campaigned on her record of securing federal investments for state infrastructure, such as rural hospitals, and she really prided herself on being a moderate Republican who apparently breaks rank with President Donald Trump. But the reality of the situation is quite different.
The Congressional Quarterly Roll Call found that her votes aligned with Trump 90 percent of the time in both of the president’s first and second terms, and voters really noticed that. They understood the difference between what she said she was, a political moderate, and her voting record, which aligned with the really far-right Donald Trump. And that’s something that Noah heard from voters as well.
Sharon McDonnell: She has had this persona of moderate cross-party stuff that’s just really eroded. If you read every article about her, it’s like, “Moderate Susan Collins.” Like, wait a minute, she’s voted with Trump. She hasn’t used her power.
MH: Collins really used that line about her being a moderate and being an independent voice in Washington as a go-to for her campaign.
In past cycles, it has worked. As we alluded to a little bit earlier, the Democrats have mounted challenges against her before. In 2020, they ran a candidate named Sara Gideon, who looked somewhat likely to oust Collins. And I think this cycle, there were a lot of reasons for Democrats to be nervous about this race.
Troy Jackson, the nominee, is a former state senator, and he ran on lowering costs, really centering working-class interests. But he had jumped into the race kind of hastily. If you remember Graham Platner, Jessie, he was the former nominee for Senate in Maine for the Democratic Party, and he was really considered a rising star, but had to drop out because of a series of scandals, and Jackson had to jump in last minute and fill his place.
But ultimately, Jackson pulled it off.
Troy Jackson (acceptance speech): We did it. Working people did it.
JW: Clearly, Jackson had a disadvantage going into this race. There were people who complained and said that he wasn’t as charming as Platner, he wasn’t as polished. But in this election, the ideas and running on affordability seems to have won the day in Maine and really throughout the country.
Collins had a reputation of delivering for the state, but clearly that wasn’t enough to overcome this blue wave across the country and some frustrations with Collins as well.
But Maia, taking a step back to look at the full scope of Democratic wins, what do you make of their gains on Tuesday? Are there other races that stood out to you? What stood out to you overall?
MH: Well, there’s the spin about the spin, which is that everybody is going to be framing this election and these results in their own interests. When Democrats win so far across the board, you can make an argument that any faction of the Democratic Party has the mandate, because Democrats of all stripes won Tuesday night.
But to my view, it’s hard to see how this is a world where there isn’t a clear demand for some kind of transformational change. So I’m wondering what Democrats do with their mandate now, especially as we think ahead to 2028.
If you recall 2020 and the last time the U.S. elected a Democratic president, you might remember that the Biden campaign was the sort of centrist, moderate return to normalcy choice, but they got there after a lot of left momentum in the primary and a really serious showing of support for Bernie Sanders, who remains one of the most popular politicians in the country.
Once Biden got into office, he arguably tried to give some of that kind of left, dare we say, populist economic message some service. There was the Build Back Better plan that had a lot of social safety net spending and Covid relief. There were climate infrastructure projects. There was the elevation of Lina Khan [to Federal Trade Commission chair].
For a little while, Biden was getting called the most progressive president since FDR, and then he threw it all away supporting the genocide in Gaza and really lost the support of the left, and then lost the support of the country when he was kind of visibly melting on the debate stage and refusing to drop out of the race.
So I’m curious what Democrats have learned from the Biden years and how that will convert into the next congressional term and the next presidential election.
JW: It really feels like I’ve lived a million lives in between now and that debate that really tanked Joe Biden’s entire political career at the end there.
I will say to your point, we’re already seeing Hakeem Jeffries, who’s likely to be the House Speaker, calling for unity and saying that people don’t want to fight. But you don’t really get a blue wave like this or a political wave like this when people don’t want to fight.
Clearly, there’s anger at Republicans. There’s anger at the cost of living. There’s anger at the war. If Democrats don’t deliver, they’re likely to see a red wave come the next cycle.
But I did want to take just a little bit of a step back and talk about Black voters and what’s happened in the aftermath of the Supreme Court voting rights decision. Black voters in this election really delivered historic victories in southern states for Democrats, but Black representation in Congress thus far appears to have been slightly reduced in this election. Now, for those who remember our discussion earlier this year about the Supreme Court decision to gut the Voting Rights Act, there were a lot of deep concerns that the decision would crater Black political representation, and so far that hasn’t come to bear, but it’s worth paying attention to in cycles that are less blue, where we’ve seen really massive redistricting.
I will shout out, there was one historic victory for Black Americans: Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, won her race for governor, becoming the first Black female governor in the country.
MH: We’ve talked a lot about these historic wins, but we would be remiss to not mention a close call in Florida, where Angie Nixon narrowly lost.
Nixon is a Black woman who’s a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and had a really shocking primary upset when she defeated the establishment favorite to get the Democratic nomination. The Democrats didn’t invest very much in her Senate race in Florida. The conventional wisdom says Florida’s not flippable, but conventional wisdom also says that South Carolina’s not flippable — and they did that.
Nixon ended up coming within about 2 [percentage] points to Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, who just won a full term after being appointed to hold the seat that used to belong to [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio. A lot of people on the left side of the Democratic Party are wondering what would have happened if Democrats had invested in a DSA candidate running statewide in Florida, which is kind of a crazy statement to make if you think of just two years ago.
JW: I mean, I listened to her [concession] speech, she is an incredible speaker, but obviously, that’s not enough to win elections. You need money, clearly, and investment from the party.
We’re going to leave it there, but there is so much more election coverage you can follow at theintercept.com.
That does it for this episode.
We want to hear from you. Tell us what you’re following or want to see more coverage of. Email us at podcasts@theintercept.com, or leave us a voice mail at 530-POD-CAST, that’s 530-763-2278.

Thank you to all of our reporters who worked late on election night: Matt Sledge, Akela Lacy, Noah Hurowitz, Jonah Valdez, and Austin Campbell, and the rest of our team.
Nara Shin is our copy editor. William Stanton mixed our show. Legal review by David Bralow.

MH: And I’m Maia Hibbett.

This is not hyperbole.

https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.title: Evicted Upper West Side Barn Owls Are Doing OK—For Now
https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.text:
Despite an unceremonious, sudden, and possibly illegal eviction, it seems like the young barn owls of upper Manhattan will be OK.   
A parliament of barn owls had been nested in a hole in the roof of the rickety water tower of an Upper West Side apartment building—but late last week, birders noticed workers doing construction on the roof of the water tower, destroying the nest that the owls had built.  
Birder David Lei told Hell Gate that the fledglings being raised in the disrupted nest began roosting out in the open on nearby buildings last week, which was unusual, he explained. 
"That owl should have been roosting in a more sheltered location, like on an air conditioner windowsill, something like that," Lei said. "But it was out in the open, fully exposed. Songbirds had been bothering it during the day, just natural behavior. But you know, a hawk could have seen it and attacked it."
Lei said that management at 15 West 75th Street had told the residents that they were doing "scheduled maintenance" on the water tower. The building's management did not respond to Hell Gate's request for comment by publication time, but we will update this story if they do.

https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-fire.title: Brooklyn fire kills 6 people, injures 7 others in Sunset Park, officials said
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-fire.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-fire.text:
Six people were killed and seven others were injured after a fire ripped through a two-story home in Sunset Park early Thursday morning, police and fire officials said.
Fire department officials said they received calls about the blaze around 1:40 a.m., and found an intense fire burning on multiple floors of the home on 58th Street and 7th Avenue in Brooklyn. It took more than 200 first responders and almost three hours to bring it under control.
Four people were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the FDNY and NYPD, while two more people died after they were taken to a local hospital with critical injuries. Both agencies said they did not immediately have identifying information for any of the victims.
Four other civilians were also hospitalized — one with serious but non-life threatening injuries, and the others with minor injuries, officials said. The three firefighters were also being treated for minor injuries, according to the department.
Officials said a lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but it’s too early to tell whether it caused the fire.
Fire marshals on Thursday morning were looking closely at what appeared to be a charred stand up scooter that firefighters brought outside the house, along with debris that firefighters were shoveling through the home’s blown-out windows.
Luis Ramos, 54, who said he lived across the street from the fire, said the house looked like “a bonfire that was out of control” where flames were “coming out of everywhere,” including the roof, windows and door.
“Whoever was in there, they didn’t even have time to get out,” he said, adding that he witnessed a body that was black and charred. “There wasn’t a spot in that building that didn’t have a flame coming out.”
Ramos said he felt for the family who lived there, especially with Thanksgiving coming in a few weeks. “Instead of, you know, of happiness, they gotta bury their family members.”
Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who spoke at the scene of the fire on Thursday morning, said helping people recover from this fire will take time and resources.
"Because we know that fires are not only devastating in the moment, but also they displace New Yorkers from their home,” he said. “And they require help and support not just from their community, but from the city at large."
Mamdani said the Red Cross has moved all the displaced people into hotels.
Jimmy Juoguo, a neighbor, said the fire was very scary.
“It’s so sad because even we [didn’t] know each other, but it’s six people, it’s too much,” he said.
The incident comes less than a week after four family members, including 11-year-old Zion Maine, died when a lithium ion battery caught fire in the Bronx.
This is a developing story and has been updated with new information.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: Where to start with: John Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Henry Eliot
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
John Berger was born a hundred years ago today. He was an artist, critic, novelist, poet, polemicist and playwright who made impassioned, idiosyncratic, fiercely attentive and deeply humane contributions to a swathe of artistic and intellectual disciplines across six decades. In fact, the diversity of his output can make it “difficult to grasp,” as Geoff Dyer observes, in his introduction to the Selected Essays. “Even admirers tend to know him in only one or two of his many incarnations.”
I hope the recommendations below provide a somewhat representative handle on Berger’s range. I have limited myself to books he assembled himself, which means I haven’t allowed myself to include anthologies, such as the excellent Understanding a Photograph, edited by Dyer, or Tom Overton’s collections Landscapes and Portraits, or the recent selection Across a Frontier, chosen by the similarly interdisciplinary critic, photographer and novelist Teju Cole.
There are many ways to approach Berger, but wherever you choose to start, you will be encountering, as Susan Sontag said of him, “a wonderful artist and thinker”.
The entry point
Berger is best remembered for Ways of Seeing, his 1972 BBC television series and accompanying Penguin paperback. Radically, he combined art and social criticism, discussing artworks in relation to advertising, mass reproduction, the female nude, the male gaze and social status. The book’s format is equally revolutionary: the text appears to begin on the front cover, and three of the seven chapters are made up of images only. Ways of Seeing is a sui generis design classic and a swift introduction to Berger’s enduring preoccupations with art, sex and politics.
The prizewinner
The same year that Ways of Seeing was published, Berger won the fourth Booker prize with G. (1972). The novel itself has been somewhat overshadowed by Berger’s acceptance speech, in which he pilloried the sponsor Booker McConnell Ltd for their “extensive trading interests” in the Caribbean, announcing that he would be donating half his prize money to the British Black Panther movement. This experimental novel follows a young man (G) and his vigorous sex life as he travels across Europe on the eve of the first world war. G is mostly oblivious – but inextricably connected to – the world-historical events taking place around him.
The quiet masterpiece
Another excellent place to start would be A Fortunate Man (1967), the first collaboration between Berger and the Swiss photographer Jean Mohr. It is a deceptively simple portrait of a country GP in the Forest of Dean, told through stark photography and haunting prose. Word and image interweave to powerful effect: the minutiae of one man’s vocation reflect compellingly on the whole of society. Berger and Mohr became close friends working on this project and collaborated several times over the following 50 years.
The one for writers
One of Berger’s lesser-known titles is Photocopies (1996), which presents a series of exquisite prose vignettes, titled as if they were photographs. Berger captures real moments, reproducing them – photocopying them – with pinpoint attention to detail. The book has an air of delicate stillness: it is a masterclass in clarity and an inspiration for prose stylists.
The one for artists
Ways of Seeing may have made his name, but much of Berger’s best art criticism is collected in About Looking (1980), which includes essays on Turner, Giacometti, Magritte, Francis Bacon and Walt Disney. It also includes his famous essay Why Look at Animals?, which considers the fact that we rarely interact with animals today, despite living in a world full of animal imagery.
The best on photography
Berger’s third collaboration with Mohr was Another Way of Telling (1982), a revelatory investigation into the art of photography. Despite its diffident subtitle – “A Possible Theory of Photography” – this landmark work stands alongside those of Walter Benjamin, Roland Barthes and Susan Sontag. A photograph is “a meeting place,” writes Berger, “where the interests of the photographer, the photographed, the viewer and those who are using the photography are often contradictory”.
The best on politics
To some extent, everything Berger wrote was political; he was always concerned with the human experience in relation to society. One topic he wrote about repeatedly was migration, most memorably in A Seventh Man (1975), another remarkable collaboration with Mohr. This galvanising book intimately documents the experience of migrant labourers seeking work in western Europe in the early 1970s, but it remains soberingly topical today.
The one that will make you cry
G. may have won the Booker prize, but To the Wedding (1995) is Berger’s greatest novel. Through fragments of conversations, songs and silences, we follow a mother and father, estranged for many years, travelling across Europe to the wedding of their daughter Ninon. It’s both a heartbreaking story and a triumphantly optimistic celebration of love and life. Colum McCann calls it “one of the greatest and most honest love stories of our time.”
The one that deserves more attention
The wonderful Here Is Where We Meet (2005) is fiction – or is it? In 8½ chapters, “John” has a series of encounters with people who are dead: he meets his mother sitting on a park bench in Lisbon, he meets his childhood mentor in Krakow market, he stands above the grave of Jorge Luis Borges in Geneva. This is Berger at his most playful, seamlessly blending novel, essay, criticism, memoir and travelogue. It’s a brilliant, unclassifiable achievement.
The one to carry in your pocket
“This is a book I carry with me everywhere,” writes the actor and director Simon McBurney, in his new introduction to And Our Faces, My Heart, Brief as Photos (1984). “It fits into the inside pocket of my jacket, a little larger than a passport.” This slim, numinous work contains scraps and scenes about mortality, art, sex and belonging. It is organised into two halves – “Once”, about time, and “Here”, about space – and manages to condense a lifetime’s wisdom into little more than a hundred pages.
- Henry Eliot edited the 2026 Bloomsbury reissues of John Berger’s work. He is the author of five books, including The Penguin Classics Book

https://www.propublica.org/article/afrif.title: Trump’s State Department Is Giving $1 Million to Controversial Group to Study Crimes Against White South Africans
https://www.propublica.org/article/afrif.author: Sharon Lerner, Anna Maria Barry-Jester
https://www.propublica.org/article/afrif.text:
After slashing funding for programs that documented atrocities and protected human rights abroad, President Donald Trump’s State Department is now granting one of its first new human rights awards to a controversial South African organization that promotes the disputed notion that white farmers are a violently targeted, persecuted group, according to multiple sources knowledgeable about the funding.
The group expected to receive the nearly $1 million award, AfriForum, is a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners, a subset of South Africa’s white population. The organization says its members, who have a “God-given calling,” fight for Afrikaner interests and self-governance. The money will be used to “document hateful rhetoric and violent acts” against Afrikaners and other minority populations in the country.
The new award comes from a State Department bureau tasked with promoting democracy and human rights internationally. Until last year, those funds were mainly spent in poor and authoritarian nations — to fight corruption in the Democratic Republic of Congo, for example, or combat child exploitation and sexual abuse in Afghanistan. Since Trump returned to office, his appointees have transformed the bureau, gutting its staff, canceling programs and reorienting some of its funding toward conservative causes in Europe.
Samuel Samson, who was appointed as a deputy assistant secretary to the State Department bureau by Trump, has claimed the U.S. has a “civilizational” connection to Afrikaners, who descend primarily from Dutch migrants and predominantly speak Afrikaans. Samson, who has met with far-right leaders in Europe since joining the administration last year, has framed the U.S. government’s financial support for Afrikaners as grounded in “a common heritage, a common culture, a common way of life, shared history and ultimately a common anthropology.”
Samuel Samson Speaks at Lex Libertas Event
There’s a long shared political history between Afrikaner groups and white nationalists in the U.S., said Audie Klotz, a political science professor at Syracuse University who has studied those connections. But, she said, “There’s no heritage connection here. It’s pure scientific racism. In the history of U.S. immigration, there’s no direct connection between South Africa and the United States.”
AfriForum met with the Trump administration in February 2025 to plead for help. The group told officials that Afrikaners are subject to racial discrimination and murders that are more frequent and asked the administration to “act strongly against hate speech that incites violence” against them, according to a statement.
South Africa is plagued by high rates of violence, and some Afrikaners have been tortured and murdered. But independent researchers have found those killings represent a tiny fraction of murders across the country, whose victims are disproportionately people living in poor urban areas, where residents are predominantly Black. Official government statistics, and two formal inquiries into the matter, do not reveal a pattern of targeted violence against Afrikaners.
But Trump subscribes to the idea that white farmers face a “genocide” and has cited disproportionate violence against them as a reason for punishing Africa’s wealthiest nation. In February 2025, he issued an executive order that cut off hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to South Africa and welcomed Afrikaners to the U.S. as refugees. Since then, the administration has opened the doors to more than 16,000 white South Africans while halting virtually all other immigration. Officials recently told Congress they plan to invite as many as 17,500 Afrikaner refugees to the U.S. in 2027.
AfriForum did not respond to specific questions for this story but said that “our understanding is that the allocation has not yet been finalised. Should the allocation indeed be awarded to AfriForum, we will make a public announcement in this regard.”
The new award is the administration’s latest show of support for the Afrikaner cause. The white South African group governed the nation for decades under a brutal system of segregation known as apartheid, which kept the Black majority an impoverished underclass until the system was dismantled in 1994. Now, with Black South Africans governing the country, white people — of which Afrikaners are the majority — remain one of the wealthiest segments of the population.
The support has caused dismay among several former high-level diplomats, who spoke to ProPublica anonymously because they fear retribution from the administration.
Two former senior U.S. officials responsible for Africa policy said that they would never have met with AfriForum, let alone funded the group, because it was considered to be politically extreme and not credible. They described the organization as cherry-picking crime statistics to create a misleading narrative. “We would certainly not have funded what we would see as a racially incendiary initiative,” said one of the officials.
The decision to direct money toward the group comes after the Trump administration halted programs that advocated for the end of violence in African countries such as Sudan, where the Biden administration determined in 2025 that there was a genocide, calling it “the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe.”
“It’s offensive to provide funding solely to this one group after we’ve cut off funding in countries undergoing real documented crises,” said David Jandura, who managed the Africa portfolio for the State Department’s human rights bureau for several years and lost his job during the mass layoffs in 2025.
Congress has also raised questions about how the award was made. A Senate aide to Democrats told ProPublica that despite repeated requests to State Department officials, they had not received a briefing outlining the recipients of funds earmarked for democracy and human rights, which they described as “highly unusual.”
“The Trump Administration proceeded with funding fringe right-wing causes internationally despite objections from Congress,” said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a New Hampshire Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, who described the lack of transparency as “unacceptable.”
In response to a series of questions about the AfriForum funding, a senior State Department official wrote in an email that the department does not comment on funding deliberations and that they routinely keep Congress informed of their actions, consulting extensively on this year’s programming. “The Administration has been clear about its concern about the abhorrent race-based discrimination and violence in South Africa,” the unnamed official wrote. “Human rights protections do not depend on a person’s income or ethnicity.”
In July, ProPublica revealed that the State Department originally intended to give the $1 million research award to Lex Libertas, a small organization founded last year by a former AfriForum executive named Ernst Roets. Trump officials later expanded the potential awardees to a small pool of handpicked organizations. The plan drew outrage from Congress over the content of the award as well as plans to bypass the typical competitive bidding process. After ProPublica’s reporting, the State Department released an open call for the funding opportunity, offering $986,500 to a nonprofit organization to “create a comprehensive record of violence affecting Afrikaner and other South African minority populations.” It’s this grant that is now being awarded to AfriForum.
Both AfriForum and Lex Libertas advocate for Afrikaner rights and have developed relationships with the Trump administration. Trump’s ambassador to South Africa, L. Brent Bozell III, visited AfriForum’s headquarters in September, praising the organization for its neighborhood watch programs while criticizing the South African government for not enacting policies requested by the Trump administration. AfriForum has also met with Trump officials in Washington, D.C., drawing public criticism from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. And in September, Roets met with administration officials.
AfriForum was founded 20 years ago and, with some 300,000 members, claims to be the biggest civil rights organization in South Africa. It says it aims to “establish self-dependence and growing self-governance” and provides some local civic services, such as garbage collection and systems for reporting pot holes and broken traffic lights. The group has said it distances itself from “white supremacist and extremist groups” and that it disagrees with Trump’s assertion that white South African farmers are experiencing a “white genocide.” But it has also said the South African government is “targeting the continued existence of Afrikaners” through racial legislation and the downplaying of farm murders, among other things. Academics and former U.S. diplomats have repudiated some of the ideas the group promotes as racist.
It unsuccessfully challenged a ban on the “gratuitous display” of the national flag flown during apartheid, which a South African court has found to be a form of hate speech. And while the group’s leader, Kallie Kriel, has said apartheid “was wrong,” he has also said it did not constitute “a crime against humanity” as the U.N. has determined, on the grounds that not enough people were killed during that time.
AfriForum has been focusing on farm attacks since at least 2009. In 2018, during Trump’s first presidency, Kriel and Roets, who was then his deputy, met with government officials in Washington, D.C., about the issue, and Roets spoke about it with Tucker Carlson on Fox News, as the chyron below him announced in all caps, “White farmers brutally murdered every week in SouthAfrica.”
Additional research on crimes against white South Africans is an unnecessary and confusing use of U.S. taxpayer dollars, said Carolyn Holmes, a professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who studies democracy in southern Africa. Holmes noted that AfriForum already produces annual reports on crimes against farming communities. “These data already exist,” she said. “You don’t need a new study. You don’t even need a far-right study, we have those.”
The U.S. support offers more than a financial boost to the organization. “For some time, AfriForum has been campaigning for recognition of their claim that white people face discrimination and persecution,” said Alex Dyzenhaus, a lecturer in international relations and African politics at the University of St. Andrews. “Before, they were only getting the Tucker Carlsons and the far right of the news ecosystem. Now they have the U.S. government on their side.”
The Trump administration has made the plight of white, rural South Africans a key foreign policy issue. In addition to the early executive order, Trump held a contentious meeting with Ramaphosa in the White House last year where Trump claimed white farmers were being executed. The administration has also considered an ad campaign focused on encouraging more Afrikaners to come to the U.S.
In September, Roets of Lex Libertas met with the White House to discuss what he sees as the crisis facing the Afrikaner community and, along with the New York Young Republican Club, placed 3,000 white crosses on the National Mall to commemorate South African farm murders.
Roets declined to answer specific questions from ProPublica but, in a text message, described the murders of several Afrikaners that he knew personally. He also wrote, “I see the suffering of black people in South Africa, I am deeply moved by it, and I spend every day of my life campaigning to make things better for us all.”
Appearing at a press conference for the Lex Libertas event, Samson, the State Department official, showcased the sharp shift the administration has made in U.S. relations with South Africa. While apartheid has been understood globally as a symbol of racist oppression, Samson described the current South African government as having discriminatory “race-based” policies and a cautionary tale for the rest of the world.
At the end of apartheid, in 1994, South Africa was a “flourishing, prosperous society,” Samson said. Since then, the country has gone to “ruin.” He blamed the fall on a “radical ideological leftist movement that wears human rights, that wears tolerance and inclusivity, as a skin suit to advance their Marxist communist worldview.”
Part of the Trump administration’s solution to this perceived crisis, he said, was to provide the research funding.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Kamala Harris on Expanding Democratic Power in the South
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Kamala Harris on Expanding Democratic Power in the South
A conversation with the former vice president about the fight for Democrats in the too-long-neglected South.
Kamala Harris made a big return to the campaign trail in the fall of 2026, heading to such battleground states as Michigan, where she boosted US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and Georgia, where she campaigned with Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. But Harris also visited places that rarely see former vice presidents, such as Columbus, Mississippi, where she appeared in a packed high-school gymnasium on behalf of Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom. This campaigning, which she referred to as her “freedom tour,” has also taken the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee to Arkansas and Louisiana. Harris says she hasn’t decided whether to run for president again in 2028. But no matter what her own next step may be, she tells The Nation, she’s committed to boosting Democratic prospects in the too-long-neglected South.
—John Nichols
John Nichols:  Let’s talk about the fight for Democrats in the South.
Kamala Harris: One of my favorite subjects.
JN: You have been appearing at party events and with candidates across the region.
KH: And for my book tour. The publisher [of the book, 107 Days] was like, “Well, we don’t normally do a lot of book tours in the South.” And I was like, “Well, we’re going to do that, and people will come.” And they did—often a thousand people.
JN: There has been a lasting debate within the Democratic Party about how to approach deep-red states. A lot of strategists make the mistake of arguing, usually behind closed doors, “Let’s just write them off.”
KH: That is a mistake…. There are people in the South who have profound needs for the things the Democratic Party says we stand for: affordable healthcare, affordable childcare, a meaningful job that leads to the ability to have opportunity for your children. The dignity of all people—equality, fairness.
That point being number one.
The other point I would raise is that if you look at what’s happening demographically in the country, there is a reverse migration happening toward the South—both in terms of families who, historically, were from the South as well as a lot of young families, because it’s more affordable. And the South, you know, in terms of topography, is beautiful.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
JN: There’s also a political side to this. In several Southern states in 2024, you ran as well as or better than you did in several Northern states that were historically identified as more competitive. There’s a base to build from in the South, right?
KH: That’s right. And I feel so strongly that you have to be able to do battle, instead of sitting back and implicitly accepting the notion that you can’t win there. You certainly won’t win if you don’t do battle. And that requires, as we know, being present. And it requires an investment. And that is part of the failure [for national Democrats], which is a failure to invest in the infrastructure that would allow us to win. And then it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Then what do we do? We abandon the people of those states who want clean drinking water? Who want the freedoms we say we fight for? Who want Medicaid, because their rural hospitals are shutting down because of a lack of federal funding? Who, as I was saying in Mississippi, know they deserve better? And who know it doesn’t have to be that way?
Well, the Democratic Party’s got to get hip to that, too: It doesn’t have to be that way.
JN: When Democrats aren’t hip to that, it narrows the party’s path to governing majorities, right?
KH: That’s my point—absolutely right. It’s about: Are we gonna play small ball?
Look, everything worthwhile requires investment. And investment, by its very nature, includes planting some seeds for a return that might be a little ways down the road but will be well worth the investment.
JN: There may also be an opening now, because of widespread disdain for the GOP administration. Have you been surprised by the implosion of Trump’s approval ratings this year?
KH: I’m not surprised. I say it publicly because I mean it: This is the most callous, corrupt, and incompetent presidential administration we’ve ever experienced.… What has happened also is [Trump] has created a party—and they’ve allowed it—in his own image. This is not Ronald Reagan’s party. That’s so cliché; everybody says it. But he has created a party in his own image, including the callous nature. So am I surprised about that? No.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Brooklyn Asylum Seeker Breaks 30-Day Hunger Strike in ICE Detention in Georgia
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Gwynne Hogan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
A Russian asylum seeker who lives in Brooklyn ended a monthlong hunger strike in a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in Georgia on Wednesday.
Andrei Gerdiukov, who’s been in ICE detention since February, and the group of 10 strikers were demanding their releases — or in his case, at least a transfer to a facility in New York so he can be closer to his wife.
He and the other remaining hunger strikers broke their fast Wednesday, 30 days after they stopped eating on Oct. 6, according to Polina Chertushkina, 27, Gerdiukov’s wife, who spoke with him over the phone.
“His hands and legs were shaking,” Chertushkina said Gerdiukov told her, as he took his first bites of a pastry, his first solid food in a month. Chertushkina lost more than 30 pounds over the course of the month, she said.
Andrei Gerdiukov, 31, was among dozens of detainees at the Folkston D. Ray James ICE processing center in Georgia who launched a hunger strike last month. As the weeks dragged on, the strike dwindled to 11 participants, including Gerdiukov, who were then sent to another ICE detention center across the street.
In recent days, the remaining participants have been threatened with being force fed, Gerdiukov told The City Reporter in a phone call from the facility earlier in the week when the fast was ongoing
“I cannot sleep at all because of hunger,” he said.
“We’re waiting for them to start force feeding,” Gerdiukov said. “They told us every day.”
“I can see my ribs,” he said.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately return a request for comment.
As the Trump administration has detained historic numbers of people as part of its mass deportation agenda, detainees across the country have turned to hunger strikes to protest the conditions of their confinement. The Guardian has reported on how ICE has force fed hunger strikers with the approval of federal courts. Force feeding is a practice widely condemned by human rights groups as a form of torture.
Gerdiukov has been in ICE detention since Feb. 22, when he and his wife were pulled over by Border Patrol agents during a traffic stop while they were on vacation in Florida with another Russian asylum-seeking couple.
All four were arrested, and the men were held in ICE detention while the women were released under orders of supervision, Chertushkina said in an interview.
In the months since, Gerdiukov has tried to win his freedom in every way he could think of. He tried to get bond in immigration court and filed a habeas corpus petition. He was denied bond and then ordered removed, a decision he’s appealing. His habeas corpus petition seeking release is still pending before a federal judge in Georgia, seven months after he filed.
He and other detainees raised grievances about food, lack of medical care and poor conditions at the facility. He and his wife requested a transfer through formal channels, reaching out to their local Congressmember Yvette Clarke (D-Brooklyn), whose office also requested he be transferred on their behalf, according to correspondence shared with The City Reporter. None of it went anywhere, he said.
“We tried every legal process. Every issue we tried to solve it here, but they didn’t listen to us,” he said. “They leave us only one choice, that’s to protest, hunger strike.”
Chertushkina said that staff approached Gerdiukov this week offering to transfer him to another facility in Georgia, but not one closer to New York. Now that the strike was over she wasn’t sure what they would do.
“Maybe other people can forget about it,” she said. “Everything will be as it was before.”
Fleeing Putin’s Russia
The couple entered the United States seeking asylum in 2024, after fleeing Russia ahead of the landslide re-election of President Vladimir Putin.
They were caught by Russian police distributing pamphlets in favor of the opposition and arrested, Chertushkina said in an interview, and Gerdiukov was beaten up.
When they were released and told to return the next week, they understood that to mean they would be put in prison if they didn’t get out of the country. They bought plane tickets right away.
“We came home, and we understood, we have to leave Russia. You have another choice, or we will be in prison,” Chertushkina said.
The couple settled in Midwood, Brooklyn, applied for asylum, got work authorization and were going through deportation proceedings, immigration court records show. Gerdiukov was working as a handyman, while Chertushkina was teaching English to Russians, Belarusians and Ukrainians in Southern Brooklyn, she said. They were settling into life in New York City.
“Everybody was very kind. In New York City I feel a lot of people support immigrants, and I thought all Americans were like New Yorkers,” Gerdiukov said. “But I was wrong. Right now, I can see the difference.”
When they decided to go on vacation with their Russian friends, they thought with their asylum claims and deportation cases pending, they were not at risk of arrest by ICE or border patrol.
“They gave me all [the] documents, I thought I was legal,” Gerdiukov said. “I brought it with me. I have nothing to hide. I’m clear.”
All four of the Russians were arrested by border patrol. The women were released on orders of supervision, which means Chertushkina cannot leave the state to visit her husband in detention.
The two men were handed off together to ICE custody and spent a week at Alligator Alcatraz before they were sent to Folkston. Gerdiukov’s friend, Andrei Mikhailov, is also partaking in the hunger strike at Folkston, while Chertushkina and Mikhailov’s wife, Ksenia Volkova, have been advocating for their detained husbands, calling elected officials and reporters across the country.
Spokespeople for Rep. Clark, Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, Senator Chuck Schumer and Governor Kathy Hochul haven’t returned requests for comment.
Gerdiukov has already faced retaliation for his protest, disciplinary records shared with The City Reporter show. He was cited with the “prohibited acts” of “engaging in group demonstration” and “conduct that disrupts” after staff said he helped orchestrate a video call with other detainees that was put online and published by several media outlets “to generate public and media attention.”
After the charges, Gerdiukov spent two weeks in solitary confinement, he and his wife said.
When Gerdiukov spoke to The City Reporter earlier in the week, he said he felt weak, exhausted and hungry all the time. Still, he said the separation from his wife hurts most.
“I’m trying not to think about that,” he said. “It’s the hardest part.”

https://gothamist.com/news/dsny-worker-a.title: DSNY worker arrested for killing a woman in Brooklyn while driving a garbage truck
https://gothamist.com/news/dsny-worker-a.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/dsny-worker-a.text:
A Staten Island man on Wednesday was arrested for striking and killing a woman in Brooklyn while driving a Department of Sanitation garbage truck last week, according to the NYPD.
Timothy A. Mcvey, 41, was charged with failure to yield to a pedestrian and failure to exercise due care, the NYPD said.
Siobhan Lynch, 30, of Brooklyn, was crossing the parkway at Cropsey Avenue around 6:35 p.m. on Oct. 28 when the garbage truck, heading east, turned right onto the parkway and hit her, police said.
Emergency services took Lynch to NYU Langone Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Mcvey stayed at the scene, police said.
“This is a terrible tragedy, and our thoughts are with the family of the victim,” Department of Sanitation spokesperson Joshua Goodman told Gothamist in an email last week.
Information on Mcvey’s attorney was not immediately available.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: One museum visit a month could improve health, new report finds
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Joe Ware
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Visiting a museum or art gallery for just one hour a month could significantly improve people's physical and mental health, according to a new report which calls for cultural engagement to become as routine as exercise and healthy eating.
The research, commissioned by the charity Art Fund in partnership with University College London professor Daisy Fancourt, recommends that people spend at least 60 minutes with art in museums and galleries every month.
However, the survey of 2,000 UK adults found that 89% fail to meet this proposed target, equivalent to an estimated 49.5 million people.
The report, “The Recommended Dose of Art: A Prescription for Health and Wellbeing”, draws together scientific evidence suggesting that regular cultural engagement can reduce stress, improve cognitive health and potentially extend life expectancy.
Previous studies have shown that regular museum and gallery visits could nearly halve the risk of developing depression over the following decade. Other studies have linked cultural participation with reduced dementia risk and lower levels of loneliness.
Viewing original artworks in galleries was also associated with a 22% greater reduction in the stress hormone cortisol compared with viewing reproductions.
Fancourt, whose book Art Cure on the scientific benefits of art came out earlier this year, says regular engagement with art should be considered a health-promoting behaviour alongside exercise, a balanced diet and spending time outdoors.
“Guidelines like eating our 5-a-day of fruit and vegetables and getting our 10,000 steps have proven effective in helping us to prioritise other health-promoting behaviours in our busy lives,” she says in a statement. “Adding regular arts engagement to this list could be a simple and joyful way of investing further in our health and wellbeing.”
But the findings also raise questions about whether Britain's struggling museums have the resources to encourage more frequent visits. Jenny Waldman, the director of Art Fund, tells The Art Newspaper that the research strengthens the case for sustained public investment in museums, including protecting free admission at national institutions and supporting local and regional collections.
“We want to see sustained, long-term public investment across the museum sector, so that all museums have the resources to care for their collections and welcome the widest possible audiences,” she says.
Waldman acknowledged that removing admission charges alone would not overcome barriers to visiting museums, including accessibility and the resources available to institutions.
She says Art Fund's research among museum directors found that 36% of museums had reduced their opening hours because of insufficient funding and staffing.
“If we want museums to play a greater role in supporting public health, we must invest in the sector and give them the means to do so,” she adds.
Waldman also points to international developments, including Greece's introduction of arts prescribing into its national healthcare system and growing recognition of cultural organisations as public health assets. She also notes efforts closer to home: “Scotland's Chief Medical Officer, Sir Gregor Smith, recently published a report recognising arts organisations as important public health assets and calling for arts and culture to be embedded more widely in Scotland's approach to public health.”
