https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: French authorities investigate claim of fraud over Picasso plates and medallions on sale
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Vincent Noce
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A criminal investigation amid a family crisis casts a dark shadow over the illustrious history of the French studio Ateliers Hugo, which produced jewellery and silverware created by major artists of the 20th century. According to a legal source, the court of Aix-en-Provence in the south of France has opened an investigation following a complaint by the Picasso family.
On 10 March, Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, representing the nine heirs of the Spanish artist, filed a complaint alleging “fraud, counterfeiting, forgery and concealment of these felonies”. The file does not name the alleged perpetrators, and their identity is not presently known. The following month the Picasso family published a formal warning in the Gazette Drouot, titled “Hugo silverware”. It urged “all art market professionals and buyers to exercise the utmost vigilance”, following the appearance of what it described as “a large number” of illegitimate silver plates and gold medallions, valued at millions of euros.
The title refers to Ateliers Hugo, a goldsmith based in Aix-en-Provence. It was founded in 1933 by François Hugo (1899-1981), the great-grandson of the famous French author Victor Hugo. In 1955 Pablo Picasso, who since 1947 had created a variety of ceramics in Vallauris on the French Riviera, commissioned François Hugo to produce plates and dishes from similar designs in fine metals, using the traditional technique of repoussé. Later, the workshop reduced them into medallions and earrings. With the help of his brother, the painter Jean Hugo, who introduced him to artistic circles, François made jewellery designed by Salvador Dalí, Max Ernst, André Derain, Jean Arp, Jean Dubuffet, Roberto Matta, Jean Lurçat and Dorothea Tanning. In 1975, his son Pierre Hugo (1947-2023) took over the company. Pierre was followed by his son Nicolas (born 1989).
Members of the Picasso family and their lawyer, Jean-Jacques Neuer, who filed the complaint, declined to comment to The Art Newspaper. But their complaint alleges that “it has been discovered that the moulds of Picasso’s works were reused for unauthorised productions of silver and gold pieces, followed by duplicates, some of them bearing three times the same number, and unnumbered specimens”.
According to a source close to the investigation, the Picasso Administration, which represents the family, says it has discovered at least 17 complete or almost complete suspicious collections, amounting to hundreds of pieces. The first red flag was raised by the Museum of Old and New Art (Mona), a private Australian museum in Tasmania. According to this source, in May 2023 the museum informed the Picasso Administration of its doubts over plates it had bought at Sotheby’s in London. An auction catalogue of 13 October 2021 describes a “complete set of 24 silver plates” bearing the signature of the artist, completed with an additional “unnumbered proof of Visage aux mains”. The pieces were “accompanied by a certificate of authenticity issued by Pierre Hugo”. The lot was sold for £1.4m. Sotheby’s declined to comment for this story.
According to the legal files, the seller was the British dealer Mark Maurice, from a now dissolved gallery named Masterpiece. The source close to the investigation says the dealer allegedly produced documents showing that he had commissioned a set of plates and a set of medallions from the Ateliers Hugo between 2017 and 2020. Mark Maurice indicated he was “unable to respond” to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries “due to strict non-disclosure agreements in place”.
In summer 2023 the ceramics museum in Vallauris, Musée Magnelli, exhibited another collection of 24 silver plates as well as gold medallions attributed to Picasso.
According to the legal files, the Picasso Administration protested, having found that they bore no number, mark or punch, as legally required. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges these facts, but tells The Art Newspaper that the works exhibited at Musée Magnelli were so-called “author’s copies, made for the exhibition, duly indicating in the catalogue that they were not for sale”. He adds that he “recovered them and had them melted after the show”. Representatives for the museum did not respond to a request for comment.
In June 2023, as reported in the legal files, the French branch of the auction house Bonhams made a request to the Picasso Administration for the right to reproduce silverware for a catalogue. The auction house was planning a sale of 95 lots from the Ateliers Hugo collection, including works by Ernst, Derain and Cocteau, valued between €400 and €50,000 each. The most valuable were 59 pieces, “made by” or “after” Picasso.
Works withdrawn from Bonhams sale
On 26 September 2023 Bonhams was informed by the Picasso Administration that these pieces were considered to be “unauthorised” editions. The auction house then decided to “delay the whole sale”, just two days before it was due to take place. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges he “did initiate, in the wake of good results obtained at Bonhams UK, this sale of pieces”, produced, he says, by his “father and grandfather”. But, he adds, “When we were informed by dealers of the presence of possible duplicates, I agreed to withdraw the sale and collaborated with the Picasso Administration to identify them.”
Bonhams declined to comment, but according to the source close to the investigation, the lots attributed to Picasso were sequestered when a British financial company, Suros Capital, tried to recover them as collateral for a €256,000 loan. A spokesperson for Suros confirmed the operation to The Art Newspaper, adding that “it was secured against not only the Picasso pieces, but a range of assets which are progressively realised, so the company expects to recover the loan in full”.
In November 2023, according to the source close to the investigation, a representative for Bonhams France informed the Picasso Administration that a Spanish collector contacted the auction house to sell 24 silver plates, estimated at £900,000. Again, the auction house refused on the basis of Picasso Administration’s doubts about the objects’ authenticity. In the legal files, the Picasso Administration claims the same collector had sold another set of 24 silver plates and one of 24 gold medallions in private sales through Bonhams in London in 2022. Neither the British auction house nor the Spanish collector made any comment.
The rights to reproduce the items disappeared with [my father and grandfather], so I have never minted any of Picasso’s creations Nicolas Hugo, Ateliers Hugo
Nicolas Hugo, who says he has not been interviewed by the investigators, claims he has no knowledge of the proceedings and “is unaware of the content of the complaint” issued by the Picasso Administration. But, he says: “The criminal investigation can only deal with facts related to the time of my father and grandfather, therefore falling under the statute of limitations and concerning persons now deceased.” He adds that “the rights to reproduce the items disappeared with them, so I have never minted any of Picasso’s creations”, and he does not have the legal status of a goldsmith. However, he says: “I have signed some certificates of authenticity, but only to confirm my father’s own signature.”
In interviews with The Art Newspaper, Nicolas Hugo describes himself as a “self-taught art dealer”. When he was around 20 years old, he started to work as an assistant in galleries in Paris, before moving to London. He is now an agent for several artists and a curator. In 2022, the French magazine Les Hardis described him as a “mix of British and Saint-Germain-des-Prés charm”. “My father became very ill in 2018,” he told the magazine. “I had an epiphany. I decided to take over the workshop. I immersed myself completely,” and started to train in manufacturing jewels.
“From 2019,” he tells The Art Newspaper, “I became involved in the history of his workshop and helped my father to showcase this heritage, for memorial and commercial reasons. I set up exhibitions in places like Barcelona or Vallauris and initiated this sale of the fonds d’atelier at Bonhams Paris. I have not taken over my father’s company and was not his partner.”
Ateliers Hugo in limbo
Nicolas Hugo says: “There have been some duplicates on the market, dating from my father’s period, but I have no idea who had made them in the workshop.” He says he has “no idea who put a collection on sale at Sotheby’s in 2021” and knows “nothing of the three sets proposed by this Spanish collector to Bonhams in 2022 and 2023”.
The criminal investigation is still at the preliminary phase. It comes at a time when the company is already in limbo. Pierre Hugo died in October 2023 and his five children have turned down his inheritance. Nicolas Hugo’s brothers and sisters declined to comment to The Art Newspaper due to the ongoing investigation.
However, sources close to the case say that Pierre Hugo’s heirs’ inheritance came with a €2.5m tax debt. According to these sources, three of the Hugo siblings said in police interviews they were “not at all” aware of the conduct of the workshop by their brother Nicolas, who had succeeded their ailing father in 2019. The sources said the three Hugo siblings were on alert after learning that Bonhams Paris declined to sell the collection from the Ateliers Hugo in September 2023. According to the same sources, when Pierre Hugo died a month later, the three siblings went to the workshop and took 21 moulds of plates that they decided to hand over to the Picasso Administration. Three moulds from the set were missing and they did not find those for the medallions.
According to these sources, the three Hugo siblings explained to the investigators that, “knowing that the rights of reproduction were extinct, they wanted to be sure this would be respected”. The siblings also asserted that they “did not want in any way to be implicated in these operations and made it clear to the Picasso Administration”, according to the sources.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-dcs-newes.title: Opinion: DC’s Newest Bosses Are From New York. They Must Deliver the IBX.
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dcs-newes.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dcs-newes.text:
Share This Article
“New York’s civic and business leaders remain pessimistic about relying on the federal government’s support to bring the IBX to life; this is exactly the moment we need commitment from this Congress.”
We learned Tuesday evening that the Democrats will take control of the U.S. House and Senate. And it appears leaders of both chambers will be not only New Yorkers but Brooklynites—at no other time in U.S. history have both chambers been led by New Yorkers.
As a rent-stabilized Queens resident and member of Queens Community Board 5, I am calling on this new federal government to make an unwavering and comprehensive commitment to the construction of the Interborough Express (IBX). Strong federal support is the last remaining key to building the IBX. Our city cannot miss this opportunity.
The IBX is perhaps the most significant American public transit project in generations, establishing a new, non-Manhattan-oriented spine connecting the Brooklyn Army Terminal in Bay Ridge to Jackson Heights, Queens. This corridor would serve 160,000-plus weekday riders and connect nearly 1 million residents across some of the most transit-starved neighborhoods in New York City. Notably, my neighborhood may stand to benefit the most: bringing our district three to four new rail stations with connections to 16 more subway lines, up from our current one, the M train.
This new Congress comes at the heels of the draft environmental impact statement’s (DEIS) publication, a make-or-break moment for the IBX. Simultaneously, New York’s civic and business leaders remain pessimistic about relying on the federal government’s support to bring the IBX to life; this is exactly the moment we need commitment from this Congress.
New York now has the leverage to steward a century-long vision through the next two years of solvable engineering challenges, financial hurdles, and bureaucratic speed bumps with executive dedication and robust public collaboration. During this crucial phase, this Congress can show both New Yorkers and Americans what a serious government can do: deliver modern marvels that materially improve all of our lives, something generations past regularly enjoyed.
This leadership must take several forms.
First, it must courageously fund the IBX. New Yorkers cannot afford delays due to MTA funding deficits, and the federal government must readily fill in gaps should they arrive. Simply put, we must secure bigger checks from this government. We deserve the investment.
Although we are working toward 50 percent federal support for the IBX through the Federal Transit Administration’s New Starts program, these grants can cover up to 60 percent. An extra 10 percent, roughly $550 million, offers capital flexibility the MTA can direct quicker as the project progresses.
Similarly, mechanisms like the Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act’s low-interest loans, greater congestion mitigation and air quality (CMAQ) grants, and expanded formula funding flexibility already have and must continue supporting nimble and adaptive budgets. Completing the IBX shouldn’t require innovative public financing—we have all the tools. We just need a Congress committed to them.
This political leadership must also embody bureaucratic excellence for the IBX. This can look like easing red-tape and ensuring smooth, synchronized partnership between federal and MTA leaders. It is already taking shape in notable ways. Federal funding is right now supporting design and engineering prerequisites for IBX transfers.
Given the highly competitive pool of New Start grant monies, however, this federal government must also classify the IBX under federal dashboard streamlining initiatives to prioritize its review, ensuring that federal agencies respond quickly to environmental impact assessments. Further, this federal government can issue swift Federal Railroad Administration regulatory waivers, protecting the IBX from freight regulatory disputes.
Ultimately, I am calling on this federal government to be nonstop cheerleaders for the IBX. It is through the constant drumming of support that the IBX can fulfill and expand its promise; Gov. Kathy Hochul, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, community boards, and countless New Yorkers are already exemplifying this.
Likewise, U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer and Congressman Hakeem Jeffries must routinely visit station sites, organize public forums, and champion the IBX throughout the media. Setting this tone has real economic value, too. The sooner the IBX is operational, the sooner both its broad economic multipliers compound and increase while its overall per-rider costs decrease.
Delivering the IBX is not only an easy political homerun for their constituencies, but with their new leadership roles, the Democrats can take significant ownership of the IBX’s success.
Take this opportunity, Sen.Schumer and Congressman Jeffries. Remind the people what America is capable of. Imagine! Congress’s two Brooklyn leaders delivering our city the promise of the IBX. Show us that the mandate you received Tuesday night can work, that neighborly politics can deliver. Show us that the government can make our lives better. We deserve it.
I cannot wait to share IBX rides with my neighbors. I cannot wait for the IBX to connect me to new neighbors. I cannot wait to look into the future knowing the IBX will be there. What I’m asking of our Congress here is to step up. We need your help. We are so so close.
Gentry Fitch is a rent-stabilized tenant of Ridgewood, Queens and member of Queens Community Board 5. The views represented here are solely his own and do not reflect the views of QCB5.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/s.title: Sunset Park Blaze Kills 6 As Lithium-ion Battery Fire Crisis Rages On
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/s.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/s.text:
The fire left lives and homes ruined. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Six Brooklynites were killed in an early morning fire that engulfed an entire wooden row house — and authorities are investigating whether the blaze is linked to this year’s 68 percent rise in fires sparked or intensified by highly flammable lithium-ion batteries.
It took smoke-eaters three hours on Thursday to extinguish the 1:40 a.m. fire, which sent flames shooting out of every window. When the smoke cleared, four people were dead on the scene and two died later in the hospital. Four others remain hospitalized, officials said at a press briefing.
Fire marshals are still investigating, but early reports linked the fire to a lithium-ion battery, though it is unclear if the battery sparked the blaze or was simply consumed by it. Two burnt-out electric bike frames were spotted outside the building on Thursday.
The Sunset Park incident comes weeks after a family of four was wiped out in the Bronx when an e-bike caught fire in their apartment.
The story behind the story
After a peak in deaths associated with the batteries in 2023, officials were quick to pass legislation banning the sale of uncertified lithium-ion batteries and e-bikes, but they are still easy to obtain online on sites like Facebook Marketplace. In addition, after-market modifications make batteries unstable.
Many batteries bought during the pandemic — when the delivery industry fueled by e-bikes boomed — are nearing the end of their useable life. The decay of lithium-ion batteries is one reason why there have been fewer deaths this year from fires, even as there have been more blazes, because more fires are occurring outside of homes when batteries are discarded.
So far this year there have been 406 fires determined by FDNY to be caused by the batteries compared to 241 last year. But, the largest increase is in non-structural fires, up to 252 from 100, meaning blazes that occur outside of a home or business. Through mid-October, as Streetsblog reported exclusively, there were 87 lithium-ion fires in garbage trucks, up from 55 in all of last year, according to the Department of Sanitation.
“There’s no comprehensive plan to deal with the battery life cycles,” Baruch Herzfeld, who co-founded the battery charging company Popwheels, told Streetsblog last month. “There’s a fictitious belief that battery fires don’t happen unless batteries are charging. People are basing their safety guidelines on something that’s not true.”
The city’s efforts to promote outdoor battery storage and charging have largely fallen flat. After a successful pilot in 2024, the city has yet to install any public charging infrastructure and companies who provide battery subscription services are hindered by a web of ever-changing safety regulations that make it nearly impossible to grow. As of last month, the city hadn’t approved any permits that would allow landlords or business owners to set up charging cabinets on the sidewalk. The application will now be streamlined since New Yorkers overwhelmingly passed the mayor’s charter revision ballot proposals on Tuesday.
Sunset Park is filled with e-bikes — on the street, inside restaurants, within the gates of the many row houses, inside apartments. Elected officials want to see outdoor charging options.
“We have had multiple trainings from FDNY that ask people, do not store your battery inside, and also do not charge when you are sleeping. So that has been an ongoing issue,” said Council Member Susan Zhuang (D-Sunset Park) at the scene on Thursday. “I am going to look and see if we can set up some stations so people can just charge outdoors, that will be helpful to the community. It’s not just the delivery people that use the bikes, it’s everyone.”
A neighbor who has lived on the block for 42 years told Streetsblog she lives in fear of battery fires.
“I am angry as hell right now. We need control of these lithium batteries coming from China,” said Rukmin DeGaray. “They are no good for neighborhoods; they shouldn’t be allowed in any building that people live in. They just blow up and these old wooden buildings, they go up like lightning.”
The driver, Timothy McVey, 41, of Staten Island, turned himself in at the 62nd Precinct station house and was booked for failure to yield and failure to exercise due care

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: We Stomped All Over the Patriarchy on Tuesday Night
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Amy Littlefield
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
We Stomped All Over the Patriarchy on Tuesday Night
Almost everywhere, abortion rights initiatives won, and pro-choice candidates prevailed. Even in Idaho, where they didn’t, women are taking heart.
I’ve always wondered what smashing the patriarchy really feels like, and on Tuesday night, we found out.
Up until then, the patriarchy had been on quite the winning streak, so much so that a newly surfaced rape allegation against the sitting president was hardly a news story. Then, on Tuesday, we got to watch a child sexual abuse survivor defeat the Republican challenger who called her a liar in the Ohio governor’s race. We got to see Max Miller, an Ohio Republican whose ex-wife accused him of holding a gun to her head while she changed their toddler’s diaper, lose his seat in a former Republican stronghold. We got to see Texans elect a Democratic Latina governor from Brownsville, Gina Hinojosa, who ran an ad about her decision to carry a nonviable pregnancy to term—and used that horrific ordeal to defend the right of Texans to choose. A Tennessee woman denied an abortion under the state’s ban won a state House seat; Virginia, Missouri, and Nevada voted to protect or expand abortion rights; and Maine Senator Susan Collin was ousted in large part because of her vote to confirm accused attempted rapist Brett Kavanaugh, to the Supreme Court.
But there were exceptions to the trend, including the success of anti-trans ballot initiatives and the defeat of an abortion rights initiative in Idaho, a state that, in the midst of the blue tsunami felt, as Idaho-based reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris put it to me, like an “island of sadness.”
Related Articles
“It was a great night in this nation for a rebuke” of patriarchy, Melanie Folwell, executive director of the ballot initiative campaign Idahoans United for Women and Families, told me. “But here in Idaho, where we had two of the wealthiest, most powerful patriarchies in the world—the Catholic Church and the Mormon Church—and then the supermajority Idaho GOP, my God, patriarchy won the day.”
Proposition 1 would have enshrined in Idaho statutes a right to abortion up until viability. But 56 percent of voters chose instead to keep the state’s near-total abortion ban. It was a gutting loss in a state where more than a third of the state’s ob-gyns have left or stopped practicing since the ban took effect, and where the campaign shared harrowing stories of women traveling to terminate nonviable pregnancies, getting med-flighted to neighboring states while miscarrying, or bleeding out while doctors whose colleagues have fled the state scrambled to save them. “I feel like the women and families and doctors were so brave telling their stories,” Suzanne Gallus, a Catholic mom of seven who knocked 1,289 doors to support Prop 1, told me. “For people to just ignore all that is especially hard to take.”
Folwell said the campaign faced uniquely strong headwinds, including an influx of new Republican residents that have turned the state into one of the country’s reddest and a convoluted explanation of the meaning of a “yes” or “no” vote that was attached to the ballot by the Republican secretary of state. The Mormon and Catholic churches donated a combined $1.3 million to an anti-abortion PAC that ran a barrage of ads in the final weeks of the campaign claiming that the proposition’s “fine print” would redefine fetal viability to exclude premature newborns who needed oxygen, allow “late-term abortion on demand,” and let minors get abortions without parental consent. The claims were false; the initiative didn’t repeal the state’s existing parental consent laws, and it would have allowed the state to ban abortion after fetal viability except in medical emergencies. But the ads forced canvassers like Suzanne Gallus, a Catholic mom of seven, to have uncomfortably technical conversations about fetal viability at the doors.
“For crying out loud, I’m not a doctor; I’m not a lawyer,” Gallus told me. “I know how to explain that, but then you’re getting into the weeds, and when you get into the weeds like that, I think you do more damage than you do good.”
Folwell said the initiative also suffered crucially from a lack of support from national organizations who balked at the fact that it could be repealed by the Republican legislature. The dozen or so abortion ballot initiatives that have passed since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in states ranging from Ohio and Arizona to Virginia and Vermont have all been more enduring constitutional amendments, not statutory provisions, but Idaho does not allow voters to initiate constitutional amendments.
“There was a lot—from national groups— a lot of gnashing of teeth about, ‘Oh, well, it could just be statutorily overturned,’ before it was even won, and a lack of investment and care because of this silly gamesmanship about what’s next, rather than focusing on tangible movement-building and wins to get things done,” Folwell told me. “And I’m [feeling] pretty crappy about it.”
But Folwell felt proud of the 2,500 or so volunteers who powered her campaign.
“The most important story out of all of this is the degree to which there are thousands and thousands of women in this state who feel less alone,” Folwell said, her voice breaking. “And that’s from people who survived something terrible to people who found community in advocacy, and that all has meaning.”
“They may have been let down in myriad ways by people in the state and outside the state, but they showed up for each other.”
Among those who showed up was Whitney Montgomery, the daughter of the architect of Idaho’s abortion ban. Montgomery drew audible gasps during a Prop 1 rally when she revealed that she was the daughter of David Ripley, who has built his anti-abortion lobbyist career on an origin story about his objections to his ex-wife’s abortion. Montgomery’s childhood memories of her dad include his stint in jail for failing to pay child support to her mother—whom he divorced before later marrying the woman who had the abortion.
“I have spent years trying to understand how someone can dedicate his life to ‘saving babies’ while ignoring one of his own,” Montgomery wrote in an op-ed for the Post Register about her decision to support Prop 1. “By his own public admission, he was a cruel and abusive husband to many of his wives. As a child, I remember hiding in a bathroom with a phone nearby, ready to call 911 if things got worse.”
I interviewed Montgomery on election night, after she had just voted at her son’s elementary school; she’d brought her 3- and 6-year-olds to the polls as part of a family tradition, and that night, they were going to make Barack Obama’s chili recipe. Montgomery conceived through IVF, another reason she objects to the agenda of her father’s political party, which opposes it. When I told her that her decision to stand up to her father—who has admitted being a “jackass” to the wife who had the abortion—felt like a symbol of the stakes for this entire election, she agreed.
“It comes down to punishing women and having that control,” Montgomery said. “He feels like he was wronged by a woman, and now it’s this punishment to women’s health.
“It’s wild.”
(David Ripley didn’t respond to my calls for comment for this article. I did speak to his fourth wife, Wendy, at 10:15 am on Election Day. She told me her husband was still asleep. They’d had a late night; among other things, they were fending off teenagers from the nearby high school who kept stealing their anti–Prop 1 yard signs.)

But outside of Idaho, women won the day, and even from the island of sadness, Montgomery felt like she was part of it.
“It was a sad night for Idaho but I’m so happy for the rest of the country and the progress that is being made,” Montgomery texted me on Wednesday. “I truly believe this fight is not over. It’s just the beginning.”
Indeed, Folwell’s critique about a lack of investment from national groups who saw Idaho as a lost cause echoed what I heard in 2021 from abortion rights advocates in Texas, who felt under-resourced, isolated, and ignored as they fought a Republican legislature that banned abortion at six weeks. To see Texas turn blue on Tuesday after the most highly invested-in Senate race in history, to see a new Democratic attorney general–elect pledge to drop lawsuits against out-of-state abortion providers, while a pro-choice Latina takes the governor’s office is a reminder that all progress is incremental, until it’s not. Before a wave grows big enough to smash the patriarchy, it starts with ripples too small to detect.
Gallus said she would keep making those ripples with the women she’d met through the campaign.
“Cultivating these little seeds here and there is really important when you’re in a place that is very extreme, because this is our home,” Gallus told me in an emotional interview on Wednesday.
“If Texas can do this, then maybe we can, too; it’s just going to take longer.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-dem.title: The Democratic Coalition Still Has a Class Problem
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-dem.author: Jared Abbott
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-dem.text:
The Democratic Coalition Still Has a Class Problem
The blue wave was undeniable. But early survey data suggest the party rode on a backlash against Donald Trump and a midterm electorate tilted toward college graduates, not a return of the working-class voters the party will need in 2028.
Democrats won a massive victory in the 2026 midterms, performing so well that Republicans’ best-laid gerrymandering plans actually backfired in a number of states, most notably Texas and North Carolina. There, Democrats held most of the seats Republicans had targeted and even flipped some districts drawn to be safely Republican. Democrats flipped Senate seats in places like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina that were considered virtually unimaginable reaches in the very recent past.
That’s of course very good for the party, and, I would hasten to add, for our fight against the ever-present threat of the far right. But Democrats’ stunning upset also brings a strong temptation for moderates and progressives alike: to read the result as proof that the party has finally turned the corner with working-class voters and can ride carefree into the 2028 sunset.
But provisional data suggest otherwise. Unless noted, the figures in this piece come from the AP Voter Poll, a large survey of voters conducted for the Associated Press around Election Day, and from its predecessor, AP VoteCast, for earlier elections. We won’t know the true shape of the 2026 electorate for months, until validated voter data becomes available, but the AP poll gives us a helpful initial look. It shows Democrats gaining real ground since 2024 with college graduates and voters without degrees alike.
But measured against 2018, the last Democratic midterm wave, the party is still deep in the hole with working-class voters, and its coalition is more lopsided by class than ever. That leaves Democrats exposed to another 2024-style loss in 2028. It also keeps out of reach the broad working-class supermajority progressives would need to deliver real change for working Americans.
It’s the (Trump) Economy, Stupid
Few doubted heading into November that Democrats would take the House of Representatives. The president’s party has lost the national House vote in each of the last five midterms. This year followed a similar script as past midterms, but it was amplified by several additional factors.
First, Donald Trump is deeply unpopular. Only 38 percent of 2026 voters approved of his job performance, and 75 percent said the economy was in poor or not-so-good shape. Some 43 percent said they voted to express opposition to Trump, against 16 percent who voted to support him.
The second factor follows from the first. Trump’s unpopularity reached into his own coalition, especially the less partisan, less habitual voters who backed him in 2024 because they were pissed off with the Democrats on affordability and immigration. With the economy still souring and Trump himself not on the ballot (despite his many exhortations that voters imagine he was), however, many saw little reason to turn out for Republicans. As a result, according to a rough estimate from the AP data, depressed turnout among Trump supporters alone was worth around 5 points to Democrats.
Third, Democrats now have a stronger midterm coalition than Republicans. For most of the twentieth century, Democrats depended on working-class voters who turned out less reliably, so low-turnout midterms tended to favor Republicans. That pattern has flipped. Democrats now draw more of their support from college graduates and other highly engaged voters who tend to show up even in off years. Republicans, meanwhile, rely increasingly on less engaged, lower-propensity voters, many without degrees, who turn out mainly when Trump is a candidate. The upshot is that the lower the turnout, the better Democrats now tend to do.
The danger for Democrats is that these advantages are temporary and unlikely to reappear in 2028 when Trump will no longer be the Republicans’ national standard-bearer, and many of the low-propensity conservative voters who sat out this year will flock back to the polls.
The Class Divide Grew in 2026
The divide between college and noncollege voters grew again in 2026, even as Democrats gained among both groups. Democrats’ margin among college graduates jumped 12 points from Kamala Harris’s 2024 showing, while their margin among noncollege voters improved by about 8 points and remained negative.
If we compare 2026 with 2018, the last time Democrats rode a midterm backlash against Trump, we see that while the party’s national margin was 2 points better in 2026, Democrats actually won voters without college degrees by 3.5 points in 2018, whereas this year they lost noncollege voters by about 5 points. Meanwhile, Democrats’ margin among college graduates grew from 14 points to 26 during the same period. The result is a yawning class gap of over 30 points, up from about 10 points in 2018.
That gap matters, because the road to the White House and sustained control of the Senate still runs through voters without college degrees. Noncollege voters remain a majority of the electorate, and in 2020 they made up a majority of voters in every one of the key swing states. With class-based support remaining so lopsided, Democrats remain vulnerable in the key presidential battlegrounds, let alone expanding their reach further into red territory in a durable way that outlasts the political manna Trump delivered to them in 2026. Relying on larger margins among college-educated suburbanites alone is arithmetically insufficient and politically unsustainable.
Democrats’ problems with noncollege voters are hardly limited to white voters. Among voters of color without college degrees, Democrats won by 57 points in 2018 but by only 34 in 2022 and 2024. This year’s rebound to 40 points, especially among Latino voters, is real, but it recovers only about a quarter of the ground the party has lost with these voters since 2018. Voters of color without degrees are now less Democratic than voters of color with them, a reversal of the 2018 pattern.
Do Democrats Even Need Noncollege Voters After 2026?
AP’s data suggest that college graduates supplied most of the national swing toward the Democrats in 2026. Based on my calculation from AP’s published breakdowns of the vote by education, voters with a four-year college degree likely accounted for more than half of the roughly 11-point move toward Democrats from Harris’s 2024 margin to 2026. This invites a tantalizing conclusion: that the party’s future lies mainly with college graduates, and that the noncollege gains are a bonus rather than a necessity. But that idea is clearly belied by the results of the red-state Senate races.
In the five red-state Senate upsets, the national pattern did not hold. There, Democrats’ margins among noncollege voters improved by 15 to 24 points over Harris’s 2024 showing, far more than the roughly 8-point gain they made with this group nationally. The figure below estimates what would have happened if each educational group in these states had shifted only as much as it did nationally.
Had noncollege voters in these states moved only at the national pace, three of the five Senate Democratic hopefuls in red states would have lost, and the other two would have won by less than 2 points. Had college graduates moved only at their national pace, four of the five would still have won. In other words, red-state Democrats did not win by riding the national wave. They won by outrunning it among noncollege voters.
Democrats Are Still Unpopular
Democrats won a landslide, but not because Americans suddenly warmed to them. In Pew’s polling of all adults, 40 percent of Americans viewed the Democratic Party favorably a month before the election, and 58 percent unfavorably. That is a recovery from a low of 36 percent in August 2025, but it is still well below the 46–47 percent Democrats drew during Trump’s first term. Gallup tells a similar story: 43 percent favorable in September 2026, up from 37 percent a year earlier but below the party’s 49 percent average since 1992.
A good share of Democrats’ 2026 margin also came from voters whose support came grudgingly. About 16 percent of voters viewed neither party favorably, and Democrats won them by 25 points, which works out to roughly 4 points of the party’s national margin.
Trust in Democrats on the issues is also thin. Asked which party could better handle the economy, 43 percent said Democrats, 38 percent said Republicans, and 19 percent said neither. That is a 6-point edge in a year when three in four voters rated the economy poorly. Republicans still led on immigration, and the parties were tied on taxes. Recent research I conducted with Joan Williams, based on a February 2026 survey, shows how shallow Democrats’ gains on immigration are. Fifty-six percent of working-class respondents agreed that Trump “has gone too far, with masked men arresting ordinary hardworking people instead of just deporting criminals.” Yet only 36 percent preferred Joe Biden’s immigration policies to Trump’s. Many working-class voters are uneasy with how Trump’s policies are carried out, but they still prefer them to Biden’s by nearly two to one.
The Dealignment Carousel
American politics over the past decade has settled into a self-reinforcing cycle of backlash that virtually guarantees heightened polarization and increasing voter disaffection. The White House has changed parties in three straight elections, and control of the House has now flipped in three consecutive midterms. After each of these elections, the winning party has claimed a mandate to finally address Americans’ growing sense of economic dislocation and political disenchantment, and each time it fails to deliver.
This is what dealignment looks like. Neither party has a stable majority coalition, so outcomes swing with the national mood and with which party’s voters turn out. In the current arrangement, that produces a reliable rhythm. In midterms, the electorate is smaller and more educated, which now favors Democrats, and the president’s party is punished, so Democrats win big when a Republican holds the White House. In presidential years, the electorate grows by tens of millions, and the added voters are disproportionately noncollege, less attached to either party, and now lean slightly Republican.
But even as each election ping-pongs back and forth between the parties, the education gap has continued to grow from 10 points in 2018 to 27 points in 2024, and now 31 in 2026. The electoral carousel goes up and down, but class dealignment continues apace.
That is why even a midterm landslide like this one does little to change the underlying shape of American politics. A wave lifts the party’s fortunes with nearly every group at once, so on election night the gains among college graduates and the modest recovery among working-class voters blurred together into a single triumphant story. But when the tide goes out, Democrats are left with the same lopsided class coalition that has plagued them for more than a decade, and Americans are left in a seemingly endless limbo where neither party can govern for working people.
Rather than overreading this year’s victory, Democrats should look closely at where they won on hostile terrain, and how they did it. The red-state Senate races offer the clearest model: as we saw above, James Talarico, Sherrod Brown, Adam Hamilton, Annie Andrews, and Josh Turek won by outrunning the national swing among noncollege voters, not by running up the score in the suburbs. The question for 2028 is whether Democrats can keep making gains like these with noncollege voters through an affirmative economic message that cuts through even without the assistance of a historically unpopular chief executive.
There is plenty raw material to work with. Seven in ten voters in the AP Voter Poll said the US economic system favors the wealthy, and those voters backed Democrats by more than 50 points in 2026. That is a ready-made audience for an economic populist message aimed at working-class voters, many of whom agree that the system is rigged but don’t yet trust Democrats to fix it. Democrats again won lower-income voters by more than higher-income voters this year, and union households backed them by 20 points, compared with 8 among nonunion voters. Those are signs that a class-based appeal can still work. But they will not add up to a durable majority unless Democrats also find a way to maintain and expand their margins among voters without college degrees.
Trump has handed Democrats a reprieve, not a realignment. They can spend the next two years taking credit for a blue wave delivered largely by outside forces, or they can use it to figure out how to build lasting support among the working-class voters they will need when the wave recedes.

https://hyperallergic.com/mfa-boston-to-.text:
MFA Boston to Allow Visitors to Watch Live Conservation of Dutch Painting
Nicolaes Eliasz Pickenoy’s 17th-century group portrait of an Amsterdam wine guild will be the star of a pop-up restoration studio that museumgoers can peer into.
Visitors to the Museum of Fine Arts (MFA) in Boston can soon watch the year-long restoration process of Nicolaes Eliasz Pickenoy's "The Founders of the Amsterdam Wine Merchants Guild" (1625).
Beginning on December 9, museumgoers can watch as conservators, scientists, art historians, and curators cycle through a pop-up studio in the MFA's Center for Netherlandish Art's Innovation Gallery.
Acquired last year, the group portrait depicts the six founding members of the lucrative Amsterdam Wine Merchants Guild, which operated until the late 18th century.

https://hellgatenyc.com/the-real-housewi.title: 'The Real Housewives of New York City' Act…Normal?!
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-real-housewi.author: Katie Way
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-real-housewi.text:
In case you haven't noticed, it's fall. Daylight has been saved; full dark hits before the workday ends. In just a few days, the idyllic stretch of weather we basked in all October will be nothing but a distant memory, little comfort in the face of November's chill. This week's RHONY episode, Season 16, Episode 9, was filmed sometime in the spring. But because it features the cast members wearing scarves and light jackets as they make their windswept way across the city, it feels, somehow, seasonally appropriate. 
And I don't know if it's just the approaching holiday season making me more charitable, but this week's episode was also surprisingly nice to watch, given how little actually happened in terms of moving the "plot" of the season forward. 
RHONY S16 has been about constructing a plausible friend group of cast members, something the previous two seasons failed at spectacularly. In that regard, despite my grousing, I think this week proved that the project was a success. Finally, after two pretty excruciating years of franchise triaging, it doesn't feel totally random that these women are gossiping with each other over lunch, or attending each others' birthday parties, because most of them seem to have some kind of actual connection to each other.

https://gothamist.com/news/queens-public.title: Queens Public Library online system downed by ransomware hack, officials said
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-public.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-public.text:
A ransomware attack Wednesday on the Queens Public Library resulted in a system-side network outage that continued into Thursday and could take some time to be fixed, library officials said.
In posts on social media, the library said while all branches are open to the public, several services including the website, on-site computers, check out and return machines, and free Wi-Fi were unavailable. The library’s app and digital media services were also down.
Services remained affected as of Thursday afternoon. CEO Dennis Walcott told Gothamist the library was working closely with law enforcement including the NYPD and the FBI to rectify the problem.
“ Unfortunately, it's part of the world that we live in right now,” he said. “So the Queens Public Library is a victim of the type of world that we're living in, where people are launching cyber attacks against various types of entities, large corporations, and now Queens Public Library.”
Walcott said the investigation is ongoing, and it’s not yet clear who is behind the attack, why the Queens Public Library was targeted or if users’ data was vulnerable.
“ We're getting information in on a regular basis, we have regular meetings with, the authorities and always getting updated information as far as the next steps that we need to take and also what the law enforcement authorities are doing as well,” he said.
In the meantime, library users will be able to check books in and out in person at their local branches, Walcot said. They should check with their local branches about virtual and in-person programs, which may be limited as the library works to get systems back up, he said. While renewals aren’t available, those who have books or other media due won’t be charged late fines, library officials said.
The Queens Public Library system includes 66 branches across the borough library system, including seven adult learning centers, teen centers, bookmobiles, and book bicycles.
This story has been updated with more information.

The Studio Museum in Harlem on November 5 announced curator, writer, and historian Ade Omotosho as associate curator. Omotosho will take up his post on November 16, reporting to chief program officer Natasha Logan and joining the museum as it celebrates its first year in its new purpose-built home. He will be tasked with shaping and overseeing the institution’s permanent collection, which comprises more than nine thousand objects—including works by more than eight hundred artists—dating from the present back to the nineteenth century.
“The Studio Museum in Harlem is delighted to welcome Ade Omotosho, an accomplished and adept curator whose thoughtful approach and breadth of experience will greatly enhance our mission to support and amplify artists of African descent through the care and growth of our permanent collection,” said Logan in a statement.
Omotosho, a 2025 participant in the museum’s Art Leadership Praxis, arrives to the Studio Museum from the Dallas Museum of Art, where he was assistant curator of contemporary art. Previous roles include those in the curatorial departments at Pérez Art Museum Miami and the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. Omotosho holds a BA in art history from the University of Texas at Austin with a certificate in African studies, and an MA from the Williams Graduate Program in the History of Art. He has contributed writing to exhibition catalogues including those published by the Studio Museum in Harlem as well as those accompanying the 2024 Venice Biennale, Made in LA 2023, and Prospect.5.
Omotosho in a statement acknowledged that he was “thrilled” to be joining the museum at a “pivotal moment” in its history. “From its inception, the Museum has championed the range of practices of artists of African descent,” he continued, “supplying a way of seeing that remains vital and necessary in our cultural landscape.”

This story was originally published by Documented. Sign up for their newsletter here.
It was around 9:30 p.m., when the loud chants began.
“La-rry, La-rry!” “Joyce, Joyce!”
Inside the two-story house in Bensonhurst, it felt as though the roof could come off. Dozens of community members and campaign volunteers for State Senate District 17 and State Assembly District 49 candidates gathered inside Tuesday night to watch the election results pour in.
Standing in the center of the crowd was Larry He, the Democratic challenger to incumbent Republican state senator Steve Chan. Beside him was Joyce Xiaoqiong Xie, the Democratic challenger to incumbent Republican Assembly member Lester Chang.
By 10 p.m., the updated vote counts flashed across a large TV screen with more cheers following from the crowd. Both He and Xie were victorious, unseating the incumbents in previously Republican-held districts — part of a wave of shifts toward Democrats that happened all over the country on Tuesday.
The following morning, WeChat groups run by local Chinese residents in Bensonhurst were buzzing with the news.
In this part of South Brooklyn, the Republican and Democratic tickets were each represented by Chinese American candidates. After leaning increasingly Republican in recent years — driven in part by local voters’ concerns about public safety and the placement of homeless shelters in the neighborhood — the neighborhood had turned blue.
Like many Democrats, Xie, the budget director and community liaison for City Council member Susan Zhuang, and He, the chief of staff to Assembly member William Colton, had campaigned on issues such as housing, affordability, supporting local families and small businesses with essential resources and improving public safety.
He handily trounced the incumbent Chan by over 14 percentage points to secure a seat in the state Senate. In the state Assembly race, Xie beat Chang by nearly six percentage points, according to the latest results from the New York State Board of Elections.
On Election Day, several Chinese voters told Documented they were concerned about public safety, citing the recent fatal stabbing of a runner in Bath Beach and a proposed homeless shelter in South Brooklyn as reasons for their concern. But more important were issues that directly affected their daily lives, such as affordability and broader economic conditions under the Trump administration that have taken precedence over broader political debates, voters told Documented. Some specifically mentioned the administration’s immigration enforcement policies.
Dan Chen, 44, cast her ballot at P.S. 97 The Highlawn in Bensonhurst before 7:30 a.m. on Tuesday, hoping to finish voting before heading to work.
“Exercising our rights as citizens is important,” said Chen, an immigrant from Fujian, China, who became a U.S. citizen in 2016.
Chen voted for Donald Trump and Republican candidates in 2024. But over the past two years, rising living costs and concerns about public safety have shifted her support toward Democrats.
“I hope Democrats can do a better job,” she said in Mandarin. “Trump did a good job maintaining border security and improving safety when many immigrants came into the country in recent years. But the cost of everything in our daily lives has gone up — rent, food, utilities, you name it. At the end of the day, what matters is our own lives.”
Kenneth Lee, 74, who has lived in Bensonhurst for more than three decades, said that while he hopes Democrats will do more to improve public safety and address immigration issues, he still voted for Democrats because he believes the party cares more about low-income residents, particularly as inflation continues to squeeze many New Yorkers.
“Food prices are so high now. Twenty years ago, you could buy several apples for $1. Now, a single apple costs more than $1, while our incomes haven’t increased at the same pace,” he said. “Many people have to rely on food stamps to get by.”
Another voter, Li, who requested to only use his last name for privacy reasons, cast his ballot for Democratic candidates at P.S. 101 in Bensonhurst. Li, who is 70 years old, said that he has voted in every election since becoming a U.S. citizen four years ago.
Li said rising prices and inflation over the past few years have made life particularly difficult for low-income residents, like him, especially after the federal government stopped reimbursing stolen SNAP [food stamp] benefits in December 2024. “Life has been very difficult,” he said.
For Li, supporting Democrats was an obvious choice.
“The simplest way to look at it is that inflation has been high under Republican leadership, and life has become more difficult for low-income people,” he said. “I hope things will get better. We ordinary people don’t know that much about policy. These are just our simple thoughts,” he added.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midt.title: Blue Tsunami’s Clearest Takeaway: People Hate Data Centers
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midt.author: Sanya Mansoor
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midt.text:
America’s data center buildout suffered a resounding defeat in the midterms at all levels of government. Candidates and ballot measures in favor of restricting or altogether stopping the development of the facilities powering the artificial intelligence boom won overwhelmingly on election night.
Newly elected Democratic governors in Georgia, Ohio, and Texas have promised moratoriums on new data center construction and all took tougher stances on regulation than their incumbent Republican opponents. The trend carried over in various congressional races, in which candidates who were critical of their competitors’ record of promoting data center development came out on top, even flipping key districts in Ohio and South Carolina.
Many local communities, mostly in Ohio and Illinois, voted directly on their AI concerns and passed a flurry of ballot initiatives restricting data center development — close to 40 proposals, according to a tracker by research firm Redbud Consulting.
“What’s good for the AI industry is clearly not good for average voters,” said Shobita Parthasarathy, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan. “I wish that data center operators and the AI industry really take this as a sign that they’re done a very poor job of considering public concern and taking it seriously.”
Parthasarathy pointed out that many Americans are now deciding how they feel about these energy-guzzling facilities based on their experience of living near one and “real knowledge” about their deficiencies. Those concerns range from negative impacts on energy bills, to the environmental and health issues, but also include anger toward the outsized power that the tech oligarchy wields.
Americans’ vote in the midterms has given them a tangible way to fight back, Parthasarathy said: Blocking the brick-and-mortar, water-sucking, heat-spewing buildings that power tech billionaires’ rapid wealth accumulation.
Tech Money ≠ Change Minds
A long track record of polls have recorded Americans’ anger about data centers. About three-quarters of voters polled by NBC News on Election Day said they opposed building these facilities in their communities. Those sentiments are consistent with a Heatmap survey from August that found a similar proportion of Americans would strongly oppose a new data center near where they live.
More than half the voters polled by NBC this week said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, though they were almost equally divided when it came to deciding which party would be better at addressing their AI concerns.
The AI industry tried to make a dent in the midterms, but much of their money was focused on a congressional primary in New York, where the cash helped defeat AI critic Alex Bores.
In the general election, an Intercept analysis found, AI super PACs dramatically scaled back their spending on congressional races compared to primaries amid growing anger toward data centers; only 5 percent of their direct expenditures went toward contested general election races. Industry observers told The Intercept that this suggested developers and tech CEOs have taken note of the electorate souring on AI and data centers.
That’s not to say that tech magnates, more broadly, have been stingy with their money. Elon Musk spent nearly $450 million ahead of the midterms, including more than $200 million in Texas, where his companies are headquartered.
“If Elon Musk wants to continue to burn half a billion dollars to get no results, there are probably other ways he can do that,” said Mitch Jones, deputy director of Food & Water Action, which has advocated for regulations on data centers on the federal, state, and local level. “It shows when an issue is deeply and broadly felt by American people, no amount of money can change their minds.”
Musk’s money wasn’t enough for the races in Texas to go his way. Surprise upsets in the state’s Senate and gubernatorial races resulted in victories for, respectively, Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa.
Talarico promised to end tax breaks for data center developers and minimum federal requirements to protect the grid, environment, jobs, and transparency. Hinojosa called for a moratorium on all data center approvals “until laws can be passed by the Legislature to protect Texans.” Outgoing Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott had already temporarily halted environmental permitting and grid connections until about the end of the year, but Hinojosa’s proposal would last longer and be more expansive.
Promises to Rein In AI
Congress’s new incoming class includes many Democrats who have promised to rein in the harms of AI. Ohio’s Democratic Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown flipped a district after portraying his opponent in ads as cheerleading the data center industry.
In typically red South Carolina, Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews defeated her opponent, Sen. Darline Graham, after accusing her of being bought by developers. Pro-AI super PAC Building the Future spent $2.5 million to support Graham, according to Politico.
In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom, who called for a temporary ban on data centers, was narrowly ahead of his incumbent opponent on Wednesday evening in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in more than four decades.
Just because Trump is expected to veto Democrats’ proposals to regulate AI, that doesn’t mean they shouldn’t push for them, said Jones, of Food & Water Action. He’s hoping Congress will approve a ban on “artificial superintelligence,” as well as a federal moratorium on new data centers.
“They should show the American public they are standing with us and taking actions to force Trump to veto those bills,” Jones said.
Although moratoriums typically target new construction and not existing data centers, Jones says they are still necessary to prevent an even more expansive buildout.
“We don’t need any more,” he said, citing a Forbes estimate that the total cost of the projected buildout ranges from $2.8 trillion by 2030 to $10.30 trillion by 2032 in the U.S.
With Trump still in charge, states led by Democratic governors may be where more forceful regulation on data centers occurs.
In Georgia, Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms promised a temporary statewide pause on data centers. Ohio’s new incoming Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton proposed an “immediate moratorium upon taking office on any new construction.” And in Kansas, Democrat Cindy Holscher, who declared victory in the gubernatorial race, has advocated for halting new development.
Ballot Measures
Local communities are getting creative, too. Jones said that some towns and cities have turned to ballot measures to bypass “elected officials who are not keeping pace with their voters.”
About half of the roughly 40 ballot measures in the midterms were in Ohio. Most succeeded by a wide margin, and as of Thursday morning, all but one vote were in favor of restrictions, according to Redbud Consulting’s tracker.
Nick Owens, who helped draft 10 local ballot measures in Ohio that restrict data center development after an unsuccessful attempt at a statewide petition, said this gave voters quicker and easier access to the ballot to curtail the “humongous growth of hyperscale data centers.”
“Communities know how best they want to govern themselves,” said Owens, who was a Trump delegate at the 2024 Republican National Convention and is currently co-founder of grassroots group Conserve Ohio. The results “just validated everything I’ve been seeing on the ground, talking to people, and in nationwide polling,” he added.
Owens is looking ahead, once again, toward pushing for a statewide moratorium, as well as curtailing the secretive use of non-disclosure agreements by tech companies and developers.
Parthasarathy, the public policy professor, said more communities may explore ballot measures as a response to developers’ lack of transparency and drive to build more.
“I don’t think their thirst for data centers is going to go away,” she said. “They might move into localities where there is less organized pushback.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ICA Miami selects architect to renovate recently acquired building
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Constanza Ontiveros Valdés
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami (ICA Miami) has appointed the global architecture firm Gensler to renovate a 30,000-sq.-ft building the museum acquired in 2024, doubling its exhibition and public-programming space.
Steps away from its current venue in Miami’s Design District, the new wing is scheduled to open in late 2027—as the museum marks its tenth anniversary at its current location. Focused on expanding the free museum’s community outreach, the project will transform the ICA into a multi-site complex and house the first permanent display of its collection.
The museum’s new building formerly housed the De la Cruz Collection, a private museum that closed after the 2024 death of its co-founder Rosa de la Cruz. Since its $25m acquisition later that year, the site has mainly hosted the ICA’s educational programmes. It will close once construction begins. The renovation is part of a $40m capital campaign, supported entirely by private funds.
The new design will adapt the existing structure. “The building was developed to house a contemporary art collection,” Alex Gartenfeld, the ICA’s director and chief curator, tells The Art Newspaper. “But with the spaces we are constructing, we intend to enhance the museum’s story-driven narrative approach to the collection and exhibitions.”
Eight new galleries will occupy the building’s first and second floors. Among them will be the museum’s first dedicated spaces for its growing permanent collection of more than 2,000 works.
“The programme between the two buildings is blended, but we will now have two full floors dedicated to our permanent collection,” Gartenfeld says. “Around every six months, we will refresh the collection display to reflect the collection’s emphasis and recent acquisitions.”
The entire third floor will be dedicated to public programming, including talks, symposia, lectures and performances. “Beyond adding galleries, this renovation will strengthen the ICA’s ability to support artists, expand learning and create a platform for exchange and belonging in one of the world’s most dynamic cultural cities,” says Bevin Savage Yamazaki, Gensler’s global culture and museums leader.
A reimagined façade with transparent components is key to the design. Gartenfeld says the façade aims to provide a connection between street-level traffic and the museum itself.
The renovations focus on visitor experience and accessibility as well. The lobby will be redesigned. And reconfigured outdoor areas will include social spaces, a sculpture deck and an expanded café. “We are aiming to create a more collective experience,” Gartenfeld says.

Democrats Would Be Insane Not to Break With Israel Now
The party has an unequivocal mandate to fundamentally change the US-Israel relationship.
The definition of insanity, famously, is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results. This should certainly be what Republican strategists are thinking to themselves after launching a needless, illegal, failed, and wildly unpopular war in the Middle East that, just like in 2006, has handed the Democratic Party control of the Senate and a commanding majority in the House in this week’s midterm elections.
Vice President JD Vance released a statement Wednesday morning that served as a rapid autopsy, naming the war with Iran and resultant rising prices as top reasons for Republicans’ generational wipeout. He also cited the United States’ relationship with Israel. These, of course, are not separate issues. In March, the State Department wrote that it had launched the Iran War in large part at Israel’s request (Benjamin Netanyahu having finally found a president foolish enough to fulfill his decades-long desire for this exact war). And the impunity that the US granted Israel for its ongoing genocide of Palestinians in Gaza, its invasion of Lebanon, and its aggressive strikes against its neighbors—including US allies like Syria and Qatar—fueled the arrogance that led to the Iran conflict.
Vice President Vance’s pointed statement was surprising in its seeming disloyalty to his boss. But in saying that voters wanted to, in his words, “change our relationship to Israel,” Vance was only reflecting a truth that millions of people have known for years—even if some within the Democratic Party still might not want to admit it.
In fact, the most glaring issue with Vance’s comments might be that they’re two years late. Americans didn’t just want a fundamental break with Israel in 2026. They wanted one in 2024, and they punished Democrats for refusing to reflect their revulsion at Israel’s actions. It’s worth remembering where we were two years ago: As polls showed a majority of swing-state voters opposing further US funding for Israel, President Biden sent Israel tens of billions of dollars in weapons to continue the slaughter in Gaza.
The Israeli government had announced in August 2024 that it had received 50,000 tons of weapons from Biden in 607 shipments over the preceding 11 months—a weapons shipment every 12 hours. At the same time, Save the Children estimated that Israel was killing a Palestinian child in Gaza every hour. By the end of Biden’s term, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated that Israel had dropped 100,000 tons of bombs on Gaza—the equivalent of seven Hiroshima atomic bombs on an area of land smaller than Detroit. Millions of Americans watched this horror livestreamed, day after day after day.
Biden even made a surprise appearance at the White House Press Briefing Room on October 4, 2024, to say that “no administration has helped Israel more than I have. None.” Meanwhile, the voters Democrats needed to turn out were calling Biden “Genocide Joe.”
We all know what happened next.
In the wake of the Democrats’ 2024 loss, our polling at the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project found that “ending Israel’s violence in Gaza” was the top-cited factor among Biden 2020 voters who defected from Kamala Harris, especially in the crucial swing states of Arizona, Wisconsin, and Michigan. President Biden’s response to the election results was to announce another $8 billion weapons package to Israel as one of his final acts as president.
And we weren’t the only ones picking up on this pattern. Earlier this year, Axiosreported that the author of the Democratic National Committee’s (DNC) 2024 autopsy report also “concluded the war in Gaza hurt Kamala Harris politically.” Concerningly, a version of the report released by DNC Chair Ken Martin made zero mention of either Israel or Gaza.
Nevertheless, many establishment Democrats continued to deny what was staring them in the face. The New York Times reported last year that Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer justified his refusal to endorse Zohran Mamdani on the belief that being “deeply critical of Israel” would be a liability in swing states in 2026. This was not reflected in polling at the time, and certainly did not bear out in polling as we approached this election, with most voters in key states including Texas, Maine, Ohio, Iowa, and North Carolina—all states Democrats ultimately flipped—saying they support blocking the transfer of bombs to Israel.
Throughout the 2026 primaries, candidates who recognized Israel’s genocide and called for a weapons embargo against Israel won with the odds stacked against them—including in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, New York, Colorado, Florida, and California. Nowhere was this clearer than in the critical swing state of Michigan, where the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent over $30 million—a record amount for one organization to spend in a single Democratic primary in US history—to defeat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. El-Sayed was able to overcome that record spending because of his moral clarity in recognizing Israel’s genocide, a position that 80 percent of Michigan Democratic primary voters agree with.
El-Sayed also won by refusing to allow AIPAC’s money and political power to intimidate him into silence. For years, advocates for Palestinian rights have tried to warn Democrats about the dangers of candidates backed by AIPAC—an organization largely funded by Republicans and whose agenda contradicts the core values of human equality that the Democratic Party is supposed to represent at its best. That warning was fully realized in Representative Haley Stevens, Senator Schumer’s recruit for the seat.
Her bizarre turncoat act in the last weeks of the election was a historic embarrassment for the Democratic Party, but it was just as much an embarrassment for the claim, so popular in the media, that there is a bitter Democratic voter divide when it comes to what the future of US-Israel policy should be. As the results in Michigan showed, there simply isn’t one.
El-Sayed coasted to a seven-point victory, just as he predicted in May, because Democratic voters fully consolidated behind him and independents broke his way. Stevens’s shenanigans and the millions spent against him by AIPAC couldn’t overcome the majority of Michigan voters—including 66 percent of Michigan independents—who say they want to end US funding to Israel. And despite endless warnings that Jewish Michiganders were set to abandon El-Sayed en masse, early exit polls showed him winning 60 percent of the Jewish vote.
It could not be clearer: Unyielding support for Israel is electoral poison, and candidates who back Palestinian rights, oppose genocide, and call for a decisive break with Israel will win. Democrats—the honest ones, anyway—know this. The question then becomes: What are they going to do about it, now that they have so much more political power?
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Unbelievably, some observers are suggesting that Democrats should elide the questions over their position on Palestinian rights, and holding Israel accountable for its ongoing genocide, that have roiled their voters for over three years. That would be a severe betrayal of the clearly stated wishes of the Democratic base that delivered this week’s historic victory.
Others might want to follow AIPAC’s lead. In October, the lobby group announced, in an admission of its own toxicity, that it would stop endorsing candidates going forward, while still continuing to spend millions of dollars in our elections through its super PAC, and presumably more untraceably through shell super PACs, as it has throughout this year.
AIPAC’s new strategy mirrors what some supporters of a close US-Israel relationship foresee for themselves as well. At the 11th hour on election morning, President Trump dubiously claimed in a Fox & Friends phone interview that he would end annual taxpayer funding for Israel’s military at year’s end. Given Trump’s penchant for lying, this is more important for its recognition of this ritual’s unpopularity than it is as a reliable indicator that such a policy change will actually come about under his watch. Regardless, his allies in Congress are, at this moment, advancing legislation to rapidly integrate Israeli weapons companies into the Pentagon procurement process—a method of providing taxpayer funding for Israeli companies at even higher levels than today, and without congressional oversight. Any Democrat who joins them will be walking down a political path they will almost certainly regret.
With the mandate voters have given them, Democrats have every ounce of leverage to strip those measures out of this year’s National Defense Authorization Act. They have every ability to strip funding for Israel’s military out of next year’s budget and send it to Trump’s desk to call his bluff. And they have every ability to bring the Block the Bombs Act for a vote and test how much their Republican counterparts have really learned from this election.
They not only have this ability; they also have every reason to become a party that is a full-throated defender of Palestinian rights—and human rights for every person. They have a mandate to stand against endless war in the Middle East, and to stand up to megadonors and super PACs that have distorted our democracy for too long.
To do anything else is the definition of insanity.
