https://hyperallergic.com/its-time-to-ta.title: It’s Time to Talk About Classism in the Art World
https://hyperallergic.com/its-time-to-ta.author: Melissa Holbrook Pierson
https://hyperallergic.com/its-time-to-ta.text:
It’s Time to Talk About Classism in the Art World
In his memoiristic new book, photographer Mark Alice Durant weaves his personal experiences into a larger rebuke of the economic inequality that governs the art world.
For something that determines so much — about the art we make, the art we get to see or not, the art that may never be made at all — the issue of class is rarely discussed in the art world. Breaking the silence, artist and writer Mark Alice Durant speaks up in his memoir-cum-rebuke, Confessions of a Working Class Artist (2026). It reads both like a Künstlerroman and an updated version of the seminal guide for the aspiring artist, Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet (1929), for our dystopian neo-Gilded Age.
For Durant, also the author of the moving photographic memoir Summer of the White Fox, and After (2024) and publisher at Saint Lucy Books, which released both titles, choosing to become an artist was an act of self-exile. He writes that he psychically uprooted himself from the working-class precincts of Boston where he grew up as well as from his extended family, with the exception of his mother, unusually open-minded and supportive of her son. Perhaps she saw herself in his youthful gift of a framed reproduction of Jules Breton’s 1884 painting of a field worker, “The Song of the Lark.” After deciding on this path, Durant writes, “I could never return home on some level.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Ex-husband of Brent Sikkema sentenced to life in prison over murder-for-hire killing
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The former husband of the late New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, Daniel Sikkema, aged 56, has been sentenced to life imprisonment for organising Sikkema’s murder in 2024. A federal court in Manhattan handed down the sentence on Wednesday (4 November).
In May 2026, after a two-week trial, Daniel Sikkema was convicted on charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country. In addition to life imprisonment, he was sentenced to five years of supervised release.
Brent Sikkema, who was aged 75 at the time of his murder, was found stabbed to death at his home in the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on 15 January 2024. According to prosecutors, Daniel Sikkema began planning the murder in 2023 in the midst of his divorce from the dealer, with whom he had been married for around 15 years and shared a son.
As the couple’s divorce proceedings became more acrimonious, Daniel Sikkema, who holds dual US and Cuban citizenship, recruited the Cuban national, Alejandro Triana Prevez, as the hitman. On the night of the murder, Prevez entered the late Sikkema’s residence and stabbed him 18 times. Prevez subsequently received $5,000 from Daniel Sikkema and was promised further payments.
Prosecutors said Daniel Sikkema made 11 payments to Prevez and Prevez’s partner in Cuba, using the identities of unwitting friends, employees and family members to conceal the transactions. Prevez was arrested by Brazilian authorities four days after the murder at a gas station on the side of the highway in the state of Minas Gerais, around 600 miles from Rio de Janeiro. He had stolen cash and jewellery in his possession. His case is being handled separately by a Brazilian court.
Brent Sikkema was born in 1948 in Morrison, Illinois, and studied at the San Francisco Art Institute before beginning his career. In the early 1990s, he founded Wooster Gardens in SoHo, moving the gallery to Chelsea in 1999. The business became Sikkema Jenkins & Co in 2003 following the involvement of Michael Jenkins and Meg Malloy.
The gallery is now known as Sikkema Malloy Jenkins and continues to operate in Chelsea. It has championed the work of artists including Kara Walker, Vik Muniz, Sheila Hicks, Jeffrey Gibson and Arturo Herrera. A representative for Sikkema Malloy Jenkins told The Art Newspaper that the gallery will not be providing any statement regarding the conviction or sentencing.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/abdu.title: Abdul El-Sayed Won His Senate Seat With a Mandate on Palestine. Can He Deliver?
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/abdu.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/abdu.text:
One senator out of the 100 who will fill the upper chamber of the 120th Congress was elected to his seat on a loud campaign promise to end U.S. complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Abdul El-Sayed will walk into a newfound Democratic majority after animating his base with pro-Palestine pledges seldom heard from a U.S. Senate contender. As a first-term senator, he’ll lack seniority on the committees to which he’s assigned. And although his critiques of the U.S. relationship with Israel have proven overwhelmingly popular in public opinion surveys and among voters at the polls, the same can’t be said for most of his soon-to-be colleagues.
“It’s going to be a fight,” said Beth Miller, political advocacy director for Jewish Voice for Peace Action, which supported El-Sayed’s campaign. “The Democratic establishment, when it’s in control, has not taken measures in support of Palestine in the past. And so this is about making sure that now they finally start listening to what the overwhelming majority of their bases say.”
El-Sayed’s run marked the first time the Jewish-led, anti-Zionist group backed a Senate campaign. Pro-Palestine lobbying groups like JVP Action have been pushing for legislation to block weapons transfers to Israel for years, aligning themselves with a small but growing number of left-leaning House members. The group helped author the Block the Bombs Act, introduced by Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., which netted 82 co-sponsors and became a pro-Palestine litmus test in some Democratic primary campaigns.
Building consensus around a single bill in the Senate is harder, but the upper chamber offers stronger levers to pull. Senators can force votes called Joint Resolutions of Disapproval that would block foreign security assistance, such as weapons sales to Israel. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has exercised this option repeatedly throughout the genocide in Gaza to try and block the sale of certain bombs, firearms, and other military equipment to Israel. While his resolutions failed in the Republican-controlled Senate, the most recent ones drew support from wide majorities of Democrats — soon to be the party in power.
Yet with the looming threat that Democrats might actually be able to pass legislation, El-Sayed would find himself under pressure from the likely Senate majority leader, Chuck Schumer, who has long maintained the support of the pro-Israel lobby, to fall in line with party priorities.
“The question is, ‘Who does he want to be?’ Does he want to be someone like Bernie, who is willing to sometimes stand up to leadership?” said Hamid Bendaas, communications director for the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which also backed El-Sayed’s run. “It’s hard to do that as a freshman and someone who’s just getting in there.”
Bendaas expressed confidence that the Michigan senator would be a champion of pro-Palestine legislation, but he noted that El-Sayed would have to balance his priorities, especially after running a campaign focused on economic populism and providing universal healthcare through Medicare for All.
Shifting Winds
There is a tension revealed by the dilemma facing Sen.-elect El-Sayed: While a growing share of Americans — and an overwhelming majority of Democrats — disapprove of the U.S. spending billions of dollars on aid to Israel, voters’ clear No. 1 concern in the 2026 election cycle was the cost of living and their own economic precarity.
Some pundits have encouraged pro-Palestine candidates like El-Sayed to put their anti-genocide principles aside, arguing that more moderate Democrats performed better on Tuesday night. They compare El-Sayed’s 7-percentage-point defeat of Mike Rogers to James Talarico’s 12-point win over Ken Paxton in Texas — and some have already asked Talarico to defy his new colleague.
But on the campaign trail, El-Sayed often connected the issues of a high cost of living and outsized U.S. spending on aid to Israel. “We ought to be spending our money here, to build schools and provide healthcare and child care here, rather than sending our money abroad to a foreign government that’s done terrible things with our money,” he said in a September interview with Bloomberg TV. El-Sayed’s approach made him the target of nearly $40 million in outside spending from the super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which supported widespread anti-Arab and Islamophobic attacks and accusations of antisemitism in an attempt to keep a vocal critic of Israel out of the Senate.
“None of it mattered,” said Yousef Munayyer, a senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington D.C. who likened the gravity of El-Sayed’s win to that of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “And this is not the Commie Corridor. This is a swing state. A lot of taboos here have been shattered, and people are going to learn from this and be emboldened now.”
In addition to bringing joint resolutions to block future weapons transfers — like the Trump administration’s planned sale of $2.8 billion in 2,000-pound bombs to Israel — El-Sayed could introduce resolutions citing the Foreign Assistance Act; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., used one to demand a State Department report on Israeli detention of Palestinian children and Israeli military and settler killings of American citizens in the West Bank. He would also be able to introduce amendments to the Pentagon’s annual spending bill that carves out billions of dollars in joint U.S.–Israel weapons research. (The Senate is currently sitting on this year’s $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act, which would even more deeply enmesh Israeli technology within the Pentagon’s programs and supply chain.)
Munayyer, the former head of the U.S. Campaign for Palestinian Rights, said that despite the uncertainty over whether moderate Democrats will be willing to link arms with progressives next session, El-Sayed’s win creates an environment ripe for accountability over Israel.
“You have a climate now where there’s going to be a lot less intimidation felt by people who had previously been hesitant to speak out on these issues because they thought it was political suicide,” he said.
Even Republicans are beginning to feel the shifting winds. On the morning of Election Day, President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Fox News that the U.S. would halt the annual $4 billion in military aid to Israel. The move would only cut off one path for Israel to get weapons from the U.S. — still allowing direct weapons sales to Israel from U.S. companies and weapons development and sharing with the Pentagon — and Trump said it was made in agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who had been previewing it for months. Tactically, Trump said the goal was to take a “talking point” away from Democrats. He cited El-Sayed by name.
While ballots were still being counted on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance, an expected 2028 presidential contender, posted on X an early post-mortem of the massive GOP losses across the country. He wrote that the party could bring back “voters who had abandoned us” if they “End the war” in Iran and “Change our relationship to Israel.”
Such recognition from the Trump White House is new territory for U.S. politics, Munayyer said.
“We are about to witness, in my view, something we have never seen before in American politics,” Munayyer said. “A robust debate in the presidential primary campaigns in both parties, where the question of the U.S.-Israel relationship is going to come up time and again. That’s never happened before, and it’s gonna be seismic.”
The question is whether Democrats will stay on top of the wave. If Schumer, a staunch supporter of Israel, remains in charge of the Senate majority, he’ll have power over appointments to key committees — giving him the opportunity to curb the influence of a figure like El-Sayed.
“I don’t think that Democrats want to have a messy fight about this stuff when the base is largely in agreement on it,” Munayyer said. But while Senate Democrats have evolved on the issue of Israel and Palestine — even Sanders expressed far weaker critiques of the Israeli state a few years ago — it’s one thing to be the dissenting party when you’re in the minority. It’s another to wield serious power.
Constant Pressure
El-Sayed is perhaps the most vocal supporter of Palestinian rights of any U.S. senator elected since James Abourezk of South Dakota, who in the late 1970s became the first Arab American to serve in the Senate. Abourezk frequently advocated for a Palestinian state and was an early critic of the pro-Israel lobby. After his time in Congress, he founded the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee.
El-Sayed, now the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, frequently referred to Israel on the campaign trail as an “ethnostate” and said he opposes any nation that organizes its government by ethnicity and religion. In an appearance on ABC News, El-Sayed argued Israel was not a U.S. ally. Two days before the election, he spent a large portion of his sit-down with “60 Minutes” calling for Palestinians’ right of self-determination and repudiated the question of whether Israel had a right to exist. In his victory speech, he criticized attempts by pro-Israel critics to conflate advocacy for Palestinians rights as “hate.”
Even so, in the lead-up to the general election, El-Sayed started being subjected to pressure from some on the pro-Palestine left. Critics chastised his decision to stump with former Vice President Kamala Harris over her complicity in the Biden administration’s support for the genocide in Gaza. Similar ire was directed at his partnership with former President Barack Obama, who has yet to name or condemn the genocide and governed over U.S. wars in the Middle East that saw the United States kill thousands of civilians.
Advocates for Palestinian rights, however, told The Intercept they recognized the utility in El-Sayed’s campaigning with the highest-profile members of the Democratic Party, and they counted it as a success that he earned their support. But they said they were not pinning all their hopes on a single individual.
On top of all the other calcified interests and long-standing political biases that shape the U.S. Senate, there’s the influence of the sprawling U.S. weapons industry, with manufacturing giants like Lockheed Martin and Boeing lobbying for their interests and showering politicians in campaign cash. That industry wants to keep profiting off the genocide in Gaza, said JVP Action’s Miller, and El-Sayed alone is not enough to stop that.
“This is not gonna be that one man comes into the Senate and changes everything,” she said. “This is that one person has been elected with a mandate that has demonstrated where the masses of people are at on this issue, and now we have to keep fighting harder than ever before.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

Just two months after Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute canceled its planned spring 2027 John Galliano show in response to a firestorm of criticism, the New York institution has set tongues wagging with the announcement of that show’s replacement. Titled “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,” the group exhibition will feature familiar garments such as puffer jackets and jeans, and humble materials including Bubble Wrap and paper, all reimagined as high fashion.
The new exhibition opens May 9, 2027 days after the museum’s annual Met Gala fundraiser, and slots into the space originally reserved for the Galliano show. That exhibition was scrapped after the museum received pushback from donors and others over the designer’s past antisemitic and anti-Asian comments. Andrew Bolton, the curator in charge of the Costume Institute, told the New York Times there had been no plan B in place at the time of the cancellation, and that the new show was meant to follow on from this year’s exhibition, “Costume Art.” Among the garments expected to go on view are Marc Jacobs’s 1990s grunge collection for Perry Ellis, and the Calvin Klein jeans worn by Brooke Shields in her infamous 1980 ad for the brand.
Anna Wintour, the global editorial director of Vogue and Met board member who typically chairs the Met Gala, was nowhere mentioned as an architect of the exhibition. Wintour had championed Galliano, known for his boundary-pushing, highly feminine designs. Page Six reports that she is expected to helm the 2027 fundraiser, as usual.
News of the replacement show was greeted with considerably less fanfare than that of Galliano’s planned exhibition.
“If you think you know your everyday outfit of T-shirt and jeans, just wait ’til you see it in the Met!” chirped Artnet News’s Min Chen with more than a hint of sarcasm, while Artnews’s Alex Greenberger characterized it flatly as “unlikely to rile up anybody.”
The Costume Institute’s annual exhibition has historically been the theme for the Met Gala, with attendees dressing to impress. With “extraORDINARY: Fashion,” the museum has sparked a question that has likely not arisen before: “So, is everyone going to wear jeans to the Met Gala now?” queried Cosmopolitan.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Bowling, burgers and civilian housing: Life on the Fort Hamilton Army installation
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: James Ramsay
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
Back in the spring, when people across the city were making summer vacation plans and debating where to find the best beach along a commuter rail line, I started hearing murmurs in my neck of southern Brooklyn about one specific priority: Everyone was jockeying for a seasonal membership at the pool club on the Fort Hamilton Army installation.
We didn’t bite — we’re a beach family — but the idea of getting a little R&R on a military compound happened to be a familiar thrill. I grew up about 10 miles south of a major Marine Corps base in Southern California, and my hockey coach, an active-duty sergeant, used to bring us on base for parties on their beach, which was essentially empty.
So the “Looped In” team decided last week to cross through the gates of Fort Hamilton — passports in hand — to see what else a civilian can get up to on base, and the answer is: a lot, starting with renting a home.
“We have approximately 212 leases, and of that, probably 40% are what we call ‘waterfall’ residents,” said Tony Mercante, the administrator in charge of the privatized housing on the installation.
“Waterfall residents” — cool code name — refers to the civilians who live on base, and at rates that are pretty competitive compared to the city’s median rent.
For $3,800 a month, Mercante said, you can get a 1,700-square-foot three-bedroom garden apartment, complete with a washer/dryer hookup, a dishwasher, a garbage disposal, most utilities included and one parking spot.
“This is a very idyllic installation,” he added. “When you come through those gates, we basically have no crime. It's a tiny, self-contained community where a lot of people know each other.”
“Idyllic” is a more-or-less fair descriptor. Walking around Fort Hamilton, a 176-acre rolling plot at the foot of the Verrazzano Bridge, feels like being on a Hollywood backlot version of an American suburb. The trees are tall and mature, the roads are windy, the SUVs actually obey the speed limit. There’s a chapel, a Post Office, a gas station and a Burger King.
But “self-contained” isn’t the same thing as “trapped.”
Garrison Command Sgt. Major Eric Riding, who moved to Fort Hamilton about a year ago from Fort Sam Houston in Texas, said the access to the city has been incredible.
“You walk out about a block and a half, you're on the [R train],” Riding said. “I think the public transportation in this city is the best I've ever seen, and I've been all over.” (He said he’s going with his family to see the Rockettes this Christmas; the R train can get them right there!)
Susan Blair, the chief of public affairs for Fort Hamilton, told us the installation’s relatively small size — and its location within the largest city in the country — means it actually relies on local civilians to keep it up and running.
“When you go to a base like Fort Bragg or Fort Hood, the entire surrounding community almost relies on the base — the base supports a lot of the economy. Where it's almost the inverse here,” she said.
And the outside community has plenty of ways to support the base’s economy, hence the private apartments, the pool club, the clubhouse bar (where Thursdays at 4 p.m. are reportedly bumpin'), the wedding and events venue space, the Harbor Defense Museum and not least, the bowling alley. (Civilians looking to visit the installation unescorted are required to fill out background check forms and submit them in-person or via fax 24-48 hours prior to visits.)
Stephen Ramosa, who lives next door in Bensonhurst, said he started working at the Fort Hamilton Bowling Center about a year ago and sees a mix of civilian bowlers and servicemembers and their families.
“ We have a senior league Tuesday mornings. That's the one that I run, and they're pretty chill,” he said. “They're pretty old, and they still bowl better than me.”
Things we didn’t see on our tour: tanks, humvees, helicopters, firearms or any kind of weaponry that wasn’t a historical artifact. Blair said that Fort Hamilton was used as a staging ground for law enforcement after 9/11, but generally, much of its significance now is related to its history.
“One of the unique things about Fort Hamilton is it's one of two bases where a Revolutionary War battle was actually fought,” Blair said.
In August of 1776, British troops landed on the beach outside what’s now Fort Hamilton and kicked off one of the largest battles of the war, one that ended with General George Washington retreating up to Manhattan.
“We did not win that one,” Blair said. “But we won the big thing.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/s.title: Some of NYC’s Worst Super Speeders Are City Marshals (You Know, The Guys With Badges)
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/s.author: Sammy Sussman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/s.text:
They get justice for private citizens — yet they endanger them at the same time.
City marshals — private citizens appointed by the mayor to secure civil court judgments on behalf of victorious plaintiffs — are among the city’s worst super-speeders, with just 30 of them racking up 647 speed-camera infractions and 102 red-light tickets, virtually all since 2020, city records show.
Streetsblog obtained a list of 30 city marshals who have been issued parking placards and found that all but one had racked up camera-issued tickets for reckless driving. And 12 of these law-enforcement officials — or 40 percent — have gotten at least 10 school-zone speeding tickets since 2020.
Two of these officers have gotten over 120 camera-issued school-zone speeding tickets:
- One marshal, who drives a vehicle with the license plate LEG6496, has received 125 camera-issued speeding tickets and 13 red light tickets since 2023. This marshal’s driving is only getting worse — between July 2025 and June 2026, they received 68 speed-camera and 10 red-light tickets.
- Another marshal, whose license plate is W857KP, has received 132 speeding tickets and 13 red lights tickets in a saga of unmitigated dangerous driving going back to 2014. That reckless driving remains a problem: Since January 2025, this driver has gotten 19 camera-issued tickets for speeding or running red lights.
Both drivers racked up enough tickets in different 12-month periods to be declared a “super speeder” under New York State law. Such drivers will soon be required to install speed-limiting devices inside their cars to prevent recklessness.
City pols were appalled to hear that marshals who are appointed by the mayor to enforce civil judgments won by private citizens in court are themselves law-breakers.
“No one is above the law,” said Council Member Kayla Santosuosso (D-Bay Ridge). “The most reckless drivers must be reined in, no matter who they work for or what they do.”
Meanwhile, the Department of Investigation, which oversees the marshals, admitted that it hasn’t tracked the officers’ driving patterns, but after told of Streetsblog’s findings, a spokesperson for the agency said it would now be “following up on these allegations.”
“DOI will be issuing a memo to all city marshals reminding them of their obligation to obey traffic laws,” Diane Struzzi, the department’s director of communications, told Streetsblog. “They are required to obey the law in both personal and official capacities.
“Any marshal found to display a pattern of reckless or dangerous driving could be subject to disciplinary action,” Struzzi added.
Who are these people?
City marshals occupy an often-overlooked niche in New York City’s sprawling law enforcement world: Marshals can seize assets on behalf of private citizens who won judgments in civil court. In exchange, the marshals can collect a bounty of up to 5 percent.
These officers are given city-issued placards, and they are granted broad powers to tow vehicles with more than $350 in unpaid fines, though it is unclear how often marshals actually do this work.
Given their role in the city’s law-enforcement ecosystem, it was especially hard to street safety advocates to accept that private individuals with quasi-police powers were abusing that power so flagrantly.
“City marshals can’t keep New Yorkers safe if they’re speeding recklessly around the five boroughs,” said Ben Furnas, the executive director of Transportation Alternatives. “We can’t accept repeat speeding in New York City.”
Soon, we won’t have to: Under the Stop Super-Speeders law passed by state lawmakers last year and making its way through the City Council, drivers with at least 16 camera-issued school-zone speeding tickets in a 12-month period will be forced to install a speed-limiting device in all their vehicles.
Had the law been in place already, at least three of the 30 placarded marshals in Streetsblog’s data cache would have been forced to install a speed-limiter — and two marshals cleared the super-speeder threshold in at least three different 12-month periods. The worst marshal, according to this data, has actually qualified as a super-speeder in four separate calendar years.
At that egregious rate of ticketing, this driver is over 50 times more likely to be involved in a fatal or serious crash than an average driver, according to a 2024 study by DOT. This reckless driver’s speeding history puts them among the 400 worst drivers across the approximately two million drivers of personal cars in New York City — and yet the city still vests them with the power to enforce judgments and tow other cars.
It’s an eerie reminder that people in official positions — i.e. New York City employees who should know better — are occasionally caught by the press for flagrant violations of the public trust. Earlier this year, Streetsblog identified a Staten Island cop with 547 speed-camera tickets. He received 187 camera-issued tickets in 2025 alone — an average of one every other day. The only discipline he has received from the NYPD is that he no longer drives a squad car on duty.
The latest records obtained by Streetsblog do not include the name of any specific marshal, rendering it even more difficult to pressure the political system for change.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/m.title: Mamdani Administration Battling Yet Another Suit By Delivery Apps Fighting Worker Protections
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/m.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/m.text:
Two delivery workers pass each other on Chrystie Street in Manhattan. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
City officials and advocates are outraged that the tech giants behind the exploitive delivery gig economy have yet again sued to block a city law that protects delivery workers from random deactivations — a key workplace improvement that also keeps streets safer.
Last week, Uber, Instacart and Amazon sued to block new requirements to give workers “deactivation” protections — that is, giving workers 120 days’ notice before kicking them off the platform permanently and providing a reason for the deactivation; creating a progressive discipline structure so that deactivation is a last resort; and creating an independent appeals process.
The law builds on the success of the delivery worker minimum pay standard and is seen as essential for street safety because it would eliminate the constant threat of deactivation that leads to workers to put street safety on the back burner in order to keep their precarious jobs. The city vowed to defend it in court.
“The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection will not back down from protecting the rights and safety of all New Yorkers,” agency Commissioner Sam Levine said. “New York City deserves safe streets and delivery workers deserve dignity and due process.”
One progressive lawmaker slammed the corporations for the latest suit, which follows an earlier effort to defeat the minimum wage law.
“Every single time we’ve passed a piece of legislation to protect these workers, the [delivery companies] have spent a ton of money to stop the bill. They lose, and then they spend a ton of money on legal challenges that they ultimately lose and end up having to settle,” said Council Member Sandy Nurse (D-Bushwick). “They have a lot of money to burn, and instead of burning it, they should just pay their workers and find ways to work with the city and DCWP to protect them and come up with fair agreements. It’s not hard, but they don’t want to jeopardize their bottom line.”
In the latest case, Amazon, Uber, and Instacart are making a federal case of their opposition, suing on Oct. 28 in the Southern District of New York to stop the law from taking effect in January. The complaint alleges that Local Law 34, which passed last year, violates the constitutional rights of the companies because it undermines their “ability to exercise their own respective business judgments about who is allowed access to their applications.”
The companies also argue that sharing details about deactivations with workers would put customers at risk and could give so-called “fraudsters” information on how to better defraud the system.
“Uber also does not disclose details of its decision when it has deactivated a courier based on fraudulent activity because doing so would provide couriers with information they could exploit to evade Uber’s fraud-detection mechanisms in the future,” the complaint reads.
Instacart had a similar rationale. The company said that even “limited detail” can allow one of its contracted workers to “identify the customers who filed the report.” The company claims around 5 percent of its workers were deactivated in the past year, thats around 600 of the 12,000 grocery delivery workers the company claimed in its city-mandated reports.
Amazon said it contracts around 73,400 “flex” workers, who use the company’s app to do deliveries with their personal cars. The Bezosian behemoth said its deactivation rate was around 2.9 percent, which translates to about 2,100 human beings.
Instacart said in a statement that the law “would make it harder to protect against fraud, theft, harassment, and unsafe conduct” and that it joined the lawsuit “to protect the safety and trust that shoppers, customers, and retail partners expect us to uphold.”
Amazon concurred, but also argued that the law is unconstitutional.
“Amazon Flex enables tens of thousands of New Yorkers to earn money on their own terms, and deactivations are rare, reserved for serious issues such as theft, fraud, safety, and service violations,” said company spokesperson Steve Kelly. “This law would put customers at risk by hampering our ability to act quickly against misconduct and uphold the standards that keep deliveries safe and reliable. A federal court has already blocked the nearly identical companion law for ride-share drivers, concluding it’s likely unconstitutional.”
Kelly was referring to a ruling earlier this year by a different Southern District judge that blocked a city law that sought to protect Uber and Lyft drivers from the same types of deactivation. That law, indeed, has yet to take effect as a result of the judge’s injunction.
Cutting through the legalese, the city’s delivery workers are adamant that deactivations lead to unsafe streets.
“These corporations use the threat of deactivation to pressure delivery workers to move faster and complete more orders, putting workers’ lives and livelihoods at risk,” the Worker’s Justice Project’s Los Deliveristas Unidos said in a statement. “Worker safety is public safety.”
That echoed a recent report by the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection that identified worker protections “essential” for street safety.
For its part, the City Council defended its work to protect the large delivery workforce.
“It is the Council’s responsibility to ensure that all working New Yorkers are safeguarded from worker exploitation and are given the opportunity to earn a sustainable living wage,” said the Council’s spokesperson Sophia Saidi. “Speaker [Julie] Menin has made worker protection a top priority, especially vulnerable and low-wage workers, as New Yorkers across the board continue to face rising costs of living.”
Uber did not respond to Streetsblog’s request for comment. It is unclear why DoorDash and Wonder, which owns Seamless and Grubhub, are not part of the suit; neither company responded to Streetsblog’s request for comment.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/o.title: OPINION: New York City’s Trash Revolution Should Be an Accessibility Revolution, Too
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/o.author: William Juhn, Anna Humphrey, Sharon McLennon Wier
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/06/o.text:
Our narrow and crowded sidewalks have always created an obstacle course for disabled New Yorkers. The city’s ubiquitous practice of piling trash bags on sidewalks is one of the biggest reasons why. Many residents consider the resulting mountains of garbage as mere eyesores, but they are a matter of life and death for people with disabilities. Huge mounds of refuse force the disabled community into moving traffic, block curb cuts and create unpredictable hazards that lead to injury and death. 
Formally known as the Citywide Containerization Program, New York City’s so-called “trash revolution” is an overdue step toward cleaner streets. The program will require residential buildings with up to nine units to use individual bins, while buildings with 10 to 30 residential units can choose between individual bins or stationary on-street receptacles known as Empire Bins. Buildings with more than 30 residential units will use Empire Bins.
Done right, the program can also serve as an “accessibility revolution” by delivering cleaner sidewalks, safer streets and a more accessible city for all New Yorkers. Unless the city designs the program with accessibility in mind, however, its leaders risk replacing one kind of barrier with another. 
Unbroken lines of bins placed on sidewalks make navigating the street difficult for low-vision or blind New Yorkers who use orientation and mobility canes to negotiate sidewalks. Rows of bins interrupt otherwise continuous building lines, creating unpredictable and hazardous obstacles that increase the risk of tripping or veering into moving traffic. 
In densely populated neighborhoods with narrow sidewalks, clusters of bins shrink the clear path needed by wheelchair users, individuals using walkers, and people using other mobility devices. Overturned bins, loose lids and misaligned containers can easily block curb cuts, bus stops and building entrances.
Empire Bins and moveable dumpsters can address these problems because they clear sidewalks of bins and bags. The city can encourage smaller buildings to share bins rather than use individual ones. To advance the City’s climate and zero waste goals, Empire Bins must be able to collect recycling and compost, too — keeping even more bags away from walking paths. 
This is a promising approach, but it will require careful planning to execute. Empire Bins can also obstruct curb access — a dangerous outcome for Access-A-Ride and taxi users who may be forced to board within, or disembark into, active traffic lanes. And Empire Bins placed too close to crosswalks or curb cuts can obstruct sightlines between shorter pedestrians or wheelchair users and oncoming traffic, increasing the risk of injuries and deaths. 
New York City can and should ensure that its waste management goals benefit all New Yorkers. We cannot sacrifice the rights, safety, and independence of pedestrians with disabilities. Accessibility must be a foundational requirement, not an afterthought. 
To accomplish all of this, the Department of Sanitation must:
1. Make sidewalks truly waste-free 
Sanitation should expand the use of Empire Bins to smaller buildings and begin working on a way to accept recycling and compost. While the agency deserves credit for launching a pilot in Brooklyn that allows smaller buildings to share Empire Bins, the larger program must formally replace individual bins and bags with Empire Bins. Sidewalks must be clear of all bins and bags. 
2. Partner with the disability community 
For decades, siloed New York City agencies stalled containerization. Now that the program is underway, Sanitation must proactively partner with the disability community and agencies such as the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities. Together, they can develop clear and enforceable placement guidelines consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act and state and local accessibility laws. 
For example: Empire Bins should never be placed within 20 feet of curb cuts, crosswalks, Access-A-Ride pickup zones or bus stops. On dense residential blocks that will receive large numbers of bins, Sanitation must consider the construction of additional mid-block crosswalks and loading zones to accommodate people with disabilities.
3. Create real oversight and accountability 
DSNY must develop transparent mechanisms for oversight and accountability, including accessibility and safety reviews for every Empire Bin location. The agency must also establish a formal process to allow people with disabilities to request relocation of bins that impede access or create safety concerns, and those requests must be addressed promptly. 
Containerization is one of the most significant changes to New York City’s streetscape in decades, and this is the rare chance to solve two long-standing problems at once. The trash revolution must also be an accessibility revolution, precisely because we want a city that every resident can access. This opportunity must not go to waste.

https://hyperallergic.com/a-view-from-th.title: A View From the Easel: Natali Bravo-Barbee
https://hyperallergic.com/a-view-from-th.author: Lakshmi Rivera Amin
https://hyperallergic.com/a-view-from-th.text:
A View From the Easel: Natali Bravo-Barbee
“As a mother, there are so many spaces in my life that are organized around other people’s needs. The studio is a space where I get to return to myself.”
Welcome to the 362nd installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Natali Bravo-Barbee moves between modes of motherhood and making while testing the limits of what photography can be.
Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.
Natali Bravo-Barbee, Governors Island and South Street Seaport, New York
How long have you been working in this space?
Three years (the spaces change every year).
Describe an average day in your studio.
An average day in the studio is rarely average. As an artist and mother, I have learned to build flexibility into my studio practice. My days usually start once my children are in school, around 8:30 or 9am. I start by making a to-do list. There is an incredible amount of administrative work that is part of being an artist and maintaining a studio practice, so I usually try to get those tasks out of the way first.
Once I clear that list, I can pick up where I left off creatively. I usually have my mate and a thermos of hot water with me, and I sip as I settle back into whatever I was working on. Sometimes that means exposing cyanotypes that I coated the day before. Most recently, it has meant going through the photographs I selected to print and spending time with the images before deciding how I want to move forward with them. I’m constantly moving between making, looking, researching, and organizing. For me, all of those things are part of the studio practice.
How does the space affect your work?
The space affects my work quite a bit, particularly because I move between my home studio and my studio on Governors Island. They create two very different conditions for working.
When I’m working from home, the day is much more fragmented. I’m able to work around my family’s schedule, but I’m also surrounded by everything that comes with running a household: laundry, groceries, dinner, and the general visual noise of home. Sometimes I’ll be in the middle of something and realize I need to switch gears completely. There is always another task waiting for me.

https://gothamist.com/news/service-upgra.title: Service upgrade coming to On The Way: An hour-long radio show on all things NYC transit
https://gothamist.com/news/service-upgra.author: Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/service-upgra.text:
This column originally appeared in On The Way, a weekly newsletter covering everything you need to know about NYC-area transportation.
Sign up to get the full version, which includes answers to reader questions, trivia, service changes and more, in your inbox every Thursday.
For three years, this newsletter and weekly radio segment on All Things Considered have dug into the nitty gritty of the subways and streets.
Now, much like an old A train getting upgraded to a sleek R211, we’re improving service for our audience. On The Way is launching an hour-long pop-up radio show on Thursdays. Starting next week, on Nov. 12, tune into WNYC 93.9 FM from 1 to 2 p.m., listen on the WNYC app, or check out our YouTube channel for the show hosted by me, Stephen Nessen. I’ll be speaking with my fellow transportation reporter Ramsey Khalifeh and editor Clayton Guse, bringing you analysis of the latest transportation news.
We’ll have special guests, including decision makers and the sharpest thinkers in the transit world. We’ll take your calls and welcome questions about your daily commutes, as well as your hopes and dreams for mass transit. Write me at [email protected].
It’s going to be a gas — consider this your invitation.
As we do in this newsletter each week, we’ll discuss the most important transportation topics of our time, from the redevelopment of Penn Station and the antiquated elements of the subway system, to the new projects like the Interborough Express and Penn Access. We’ll look at the ongoing issues in the transit system like fare evasion, subway signals, and the future of the taxi industry.
We’ll also look at the subway bottlenecks that slow your commutes, and share tips on how to legally avoid paying for the AirTrain, or navigate Exit 31 on the BQE without pulling your hair out.
Speaking of the BQE, you can bet we’ll get into that too.
The Curious Commuter segment will continue, so please keep the questions coming!
As always, we welcome your thoughts on our coverage on the web, on the air and in your inbox. Talk to you on the airwaves.
NYC transportation news this week
Bus and bike lanes galore to come. Advocates say that a ballot measure that passed on election night will reform the process for the construction of bus and bike lanes and means more street safety projects throughout the five boroughs. The measure will amend the city charter to “simplify the review of street safety projects to reduce construction timelines,” according to the text of the ballot question.
“This really just defangs some of the opponents who have sought to slow down and stop these street safety projects,” said Ben Furnas, executive director of Transportation Alternatives.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office estimated construction timelines on major bus and bike lane projects could be reduced by at least 33%. But the measure still requires the city to solicit input from community boards before moving forward with any street redesign.
SoHo basketball court set to leave MTA construction purgatory. The refreshed Grand Canal Court at Sixth Avenue, set to open at the end of November, will feature new benches, a water fountain, upgraded lighting and fencing. The courts were originally ripped up in 2022 so workers could build a new substation that provides electricity to trains.
Scary good ridership for the MTA over Halloweekend. On Halloween Saturday, 3.27 million riders got on the subway, the most on a Saturday since 2016. And during the New York City Marathon, the subway saw its highest Sunday ridership on record.
NYPD seizes e-bikes along a clogged East Village street. Eleven e-bikes parked along East 11th Street and First Avenue were confiscated by police last week. Neighboring business owners and residents have been complaining for months about idle delivery bikes clogging sidewalks and curbs, sometimes by the hundreds.
Watchdog says MTA should eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget woes. The budget watchdog Citizens Budget Commission recommends the MTA should make sweeping cuts to positions that it argues technology has made obsolete as the agency could be looking at a nearly $900 million funding shortfall as spending outpaces fare revenue.
Curious Commuter
Have a question for us? Use this form to submit yours and we may answer it in a future newsletter!
Question from Charles in Brooklyn
Charles from Brooklyn asks: Why on earth did the MTA eliminate over half of the seats on the new D trains?! We have long commutes and need those seats!
Answer
The MTA has been slowly replacing some of the oldest subway cars (in lines like the A, C and now D) with new R211 trains. They’re noticeably different from the trains of yore with “conversational” yellow-and-orange seats. The newer subway cars have wider doors to allow for more people to easily get on and off the trains. And yes, there are notably less seats. More standing room means more space for people in a single subway car than previous models with more seats. While riders with longer commutes have a lower chance of snagging a seat on one of these new train cars, the modern equipment is less likely to break down, meaning better service all around.
Join us for a conversation with MTA Chair Janno Lieber
Lieber joins WNYC’s “On The Way” at The Greene Space on Nov. 17 for an in-depth conversation on the country’s largest mass transit system. Lieber is the 14th person to run the transit agency, but only the fourth person to hold the job for more than five years. He joins WNYC Transportation and Infrastructure Editor Clayton Guse in The Greene Space to discuss what the transit agency means to New York and the future of the transportation networks used by millions of people every day. “On The Way” subscribers can use promo code “OTW” for 20% off tickets. Information and tickets are available here.

https://hellgatenyc.com/looking-back-at-.title: Looking Back at New York's Glamorous, Silent Film Past
https://hellgatenyc.com/looking-back-at-.author: Kelly Faircloth
https://hellgatenyc.com/looking-back-at-.text:
To walk into "Goddesses in the Machine: Fashion in American Silent Film," the new exhibition at the Bard Graduate Center, is to feel a little bit like a kid in a candy shop—or rather a theater kid turned loose on the Paramount backlot, circa 1922. Everywhere you look, there's another lighter-than-air silk gown, or pair of beautiful metallic pumps, or bedazzled brassiere.
If you have a mental picture of silent film, there's a good chance it involves tinny piano music and overdramatic facial expressions—the era as retold by "Sunset Boulevard." This exhibition, which aims to tell the story of style and costume in early film, will overturn that impression, conveying just how vibrant, thrilling, and downright sexy these movies and their stars must've seemed to contemporary audiences. One of the displays quotes a costume designer who wrote that in the silent era he "wallowed in rhinestones and feathers and furs and loved every minute of it." That opulence and enthusiasm come through loud and clear in the exhibition.
What's more, the exhibit offers a rare window into a fascinating chapter in the history of the American movie business: when its beating heart was not on the West Coast, but in New York City.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-wor.title: Working-Class Democratic Candidates Won Big in the Midterms
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-wor.author: Jared Abbott
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-wor.text:
Working-Class Democratic Candidates Won Big in the Midterms
After this week’s elections, Democratic congresspeople from working-class backgrounds are set to grow their numbers by 75%. They have a chance to push the party’s agenda in a pro-worker direction. Organizing in a congressional caucus can help them do that.
In January, a logger from Maine’s North Woods will take a seat in the US Senate. Troy Jackson spent his adult life cutting timber before he ran for office, and he will be the only Senate Democrat whose working life before politics was spent mostly in a working-class job. But he won’t be alone on Capitol Hill. Across the House, a union ironworker from suburban Cleveland, a Bethlehem firefighter, a Wisconsin waitress, an emergency room nurse, a Montana smoke jumper, a Rochester math teacher, and a former Trader Joe’s worker from Queens are heading to Washington too.
By my count, twenty-one Democrats in the next Congress will have spent at least half of their working lives before politics in working-class jobs. Today there are just twelve. Working-class Democrats will still represent a woefully small fraction of the party caucus in the new year, but the 2026 midterms have swelled their ranks fast, and that gives them a real opportunity to come together to lead on a pro-worker agenda.
Having more workers in Congress isn’t just a matter of symbolism; it can meaningfully change what government does and how ordinary people feel about their elected officials. Political scientists Nicholas Carnes and Noam Lupu have shown that when workers don’t hold office, economic policy tilts toward the haves and away from the have-nots. Their work demonstrates that when working-class people are underrepresented in office, legislatures are less likely to pass pro-worker policies, governments tend to build less generous welfare states, and citizens have lower trust in their elected officials.
A Working-Class Wave
Of the over 250 Democrats serving in the current Congress (counting both the House and the Senate), just twelve (4.6 percent) spent most of their pre-political careers in working-class jobs. Meanwhile, roughly half of American workers hold working-class jobs.
I count a member of Congress as working class only if they spent at least half of their working life in working-class jobs before entering public office. That means jobs like factory work, waiting tables, office support, teaching, nursing, firefighting, and enlisted military service. A summer job or a few years of college shifts doesn’t count. That rules out many Democrats with real but limited working-class history, whose time in those jobs was too short or too uncertain to count.
The ten newcomers who clear that working-class bar mostly won hard-fought, highly competitive races. Indeed, nine of them won or lead in still-uncounted races for seats that Republicans hold today: Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s 7th District; Bob Brooks and Bob Harvie in two Pennsylvania districts; Rebecca Cooke in western Wisconsin; Mitchell Berman in southern Wisconsin; and JoAnna Mendoza, Jake Johnson, and Sam Forstag lead in Arizona, Minnesota, and Montana, respectively. Troy Jackson took a Republican-held Senate seat in Maine. The tenth, Claire Valdez, won an open seat in Brooklyn and Queens, one of the most heavily Democratic districts in the country.
These candidates’ résumés read like a cross section of the American working class:
Many of these working-class candidates are also union members, and several have held union office: Poindexter as an organizer and apprenticeship instructor, Brooks as president of Pennsylvania’s firefighters’ union, Forstag as a vice president of his Forest Service local, and Valdez as a unit chair in the United Auto Workers. They join eleven returning members with similar backgrounds, from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the former bartender, to Stephen Lynch, the ironworker who ran his union local, and Norma Torres, a former 911 dispatcher.
Working-Class Democrats Span Every Wing of the Party
The working-class Democrats come from a wide range of the party’s caucuses. Among current members, they include Congressional Progressive Caucus stalwarts like Ocasio-Cortez and Maxine Waters, New Democrats like Lucy McBath and John Mannion, and Blue Dog Jared Golden.
The incoming class is just as mixed. Valdez was backed by Justice Democrats and the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Jackson was Bernie Sanders’s pick. Harvie was endorsed by the New Democrats’ PAC, Johnson and Berman by both the New Democrats and the Blue Dogs. And Poindexter, Brooks, and Forstag managed something that should be impossible under the party’s factional logic: they were endorsed by both the Progressive Caucus PAC and the Blue Dog PAC.
But despite their ideological range, this crop of new working-class Democrats is more progressive on economics than it might at first appear. When I coded the campaign positions of the nine newcomers who ran in swing seats, five came out progressive or leaning progressive, including three the Blue Dogs endorsed. Troy Jackson and Bob Brooks both ran on Medicare for All. Sam Forstag proposed a 5 percent wealth tax on fortunes over $1 billion, Bob Harvie backs the PRO Act and a $15 federal minimum wage, and Brian Poindexter wants to make it easier to join a union and to make the wealthy pay their fair share to shore up Social Security funding. Claire Valdez, who ran in a safe seat in New York City, made Medicare for All one of her three platform pillars, alongside “unions for all” and “housing for all.”
Even the newcomers who lean moderate or show no clear lean hold robust pro-worker positions. Rebecca Cooke supports a $15 minimum wage and expanding Medicare to cover dental, vision, and hearing. Mitchell Berman calls for a living wage of about $21.54 an hour and joined striking nurses on the picket line. Jake Johnson wants a new top tax bracket for the highest earners and to break up big corporations that exploit workers. JoAnna Mendoza backs the right to unionize and expanding Medicare as well.
Whatever wing of the party they come from, this group’s shared working-class background grounds them in the bread-and-butter, kitchen-table issues that working people care about most and makes them ideal tribunes for working people’s interests on a national stage. They share an experience: of hourly pay, of shift work, of what a health insurance deductible means when you’re living paycheck to paycheck, and of the value of a union contract to families’ financial stability.
We Need a Working-Class Caucus in Congress
Congress has caucuses for nearly every region, industry, and ideological tendency. The Democrats’ main ideological blocs in the House are the Progressive Caucus, the New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dogs. But Congress doesn’t have a caucus by and for working people, dedicated purely to delivering material gains that improve the lives of ordinary Americans. The Labor Caucus does important work championing workers’ rights on the job and the priorities of the labor movement, from the PRO Act to a higher minimum wage. A working-class caucus would build on that work with a broader vision: raising the standard of living for all working people and making sure every working family has what it takes to thrive. Such a caucus, of course, wouldn’t need to police who does or doesn’t count as working class, but lawmakers with strong working-class backgrounds, who know firsthand the pressures that working families face, would play a central role. That would give working people not only allies in Congress but a voice of their own.
A working-class caucus could do things the existing ones cannot. To start, because working-class lawmakers already sit in caucuses across the party’s ideological spectrum, a working-class caucus could build coalitions across factional lines on bread-and-butter issues like wages, labor law, health care costs, and housing. Each faction supports progress on many of these issues in principle, but an organized bloc would be better placed to push back when party leaders are tempted to let those priorities slide down the agenda. Nick French has made a similar case for the record number of socialists heading to Congress: even a small minority can exert meaningful leverage when it organizes as a bloc.
Second, the issues that shape working people’s daily lives would sit at the top of the caucus’s agenda: making sure a full-time job pays enough to support a family; bringing down the cost of housing, health care, and childcare; protecting retirement security; strengthening workers’ right to organize; and investing in the towns and regions that decades of bad economic policy have left behind.
Finally, there is the bench of future working-class candidates to build. The 2026 results showed that working-class Democrats can win the competitive seats that decide control of the House, and a caucus could recruit, train, and fund more of them, so that a waitress or an electrician thinking about running knows there is a bloc in Washington that wants her to be there.
Organizing twenty or so working-class members of Congress into an organized caucus obviously won’t remake the Democratic Party into a party of the working class on its own. It can’t fix the deeper problem that working people have too little organized power in American politics. But it would give workers more leverage inside the party, because an organized group of pro-worker champions in strategic positions across the party can keep its leadership focused on working people’s priorities and hold the party brass accountable when it strays.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: What's Behind Trump’s Obsession With Butts?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
One of the mysteries of the 2026 midterms will always be why Donald Trump thought he could charm voters by repeatedly and lasciviously celebrating the human buttocks.
On October 12, Trump astonished a rally in Ohio with his lurid leering at Senator Jon Husted. “I started examining his body because I didn’t know he was a great athlete,” Trump said, alluding to Husted’s history as a college football player. “And I looked—I watched up, and down, I looked at his ass, and I looked at the whole…” Tributes to Husted’s rear would remain a staple until the end of the campaign.
But Trump wasn’t content to ogle just Husted. Speaking in Michigan on October 25, Trump made similar comments about both the singer Nicki Minaj (credited with “one hell of a beautiful ass”) and senatorial candidate Mike Rogers. Trump added, “I’d say that about your ass too, Mike, if it gets you a guaranteed victory.”
The degree to which Trump talks about other people’s bums really is bizarre and arguably without precedent in American political history. Abraham Lincoln did enjoy making scatological jokes about bodily functions, but that was in keeping with his persona as a son of the soil born in a log cabin—and he was not known to constantly praise, say, Charles Sumner’s behind on the campaign trail. In 2020, then–vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin appeared on The Masked Singer to perform “Baby Got Back,” Sir Mix-a-Lot’s classic rap tribute to the posterior. This was unusual but a one-off event—and by that point, Palin had long transitioned from a serious political figure to, well, the kind of D-list celebrity who sings about butts on television.
By contrast, Trump’s butt commentary is relentless, and coming from the incumbent president of the United States. And because of the cult-like hold that Trump has over the Republican Party, ass-talk started to proliferate. On October 29, during an appearance on Fox News, vice president JD Vance was asked a serious question from a voter about how the affordability crisis was harming young people. Inexplicably, Vance responded, “I want to point out that I’ve only gotten one question about Jon Husted’s ass.” A few days later, Florida senatorial candidate Ashley Moody told a rally, “Maybe I should be upset [Trump] didn’t talk about my asset.”
All of this loopy bum talk didn’t help the Republicans, despite Trump’s absurd claim that his praise of Husted’s rear caused the senator’s poll numbers to vault 14 points. Husted and Rogers went down to defeat, while Moody won an unexpectedly narrow race, helped by the fact the Democratic Party didn’t sufficiently fund her rival Angie Nixon.
After the Republicans were soundly trounced in the worst midterm defeat in half a century, Republican operative Todd Gillman told Politico, “Honestly, we need to move as far away from Trump as we can. I think Republicans might be screwed all the way until ’30. Talking about Nicki Minaj’s fat ass. All that stuff is just wearing people out.”
Even if it is politically ineffective, Trump’s ass-talk is a political fact, one that demands an explanation. On November 1, The New York Times published a lengthy analysis of Trump’s increasing verbal incoherence, including “his baffling fixation with admiring men’s posteriors.” “He is cruder than he used to be,” the paper reports, “using nearly 15 swear words per 10,000 words compared with 14 two years ago and six a decade ago, a change consistent with age-related disinhibition.”
It makes sense that, at the age of 80, Trump is less willing or perhaps less able to censor himself. But while this cognitive explanation offers a necessary context for Trump’s rough language, it doesn’t explain the specific content of the speech. Why does he have an anal focus, rather than, say, a genital or oral one?
Further, the fact that Trump’s ass talk was echoed by respectable Republicans such as Vance and Moody means it has a social meaning that goes beyond the peculiarities of Trump’s admittedly twisted personality. Trump is a freak but not an isolated case. He’s a weirdo with an immense mass following, so his quirks have a wider social resonance.
Saturday Night Live, less restricted by the rules of propriety than The New York Times, offered an unvarnished sexual explanation in a recent skit that shows the president suffering from “gay dementia.”
This joke is, as often with SNL, both too glib and borderline offensive. The truth is that Trump’s ass-talk is only occasionally sexual but more frequently involves excretion; it targets women as well as men, and is as much about asserting domination and humiliation as about expressing desire. In other words, Trump’s fixation is scatological and anal, rather than narrowly erotic.
Consider Trump’s description of Norway as a “shithouse country” (a term of abuse Trump has used against other nations in the past). Similarly, Trump has obsessed in speeches about the dangers of low-flow toilets, lamenting in 2019 the need to flush “10 times.”
Writing in Rolling Stone, Jack Crosbie argued that Trump’s ass talk is “ripe for armchair psychoanalysis: Trump is self-conscious about his own aging body, Trump values the superficial and material above all other things, Trump sees validation from the strong and tall and beautiful as evidence that what he is doing is good and just.”
This is all very suggestive, but it’s useful to move beyond such amateur speculation and consult the work of a true expert. In thinking about Trump’s anal fixation, few works are more illuminating than Normal O. Brown’s towering study Life Against Death: The Psychoanalytical Meaning of History. Brown was a distinguished classicist, and the virtue of his book lies in its provocative application of Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytical theories to social and political analysis. As such, it rivals other mid-20th-century works of daring, psychologically informed social theory by figures such as Herbert Marcuse and Wilhelm Reich.
Surprisingly, Brown’s book has a Trump connection. It was originally published to obscurity by an academic press but found fame when it was championed by Norman Podhoretz, a New York literary critic and editor at Commentary. Podhoretz would later become one of the founding fathers of neoconservatism and, late in life, one of the most prominent pro-Trump intellectuals. In a 1999 essay in Harper’s, Christopher Hitchens noted that Podhoretz and other neoconservatives have an “obsessive” and prurient focus on anal sex.
In a brilliant and celebrated chapter on “the excremental vision” of Jonathan Swift, Brown notes,
according to Freudian theory the human infant passes through a stage—the anal stage—as a result of which the libido, the life energy of the body, gets concentrated in the anal zone. The infantile stage of anal eroticism takes the essential form of attaching symbolic meaning to the anal product. As a result of these symbolic equations, the anal product acquires for the child significance of being his own child or creation, which he may use either to obtain narcissistic pleasure in play, or to obtain love from another (feces as gift), or to assert independence from another (feces as property), or to commit aggression against another (feces as weapon).
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The anal stage is universal, but as the infant matures, these impulses are sublimated into more socially acceptable behavior. If Trump is in fact suffering cognitive decline, it could be that sublimation is no longer possible. It’s broadly true that for Trump, subtext and text are often one: He doesn’t sublimate desire but gives it free vent, often in erratic and socially aggressive ways.
In the writings of Swift, one sees anal aggression brilliantly sublimated into a harsh and compelling satirical vision of humanity. Brown demonstrates that this is both Swift’s practice as a writer and his thematic concern. Trump, lacking Swift’s genius, turns anal aggression into mere verbal abusiveness: In the vernacular, Trump is a man who loves to shit talk.
Elsewhere in his study, Brown links the anal stage to hoarding, particularly of gold. Very slightly sublimated, hoarding gold turns into a love of the gold standard. This cluster of compulsions (narcissism, abusive language, hoarding, the fetishization of gold) can easily serve as a quite acute account of Trump’s psychology. Even if one doesn’t accept the scientific validity of Freudian categories, there is no denying that it offers a fresh and original way to think about commonly linked character traits.
While Brown was fully aware of the sadism of the anal stage, he also entertained the utopian hope that humans might be able to deprogram themselves of their social conditioning and achieve a return to the childhood ecstasy in the polymorphous perverse. The case of Trump suggests that this program might be dangerous if applied unilaterally. If one individual reverts to the anal stage while the rest of society remains committed to sublimation, you have a recipe for tyranny: the alpha male baboon who smears his shit over everyone in order to assert dominance. In other words, Trump’s impulse to constantly talk ass is symptomatic of the fact that he is an asshole.
