https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New Miami art space to champion photography, film and video
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sarah Cascone
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A beloved Miami art space returns this month, opening on 30 November in Little River as Mitrani Art, a photography, film and video venue with exhibition galleries, a screening room and artists’ studios. It is a long-awaited new chapter for the Mitrani Warehouse, which sisters Dina and Rhonda Mitrani began out of their family’s longtime Wynwood clothing factory in 2002, watching the neighbourhood around them transform into a thriving arts district.
“We want to continue that same model that we had in Wynwood, creating a community with art studios and event spaces,” Dina tells The Art Newspaper. “We still want to welcome emerging and established artists to use it as a place to experiment and create new work.”
The inaugural exhibition is a group show of lens-based art titled ReExposures: The Magic Within. One expected highlight is Suddenly We Jumped by the Miami-based artist Antonia Wright. The video captures a live performance from 2013 in which the artist actually shattered a glass ceiling, dramatically jumping onto a pane of glass and falling to the floor below.
“Antonia makes really creative work and focuses on important social issues that need change,” Rhonda says. “This one is very impactful.”
Both Mitrani sisters left their native Miami for university, and found their way to New York after graduating.
Dina worked at Christie’s and then at two different galleries, including one specialising in Latin American photography. After having children, she decided to move home and open a photography gallery in her home city. Rhonda, who had a thriving film production career, was more reluctant to return.
“I had no intention of leaving New York,” she admits. “I ended up making a documentary film about my father going back to Cuba, and that brought me back to Miami to finish editing it. During one of those visits, Dina said, ‘Why don’t you stay here? There’s something going on in the art community.’”
At Mitrani Warehouse, the sisters started small, with art studios on the second floor, and gradually took over the building. Dina, who has a photography background, started a contemporary photography gallery, Dina Mitrani Gallery, and Rhonda opened the Screening Room, the first dedicated space in Miami for film-makers and video artists to show their work.
But as the years passed, the sisters watched as artists and galleries slowly got priced out of the neighborhood. “We realised the Wynwood Art District was shifting. We held on for as long as we could, because we had an emotional attachment to that space where our parents had their business, our grandmother worked there, so many cousins, uncles,” Dina says. “But we realised it was time to go.”
When the Mitrani Warehouse closed in 2017, the sisters immediately began looking for a new location. In 2019, they purchased a mechanic shop in Little River with high ceilings and space to expand by building a separate studio facility. To design the new facility, they hired R&R Studios, a local multidisciplinary architecture firm run by Argentine artists Roberto Behar and Rosario Marquardt, who were longtime residents of the Mitrani Warehouse studios. The project took considerably longer than expected due to the pandemic, permitting and other roadblocks.
“It’s been seven years in the making, so we’re very excited to open. There’s a lot of anticipation,” Rhonda says.
The opening of Mitrani Art means a new permanent home for the Screening Room and Dina Mitrani Gallery, which have relied on pop-up programming across the city since the closing of the warehouse. The sisters have also started a new non-profit, Mitrani Art Projects Inc, that will run educational programmes in the space.
And artists are already moving into the new building, which has four studio spaces, each big enough for two artists. Rent is at the lower end of the market rate for the neighbourhood, the sisters say, and they hope to keep it that way by securing grant funding in the future.

https://apache.be/2026/11/06/onderzoeksr.title: Onderzoeksrechters worden pion van beleid in nieuwe wet op woonstbetredingen
https://apache.be/2026/11/06/onderzoeksr.author: Walter De Smedt
https://apache.be/2026/11/06/onderzoeksr.text:
De voormalige voorzitter van de vereniging van onderzoeksrechters, Walter De Smedt, maakt brandhout van de net gestemde wet over woonstbetreding. Die wet, met als enige doel het verwijderen van mensen zonder papieren, gaat volledig voorbij aan de kerntaak van een onderzoeksrechter: onafhankelijk onderzoeken en voorlopige maatregelen nemen.
In de twaalfde eeuw maakte de Luikse prins-bisschop Albert de Cuyck een charter. De voornaamste regel daarin, “Pauvre homme en sa maison est roi”, heeft de geschiedenis − inclusief twee wereldoorlogen − overleefd.
Daar is nu verandering in gekomen. Mensen zonder papieren die een uitvoerbare verwijderingsmaatregel hebben, die weigeren mee te werken én door hun gedrag een gevaar vormen voor de openbare orde of nationale veiligheid moeten kunnen worden aangehouden, zelfs indien daarvoor de woning moet worden betreden. Daarvoor is de tussenkomst van een onderzoeksrechter voorzien. Die kan een “machtiging” verlenen en de modaliteiten ervan bepalen. Ongeacht of deze ingreep nodig en grondwettelijk is, moet de vraag gesteld worden wat een onderzoeksrechter in deze “politiek-bestuurlijke” procedure komt doen.
Advocaten en onderzoeksrechters tegen
Een onderzoeksrechter is een rechter die in het kader van een strikte procedure even strikt omschreven opdrachten heeft. Hij treedt enkel op in een voorlopig strafonderzoek, een onderzoek naar mogelijke gepleegde strafbare feiten. Het is zijn opdracht alle maatregelen te nemen die de rechtscolleges in staat moeten stellen met kennis van zaken te oordelen. Daartoe kan hij ook, met aanhaling van de redenen, grondwettelijk beschermde rechten schenden, een aanhoudings- of een huiszoekingsbevel verlenen.
Deze maatregelen zijn enkel voorlopig. Vrijheidsberoving wordt door de onderzoeksgerechten, de raadkamer en de kamer van inbeschuldigingstelling, beoordeeld. Alles moet nadien door de strafrechter worden overgedaan in een openbare en tegensprekelijke procedure waartegen ook de rechtsmiddelen van verzet, beroep en cassatie openstaan. Geen wonder dat de onderzoeksrechters én de twee advocatenordes een negatief advies gaven.
In voorliggend wetsvoorstel gaat het niet om een strafonderzoek. Het gaat evenmin om een voorlopig vooronderzoek dat onder toezicht van de onderzoeksgerechten staat en evenmin wordt overgedaan in een openbare en tegensprekelijke procedure. Het enige doel is de verwijdering van mensen zonder papieren. Het gaat hierin ook niet om een rechterlijk bevel maar om een rechterlijke “machtiging”. De onderzoeksrechter kan weigeren en de modaliteiten bepalen. Toch is het duidelijk dat hier beroep gedaan wordt op een rechter omdat het niet anders kan, maar dat die daarvoor uit zijn eigen procedure en de daarin voorziene waarborgen moet treden. De essentie van zijn opdracht, zelf onderzoeken en voorlopige maatregelen nemen ontbreekt. Ook het toezicht van de onderzoeksgerechten en van de strafrechter in een openbare en tegensprekelijke behandeling ontbreekt.
“Verkrachters, drugsdelinquenten en haatpredikers”
Even opmerkelijk als de vorige bezwaren is het echte doel van de wet. Volgens de minister van Asiel en Migratie Anneleen Van Bossuyt (N-VA) gaat het om “verkrachters, drugsdelinquenten en haatpredikers” die uit het land moeten worden gezet. “Die mensen zullen zich nu niet langer achter een voordeur kunnen verschuilen”, zegt ze aan VRT.
De vraag is hoe er voor deze opvatting een meerderheid kon worden gevonden. Zelfs de beweerde liberalen van Anders stemden mee. Als het om de uitzetting van verkrachters, drugsdelinquenten en haatpredikers gaat is de wet de meest grove miskenning van de rechtsstaat. Voor dergelijke misdrijven is er immers een strafprocedure met een vooronderzoek, een tegensprekelijk en openbaar onderzoek ter zitting waarin de rechten van de verdediging moeten worden gerespecteerd.
Buiten de reguliere rechtspraak
In 1933 vaardigde Duits president Paul von Hindenburg de Rijksdagbrandverordening uit over de brand van de Reichstag, het Duitse parlementsgebouw, op 27 februari 1933. Door deze Schutzhaft (“beschermende bewaring”) konden de Gestapo (Geheime Staatspolizei), de SA (Sturmabteilung – de milities van de nazipartij) en de SS (Schutzstaffel – de lijfwacht van Hitler) volledig buiten de reguliere rechtspraak om burgers willekeurig en voor onbepaalde tijd opsluiten.
Deze Schutzhäftlinge kwamen niet in reguliere gevangenissen terecht maar werden direct naar concentratiekampen gestuurd. In het begin ging het om communisten, sociaaldemocraten, vakbondsleiders en tegenstanders van het regime. Daarna werden Joden, Roma en Sinti, Jehova’s getuigen en homoseksuelen opgepakt. Later ondergingen daklozen, bedelaars, sekswerkers en langdurig werklozen hetzelfde lot. Onder de benaming Sicherheitshaft werden tijdens de bezetting van België burgers en verzetsstrijders door de Sicherheitspolizei (Sipo-SD) opgepakt en naar het Fort van Breendonk gebracht en vandaar naar de concentratiekampen.
Machtiging
Het voorstel van de woonstbetredingen staat niet alleen. Ook bij de toepassing van de afkoopwet werd het rechterlijke bevel omgezet in een rechterlijke “machtiging”. Dat is een bevestiging van de toegenomen opdrachten en bevoegdheden van het openbaar ministerie als ambtenaar van het door slechts één minister bepaald strafrechtelijk beleid. Ook de afhandeling van het strafproces neigt steeds meer naar een enkele “machtiging” van de openbare vordering.
Vraag is natuurlijk wat de onderzoeksrechters er van gaan maken. Dat heeft het voorstel echter reeds voorzien. Als de éne weigert kan een andere worden aangesproken. Dat was onder de Sicherheitshaft evenzo: de onwillige rechters werden ook afgevoerd.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/defe.title: Defeating Zionism to Free Palestine
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/defe.author: Noura Erakat, John Reynolds
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/defe.text:
The World at a Crossroads
Three years on from the onset of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, we are at a crucial hinge point. The world today, when it comes to Palestine, stands at the crossroads: meaningful support for liberation and decolonization, or the normalization of colonial expansion and erasure.
Since the 2021 “Manifesto of Dignity and Hope” and the unified call of Palestinians to confront Zionism, the Israeli political sphere has only continued to sustain and entrench its fascist trajectory and its racist laws. After 2023, Israeli settler colonialism and domination escalated into all-out destruction and elimination. Palestinians who had been enduring suffocating apartheid and siege for far too long were now subjected to genocidal assault. Though the context on the ground shifted, the urgent need for a better understanding and challenge to Zionism on political, legal, structural, and ideological grounds remained.
It was a new generation of Palestinian activists who produced the Manifesto of Dignity and Hope, but their text was shaped by the legacy and spirit of Palestinian revolutionaries and anti-colonial thinkers from earlier periods. Common language echoes through the generations. A quarter-century ago, Palestinian intellectual Edward Said wrote the core of the issue of Palestine “is intellectual truth and the need to combat any sort of apartheid. We should concentrate our resistance on … fully confronting the apartheid provisions inherent in Zionism.” And as diplomat Fayez Sayegh captured it in 1965: Racism is not an acquired or incidental or passing feature of the Israeli state; it is “inherent in the very ideology of Zionism.” Today, we can draw inspiration from these intergenerational reverberations across Palestinian theory and activism, in their consonant commitments to confronting Zionism.
Part of our own task as anti-colonial legal scholars is to expand our analysis of the limitations of narrow liberal legal readings of apartheid and inequality, and to highlight how a radical critique of Israeli apartheid is essential to dismantling Israel’s apartheid regime. This requires scrutiny not only of Zionism and Israeli settler colonialism, but also of the concept of apartheid itself. Apartheid was previously understood in the context of the African anti-apartheid struggle, in a formulation originally coined by the South African Communist Party, as “colonialism of a special type.” By the late 1990s, however, apartheid had been stripped in mainstream understandings of its global character and colonial essence, and effectively reframed as “racial discrimination of a special type.”
One factor in this analytical shift was the domestication of racism in international law, which has obscured its relationship to global capitalism and transformed racism into a problem for individual countries to resolve through juridical reform or diversity, equity, and inclusion programs. Racism is not merely abhorrent because people’s feelings are hurt or one feels unseen, however, but because it is entangled with power and economic structures, and because materially, the continuum of racist violence culminates in genocide, which is squarely understood as a global phenomenon. Martin Luther King Jr. pointed to this in 1967 when he said: “In the final analysis, racism is evil because its ultimate logic is genocide. … If one says that I am not good enough to eat at a lunch counter, or to have a good, decent job, or to go to school with him merely because of my race, he is saying consciously or unconsciously that I do not deserve to exist.”
International law attempts to capture this continuum. Three of the specific acts conducted to maintain apartheid are identical to the acts conducted to commit genocide under their respective legal definitions. In the former, they are done with the intent to dominate; in the latter, with the intent to destroy. These are not mutually exclusive, but rather interact with each other: Colonialism, apartheid, and genocide combine under the Zionist project in Palestine to produce a system of oppression based on conquest, structural racism, dispossession, and elimination.
Palestinian opposition to Zionism and the imperatives of decolonization — for political emancipation, material survival, and cultural flourishing — are the central thrust of our work. The colonial origins and early legal mechanics of Zionist settler colonialism and Israel’s apartheid regime reveal how Zionism functioned both as a colonial initiative and a racializing project. This manifested in colonial institutions even before the state was established in 1948, after which they were enshrined in racist legal regimes. A broad structural analysis of the institutional and economic processes of land and capital accumulation that have occurred under settler colonialism in Palestine is necessary to understand the machinery of conquest and dispossession — and the role that racism has played in driving it forward. Drawing on the anti-colonial Palestinian intellectual tradition, we can see that an antiracist analysis has been organic to the Palestinian liberation struggle and is precisely what shaped U.N. initiatives in the 1960s and 1970s that condemned Zionism as a form of racism and racial discrimination alongside apartheid and colonialism.
Despite all the analysis of Israeli state racism and colonial violence since 1948 and all of the mass popular mobilizations and legal advocacy against Israeli apartheid, nothing substantive was done at an international, political, or institutional level to address or redress it. This inaction and the impunity afforded to Israel inevitably culminated in the situation that the world found itself in after October 2023: unsanctioned apartheid accelerating into unadulterated genocide — and given the green light by those who had the power to stop it. There was a decade of increasingly flagged warning signs leading up to this. But Palestinian scholars and international lawyers who had warned of a “prelude to genocide” or “slow-motion” genocide over the years were largely ignored, and in some cases castigated. The consequences have been catastrophic. The United States actively funded, armed, and cheer-led the butchery in Gaza. European Union leaders chose to “stand with Israel” as it announced its starvation policy and war of annihilation.
We would not have ended up in this present moment if the critiques of Zionism as colonialism and racism and the reality of Israel as an apartheid regime had been taken seriously. In 1975, the U.N., led by a Third World majority, declared “international co-operation and peace require the achievement of national liberation and independence, the elimination of colonialism and neocolonialism, foreign occupation, zionism, apartheid and racial discrimination in all its forms, as well as the recognition of the dignity of peoples and their right to self-determination.” Against this, the Western world, led by the United States, has worked to normalize Israeli apartheid.
We see part of our task now as one of continuing to build on the recent “mainstreaming” of condemnations of Israeli apartheid and genocide, but in a way that decisively resists the drift toward narrower, liberal articulations and insists on the importance of radical, anti-colonial, and anti-imperial analysis and praxis. In our work as critical legal scholars, we situate apartheid and the shape it has taken as a category in international law, and we explore the limits and potential of legal tactics, arguments, and institutions to dismantle Israeli apartheid and end the genocide in Gaza. We argue that while legal actions should be pursued in the service of political and social movements, legal logic is insufficient in itself — and can risk narrowing or distorting the horizon of Palestinian liberation. In our view, the proliferating condemnations of Israel by major human rights organizations and mainstream figures in recent years have belatedly reflected the popular consensus and a political reality that Palestinian activism had made undeniable. They also fit, to varying degrees, within a wider pattern of containment.
As one example, take the case of European officials and states finally beginning to acknowledge the heinousness of Israel’s obliteration of Gaza in mid-2025, but doing so primarily in the form of calling for a Palestinian state. They did so only after almost two full years of enabling untold destruction, and refusing to impose any serious sanctions to stem the genocide. Their moves to recognize Palestinian statehood were not about any genuine support for Palestinian self-determination, but rather a way to stabilize the apartheid status quo and try to slow down the Israeli–U.S. drive to continue the erasure of Gaza and full annexation of the West Bank.
With all of that in mind, it is important to situate the political moment we are in — the increasing focus on Israeli apartheid in recent years and subsequently on the genocide in Gaza — alongside the urgency of thinking about Palestine’s future and our collective responsibilities. In doing so, we have several core aims: to offer a deeper understanding of the nature and extent of Israel’s colonial rule over Palestinian lands and lives; to think through the relationship between the practices of Israeli settler colonialism, apartheid, and genocide on the one hand, and the institutions and ideology of Zionism on the other; to situate Palestinian liberation and its global solidarity alliances as an antiracist struggle and an anti-colonial movement; and to insist on the need for systemic anti-imperial understandings and critiques of Zionism. To properly confront Zionism and avoid the pitfalls of neo-apartheid, we must be attentive to the necessities and practicalities of decolonization.
The decolonization of Palestine today continues a legacy of other liberation struggles — against European colonization globally, against domestic regimes of fascism, against apartheid in southern Africa, and against white supremacy in the United States and elsewhere. These are political orders that Third World, antiracist, partisan, and socialist movements have fought against throughout the past century and more. We must continue that tradition in the service of decolonization by fleshing out the political, legal, historical, and moral reasoning of anti-colonial and anti-Zionist thinking and movements. In our own writing, we feel we are merely providing footnotes to the political education and organizing that has fanned out from Palestine around the world, and that has shaped what millions of activists and people of conscience have viscerally felt: that Zionist colonial rule should and can be dismantled, and that Palestinians must be supported in their struggle to do so.
The stakes of confronting Zionist settler colonialism are high for the entire world: first and foremost for Palestinians’ own liberation, but also because their struggle is at the epicenter of wider global struggles against structures of domination and exploitation. Zionism is a colonial project in Palestine, but also a vehicle of imperialism in the region — agitating for U.S. war and intervention, acting as an antagonist of imperial aggression against Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Yemen and beyond, and actively collaborating with reactionary geopolitical forces globally. Zionism has been further mobilized by ethnonationalists and imperial projects as a proposition on how to organize a society on a basis of racial hierarchy that leaves its excluded groups to perish. Palestinian revolutionary intellectual Ghassan Kanafani always insisted on the importance of understanding the Palestinian struggle in the context of “the alliance between Zionism and imperialism.” And in positioning Kanafani’s analysis in the context of global movements against imperialism today, educator and organizer Layan Sima Fuleihan reiterates the Palestinian cause is “a banner for all of humanity.”
Naji al-Ali, the Palestinian political cartoonist famous for his iconic Hanzala (or “Handala”) character who symbolizes Palestinian resolve and future return, was himself displaced from northern Palestine as a boy during the Nakba and grew up in refugee camps in Lebanon. Kanafani came across Al-Ali and his artwork in Ein al-Hilweh camp and began to publish his drawings in the early 1960s. Al-Ali went on to produce tens of thousands of cartoons over the next 25 years, and through his art was renowned as a voice of Palestinian and Arab political consciousness. In 1984, just a couple of years before he would be assassinated, Al-Ali reflected on what Hanzala and Palestine represented:
I feel that I can recall and sense every bush, every stone, every house and every tree I passed when I was a child in Palestine. The character of Hanzala was a sort of icon that protected my soul from falling whenever I felt sluggish or I was ignoring my duty. That child was like a splash of fresh water on my forehead, bringing me to attention and keeping me from error and loss. He was the arrow of the compass, pointing steadily towards Palestine. Not just Palestine in geographical terms, but Palestine in its humanitarian sense — the symbol of a just cause, whether it is located in Egypt, Vietnam or South Africa.
In the decades since then, the idea of Palestine as the compass has resonated in struggles for justice around the world. Most recently, in 2025, the Palestinian Youth Movement and a coalition of solidarity groups brought thousands of activists together for the People’s Conference for Palestine, under the banner “Gaza is the compass.”
A wide array of voices, from community activists to trade union organizers to political representatives, emphasized how central Palestine is to all of the social struggles they are engaged in.
Palestinian doctor Mohammad Mustafa articulated the perspective of the many involved in movements for justice across the globe: “Gaza is the measure of our humanity. It is the litmus test that reveals who we are; as individuals, as a nation, as a world. … The compass points in one direction no matter who you are or where you are. In this way it provides a mandate and direction towards freedom for everyone.”
Lawyer and organizer Huwaida Arraf echoed these ideas: “Gaza is our compass because it points us to the truth. … When we’re fighting for Gaza, we’re fighting for a world where no people live in cages or under siege, under the boot of militarism or of fascism.”
Monadel Herzallah from Gaza, who lost five family members in the genocide, insisted the same: “To fight for a free Palestine is to fight for a free Haiti, a free Congo, a free Sudan — a free and just world which will be molded by all of us.”
Palestine is the compass because of what it represents as a banner for all humanity, and because of the horizons it opens up everywhere in imagining and building a new world.
Excerpt adapted from “Confronting Zionism: Decolonizing Palestine and Building the World Anew,” coming from Haymarket Books on November 10, 2026.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.propublica.org/article/burgu.title: Trump Official Who Wants Data Centers on Public Lands Has Tens of Millions Invested in AI Industry
https://www.propublica.org/article/burgu.author: Mark Olalde
https://www.propublica.org/article/burgu.text:
The Trump administration has likened the need to build out the nation’s artificial intelligence infrastructure to the Manhattan Project, the World War II effort that produced the world’s first atomic bomb.
The White House’s point person on the effort, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, has spoken of the “AI arms race” with China as an existential issue for the nation. “AI is manufacturing intelligence, and, if we don’t manufacture more intelligence than our adversaries, it affects every job, every company and every industry,” he said during his Senate confirmation hearing in January 2025.
But advancing the administration’s AI objectives also could benefit Burgum’s own finances.
Much of his wealth is held in Arthur Ventures, an investment firm he co-founded, according to his 2026 financial disclosure form, which has not been previously reported. Between $18.1 million and $64.4 million of those investments are in AI companies, according to an analysis of the companies’ marketing materials shared with ProPublica by public lands advocacy group Save Our Parks. (Government financial disclosure forms allow filers to report wide ranges instead of the specific value of their investments.)
Burgum made his fortune 25 years ago when he sold a software company to Microsoft and has remained heavily invested in technology. In the year before joining the administration, when he was North Dakota’s governor, he made between $2.1 million and $11 million in capital gains from AI-related investments, Save Our Parks’ analysis showed. In 2025, he sold millions of dollars of stocks and equity in AI companies, bringing in capital gains worth between $2.5 million and $15.1 million.
In the ethics agreement Burgum signed as part of his Senate confirmation, he agreed to resign from his positions at Arthur but not give up his financial interests there.
“Secretary Burgum has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure obligations,” a U.S. Department of the Interior spokesperson told ProPublica in a statement. “Any suggestion that his office decisions are driven by personal investments are false and completely unsupported.”
Officials across the Trump administration also stand to profit from the White House’s support for AI and data centers. For example, 380 of President Donald Trump’s political appointees or their spouses hold stocks or have other financial connections to Nvidia, which has become the world’s most valuable company thanks to the data center boom. More than 320 have ties to Alphabet, Google’s parent company, which plans to spend at least $195 billion this year building data centers and AI-related technology. And more than 240 are invested in or otherwise have financial ties to Meta Platforms, which is developing a “fleet” of data centers. This is according to an analysis of records added last week to the Trump Team Financials database developed by ProPublica to make accessible the financial disclosures of administration officials.
Federal officials’ activities are governed by a criminal statute that sets a high burden of proof for potential wrongdoing — for example, approving permits for a company in which they are substantially invested, multiple ethics professors and lawyers told ProPublica. They said that Burgum’s investments appear to be acceptable under this law.
But ethics rules that do not carry criminal penalties also apply, explained Cynthia Brown, senior ethics counsel with Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a government watchdog group. These rules, she said, “instruct officials not to work on anything that would create the appearance of a conflict of interest.” She said this would include Burgum’s support for data centers on federal land while holding investments in AI.
Richard Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and President George W. Bush’s chief ethics lawyer, agreed that Burgum should avoid making decisions benefiting an industry in which he is heavily invested. “I, as the ethics lawyer, would insist he stay away from it,” Painter said. “In the Bush administration, the answer would’ve been ‘he has to recuse,’ I can guarantee you that.”
A review of recent Interior Department secretaries’ financial holdings suggests it’s common to have some potential conflicts, but Trump’s appointees are more heavily invested in the industries they oversee than their predecessors. Deb Haaland, President Joe Biden’s appointee, held no direct financial investments in companies the department regulated. President Barack Obama’s first appointee, Ken Salazar, listed ownership of his family’s ranch but few other investments. Obama’s second appointee, Sally Jewell, held stocks in oil and gas, which she agreed to divest as a condition of her confirmation.
Ryan Zinke and David Bernhardt served as Interior Department secretaries during Trump’s first term. The former was found by the agency’s Office of Inspector General to have improperly assisted a development in his hometown, while the latter had so many potential conflicts that he reportedly carried a card listing them. (Zinke said the OIG investigation was a political attack, while Bernhardt recused himself from several decisions in which there would have been clear conflicts.)
More recently, as the effort to build data centers has run headlong into broad public opposition, the current administration has offered federally managed public lands to them. Unlike local or state processes, where concerns about water use, power consumption and the lack of transparency around permitting have slowed or halted projects, the public has less ability to stop them on federal property. The Interior Department oversees most of this land.
A little-noticed U.S. Geological Survey report released earlier this year found at least 91.3 million acres of public lands managed by the Interior Department — an area comparable to Montana — could potentially host data centers.
The department’s mandate includes overseeing tribal affairs, managing national parks, regulating extractive industries like coal and operating dams across the West. Burgum, though, is spending significant time on other things. This includes meeting with representatives of companies such as Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet more than 20 times from January through November 2025, according to a compilation of his schedules shared with ProPublica by public interest watchdog group Public Citizen.
In response, several Democratic senators sent a letter to Burgum in October saying, “We demand that you immediately cease all efforts to hijack public lands for the development of data centers, and urge you to provide full transparency on your role in the DOI’s efforts to site data centers.”
Some of Burgum’s meetings have been previously unreported, including a June 2025 dinner with a high-ranking United Arab Emirates delegation in the wine room of the upscale Italian restaurant Cafe Milano in Washington’s Georgetown neighborhood. The small guest list included the United Arab Emirates’ AI lead, Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, as well as Amos Hochstein, a prominent American proponent of AI data centers via his investment firm TWG Global.
Several months later, Burgum signed a memorandum of understanding with the Emirati delegation, pledging to work together to deploy AI.
Neither the Emirati Embassy nor TWG Global responded to requests for comment.
The Interior Department spokesperson said that Burgum “is responsible for helping unleash American energy production and ensuring our nation has the resources and infrastructure necessary to lead the future. That mission requires engagement with industry leaders, stakeholders, and international partners.”
In an August Fox News appearance to promote the administration’s AI efforts, Burgum was asked about the network’s poll showing 70% of voters opposed data centers. He countered by alleging that “foreign influence” and “misinformation” had played a large role in fueling public opposition.
Jayson O’Neill, a spokesperson for Save Our Parks, said Burgum and others in the administration are out of touch with public concerns. “His almost myopic focus on artificial intelligence and the data center build-out at the expense of our public lands serves not only the globalist tech titans behind and within the Trump administration, but also him and the tens of millions of dollars of his own personal wealth invested in the industry.”
Potential Conflicts of Interest Across the Administration
Across the administration, political appointees whose offices have AI business before them hold significant investments in the industry.
Steve Pearce is director of the Bureau of Land Management, the Interior Department agency that administers more land than any other entity in the country. The former New Mexico representative was confirmed over Democrats’ concerns that he favors selling public lands and that his career in oil and gas presents a conflict of interest involving an industry the agency regulates.
But public lands advocates say his AI investments now worry them. Pearce owned stock in Nvidia, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other AI-focused companies, according to his most recent publicly available financial disclosure, signed in October 2025. He also is invested in Titan Development, a real estate company that has managed several land acquisitions for data centers in the Southwest. (He pledged to divest many of his AI investments, but not Titan.)
An agency spokesperson pushed back on the concerns. “Director Pearce complies with all applicable federal ethics requirements and financial disclosure obligations,” the spokesperson said in a statement, adding that “conflating lawful disclosure of financial holdings with an actual conflict of interest ignores the federal ethics framework designed to identify and address precisely these questions.”
The BLM is reviewing permit applications for about 15 data centers and 17 associated infrastructure projects, including nuclear power plants and transmission wires, in Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Wyoming and Idaho. This is according to an agency spokesperson and its Mineral & Land Records System.
The project that was to be the first data center on BLM land, near Boulder City in southern Nevada, had earned a permit to build a solar plant, before changing its plans. The BLM approved the change in June without studying the potential environmental implications. (An Interior Department appeals board has since paused the project, sending it back to the agency for further review.)
Meanwhile, it remains unclear how much the public will benefit from data centers on BLM land. The foundational federal land management law was passed in 1976, so it does not envision data centers. Even so, the department said it is relying on this statute to permit data centers.
Businesses pay the government to use public land. Oil and gas drillers pay a royalty on each barrel they produce. Solar power plants pay a per-megawatt fee.
For data centers, the main charge appears set to be an “annual fair-market-value rent,” an Interior Department spokesperson said. But such rental fees can be quite low, so the economic benefit to the public won’t be known until the data centers are permitted.
Another key official with a land management agency who’s heavily invested in AI is Michael Boren. He first served as acting assistant secretary of the Interior Department before transitioning to U.S. Department of Agriculture undersecretary, where he oversees the Forest Service, second only to the BLM in the land area it stewards.
Among his many investments in AI companies, Boren reported between about $1.5 million and $6.1 million worth of financial interests in Elon Musk’s xAI, which has since been acquired by SpaceX. Additionally, he has up to $500,000 invested in Valar Atomics, which is pushing to build a data center complex called Project Beehive on thousands of acres of BLM land in Utah, complete with more than 450 small nuclear plants to power it.
“Undersecretary Boren has fully complied with all federal ethics laws and requirements and will continue to follow the advice of USDA’s excellent ethics attorneys,” an Agriculture Department spokesperson said in a statement.
Lee Zeldin, whom Trump appointed to head the Environmental Protection Agency, has also emerged as a major AI booster. He too has dabbled in AI investments. Zeldin’s financial disclosure forms reveal that in May 2025 he bought and sold up to $15,000 worth of shares of Datavault AI, a company selling AI-, data- and blockchain-based products.
“Administrator Zeldin followed every ethical rule to a tee in his disclosure without exception,” an EPA spokesperson said in a statement. The agency added that he was cleared by its ethics officials and that he has no obligation to explain such transactions.
The EPA under Zeldin has taken steps to minimize oversight of data centers and power plants built nearby to keep them running. This includes a rule the agency proposed in July to end a requirement that states gather public feedback as they consider air permits for certain facilities, including data centers.
In October, a group of Democratic senators sent a letter to Zeldin asking the EPA to withdraw the proposed rule. “The federal government should encourage transparency and public engagement around these projects, not make it easier to shroud their construction in secrecy,” they wrote.

Intermedia + Digital Arts MFA Program at UMBC Now Accepting Applications
Funding for tuition, healthcare, and stipends is available. Apply to the University of Maryland, Baltimore County program by Feb 1 to be considered for financial support.
The Intermedia and Digital Arts (IMDA) MFA Program at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC) invites applications from interdisciplinary artists seeking to expand or reinvent their practice. IMDA is a three-year, 60-credit graduate program with private studios in Baltimore’s progressive art community. IMDA faculty are nationally and internationally recognized artists, filmmakers, designers, and scholars with active exhibition and publication records.
IMDA offers a multidisciplinary program with one on one feedback from world-renown visiting artists, independent teaching opportunities, professional exhibition venues, and dedicated fabrication, media, and physical computing labs. UMBC is a top-ranked R1 Research University with an inclusive culture that provides students with access to research centers and broad interdisciplinary opportunities. Graduate Assistantships that include full tuition remission, health insurance, stipends, and other merit based financial support are available.
IMDA supports a broad range of interdisciplinary creative practices including socially-engaged, community-based, interactive, and studio-based artworks made using cutting edge and traditional methods and technologies. Alumni present their work at distinguished venues around the world, receive prestigious grants and residency awards, and are academic leaders at internationally recognized art academies and universities.
Visiting artists include: Janine Antoni, Zoe Beloff, Lynda Berry, Paul Chan, Annica Cupetelli and Cristobal Mendoza, Paul DeMarinis, Tony Dove, Hasan Elahi, Karen Finley, Guillermo Gómez-Peña, Guerrilla Girls, Barbara Hammer, Nina Katchadourian, Alison Knowles, William Pope.L, LoVid, Matmos, Michael Rakowitz, David Rokeby, Paul Rucker, Frances Torres, Mark Tribe, Levester Williams, Stephanie J. Williams, Fred Wilson, Martha Wilson, Krzysztof Wodiczko, Karen Yasinsky, and The Yes Men.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-s.title: NYC schools’ standoff with Google over AI raises prospect of no search in class
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-s.author: Jessica Gould
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-s.text:
Google is locked in a standoff with the nation’s largest public school system as the debate over AI’s place in the classroom pits parent groups against the tech behemoth.
Earlier this week, Google said schools that ban artificial intelligence will lose access to Google search, prompting cries of blackmail and a swift rebuke from Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” Mamdani wrote on X. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.”
In September, Mamdani announced a one-year ban on most AI programs in city schools and tighter limits on screens, especially for the youngest students. The moratorium was a major win for city parents who oppose the use of artificial intelligence in public school classrooms.
But Google’s threat to pull the plug on search in classrooms underscored how deeply the technology’s products are woven into the fabric of education.
This is a perfect time for us to figure out how we wean ourselves off of Google so that we don't have companies able to blackmail us in order to create a captive audience of students
Google products are ubiquitous in schools. Since the pandemic, many students have been issued individual Chromebooks for schoolwork and remote learning. City officials said the school system has 1.3 million Chromebooks, with about 500,000 assigned to students, and another 800,000 in schools. Teachers post assignments to Google Classroom, and students, like many adults, rely heavily on Google Docs and search.
“It would be incredibly difficult for us to disentangle our school system entirely from Google, and that's what they're betting on,” said Kelly Clancy, part of the coalition calling for a total ban on AI in the city’s public schools. She said all three of her children are required to use Google Classroom for remote learning and homework.
“But I think what they're not counting on is the fact that parents across the country have mobilized against this,” Clancy said. “And this is a perfect time for us to figure out how we wean ourselves off of Google so that we don't have companies able to blackmail us in order to create a captive audience of students.”
Google has insisted it’s impossible to separate the company’s search function from AI.
Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that “search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” so turning off AI will also mean turning off the search engine. The company said the new policy would go into effect early next year. It did not respond to Gothamist’s requests for comment.
But over the past year, an influential movement of parents, educators and lawmakers have sought to beat back the creep of artificial intelligence in schools. They argue AI summaries and bots enable cheating, short-circuit learning and seduce children into inappropriate and even dangerous relationships. This week, parents of a North Carolina 13-year-old sued Google alleging she made plans to end her life after interacting with its AI Mode.
Education officials said they were still trying to figure out how Google’s new policy would affect search in schools.
Officials are “reaching out to Google to discuss this update further,” public schools spokesperson Nicole Brownstein said.
She said the city has disabled the Gemini chatbot and AI mode on Google Chromebooks issued to students, and they’ve made requests to Google to disable the AI Overview that continues to appear in search results.
“We will keep students and school communities updated as we continue to place student safety and wellbeing above all other interests,” she said.
Following the Times report, Google posted additional information about its plans on X.
It said the announcements give schools "more choice, not less" and that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will be off by default, and schools will be in charge of which service, if any, is turned on.
The company emphasized the changes were made in response to feedback from K-12 schools. Google said it’s also changing how AI will function within search “to make it better for learning.” The company said both AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guidance through problems” rather than just “quick answers to schoolwork.”
Assemblymember Alex Bores noted that Google has made “deep investments” into its educational offerings over the years, aggressively and successfully marketing its suite of products to schools.
“This is a product choice that Google is making, and it's a profit maximizing one,” said Bores, who worked at Palantir and recently co-founded Who Decides, an advocacy group for AI safety and regulation.
“Competitors like Duck Duck Go let people opt in or opt out of AI search. And Google could do the same. They could also do the same only when it comes to children if they wanted. But they're making an intentional choice not to, and I think that's a disappointing one,” he said.
Anti-AI parents and educators said Google’s threat should encourage the city to cut ties with the company, and invest in other search engines instead. Naveed Hasan, a member of the Panel for Educational Policy, which votes on education contracts, said the city should consider writing limits into contracts to prevent tech companies from unilaterally changing the software the school system has already purchased without permission.
“We should revisit how we look at technology contracts when companies change their features mid contract,” he said.
Zephyr Teachout, professor at Fordham Law School, said the company’s move may also face legal challenges. “What Google is doing is illegal under antitrust law and I expect there will be investigations from the Attorney General’s office and other places soon,” she said. “It’s simply not credible to me that Google cannot provide search without AI overviews.”
Clancy saw an opening for the school system to rethink how it teaches students to do their work.
“This is an exciting opportunity for us to figure out [how] to teach kids the fundamentals of research,” she said.
Maybe instead of spending so much on Google, Clancy added, the city could invest in school libraries and books.

https://hellgatenyc.com/carl-heastie-spo.title: NY Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie Goes to a Celtics Game…
https://hellgatenyc.com/carl-heastie-spo.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/carl-heastie-spo.text:
Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie, one of the most powerful people in New York, is a man of sundry interests. He loves cars, he loves bail reform, he loves his dog, he LOVES Prince. And he really loves sports. Specifically, the strange combination of the Dallas Cowboys, the Boston Celtics, and the New York Yankees. 
As New York Focus reported this week, you can find evidence of Heastie's sports mania in the campaign finance filings of the Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee, which, since Heastie became speaker, has spent upwards of $1 million on sports-related expenses including luxury box tickets, meet-and-greets, and lavish concessions. And Heastie's social media is full of honestly envy-inducing sports experiences. 
The DACC is supposed to be a fundraising mechanism for Assembly Democrats, and Heastie has claimed that the sporting events were fundraisers. "That story is beyond pointless," Heastie's spokesperson Mike Whyland wrote in an email to Hell Gate. "Those sporting events raised more than $10 million and after Tuesday it looks like it was money well spent." Heastie responded to the New York Focus story on Instagram, writing in part, "For years this newspaper has been trying to insinuate illegal and unethical things…It’s called fundraising stupid." But it's not always clear how the luxury tickets benefited any New York assemblymembers' campaigns—especially when some took place at Boston's TD Garden. In its filings, the committee characterized much of its sports spending as "office expenses."

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-republ.title: Trump Hurt Average Americans, So They Voted Against the GOP
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-republ.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trump-republ.text:
Trump Hurt Average Americans, So They Voted Against the GOP
Populism isn’t just a switch the GOP could have chosen to flip on in this election but didn’t. Its governing record under Donald Trump has been one of harm and contempt for working people. Voters knew that and punished Republicans for it.
You didn’t even have to look at the numbers on Wednesday to know the election was a rout. You could have just guessed it by the fact that Donald Trump didn’t deny the results, call the whole thing “rigged,” or vow to fight the cheaters to the bitter end. Instead he meekly congratulated the Democrats, insisted none of it was his fault, and offered to work with his opposition before getting back to the truly important work of his ballroom.
In a two-week period that saw right-wing leaders across the world refuse to concede and try to find ways to deny election results, Trump, the man who first gave them the playbook to do it, was the only one to accept his defeat. It’s a measure not of any change in the president but of how emphatically he was rejected by the country.
By now, everyone knows this past Tuesday was a generational calamity for Republicans, and the party is of course now yelling over each other to explain what went so badly wrong.
“We forgot that we’re a populist party,” one GOP operative told Politico about the party’s lack of an affordability message.
“President Trump’s message won. Unfortunately he wasn’t the messenger,” Trump’s former campaign deputy communications director told Fox News, complaining that his team had “allowed his winning message in 2024 to be co-opted by his opposition.”
The issue was just that the GOP “forgot how to win,” wrote outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn, blaming the poor “character and integrity” of its candidates and urging the party to be more “likeable.”
For Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, now eagerly positioning himself as captain of this shipwreck, the problem was that Republicans were too obsessed with fighting “wokeness,” which was “yesterday’s battle.”
It’s not surprising that a party that would allow itself to get destroyed so thoroughly would in the aftermath still be completely oblivious about why they lost. Technically, yes, it was many of these things: the lack of populism, the bad candidates, the ignoring of affordability, the obsession with wokeness.
But that’s really underselling it. The reason the Republicans have been decimated is that the party did everything they could possibly do to make almost everyone in the country’s lives dramatically worse for the past twenty-two months: it pushed four hundred thousand people out of their jobs, it is throwing millions of people off of their health care, it wrenched Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits — also known as food stamps — from 5.5 million people, and raised their insurance premiums by 26 percent, with another 13 percent to come next year.
This was part of the party’s genius idea of slashing federal support for health care more than anyone had ever done in US history, to the tune of $1 trillion. This is all before you factor in the average of $471 per person in fuel costs alone added to US households’ expenses by the Iran war and the $1,745 more per family they’ve had to pay because of Trump’s blanket tariffs.
Mind you, all this was as Trump and the GOP shoveled a trillion dollars in tax cuts — the same amount they had cut from most people’s health care — to the top 1 percent, in a cut that gave 70 percent of its benefits to the wealthiest fifth of Americans. At the same time, it presided over record-high wage theft by employers and actively decided to let hundreds of corporate crooks who gave money to Trump off the hook for a variety of alleged wrongdoing, including price-fixing, workplace discrimination, and forced labor — all while the president and his family lined their own pockets in a way that’s never been seen before in US (or really, human) history, with the president alone growing his net worth by $3 billion through crypto scams that tricked his own voters into buying and being stuck with worthless Trump-themed digital currency.
We’re not even getting into the way Trump’s deportation crusade has caused terror, havoc, and death even among US citizens while directly hurting the farming communities that had lent him their support.
You will note the problem here is not that Trump and the Republicans were not talking about affordability. Trump could have spent the final weeks of the campaign actually talking about the high cost of living instead of droning on about his reflecting pool and men’s asses, and the reality is people’s lives still would have been significantly, materially worse off because of the policies they sunk untold months, energy, and political capital into to pursue — the same decidedly anti-populist policies Republicans have pushed for decades.
Those policies are not the ones desired by ordinary Trump voters, who — if you look at polling and the election results for ballot measures and candidates — want things like a higher minimum wage, a clampdown on price gouging, affordable childcare, and more generous employer benefits. Instead they got the bog-standard neoliberal agenda that the GOP’s donors and corporate sponsors promote, lobby for, and force onto the legislative agenda, because it benefits their bottom lines.
It’s not that Republicans suddenly forgot to be populist going into the election. It’s that they had nothing to be populist about.
The problem for the GOP here is the same one that the similarly corporate-backed Democratic Party has been wrestling with for decades: the interests of its working-class voters are fundamentally at odds with the interests of the people who fund its campaigns, who bankroll the think tanks they rely on for their policy ideas, and who are often the 1 percenters who make up its roster of elected officials.
The Democratic Party is, thanks to the left insurgency in its ranks, currently in the middle of a battle to try and resolve that contradiction. The GOP appears completely oblivious that that contradiction even exists — and as a result, has no real idea why voters just gave it a historic rebuke.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New museum dedicated to Italian Modernist Mario Sironi must not become ‘endorsement of fascism’, art historians warn
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James Imam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Plans by Giorgia Meloni’s government to open a new museum in Rome dedicated to Mario Sironi, the Modernist painter who was a supporter of Benito Mussolini, risk sanitising Italy's fascist past, two leading historians have warned.
The state-run museum is expected to open next year within the Associazione Nazionale fra Mutilati ed Invalidi di Guerra (National Association of War Disabled and Wounded Veterans), a monumental fascist era building inaugurated in 1928. The building is home to two major frescoes by Sironi painted ten years later. One depicts Mussolini on horseback.
The museum will display 30 works recently acquired by Italy's culture ministry from the Mario Sironi Archive in Rome, including paintings, drawings and preparatory sketches. A further 90 works will be loaned by the archive.
Unveiling the plans on Tuesday, Alessandro Giuli, the culture minister, said the project was “the defining achievement of my term in office, and the one of which I am most proud”.
Meloni's Brothers of Italy has political roots in the postwar Italian neo-fascist movement. Press materials for the museum do not mention fascism or Mussolini.
Sironi joined the fascist movement in 1919, contributing more than 1,700 political cartoons and illustrations to Il Popolo d’Italia, Mussolini’s newspaper. The museum will feature works spanning more than four decades from the 1910s to the 1950s, covering distinct phases from Sironi's artistic development including Futurism, metaphysical-influenced works and monumental commissions awarded under the fascist regime.
Members of Italy’s cultural sector have emphasised the need for the institution to address Seroni’s politics.
Tomaso Montanari, an art historian and rector of the Università per Stranieri di Siena (University for Foreigners of Siena), said that he did not oppose the museum but insisted it must explicitly distance itself from fascism.
“Since Italy is a republic founded on anti-fascism, the museum's educational material must make clear that there is no endorsement of fascism," Montanari told The Art Newspaper.
Montanari, who sits on the culture ministry's scientific committee, said that the initial project for the museum focussed “overwhelmingly” on Sironi's fascist period work. He added that the ministry "partially" heeded his argument for works from other periods to be included.
The art historian and curator Fabio Benzi, who is on the Sironi museum's scientific committee, told the French-language publication Le Journal Des Arts: "The danger is of legitimising a certain authoritarian aesthetic under the guise of cultural rediscovery".
The culture ministry has been contacted for comment.
Last year, the ministry announced it had acquired the former Rome home of Giacomo Balla, the futurist painter who initially supported fascism, which operates as a museum.
On Thursday [5 November], key members of Meloni's government presented a new exhibition celebrating the 90th anniversary of the EUR district in Rome, the city's grandest example of fascist-era planning.

https://apache.be/vaarwel-big-tech.title: Overheden, onderwijs en ziekenhuizen houden bezoekers in greep van big tech
https://apache.be/vaarwel-big-tech.author: Jan Walraven
https://apache.be/vaarwel-big-tech.text:
Apache wil af van Amerikaanse en andere big tech en kiest maximaal voor meer ethische, Europese en opensource-alternatieven. In deze blog houden we je ongeveer tweewekelijks op de hoogte van onze odyssee weg van big tech. De berichten verschijnen hieronder, met het meest recente bovenaan.
Overheden, onderwijs en ziekenhuizen houden bezoekers in greep van big tech
door Jan Walraven
Bij welke leveranciers ‘kopen’ Belgische gemeenten, ziekenhuizen, scholen, universiteiten, … hun digitale diensten? Het antwoord op die vraag wordt best gegeven met een Amerikaans accent, blijkt uit een analyse van vzw BeLibre. Verschillende gemeenten, scholen en ziekenhuizen zetten bovendien trackingtechnologie in van onder meer Google om het gedrag van bezoekers in kaart te brengen.
Eerder dit jaar bekeek ook Apache de digitale (on)afhankelijkheid van federale, Vlaamse en lokale overheden. Vooral Amerikaanse bedrijven zoals Microsoft zorgen ervoor dat die overheden kunnen mailen en dat overheidswebsites online blijven. Een gelijkaardige, maar steeds uitgebreidere oefening maakt BeLibre via een geautomatiseerde scan.
BeLibre controleert niet enkel op welke techbedrijven overheden en (semi-)publieke instellingen rekenen voor hun mail en hun website. Via een tool voor ‘lekdetectie’ bekijkt de vzw ook of er gebruikersdata naar externe partijen worden doorgestuurd wanneer je de website van een ziekenhuis of school bezoekt. De tool van BeLibre-bezieler Jurgen Gaeremyn bootst een kort websitebezoek na zonder ergens op te klikken, dus ook niet op ‘cookies aanvaarden’.
Onder meer de trackingtechnologie van Google blijkt populair. De techreus biedt de standaardversie van Google Analytics dan ook gratis aan. Dit betekent, zo stelt BeLibre het, dat de “analysegeschiedenis en de beslissingen die erop gebouwd zijn” verzameld worden “binnen een door de VS gecontroleerd platform”, wat voor “een groeiende afhankelijkheid onder buitenlandse rechtsmacht” zorgt. In sommige gevallen is Google Analytics zo ingesteld dat de techreus de verzamelde gebruikersgegevens kan inzetten om bijvoorbeeld advertenties op andere sites beter af te stemmen op het surfgedrag van bezoekers.
Sommige (overheids)organisaties laden ook een cookie van Google Ads direct op de eigen website. Hierdoor worden gegevens over een websitebezoek expliciet gekoppeld aan het advertentieprofiel dat Google opstelt van de bezoeker.
“Door deze tools te gebruiken, maken deze organisaties zich voor hun bezoekersanalyse niet alleen afhankelijk van Amerikaanse bedrijven, waarover ze weinig of geen inspraak hebben, maar bovendien drijven ze zo mee handel in bezoekersgegevens”, zegt Gaeremyn.
Ook de Meta Pixel van de techreus achter Facebook en Instagram duikt verschillende keren op. Via dit stukje code kan ook het bedrijf van Mark Zuckerberg bezoekers volgen op verschillende websites om zo een profiel van hen op te bouwen.
Willen (en weten) burgers dat hun bezoek aan de website van een ziekenhuis via Google en Meta gevolgd en gemeten wordt? Dat Facebook weet dat ze informatie over pakweg een fertiliteitsbehandeling hebben geraadpleegd? Wat alleszins opvalt op verschillende websites, is dat een bezoeker die gegevens deelt zonder dat daarvoor toestemming werd gegeven.
“Ik ben ervan overtuigd dat de meeste overheden en diensten wel van goede wil zijn, maar vaak niet stilstonden bij de consequenties van keuzes die tien of vijftien jaar geleden gemaakt werden en intussen vaak vergeten zijn”, zegt Gaeremyn. “Daarom is het nuttig dat we diensten en overheden attent maken op deze consequenties en de bijhorende risico’s.”
De gegevensuitwisseling tussen de EU en de VS wordt in principe wel wettelijk geregeld door het EU-US Data Privacy Framework. Met dit akkoord belooft de Verenigde Staten in essentie dat gegevens van Europese burgers en bedrijven volgens (strenge) Europese regels behandeld zullen worden. Zonder dit raamwerk zouden Europese overheden en bedrijven in principe geen Amerikaanse technologieproviders meer kunnen gebruiken.
Dat raamwerk staat zeker sinds het aantreden van president Donald Trump steeds meer onder druk. Critici wijzen er wel al veel langer op dat de Amerikaanse garanties niet gebaseerd zijn op eenduidige Amerikaanse privacywetgeving, maar wel op een poreus lappendeken van richtlijnen en regels, waaronder ook presidentiële decreten van Trumps voorganger Joe Biden. En ook dat het toezicht op die diffuse regels actief wordt uitgehold door de regering-Trump.
Bovendien baart andere wetgeving ook kopzorgen. Onder meer de Amerikaanse Cloud Act en een clausule uit de Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act maken het voor Amerikaanse autoriteiten en inlichtingendiensten mogelijk om Amerikaanse bedrijven te dwingen om gegevens vrij te geven. Ook als die gegevens op dataservers in de Europese Unie zijn opgeslagen door het Europese dochterbedrijf van pakweg Microsoft.
“Als het bedrijf in kwestie onder controle van een Amerikaanse entiteit staat, gelden die Amerikaanse wetten”, zei Hans Graux, voorzitter van de Vlaamse Toezichtcommissie, eerder aan Apache. Het gebruik van de diensten van buitenlandse techbedrijven houdt dus wel degelijk risico’s in.
Trump maakte de wereldwijde dominantie op vlak van technologie tot een kwestie van nationale veiligheid. In het Witte Huis vinden bigtechbedrijven dan ook een uitgesproken bondgenoot voor deregulering. Ook de Europese regels rond onder meer online privacy zijn daarbij een legitiem doelwit.
De lobbymachine van Amerikaanse bigtechbedrijven draait op volle toeren, blijkt uit onderzoek van ngo Corporate Europe Observatory. Techbedrijven willen met name persoonlijke data gebruiken “in de context van AI”, zonder dat ze daar nog toestemming voor moeten krijgen van gebruikers. Een recent voorstel van de Europese lidstaten zit volledig op die lijn. De pogingen om de strenge Europese regels uit te hollen, lijken te slagen.
De afhankelijkheid van met name Amerikaanse bigtechbedrijven blijkt groot in de (semi-)publieke sector, maar dat hoeft niet zo te blijven. Zeker in de ons omringende landen wordt volop gezocht naar alternatieven. Deze week nog kondigden vijf Duitse deelstaten aan dat ze voor het onderwijs af willen van de diensten van Google en Microsoft. Ze starten met de ontwikkeling van een platform op basis van Nextcloud. Ook Apache stapte recent over op die opensourcetoepassing.
“We moeten ook accepteren dat migreren niet van vandaag op morgen gaat”, zegt Gaeremyn. “Ik denk dat het verhaal van Apache zélf daar getuige van is. Met BeLibre willen we dan ook de hand reiken naar organisaties en overheden om op zoek te gaan naar wat gemigreerd kan worden op korte en op lange termijn.”
Mediahuis gebruikt én kopieert big tech
door Jan Walraven
Bij de meeste Belgen doet de naam Hyves wellicht geen belletje rinkelen. In Nederland ging de nostalgiemeter wél in het rood bij de aankondiging dat het sociaal netwerk een tweede leven krijgt. De Telegraaf had de primeur: met Hyves gaat moederbedrijf Mediahuis de concurrentie aan met de Facebooks en Tiktoks van deze wereld. Hyves was in Nederland begin jaren 2000 nog de populairste socialenetwerksite, maar gaf dertien jaar geleden de strijd tegen de Amerikaanse concurrenten op. Drie jaar eerder, in 2010, had Telegraaf Media Groep (TMG) nog 43,7 miljoen euro veil voor het platform. TMG werd inmiddels opgeslorpt door Mediahuis, de Belgische uitgever van onder ander Het Nieuwsblad en De Standaard.
Mediahuis ontkent dat de reanimatie door nostalgie werd ingegeven, maar probeert het te verkopen als ethisch alternatief voor big tech. De uitgever plaatst Hyves’ herrijzenis nadrukkelijk binnen twee trends. Enerzijds speelt het in op toenemende kritiek op de schadelijke effecten van de verslavende algoritmes van grote platformen, anderzijds surft het mee op de golven van de beweging die pleit voor meer Europese digitale autonomie.
“Hyves wil het anders doen”, klinkt het. Maar wie de gebruiksvoorwaarden en privacyverklaring leest, ziet meteen dat je dit best met een korrel zout neemt. Hyves wordt een zoveelste advertentieplatform voor Mediahuis, zoals elke ‘mediamerk’ dat eigenlijk is. De gegevens die Mediahuis over gebruikers van Hyves binnenhaalt, kunnen gebruikt worden om ook de advertenties op andere sites van Mediahuis op maat van gebruikers te snijden.
Of het nu van Mediahuis of DPG Media is: op basis van de gegevens die de uitgevers verzamelen, krijgen gebruikers ‘gepersonaliseerde’ reclame te zien: surveillance capitalism in de Lage Landen. Op kleinere schaal, maar in essentie blijft het hetzelfde verdienmodel als dat van Facebook, Instagram, … (Moederbedrijf Meta lanceerde tot grote tevredenheid van de beurs een ‘persoonlijke’ AI-agent voor zijn gebruikers en daarmee wil Meta uiteraard ook gebruikersgegevens opslurpen en gebruiken.)
Het Nederlandse platform voor onderzoeksjournalistiek Follow the Money ontdekte bovendien dat gebruikersgegevens van Hyves gewoon verwerkt worden via Amerikaanse software. Ondanks de belofte van “een overwegend Europese technische architectuur”.
Een commercieel mediabedrijf dat gebruikers wil insluiten op een commercieel sociaal medium. Denken we echt dat dit een oplossing is? Een stukje macht van vooral Amerikaanse big tech afknijpen en overdragen aan commerciële bedrijven van ‘eigen bodem’? Nochtans toont een andere krant van Mediahuis dat het ook anders kan. Lezers van NRC konden de voorbije weken de queeste van techjournalist Marloes de Koning volgen om de krant aan het open sociale web toe te voegen. Het leidde tot een plan om een NRC-server te openen op Mastodon, waarop “mensen van binnen en buiten NRC met elkaar in gesprek kunnen gaan, onder onze eigen voorwaarden en op onze infrastructuur”.
Mastodon is onderdeel van het fediverse, een verzameling van alternatieve sociale netwerken die onderling verbonden zijn. Zoals bij e-mail maakt het niet uit of je nu een account hebt bij NRC of bij een andere dienstverlener: je kan met anderen in gesprek gaan. (En van dienstverlener wisselen als je ontevreden bent.) Om dit mogelijk te maken, rekent dat fediverse op het ActivityPub-protocol; een set van regels over hoe systemen met elkaar moeten communiceren.
Een community voor Apache
Ook Apache wil met dat protocol en dus sociale netwerken experimenteren. (Wees gerust, we gaan je gegevens niet gebruiken om reclames te tonen. We blijven reclamevrij.) Als nieuwscoöperatie zoeken we steeds naar manieren om onze coöperanten, betalende leden en potentiële lezers beter of anders te betrekken. Nu blijft de interactie rond onze onderzoeken en analyses beperkt tot de commentaarsectie, of praten we enkel echt met onze coöperanten tijdens de algemene vergadering. Dat zou wel wat meer kunnen zijn.
De komende weken zetten we daarom een test op met Bonfire, nieuwe opensourcesoftware gericht op het smeden van meer online betrokkenheid. De eerste tests voeren we intern uit. Als die goed zijn, schakelen we mogelijk ook jou en andere geïnteresseerde lezers in. We laten ons daarvoor inspireren door wat het magazine Jacobin in Duitsland doet met Bonfire: een sociaal netwerk bouwen met en voor lezers. “We wilden een platform dat niet uitgezet kon worden door een buitenlandse regering of opgekocht door een miljardair”, verklaarde Magdalena Berger van Jacobin DE de “politieke keuze” om een eigen online ontmoetingsplek te bouwen.
Bovendien maakt Bonfire gebruik van hetzelfde protocol als Mastodon. Zo wordt het in theorie mogelijk om ook met bijvoorbeeld gebruikers van de eerder vermelde NRC-server in gesprek te gaan. En Jacobin kan volledig zelf bepalen in welke mate het die verbinding maakt, met het fediverse of met andere alternatieve sociale media, zoals Bluesky. Alsof je met een account op YouTube het Instagram-account van iemand anders kunt volgen. Het klinkt voorlopig allemaal nog wat technisch, daarom willen we eerst zelf de mogelijkheden testen.
Onze reis weg van big tech begon met onze online werkomgeving (het lukt ook zonder Google!) maar we kijken verder dan dat. Wordt vervolgd …
Apache migreert succesvol naar Nextcloud
door Jan Walraven
Op de redactie van Apache heerste woensdag (16/9) de sfeer en nervositeit van een eerste schooldag. De ene keek er al meer naar uit dan de andere, maar rond 10u verzamelden we uiteindelijk met opengeklapte laptops allemaal rond een (iets te kleine) tafel. Klaar om aandachtig te luisteren naar docent-voor-een-dag Stijn van vzw Tactic. Wat ons daar samenbracht? Eerder dit jaar kondigden we ons afscheid van big tech aan. Een van de dikste banden zouden we nu doorknippen, door Google Workspace in te ruilen voor Nextcloud.
De voorbije weken probeerden we dit moment zo goed mogelijk voor te bereiden. Bestaande Google Drives werden van ballast ontdaan, bestanden werden in mapjes ondergebracht, en in onze mailboxen gingen we genadeloos op zoek naar digitaal bestofte persberichten van tien jaar oud die we nooit meer zouden herlezen. Delete, delete, delete. Helemaal klaar voor De Grote Oversteek.
Nextcloud is een Europese opensource-toepassing voor zogenoemde kantoorsoftware. Om dit softwarepakket te kunnen gebruiken, moet je geen klant worden bij het gelijknamige Duitse bedrijf. Dit in tegenstelling tot Google Workspace, waarvoor je enkel bij Google zelf terechtkan. Verschillende bedrijven en organisaties bieden een Nextcloud-omgeving aan, maar je kan het ook zelf installeren – mits voldoende technische kennis en apparatuur. Apache klopte hiervoor aan bij Tactic. Deze Brusselse vzw installeert al sinds 2002 “vrije, duurzame en ethische tools” voor verenigingen en collectieven en begeleidt hen ook om zelfstandig te leren omgaan met deze tools.
Een Nextcloud-omgeving kan je bovendien naar eigen smaak inrichten. Zoals je een App Store hebt voor je smartphone, kan je zelf extra toepassingen installeren. Nextcloud zelf (het bedrijf) biedt verschillende modules aan, zoals Talk, waarmee je kan chatten en videobellen. Maar omdat de technologie opensource is, kunnen andere ontwikkelaars ook zelf apps maken die elke gebruiker aan zijn Nextcloud-omgeving kan toevoegen. Van een klassieke agenda of alternatief voor Doodle, tot een module om röntgenfoto’s en andere medische beelden te analyseren. De mogelijkheden lijken eindeloos.
Maar wat gaat Apache dan zoal doen met Nextcloud? Geen röntgenfoto’s analyseren. Zoals de naam doet vermoeden gebruiken we het ten eerste als ‘cloud’ om allerhande bestanden, foto’s, … online in op te slaan. In Nextcloud Office kunnen we samen aan tekstbestanden of spreadsheets sleutelen, ook met freelancers. Talk wordt onze voornaamste tool voor interne communicatie: om te chatten over artikels (of om stoom af te laten met flauwe moppen), om te videobellen, om bestanden te delen, … Verder zijn er nog de kalenderfunctie en een tool om ‘doodles’ en andere peilingen te maken. Gaandeweg komen daar mogelijk nog apps bij, maar dat zal de toekomst uitwijzen.
Ook om e-mails te kunnen versturen en ontvangen rekenen we niet langer op Google. Tactic zette voor ons een e-mailserver op. Een mailarchief overzetten dat voor sommige journalisten tot zestien jaar teruggaat, gaat niettemin met horten en stoten. Maar ook de slak bereikt de ark! Vanaf nu beheert een Belgische vzw onze mailcommunicatie via een server op Belgisch grondgebied, dus over de jurisdictie bestaat alvast geen discussie meer. Met andere woorden: we zijn voor onze online communicatie niet langer gebonden aan een Amerikaans bedrijf dat aan de wensen en grillen van de Amerikaanse overheid moet voldoen.
Apache bereidt zich voor op de overstap van Google naar Nextcloud
door Kasper Nollet
“Het hele op data-extractie gebaseerde model van big tech culmineert finaal in het product dat AI is.” Dat zei onze redacteur Jan Walraven onlangs in de podcast van Annacon, de vzw die zich inzet voor goede informatiebeveiliging en genderevenwicht in de cybersecuritysector.
Terwijl de redactie van Apache volop bezig is met de voorbereiding voor de overstap van Google Workspace naar Nextcloud, mocht Jan in de podcast Tijdstof komen vertellen over onze plannen en over de moeilijke beslissingen en vraagstukken die daarbij komen kijken.
Betekent weg van Amerikaanse tech dat we onmiddellijk Europese alternatieven moeten omarmen? Is open source altijd de juiste keuze? Hoe zit het met onze eigen informatiebeveiliging? En hoe zorgen we dat we mensen meekrijgen naar de alternatieve platforms waarop we ons aanbod (willen) uitrollen?
Over een paar weken doet Apache dus de definitieve overstap van Google Workspace naar Nextcloud. Daarvoor moeten alle gegevens die nog op onze Google Drive staan, overgezet worden. Voor de redacteurs blijkt het de ideale gelegenheid om hun persoonlijke mappenstructuur en ongebruikte bestanden onder de loep te nemen.
Jan spreekt in Tijdstof verder nog over zijn eigen journalistieke parcours, over waarom we AI niet als product maar als winstmodel moeten zien en over waarom je niet beter zelf de stuurprogramma’s van je MacBook installeert.
