https://jacobin.com/2026/11/oil-currency.title: The Dollar’s Power Never Came From Oil
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/oil-currency.author: Matías Vernengo
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/oil-currency.text:
The Dollar’s Power Never Came From Oil
The emergence of the dollar as the world’s currency was the result of the rise of the US as the preeminent global power. But the slow erosion of US economic and political power will not automatically spell the end of the dollar system.
The war in Iran and the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have renewed an old debate about the foundations of American global power. Oil has been central to the geopolitical order dominated by the United States since World War II. The dollar is the principal international currency, oil is overwhelmingly priced in dollars, and American military power has been essential to controlling access to petroleum, particularly in the Middle East. The question raised by some analysts is whether the erosion of this arrangement, accelerated by the transition to cleaner sources of energy, signals the end of American hegemony and of the privileged position of the dollar.
There are good reasons to take this possibility seriously. China has become the leading producer of solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles, and many of the technologies essential to the transition away from fossil fuels. The transition to new energy technologies could therefore profoundly reshape the distribution of global economic power at a time when American military superiority is being questioned.
But there is a problem with moving directly from the decline of petroleum to the decline of the dollar. International monetary hegemony does not depend primarily on which commodities are traded, and only secondarily on which country possesses technological superiority in the industries of the future. It rests on a broader structure of fiscal, financial, productive, and military power that has historically developed over centuries. Understanding that distinction requires looking beyond oil to the historical relationship between money and empire.
The Hydrocarbon Dollar Thesis
An influential interpretation of international economic power emphasizes the relationship between energy technologies and geopolitical hegemony. Britain’s rise coincided with the coal-powered Industrial Revolution, while American dominance was associated with the age of petroleum, particularly as oil became essential to modern warfare and transportation. In this interpretation, China’s predominance in renewable energy technologies raises the possibility of another hegemonic transition. Daniel Bessner has suggested that China’s predominance in renewable energy technologies may herald that transition.
Helen Thompson, in her book Disorder: Hard Times in the 21st Century, provides a sophisticated historical version of this argument. She shows how successive energy regimes shaped imperial rivalry, international finance, and the geopolitical conflicts of the twentieth century. For her, oil altered the material foundations of military and geopolitical power, creating a structural disadvantage for Britain and an advantage for the United States. Britain had become the leading industrial and naval power during the age of coal, a resource it possessed in abundance. The transition to oil, initially for naval propulsion and subsequently for motorized transportation and aviation, changed the strategic equation.
In 1911, Winston Churchill, as First Lord of the Admiralty, decided that oil should replace coal in the Royal Navy. Oil-powered ships offered military advantages, but the change created a serious strategic vulnerability. The energy transition forced Britain to import a resource it previously did not need. In addition, the United States possessed an enormous advantage in oil production. Its rapidly expanding oil industry gave it the capacity to supply both its own economy and the Allied war effort. Thompson notes that approximately 80 percent of the oil used by the Allies in World War I came from the United States.
During the interwar period, British governments tried to establish secure supplies through their Middle Eastern concessions. Nevertheless, their reliance on western hemisphere oil persisted. During World War II, Britain again needed oil supplied by American companies, paid for in dollars. Thompson’s point is not simply that oil was a superior energy technology. It is that the geographical distribution of petroleum reserves fundamentally altered the capacity of competing states to sustain modern warfare. More importantly, Thompson’s contrast between Britain’s ascent during the age of coal and America’s ascent during the age of oil suggests that, in the next renewable energy age, based on minerals, batteries, and electrification, China might become the key player.
There is much to this argument. Countries that depend heavily on imported oil are vulnerable to changes in international oil prices and the availability of foreign exchange. The expansion of renewable energy can reduce these vulnerabilities. It may also weaken the strategic importance of oil-producing regions and the influence of countries that dominate them. But reducing the external dependence associated with energy imports is not the same thing as escaping the international monetary hierarchy.
The ascent of the United States implied that the infrastructure of international trade and finance was organized around the dollar — most clearly after the Bretton Woods Agreement in 1944. Many internationally traded commodities, including oil, were priced in dollars. By the 1970s, after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system and the two oil shocks, oil-exporting countries earned large dollar surpluses and recycled their revenues through American banks and Treasury bonds. The petrodollar system thus helped sustain the international demand for the dollar. A conventional fear is that international investors might lose confidence in the dollar and shift their holdings into other assets. If the international demand for dollars is partly sustained by the hydrocarbon economy, then a transition to renewables could reduce that demand and thereby weaken dollar hegemony. In that sense, petrodollars might become eventually battery-renminbis.
However, pricing oil in another currency would not necessarily undermine the international role of the dollar. Foreign exchange markets make it possible to acquire currencies for particular transactions without fundamentally changing the denomination of international debts, the composition of reserves, or the structure of international credit. The critical question is therefore not simply what currency is used to purchase oil, even if that matters. It is why the rest of the world continues to need dollars, and why the United States does not face a comparable need for foreign currencies.
Money and the Fiscal-Military State
Another explanation, developed recently by Ho-fung Hung in Greenback Empire, places geopolitical and military power at the center of international monetary relations. The postwar international monetary order was intrinsically connected to the overwhelming predominance of the United States following World War II. First its wartime allies, and subsequently even its former enemies, Germany and Japan, became dependent on American military protection.The United States also exercised considerable control over access to strategic commodities, particularly petroleum, and maintained close security relationships with major oil-producing countries, even as they sought greater autonomy through the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC). Even geopolitical adversaries remained, to varying degrees, dependent on the dollar-centered international financial system. The widespread use of dollars and accumulation of American financial assets cannot be separated from these political and strategic relationships. The resulting system is self-reinforcing. American military superiority supports the international role of the dollar, while dollar hegemony allows the United States to sustain military expenditure and international commitments on a scale that would be considerably more difficult for other countries.
Nevertheless, a fuller explanation requires placing these relationships in a longer historical perspective. The fiscal-military state was central to the development of modern capitalism and the rise of successive hegemonic powers. Public debt, central banking, and military expenditure did not merely support economic development after the fact. They were essential institutions in the creation of modern capitalist economies.
The Bank of England, founded in 1694, was established principally to finance the British state during its wars against France. Public debt became the foundation of an expanding financial market. The central bank helped transform government obligations into liquid financial assets, supporting both private finance and state expenditure. The development of the British fiscal-military state, to use John Brewer’s apt concept, allowed the government to finance its navy, sustain prolonged wars, protect commercial routes, and promote the international expansion of British capitalism. This process helped establish the foundations of sterling’s international predominance. It was not simply that British industrial and naval power made sterling an international currency. The institutions associated with public finance and monetary development helped create that industrial and naval power in the first place.
The same relationship would later emerge in the United States. Government expenditure, public credit, and the creation of financial institutions supported national economic integration and industrial development. Alexander Hamilton understood the significance of public debt and banking institutions for the construction of a national economy. The federal fiscal and monetary apparatus developed further during the Civil War, while the creation of the Federal Reserve in 1913 helped establish the financial infrastructure required for the dollar’s international expansion.
The relationship between fiscal-military and monetary power is circular. The fiscal capacity anchored in taxation, public debt, and central banking makes possible government expenditure on military procurement and research that promotes technological development and military power. These capabilities, together with geopolitical alliances and financial institutions, help sustain the international use of the hegemonic currency as the unit of account in trade and debt contracts, and as the main reserve asset. Monetary predominance then reinforces the original advantage. The hegemonic state can borrow and settle its external obligations in its own currency without having to accumulate foreign exchange as other countries do. It also acquires leverage over the external financial constraints faced by other states through its control over international liquidity and financial infrastructure. Rather than deriving simply from commodity pricing, market confidence, or network effects, monetary hegemony is thus both a product of fiscal-military power and a central means of reproducing it.
How Britain Actually Lost Monetary Hegemony
The transition from British to American hegemony provides a particularly revealing historical example of how currency competition works. It is tempting to associate Britain’s decline with the transition from coal to petroleum, just as it is tempting to interpret America’s current difficulties as a consequence of its attachment to fossil fuels. Energy certainly mattered. Coal was fundamental to British industrialization and naval power, while petroleum became increasingly important for modern transportation and warfare. But the crucial transformation in the international monetary hierarchy occurred through a different mechanism.
During the nineteenth century, Britain was the world’s principal financial center. London supplied international credit, financed trade, and exported capital on an enormous scale. Sterling became the leading currency of international transactions. As Jay Sexton shows in Debtor Diplomacy, the United States, despite its growing productive capacity, remained dependent on British finance. American railroads, infrastructure, and industrial expansion benefited from access to London’s capital markets, which British financial diplomacy helped facilitate. By the beginning of the twentieth century, however, the United States had become the world’s largest industrial economy. Its productive predominance was not yet matched by equivalent international monetary power.
World War I transformed this relationship. Britain entered the war as the leading international creditor but became increasingly dependent on American productive resources and finance. Maintaining its military commitments required massive purchases from the United States, financed through the liquidation of foreign assets and increasingly through American credit. By 1917, Britain could no longer sustain its war effort without substantial American financial assistance. The United States, which had previously depended on British finance, emerged from the war as the principal international creditor. John Maynard Keynes, who worked at the British Treasury dealing with the interallied web of debts, observed that “[i]n another year’s time we shall have forfeited the claim we had staked out in the New World and in exchange this country will be mortgaged to America.”
The transformation of monetary power followed. The creation of the Federal Reserve supported the development of dollar-denominated trade finance. As suggested in Charles Kindleberger’s classic account of the interwar period, The World in Depression, 1929–1939, the economic collapse and the geopolitical turbulence that led to two world wars were intrinsically connected to the global crisis of British hegemony and the absence of a clear hegemonic power. World War II and the establishment of the Bretton Woods system institutionalized American monetary predominance. Sterling continued to play an important international role, particularly within the sterling area, but Britain had become subordinate to the United States.
As David James Gill shows in The Long Shadow of Default, American financial assistance through Lend-Lease, the 1946 Anglo-American Loan, and Marshall Plan aid had cushioned Britain’s decline. At Suez, Washington demonstrated that it could also use its financial predominance to impose constraints. The Suez Crisis of 1956 dramatically demonstrated the limits of American support. When Britain and France, together with Israel, intervened militarily against Egypt following the nationalization of the Suez Canal, the Eisenhower administration opposed their operation. Britain faced a financial crisis as sterling came under speculative pressure and its dollar reserves declined. The United States had the capacity to provide the financial assistance Britain required, but withheld support until the British government agreed to withdraw.
The significance of Suez was not simply that Egypt could disrupt an important petroleum route, as Iran is doing now in the Strait of Hormuz. It was that Britain could no longer conduct an independent imperial military operation when the United States opposed it, because Washington could impose an external financial constraint that London could not escape. Suez did not create Britain’s monetary subordination. It made visible the hierarchy that had emerged through the two world wars. An equivalent moment for the United States would require another power capable of imposing a comparable external constraint on Washington. Disrupting international petroleum supplies is not by itself sufficient, in particular because the United States is not dependent on imports of energy commodities.
The Global Fiat Dollar Standard and the Rise of China
The history of international monetary standards reinforces the argument. The transition from Dutch to British hegemony coincided with the gradual displacement of silver by gold as the principal international monetary standard. The transition from British to American hegemony eventually produced a more radical transformation, namely, the demonetization of gold itself.
The gold standard collapsed during the interwar crisis of the 1930s, although gold remained central to the international monetary arrangements established at Bretton Woods. Under that system, foreign monetary authorities could convert dollars into gold at a fixed price. When President Richard Nixon suspended dollar convertibility in August 1971, many observers expected American monetary predominance to decline. The United States could no longer guarantee the metallic backing of its international liabilities. Yet the dollar did not lose its position as the principal international currency. On the contrary, the eventual consolidation of the global fiat flexible dollar standard eliminated the requirement that the United States settle foreign official dollar claims in gold. The international monetary system remained organized around American liabilities but without the same metallic constraint.
The aggressive reassertion of American monetary power in the early 1980s was central to the restoration of American hegemony, as Maria da Conceição Tavares argued at the time. Susan Strange similarly challenged the conventional view that American structural power was declining. The Volcker shock demonstrated the international consequences of American monetary power. The sharp increase in American interest rates helped produce the debt crisis of the developing world, forcing countries throughout Latin America and elsewhere into painful external adjustment. The aggressive reassertion of American monetary power in the early 1980s was central to the restoration of American hegemony.
This history presents a serious problem for interpretations centered on the material backing of money or the pricing of particular commodities. The disappearance of gold convertibility did not end dollar predominance. The petrodollar arrangements of the 1970s reinforced an already existing monetary hierarchy. They did not create it. Together with the expansion of offshore dollar markets and private international banking, they helped consolidate what Peter Gowan called the Dollar-Wall Street Regime. Neither the deindustrialization of the United States nor the rise of Japan, the Asian Tigers, and China necessarily implies the end of American hegemony or of the international position of the dollar. The Dollar-Wall Street Regime survives even if the United States has been challenged in the productive arena.
The distinction between productive and monetary predominance is essential for understanding the current international order. China has become a leading industrial power and an increasingly important source of advanced technology. In renewable energy, China clearly challenges the productive predominance long enjoyed by the United States. But China does not possess an equivalent position in international finance. The dollar remains the principal currency of international credit, foreign exchange trading, and official reserves. China itself continues to hold substantial dollar reserves, and much of its international lending and trade remains connected to the dollar system. The United States does not face a symmetrical dependence on the renminbi.
This asymmetry is the foundation of American monetary privilege. The United States can finance international commitments and external liabilities in its own currency. Most other countries, including China, must continue to consider their access to the principal international currency. More importantly, the dollar’s position allows Washington to influence the external financial constraints faced by other countries. American sanctions can restrict access to international payment systems and financial markets. Conversely, the Federal Reserve can provide emergency dollar liquidity to selected foreign central banks, alleviating pressures that might otherwise produce financial crises. This ability to impose or relax external constraints is not simply an incidental benefit of the dollar’s international role. It is one of the central mechanisms through which monetary hierarchy sustains geopolitical power.
China’s growing technological capabilities could certainly alter this balance over time. Dependence on Chinese strategic minerals, equipment, and manufacturing capacity already creates vulnerabilities for the United States. But dependence on particular imported commodities or technologies is different from financial dependence on another state’s currency. For a transformation comparable to the British-American transition, the United States would have to become dependent on Chinese-controlled resources or finance under conditions in which China could determine the terms of access. The emergence of substantial international borrowing, credit, and settlement in renminbi could form part of such a transformation, but nothing of the sort is in the cards in the near future.
The Resilience of the Dollar
None of this means that American monetary hegemony is permanent. China’s advances in batteries, electric vehicles, and renewable energy could erode American productive predominance, at least in some sectors. The increasing use of financial sanctions and other coercive measures may also encourage countries to develop alternatives to the dollar. But greater currency competition is not the same as a reversal of the underlying international financial hierarchy.
Britain’s loss of monetary hegemony was ultimately tied not only to its dependence on American production but also to its reliance on dollar financing during the two world wars. Suez demonstrated that Washington could use that dependence to constrain British policy. The United States, by contrast, does not need to borrow in renminbi to sustain its international commitments, and China cannot yet impose a comparable external financial constraint on Washington. China’s challenge to American productive predominance is real, but no significant decline in the dollar’s international market share has occurred. Even if such a decline were to take place, it would not by itself establish a new monetary hegemon.
Indeed, as America’s productive lead and the legitimacy of its international leadership erode, its reliance on sanctions, financial exclusion, and military pressure may increase. The problem may therefore be less the imminent disappearance of American monetary hegemony than its increasingly coercive character. The transition away from fossil fuels is essential for addressing climate change and could substantially reduce the external vulnerabilities of oil-importing countries. But it will not automatically create an alternative international monetary order. To paraphrase John Connally’s famous dictum, the dollar remains America’s currency and the rest of the world’s problem.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: London’s National Gallery publishes recommendations of its citizens’  assembly
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The National Gallery in London says in a new report that a new public body founded to advise the UK national museum on its future policy and direction has given it “a mandate to be brave”.
The new initiative, titled NG Citizens, was announced in July last year. The museum aims to transform its governance model by launching a citizens’ assembly made up of members of public from across the UK.
The accompanying report outlines the recommendations and shared vision developed by 55 participants who took part in five sessions between November 2025 and March 2026.
The new assembly recommended that the museum should “embrace and grow commercial opportunities” and also use technology to support personalised itineraries, especially for “under-represented” groups, among other objectives.
Other key recommendations for the museum include being more informative about its wider history, representation and context behind the art. The collection also urgently needs to be a true reflection of the UK, said the assembly members.
The overarching question put to the assembly members was: “What do you want from the UK’s National Gallery? How can it bring people and paintings together in authentic and meaningful ways, now and in the future?” A series of eight principles, defined as the “core values that guide how the gallery can move towards the vision”, were discussed at the sessions.
Core challenges on the agenda included: “How can the National Gallery balance its role as a free public gallery whilst being commercially minded? What is the social value of art? How can art galleries explain and support this? Can art ever be open to everyone?” Other issues discussed include “how to bring in new, diverse and loyal audiences.”
Over the next four years, a series of smaller panels, made up of assembly members, will work directly with the gallery to oversee the implementation of these ideas. “NG Citizens will now continue into its second phase: the Citizens’ Panel. The panel will consist of three separate cohorts between 2026 and 2030,” says the report.
Some issues were not up for discussion at the sessions says the report, such as ideas that would result in significant changes to existing buildings; ideas that involve buying or selling paintings; and ideas that might compromise the gallery’s role as an arm’s length body of the UK government.
The report concludes: “The National Gallery was the first of its kind to do this on this scale, in the world. We can accept it was never going to be perfect; it would present challenges, but we hope observers can learn from our experience… To have a group of people that we can work with over future years, who will maintain a critical and supportive perspective, presents opportunities far beyond the usual focus group approach.”
Maurice Davies, a UK culture consultant at Cultural Associates Oxford, says the report is “quite remarkable” but questions whether the National Gallery will be “bold and brave enough” to take forward the assembly’s recommendations.
He tells The Art Newspaper: “The panel have concluded that the gallery needs to be far more than it currently is; a collection of European paintings based in the centre of London. They say the collection ‘urgently’ needs to be far more diverse and to represent the diversity of the UK so it needs to change its collecting policy significantly.
And they say the gallery should share ‘paintings and resources’ throughout the UK which suggests the gallery might want to reconsider its current hugely expensive project to extend its building in central London in favour of using resources to work with museums and galleries in a wide range of locations.”
Last September, the National Gallery received pledges of £150m each (from Michael Moritz’s Crankstart foundation and the Julia Rausing Trust) for its planned major new extension scheduled for completion in the early 2030s.

https://gothamist.com/news/1-dead-after-.title: 1 dead after early morning fire rips through Hamilton Heights apartment building, FDNY says
https://gothamist.com/news/1-dead-after-.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/1-dead-after-.text:
One person died and at least five others were injured after a fire tore through a six-story Hamilton Heights apartment complex Monday morning.
An FDNY spokesperson said the fire started in a heavily cluttered 3rd-floor unit at the Riverside Drive building around 1:30 a.m.
First responders transported one person with life-threatening injuries to a nearby hospital, and two others were treated for minor injuries. FDNY officials said two firefighters were also injured in the blaze.
One person, who has not yet been identified, was pronounced dead on scene.
Firefighters got the flames under control Monday morning. Investigators are still determining exactly what caused the fire.
Eighty-seven people have died as a result of fires this year, according to FDNY data. That’s up from 45 by this time last year.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.title: Proteste in Frankreich | »Das ist eine Revolte gegen die bestehende Ordnung«
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.author: Diego Chauvet
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120375.text:
- Politik
- Proteste in Frankreich
»Das ist eine Revolte gegen die bestehende Ordnung«
Pünktlich zu den jugendlichen Protesten in Europa hat Enzo Traverso ein neues Buch veröffentlicht – ein Gespräch mit dem linken Historiker.
Ihr neues Buch »Survivances de la révolte« (Fortleben der Revolte, La Découverte) erscheint, während Frankreich sich erhebt. Was sehen Sie in dieser Revolte entstehen?
Ich bin angenehm überrascht, eine Resonanz zwischen den Themen festzustellen, die ich in meinem Buch behandelt habe, und dem aktuellen Geschehen, das von einer Revolte geprägt ist, die sich in Frankreich besonders eindrucksvoll, ja spektakulär äußert. Doch es handelt sich um ein globales Phänomen. Am 17. Oktober waren die Aktionsformen in mehreren italienischen Städten denen in Frankreich sehr ähnlich.
Ich denke, wir erleben die Symptome einer Revolte, in der die jungen Generationen eine besonders bedeutende Rolle spielen. Über die unmittelbaren Forderungen hinaus ist es eine Revolte gegen die bestehende Ordnung, gegen das auferlegte soziale und politische System, das von den jungen Menschen als regelrechter eiserner Käfig, als Zwangsjacke, als Strafe empfunden wird.
Im Mai 1968 gab es eine Generation, die die ihr angebotene Zukunft nicht akzeptierte. Heute revoltiert die Jugend gegen ein System, das ihr überhaupt keine Zukunft bietet – oder vielmehr eine Zukunft, die für die überwältigende Mehrheit schlechter sein wird als die ihrer Eltern: eine Zukunft in sozialer Unsicherheit, aber auch geprägt von Ökozid und Bedrohungen der grundlegenden Lebensbedingungen der Menschheit auf diesem Planeten. Die jungen Generationen sind sich dessen viel stärker bewusst als meine Generation. Sie haben also allen Grund, sich aufzulehnen.
Wie führen der Lehrkräftemangel und überfüllte Klassen zu einem so tiefgreifenden politischen Protest?
Diese Bewegung ist nicht – wie andere Bewegungen in der Vergangenheit – gegen eine Reform entstanden. Sie ist aus untragbar gewordenen Studien- und Lebensbedingungen hervorgegangen. Das Gefühl von Ungerechtigkeit ist unerträglich geworden. Als Historiker kann ich feststellen, dass Revolten im Nachhinein immer vorhersehbar sind. Doch niemand hätte sich vorstellen können, dass junge Menschen am selben Tag in Paris, Marseille, Lyon oder Mailand auf die Straße gehen würden – und dabei ganz ähnliche Ausdrucksformen finden.
Die politische Dimension dieser Revolte ist unbestreitbar. Eine Analogie zur Pariser Kommune fällt mir besonders auf: Der antikommunardische Diskurs ähnelt stark dem, der sich heute verbreitet. Er weigert sich, nach den sozialen und politischen Ursachen der Revolte zu fragen, und begnügt sich damit, sie zu kriminalisieren, manchmal auch, indem er sie rassifiziert. In Frankreich wie in Italien wird die Revolte in gewisser Weise ethnisiert oder biologisiert. Das war schon im antikommunardischen Diskurs der Fall: Paris wurde als in den Händen der »Wilden« und »Barbaren« dargestellt, die Zivilisation als bedroht.
Anschließend haben wir extreme Polizeigewalt erlebt, bei der jungen Jugendlichen Augen ausgeschossen und sie verstümmelt wurden. Doch der vorherrschende Diskurs konzentriert sich auf das Eigentum. Ich denke aber, dass diese Jugend weiß, dass in einem multinationalen Konzern viel mehr Gewalt steckt als in der Handlung eines jungen Menschen, der einen Stein gegen ein Schaufenster wirft.
Politisiert sich gerade eine Generation?
Eine Generation bildet sich heraus, sie formt sich um ein Gründungsereignis. Der 17. Oktober hat eine Generation politisiert. Doch eines ist sicher: Diese Jugend will kein System, das zugleich ein anthropologisches Modell ist, das auf Konkurrenz und Individualismus beruht. Sie lehnt die Vorstellung einer Zukunft ab, die auf eine privatisierte Utopie zusammenschrumpft und in der man Zukunft nur noch als individuellen Erfolg und berufliche Laufbahn denken soll. Es ist eine Revolte gegen eine Zivilisation und gegen ein Wertesystem, das sich als unveränderliche Lebensform durchgesetzt zu haben schien.
Bei den Demonstrationen habe ich diesen Slogan gesehen: »Wir wollen aus der Gegenwart ausbrechen.« Es ist ein Protest gegen den »Präsentismus«, jenes Regime des Geschichtsbewusstseins, das in der Gegenwart gefangen ist und keinen Erwartungshorizont kennt. Die Demonstrierenden wollen diesen eisernen Käfig aufbrechen. Ich glaube, in einem solchen Slogan kommt ein Geschichtsbewusstsein zum Ausdruck. Zwanzig Jahre lang waren soziale Bewegungen, mitunter machtvolle, nicht in der Lage, sich eine Zukunft vorzustellen. Ich sage nicht, dass dieses Problem gelöst ist. Wir wissen noch nicht, wohin wir gehen; wir befinden uns mitten in einer anhaltenden Krise. Aber vielleicht zeichnet sich gerade eine Alternative ab.
Beobachten wir über die von Ihnen beschriebene Generation hinaus eine Konvergenz der Kämpfe?
Das ist eine Forderung, die aus dieser Revolte hervorgeht. Die jungen Menschen, die auf die Straße gehen und Gymnasien und Universitäten blockieren, wissen, dass sie nicht gewinnen können, wenn ihre Bewegung ihre eigenen Grenzen nicht überschreitet. Die Kämpfe müssen sich also verbinden. Das hat begonnen.
Der Historiker Patrick Boucheron beschreibt in der französischen Tageszeitung »Libération« eine »präautoritäre« Phase statt einer »prärevolutionären«. Was halten Sie davon?
Ich würde sagen, dass die Dialektik der Geschichte gerade durch diese Ungewissheit gekennzeichnet ist. Warum nicht eine prärevolutionäre Situation? Die Voraussetzungen sind vorhanden. Damit bezeichne ich die gegenwärtige Krise nicht als prärevolutionär; dafür ist es noch zu früh. Doch wenn sich diese Bewegung zersetzt und erschöpft, wenn die Konvergenz der Kämpfe weder einen politischen Ausdruck noch Formen des Widerstands gegen die brutale Repression findet, die heute ausgeübt wird, dann zählt auch eine autoritäre Wende zu den möglichen Ergebnissen. Alles ist bereits vorbereitet. Ich würde sogar sagen, dass die Gewalt dieser Macht umgekehrt proportional zu ihrem Maß an Legitimität ist.
Es gibt weder eine Verschwörung noch eine verborgene Kraft, die die Ereignisse planen würde. Revolten brechen spontan aus. Das Gedächtnis, das ich in meinem Buch untersuche, ist ein unterirdisches Gedächtnis, ein Gedächtnis, das ich »marranisch« nenne. Das Gedächtnis der Revolten und der emanzipatorischen Bewegungen ist eine Alternative zu dem, was Pierre Nora als »Erinnerungsorte« bezeichnet hat: Sie sind institutionalisiert und durch Erinnerungspolitiken sakralisiert, die Machtpolitik sind.
Die Erinnerungen an die Revolte sind unsichtbar. Sie werden wie unterirdische Flüsse weitergegeben und tauchen plötzlich wieder auf, in Gestalt einer Explosion. Um diese Bewegungen zu verstehen, muss man darauf achten, was unter der Oberfläche geschieht.
Seit dem 7. Oktober 2023 wurde das Gedächtnis an die Schoah, das jahrzehntelang ein Instrument im Kampf gegen Rassismus und Diskriminierung gewesen war, dialektisch in sein Gegenteil verkehrt. Es wurde mobilisiert, um einen Genozid zu legitimieren. Was jetzt geschieht, ist eine Bewegung, die diese ganze zu einer Lüge gewordene Vorrichtung umkehren will.
Die französische Tageszeitung »L’Humanité« wurde 1904 vom Sozialisten Jean Jaurès gegründet. Ursprünglich als Sprachrohr für die sozialistische Bewegung gedacht, vertritt sie seitdem konsequent linke und sozialistische Positionen. Sie setzt sich für soziale Gerechtigkeit, Arbeitnehmer*innenrechte und weltweiten Frieden ein.
Die Zeitung ist das ehemalige Zentralorgan der Kommunistischen Partei Frankreichs (PCF). 1999 entfiel der explizite Hinweis auf die Partei. Seit 2004 gehört die Zeitung zu 40 Prozent der PCF, Freund*innen und Mitarbeiter*innen halten je zehn Prozent, die Gesellschaft der Freunde 20 Prozent und Großunternehmen wie Sparkassen, der Sender TF1 und der Rüstungskonzern Lagardère den Rest. Heute arbeiten bei der »L’Humanité« etwa 60 Redakteur*innen; die Zeitung hat etwa 40 000 Abonnent*innen. Das 1930 erstmals begangene Pressefest, die Fête de L’Humanité, ist bis heute ein wichtiger Termin des gesellschaftlichen Lebens in Frankreich.
Wird nicht auch der Laizismus gegen die Muslime gewendet?
Ja. In den extremen Rechten, die ich als »postfaschistisch« bezeichne, hat ein Übergang vom Antisemitismus – einem der Grundpfeiler nationalistischer und faschistischer Kulturen in der ersten Hälfte des 20. Jahrhunderts – zur Islamophobie stattgefunden. Sie ist heute das verbindende Element aller extremen Rechten.
Das erklärt die Beziehungen dieser Bewegungen zu Israel und ihre Unterstützung des Genozids in Gaza. Das bedeutet weder, dass der Antisemitismus als Vorurteil verschwunden wäre, noch, dass die extremen Rechten nicht weiterhin zu seinen Zentren gehörten. Doch die ideologische Achse dieser extremen Rechten ist heute die Islamophobie – verbunden mit der Umwandlung des Laizismus, eines Grundsatzes, den es zu verteidigen gilt, in eine Waffe gegen eine Minderheit, die muslimische Minderheit.
Welchen politischen Ausweg gibt es für diese Revolten, nachdem mit dem Scheitern der kommunistischen Länder der revolutionäre Horizont verschwunden ist?
Ich denke, wir suchen noch immer danach. Im 20. Jahrhundert verfügte die Linke über Modelle: ein sozialdemokratisches und ein kommunistisches Modell. Sie bot eine Alternative an, und im kollektiven Bewusstsein galt der Kapitalismus nicht als alternativlos. Dieser Horizont schloss sich 1989 – ein Ereignis, das ich selbst als befreiend erlebt habe.
Doch sehr schnell wurde uns bewusst, dass es zugleich das Ende eines historischen Abschnitts markierte: das Ende der Revolutionen des 20. Jahrhunderts. Seitdem war die Linke nicht in der Lage, neue Modelle zu erfinden. Der Kommunismus hat als revolutionäre Perspektive die Bühne der Geschichte verlassen.
Die Bewegungen, die danach entstanden, waren also Bewegungen ohne Gedächtnis. Sie kritisierten die bestehende Ordnung, konnten sich aber nicht mehr in eine Kontinuität einreihen. Ich nenne oft das Beispiel der Kommunisten, die in die Lager der Nationalsozialisten deportiert und dort hingerichtet wurden. Als sie starben, wussten sie, dass ihr Opfer nicht vergeblich war, weil sie einer Bewegung angehörten, die ihren Kampf fortsetzen konnte.
Dieses Geschichtsbewusstsein, einer Bewegung anzugehören, die in die Zukunft schreitet, barg viele Illusionen, besaß aber eine außergewöhnliche Kraft: »Die Zukunft gehört uns. Ich kann sterben, andere werden meinen Kampf fortführen.« Der Verlust dieses Orientierungspunkts war verheerend.
Ich glaube, zwischen dem Reichtum des zeitgenössischen kritischen Denkens und der Unfähigkeit, eine politische Alternative aufzubauen, klafft eine beträchtliche Lücke. Doch diese theoretische Ausarbeitung war noch nicht in der Lage, eine politische Bewegung zu tragen, die in den Augen der subalternen Klassen, der arbeitenden Klassen, eine Alternative entwirft. Wie das gehen soll? Ich weiß es nicht. Intellektuelle können Projekte formulieren, doch sie müssen aus den sozialen Bewegungen selbst hervorgehen. Man kann sie nicht am Schreibtisch ausarbeiten.
Erschwert das Scheitern des historischen Kommunismus also die Erfindung eines neuen Ideals?
Das Hindernis ist enorm. Wir leben in einer Situation, die mit der Welt zu Beginn des Ersten Weltkriegs vergleichbar ist, als Rosa Luxemburg die Losung »Sozialismus oder Barbarei« ausgab. Doch es gibt einen großen Unterschied. Im 21. Jahrhundert müssen wir feststellen, dass der Sozialismus an die Macht gelangt ist, dass es erste Umsetzungsversuche gab und dass er in mehreren Fällen zu einer der Dimensionen der Barbarei selbst geworden ist. Das können wir nicht ignorieren.
Das bedeutet, dass es kein Zurück geben kann. Es gibt kein Modell, das man wiederherstellen könnte. Man kann nicht sagen, die Lösung bestehe darin, zur Sozialdemokratie der 1950er- und 1960er-Jahre oder zum Kommunismus der 1920er-Jahre zurückzukehren. Wir müssen also etwas anderes erfinden.
Es gab Versuche in Lateinamerika, in Griechenland mit Syriza und in Spanien mit Podemos. Sie sind gescheitert. In den Vereinigten Staaten ist eine sozialistische Bewegung im Aufstieg begriffen. Doch ich kann heute nicht sagen, welche Gestalt ein neues Modell annehmen wird.
Kann uns die Erinnerung an die vergangenen Revolutionen dabei helfen, etwas anderes zu erfinden?
Während Frankreich und andere europäische Länder von einer enormen sozialen Wut erfasst werden, fragt der in Paris lebende italienische Historiker Enzo Traverso danach, was die Revolten nährt und in welchem Verhältnis sie zu den Kämpfen der Vergangenheit stehen. Mit seinem jüngsten Buch »Survivances de la révolte« (Fortleben der Revolte, La Découverte) schließt er eine Trilogie ab, die mit »Mélancolie de gauche« (Melancholie der Linken, 2016) begann und mit »Révolution« (Revolution, 2022) fortgesetzt wurde. Er spricht über die Rolle der Jugend, die unterirdischen Erinnerungen an die Kämpfe und die Schwierigkeit, eine politische Alternative entstehen zu lassen.
Ich denke, ohne Geschichtsbewusstsein lässt sich keine Zukunft aufbauen. Das zu sagen, ist eine Binsenweisheit, aber ich bin davon überzeugt. Das Gedächtnis des Antifaschismus etwa ist unverzichtbar, um Demokratien zu bewahren und zu verändern. Zumal die neuen Faschismen vorgeben, die Demokratie zu verteidigen, und sich innerhalb der Institutionen durchsetzen wollen, um sie von innen heraus zu verändern und ihres Wesens zu berauben.
Bei den Demonstrationen habe ich Plakate gesehen, die an die Pariser Kommune und an das Massaker an den Algeriern in Paris am 17. Oktober 1961 erinnerten. Man sollte nicht versuchen, Bewegungen künstlich ein Gedächtnis einzuflößen, als wären sie ohne eines. Sie besitzen bereits ein Gedächtnis, das mitunter im Unbewussten und in der kollektiven Vorstellung eingeschrieben ist. Vielleicht muss man ihm Sichtbarkeit und eine Form geben.
In meinem Buch führe ich das Beispiel jener ikonoklastischen Welle in den Vereinigten Staaten an, bei der Statuen gestürzt wurden, die die Sklaverei oder den Kolonialismus feierten. Diese Bewegung wurde als barbarisch gebrandmarkt. Ihre Akteure wurden als Ignoranten dargestellt, die die Geschichte zerstören wollten. Dabei waren diese Bewegungen ein außergewöhnlicher Moment, in dem sich die Gesellschaften die Vergangenheit wieder aneigneten.
Gemeinsam mit Walter Benjamin bin ich davon überzeugt, dass man von einer Reaktivierung der Vergangenheit sprechen kann. Natürlich lässt sich das Geschehene nicht verändern, doch die Vergangenheit ist kein kalter, archivierter, erschöpfter Kontinent, der radikal von der Gegenwart getrennt wäre. Unter bestimmten historischen Umständen bedeutet die Gegenwart zu verändern auch, die Vergangenheit wiedergutzumachen. Benjamin verwendete sogar einen theologischen Begriff: die »Erlösung der Vergangenheit«. Es geht darum, den Besiegten der Vergangenheit Gerechtigkeit widerfahren zu lassen, sie zu erlösen.
Dieser Text ist am 5. November 2026 in unserem französischem Partnermedium »L’Humanité« erschienen. Er wurde übersetzt und nachbearbeitet.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Diante de Milei e população, papa Leão 14 aborda crise na Argentina e defende preservação da democracia
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Opera Mundi
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Em visita à Argentina, no âmbito de sua agenda pela América Latina, o papa Leão 14 declarou, no domingo (8), que a “economia deve estar a serviço da pessoa, e não a pessoa a serviço da economia”. A primeira mensagem no território argentino se deu no Palácio Libertad, onde estavam presentes o presidente Javier Milei e outras autoridades políticas, além da população civil.
“Estou pensando de uma forma particular nas famílias que carregam o peso da incerteza, naqueles que procuram trabalho, nos idosos que contribuíram por anos para a construção da sociedade e naqueles que, mesmo trabalhando, têm dificuldade em atender às necessidades de seus lares”, disse.
De acordo com o jornal argentino Página 12, o discurso do pontífice teria deixado Milei “desconfortável”, no que analistas locais interpretaram como uma mensagem enfática ao presidente argentino. No local, o papa pediu que “o crescimento fosse permitido alcançar também aqueles que enfrentam maiores dificuldades”.
Atualmente, o governo da Argentina promove um programa ultraliberal de cortes que dizimou o poder dos salários, emprego, economia familiar e programas sociais, pensões e subsídios, disparou a pobreza e atacou ciência e educação, atingindo, ao mesmo tempo, o setor empresarial, o investimento, o consumo interno e a classificação do país.
“A Argentina tem muitos recursos humanos”, mas “fazer essa riqueza dar frutos para o benefício de todos exige prestar atenção especial aos jovens”, disse o líder católico. “As oportunidades que encontrarem hoje dependerão em grande parte de conseguirem desenvolver seus projetos de vida aqui.”
Leão 14 sustentou que uma nação deve se questionar “o que deu errado” quando uma categoria de jovens prefere deixar o país para realizar seus sonhos fora, e também a que a criação de condições em prol do futuro juvenil “exige fortalecer a educação, a formação profissional, a universidade e a pesquisa de uma maneira específica”.
Defesa da democracia
Diante de Milei e das autoridades políticas presentes, o pontífice enfatizou que a democracia “se fortalece com a disposição de ouvir, com o cuidado da palavra, com a busca paciente por acordos e com a capacidade de reconhecer aqueles que pensam diferente”.
Milei, cuja aprovação entre os argentinos caiu para cerca de 30% por meses, faz ataques frequentes a figuras da esquerda, à imprensa e a qualquer um que discorde de sua linha. O presidente continuou sua austeridade e reformas, apesar de relatos que revelam o fracasso econômico de sua gestão, além das crescentes mobilizações populares no país, que acabam fortemente reprimidas pela polícia.
“Aqueles que exercem autoridade também têm o dever de agir com prudência, de reconhecer os limites do poder que lhes foi confiado e de direcionar suas decisões para o bem de toda a comunidade”, afirmou, destacando que é preciso aprender a conviver mesmo quando há diferenças, o que eventualmente abre caminho para o diálogo.
“A democracia pertence a esse patrimônio que deve ser protegido. Aqueles que têm responsabilidades públicas têm uma tarefa particularmente exigente”, disse.
Bem-estar da Argentina
A administração de Milei também cortou assistência para pessoas com deficiência e orçamentos de saúde. O papa enfatizou que a dignidade “exige atenção especial à doença, dependência e deficiência.”
“A Argentina foi abençoada por Deus com uma riqueza natural extraordinária. Seus campos, suas reservas de água, suas fontes de energia, seus minerais e a diversidade de seus ecossistemas oferecem amplas possibilidades para desenvolvimento”, afirmou.
“Uma ecologia autenticamente humana sabe como unir o cuidado da criação com o das pessoas, garantindo que o uso desses recursos contribua para o bem-estar das comunidades e preserve as condições que tornam a vida e o trabalho possíveis em seus territórios”, acrescentou.
O papa Leão 14 segue no país pelos próximos dias. A expectativa é de que, nesta segunda-feira (9), visite Cottolengo Don Orione, um centro para pessoas com deficiência na cidade de Claypole, em Buenos Aires, onde presidirá uma missa no Monumento aos Espanhóis.
Na terça-feira (10), ele viajará para Córdoba e, na quarta-feira (11), coroará sua visita com uma missa na Basílica de Nossa Senhora de Luján. Depois partirá para o Peru.
*Com Telesur.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/09/isra.title: Tons of “Bunker-Buster” Bomb Parts for Israel Go Through JFK Airport
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/09/isra.author: Noah Hurowitz
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/09/isra.text:
An Israeli airline shipped thousands of pounds worth of parts for controversial “bunker-buster” bombs through John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York during the height of the Israeli–U.S. war against Iran, according to a new investigation by a left-wing research group.
Challenge Airlines, a cargo hauler based in Israel, made three flights this spring carrying the bomb casings for BLU-109s — a 2,000-pound munition that has been tied to numerous mass-casualty attacks on civilian neighborhoods in the Gaza Strip, Lebanon, and Iran in recent years — according to open-source data obtained by the Movement Research Unit and reviewed by The Intercept.
The airline also made more than 100 shipments of guidance kits known as joint direct attack munitions, or JDAMs — which are used to convert so-called “dumb bombs” into GPS-guided munitions capable of striking a specific target — according to data shared with The Intercept. Many of the guidance kits were marked for use on the MK-84, another 2,000-pound bomb Israel used in its campaign to level Gaza, where fragments of JDAMs have repeatedly been found at the site of airstrikes.
The 2,000-pound bombs present a serious risk of civilian casualties, according to Josh Paul, a former State Department official who resigned at the outset of the war in Gaza to protest the Biden administration’s sale of weapons to Israel.
“If you look at historic U.S. use of 2,000-pound bombs, in the entire counter-ISIS campaign, there were just two that were dropped in the vicinity of the city of Mosul precisely because there is no way to use a 2,000-pound bomb discriminately in an urban environment,” Paul said, referring to an American air war during the final years of the Obama administration to end the Islamic State’s control of the Iraqi city of Mosul.
Israel hasn’t shared the United States’s reservations. The country made extensive use of the weapons to attack targets in Gaza and Lebanon, including a deadly strike on Gaza’s Jabaliya refugee camp that killed dozens of civilians, according to an analysis by the New York Times.
“If you look at a picture of Gaza right now, I would say Israel’s use of these weapons is functionally indistinguishable from indiscriminate bombing,” Paul said.
Challenge Airlines, and the Israeli military did not respond to request for comment.
“We work closely with all airport partners to ensure the safety of public, neighboring communities, and airport personnel,” said a spokesperson for the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates JFK Airport. “The federal government and commercial airlines have primary responsibility as to what is allowed to be shipped on aircraft. We are pre-empted under federal law from interfering with these activities.”
While the shipments of JDAMs and bomb bodies for BLU-109s did not include active munitions, previous shipments of weapons through JFK have included explosives, including 14 tons of nitrocellulose bound for Israel in May 2025.
The Intercept verified the data showing all three shipments of bunker-buster bomb bodies, and verified a portion of the data showing shipments of JDAM kits. Movement Research Unit, an investigative outlet whose prior work has uncovered shipments of drone tech to Israel and the transport of fighter jet parts by United Airlines onboard civilian passenger flights, shared the data on the condition that some specifics of its methods be withheld to prevent a crackdown on the availability of such data.
In response to the flow of weapons and materiel through JFK, the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America has been organizing a campaign to stop the flow of weapons to Israel through the airport.
“This is another example of a growing body of reporting that shows how civilian infrastructure is used for the genocide in Gaza,” said a DSA member named Henry, who asked to be identified without his last name in order prevent retaliation from his employer. “Civilian air travel should prioritize passengers, travelers, and the international community — not weapons — and no worker should be forced to serve the militarized supply chain.”
Tons of Pressure
Challenge Airlines shipped the bunker-buster bomb bodies on flights leaving JFK for Tel Aviv on March 12, April 30, and May 6, according to the data shared with The Intercept.
They shipped the guidance kits far more frequently, with 109 shipments leaving JFK for Tel Aviv between December 22, 2024, and June 7, 2026. Cargo documents indicate that most of the shipments were of JDAM kits designed for 2,000-pound MK-84 bombs but also included at least one shipment of kits for bunker-buster bombs.
In total, the airline shipped 175,884 pounds of BLU-109 casings and more than 5 million pounds of JDAM kits between December 22, 2024, and June 7, 2026, according to the data obtained by Movement Research Unit.
JFK Airport is the main export hub for such munitions flying by air to Israel, according to federal data: More than half of all Israel-bound air shipments of weapons that fit the government export category for bombs and missiles was sent abroad from JFK.
It was not immediately clear where the bunker buster and JDAM shipments originated, but sales of military hardware to Israel typically either come from deals between the Israeli and U.S. governments or direct commercial purchases under a special export license made by the Israeli military from private companies.
In the first two years of Israel’s war on Gaza, the U.S. spent $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel, according to a study by analyst William Hartung. That has included multiple shipments of 2,000-pound bombs like the BLU-109 and the MK-84, as well as JDAM kits to equip the weapons with GPS guidance.
The Biden administration in May 2024 halted the shipment of MK-84 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, citing the potential harm to civilians, but President Donald Trump resumed shipments of the heavy munitions within weeks of retaking the White House.
News of the shipments comes just over a month after the Associated Press revealed plans in the works for the U.S. to ink a vast $2.8 billion arms sale to Israel that would include thousands of 2,000-pound bombs.
The ongoing sale of such heavy weapons to Israel underscores the need for a federal solution, according to Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., who sponsored last year legislation dubbed the “Block the Bombs Act,” that would bar the U.S. from selling BLU-109s, JDAMs, and other munitions central to Israel’s war effort.
“It’s the only bill that prohibits these weapons transfers from happening, and the only bill that creates a comprehensive process of oversight,” Ramirez told The Intercept. “There’s been a big push, particularly in New York and around JFK, to block these transfers and it’s good that people are putting pressure locally, but ultimately it is Congress’s responsibility to make that happen.”
First introduced in May 2025, the bill has gathered more than 80 co-sponsors but has thus far languished in legislative limbo. With the House of Representatives soon to be under Democratic control, Ramirez said she plans to bring the bill to the floor next session.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.title: Firm Linked to Trump’s Sons Got Nearly $40 Million in Federal Contracts to Screen for Ebola and Other Diseases
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.author: Sharon Lerner, Anna Maria Barry-Jester, Robert Faturechi
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.text:
The Trump administration awarded a small biosecurity company nearly $40 million to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases just months after a firm linked to President Donald Trump’s elder sons invested in its parent company, according to records and interviews.
The contracts, one to screen for Ebola in several U.S. airports and the other to respond to disease outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, are seven times the total value of government contracts the company had directly received before.
The company, XpresTest, has years of experience monitoring for COVID-19 and other diseases for the government at U.S. airports. That makes its parent, XWELL, an unusual hybrid, selling both spa treatments and biosecurity services. Last year, it made most of its money from waxing salons and airport spas that offer manicures, massages and “chakra beds.”
The contracts are the latest example of the president’s family benefiting financially from his administration’s actions. And the stakes for these deals are particularly high. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an Ebola outbreak has killed more than 5,000 people this year, and the federal government is trying to stop the pathogen from coming to the U.S.
XpresTest has never worked with Ebola or provided biosecurity services abroad, let alone in the kind of volatile locales it’s now expected to work in. The CEO of its parent company, Ezra Ernst, said XpresTest won both contracts in a competitive bidding process and pointed to its years of experience doing screening for COVID-19 and other pathogens at American airports. But even he acknowledged that working internationally is “a new thing for us” and expressed uncertainty about being able to complete the work in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
“This is a risky contract. I’m not sure we can do it,” Ernst said in an interview.
Jeremy Konyndyk, who helped oversee the U.S. government’s response to a 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, said there are some parallels between monitoring for COVID-19 and Ebola at airports, but he said it’s concerning that the government would award such a lucrative contract to a company that has no experience in Africa.
“There are countless organizations in the world that have decades of experience doing this work,” Konyndyk said. “I have to wonder why the hell they’re not going with someone who has actually done this before.”
Under previous administrations, the U.S. government addressed international disease outbreaks in partnership with the World Health Organization. But Trump withdrew from the group last year, dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development, which handled much of this work, and dramatically scaled back the global presence of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
At the same time, the State Department launched the America First Global Health Strategy, which calls for the U.S. to use aid to foreign countries to “promote American companies and American innovations abroad.” This March, the State Department announced it would be giving up to $4.5 billion in funding for various purposes, including responding to infectious disease outbreaks.
Under that program, XPresTest was awarded $20 million. Other funding went to better-known global aid nonprofits, including International Medical Corps, Save the Children and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, whose awards ranged from $25 million to $35 million.
The CDC also awarded XPresTest a contract, for $18.8 million.
In response to questions from ProPublica about XPresTest and its parent company, XWELL, the State Department noted the firm’s previous work screening for diseases at airports under a contract with the CDC and said its own award was made “through a competitive process that builds on this successful model.”
The CDC did not respond to a request for comment.
A spokesperson for the president’s sons Donald Jr. and Eric Trump said that they are “merely passive, minority investors in a fund that invested in this company,” and that they had no “involvement in or knowledge regarding the negotiation or procurement of any of its contracts, including any government contracts.”
“Both are private citizens who hold no government positions, broken no laws and who have every right to pursue lawful business and investment opportunities,” the spokesperson said.
The Trump sons’ connection to XWELL was established in February, when a fund called American Ventures invested in the company. The fund was launched by Dominari Holdings, a small financial firm with offices inside Trump Tower in New York. The leaders of Dominari hired the Trump sons as advisers after their father was elected to a second term and granted them a stake of more than 10% in Dominari.
Anthony Hayes, the CEO of Dominari Holdings, told ProPublica, “We have never seen or even heard of Don or Eric using their family name to influence the granting of a government contract.”
American Ventures has taken stakes in other companies that have benefited from Trump administration actions. The Florida-based drone company Powerus got a contract worth up to $90 million from the U.S. Air Force five months after the Trumps’ involvement was announced. Through American Ventures, Donald Jr. and Eric Trump also are acquiring a stake in a critical minerals group that has received U.S. government support to mine for tungsten in Kazakhstan. The Trumps have described themselves as passive investors who do not advocate for the companies they have stakes in before their father’s government.
XWELL was founded in 2006 as a line of airport-based spas that provided massages and facials. During the pandemic, the company, then known as XpresSpa Group, got $5.5 million from the CDC to offer travelers COVID-19 testing. It also collected waste from airplane toilets to check for new viral strains. It has done similar work for at least one other company that has received government contracts.
In January, XWELL announced that it was hiring a former senior adviser at the CDC who created and led the agency’s traveler surveillance program. The firm said the move was part of a plan to expand “its traveler-based pathogen surveillance capabilities to support international travel hubs and large-scale mass gathering events worldwide.”
The following month, American Ventures invested about $30 million in XWELL. The company had lost money the previous year. “We were so cash-strapped, close to bankrupt,” its CEO said.
Its valuation before the cash infusion was just $3 million. In exchange, American Ventures got a roughly 10% stake in the company to start, with an option to essentially print and sell millions of shares in the future.
Why American Ventures would invest so much in XWELL is unclear. In other cases, when the fund has invested in similar tiny publicly traded companies, some of those firms have moved into hot new sectors and drawn publicity for their connection to the Trumps, then Dominari has offloaded shares. In this case, there is no indication it has sold any of its stake yet.
In June, XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract for what a public notice about the grant said was “Ebola entry screening services.”
XpresTest then received the State Department grant for “rapid, effective, and coordinated outbreak response” to infectious disease threats in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in September, according to a government database. The company is also planning to work in Kenya and Morocco. XWELL’s website shows it is now hiring specialists in Ebola response training and biosecurity in the U.S.
In July, after XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract, XWELL announced plans to sell the subsidiary along with its line of spas to a private facial spa company. Ernst, the CEO, said the government contracts played a role in the $13 million sale price and will follow XpresTest to the new company.
That means XWELL, the company that the Trump-linked investment fund took a stake in, will benefit financially from the Trump administration contracts if the sale closes, even though it won’t be involved in doing the work for the government.
XWELL said in a public filing that the sale was part of an effort “to pursue a new direction in the national security sector.” Ernst said he didn’t know the exact plans but thought the parent company might be looking to work with the Department of Defense.
XWELL did not announce either of XpresTest’s biosecurity contracts, which recently became public in federal contracting disclosures. Public companies like XWELL are required to report so-called material events, developments that could affect their share price, such as a large government contract. XWELL has publicized previous work for the federal government, including a $2 million, eight-week pilot program for testing COVID-19 in 2021.
When asked why his firm didn’t announce the awards, Ernst gave various reasons, including the possibility that XPresTest might wind up not being able to do the work — either because of its own inexperience working internationally or because the Trump administration might suddenly shift priorities and only pay for a fraction of the contract.
“None of these contracts are guaranteed,” he said.
The biosecurity awards add to the questions about the Trump family’s enrichment during his second term. The Trump family’s business activities extend far beyond Dominari and American Ventures. The president himself has made more than $1 billion from cryptocurrency ventures whose value has ballooned as his administration has taken a friendly stance to the industry. And other companies backed by his sons Donald Jr. and Eric have received billions of dollars in federal deals. Earlier this year, ProPublica reported that the Pentagon granted a small North Carolina startup linked to Trump Jr. a $620 million loan after a top aide to the president intervened on the company’s behalf. The Pentagon denied preferential treatment, and a spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he played no role.
The Trumps’ financial ties to government deals and actions are expected to be a primary focus of Congress in the coming months after Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House in last week’s midterm elections.
“When the government is corrupted for personal gain over the public interest, Americans lose trust and taxpayer dollars are wasted,” Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, wrote in a letter to colleagues last week.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Chad Harbach’s Novel of Millennial Intellectuals
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Kevin Lozano

A Dangerous Feeling
Chad Harbach’s novel of millennial intellectuals
Chad Harbach’s Novel of Millennial Intellectuals
In The Brightness, Harbach examines life before 2016.
In season six of Sex and the City, Carrie’s budding relationship with her new boyfriend, a novelist named Jack Berger, falls apart after they argue about an article of clothing that features prominently in his latest book. Carrie can’t get over the scrunchie. No New York woman, Carrie insists—especially the protagonist of his novel—would be caught dead wearing one. Berger dismisses her, but the argument still gnaws at him: He is keen to prove Carrie wrong, and he thinks he does when he spots a scrunchie-wearing woman at a “hip downtown restaurant,” but she ends up being a tourist. The fashion choices of early 2000s tourists aside, the entire fracas highlights a greater issue in their relationship: Why did he think he knew better in the first place?
Books in review
The Brightness: A Novel
Buy this book
The matter of the scrunchie is more than just a relationship mishap; one can’t help but wonder if Berger is all that competent in his chosen field. If he got the scrunchie wrong, how much else did he miss? Put another way, what is the proper barometer for judging realism in fiction: Is it meant to hold up a mirror to our world so that we might see it more clearly? Or more pointedly: What does Berger’s insistence say about his ability to understand and make claims on what women are like? Most readers might agree with Carrie here—that the scrunchie is not just a scrunchie, but a sign that Berger is a man (and a writer) whose sense of the world is not to be trusted.
In Chad Harbach’s new novel, The Brightness, we are transported back to 2015 and 2016, when the great signifying detail in the dress of urban millennial men is described as follows: “The trend in menswear” in this period “was toward an insinuation of gayness, in the form of slim striped tank tops and tight-fitting shorts.” We could debate what Harbach means by “insinuation,” but the point is clear enough: Truly fashionable dudes can see around the corner and have stocked up on big pants and flowing fabrics. And his idea of heterosexual male attractiveness flatters that of the putative novel reader: the kind of guy who wears “moss green jacket[s]” and “cognac boots” and writes book reviews for New York’s little magazines.
It’s the women of The Brightness—a mixed cohort of feminist students at Westish College, early-career editors and writers, and in one case the owner of a small brewery in Red Hook—whose modes of dress Harbach spends many pages describing. More than once, a student’s red lipstick is made to indicate her determination to court notoriety. The game of attention-seeking moves beyond makeup, Harbach tells us, because women, more than men, must think about how they look and what it says about them—whether it’s owning things like “wide-legged golden jumpsuits” or a vintage “kimono-like mini-wrap,” or knowing that “a certain shade of yellow, a rich pastured egg-yolk hue, [is] destined to rule New York that season.”
If Carrie compelled us to consider the scrunchie, what do we think Harbach is trying to do here? What does all this grousing about clothing say about that fateful year before the American lexicon expanded to include phrases like “shithole country” and “pussy hat”? Is he saying that we shouldn’t take for granted how easy we once had it? Does he mean to mourn these years? Or is his verdict on 2015 and 2016 much uglier—as ugly as a wide-legged golden jumpsuit?
Like many a campus novel before it, The Brightness begins with a prank. It’s the start of the school year at Westish, and before classes have commenced, frat row is crowded with revelers. Three students—Irma, Pammy, and Dahlia—have been talking all summer about making a statement at their little Midwestern school’s annual bacchanal, known as “the Parties.”
The three call themselves the “Witches of Westish.” And what they mean to expose is something rotten at the heart of the campus experience: what in the 2010s was often called “rape culture,” the latest moniker for a source of conflict and pain that every generation of college students has faced in one way or another, including today. (It should be no surprise that there remains little accountability on the matter within higher education, as the ongoing case of the Cornell 7 has recently made clear.)
To address the violence and assaults on their campus, the Witches of Westish set out to do a performance piece. Targeting a trio of incapacitated jocks at the Parties, they plan to stamp temporary tattoos on their foreheads that read “Rape Victim.” The next day, the jocks would wake up, look in the mirror, and discover the message imprinted on them, in ink that is very hard to wash off. They would be walking advertisements for the project’s goal: To make visible the sexual violence that pervades college life.
The Witches only manage to tattoo two of the jocks, because Irma is excused from her duties. She has too much to lose: A child of working-class rural Wisconsin, Irma is a scholarship kid, and the coven doesn’t want to risk screwing up her life. Her job instead is a more literary one: She is responsible for writing the Witches’ “manifesto,” which the college newspaper publishes soon after the men are tattooed. In a few weeks’ time, the prank makes the national news, and the Witches are famous, Dahlia most of all. After being suspended, she becomes, in short order, a martyr, then a blogger and podcaster for an online feminist magazine (à la Jezebel) called The Brightness. The other two Witches are noticed as well: At a wedding later in the novel, Irma is even offered the chance to write for The New Yorker.
That this might all sound a bit confusing is natural—Irma, our guide for most of the novel, spends her last year of college utterly bewildered—by her future, by all the attention, by desire. Yet the fact that this opening set piece might be more than a little ridiculous is perhaps the point. In many ways, The Brightness bears a striking resemblance to Tom Wolfe’s 2004 novel I Am Charlotte Simmons—a bleak right-wing satire of campus politics in which Wolfe targeted what he felt to be the crass sexual mores and hollow politics of university students. But Harbach’s handling of the Witches’ scheme is more curious: He can’t quite seem to decide whether his subjects are half-baked pseudo-intellectuals or are perhaps worth taking seriously.
What is stranger still is that the prank is only one of the novel’s many tangled plot lines, all which converge at a New England wedding to celebrate the nuptials of Owen Dunne, a young gay novelist who first appeared as one of the heroes in Harbach’s debut novel, 2011’s The Art of Fielding, and who has also written a critically acclaimed novel by the name of The Art of Fielding.
The veil between the two novels is lifted by Pella, another of the heroes of The Art of Fielding. In that book, Pella was 23, about to divorce her much older husband, and she landed at Westish looking for safe haven with her estranged father, the college’s president. By the novel’s end, her father has died after a heart attack (brought on, it is implied, by his invigorating affair with Owen), and Pella has shacked up with the captain of the baseball team, Mike Schwartz, and decided to get her life back on track by enrolling at Westish.
Four years have passed when we meet her again in The Brightness. Pella is now a recent graduate and engaged to Mike. She is also, we learn, best friends with Irma and was the first (but uncredited) editor of Owen’s now-successful novel. And despite publicly professing happiness for her friends, she feels somewhat used by them, or at least underappreciated, and her attraction to Mike has waned. The novel’s second (and, arguably, primary) plot involves Pella’s post-college life and her fumbling attempts at cultivating an identity away from the people she has helped nurture. And it should be no surprise that her bildungsroman is pockmarked by many indignities; more than any other character in this novel, Pella is a tragic figure.
The metafictional sleight of hand at the center of The Brightness lacks a certain elegance; it is hard to justify, I think, the need for an Art of Fielding Extended Universe. Still, it is worth pausing here to examine the binary that Harbach’s two books represent. The Art of Fielding is about male friendship and presents a vision of a nontoxic version of it, in which throwing a baseball and quoting Marcus Aurelius might allow men to find the best in each other. The Brightness, on the other hand, is about the mysteries of female friendship, which, in Harbach’s telling, is passionate, without logic, and guided by petty jealousies. Irma and Pella, the novel’s main dyad, spend most of the book apart, their friendship strained by the tattoo prank and what it says about their divergent ambitions: Irma is hungry for accolades and attention, while Pella is more than willing to follow a traditional path after having such a late start to her adulthood.
The two novels differ in another crucial way. The Art of Fielding was confined to what took place either on the baseball diamond or on the campus itself; it made no attempt to supply its readers with an argument about the state of the world at the time. Certainly, a lot was happening in 2012 that was on the minds of college-age kids: America had yet to recover from the 2008 financial crisis, though the anger and sense of precarity that suffused the elder members of the millennial generation are completely absent from that novel’s idyll. In part, that separation from the world was to the novel’s benefit: It allowed The Art of Fielding to be charming and spritely precisely because of its light touch and its pleasing accounts of baseball; indeed, Harbach marked himself as one of the most talented describers of the act of fielding itself—the fluid beauty of a shortstop at work. The world, by contrast, weighs down The Brightness. Leaving aside all the acrobatic leaps required to make the novel fit within the fictional world of its predecessor, The Brightness is crammed with references to recent history: There are mentions of Trump and Bernie, Lana Del Rey and blogging, and, of course, all of those clothes and Harbach’s many thoughts on how people looked and acted in the 2010s.
The accumulation of proper nouns and era-specific details invites us to judge Harbach’s rendering of the 2010s against our own experience.
