Im Zeichen der Friedenstaube: Berlins Fußballerinnen in Liga zwei
Den Gedanken, Bayern abzuschaffen, formuliert unser Kolumnist über den Fußball hinaus – mit einem Herz für die Kleinen und im Sinne der Gerechtigkeit.
Dieser Tage erfreute Jochen Seitz unser Herz. »Die Regionalliga Bayern muss aufgelöst werden«, forderte der ehemalige Coach von Lok Leipzig mit köstlicher Ironie. Als doppelt geschädigter ostdeutscher Nichtaufstiegstrainer trotz Meistertitel darf er das.
Wir alle wissen, was ein schweres Trauma mit Menschen anstellen kann, und sind vereinigungsbedingt immer aufseiten der Opfer. Insofern fällt es uns leicht, Bayern mit Ausnahme der Städte Nürnberg, Augsburg und München (die werden Thüringen geschenkt, und München wird neue Landeshauptstadt) sogleich Österreich zuzuführen. Bayern ist viel zu groß und Österreich sooo süß und sooo klein. Alpenrepublik ÖsiBayreich, das tönt doch perfekt!
Mein Herz für die Kleinen erfüllt mich auch in Berlin. Deshalb war es mir Ehre und Pflicht zugleich, mich trotz schwerer Erkältung in Westberliner Vorgärten zu expedieren, um dort den Zweitligakick der Fußballerinnen von Viktoria Berlin gegen Hertha BSC zu bewundern. Flink bis Lankwitz mit der S-Bahn und dann vorbei an mürrischen, mit Besen und Harke versehenen Omas – im Kampf gegen das Laub und die gute Laune der Bürgersteigbenutzenden.
Frank Willmann blickt auf den Fußball zwischen Leipzig, Łódź und Ljubljana.
Im Stadion Lichterfelde erwarteten uns über 3333 Zuschauende, die in der Folge eine recht smoove Fußballparty feierten. Vorm Spiel wurde auf der Anzeigetafel allen ehrenamtlichen Helferinnen und Helfern Viktorias mit Foto und Text gedankt. Es gab eine kleine Aktion von beiden Fanlagern gegen Rassismus, und die Berliner Kältehilfe warb großflächig für Spenden. Zivilgesellschaft at her best.
Ich sah keinen einzigen Polizisten. Warum nur? Im Casino hatten sich ein paar weißhaarige, als Rocker verkleidete Opas hinter ihren Mittagsbieren verschanzt, die sich das Spiel nicht entgehen lassen wollten. Auch sie hielten die Fäuste unten.
Die Viktoria-Frauen dominierten die Gäste, auf der Tribüne tirilierte aber Hertha am lautesten. 5:0 siegte Tabellenführer Viktoria Berlin, das dürfte stark Richtung 1. Bundesliga gehen. Ich gönne ihnen ein vernünftiges Stadion, der Jahn-Sportpark scheint mir für das angenehm bunte Volk geeignet: viele Kinder, viele Frauen, ein cooler Nachmittag im Zeichen der Friedenstaube. Mal gucken, was der notorisch nörgelnde Berliner dazu sagt, wenn er Fledermaus und Spatz in Stellung bringt, um den Stadionumbau zu verzögern. Ganz zu schweigen vom Beamtenmob des Berliner Senats.
Am Vorabend hatten Herthas Männer die VW-Lümmel aus Wolfsburg zurechtgewiesen. Eine große Tat, der ich viel Bewunderung entgegenbringe. Die Blau-Weißen auf dem Weg in die 1. Bundesliga – dort gehören sie hin: Fast 70.000 Zuschauer sahen es genauso beim fetzigen Wolfsburgverkloppen (Symbolwort).
Wie sehen eigentlich die Autobauer vom Fließband die Geldvernichtungsmaschine KMS (Keiner mag Sie, Wolfsburg)? Die Ex-Berliner Großklappe Fips Reese für viele Millionen in das Fass ohne Boden rödeln und VW-Standorte schließen? Wäre Reese nicht auch einer für die ösibayreiche Nationalmannschaft? In diesem Sinne: Haltet immer schön euren Rumpf sauber!
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Trazer mais estudantes da rede pública para fazer o Enem’: com inscrição automática e prova na escola, governo amplia presença no exame
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O primeiro dia de provas do Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) 2026, realizado no domingo (8), registrou aumento na participação de estudantes da rede pública. Segundo o ministro da Educação, Leonardo Barchini, a aplicação transcorreu sem grandes contratempos.
No total, 68% dos inscritos compareceram ao primeiro dia de prova. Os concluintes do ensino médio na rede pública somaram mais de 1,9 milhão de inscrições, o que representa 39% do total. Cerca de 65% desses alunos fizeram o exame no domingo.
“Era esse o nosso objetivo: trazer mais estudantes da rede pública para fazer o Enem. Por isso, a gente deu todas as facilidades para que eles possam fazer as suas provas em sua própria escola, sua própria sala de aula, e que tenham essa inscrição automática”, destacou o ministro em entrevista coletiva.
A inscrição automática é uma das novidades desta edição. Os estudantes de escola pública passaram a ser inscritos pelo Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais (Inep), que organiza o exame, com base nos dados fornecidos pelas redes de ensino. O procedimento dispensa o preenchimento inicial da inscrição, mas o aluno ainda precisa acessar a Página do Participante para confirmar a inscrição, conferir os dados, informar o município onde deseja fazer a prova e escolher a língua estrangeira. A medida busca reduzir obstáculos burocráticos e ampliar a participação da rede pública no exame.
“No ano passado, por exemplo, somente 53,8% dos concluintes da rede pública fizeram o Enem. Esse ano, temos um número esperado de 65%. A maioria dos estudantes fez a prova na própria escola, mais de 85% realizou a prova na própria escola onde faz o ensino médio, e isso facilita a vida dos estudantes”, afirmou Barchini.
De acordo com o ministro, o número de alunos da rede pública inscritos no Enem cresceu em cerca de 250 mil.
Inscrições no Enem PPL crescem em São Paulo
Nas unidades prisionais paulistas, a participação no exame também aumentou. Segundo a Polícia Penal do Estado de São Paulo, 24.601 pessoas privadas de liberdade se inscreveram neste ano no Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio para Pessoas Privadas de Liberdade (Enem PPL), distribuídas em 175 estabelecimentos penais. Em 2025, foram 22.439 inscritos em 170 unidades. São 2.162 inscrições a mais, uma alta de 9,64%. De acordo com o órgão, é o quarto ano consecutivo de crescimento.
Na Região Metropolitana de São Paulo, 27 estabelecimentos penais somam 3.105 inscritos. Só na capital paulista, dez unidades prisionais inscreveram 1.231 estudantes.
As provas do Enem PPL estão previstas para 15 e 16 de dezembro, mesmas datas da reaplicação do exame regular, e os gabaritos devem ser divulgados em 28 de dezembro. O exame também é realizado pelo Inep e tem o mesmo nível de dificuldade da versão aplicada fora dos presídios. São quatro provas, que somam 180 questões, e uma redação em língua portuguesa.
Assim como no Enem regular, a nota do Enem PPL dá acesso ao ensino superior pelo Sistema de Seleção Unificada (Sisu), que oferece vagas em universidades públicas, pelo Programa Universidade para Todos (Prouni), que concede bolsas integrais ou parciais em instituições particulares, e pelo Fundo de Financiamento Estudantil (Fies), que financia os estudos.
Segundo a Polícia Penal, desde a edição passada, o participante, tanto do Enem PPL quanto do exame regular, pode obter a certificação de conclusão do ensino médio ou a Declaração Parcial de Proficiência. Para isso, precisa atingir ao menos 450 pontos em cada uma das quatro áreas de conhecimento e 500 pontos na redação.
Abstenção sobe e prova será reaplicada em dezembro
Em balanço preliminar, o Inep registrou 32% de ausências entre os pouco mais de 5 milhões de inscritos. O índice é superior ao do ano passado, quando a abstenção foi de 27%.
O número de ocorrências ficou dentro do esperado para a maior operação logística do governo federal, que mobiliza mais de 596 mil profissionais. Pelo balanço preliminar, 4.359 candidatos foram eliminados por violar alguma regra do exame.
Por causa de eventos climáticos graves, duas escolas em Santa Catarina tiveram os locais de prova transferidos. Houve ainda falta de energia em 39 locais de prova no Amapá, em Minas Gerais e no Rio de Janeiro. Os estudantes afetados poderão participar da reaplicação do Enem 2026, prevista para 15 e 16 de dezembro.
A reaplicação é destinada a participantes que tiveram a prova comprometida por situações previstas no edital, como problemas logísticos ou doenças infectocontagiosas. O pedido deve ser feito pela página do participante e depende de análise e aprovação do Inep.
Ao todo, o Enem foi aplicado em 1.901 municípios, em 14.868 locais de prova, com 15.494 coordenações e 184.095 salas.
Redação sobre o SUS foi ‘muito celebrada’, diz ministro
O tema da redação deste ano foi a valorização do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS). Barchini elogiou o trabalho de formulação das provas feito pelo Inep.
“Um tema muito celebrado nas redes, uma avaliação muito positiva, os próprios estudantes tiveram uma avaliação positiva”, avaliou o ministro.
O segundo dia do Enem 2026 será no próximo domingo (15), com duas provas objetivas de 45 questões cada. A de Ciências da Natureza e suas Tecnologias abrange biologia, física e química, e a outra é a de Matemática e suas Tecnologias. Os candidatos terão cerca de cinco horas para responder às 90 questões. Os portões abrem às 12h e fecham às 15h, no horário de Brasília. As provas começam às 13h30 e terminam às 18h30.
Com informações da Agência Brasil.

https://www.propublica.org/article/post-.title: Lawyers in This State Are Allowed to Ghost Clients for Years. Why Don’t More Judges Stop Them?
https://www.propublica.org/article/post-.author: Samantha Melamed
https://www.propublica.org/article/post-.text:
One morning in July 2025, I was the lone spectator in Judge Frank Palumbo’s courtroom in Philadelphia, watching prosecutors and public defenders haggle over the fates of defendants.
Palumbo paused the proceedings to talk to a lawyer he’d appointed to help a prisoner who had ineptly challenged his conviction. The lawyer profusely thanked the judge for the job. Then, Palumbo offered a bit of guidance: “I think I know where this is going to go. I don’t want to make it overly complicated. It’s real simple.”
The judge said he’d pass along a brief that a different lawyer had filed arguing that there was no merit to the man’s claims in a related case. “I’m not saying plagiarize,” the judge said.
The attorney told the judge he got the message. “So it’s called a Finley letter,” he said, using the common legal term for that no-merit brief, in which an attorney can argue against the client’s claims and ask to withdraw from the case.
“It’s looking like it’s going to be a Finley dismissal,” the judge agreed after a bit more discussion, “but every option is open.”
I’ve spent years covering criminal justice in Pennsylvania, including the post-conviction system that allows people to argue that their lawyer had mishandled their case or to raise newly discovered evidence. That day, I left the courtroom wondering how what I’d observed squared with the state’s promise of effective legal representation in cases like this.
That question sent me on a yearlong reporting odyssey, during which I read hundreds of Finley letters, tracked down court financial records from all 67 Pennsylvania counties, interviewed dozens of lawyers and analyzed thousands of court dockets. What I wanted to know was: Why has it become the norm for Pennsylvania’s lawyers to argue against their own clients? And who is this system serving?
I found that lax rules, low pay and heavy caseloads have compromised legal representation under the state’s Post Conviction Relief Act. Over the past year, I’ve reported on how lawyers, working under fee structures banned in other states, fell years behind on their cases. I spoke with prisoners who’d waited nearly a decade for their lawyers to file anything and others whose lawyers filed Finley letters despite compelling evidence of innocence. I also looked at three years’ worth of invoices and found that, three quarters of the time, Philly lawyers who wrote Finley letters had never spoken with their clients, contacted the trial lawyer or obtained available police files before deciding their claims had no merit.
None of those seemingly basic steps, I was surprised to learn, is required under the law. In fact, dozens of lawyers I spoke to expressed sharply divided opinions about the extent of their obligations to these clients.
But court-appointed lawyers are not working unsupervised. Judges are largely in charge of appointing them to cases, and those same judges are supposed to make sure they’re doing a timely and diligent job.
I noticed that judges continued to assign lawyers more cases even after appeals courts flagged serious issues with their work. And when it came to Finley letters, judges accepted almost all of them over the three years of cases I reviewed, despite the lawyers’ minimal investigative efforts. Some of the letters they approved contained obvious factual errors or even named the wrong client.
Last fall, after Palumbo gave the lawyer a copy of a Finley letter, the lawyer followed the template. His no-merit brief said that his client’s claim could not be considered because he’d missed his filing deadline. The bulk of the document was, in fact, identical to the other lawyer’s brief.
Palumbo, who didn’t respond to my requests for comment, accepted the Finley letter anyway, let the lawyer drop the client and dismissed the claim.
Who Judges Judges?
I thought a fair way to evaluate judges would be to look at the rulings of the Pennsylvania’s Superior Court, the state’s appeals court that hears hundreds of challenges to judges’ rulings on post-conviction matters each year.
And boy, did the Superior Court have thoughts on how judges are handling post-conviction cases.
In one withering opinion, a judge bemoaned an “embarrassing saga” of deficient lawyering that a Berks County judge had tolerated. Another derided a Philly judge and the five attorneys she’d appointed who all missed appeals deadlines, writing, “As Hall of Fame manager Casey Stengel said of the hapless 1962 New York Mets, ‘Can’t anybody here play this game?’”
After logging hundreds of rebukes laid out in Superior Court opinions by hand, I asked some colleagues with data skills to help identify as many of these cases as possible across the last 14 years, the time frame for which opinions were reliably posted online.
We found that the appeals court flagged more than 250 cases in which judges didn’t intervene as lawyers provided what the court labeled ineffective representation: “sandbagging” a client at a hearing, stonewalling a petitioner who’d mailed two dozen letters to the lawyer’s office or filing boilerplate appeals so vague that they doomed their clients’ cases. In hundreds more cases, judges failed to appoint a lawyer at all, held hearings where petitioners went unrepresented or allowed a lawyer to drop a case, leaving the client stranded on appeal. More than 200 times, they oversaw lawyers who abandoned clients, tanking their appeals or stalling their cases for years.
“Judges are in a terrific position to be able to prevent these kinds of injustices,” said Marissa Boyers Bluestine, a longtime post-conviction lawyer who now works at the University of Pennsylvania’s law school.
The scathing reversals aside, the Superior Court affirms about 80% of lower-court rulings. That’s expected given the strict deadlines and complicated rules about how appeals must be filed. The appeals court is also required to defer to the lower court’s factual decisions. And when it reverses due to an error, the recourse is generally limited to ordering a do-over or, on rare occasions, instructing the lower court to explore sanctions. In one opinion, the court resorted to using boldface to call out an egregious failure: “The PCRA court did nothing in this case for 20 years.” Then, it told the lower court to try again.
Judges do have the authority — and, in fact, an obligation under state rules — to make disciplinary referrals. Because complaints are confidential, there is no way to know how often they do so. But only six lawyers in the last decade have been publicly sanctioned for work on court-appointed post-conviction cases.
Judicial discipline is even rarer. No lower-court judge in at least a decade has been publicly disciplined for mishandling a post-trial matter. Judges who, according to the Superior Court, exhibited biases, imposed vindictive sentences or improperly denied recusal requests remained on the bench.
Even after the Superior Court raised alarms, more than 100 cases ricocheted between the appeals court and county judges two, three, four or more times, as judges repeated errors or reappointed lawyers to cases they’d already mishandled.
One such case played out after Jefferson County’s only judge, John Foradora, sentenced a woman to up to 22 years in prison for passing two narcotics pills in prison. Her lawyer failed to object to or appeal the lengthy sentence. After she filed a PCRA, the Superior Court found that her lawyers’ inaction enabled the “unduly harsh and clearly unreasonable” punishment to stand. But each time the Superior Court reversed, Foradora again imposed a lengthy term. After three such reversals, the woman wound up serving more than eight years. Foradora said through a court spokesperson that he was unable to comment.
Shannon McDonald, an attorney in the Philly suburbs, said that “some judges don’t consider PCRA a priority.”
She described waiting as a petition languished on a Delaware County judge’s desk for two years, until her client had finished his sentence and been released from prison. Then, the judge finally ruled, dismissing the claim.
The Finley Problem
Like lawyers, judges I’ve spoken with seem to be divided on their obligations, especially when it comes to the no-merit letters known as Finley letters. The state Supreme Court says that when a lawyer submits a Finley letter, the judge needs to conduct a review of the merits of the case.
Attorney Rob Perkins, who leads the nonprofit Allegheny Lawyers Initiative for Justice, told me that while he’s encountered some judges who take post-conviction matters seriously, others seem to view them as a nuisance. He said several lawyers told him that they were afraid that if they litigated cases too aggressively, judges would withhold future assignments. The no-merit letter becomes the simplest path forward: “When a judge is handed a no-merit letter that sounds good, I think their inclination is to accept that the attorney did their job.”
Superior Court opinions reflect this pattern as well. In my review, I found hundreds of cases overruling lower-court judges who accepted flawed Finley letters. The appeals court noted that lawyers claimed, incorrectly, that their clients had missed filing deadlines, rejected legitimate claims as meritless or failed to notice that their clients were serving illegal sentences.
In dozens of cases, judges approved defective Finley letters that did not fulfill basic rules, such as including a notification to the client or addressing all the claims the client wanted to raise.
Several judges told me that Finley letters serve an important purpose, in shutting down frivolous challenges that waste resources.
“Not all [claims] have merit,” Judge John J. Mead of Erie said. “A lot of them initially you could look at and make a determination [as to] whether or not it’s going to require a hearing.”
I’ve noticed that the system makes accepting Finley letters the simplest choice for judges. A judge who rejects a Finley letter must either find a new lawyer willing to take the case, or force the same lawyer to pursue a matter they previously deemed meritless.
Judges who take that path risk pitting a lawyer against his own client, the Superior Court wrote in one recent case, finding the judge’s actions resulted in the denial of a man’s right to counsel. His lawyer, forced to handle a hearing after writing a Finley letter, treated it “more like a cross-examination of a witness that [he] does not believe than a direct examination of his client.”
Jon Auritt, who retired after more than 50 years as a lawyer in Delaware County, said that these failures stem from a common cause: Instead of working independently, lawyers are beholden to the local judges who appoint them.
Even if judges are not as explicit as Palumbo was with their instructions, Auritt said, their message is often clear: “The judges are never incentivized to appoint a lawyer who might earnestly find a reason to overturn the conviction.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Russia’s Last Independent Newspaper Is Going Dark
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Katrina vanden Heuvel
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Russia’s Last Independent Newspaper Is Going Dark
Novaya Gazeta’s closing marks the end of what little press freedom remained in Putin’s Russia.
Russia’s Last Independent Newspaper Is Going Dark
The closing of “Novaya Gazeta” marks the end of what little press freedom remained in Putin’s Russia.
Novaya Gazeta—one of Russia’s last bastions of independent journalism—will publish a final issue and shut down next week.
The paper has faced mounting institutional pressures: It was evicted from its office space and labeled a foreign agent by the Kremlin, and banks have refused Novaya their services. Its reader-supported funding platform was also shut down.
The fact that the publication survived for this long is a testament to its reporters’ extraordinary bravery. Since its founding in 1993, Novaya has earned international acclaim for reporting in areas including human rights violations during the second Chechen War, the persecution of Chechnya’s LGBT community, and abuse inside Russian prisons. Over its years of courageous muckraking, six Novaya journalists were killed, including the crusading reporter Anna Politkovskaya.
After Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the free-speech crackdown that followed, much of the paper’s staff fled to Latvia, where they launched Novaya Gazeta Europe. This outlet is expected to continue operations—but its website is blocked in Russia.
However, while the original paper will soon cease publication, readers and historians can still access its work. Kronika, a project from PEN America and Bard College dedicated to preserving journalism at risk of suppression, is digitizing the newspaper’s entire archive. In doing so, the project is keeping Novaya’s ideals and principles alive.
Novaya cofounder and former editor in chief Dmitrii Muratov told Columbia Journalism Review that, if not for the archive, decades of Russia’s historical memory could vanish. And if such a public record were lost, he said, “we would not know how dictatorships take shape.”
To mark the legacy of this singular newspaper, The Nation is republishing the piece below, which I originally wrote when Muratov and the Filipino American journalist Maria Ressa were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021.
In the Nobel lecture he delivered later that year, Muratov saluted his colleagues, who risked their lives to hold those in power to account and promote the public interest.
“We are the prerequisite for progress,” he said. “We are the antidote against tyranny.”
The following was originally published in The Nation, October 8, 2021.
A Courageous Voice for Press Freedom and Independence in Russia
As the Nobel Prize committee recognized with today’s award to Dmitrii Muratov, independent journalism and media freedom in Russia confront growing threats.
katrina vanden heuvel
I and my late husband, Stephen Cohen, first met Dmitrii Muratov in 1993. He and a few other colleagues had gathered in the basement cafeteria of Moscow News—then a bold newspaper of the glasnost era—to plan the launch of Novaya Gazeta. Survival was on their minds at that time; they were beginning the paper with two computers, one printer, two rooms—and no money for salaries. A few months later, an initial boost of support came from President Mikhail Gorbachev, who contributed part of his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize money to buy the newspaper its first computers.
Nearly 30 years later, the newspaper has another Nobel in its history. On October 8, Muratov was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize with Filipina journalist Maria Ressa “for their efforts to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace.”
I knew in 1993 that “Dima” was a bold and creative editor. What I did not foresee was that he would become such a vital defender and advocate of press freedom in Russia. The newspaper, which continues to publish against great odds, has paid a heavy price for its crusading investigations into Putin’s and other high-level officials’ corruption, human rights violations, the persecution of the LGBT community in Chechnya, right-wing nationalist extremism, and abuses of power. The paper has also spent decades carefully tracing Stalin’s crimes in newly opened archives.
Six of its courageous reporters—among them Anna Politkovskaya, who was killed exactly 15 years ago—have been murdered for their unflinching investigations. (Fewer than half the killings have been solved.) “When Anya was killed, I called an emergency editorial meeting and wanted to close down the paper,” Muratov told me once. “I told my staff no story is worth dying for. But they wouldn’t let me do it.… I knew we had to go on.”
Muratov is not afraid to publish dissenting, oppositionist views on Crimea, Donbas, Syria, and growing poverty and the abuse of civil liberties in Russia. He handles at least 10 lawsuits a month—filed by official organs. It is remarkable that amid the escalating crackdown on press freedom, he has managed to preserve a sense of humor and visibly enjoy mentoring a new generation of investigative journalists—and readers. Elena Milashina, who started at Novaya in her late 20s, is one of those journalists; since the publication of her article in March documenting the murders of LGBT people and reporting on the cold-blooded murders instigated by Chechnya’s leader Ramzan Kadyrov, she has faced physical threats and death threats.
Indeed, most of the journalists working at the paper are like Milashina: the same age as, or a few years older than, the publication itself. Younger generations may not read the print edition, but Novaya’s print circulation as of October 2021 is 90,000, social-media traffic is 30 million a month, and its website receives 8 million to 11 million monthly page views.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The paper’s founding independence was boosted by the fact that, until 2006, Novaya journalists owned 100 percent of its stock. In 2006, to secure a capital infusion, Muratov persuaded his staff to sell 49 percent of their stock to Gorbachev (10 percent) and a partner, mini-oligarch Aleksandr Lebedev (39 percent). Lebedev invested nearly $4 million to raise staff salaries, upgrade the paper’s offices, and turn Novaya into a paper with national reach. (In 2015, Lebedev stopped funding Novaya, revealing in a Guardian interview that he had ceased because of the expense and also the strain.)
Fifteen years after Politkovskaya’s murder, nearly 30 years after Novaya was founded, independent journalism and media freedom in Russia confront growing threats. An array of media regulations and laws, the labeling of independent media outlets as “foreign agents,” and increasingly restrictive regulation of the Internet are all deeply troubling. Some Russian media analysts and journalists believe that many of these new restrictions are fueled by the West’s anti-Russian sanctions, increasing political tensions, and a deepening and dangerous cold war. In such times, the already narrow space for diversity of views and freedom of speech shrinks. Many analysts also see the culture of impunity—the ongoing failure to hold accountable those who threaten, attack, or kill journalists—as posing a grave threat to media freedom and democracy itself.
How Dmitrii Muratov has navigated for decades the dangerous waters of Russian politics—he has friends across all levels of Russian society, including top politicians—often irritates members of Russia’s more hard-core opposition and some Western observers, who think he has sold out to the Kremlin. As I ventured onto Twitter this morning to post a congratulatory note, a cat lover named Svetlana posted: “With tremendous respect to Dmitry—in Russia there is a saying, ‘If he’s still alive, he’s working for them.’ I admire his courage. And so did Peskov [Putin’s press secretary]. Where does it leave us? Thank you.”
Muratov has used his influence and connections not for his personal ambitions, nor to enrich himself, but to keep alive one of the last havens of investigative journalism inside Russia. The Nobel Prize will likely give Novaya and Muratov domestic protection, but may well also earn Muratov more enemies among the Putin elite, who will allege that he has betrayed the country for awards and foreign funds. What matters, as Muratov said on learning of Oslo’s call, are “Igor Domnikov, Yuri Shchekochikhin, Anna Politkovskaya, Stas Markelov, Nastya Baburova—these are the people who won the Nobel Prize today.”
Today’s prize will be wind at the back for all Russian investigative journalists.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: E-Bike Battery Fires Hit Record in NYC, But Solutions Remain Elusive
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
It’s a record. Already in 2026, New York City has suffered 406 lithium-ion battery fires, sparked by the electric cells that power an ever-growing fleet of e-bikes and electric scooters.
Since 2019, when the Fire Department first started keeping these stats, such blazes have resulted in 46 deaths and 628 injuries.
All this occurred despite an aggressive effort to end this grim but persistent trend. Laws were passed. Policies changed. The FDNY warned people again and again not to charge off-label batteries without safety certification.
And yet last month, four tenants of a Bronx public housing development perished in a fast-moving fire triggered by a battery charging inside their apartment.
Then last week, six people died in a Sunset Park blaze. A cause has not been officially released, but FDNY officials noted two charred lithium-ion battery-powered devices were removed from the scene. Not counting the victims of the most recent Brooklyn fire, that’s nine battery-fire deaths already this year.
And once again, elected officials are calling for reforms.
Last week, the City Council announced it will hold an emergency hearing on this issue on Nov. 20. And on Friday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani told reporters his administration is focusing on finding a solution, “whether it’s exploring additional legislation or it’s exploring additional policy that we can make at the administrative angle.”
Dwindling Enforcement
The solutions may not be so simple.
Workers who rely on e-bikes continue to buy and charge unsafe, off-label batteries, which are less expensive. Retailers and on-line outlets continue to sell them.
At times, the city bureaucracy has struggled to respond, even when they’re clearly warned of potential danger. In February 2023, journalist Fazil Khan perished in a raging fire in Harlem that erupted in an apartment below him where tenants were charging multiple batteries. Callers to 311 had warned the city weeks earlier, but there was no response.
That same year, the City Council took the first major step to confronting this issue, passing a law banning the sale of lithium-ion batteries that were not safety certified. This was a crucial step: Fire officials say batteries that are certified by the Underwriters Laboratory (UL) or aren’t charged via their manufacturer’s approved charger are vulnerable to bursting into flame. The resulting chemical fire is difficult to extinguish — and spreads quickly.
Since then, however, enforcement of the ban has wavered, according to Department of Consumer & Worker Protection (DCWP) records obtained by The City Reporter.
The law went into effect Sept. 1, 2023, while Eric Adams was mayor, and in the first four months his DCWP launched a wave of inspections citywide, issuing summons to 105 retailers at a rate of more than 26 per month.
In 2024 the agency issued summons to 108 businesses over 12 months, which dropped the rate to nine per month. Then in 2025, the last year of the Adams administration, enforcement fell even further, with summons issued to just 46 sellers all year for a rate of less than four per month.
In 2026, the first year of the Mamdani administration, enforcement got off to a slow start. By the beginning of August, DCWP had issued summons to just 26 sellers, but in August and September the city launched a sweep, bringing the total to 68 retailers hit with summons by last week. That was still a rate of just under seven per month.
And records show some of these retailers broke the law again and again, with some being hit with multiple summons for selling unsafe batteries since the law went into effect.
DCWP spokesperson Stephany Vasquez Sanchez said the agency “focuses on bringing businesses that remained in violation of (the law) into compliance,” and the agency’s tactics of shutting down repeat offenders “have improved compliance.”
“We’ve found that the majority of businesses stay in compliance once they learned to sell safe and certified devices,” she said. “We will continue our work to ensure compliance in this industry, especially to hold recidivist businesses accountable with our full authority.”
Another effort to get the delivery drivers who rely on e-bikes to stop using non-certified batteries kicked off in June 2025 under a law sponsored by then-Councilmember Keith Powers. The law created an exchange program for eligible drivers to turn in their unsafe batteries for those that were UL listed.
But the exchange program expired in 2025.
Last week after the Sunset Park catastrophe, Powers, now a state assemblymember, took to social media to call on the Mamdani administration to “resume that program and save lives.”
What Can Washington Do?
Another elected official who’s tried to staunch the sale of unsafe batteries is Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-The Bronx), whose district includes the Patterson Houses where a battery fire last month killed four tenants, including an 11-year-old boy, two teenage boys and a 33-year-old woman.
In 2024, and then again in 2025, Torres sponsored a bill that would require the Consumer Product Safety Commission to establish a safety standard for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in micromobility devices such as electric scooters and bikes. Nationally retailers would be barred from selling batteries that don’t meet those standards. In both years, an overwhelming and bipartisan House majority voted for it.
The bill, nevertheless, has been unable to get to the floor of the Senate, where Torres said it would also be overwhelmingly supported. The obstacle, he says, is Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky), who’s employed a tactic that allows a single senator to block a bill from getting to the floor, without explanation.
Torres is marginally optimistic that the Democratic wave gave control of Congress to his party “would improve the prospects” of the bill seeing the light of day.
But, Torres added, “a Republican minority in the Senate could remain an obstacle.”
“I see it as a matter of life and death,” the congressman said. “Poorly manufactured lithium ion batteries are literally ticking time-bombs and it’s communities like the Bronx that are hardest hit.”
Finally the deadly fire in the Patterson Houses in The Bronx last month cast a spotlight on another attempt to prevent more of these fires from costing lives.
In 2023, the same year the council passed the law barring the sale of uncertified batteries, the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) was considering prohibiting the charging of e-bike batteries, certified or not, on all public housing property. That September they dropped that plan and instead adopted a compromise: households could charge one battery per unit, as long as it was safety-certified and the charging could not block any exit from the apartment.
Since then, that compromise solution has been followed by no fewer than 53 e-bike battery fires in NYCHA apartments. In the Patterson Houses blaze, the residents were charging the battery in the kitchen, in a place that blocked the family from escaping.

Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Parents and teachers decry Google pledge to yank Search if schools block AI: ‘This threat is nothing but extortion’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google’s announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search.
Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google’s AI tools will also lose access to its search engine.
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” said Chris Phillips, vice-president for education at Google. “After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”
Parents and teachers across the country raised concerns to the Guardian about AI’s potential to weaken students’ critical-thinking skills and the growing influence of big tech in education.
Some called on schools to consider alternative search engines, while others argued that students should be taught how to use AI responsibly rather than prevented from accessing it altogether.
Jen Atay, a 51-year-old teacher in Hawaii, lambasted Google’s approach, saying: “When the software is free, you are the product, and it is inappropriate for Google to test or develop AI with minors. This should not be allowed at all.”
A 44-year-old father of two boys in Amissville, Virginia, said he worries that “AI will weaken people’s ability to think critically. I use AI in my work, but it would not be effective if I did not have well over a decade of experience under my belt. Even the best models are often flat-out wrong in their responses.”
“These tools are not something that should be introduced to children at such a young age. I’m hopeful that a Democratic Congress will force the adoption of legislation that will protect our schools from corporate malfeasance such as this. This threat from Google is nothing but extortion and it should be treated as such,” he added.
Similarly, Eyla Whitemoon, a mother and educator based in Kernville, California, said: “By infiltrating or ‘partnering’ with our institutions, Google and Meta et al, created a false dependency and our starved public education system happily merged with their ilk. And just like any good mob boss, drug dealer or capitalist minion, these companies got society hooked on their products and now are raising the cost of their supply … My heart aches for what our children won’t experience in a future where AI is in charge and the mega technoautocrats sit in their bunkers and hide.”
Meanwhile, a 64-year-old educator based in Ann Arbor, Michigan, said: “Thankfully, after having to revamp all teaching in response to AI, Gen Z has begun appreciating what they stand to lose on account of surrendering their cognitive skills to AI. There are alternative search engines to Google and those will now be what we turn to. Teachers and students alike detest the tech industry’s demand that we kiss their feet and give ourselves up to be their peons.”
Others questioned why schools should depend on Google at all.
An 84-year-old retiree and mother in Maryland, said: “Google decided to follow the evil path to riches. When they started, they were great. Today they are simply evil money grubbers … Schools should tell Google to go pound sand and simply have kids use DuckDuckGo or one of the other search engines … There is nothing Google offers that is not available from some other source.”
Rachel Dominguez, a 42-year-old parent in Minneapolis, Minnesota, also suggested that schools turn to academic databases instead of relying on Google Search.
“Seeing as how Google Search has turned into an AI slop-first service, maybe it’s better that the kids learn how to use databases such as Academic Search Premier, JSTOR, and arXiv. Most school districts have subscriptions to these services, and students learning to use them would be better prepared for college. A trip to the media center is not some abnormal chore … That is, if the librarian still has a job in the first place,” she said.
Not everyone believes blocking AI is the answer. Some argued that schools should focus on teaching students how to use the technology responsibly.
A 67-year-old emerging technology teacher in Texas said: “I do not blame Google. AI is not going away. I’ve been very frustrated this year trying to teach AI literacy with AI blocked. Schools need to teach how to properly use AI, not block it.”
A California resident echoed that view, arguing that schools could use Google’s AI tools to teach students to question the information they receive.
“Google Search has existed since the 90s and it’s crazy of them to completely remove it instead of just removing Gemini. That being said, I would like to see schools actually permit the use of Gemini and use it as an opportunity to show students how its sources aren’t always valid and you can’t trust everything an AI tells you,” they said.

https://taz.de/Was-Nvidia-so-wichtig-mac.title: Was Nvidia so wichtig macht: Die Hardware hinter KI
https://taz.de/Was-Nvidia-so-wichtig-mac.author: Svenja Bergt
https://taz.de/Was-Nvidia-so-wichtig-mac.text:
Was Nvidia so wichtig macht: Die Hardware hinter KI
KI-Chatbots wären in ihrer heutigen Form nicht denkbar ohne die Chips von Nvidia. Auch Deutschland will dem US-Konzern nahe sein.
Erst kürzlich hat Deutschland ein bisschen was abbekommen, vom großen Nvidia-Hype. Das Unternehmen hielt seine Hausmesse GTC, die sonst meist im kalifornischen San José stattfindet, in Berlin ab. Jensen Huang, Mitgründer und Unternehmenschef sprach und Fans jubelten ihm zu wie einem Popstar. Beim Investorengipfel der Bundesregierung gab es dann auch etwas Glamour für die Politik: Wirtschafts- und Forschungsministerium unterzeichneten eine Absichtserklärung mit Nvidia zur Kooperation in Sachen künstliche Intelligenz.
Nvidia, 1993 gegründet, ist der global wichtigste Hersteller von KI-Hochleistungschips und einer der am höchsten bewerteten börsennotierten Konzerne. Der aktuelle Börsenwert liegt bei rund 5 Billionen US-Dollar. Obwohl Nvidia schon 1999 an die Börse gegangen ist, lief es in der öffentlichen Wahrnehmung lange etwas unter dem Radar. Der Fokus lag eher auf den Tech-Unternehmen, mit deren Produkten die Kund:innen in direkten Kontakt kommen: Google, Amazon, Facebook (später als Teil von Meta), Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft.
Einen Schub sowohl was die wirtschaftliche Bedeutung angeht als auch in Sachen Bekanntheit, erhielt Nvidia mit der Popularität von großen Sprachmodellen aus dem Bereich künstliche Intelligenz. Diese Modelle sind die Basis für KI-Chatbots wie ChatGPT oder Claude. Und gerade für das Training der Modelle sind spezielle Hochleistungschips nötig. Nvidia ist bei der Herstellung dieser Chips Marktführer, zur Liste der Geschäftspartner zählen unter anderem Anthropic, Google, Meta und Microsoft.
Für sorgenvolle Blicke auf die Branche sorgt jedoch, dass Nvidia eben nicht nur Zulieferer ist für Chips – sondern auch Investor in KI-Unternehmen, zum Beispiel in Anthropic, und auch Kunde für KI-Dienste. In derart eng verflochtenen Konstellationen kann schon eine umstrittene Unternehmensentscheidung, eine Fehlinvestition oder eine Änderung der politischen Rahmenbedingungen Rutschbewegungen in der gesamten Branche auslösen.
Heilsame Kursverluste
Branchenbeobachter:innen zufolge könnten daher die jüngsten Kursverluste nach den Zwischenwahlen in den USA eine heilsame Kurskorrektur sein. Wenn die Bewertungen der KI-Unternehmen tatsächlich flächendeckend zu hoch sind und damit eine Blase entstanden ist, könnten schrittweise Kurskorrekturen ein abruptes Platzen verhindern.
Und Deutschland? Die jüngst vereinbarte Kooperation mit Nvidia sehen Expert:innen zwar grundsätzlich positiv, weil sie der hiesigen Industrie Zugriff verschafft auf die marktführende Chip-Technologie. Gleichzeitig aber birgt sie ein Abhängigkeitsrisiko: Eine solche Kooperation dürfe nicht mit technologischer Souveränität verwechselt werden, warnte Patrick Glauner, Professor für künstliche Intelligenz an der Technischen Hochschule Deggendorf, gegenüber dem Science Media Center: „Europa muss parallel eigene Anbieter bei Hardware, Infrastruktur und Software stärken.“
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/deserts.title: La hausse du nombre de médecins ne soigne pas les inégalités territoriales
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/deserts.author: Christophe Prudhomme
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/deserts.text:
La hausse du nombre de médecins ne soigne pas les inégalités territoriales
Selon les derniers chiffres connus, en France, le nombre de médecins en activité début 2026 est de 242 400, soit une hausse de 14 % depuis 2010. On peut se féliciter de la fin du creux de la vague. Mais il ne faut pas oublier que le problème de démographie médicale est la conséquence de la réduction drastique du nombre de médecins formés, résultant des préconisations d’économistes néolibéraux qui souhaitaient réduire le « trou » de la Sécurité sociale en diminuant leur nombre. Cette augmentation ne règle pas la fracture territoriale.
Des départements ruraux ou périurbains comme la Nièvre ou la Seine-Saint-Denis ont vu leur nombre de médecins s’effondrer de près de 20 %. Quand d’autres, comme la Gironde, ont enregistré un bond de plus de 30 %. Notons que la hausse profite principalement aux médecins spécialistes (141 000 en 2026) au détriment des généralistes (101 000). Cette évolution pose un problème majeur au regard des besoins d’une population vieillissante, atteinte de maladies chroniques, pour laquelle le rôle de coordination du médecin généraliste devient de plus en plus essentiel.
Des déserts médicaux qui subsistent
Le gouvernement se félicite de l’arrivée de 3 000 docteurs juniors auprès des médecins généralistes pour répondre aux déserts médicaux. Il faut préciser que ces docteurs juniors proviennent de la création d’une dixième année d’études permettant de les utiliser comme main-d’œuvre à bon marché pendant un an supplémentaire. Alors que les études de médecine sont déjà longues, il n’est aucunement besoin de cette année de plus pour leur formation.
Par ailleurs, ils iront exercer là où des médecins sont déjà présents, donc l’effet de leur arrivée sur la résorption des déserts médicaux est illusoire. Au mieux, cela permettra d’augmenter le nombre de consultations dans les cabinets déjà existants. Pour les patients, cet effet sera transitoire car les stages durent six mois et ils seront obligés de changer de médecin lors de chaque nouvelle affectation.
Les jeunes médecins concernés sont plus que critiques sur ce nouveau dispositif. Une de leur représentante syndicale est très sévère : « On ne résout pas une pénurie de médecins en retardant leur arrivée dans la vie professionnelle. La France a besoin de médecins qui s’installent, restent et assurent durablement le suivi de leurs patients. »
La bonne solution pour que chacun puisse disposer d’un médecin traitant disponible et de l’accès à un spécialiste sans dépassement d’honoraires est de proposer aux jeunes médecins un autre mode d’exercice : la médecine salariée dans des structures collectives qui s’appellent les centres de santé. Il est possible de répondre ainsi aux aspirations de professionnels en termes de conditions de travail et de rémunération ainsi qu’aux besoins de la population avec un service public de proximité.
Aux côtés de celles et ceux qui luttent !
L’urgence sociale, c’est chaque jour la priorité de l’Humanité.
- En exposant la violence patronale.
- En montrant ce que vivent celles et ceux qui travaillent et ceux qui aspirent à le faire.
- En donnant des clés de compréhension et des outils aux salarié.es pour se défendre contre les politiques ultralibérales qui dégradent leur qualité de vie.
Vous connaissez d’autres médias qui font ça ?  
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Syria confirms sending troops to Saudi Arabia amid battle against Houthis
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Syria confirms sending troops to Saudi Arabia amid battle against Houthis
Syrian officials deny reports Damascus is sending troops to Yemen, but Syrian security integration appears under way.
Shortly after Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s visit to Riyadh last week, reports emerged that Damascus was aiding Saudi Arabia in its war against Yemen’s Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) and backed by Iran.
Security and financial aid appeared to be the cornerstone of the meeting between al-Sharaa and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, which concluded with Riyadh pledging $403m in loans to help Syria rebuild infrastructure damaged by 13 years of its civil war.
Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates noted that cooperation between the two countries’ defence ministries was the “most notable” of the deals, but it did not elaborate.
Days after the visit concluded, media reports suggested Syria was sending fighters to Saudi Arabia to help fight the Houthis. The Reuters news agency reported that Syria was providing Riyadh with military advice and training inside the kingdom after Saudi cities were targeted in hundreds of Houthi missile attacks.
On Sunday, Syrian officials told The Associated Press news agency that Damascus has already sent Syrian military advisers to Saudi Arabia and 600 special forces were due to arrive in the kingdom next week.
Despite denying the initial reports, a Syrian government official told the state’s news agency SANA that Syrian soldiers were sent to Saudi Arabia in a “training, expertise exchange and military consultations” capacity.
“The Syrian role would probably count for more in Riyadh than on Yemen’s front lines because it would show that the new Syria can share a partner’s security burden,” Nanar Hawach, a Syrian analyst, told Al Jazeera, adding that even a training and support role from the Syrian government rather than a direct combat role would satisfy Riyadh.
“The reports and the denials can both be partly right since Syrian officers training Yemeni forces inside the kingdom is different from Syrian troops fighting in Yemen. If Syrian forces are involved, Damascus has good reasons to avoid acknowledging it, from avoiding retaliation to reassuring Syrians that rebuilding at home comes first,” Hawach explained.
Houthi threat
Yemen has been a central concern for Saudi Arabia since Houthi fighters captured the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014. Saudi Arabia has led an Arab military coalition to support Yemen’s internationally recognised government since March 2015. It has provided material and air support to anti-Houthi forces.
Saudi Arabia has been eager to form a regional military alliance that would help counter the threats from the Houthis and their patron Iran.
Tehran’s attacks on its Gulf neighbours since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28 and recent Houthi missile strikes on Saudi cities have highlighted the need for a regional security umbrella.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, agreed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan in August, has been viewed as a mechanism for this collective defence by many in Riyadh.
Syria and its thousands of battle-hardened soldiers with some expertise in drone warfare would be considered a useful addition to this alliance. The Syrian official who spoke to SANA said the current military arrangement between Damascus and Riyadh could lead to Syria joining the Mecca Defence Alliance.
“Interest in the Mecca pact could reflect Syria’s wish to anchor its recovery in a regional security framework. Yemen is far enough away for Damascus to present any role as standing by an Arab partner while Lebanon is next door, and intervention would reopen its history there and risk destabilising Syria itself,” Hawach said.
“However, distance does not make it cost-free. Confronting Iran’s allies anywhere invites retaliation, and soldiers killed far from home would be hard to justify to a public that expects peace to bring recovery.”
Syrian expertise
Syria’s post-war government has already come under pressure to act militarily outside its borders. US President Donald Trump has spoken numerous times this year about trying to get Syria to intervene in Lebanon to help disarm Hezbollah, another Iran-backed group.
Syrian rebels have been deployed to other conflicts in the Middle East and North Africa during their attempts to overthrow Bashar al-Assad’s government from 2011 to 2024. Syrian fighters allegedly took part in Azerbaijan’s war against Armenia in 2020.
“Syrians are combat-experienced and -capable, and they’re cohesive, so there’s a potential tactical advantage there,” Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer on security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
“Overall, this is very much a common Saudi approach to strategy and security issues, basically leaning on partners they courted through diplomatic links.”
Since the fall of al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Saudi Arabia is believed to have been instrumental in helping the US remove Assad-era sanctions on Syria, which has been critical in legitimising the post-war government in Damascus.
With Saudi Arabia now fully embroiled in the Yemen war by backing its internationally recognised government and being targeted by regular Houthi air attacks, the deployment of Syrian troops would provide it with additional expertise and guidance on how to confront the Houthis.
The AFP news agency reported that Syrians in Yemen are now leading drone operations against the Houthis although the Syrian government has denied these claims.
Samy Akil, senior programme adviser with The Syria Report website, said Syria’s cooperation gives Riyadh another ally in the region and potential partner in the Mecca Defence Alliance.
“Syria has so far tried to navigate different competing regional interests across several regional capitals. It tried to not align itself with a specific camp, but I think as time goes on, it needs to kind of start settling on [a] hierarchy in terms of regional partners, and obviously, Saudi Arabia is one of the top contenders to do so,” he told Al Jazeera.
“It’s basically signalling that Syria is willing to support and help with the limited resources and capabilities it has, but it also inadvertently legitimises the Syrian government’s foreign policy approach of supporting regional countries and kind of showcase that it is not only a country that is asking for support, but it is also a country willing to provide support.”
With Israeli raids and attacks on southwestern Syria continuing, Damascus could also benefit from having a regional power such as Saudi Arabia as an ally.
“The fact is that Syria recognises that it has little policy options to deter a further entrenchment of Israeli forces into southern Syria in [the] hope that the potential of joining the [Mecca] agreement would act somewhat of a deterrence to, at the very least, stop further encroachment of Israeli troops in Quneitra and Daraa.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/irani.author: MEE correspondent
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/irani.text:
Iranian press review: Newspapers warn of war reaching 'heart of Europe'
IRGC-linked outlets publish list of potential targets in Europe
Daily newspapers close to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) have published a list of potential targets across Europe, following US strikes on Qeshm Island last week.
The reports came as speculation grows over a possible return of the US to the war with Iran.
On Tuesday, the Hamshahri daily published a map of Europe on its front page, marking US-used bases in the UK, Germany, France, Italy, Romania, Greece, Albania and Portugal as the “target bank of the Iranian armed forces”.
Hamshahri described Iran’s new military strategy as one “of confrontation without geographical limits”, borrowing a term the country's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei previously used.

Under this strategy, the daily wrote, “US support centres, air and naval bases, and logistical infrastructure in Europe have been raised as potential targets”.
The Kayhan daily, whose editor is appointed by the supreme leader, also issued a warning. It said that if the US did not accept Iran’s conditions for a peace deal, “the geography of the battle will expand to the heart of Europe and the depth of overseas bases”.
It added that Iran’s military doctrine towards the US, Israel and their allies had become “more direct and more offensive”.
Among European countries involved in the war against Iran, Kayhan singled out the UK, saying it had played “the most key and prominent role”.
Could Iraq's 2006 experience be repeated in Iran in 2026?
As senior Iranian officials welcomed the Republican Party's defeat in the US midterm elections as a blow to President Donald Trump's hawkish policies, the news website Khabar Online drew comparisons with the 2006 midterms, held during the US-led occupation of Iraq.
In its report, Khabar Online warned that “a change in the congressional majority and opposition to war policies do not necessarily mean an immediate retreat by the president or an end to military operations”.
The report recalled the Republican Party's similar defeat under the then president George W Bush and examined its impact on the war in Iraq, including the extensive powers the US president used to continue military operations.
It also looked at US military operations in Iraq after 2006, when Washington increased the number of troops on the ground.
“The expectation of some opponents of the war was that a Democratic victory would pave the way for a rapid withdrawal of US forces from Iraq. But what happened in the following months was the opposite,” the report said.
Drawing on the comparison, Khabar Online concluded: “The Bush experience shows that even an anti-war majority in Congress cannot, on its own, stop the government's military course without political unity and the ability to overcome a presidential veto.”
Israel sought to break up Iran, former Israeli negotiator says
Daniel Levy, an Israeli peace negotiator who took part in the 1993 Oslo-B talks, said Israel's reasons for launching a new war against Iran on 28 February were to break it up and follow a policy similar to what happened in Iraq and Syria.
“Israel's goal was the collapse of the state, the creation of chaos in Iran and the break-up of the country - something similar to what we saw in Iraq and Syria,” he said in an interview with BBC Persian.
He added: “I don't think the Israelis themselves even believed their own propaganda narrative that regime change could be achieved in Iran.”
On the plan to divide Iran, Levy also pointed to reports in the early days of the war about weapons being sent to Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Iraq.
He said the initial idea was to establish a liberated area inside Iran, where resources and military forces could be concentrated to continue the war against the central government.
Levy also referred to Reza Pahlavi, the son of Iran's deposed shah, who had received public support from Tel Aviv since Israel's 2025 attack on Iran. He described Israel's backing of Pahlavi as a temporary strategy aimed at advancing its longer-term goals.
“The Pahlavi family was a useful tool for Israel. A tool for creating chaos. I don't believe they thought the end result would be regime change. I don't even think they considered that a desirable outcome,” he said.
Tehran looks to Beijing as war diplomacy intensifies
Speculation is growing over China's possible role in efforts to secure a ceasefire between Iran and the US, as diplomatic contacts between Tehran, Beijing and Muscat point to a possible new channel for negotiations.
The pro-reformist Shargh daily reported that security official Ali Bagheri Kani's recent meetings in Beijing could signal the creation of “a parallel diplomatic path” led by China and Oman.
Shargh added: “Bagheri Kani's visit, within this framework, could be part of Tehran's consultations to assess new diplomatic initiatives and explore the capacity of influential countries to prevent the crisis from escalating.”
Meanwhile, the conservative Jame Jam daily also covered Bagheri Kani's visit, describing it as part of Iran's efforts to bring Beijing and Moscow on board with its regional policies.
According to Jame Jam, Tehran's diplomatic efforts and consultations with China and Russia, alongside the use of mediators such as Qatar and Pakistan, are part of Iran's attempt to manage the war it has faced since February.
However, the daily stressed that statements of support from China and Russia alone could not prevent the conflict from continuing. It said the effectiveness of their policies depended on practical action to prevent US unilateralism in the region.
